work.author: Cyrill of Alexandria
work.title:
De adoratione et cultu in spiritu et
     ueritate

paragraphs.text: BOOK 1. On humanity's turning aside into wickedness and its captivity to sin; and also on the calling and return that come through repentance, and on the way back up to the better state.

BOOK 2. That it is impossible to escape the death that comes from sin and the greed of the devil except through the sanctification that is in Christ. And that justification is not in the law, but in Christ.
BOOK 3. On the same subject.

BOOK 4. That the one who has been called by God to justification and redeemed must follow him, and must reject the slackness that leads to wickedness, and rather strive to live lawfully and vigorously.
BOOK 5. Further on courage in Christ.
BOOK 6. That we must hold fast to the God who is God by nature, and to him alone, and love him with our whole soul and heart.
BOOK 7. On love for our brothers.
BOOK 8. Further on love for our brothers, and against the one who steals a calf or a sheep.
BOOK 9. On worship in spirit and in truth, and on the holy tabernacle, showing that it was a type of the Church in Christ.
BOOK 10. On the things in the holy tabernacle.
BOOK 11. On the priesthood, and that the priesthood under the law was a type of the priesthood in Christ.
BOOK 12. On the priesthood.
BOOK 13. Further on the priesthood.
BOOK 14. That those who wish to attend the churches must be pure and washed clean of the stain of sin, and so present themselves before God.
BOOK 15. That we must present ourselves before God pure and washed clean of sin. And that our cleansing, again, is in Christ.
BOOK 16. That we must bring spiritual sacrifices and offerings to God.
BOOK 17. On the holy feasts.
On humanity's turning aside into wickedness and its captivity to sin; and also on the calling and return that come through repentance, and on the way back up to the better state.
There is no need to ask where you are going or where you have come from, I suppose. I know well that you would answer at once that you have come from home, and to us.
True.
And this book you are holding in your hands: what is it?
A Gospel book, containing the writings of Matthew and John.
And where, and to whom, do you think you need to carry it? You would hardly study it while walking about out of doors, Palladius. Labors of this kind are sweeter at home and at leisure.

You are right. I have come to consult you, and I bring the sacred book. I have labored over it countless times, but I am no closer to understanding what our Lord Jesus Christ could mean in Matthew, when he says: "Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke, will pass from the law until all things have come to pass." And in the writing according to John, he says to the woman from Samaria: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth."
Then what is it in these passages that seems to you so steep? What is deep and hard to reach? I am asking: tell me.

The sacred word commands us to depart from the more ancient customs, and says that we must cease from the righteousness that is in the Law. Paul said to those who sought that righteousness even after coming to faith: "You have been cut off from Christ, you who would be justified by the Law; you have fallen from grace. For through the Spirit, by faith, we eagerly await the hope of righteousness." And concerning the way of life under the Law, though he shows us the splendid and great things he could boast of in it, he says again: "Whatever was gain to me, I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing our Lord Jesus Christ. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as rubbish, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the Law, but the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God." He also plainly affirmed that the ancient commandment was not blameless. That is why he says that in its place a new commandment, the one through Christ, that is, the Gospel, has been brought in for our benefit. He writes as follows: "For a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, since the Law made nothing perfect, and a better hope is brought in, through which we draw near to God." And again: "For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and so I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts." And understanding and interpreting the word "new" with special care, he says: "In speaking of a new covenant, he has made the first one old; and what is becoming old and growing aged is near to vanishing." If, then, the Law perfected nothing, and the ancient commandment has been set aside and a second one brought in, which makes us God's own, why does the Saviour say, "I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill"? And why does he say that we ought to worship God the Father in spirit and truth? For this shows, I think, that we must give up the customs and the worship prescribed by the law.

How far out you have sailed onto the broad sea of questions! What mind would be equal to gazing clearly at such subtle matters of contemplation? For it would have to show us that the new Scripture is a sister and neighbor, as it were, to what was decreed long ago through the all-wise Moses, and passes through the same matters; and that life in Christ is not far removed from the way of life under the Law, if what was ordained for the ancients is brought to spiritual contemplation. For the Law is a type and a shadow, the outline of true religion still in its birth pangs, as it were, holding the beauty of the truth hidden within itself. Or will you say that what I have said is not so?

Certainly it is so. But how can this be made clear? In what way can someone who lives by the Gospel still be considered attached to the ancient commandment, and be thought to fulfill what was given through Moses?

The answer is not as simple as one might suppose. Virtue, I think, is something with many branches and many forms, and the glories of the life in Christ are embroidered for us through a great variety of good deeds. Indeed the divine David, in the forty-fourth psalm, presents the Church to Christ as a pure virgin with the rank of a queen, and clothes her in a robe of gold and many colors, saying: "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment woven with gold, arrayed in many colors." The gold, as I think, signifies what is precious and illustrious, and the many colors signify very aptly the manifold nature of virtue. For the Church is exceedingly comely, having an adornment perceived by the mind, not seen by the eyes of the flesh but within, in mind and heart. Through a great many beauties it gracefully displays to us the one who is understood to be a Jew in secret, noble and exceptional. For as blessed Paul writes: "For a person is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision something outward in the flesh. Rather, a person is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in spirit, not in letter. Such a person's praise is not from human beings but from God."

Tell me, then: now that circumcision in the spirit has been introduced, the sacrifices prescribed by the law overturned, and that way of life has no place among us, does it not seem somehow implausible that Christ said, "I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill"? Or if that is not so, then nothing, I suppose, would prevent us too from honoring the God of all with sacrifices of oxen and with incense, offering him turtledoves and pigeons, and from eagerly fulfilling ourselves whatever else the ancients were accustomed to do.

And yet, my friend, you are drifting far from what is fitting. You think the law has been overturned, so that we gain no benefit from it at all and it is entirely useless for showing us anything necessary, rather than that it has been transformed to display the truth. Yet blessed Paul writes: "Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law." For the law is a tutor, and it leads us well to the mystery of Christ. And we say that what was decreed long ago through Moses for the ancients are the elementary principles of God's oracles. But if we push the tutor aside, who will still bring us to the mystery of Christ? And if we refuse to learn the elementary principles of God's oracles, how, or from where, shall we ever arrive at the goal? Or is not Christ, according to the Scriptures, the fulfillment of the law and the prophets?
Yes.

For so it is written. And he would be the fulfillment of the law and the prophets, I suppose, because every oracle of the prophets and of the law looks and is turned toward him. That is why, putting the disobedience of the Jews to shame, he said: "Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" So when he says that he has come not to abolish the law at all, but rather to bring it to completion, do not suppose that he brought about a total overthrow of what was decreed of old. Rather he brought about a kind of refashioning, a re-engraving, so to speak, of what existed in types into the truth.
You are right.

And indeed this is just what had to be done by Christ. Those who have mastered the art of painting on panels do not give their pictures a form that lacks nothing and is complete in every respect the moment they begin to paint. First they sketch it out skillfully in outline and in plainer color, displaying in advance the outlines of whatever subjects they have chosen while these are still faint. Then, laying over the shadowy sketch the shape that fits and best suits each part, they bring the outlines into a clear form, incomparably better than the one at the beginning. Or is that not so?
I agree.

And those who practice the craft of bronze-working, if they want to cast a statue, first mold it in wax into a rough form; then, melting the wax with fire, they pour in the bronze, and so bring the work to a finished form and real beauty. Once the variety of colors has been laid over the sketch, and once the bronze has melted away what was made of wax, the first, original shapes might seem for a moment to have been set aside and overturned. But that is not how the matter really stands. For the bronze-worker and the painter would both say, and say truly: "We have not destroyed the sketches; we have not reduced the outlines to complete uselessness; rather, we have fulfilled them. For what could be seen in sketches and outlines, still rather obscure and less beautiful, has advanced to what is better and clearer."
Well said.

And if anyone chooses to examine the sacred and divinely inspired Scripture closely, he will surely know that what I say is true. For Moses put a veil over his face, because the children of Israel could not gaze at his face, as it is written.
And what does this indicate?

The minds of the Jews were still rather dull. The outward things of the law, by which I mean again those conveyed by the letter alone, were somehow bearable to them; but the things hidden within, the true face of its meanings, so to speak, were wholly unbearable and beyond their reach. That is why the divine Paul writes to us: "For to this very day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not lifted, because only in Christ is it taken away. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart." But let that suffice concerning the Jews. "But we all," he says, "with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit; and the Lord is the Spirit." Those who look into a mirror see an image and imprint of the real thing, and do not behold the real thing itself. In the same way, I think, those who long to see the beauty of the life in Christ will best attain what they desire by using the law as a mirror. For by refashioning that same image of the realities into the truth, they will know clearly what is most approved by God and well-pleasing to him.
Then what might be the reason why the new oracle of the Gospel was not given to the ancients at the beginning, but types and shadows were laid down as law instead?

The precise account of God's dispensation, and how these things truly stand, must reverently be left to God, who knows all things. Yet our reasonings, which do not allow us to go without good thoughts, can bring us at least to a modest knowledge, or perhaps to a seeming knowledge, of the reason for the dispensation. We say, then, that those redeemed from Egypt needed a great deal of tutoring, and an upbringing suited, in a sense, to infants. For they were still dull of mind and all too easily carried off toward any of the most jarring evils. They were sick with a love of the flesh that was almost impossible to wash away, and gripped by passions hard to escape. For such people it was still somehow out of reach, and not easy, to be able to leap up at once to what is exceedingly fine, so as to adopt a way of life so splendid and extraordinary that they would walk on earth but have their citizenship in heaven, as it is written. For is not solid food for the mature, while milk is more suitable for those who are still infants?
Very much so.

So those who were still infants needed tutoring through types, and, so to speak, a gentler upbringing, not the word that prescribes perfection and can carry people to completeness. The people of Israel would be found to be so fickle, so foolish, and so readily drawn into every kind of passion that, had their character and conduct been strictly tested, they would not, I think, have been found worthy even of the shadow. Moses demonstrated this. At God's command he went up the mountain himself to receive the law, but they immediately slid into apostasy. They made a calf, and the wretches dared to say: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." Moses was grieved at such dreadful fickleness, and he broke the tablets on which the law was written. He did not consider them worthy of shadow or types, or indeed of any tutoring from above at all, people whose minds were so senseless that they forgot the great wonders performed on their behalf by divine power, gave their reverence once again to a calf, and called to mind the worship they had practiced in Egypt. Yet at that time the law was sketched in shadow for the ancients on tablets of stone by the finger of God, as it is written. Those things were a type of what we believe has come about for us in Christ. For God, the Master of all, writes the knowledge of his will within us, as it were, using the Son as a pen in the Spirit. For he called him this through David, saying: "My tongue is the pen of a swift scribe." For the Father's pen, that is, the Son, has engraved on the hearts of all the knowledge of every good, using as a kind of finger of God the Spirit, who is both the Father's and his own. For he called the Spirit of God a finger, saying at one time, "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God," and at another, "But if I cast out demons by the finger of God." And Paul too called us a spiritual letter, saying: "You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by all people; you show that you are a letter of God delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts."

I myself would also say that the things of the law are types and shadows; be well assured of that. Come, then, let us apply a subtle and precise mind to what was prophesied in types, and let us investigate thoroughly the beauty of the truth. In this way the mystery of worship in spirit would no longer be obscure to anyone at all.

And yet, my noble friend, I shudder at this, and with good reason, and I am exceedingly reluctant to undertake it. For matters whose contemplation is so lofty and so far beyond us would not, I think, be within the grasp of people like us. Anyone who considers the depth of the insights in the law ought, I think, to say: "Who is wise, and will understand these things? Who is discerning, and will know them?"
The matter is not without its difficulties, my good man. Yet Christ says: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."

Then we must set out eagerly to hunt for what will be of benefit. And first let us lift up a prayer, saying: "Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive the wonders of your law." But it seems that before anything else we must speak of man's turning aside into wickedness, and of the slavery and captivity under the enemy of all, and of how and in what way these things come about through us and within us. Then we must go on to say how one ought to turn away from evil, to shake off the yoke of slavery to it, and to leap back up to the state we had at the beginning, with God saving and helping us. If our discussion proceeds along this fitting road, then the rest, I think, will follow fittingly.
Your thinking is entirely right.

For to be able to bear fruit for God and to offer spiritual sacrifices, that is, to act courageously and win approval as people who wish to achieve virtue, would surely not befit those [?] freed from slavery and from the compulsion of the passions, but rather those whose minds are already somehow sobering up toward freedom and who are practiced at shaking off the yoke of the devil's greed.
I agree; you think rightly.

So let us say that in the beginning man was made with a mind still somehow above sin and passions, yet not entirely incapable of turning aside to whatever he might choose. For it seemed right to God, the supreme craftsman of all things, to place in man's hands the reins of his own will, and to leave him to do what seemed good to him by impulses of his own choosing. For virtue had to be a matter of choice, and not seen as something compelled, nor fixed unfailingly by laws of nature; that would belong only to the essence and preeminence that is highest of all. And once the living creature had been completed by God's craftsmanship according to the principles of its own nature, it was at once enriched with likeness to him. For the image of the divine nature was engraved on him when the Holy Spirit was breathed into him. For the Spirit is the breath of life, since God is life by nature.
Did the divine Spirit, then, become man's soul?

How could it be anything but utterly absurd to think so? For in that case the soul too would have remained unchangeable, whereas in fact it is changeable. But the Spirit is in no way changeable. Or, if it is subject to change, will not the blame reach up to the divine nature itself? For the Spirit belongs to God the Father, and also to the Son, being poured forth in essence from both, that is, from the Father through the Son. It is ignorant, then, to think that the Spirit was transformed into a soul and passed over into human nature. Rather, what had been fashioned was given a soul by an ineffable power, and was immediately made beautiful by the gift of the Spirit. For there was no other way for us to be enriched with the divine image.
Well said.

So God, having thus adorned his handiwork, granted him life in paradise. But one so splendidly adorned and crowned with an abundance of good things from above had to be kept from being easily carried away into arrogance, as he would be if he did not know what servitude is, or that there is a measure proper to those who serve. For excessive glory and unlimited freedom lead to the haughty and accursed passion of pride. So a law of self-restraint was given to him, as a means of not forgetting his Master, so that through it he might always be called to remember the one who had commanded him with authority, and might know clearly that he was yoked under the ordinances of the one who rules. But that unholy and God-hated beast would not keep still.

You mean, I suppose, Satan, who was hurled down from the vaults of heaven like lightning. For he was childishly sick with the desire to be God, and he indulged in fantasies, hinting at things beyond his own nature.

You judge rightly. Being the inventor and father of envy and sin, he would not leave alone the living creature on earth, that is, man. Creeping in with cunning and deceit, he led him astray into disobedience, using the woman as the instrument of his villainy. For the pleasures that are with us and within us are always somehow pushing us toward what is ugly, that is, into sin. The woman is a type of pleasure, and the mind, beguiled by the flatteries of pleasure, often rushes headlong into what it did not want. So what is seen to have happened in Adam in concrete events and in a way the senses can perceive, one may see fulfilled in each of us as well, in a way perceived by the mind and hidden. For pleasure springs up first and bewitches the mind, and little by little draws it into thinking at last that transgression of the divine law is nothing at all. The disciple of Christ confirms this when he says: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God.' For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each person is tempted when he is dragged away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, brings forth death."
What you say is true.

So human nature, having bartered away the grace it had from God and being now stripped of the good things it had at the beginning, was sent out of the paradise of delight. At once it was refashioned into ugliness, and from then on it was shown to have fallen into corruption.

Necessarily so. For to lack God's gifts is, I think, nothing other than to fall away from every good. And human nature would very easily succumb to being carried off into every kind of monstrous evil, unless the grace of the one who saves held it up toward virtue, enriching it with good things from above and from itself.

You speak well, and I would agree, with very good reason. The living bread, that is, the Word of God, nourishes us into spiritual strength, for it is written: "And bread strengthens the heart of man." It frees us from slavery and from the passions, and gilds us splendidly with the glories of freedom. But when God, as it were, draws back his hand and does not hand out to us his provision in these things, it is altogether necessary that we somehow fall into evils against our will. We slip away from all virtue and come, as it were, under another's yoke. We reach such a pitch of evil and greed that we come close to losing even the understanding that lives with us and serves us for every good thing. Then the heart of the one who suffers this is shown to be utterly empty of godly wisdom, prostituted, as it were, to Satan, and easily brought under his outrages and lewdness.
Could you show how? Or will you leave us floating on bare reasonings?

Not at all. I will show, as well as I can, what happened to the ancients, shaping it skilfully into a type of spiritual realities. Things that strike the senses and that we see with meaningful sight would give us vivid and very clear images of what is grasped in subtle contemplation. So it is written concerning the forefather Abraham: "And there was a famine in the land, and Abraham went down into Egypt to sojourn there, because the famine was severe in the land." He had left the land that was dear to him and had given him birth, and had moved to another, which God showed him. For "Go out," he says, "from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you." But when the famine weighed heavily and brought a hardship very hard to escape, he was forced, not willingly, to turn toward Egypt. And he did not settle there, but rather sojourned in it.
What then of this?
It gives shape for us to an excellent contemplation of more hidden things.
In what way?

Rebuking the disobedience of the Jews, God said somewhere: "Behold, I am bringing a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And from the east to the west they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it." Think, my friend, of those who happen to be crushed by such a famine. They have lost the supply that holds them firm in virtue and have no food from heaven and from above. Is it not altogether necessary that they make their mind something like an emigrant and a fugitive? It then runs off to baser things, and, driven out of its strength in virtue as out of its own land, it goes down into another state and another will. That state is no longer under God, but is rather subject to diabolical sceptres. For the father and king of sin, I think, is the one who first brought it into the world. One might take Pharaoh, ruler of the Egyptians, as his image and type, I think, and with very good reason. Among the Egyptians the darkness of error was very deep, and there was absolutely no form of wickedness they did not practise.
And what grief came to blessed Abraham from going down into the land of the Egyptians?

A very great deal. He came within a hair of the worst evil of all. You can easily learn this too, for holy Scripture says: "And it came to pass, when Abraham entered Egypt, that the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful; and the princes of Pharaoh saw her and praised her to Pharaoh, and brought her into Pharaoh's house." See, then, my good man, that he very nearly lost his wife.
What a bitter thing, and enough to cause deep grief!

And indeed this will also happen to us, in a spiritual sense. Some slip away from their homeland, their own as it were, that is, from the good order and virtue that were familiar and dearest to them. They come down to worse things and come under diabolical sceptres. Then the wicked and hostile powers cling to them in every way and plot terribly against them. If they see anyone who has come under their power and is able to have an understanding not lacking in beauty, they are eager to win him over for their own leader and to bring him under that one's sowings, so that he may bear fruit no longer to God but rather to Satan. For his food, as it is written, is choice. They bewitch, as it were, the mind that has been captured and has slipped, so that it may not look much toward freedom and leave their service. To this end they sometimes procure earthly pleasures for it, and enrich it, so to speak, with delights that come to nothing. In just the same way the princes of the Egyptians, when blessed Abraham was losing his wife, fawned on him as it were with honours and presents of gifts, wanting to relieve him of his great grief. For it is written: "And they treated Abraham well on her account" (meaning Sarah, clearly) "and he had sheep and calves and donkeys, menservants and maidservants, mules and camels." For Satan overreaches us in the most vital matters and robs us, as it were, of free offspring and fruitfulness. He greedily subjects the noble mind to his own outrages and lewdness, and binds it fast with the delight of earthly things. He once went so far in madness as to bring his test even upon Christ himself. For "leading him up," it says, "he showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and the devil said to him: To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish. If you, then, will worship before me, all will be yours."
That is right. But tell me, since I ask: what benefit or help could there be for those who suffer this?

God, my noble friend, and the grace that comes from him. That grace does not allow the weakened mind to remain under diabolical feet forever, but shields and rescues the one who can do nothing to help himself. If you wish, you can see that this happened in the case of the forefather Abraham too. When the righteous man had given up and could do absolutely nothing, God stepped in and freed his wife from the lewdness of the Egyptians. "For the Lord afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great and grievous afflictions because of Sarah, Abraham's wife." Only so, and with difficulty, did Pharaoh let the righteous man's wife go free of outrage. God alone, then, can rescue the captured mind from the devil's hand, and he will restore it to its original good order.
So when we are thrust down by want of the good things from above, we sometimes go down to shameful and loathsome things.
So I say.
But surely it would be entirely fitting for God, who loves the good, not to let us fall into any such things.

That is indeed most fitting for God, my good man, and it is what he wills too. He would hardly be good, and no great lover of virtue, if he did not have this aim toward us. But we ourselves share the blame for our suffering, because we provoke the Lord of all to anger, and so he gives us over to a weak and unmanly mind. Or do you not hear him crying out through one of the holy prophets: "Behold, I am giving weakness to this people, and fathers and sons shall grow weak in it; neighbour and his fellow shall perish"? The most wise Paul also writes concerning some: "And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting." And the inspired Isaiah establishes this more clearly still, speaking as if in the person of the sons of Israel, that is, of those who had slipped into sins: "Behold, you were angry, and we sinned."
Tell me, then: when we grow careless of what is fitting and are caught by sins, shall we throw the blame on God and charge him with his anger, as though we had sinned because of it?

We shall not accuse him, for that would be madness. When we say, "You were angry, and we sinned," we mean something like this: "If we do not have your favour, O Master, nothing keeps us from being tyrannized by sin because of the weakness of our nature, and from then being caught in every evil."
I understand what you say.

So when we are stripped of the care and the protection that come from above, and are paying the penalty for our utter dissipation and our unrestrained inclinations toward what is base, we are shown to be weak and easily captured. Indeed, which of these ailments are we not shown to suffer? You can see this clearly by turning to the words of Jeremiah. The savage multitude of the Jews lived in great luxury and was richly enlarged by God's generosity. It had overcome all its enemies and had reached perhaps the very height of glory among men. Yet it practised a hard and unbreakable disobedience. They all but bade farewell to the commandments given through Moses and counted what God had decreed as worth almost nothing, and so they were swept along unchecked toward destruction and ruin. "Under oak and poplar and shady tree," as the prophet says, they built altars. In the most thickly wooded groves they set up sacred precincts for demons, and saw fit to honour them with sacrifices of oxen, with incense and with all the rest. They did not blush to call the works of their own hands gods and saviours and what not besides. At one point they reached such folly that they counted the unholy slaughter of their children among their boasts, and thought that in this way they were kindling the richest sacrifice. Nor did the impiety of the people of Israel stop there. They kept adding fresh audacities, as it were, to their former ones, an unbridled departure into every sort of outrage. And so they provoked the lawgiver to no small anger against themselves, kind though he was. Since they brazenly shook off their service to him, he then let them be overpowered by their enemies too, and carried off into forced servitude, I mean under the Chaldeans and Babylonians. The enemy came, leaving their own homes, enslaved them and burned the holy and famous city. Only at the last did those under attack decide to ask the prophet Jeremiah how the disaster would end for them. "And Jeremiah said," it says, "Thus shall you say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am turning back the weapons of war with which you are fighting the Chaldeans who have shut you in outside the wall, into the midst of this city. And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a mighty arm, with wrath and great anger. And I will strike all who dwell in this city, both men and beasts, with a great death, and they shall die." Then, after other things: "And to this people," it says, "you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I have set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who stays in this city shall die by the sword and by famine. But he who goes out to surrender to the Chaldeans who have shut you in shall live, and his life shall be his spoil, and he shall live. For I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good. It shall be handed over into the hands of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire." Do you understand, then? When we grieve God in return for the generosity he once showed us, we wretched people will be unable to resist the strength of our enemies. Instead, with God's wrath pressing hard on us and, as it were, leaping upon us, we shall be slaves instead of free, and we shall live out an inglorious and pitiable life.
You speak well.

For the law of God carries the one who is gentle and docile toward a blameless way of life, and becomes a kind of lamp for each person, showing what is useful and necessary. Whoever yields to reverence for it would live, I think, a life not unworthy of admiration. Firmly fixed in virtue and established in piety, he will dwell, as it were, in a holy city. But suppose someone chooses to rush eagerly into worldly pleasures, as into a thicket or a forest full of flowers and fine timber, and to linger fondly among the delights of this life. Suppose he receives the many-shaped pleasure into his mind and heart like a swarm of idols, and burns the fruits of his own eagerness as incense to the demons. Then, yes then, and with very good reason, he will slip away from the protection from above, and will lie there as the readiest prey for those who wish to capture him. Driven out of his original good order as out of a holy city, he will then depart, as under a forced yoke, to do whatever his masters please. He will be far from God in the disposition of his mind, enduring deportation to Babylon, that is, beyond the borders of the holy land, in which God is known and his name is great. That is why those who endure such hard toil, who have fallen into the hands of enemies and cannot bear the servile, slavish life among them, cry aloud: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion." For the human mind, I think, suffers from some such ailment.
What do you mean?

It is always somehow careless and slack in its desire for the good things it has at hand, and does not long very much for what lies within its power. But if there is a change to the opposite, and it comes to lose the splendid things it had, only then does it barely perceive what it has suffered. Yet it ought to have repelled this with all its strength, forestalling the attack rather than letting it come and learning by experience.
True.

It is necessary, then, and wise, and among the most profitable things of all, to forestall thoroughly what is wicked and the approach of unwanted servitude. We should try to turn away quickly, in advance, from things which, if we came to experience them, would leave us lying in every evil.
So it is.

If the yoke of forced servitude is brought upon us by divine wrath, and with it the necessity of sinking into a debased mind, it is not easy to resist. But I would say it is useful at least simply to remember from what state to what state we have been turned, and to lament bitterly our neglect and our lack of help from above. For "godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." But when divine wrath is not hanging over us, and it is in our power to choose and do what seems good, we can still hold the inclination toward both, toward evil, I mean, and toward good, as something free and wholly uncoerced. Then we must nobly refuse to grow soft toward wickedness. I think we must shake off any love for the pleasures our enemies offer, and refuse to act under the hand of the enemies who are said to rule this age. Even if what they offer happens to bring some share of prosperity, I mean the prosperity the world honours, it always ends in a shameful and ugly outcome.
How did you put it?
Would you like me to explain by taking examples from ancient times?
By all means.

When famine was wasting those throughout, so to speak, the whole earth, the sons of Jacob decided to go down to the Egyptians. They were young men, about ten in number, and the purpose of the journey was to buy food and nothing else. When they had come there and were finally recognized as Joseph's brothers, Joseph was at that time distributing grain and governing the Egyptians, and the news of what had happened reached Pharaoh's ears. "And Pharaoh said," it says, "to Joseph: Say to your brothers: Do this: fill your sacks and go into the land of Canaan, and take your father and your possessions and come to me. I will give you all the good things of Egypt, and you shall eat the marrow of the land. And you, give this command: that they take wagons from the land of Egypt for your children and your wives, and bring your father and come. And do not let your eyes grieve over your goods, for all the good things of Egypt shall be yours." So the ruler of the Egyptians promised them rest and to fatten them well with luxury, and even provided wagons, smoothing the way down, I suppose, for any who hesitated. And they went down at once with their whole households. Somehow, I do not know how, they had preferred the passing enjoyment of food to the land and country given by God. Surely it would have been far stronger and better to dwell in that land, even if it had to be achieved with a little toil. When they came to Egypt, they perhaps thought that they had escaped the toils of home from then on, and the feeling of immediate delights was somehow sweet to them. But as time went on, that multitude, noble and free from of old and from their fathers, came under the inglorious yoke of slavery. So if a fall into baser things comes along with worldly prosperity, we must refuse it, my good man, if freedom counts for anything with us, and we must regard servile ways and a servile mind as loathsome and hateful.
Excellently said.
What then? Shall we not also mention another example, which, it seems to me, yields no small benefit in harmony with what we have just said?
What do you mean by that?

Rabshakeh the Babylonian, general of the Assyrians, once led a multitude of spearmen beyond counting and came to besiege the holy city. Or rather, he supposed that he would capture the whole of it, from its foundations, with very little effort. Then, ahead of his weapons, he let loose his abusive tongue against God, which was well practised and long accustomed to it. After saying countless blasphemous things, he finally called out to those who lived in the holy city: "Thus says the king of the Assyrians: If you wish to be blessed, come out to me, and each of you shall eat of his own vine and his own fig trees, and you shall drink water from your own cistern, until I come and take you to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine and bread and vineyards." Notice, then, that he too promises the luxury and delight of the vine and the fig tree; and he added, "and you shall drink water from your own cistern."
But what would these things mean, if taken up into spiritual contemplation?

The power of wickedness, I think, does its work in us in two ways. People who are easily led into sin are persuaded, by themselves or by others, to revel either in pleasures from outside or in those that are innate and within us. Then they slip and are caught in every sort of most repugnant thing. The Saviour's disciple would show us that this is true, when he says somewhere: "For all that is in the world, the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the pride of life." The desire of the flesh is innate, rooted and abiding in us ourselves; the divine Paul too named it for us the law of sin, dwelling in the members of the flesh. But the delights and pleasures that come from outside and are brought in are those that come through the eyes. For the things wealth brings are admired through the eyes, and fine clothing too, and whatever things people are attached to, when they cast no mean vote for them as giving the sweetest enjoyment. So the vine and the fig tree would stand as a type of the delight and luxury that come from outside and are brought in. They aptly show at the same time how passing and quick to wither the things of the world are, and also how sweetness goes together with what usually darkens the mind. For all worldly luxury tastes sweet at the moment of sharing in it, but greatly darkens and terribly intoxicates whoever has taken it in. And the cistern is an image of the innate impulses within us. These are not brought in from outside like the others, but spring up within us, as it were, welling up from the flesh itself. The wicked powers tell us that we shall share freely in all these things, natural and imported alike, and enjoy them without limit, if we abandon self-control, which is like a holy and unshakeable city, and go over to the king of Babylon, who was a type of Satan. Rabshakeh, then, promised to let them have and to grant them immediate delight if they went over to the Babylonians. But they were not persuaded, for they thought rightly. For the choice to want worldly things will surely be followed by having to fall into unwilling slavery and to be counted among the captives of war.
Your account is accurate. But what would be the remedy for these things? Please tell me, since I would be glad to know.

What else but the one that is the opposite of the first and original fault? We turned aside, by the leanings of our own wills, toward wanting to live shamefully, and we thrust aside the refinement of a blameless way of life. So we fell into an ignoble and servile mind, thinking only of the things on earth and given over wholly to the pleasures of the flesh. That is why God let us slip into a debased mind.
So it is necessary to run back to virtue?

Without a doubt, my good man. We must no longer long for life in the world, entirely in keeping with what was rightly said through Paul's voice: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." Rather, we must thirst for enrolment in heaven, make the city above our homeland and our city, as it were, and cry out earnestly to God: "Spare me, for I am a sojourner on the earth and a stranger, as all my fathers were." For whoever walks on earth but has his splendid citizenship in heaven would rightly appear, from the facts themselves, to be truly a sojourner and a stranger. Indeed the Saviour's disciple bids us make this our own illustrious and seemly boast, when he says somewhere: "Brothers, I urge you as sojourners and strangers to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul."
Would such a disposition, then, be enough for achieving virtue? I mean ceasing from the desires of the flesh.

Yes, if we are wise enough to add the things that belong to the other kind of goodness, which is clearly the spiritual kind. For it is written: "Your commandment is exceedingly broad." Or is not the defilement in us twofold, of soul and of body? I would think, and with very good reason, that what usually defiles us must be matched by cleansing remedies of equal strength and effect.
You are right.

So just as the filth is twofold, of soul and of body, the cleansing would rightly be of soul and of body as well. But those so minded will profit from seeing, without much effort, that we ought to make a habit of regarding life in the world as a sojourn in a strange land, if they choose to take Abraham as an image of the matter. To him God said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house, and come into the land that I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be blessed; and I will bless those who bless you, and those who curse you I will curse; and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” Do you see how he commanded him to depart not only from his land and home, but also from his kindred, and indeed from his father's house, and to come into a land that the one who called him would himself show him?
But what does this mean?

Surely it is plain, then, that when God calls us to follow him (to follow spiritually, clearly) and wants us to creep out of life in the world (by which I mean once more life spent in pleasures and in love of the flesh), it is utter madness to think any of the people we might choose to honor better than such a one. Let a person count as nothing his homeland and family, his father's house, and the possession of earthly things. For this reason the Savior himself called us to the same courage when he said: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.” And he added: “And everyone who has left brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields or houses for the sake of my name will receive many times as much, and will inherit eternal life.” Or would you not say that a courage so brilliant and so conspicuous, which counts these things as nothing and treats following Christ as a matter of great importance, is the work of the utmost strength, the strength understood to be in Christ?

Certainly I would, since those who were invited to the wedding but refused to come lost their grip on the best of hopes and on the joy that is in Christ. One of them said, “I have married a wife, and I cannot come.” Another said he had bought a field, and so ranked temporal things above the invitation.

Well said, Palladius! You delight us by saying what is fitting, and your great quickness of mind makes you leap ahead eagerly to grasp where the argument is going. Notice, then, that those who follow God wholly and in every way, and who have put the things of the flesh and worldly love of pleasure second to their hope in him, will certainly go on to receive a rich share of blessing from above. For what does he say to Abraham? “And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you,” and what follows. Do you see what a multitude of spiritual goods he heaped upon him? And is it not worth seeing how Abraham departs from the land that bore him? “He took,” it says, “Sarah his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had acquired, and every soul that they had acquired in Haran. And they set out to go into the land of Canaan, and Abraham passed through the land along its length as far as the place Shechem, to the high oak.” He left Haran without leaving any remnant of himself behind in it; with all his kin, as it were, and all his household, he hurried most eagerly over into the land of Canaan, which God had shown him. Then he passes through the land along its length and comes to the high land. For whoever has resolved to follow the divine commands closely, and to count the call from above worthy of his best care, must go out entirely from life spent in worldly pleasures, with all his kin, so to speak, leaving no remnant of his mind behind among the things in which he once lived. For so he departs rightly, and he will pass through the land, since he has been called by God, so that, as the blessed Paul writes, he may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth of the mystery of Christ. Then he will rightly go up to the high land, that is, to a disposition that dwells on high among the virtues and no longer has anything about it that has been flung down into love of the flesh. And what further good will come to him once he has reached this point, we shall learn from the sacred Scriptures themselves. “The Lord appeared to Abraham,” it says, “and said to him, ‘To your offspring I will give this land.’ And Abraham built an altar there to the Lord who had appeared to him.” While he was still lingering in the land of his fathers and had not yet moved to the holy land, he was given only the oracle that he must move to another land, having let go of the one that bore him. But when he had come into the land of Canaan with all his household and all his goods, and had sprung up to the holy land, he was given the grace of seeing God, the security of hope in the firm possession of freedom, and the right thenceforth to raise an altar. So it is with us too, by the same pattern of reasoning. If we stay with the world and with its most loathsome pleasures, there will be no grace from God for us. But when we have been called and yield to the divine laws, and spring up, as though to a high land, to the desire and eagerness for every kind of good, God instills in us the knowledge of his own glory and promises the firm foundation of our hope. He makes the mind within us so strong that it is now in some way able to offer spiritual sacrifices and to become the fragrance of Christ to God the Father, as it is written; and also to present the body to him as a living sacrifice, well pleasing to God, the reasonable and spiritual worship acceptable to God. For he gladly receives the forms of worship in the Spirit and regards the thing as a spiritual sacrifice.

We ought, then, to move to better anchorage, setting sail from what is more shameful; to welcome the call from above with the greatest gladness, and to make a point above all of lingering among the things the law honors, which have won the highest verdict with God. For to seek to go back and to return to any of the things that habitually do us wrong is something we shall not clear of blame.

No indeed, my friend. It is a grievous thing to choose to fall sick again with what one has left behind. For those whom God's power has once rescued from a worldly way of life, it is very dangerous even just to look back at it, and, as it were, to go over the memory of their sins, setting their minds on loving them. So the inspired Psalmist pleaded, saying: “Turn my eyes away from looking at vanity.” For the distraction of this life and the empty enjoyment of temporal things are truly vanity. That anyone who has truly chosen to walk upright must stand apart from them and leave them behind, and must refuse even to contemplate them with pleasure in his thoughts, one could easily learn from the following as well.
From what, do you mean?

The inhabitants of Sodom were savagely driven mad by unnatural pleasures. They dishonored the law of intercourse that nature set for the begetting of children and were inflamed by the youthful beauty of males; and what utterly outrageous deed did they not carry out? So they provoked the Creator to anger and in a sense forced him to proceed to punish them, even though he is a lover of humankind. And when the time for them to suffer was at the door, his forbearance toward them having been, as it were, used up, those who were to carry this out entered Sodom. It is written thus: “Two angels came to Sodom in the evening. Lot was sitting by the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground, and said, ‘Look, my lords, turn aside to your servant's house and lodge, and wash your feet, and rising early you shall go on your way.’ And they said, ‘No; we will lodge in the street.’ And he pressed them hard, and they turned aside to him and entered his house, and he made them a drinking feast and baked them unleavened bread, and they ate before they lay down.” For Lot, being of Abraham's blood, brought up in the laws of uprightness, and caring in no small measure for piety toward God, was living as a sojourner in Sodom. Among them he was a newcomer and a stranger both by race and by way of life. “For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?” as it is written. Looking down on the local evils and walking the road of life that was customary for him, he held fast to holy pursuits; and honoring the law of hospitality above all, he sat at the entrances of the city and warmly welcomed those who came in, knowing that this is dear to God. When those arrived who were to bring punishment on people who had gone raving mad with unbridled licentiousness (they were a pair of angels), he went quickly to meet them, and in his greeting he showed a clear sign of the kindness that was in him. For he bowed with his face to the ground, and urged them to come to his home and enjoy the laws of love to the full. But they said, “No, we will lodge in the street.” By this they indicated that they were strangers without a hearth, but also, I think, stirred the man who had chosen to be hospitable to more intense zeal, all but hinting, with some wit, that he could hardly decently let them go without a home and cast out at the very crossroads. The righteous man understood this and pressed them all the harder, and did not snatch at their refusal as a feeble and weak-spirited mind would. So he brings them into his house, sets unleavened bread before them, and prepares a drinking feast. So much for the righteous man. But the Sodomites, sick with naked and shameful lust, impiously surrounded the righteous man's dwelling and went past the very limit of shamelessness: they demanded to be allowed to do their customary deeds, and when they should have chosen hospitality, they wanted to do harm through unnatural licentiousness. When Lot tried to hold them back from such savage and loathsome undertakings, they wanted to overpower him, and he might perhaps have been caught and suffered it himself, had his rescuers not been there. “The men,” it says, “stretched out their hands and drew Lot into the house to them and shut the door of the house. And they struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, from small to great, and they wore themselves out looking for the door.” Yet the help given him is not measured by these things alone. For again it is written: “When morning came, the angels urged Lot on, saying, ‘Get up, take your wife and the two daughters you have, and go out, so that you too may not perish with the lawless deeds of the city.’ And they were troubled, and the angels took hold of his hand and the hand of his wife and of his two daughters, because the Lord spared them.” This is a very clear proof for you that we are not only spurred on by words and urged in our minds to depart from sin, but that God, the Savior of all, also goes so far in his gentleness toward us as to make his help active, according to the words: “You held my right hand, and in your counsel you guided me.” For since human nature is not very strong, nor sufficiently able to escape from evil, God somehow strives together with it toward this. He is seen to bestow a twofold grace: persuading us by admonitions, and providing help, and making us superior to the evil that is close at hand and tyrannizes over us. You would also find this to be true: that those who care for righteousness are very few, and that good men are very rare in this life; for a faithful man is hard to find, as it is written. Yet such a man is chosen and deemed worthy of no casual care from above. For even if he lives in the world mingled with others, he suffers no harm from it; he is snatched out like a lily from among thorns, and the righteous would not perish with the ungodly, as the voices of the saints say.

It is settled, then, that by God's sparing mercy and the help of holy angels we shall wash off the greed that comes from wickedness, and shall beyond dispute find that we are never in any way caught in the punishments of the wicked, if we trust God, who has cried out plainly through one of the prophets: “I am the Lord your God, who holds your right hand, who says to you, ‘Do not fear, Jacob, Israel few in number; I have helped you,’ says the Lord, ‘who redeems you, Israel.’”

For would not the fact that Lot hung on the hand of the angels show that the all-powerful God is a helper to the saints? For these would be a figure of God: at first three of them came to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while two visited Sodom. For the Father judges no one, according to the Savior's own words, but has given all judgment to the Son, with whom, clearly, the Holy Spirit is also present and in whom he exists by nature.
You understand very well. Let us look at what comes next, if you agree.

Most readily; and I will tell you. “And it came to pass,” it says, “when they had brought him outside, they said, ‘Save your own soul; do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in the surrounding country. Flee to the mountain to save yourself, lest you be taken along with them.’” In the words “Save your own soul,” I say it is plainly being said: “Keep yourself pure, and do not share in other people's sins.” Rise above the snares of the world; for the whole universe is nothing in exchange for a soul. “For what will a person gain if he wins the whole world but forfeits his soul?” The command to make the journey without turning back perhaps signifies that we should not, by turning back toward wickedness, choose again to think as those do who were brought under the punishment of fire through their lack of self-control (“For no one,” it says, “who puts his hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of heaven”); rather, we must hold to the road to salvation, not being dragged this way and that, and not having a mind that is light and easily scattered by the stale fancies of worldly desires, but keeping within ourselves a mind that is whole and sleepless and trained always to look straight ahead. And I will say something greater still: the angel does not only say that he must now make his journey without turning back, but usefully adds, “Do not stop anywhere in the surrounding country. Flee to the mountain to save yourself, lest you be taken along with them.”
And what might “Do not stop anywhere in the surrounding country” be meant to show?
That being sluggish and slack when we ought to fly out of evil is, I think, dangerous and harmful.
Explain how.

A prophetic word said: “Woe to those who do the work of the Lord carelessly.” And the inspired Paul himself says somewhere: “Run so that you may obtain.” For to be unwilling to make our escape from shameful things with all our strength and in haste, while the mind is hard to tear away from its old ways and departs from each wicked thing as if in gloom, and moves over most reluctantly to what is by nature beneficial, would be nothing other than to stop in the country surrounding evil, when we ought to be leaving at a run. Or rather, it is quite possible that, always delaying and hanging back, we would be overtaken by punishment before getting outside the boundaries of evil, before cleansing away the stain, before washing off the defilement that our old laziness has melted into the soul, before unloading our charges and taking up the saving yoke to find rest through Christ. So the best of commands is “Do not stop anywhere in the surrounding country,” that is: do not delay and be caught in any form of wickedness, but rather go up, as to a mountain, to a choice and conspicuous life, which has nothing in it that is flung down to the ground, but is distinguished by high and lofty virtue and freed from the lowest way of thinking, that is, the earthly and fleshly. For it is written: “The mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they have been greatly exalted.” For the mind that befits the saints is far above earthly things. And “the young of the vulture fly to the heights,” as it is written, if indeed they have their citizenship in heaven, as on a mountain, and lay claim to the homeland above. And Paul writes somewhere: “Seek the things above, not the things on earth.”

So the mountain, understood spiritually, is the life of holiness and the surpassing height of the exalted way of life, while the life spent in impurities and love of sin, melted into earthly things, is understood to be somewhere below.
Well said; for the passage shows us exactly this. But you would also marvel at the following.
At what?

The blessed angel told the inspired Lot, as he ran on without hesitating and without turning back, that he must leap up to the mountain. But Lot pleaded, saying: “I beg you, Lord: since your servant has found mercy before you, and you have magnified your righteousness, which you are showing in keeping my soul alive, I shall not be able to reach safety on the mountain, lest evils overtake me and I die. Look, this city is near enough for me to flee there, and it is small; there I shall be saved. Is it not small? And my soul shall live.” And he said to him, it says: “Look, I have respected your person in this matter too, so as not to overthrow the city of which you have spoken. Hurry, then, to be saved there, for I shall not be able to do anything until you have entered it.” This is why he called the name of that city Zoar. The sun rose over the earth, and Lot entered Zoar.
And what benefit might come to us from this too? I would like very much to learn it, believe me.

Do you not see, though you lean so strongly toward quick understanding, that for those who have just run out of wickedness and think they must set out on the path of salvation, virtue cannot be captured at once, nor can what seems right be walked at the first attempts? No one could easily be carried up to an exalted way of life, nor get far from the passions that have, as it were, been reared together with him. He will be outside them only gently, so far as concerns his eagerness for better things and the beginnings of his undertakings; not very high, nor very far. He would all but move over, as to another land, to a life that is praiseworthy but has not yet won a high and conspicuous glory, such as was the training under the law, which leads up to the beginnings of the best and good life. For it is written: “The beginning of a good way is to do what is just.” For just as, for those who are eager for knowledge and long for mystical contemplation, the word of catechesis would be suitable and most fitting at the beginning, while for those already darting on toward mature manhood and to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, the more solid food would now in some way be appropriate, that is, discourse about the highest things, and thereafter the whole path of doctrinal inquiry, so I say it is here too, that is, in the correction of character and conduct: it is not possible for anyone to leap up at once to what is blameless, that is, to a surpassing and lofty way of life. It is fitting, I think, to proceed little by little toward the perfect disposition, beginning from small and moderate things, and running ahead, as it were, into a small city that is a neighbor to a high mountain, that is, into the way of life that ranks below the exalted and lofty life and is concerned with lesser things. In this way the righteous Lot, too, would be a figure of those so disposed, asking to lodge not at once on the mountain, but in the small city of Zoar. Will we not often find such accommodations made for believers in the preaching of the Gospel as well? So the blessed Paul writes: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband. I say this by way of concession, not of command. For I wish that all people were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.” Do you see how he showed us the surpassing excellence of self-control as a mountain when he said, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” but allowed us to lodge in Zoar, that is, in the way of life that still ranks below the perfect, meaning the permission to have intercourse only with one's own wife? The Savior said that the best soil would yield fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold. He also distributed the talents not in equal measure, but to one five, to another two, to another one; by this, I think, showing the unequal strength of people's dispositions, and assigning to each according to his fitness and resolve. For, as we said just now, “each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.”
You speak well.

The blessed angel allows him to lodge in Zoar. “Look,” he says, “I have respected your person in this matter too, so as not to overthrow the city of which you have spoken. Hurry, then, to be saved there.” Then it says: “The sun rose over the earth, and Lot entered Zoar.” You would marvel, my friend, on learning what the meaning of this is too. “I have respected your person,” it says, “so as not to overthrow the city of which you have spoken.” In truth, a way of life that is not perfectly given to virtue is not what God wills, and to be overcome by the passions in any respect at all is rejected by him and not far from condemnation. Yet out of his love for humankind he makes allowance, and measuring what is attainable at the beginning against our nature, he commands that those who are still practicing the good, and are not yet walking a wholly blameworthy course, be saved. But for those who have reached this measure and are entering this state, the entry cannot happen without the divine light and the torch-bearing from above. For “the sun rose,” it says, “and Lot entered Zoar.”
How very fitting your words are!

So the godlike Lot entered the city that was still small, since God allowed him to. But the wife who followed him and fled out with him proved too weak even for this. For she looked back, it says, and became a pillar of salt. Notice that a courageous mind and a youthful spirit, even if it perhaps does not fully attain to what pleases God, once it has begun to achieve virtue, still moves little by little out of its habits of passion toward a better state. But the weak and unmanly mind, of which the wife is a sign, is made completely useless by its turnings toward wickedness. This, I think, is what becoming a pillar of salt shows: it would be a symbol of a mind that has withered, a mind inclined to pass over into foolishness and already driven, in a way, to the utmost insensibility. The Saviour himself said that salt which has lost its savour will no longer be good for anything, but will be utterly useless, thrown out and scattered under people's feet. So the wife was turned to stone, but before long Lot supplied what was lacking. For it is written: "Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the mountain, he and his two daughters with him; for they were afraid to live in Zoar. And they lived in the cave, he and his two daughters with him." For the mind advances as if by steps toward what is perfect, and rises little by little from what it was at the beginning, when it was neither suitably disposed nor fully capable. It advances and climbs toward the better, leaning on prudence and spiritual courage as on its own daughters, and leaving somewhere below the pleasure-loving and unmanly, of which the wife is a type. From then on it dwells as in a mountain and a cave. The mountain signifies for us what is lofty and raised up to spiritual health, and the cave what is fixed and steadfast in perseverance in virtue, and both signify it very well. For it is written thus about good men: "He who walks in righteousness, who speaks a straight way, who hates lawlessness and injustice, who shakes his hands free of bribes, who stops his ears so as not to hear a judgment of blood, who shuts his eyes so as not to see injustice—he shall dwell in a lofty cave of strong rock." But our account of this might also be taken another way, and not implausibly. For the rock is Christ, because of the strength and invulnerability of the essence that is highest of all. And the cave in Christ may be understood as the Church, the lodging of the saints, the shelter of the godly, in which the righteous dwell, and indeed all who escape punishment by fire.

How well our discussion is going, my friend! For my part, I would like the exercise to go on through as many other demonstrations as we have. For to love to know richly what leads to our benefit I would count worth everything.

Indeed, Palladius, what you say is fitting. The thing would be the fruit of a mind as eager to learn as can be, and my discourse will be better than hesitation, since it does not seem right to me to practise an untimely silence that would creep in upon such splendid and lovely narratives. So then: that we must sever ourselves entirely and in every way, as far as possible, from any inclination toward or fellowship with what is base; and moreover, that the ability to look up toward virtue could come about in no other way than by this very means—this we shall see without effort if we turn the eye of the mind carefully both to the story of the godlike Abraham and to the things accomplished beyond all reason at the exodus of the Israelites, which they made in their time when they broke the bonds of Egyptian oppression.
Then explain it part by part. For be assured that you will delight us greatly if you choose to do this.

We were saying, then, that the godlike Abraham, once hard pressed by an unbearable famine and by the lack of necessities, went down into Egypt unwillingly and yielded to necessity. And because he was a stranger and a newcomer, Pharaoh mistreated him with vexations and oppression. For, inflamed by unrestrained pleasures and longing for shameful deeds, he wanted to take from him the woman who lived with him. But God did not allow him to accomplish this. For he afflicted Pharaoh, it says, with great afflictions because of Sarah, Abraham's wife. Pharaoh is an image and type of diabolical incontinence. For the devil's aim, and the object of his greatest zeal, is to sow the seeds of the impurity within him even in the minds of the saints, so that they may choose to bear fruit that is dear and pleasing to him. And these, I think, would be the offences that lead into sin of every kind. Anyone at all might be caught, and will be subjected to his oppressions against his will, for nature suffers from feebleness; yet God by no means permits it, but in a way reins in the attempts against the saints and the plots of the evil one. And it turned out that the godlike Abraham escaped harm in no other way than by leaving the land of the Egyptians and returning to the original, God-given place, where on his arrival he devoted himself at leisure to the care of good pursuits. It is written thus: "Abraham went up out of Egypt, he and his wife and all that was his, and Lot with him, into the desert. Now Abraham was very rich in livestock and silver and gold. And he went back to where he had come from, into the desert as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been before, between Bethel and Ai, to the place of the altar which he had made there at the beginning. And there Abraham called upon the name of the Lord." Do you understand, then, that those who hurry away from worldly incontinence to another, holy life must take with them, so to speak, everything that is theirs? For our forefather Abraham fled from the land of the Egyptians with his whole household and his whole family—and I would add, with all his goods. For we must depart completely and be willing, as it were, to move with our whole household into the desert, that is, into an undisturbed and pure state of mind, from which human nature also went out at the beginning, when through want of the goods from above it declined toward the worse. This is what the descent among foreigners would signify in a riddle: a departure from the land, so to speak, and from the original and most beloved tent, in which there was also an altar. For when we run back in this way until we come to the place and region of the original altar—that is, of the holiness that was natural to us of old—we too call upon the God of all, saying that prophetic address: "Lord, besides you we know no other; we name your name."
Very elegantly said.

You would see that the matter holds no differently for us if you also carefully examine what happened to the sons of Israel in their time. The Egyptians, having got them into their power after famine had first driven them down there—men descended from saints, from the root upward, and free men—yoked them to a servitude unexpected and unfamiliar to them and oppressed them savagely, having contrived some such pretext for their cruelty toward them as this: "There arose," it says, "another king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. And he said to his nation: Behold, the race of the sons of Israel is a great multitude and stronger than we are. Come, let us deal craftily with them, lest they multiply, and, whenever war breaks out, they too join our enemies, and after fighting against us go out of the land." For it grieved the ruler of the land of the Egyptians, I think, that those held by a forced bond, yoked against their will, might ever choose even to look toward freedom. "And he set over them," it says, "overseers of the works, to afflict them with their labours, and they built strong cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses and On, which is Heliopolis." For the fruits of that unbearable oppression were endless miseries over clay and brickmaking, cities fortified with walls, and the raising of earthworks in the fields; and all this was carried out by the labourers without pay and with long sweat. For the world-rulers of this age, having taken the wretched souls of men under their hand, wear them out with clay and brickmaking and with things done on the earth and concerned with the earth; and binding them to an evil and profitless trial (for such appear to be the works of the flesh and what concerns it), they force them to accept a bitter and utterly toilsome life, which will in no way bring any benefit to those compelled to pursue it. For how will the works and passions of the flesh help our wretched soul? Rather, it will be laid up by us as gain for the devil and the demons, and will be the wealth and boast of the kingdom of our adversaries—just as Pharaoh, no doubt, thought it brought him no small glory that the Israelites, compelled to it without food and without pay, built cities for him.
So it is. And indeed the account is very clear.

The labour of the Israelites, then, sets down for us a representation and, as it were, a clear image of our vain and unholy pursuits on earth, with Satan himself and the evil powers with him pressing upon us and assailing us; these the divine Scripture signifies by the name of taskmasters. This, for my part, I would call the evil distraction, full of sweat and toil, and filled, as it were, with clay and impurity and miry pleasure. But even then God had pity on those who were so impiously and savagely mistreated by the oppressions of the Egyptians and enslaved against all right. For he at once made the most excellent Moses the minister of his gentleness toward them. Or shall we not find God doing this for us too? For when we have slipped into sins, he grants us mercy, and at once places his own law in the hearts of all, as a mediator, so to speak, leading us back to a free life.
I understand what you mean.
Shall we, then, cut short the breadth of the story and say what is fitting as far as we can?
By all means.

It is written thus: "And after this Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Send my people away, that they may keep a feast to me in the desert. And Pharaoh said: Who is he, that I should listen to his voice and send away the sons of Israel? I do not know the Lord, and I will not send Israel away." Moses and Aaron insisted that Israel must be released from the country and land of the Egyptians, since God was calling them to a feast. For it is truly a real feast to cast off the yoke of unwilling slavery, and thereafter to be under God and to do what pleases him, with no one opposing, or forcing one to prefer and love what seems good to himself instead. But Pharaoh speaks with wholly unbridled tongue and is insolent toward the glory of God, saying both that he does not know who the Lord is and that he will not release Israel. Yet the godlike Moses by no means gives up, but firmly insists that what God has decided must be carried out. For when Satan hinders those who were under him from going out to freedom, they must play the man and rise above every obstacle, I think, and least of all be seen to be cowards, but press on, saying: "The God of the Hebrews has called us. So we will go a three days' journey into the desert to sacrifice to our God, lest death or slaughter meet us." For this is what the wise Moses cried out then on our behalf. "We Hebrews," he says, "do not, like you Egyptians, revere a calf, nor a pig or a goat, nor the statue of a man, nor the outlines of birds and the images of reptiles that are set up in shrines. But the God and Master who fashioned this whole universe has called us." Great, then, is the God of the Hebrews, not to be ranked with the gods of the Egyptians, and above all creation, who calls us into the desert to offer him there the sacrifice that is pleasing to him. Now Egypt is interpreted as "darkness," and I think that we who are spiritual must approach spiritually what is set out in shadow and types. For we must withdraw thoroughly, I think, from everything that is wont to darken us, and, as people who have left a country lying under the tyrant—I mean Satan—namely the easy slide into sin, we must hasten vigorously to move over to a free and purer life and to travel the road of a lawful way of life that is not subject to demons. For then we shall be able to offer the fruits of righteousness to God as we should.
