And he insisted that the Israelites must set out on a three days' journey into the desert, showing by this that they must not be near the borders of wickedness and of a life under tyranny. The godlike Moses also puts forward a wise pretext, and with very good reason says that those called by God must withdraw from Egypt: "lest death," he says, "or slaughter meet us."
And what does that mean? For it is not easy to grasp, even for those who want to understand.

I will explain. It was a custom of the Egyptians, and it is kept to this day among idol-worshippers, that those who enter temples must avoid coming upon a dead body. For they say that it is the greatest defilement not only to touch one, should anyone choose to, but even merely to happen upon such a sight. So, on the basis of their own customs, he persuades them to believe that they could not sacrifice in purity if, just as they began to do so, a corpse or a slaying should unexpectedly meet them from somewhere—that is, someone who had died by the law of nature or someone violently killed by murderers. "For you," he said, "have temples and sacred precincts, bars and gates, and once you have run inside them you can sacrifice purely, as you yourselves suppose; but we must sacrifice in the middle of the city, at crossroads and in the fields, and be defiled by the sight of the dead. For there is nothing at all to shut them out by boundaries." The literal account, then, would have its plausibility from the customs of the Egyptians; but what the all-wise Moses said would be rightly said even if it were understood spiritually. For we must sacrifice as in a desert and keep a holy feast to God, departing from the land of the Egyptians, and we must avoid the sight of death. For with a mind at leisure and far removed from worldly darkness, and turning our eye away from what leads to deadness and corruption, we shall sacrifice purely to God who rules over all. Dead works would be the works of the flesh. And worldly darkness is the clouding that comes from evil and vain distractions, defiling the pure and clear air of the mind. That those who wish to worship sincerely ought to keep well away from these things, the literal account also persuades us.
Indeed, this is not unclear. So carry on with what comes next for me.

An unbearable and sharp longing, I think, for their ancient freedom came upon the Israelites; and since they had already inclined toward it, they terribly provoked to anger the one who held them bound under the yoke of slavery. Saying that desires for such things were the product of idleness, he orders that the sweat of their labours be increased: the customary quota was demanded without delay, while the allowance of straw was cut off from them, contrary to custom. For he said: "You are idle, you are idlers; that is why you say, Let us go and sacrifice to our God. Now then, go and work; for straw will not be given you, and you yourselves shall deliver the quota of bricks." So the scribes of the sons of Israel saw that they were in trouble, being told: "You shall not fall short of the daily due of bricks." "And they met Moses and Aaron, who were coming to meet them as they came out from Pharaoh, and said to them: May God look upon you and judge, because you have made our smell abominable before Pharaoh and before his servants, so as to put a sword into his hands to kill us." Or do you not say, my dear friend, that it is true that when someone chooses to throw off the yoke of the devil's oppression and to take up instead the splendid and free glory of the worship of God, to be at leisure and to know the true Master, according to what is sung in the Psalms—"Be still and know that I am the Lord God"—the enemy of all will accuse us of this leisure and will as though it were something unholy, and will rise up, together with the other evil and unclean spirits, savagely compelling us to cling unceasingly to fleshly and earthy impurity and to the things of the world, according to each one's habit, and least of all permitting us to abstain from our familiar wickedness, yet making even this hard to come by, so that the evil may not, through being all too readily available, be spat out and lead to satiety? This, I think, is what is meant by vigorously demanding the quota of bricks while taking away the means by which it could easily be produced, that is, the straw. For we are somehow so made that we seek what we are accustomed to most eagerly and vigorously, and burn for it with hotter desires, precisely when something appears in between that keeps us, as if by necessity, from being able to obtain it. And when the divine law is re-educating the human mind away from more shameful things, then above all a great longing creeps in, calling it back to those same things and all but persuading it to cry out against the lawgiver. Of this, again, the scribes of the sons of Israel are a demonstration, as in shadows: worn out by the work and seeing no easy way to accomplish it. For they were short of straw, and they bitterly blamed Moses and Aaron for the charge brought against them, saying that these men had been the cause, and that they were enduring a heavier assault of oppression for no other reason than that a longing for freedom had come upon them, persuaded by their words.
Don't you think this is fitting and true?

Entirely so, Palladius. For as soon as a good desire and a good thought stir us, perhaps, to choose what pleases God, and we call to mind the law that leads to piety, the enemy of all, whose nature it is to do harm, chokes us all the more cruelly; but God rescues and saves. And so he said to Moses: "Go, speak to the sons of Israel, saying: I am the Lord, and I will bring you out from the domination of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from their slavery, and I will redeem you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment, and I will take you as a people for myself. And I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the domination of the Egyptians." For while Satan turns us away, rises up against every good desire, and pushes aside our inclinations toward it by whatever means he can, the law of God urges us on toward a good will, showing that our helper cannot be broken, sharpening us to courage with the richest hope, strengthening us with faith, and committing us to God, who is truly our saviour and redeemer.
What a most excellent and saving thing faith is, and a thirst to follow God!

You are right. And that faith moves toward a good end you will know well as our discourse reaches its proper goal. When Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh again to speak with him, intending to persuade him to release Israel from the land of the Egyptians and free them from their long-standing bonds, they wanted to shame him into compliance with signs beyond reason. They displayed the transformation of a staff into a serpent, and they plainly announced that through God they could very readily accomplish even greater and more surpassing things. But he ordered his own magicians to do the same, all but crying out by this: "We are not ignorant of such works. There are far more of them among the Egyptians than among you; and working wonders is the business of magicians, among whom you too are numbered." But since he was utterly hardened and would not release Israel, four terrible plagues were brought upon him, each worse than the last. Water was miraculously changed into blood, and frogs and gnats, and finally the dog-fly, at last made Pharaoh somewhat softer, as though under unbearable necessity. Calling Moses and Aaron, he says: "Go in and sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land." "And Moses said: It cannot be done so; for we shall be sacrificing the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God. If we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God before their eyes, we shall be stoned. We will go a three days' journey into the desert and sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he told us. And Pharaoh said: I will send you away, and you shall sacrifice to the Lord your God in the desert; only do not go very far away." For against Satan, who opposes us and has resolved to fight stubbornly against our eagerness for the good, God raises up his own hatred of evil; he chokes him in his insolence and tames him with blows. Then Satan barely gives way, and unwillingly; yet even so he tries to persuade us to offer God a worship that is not exact, and not yet to depart completely from slavery to him. For he ordered the Jews to sacrifice not outside his own land but within it. But Moses very wisely says: "It cannot be done so." For the inventor of sin is always the one who proposes evil things; but the divine law sends them away and forbids doing whatever seems good to him. Therefore those who wish to live rightly must pay attention, not to what the Evil One says to deceive them, but to what the divine oracle proclaims to us. For "your law," it says, "is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths."
True.

So when the Evil One holds us fast, that is, when he wants to shut us in and bring us under his power, we must worship the God who alone is God by nature. Let us go as far as we can from double-mindedness and say, "It cannot be done so." For no one can serve two masters: either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. And again it is written, "Woe to cowardly hearts and slack hands, and to the sinner who walks on two paths." For my part I say that we must offer pure and blameless worship to God who rules over all, having left the worship that is under the Evil One completely behind, and in this way seek to go on nobly toward what is better. Besides, "We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God," he says. "For if we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians before their eyes, we shall be stoned." As far as the historical account goes, the excuse is well founded. Here he calls the objects of worship "abominations," and what the Egyptians worshipped were calves. "If we sacrifice these to the God of the Hebrews," he says, "we shall stir the Egyptians to anger in every possible way, since they will find it unbearable." The argument is plausible enough. But taken as spiritual contemplation, it offers no small benefit. For when we put to death what the host of demons most honours, values highly and counts worthy of all regard, we offer God the most pleasing worship.
What do you mean?
Are the passions of the flesh not precious to them? This is not for the passions' own sake, of course, but because through them we perish and are bound fast in slavery under the demons.
True.

If we put these passions to death and, as it were, slaughter them, we shall be a fragrant aroma to God. Paul writes as follows: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, well-pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship." A person would do this rightly by putting to death the members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness. Each of the passions in us, then, is an abomination of the spiritual Egyptians, that is, something they hold most sacred. God shows that divine Scripture customarily calls whatever stands in the place of an idol an "abomination," as a kind of object of worship, when he says through the voice of Jeremiah concerning the synagogue of the Jews: "Why has the beloved committed abomination in my house?" But if someone wanted to take "abomination of the Egyptians" to mean what they hate and reject, he would not stray from the fitting sense. For the things the unclean spirits always hate and abhor will be offered by us to God as a fragrant aroma and a spiritual sacrifice: faith, gentleness, self-control, temperance, love for one another, and the glories of sincere devotion to God.
And who would be those who sacrifice in the Evil One's land? And who should be understood as those outside the land?

Those who have not yet gone out of Egypt and sacrifice to God within it are very many, perhaps beyond number. Those outside it and in the desert are very few and chosen. For "many are called," it says, "but few are chosen." We have all been called to freedom through faith in Christ, and we have been redeemed from the devil's tyranny. It was Christ who carried us off to this freedom, and he was fittingly prefigured for the people of old in Moses and Aaron, so that you may understand that Emmanuel, in the divine plan of salvation, is lawgiver, high priest and apostle all at once. But most of those who have been called still cling fondly to their old evils. In their minds they have not yet wholly left worldly deceit behind, and so they worship God by bare faith alone. These, we say, are the ones who sacrifice in Egypt, or who have gone only a little way outside it. For hard-hearted Pharaoh says, "You shall not go far, even if you run out of the land of Egypt." But those who wish to please God by turning completely to the good, and who are entirely free of worldly confusion, are carried out of Egypt and escape the tyrant's hand. As if in the desert, in a life of quiet and freedom, they offer pure sacrifice to God, being pure themselves. I would also put it another way. Those who are running toward the truth, away from worshipping the creation rather than the Creator, and who have been called to the knowledge of him who is God by nature, must go as far as possible from the land of Egypt. For those who have not yet scrubbed the remnants of the ancient deceit from their minds have not yet gone out completely. Some observe days and months and seasons and years. Although these people have been called through Christ to the dignity of freedom, they still live in Egypt and sacrifice to God there, keeping up a way of life that Satan would not dislike. But if someone goes out completely and bids farewell to the older customs, he sacrifices in the desert and pursues a life worthy of all praise.
I agree, for you understand rightly. But let our discussion resume its course.

Well then, Pharaoh lies and goes back on his promise, and he still does not release the Israelites. He was then tormented by three more plagues and barely gives his consent, saying he will let them go, and again he was caught lying. For he is a liar and does not stand in the truth, as the Saviour says. God threatens the Egyptians with a most violent hail and then actually sends it on them, and the locust as well, the "ravager of fields," if we may borrow a word from the Greeks too. Then, and only then, and barely, the shield-bearers of Pharaoh's loathsome wickedness, who had earlier been so fierce and unbreakable, raise a great outcry against him, saying: "How long will this be a snare to us? Send the men away, so that they may serve the Lord their God. Or do you want to find out that Egypt is ruined?" From this it occurs to me once again that Satan is perhaps "superior" to the powers under him in those things where it would suit him to win. For they, it seems, are very hard and utterly implacable, yet late and barely they still come to some modest sense of God's wrath. He, however, surpasses them in a savagery beyond all reason and is hardened to the utmost. For it is written: "His heart is set like stone, and he stands like an anvil that cannot be beaten." So when a great outcry had been raised against him, he reluctantly said to Moses and Aaron: "Go and serve the Lord your God. But who are the ones who will go?" And Moses says: "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and daughters, and with our sheep and cattle, for it is the feast of the Lord our God." And he said to them: "May the Lord be with you, as surely as I am sending you away! And your household too? See that evil is before you. Not so; let the men go, and serve God, for that is what you yourselves are asking." Notice then, my friend, that Moses said the departure must be made in the best way, but Pharaoh says, "Not so." He said he would release them only in part, and that the rest, along with the household itself, must stay behind in Egypt as a kind of hostage to guarantee that those departing would return. "Let every young man of yours go," he says, "every one in his prime." But the divine Moses firmly insists that they must leave with no one overlooked: those in youth and those in the decline of life together, sons and daughters, herds of cattle and other livestock. For indeed those who are eager to lay claim to true freedom ought to be glad to be rid of the evils in the world and to travel the path of virtue. They must leave behind no remnant whatever of their soul and mind, through which they might once again be dragged under the Evil One's greed. The divine law calls to this young men and maidens, old men with younger ones, as the Psalmist says, and every kind of age as it is understood in Christ. The inspired John also addressed these, saying: "I have written to you, children, because you know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one." They could also be understood in another way: the young men as a type of courage, the old men of prudence, and the sons and daughters of the childlikeness that is understood in Christ. For with courage and prudence and godly simplicity we shall depart from sin into holiness. "Be courageous," it says, "and let your heart be strong." And again: "Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves." And when he says that the sheep and cattle should go along with them, I think he indicates that we must not abandon to Satan even the bodily and more irrational of our impulses. Indeed the inspired Paul writes: "For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness."
Why then does Pharaoh release those in their youth and prime, but lay claim to the others?
Who do you say were the ones who stayed in Egypt?
They were, I suppose, the women of course, the children not yet grown, the feeble old men, and the livestock.
Then, my excellent friend, how is it that you do not see the point at once?
What point do you mean?

Those who are vigorous and young, whose disposition toward godliness is more robust, he regards as a burden. He is eager, I think, though against his will, to be rid of those who stand against him, since they are able to fight back and defend themselves when wronged, according to the saying, "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." But he lays a strong claim to whatever is not by nature inclined to courage, as a feeble and unwarlike kind. He loves a mind that is sick within itself, womanish and soft, as if past its prime and without strength, or still childish, and he loves what is gross and more irrational, as symbolized by cattle and sheep.
Well said.

Once again the hard-minded and unbending Pharaoh lies. Then, when the swarms of locusts had devoured almost their whole country, so to speak, he sends for Moses, and Aaron comes in with him, and he says: "Go, serve the Lord your God; only leave your sheep and cattle behind, and let your household go with you." And Moses said: "No, you too shall give us whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, which we will offer to the Lord our God. Our livestock shall go with us, and we shall not leave a hoof behind, for from them we shall take what we need to serve the Lord our God."
And what meaning should we attach to these words of the all-wise Moses? Or how could someone take things from Egypt and from Pharaoh and dedicate them to God?

Indeed, my friend, the meaning is clear. The one who opposes and fights those who wish to live godly lives, if he cannot have some people wholly subject to him, wants at least to have them in part. But the law of God teaches us to make the sharpest possible break, by no means allowing anything to lie and remain under his power: no part of the soul or of the mind, and no occasion for bodily impulse. It teaches, further, that we must also bring to God the finest and choicest things of life in the world. This, I think, is what taking from Egypt and sacrificing to God signifies. Or is this not what is done by those who use worldly wisdom to fight for our holy and divine doctrines, pursuing brilliance of style and sharpness of knowledge, and so offering God their spiritual worship? For all wisdom is from the Lord, as it is written. Yet we say that the poets and prose writers of the Greeks attained such brilliance of eloquence in a worldly spirit. Indeed the inspired Paul says: "We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might understand the things freely given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit." Moses, while he was still among the shadows, truly said that the choice things of life in the world would not be rejected by him who is God by nature, and he immediately shows this clearly, though only in type and shadow. For when God commanded them to plunder the Egyptians, Moses said that they must borrow gold and silver vessels from the people they lived with and from their neighbours, and this was carried out through the women. For women are always somehow given to whispering and great talkers, and they are clever at deception. The gold and silver vessels taken from the Egyptians would be, I think, as I said just now, the things in which some people in the world would naturally pride themselves, even if they had come to know the true God. What I mean is again something like this. The impulses of mind and soul are common to all human beings, as is the capacity for anything at all, good or evil. Those who use the advantages of nature well achieve a glorious and outstanding life. But those who very foolishly turn them aside to improper ends somehow debase the goods of nature and walk the most shameful path. Courage and prudence are good for those who use them best, but harmful to those who do not possess them rightly. One can be courageous and prudent and win praise and applause; but one can also have these same qualities and draw great outcry. These qualities are common and found in everyone, both in those still in error and in those who know God. So when courage, which was once a worker of wickedness, and keenness of understanding are turned by us to what pleases God, they will become holy and acceptable to God, as though taken from the Egyptians and from life in the world. For they are reshaped for the service of virtue and the ministry of holiness, just as the gold and silver vessels from Egypt proved useful for building and completing the holy tabernacle. After they had plundered the Egyptians, and after the death of the firstborn, the Israelites were at last redeemed, having sacrificed the lamb as a type of Christ. There was no other way to obtain such a thing, since all redemption is in Christ, and through him comes every good gift. They are sent out of Egypt at midnight, as if they were being freed from darkness and slavery at the same time. For slavery to sin always tends to exist in spiritual darkness, and not in the divine light. "Everyone who does evil hates the light," as the Saviour says. The dough is carried out unleavened, and they flee without provisions. "For the Egyptians pressed the people," it says, "to send them out of the land in haste, for they said, 'We are all dying.' And the people took up their dough before it was leavened, with their kneading bowls bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders." For I do not think that those who are about to cleave to God and who have chosen to belong to him should carry along any remnant of worldly wickedness. Nor should they be supplied with foreign and unholy food, meaning, clearly, spiritual food. Their bread should be unleavened, which signifies that from now on they desire him who gives life to the world. Such people would keep the feast purely, and by offering the worship acceptable to God they remain under him for ever.

It is settled, then, that those who love God and are good must reach the life that is under Christ and free from tyranny, as though it were a holy and sacred land. And they must hasten to sacrifice not in the land of their enemies, that is, not while they are in a state that loves sin and is far from blameless, but rather in eagerness for virtue, with a settled character that has been banished from the devil's tyranny.

Do not suppose it to be otherwise than this, my good friend, for our argument has been made rightly. But if you like, we may also consider these things through another image. The inhabitants of the holy city, I mean Jerusalem, dared to grieve God, the Saviour of all, by running off into every kind of outrage. So they came under the hand of the Babylonians, who took them as captives of war and ordered them to serve, for they had no choice but to yield to their masters, even against their will. Greatly distressed, and lamenting their unexpected misfortunes, they sometimes sought to find at least a little relief from their suffering. This relief was to dull the sharpness of the grief within them by singing hymns to God. "I remembered God and was glad," said the divine David, showing that singing hymns to God is a spiritual feast. But those who wanted to sing and keep up their custom somehow felt it shameful to let so sweet a sound enter the ears of foreigners, and to throw their sweetest and most melodious song to the winds, as it were, while the Babylonians sometimes mocked them and were thoroughly annoyed by songs accompanied by instruments. Therefore they said: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion." In Zion, according to the laws and customs of the Jews, the sacrifice of praise was offered with strings and instruments, charming with its melodies those who came to the divine temple. But since they were bound fast under a foreign yoke of slavery, they lament and say: "On the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments," thereby indicating that they had given up singing. For the willow is a fruitless plant, or rather one that loses its fruit; that is what it is called by the [?] of the Greek poets. So the instruments of song were set aside for idleness and fruitlessness, and they cry out the reason for this inactivity, saying: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" And when Baruch brought them the words of Jeremiah, "they all wept," it says, "and fasted and prayed before the Lord. And they collected money, as much as each one could afford, and sent it to Jerusalem to Joakim the priest, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, and to the priests and to all the people who were found with him in Jerusalem." And after some other things: "And they said: Here we are sending you money. With the money buy burnt offerings and sin offerings and incense, and prepare grain offerings, and offer them on the altar of the Lord our God." For they thought it fitting that they themselves should no longer sacrifice, since they had been banished from the holy land and for the time being no longer lived under God, but were yoked, as it were, to another and had fallen into a tyrant's hands. Instead they assigned the worship to those who still lived in the holy city and had been allotted the honour of the sacred ministry. In this they clearly reasoned rightly in considering what was fitting and necessary. And the most wise Daniel himself held to his sacred pursuits, yet, being a captive along with the others, he found a wise way around the constraint. I will tell you how. He prayed three times a day, but the windows of his upper room faced and opened toward Jerusalem; for so it is written. For he thought his prayer would hardly be acceptable to God unless, even if he perhaps could not do so in the flesh, he at least withdrew in thought from that foreign and hateful land, and, looking with the eyes of the mind toward the land most dear to God, offered his prayer for whatever he wished as though he had entered the temple itself.
Excellent! Our whole argument has truly been brought to completion.

That it is impossible to escape the death that comes from sin, and the grasping greed of the devil, except through the sanctification that is in Christ; and that justification is not in the law, but in Christ.

Our discussion, Palladius, and no mean one, has shown that we ought to love keeping ourselves away from what by nature does harm, and ought to aspire to service under God, since it is both glorious and profitable.
Quite so.
And we firmly established that, once we have turned away completely from what is shameful, it is fitting for us to seek what is better.
Certainly.

It then seemed to follow that we must put the pleasure-loving life of the world, and the turmoil that goes with it, as far from us as possible, and hasten to dedicate ourselves to God. Having entered, as it were, a wilderness in the disposition of our minds, we must offer him a worship that is free from distraction and wholly pure, one that defilement cannot reach, a worship that is beautiful and acceptable to him.
Yes, that was our view.

And did it not become clear from countless examples that, while Satan in his greed was shutting us up under himself and trying to keep us in his grip, the divine law was calling us to the dignity of freedom? It set its teaching about what is best against his abominations and trained us toward better things.
True.

God, then, is the giver of salvation and the ruler over all our well-being, and he shows us the way to intimacy with himself, with Christ as mediator. For would not the mediation through Moses be a type, and a very clear one, of the mediation through Christ?
In what way?

The inspired Moses brought Israel out of bodily slavery and rescued them from the labor of brickmaking and from work on the land. Standing as a kind of go-between for God and men, he carried to them the words from above. But our Lord Jesus Christ, who recasts into truth what was given in types and shadows, draws us out of spiritual slavery. He drives out the sin that had long tyrannized over us and overthrows the devil's power. He persuades those who think they must follow him to abandon an earthly mind and the pursuits of the flesh, and he reshapes them, as it were, toward the desire for virtue. And he announces to us with perfect clarity the will of God the Father. That is why he said, "The words that I speak are not mine, but his who sent me." And again, "I do not speak on my own; the Father who sent me has himself given me a command about what to say and what to speak." Indeed, Moses presented his own role as an image and outline of the mediation in Christ when he said to the Israelites, "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, on the day of the assembly." So what came through Moses, and the power of his mediation, existed as a type and an image, but the manner of the mediation in Christ is more ineffable. Moses was a servant of the law and the shadow, and a bearer of instruction from above; Christ, as Lord of the law and the prophets, lays down whatever laws he pleases. And he was mediator because in him divinity and humanity run together and, as it were, come into one, for both together are understood to be Christ. Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, but Christ as a son over his own house, and we are his house, we who through faith in him have been led to true freedom. It stands firm, then, that the sacred teacher Moses was the mediator of a fleshly freedom, of the letter and the shadow, whereas our Lord Jesus Christ introduced what is beyond the law and grants a freedom incomparably better than the fleshly kind, namely freedom according to the Spirit. That is why he said even to the Israelites, who had been freed in the flesh, "If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free." And again, "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed."
You have put it excellently.
Let us boast, then, not in what is splendid according to the flesh, but in what is in the Spirit and in the righteousness that is according to Christ, not the righteousness according to the law.

For if whatever is under sin is still enslaved, and the law, far from justifying, rather condemns and records people as transgressors, how could it fail to be clear to everyone that all justification is in Christ, and that perfection in the Spirit through sanctification comes through him and in him? So the most wise Paul writes, "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" And he records the uselessness and powerlessness of the old law in these words: "Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for 'the righteous shall live by faith.' But the law is not of faith; rather, 'the one who does them shall live by them.'" In Christ, then, we are justified through faith, and we have been redeemed from spiritual slavery.
Is the law useless, then?

That is not what I am saying. It was not proclaimed in vain; rather, it was given as a help, as it is written. Insofar as it served for instruction, for knowing what is wrong, and for receiving the first principles and elements of God's oracles, how could it not be considered useful? But it is too feeble to wash away sin and to bring people to perfection in sanctification. So the inspired Paul told us, "Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no flesh will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin." The law, then, points out sin; it does not procure the glories of virtue. For to say, for instance, "You shall not commit fornication, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not swear falsely," and whatever else belongs with these, is to mark out the kinds of wickedness and to remove impurity, not to bring in the knowledge of virtue or to make the knowledge of a genuine life fully plain to the hearers. To count merely not doing shameful things among the ways of an exceptional life would be, I think, ignorant. Rather, I think, and with very good reason, that we can hardly be crowned with the verdict that belongs to all things praiseworthy unless we let go of evil, thrust it away, and leave it somewhere below, since it is not free from the suspicion of wickedness and profane abomination, and leap up to the very glories of virtue. So our Lord Jesus Christ says, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." You understand, then, that the Savior has commanded us to choose a righteousness beyond that according to the law. Knowing this to be the best thing, the wise Paul writes, "If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless. But whatever gain I had, I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus our Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ."

I understand, for the argument is clear. But tell me this: if the old law is not sufficient for perfection, why was righteousness through faith, and the sanctification that goes with it, not ordained for us at the beginning instead?

Because, my friend, I would say, it is what is dirty that is properly washed, what is stained that is scrubbed clean, and what is darkened that is made bright. And it would be fitting, I think, in keeping with the Savior's words, that it is the sick who are healed, and that those called to repentance are not the sanctified but those weighed down by their sins. Must not those who are called to forgiveness first be condemned, and those endangered by the weakness within them then be seen to be redeemed? So it was necessary for the law that points out sin to appear first, as a kind of reproof and exact accuser of the weakness of all, so that the greatness of the divine gentleness shown to us through Christ might not go unrecognized. For where or how could there be the grace of forgiveness if there were no charges laid? And if I may be brief and jump back to some ancient narratives, I will say again that God promised Abraham the grace that comes through faith; and in him, as the firstfruits of those who have received mercy, he made forgiveness out of gentleness older than the law. For it is written, "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." And Paul adds his testimony, saying, "How then was it counted? While he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not while circumcised, but while uncircumcised. He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith that he had while still uncircumcised." And he clearly heard God say, "In you all the nations shall be blessed." "In you" would mean "after your likeness." Paul understood it this way when he said, "And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.' So then those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith." Circumcision, then, is a sign of the faith he had while uncircumcised; he was not justified by works of the law, and the glories that come through faith are shown to be older than circumcision in the flesh. For he was called the friend of God.
Then I might fairly raise this difficulty: what was the reason for the delay of sanctification by faith? Why, I mean, was the sign set in the earlier place and the superior thing in the second?

Did we not say just now that it was the work of an admirable and ineffable skill that the condemning law should spring up in time before the justifying faith? Or does not the light shine in the darkness, and is not power made perfect in weakness, as it is written?
You are right.

So the law came in so that the trespass might increase. For where there is no law, there is no transgression either. And how could anyone see forgiveness for transgression and for the ease with which we fall into it, if the law had not first condemned us? Paul will support me in showing that what I say is true, and that the argument on this point is neither faded nor without beauty, when he says, "Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels." Being very wise, he sometimes tries to cut off in advance the quibbles and objections that some would raise. For it was likely that some would find fault with the delay of righteousness in faith and would say that the law's slipping in between had come about to annul that ancient promise. So he says, "Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed to us. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian, for you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus." And he clears up the difficulty, as it were, by adding very aptly, "This is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise." So the law, having shut us up under sin, trained us for Christ, for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets. That is why he said to the Jewish people who disobeyed him, "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me." So we are justified not by works of the law but rather by faith in Christ. "For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, 'Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, and do them.'" But Christ redeemed everyone from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree"—so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
But, my good friend, if you agree, let us go on instead to some other point of Christ's teaching, for this is enough about the law and its dispensation.
Then tell me whatever you like, as long as it is not entirely beyond my power to answer.

The question is not too steep or untrodden, and what we are looking for will, I think, be found quite effortlessly, since Christ puts the divine light into us. Shall we not, then, we who have received justification by faith and have set aside worship in shadows and types, honor God with bloodless offerings?

You are right. For it is written, "Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and give him the firstfruits of your fruits of righteousness." For with such sacrifices God is well pleased, according to the words of the saints.

Then it is pointless to be eager to sacrifice oxen and to carry out what was brought in for us by the ancient commandment. Slaughtered sheep and incense, and cakes as well, fine flour mixed with oil, turtledoves and pigeons: these were the offerings of worshipers in that age. But tell me why God did not reject these things from the beginning, and why he is now seen to legislate for the things in which he delights and to reveal to us the forms of spiritual sacrifice.

Do you really think, and dare to say, that the Divine made a wrong decision at the beginning, and, having missed, as it were, what is perfectly good, only barely managed to find the greater thing? Or that he chose the things in shadows then, as fully satisfying what pleased him, but in our time came to suffer a fondness for novelty, so that he shifted his preference to other things and invented for us a worship not recognized long ago?

Not at all. That, I think, is nonsense. I would never suppose that the capacity to err in any way at all could belong to him. But I would be very glad to learn what moved him to give those laws to the people on earth then, and these now.

Your question forces us, as it were, to go back again. Did I not say that the law was a tutor, that is, the instructor of those still infants and of those not yet able to understand what is truly good? And that it hinted in riddles at what the will of God is, the perfect and well-pleasing will, still marking it out, as it were, in crude types? You will know, you will know, and without much sweat, the nature of spiritual worship: that it was always, even from the beginning, deeply desired by God, but still hard to approach and beyond the grasp of the souls of the Jews. For this reason they needed language suited to infants, simple lessons, and a carefully managed upbringing that had nothing steep or harsh about it. So God, in ancient times, legislated what was in types. Yet he also showed in advance that the things belonging to true worship would come and be present in their own times; and he rejected approach through blood, and the shadow, and he shook them off, saying through the prophet Amos, "I hate, I reject your feasts, and I will take no delight in your festal assemblies. For even if you offer me your burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not look on them. Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not listen to the melody of your instruments." And through Micah he introduced the persona of a man eager to learn how he might accomplish what is good without blame: "With what shall I come before the Lord, and lay hold of God Most High? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the Lord accept thousands of rams, or tens of thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my ungodliness, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" Then, directly following: "Has it not been told you, O man, what is good? And what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?" Is this not clearly what Christ said: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me"? And again, "Whoever loves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also." Worship according to Christ consists not in legal observance but in what is holy and spiritual.
You have spoken most rightly.

And through the voice of Isaiah he rebukes the Israelites more sharply, saying, "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah! What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs and goats. Nor should you come to appear before me, for who has required this from your hands? You shall no longer trample my courts. If you bring fine flour, it is vain; incense is an abomination to me. Your new moons and Sabbaths and the great day I cannot endure. Your fasting and rest and your feasts my soul hates; they have become a surfeit to me." And through the prophet Malachi he says the same thing to people who had become thoroughly hateful to him, and he mentions the times when those throughout the whole earth would offer him the incomparable fragrance of the bloodless and spiritual sacrifice. For he said this in turn: "I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty." You see that he says incense and a pure sacrifice will be offered to him from every nation. And just as, by calling the covenant given to us in Christ "new," he has made the first one old—for the inspired Paul writes this to us as well—so here too, by calling the sacrifice that would in due time come from every nation "pure," he passes judgment on the ancient one for not being so. For in what way could that be pure which neither cleanses nor has the power to bring to perfection in virtue? That is why the blessed Paul says that it was not faultless, and that what comes through Christ was necessarily brought in, and a place was sought for the second.
Is worship in shadows, then, entirely unwelcome to the all-holy God?

Entirely so. One can hear him clearly saying to the Israelites through the voice of Jeremiah, "Thus says the Lord: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the meat. For I did not speak to your fathers or command them on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Listen to my voice.'" As far as the lawgiver's precise wish was concerned, the law in shadows would never have been proclaimed at all at the beginning, with spiritual worship passed over in silence. But since the matter was burdensome, and the power to fulfill what is perfectly good was, for the people of that time, not merely beyond their reach but, I would say, hard and far from smooth, the written law was ordained by way of accommodation, as a kind of training suited to infants, containing the outline of the truth. Still, the One who fixed the laws for us made it plain that those things were not what pleased him most, but that what comes through Christ is what he deeply desires. Thus he said again, "Therefore I have cut down your prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment will go forth like light. For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings." For in God's eyes love for one's brothers, which is the fulfillment of the law, and the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ, through whom the Father himself becomes known to us, are far better than a falling calf and a slaughtered sheep. And no one could doubt that this brings eternal life, since Christ says to the Father in heaven, "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." And how can anyone doubt that the truth will prove true in every way and in every respect?
No one can.

Israel slipped away from its close relationship with him, since it did not accept the faith and did not know God. He says very plainly that it will not return to what it was at the beginning except through Christ alone, once it has given up the customs of the law. For again it is written: “For the sons of Israel will remain many days without altar, without priesthood, without manifestations; and afterward the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they will be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last of these days.” For when the full number of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved, but in Christ. He is called David because he is of the seed and of the tribe of David. That the sacrifices of the law themselves would also be abolished he affirmed clearly through Joel, saying: “Gird yourselves and lament, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar; go in, lie down in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering have been withheld from the house of your God.” And again through the same prophet: “Sacrifice and drink offering have been taken away from the house of the Lord; mourn, you priests who minister at the altar.” In addition to this, he promised that the tabernacle itself would also be removed, saying: “And it shall be, when you are multiplied and increased in the land, says the Lord, in those days they will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant of the Holy One of Israel’; it will not come to mind, nor will it be named, nor will it be visited, and it will not be made again.” For once the sacrifice that was still in types and through blood had been entirely overturned, it was in a way necessary that the tabernacle itself should also be removed, since a truer one had been raised up in its place, that is, the Church, of which Christ himself said: “Here I will dwell, for I have chosen it.” And that the manner of worship will pass over and be changed for the better, to the new worship in Christ, will be clear when Malachi writes to us about God: “And he will purify the sons of Levi, and pour them out like gold and like silver; and they will bring the Lord a sacrifice in righteousness, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God, as in the days of old and as in the former years.” So do you understand that he is saying there will be something very like a reforging and refashioning of both the priesthood and the sacrifices?
I understand.
For the words “he will pour out and purify,” spoken as though of gold and a goldsmith, are surely meant to lead us to this thought?
Certainly.

For that the Word, once he had become man, would accomplish something of this kind in a spiritual sense, God the Father has fully assured us when he said: “Suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he is coming, says the Lord Almighty. And who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears? For he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like the fullers’ herb. And he will sit smelting and purifying as silver and as gold.” So he is saying that there will be a renewal and a refashioning of the priesthood; and as for the manner of the service, he points to nothing other than the mystery of Christ. Again he spoke through the voice of Ezekiel about those to whom the priesthood had been allotted: “These will draw near to me to minister to me, and they will stand before my face to offer me sacrifice, fat and blood, says the Lord God. These will enter my holy places, and these will approach my table to minister to me.” And the fat and the blood and the ministrations at the table—would they not rightly be said to be the mystery of Christ?
You speak well.

God has also made perfectly plain to us the very time at which the change of all things for the better, the manner of the renewal, will take place, when he says: “And from the eighth day onward the priests will offer your whole burnt offerings and your peace offerings on the altar, and I will accept you, says the Lord.” By the eighth day he means the time of our Savior’s resurrection, at which the whole burnt offerings—that is, the complete and entire consecration of believers to God—are acceptable to God, a spiritual bringing of gifts. The divine Paul teaches this when he writes: “Through him, then, let us continually offer up to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.” And again: “Do not neglect to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.” For what other fruits could we who have been justified by faith offer to God than long and unceasing praise? And the purest sacrifice of a blameless life is a fragrance beyond compare.

Our argument stands very well, and it is true that a person is justified not at all by the law but rather through faith in Christ and the initiation of the gospel. But I would like you to take the explanation forward with clear examples as well, and to learn it from the sacred Scriptures themselves.

Well then, my friend, I am ready to do this, since you wish it. But you, in turn, must examine each of the points with your precise and finely polished mind. And if I seem to you not to understand or speak quite correctly, soberly correct me and clearly set me on a better course, imitating the best of carpenters, who, whenever the work in their hands departs from the proper measure, skillfully reshape it to what seems best. Let us make the blessed revealer of sacred things, Moses, a kind of starting point for our discussion of these matters. Touching briefly on his history, I will try to give full assurance and to show clearly that the law brought nothing to perfection and is not sufficient for salvation, but that Christ is the redeemer and savior of all.

You should know that you are conferring no small benefit, and in this too you show yourself above hesitation. For the matter in hand is very hard to grasp, and knowledge of what we are seeking is extremely difficult to discern; but God, who reveals it, is rich.

You speak well, and your words spur me on, like the keenest-scented hounds, to follow the trail of the deep and more hidden meanings. Once, then, in the desert of the land called Midian, when the blessed Moses was tending flocks of sheep and was at the very foothills of Mount Horeb, a strange and marvelous thing was shown to him as God brought it about. “An angel appeared to him,” it says, “in a flame of fire out of a bush; and he saw that the bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, ‘I will turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned up.’” Now the bush is not a cultivated tree; it is rather a kind of wild thorn, a plant rooted in the mountains, and on it the awe-inspiring miracle was performed, which very well fulfilled the type of a mystery. For the angel was there as if in the form of fire, consuming it through and through, yet giving the wood no sense of the fire’s working; it was as though he were not even there, since the wood did not share, so to speak, even a trace of heat such as fire gives.
What, then, does this mean?

Israel had become like a wild tree that bore no cultivated fruits of righteousness, for they were nourished on the laws of the Egyptians. The law that was to be given through angels was able to give light, if only it were understood spiritually, and to drive away the darkness from the mind, for this too is the working of fire. Yet it was of no benefit to those who received it. This was not at all the fault of the law itself, but because those to whom it was addressed did not receive the light into mind and heart; they possessed the letter outwardly as a mere semblance of illumination, and so what they thought they had they did not truly have. Therefore the fire being seen around the bush, while still giving the wood no sense of heat, points, as it seems to me, to something of this kind. That the light from the law proved of no benefit to the Jews the Savior himself will make clear when he says: “You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify about me. Yet you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have eternal life.” And again, a little later, to the teachers of the Jews and to all the people: “Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; your accuser is Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” For those who in their utter ignorance thrust away the elementary instruction given through the law, how could they receive Christ, who brings the knowledge of what is perfectly good? Seeing the bush burning yet not consumed, and not even yielding to the fire, the blessed Moses was astonished: why is the bush not burned up? For one might well be astounded at the complete insensibility of Israel. They received the law from God as a helper and ally and were enriched with the illumination it gave; then, counting the gift as worth nothing and not taking what had been given into mind and heart, they remained without benefit, for their mind was, fittingly, as it were dead and cold. One might rightly say of them too: “Why is the bush not burned up?” For otherwise they would have become, with us, fervent in spirit.
Well said.

The event also seems to suggest to us a not unlearned contemplation of other ideas. For the Israelites were now about to depart from the land of the Egyptians and, as never before, to shake off the yoke of their unwilling servitude, and for that reason to fall foul once more of the anger of the ruler. So God gave them as a sign what was happening at the bush: that they would prove far stronger even than fire itself and would not be caught by those able to do them wrong, in keeping, I think, with the words spoken in a manner worthy of God: “Do not fear, for I am with you. The flame will not burn you; rivers will not overwhelm you.”
An apt interpretation.

So Moses was amazed at the sight in this way, and he hurried forward, longing to come near. “When the Lord saw,” it says, “that he was coming near to look, he called to him from the bush, saying, ‘Moses, Moses.’ And he said, ‘What is it?’ ‘Do not come near here. Take the sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.’” Now the blessed Moses will be for us a type of the law, for “they have Moses and the prophets,” says the blessed Abraham in the sayings of the gospel. Does this statement seem implausible to you?
Not at all, for Moses represents the law.

Israel, then, has been called, the flock that lives according to the law and under the law. For “the Lord, the God of the Hebrews,” it says, “has called us.” And it obeyed God who called, just as Moses did: “All that the Lord God has said we will do, and we will obey.” But since the power of submission to the law is not sufficient for cleansing—for “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins”—Moses is prevented from approaching God. “Do not come near here,” it says. For the good is unapproachable through the law, and the power of the way of life according to Moses is quite insufficient to bring us to God. But Christ presents us to him through sanctification. For those who are eager to cleave to the holy God must be holy: “You shall be holy,” it says, “for I am holy.” And that the manner of life according to the law is not altogether blameless he taught at once, saying: “Take the sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” For he commanded Moses, the revealer of sacred things, to take the sandal off his foot, showing that the course of life under the law was not yet pure, nor entirely free from the works of corruption and deadness. The divine Moses was being instructed, through the custom of the Greeks, that it is not lawful for one who bears the remains of deadness and corruption to draw near to God. For they did not go into their temples wearing on their feet sandals made from dead animals; their laws recorded this as a kind of defilement. But it was not the law, my good friend, nor the course of life according to the letter of Moses, that freed us from deadness and corruption and from the impurity that comes from them, but rather faith in Christ and the most perfect cleansing of the gospel way of life. Or is what I say not true?
Of course it is.

When he had taken the sandal off his foot and then ran forward and came near, God addressed him: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. And Moses turned away his face,” it says, “for he was afraid to look before God.” For when we have put off the mindset of death and walk the road of the way of life in Christ, as it were with a clean and free foot, we will be near to God—in a spiritual relation, clearly, and not by distance in space. For the things of Moses were types and shadow. And so we will be enriched with the teachings of the heavenly initiation and gather within ourselves the knowledge of God, as the Father reveals himself to us in the Son. For we will see him, and incomparably better than the people of old did, represented as they were in the person of Moses. For he turned away his face, “for he was afraid to look before God.” By this is signified the weakness of understanding of those being schooled under the law, which in some way does not wait upon God and is not able to see his glory, in keeping with what is sung in the Psalms: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see,” or again: “Behold, a foolish and senseless people; they have eyes, and do not see.” But we, approaching the teachings about the ineffable nature with pure and enlightened eyes, behold the beauty of God the Father shining forth in the Son. And to the Jews, who thought they had seen the Father, Christ wisely said: “You have neither seen his form nor heard his voice.” But when Philip, who was very eager to learn, asked—more crudely than he should have, yet still out of a love of learning—and said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” Christ answered: “Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” That the contemplation and instruction given through the commandment of the law, as in shadow and riddle, is not very strong and not sufficient for an accurate and faultless showing of God, we will see also through the two daughters of Laban. For it is written: “Now Laban had two daughters; the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the other Rachel. Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and very lovely to look at.” And the patriarch Jacob was devoted to Rachel, yet he married Leah before her. When the type passes over into the truth, you will see the mystery of Christ. For there are two wives called to spiritual kinship and joined to him. The elder is the first, the synagogue of the Jews, represented as it were through Moses, to whom God said through the voice of the prophets: “Behold, your eyes and your heart are not good, but are set only on your greed and your wrongdoing and on committing murder.” The second was the young and more beautiful one, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, to whom the divine David said: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, for the King has desired your beauty.” Somewhere this too is said to her: “Your eyes are doves.” But the beauty of the Church is spiritual and truly beyond this world. For it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is Esebon.” Now “Esebon” in the Hebrew tongue means “within.” For it cannot be grasped by the eyes of the body, but is readily discerned by the gaze of a pure mind. Or is it not so?
Certainly it is.
So it is not through the schooling of the law that one could behold the divine and pure beauty, but rather in Christ and in the teachings that come through him.
True.

And what is able to redeem, Palladius, and to deliver from the hand and tyranny of the devil, is not Moses or the law, but the Master of Moses, that is, Christ, and the power of his mystery. Indeed, when God says, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their taskmasters; for I know their suffering, and I have come down to deliver them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them out of that land into a good and large land, a land flowing with milk and honey,” and adds at once, “And now, behold, the cry of the sons of Israel has come to me, and I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them. Come now, I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall bring my people, the sons of Israel, out of the land of Egypt,” Moses cried out clearly and explicitly: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and that I should bring the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt?” Is not the type plain, then, and does not the manner of his refusal point to the one who is incomparably superior and supreme, that is, Christ? For him it would be unfitting to say “Who am I?”; for him it is very easy to deliver peoples, to save nations, and to bring them to freedom, once the one who holds them in slavery, that is, Satan, has been crushed and rendered powerless.
Very easy indeed; you have spoken rightly.

What then? Can we not also see from this, with no trouble at all, that the Only-begotten has become the author of the salvation of all? For through him we have been redeemed, and the prophet says: “Not an ambassador, not an angel, but the Lord himself saved us.”
How do you mean?

The God of all plainly commanded Moses to go without any hesitation to the sons of Israel and to tell them openly that, having received the all-powerful God as their helper and ally, they would easily throw off the heavy burden of their slavery in Egypt, would set out for home again, and, returning to the freedom of their fathers, would dwell in the holy land and there richly enjoy the good things he would give them. “Moses answered,” it says, “and said, ‘If they do not believe me or listen to my voice—for they will say, “God has not appeared to you”—what shall I say to them?’ And the Lord said to him, ‘What is this in your hand?’ And he said, ‘A rod.’ And he said, ‘Throw it on the ground.’ And he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses fled from it. And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail.’ And he stretched out his hand and took hold of its tail, and it became a rod in his hand.”
What an extraordinary miracle, my friend! But tell me yourself, again, what it is meant to show.

I will tell you. The Israelites had lived with the Egyptians for a long time, had slid into every kind of sin, and took pleasure in the luxuries of the country. Moses was well aware that they would be slow and very hard to bring round to good order; but he wisely supposed that the toil of their labors would push them, even against their will, toward obedience, if they saw him working miracles. For pleasure is truly something hard to escape, and the wildness of the passions within us is not easily tamed. But when sweat is wringing them and toils hang over them, the one who promises to free them could easily persuade them to despise even the sweetest things. And I think that God, who has knowledge of every good, allowed the greed of the Egyptians to fall on the Israelites as something especially hard to bear and painful at that very time, and did so with the wisest providence, so that they would be ready to flee, and not, bound by the pleasures they had grown up with, become hard and quite unmanageable, slighting the grace of the one who called them to freedom and making their servitude in Egypt a willing one, sometimes preferring the pleasure of the moment to a few toils. Rather, they even reckoned these things better than the gifts of God. And so, though they had most gladly escaped the greed of those who had long tyrannized them, and were camping in the desert and fed with food from above and from heaven—I mean the supply of manna—they remembered the luxury of Egypt not without tears. They even went so far as to insist that it would have been far better and preferable for them to have died while reveling at the tables of Egypt, crying out childishly: “If only we had died, struck down by the Lord in Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full!”
You speak well.

So Moses knew that the working of miracles would be necessary to bring them to obedience. That is why he says: “If they do not listen to me—for they will say, ‘God has not appeared to you’—what shall I say to them?” But the God of all at once ordered him to perform the miracle as a kind of rehearsal, persuading his minister in advance by experience, I think, that what was done would be sufficient for everyone else, as it was for him, as a clear proof that he had been called by God. For the ability to change the natures of things into whatever one might choose would befit no one else but the Creator of all alone. At the same time he made the marvel very fittingly a kind of veiled indication of the salvation through Christ. For we will see in it the refashioning of human nature to its original state in him, and as it were its transformation back into what we were in Adam when we were first brought into being, and before we had been deprived of the glory and sanctification from above.
How do you mean? Your meaning is unclear.
Would not the rod, or scepter, be for us a symbol of kingship, Palladius?
Certainly, since some of the ancients who were accustomed to sing the stories of the Greeks say that it was even made something to swear by.
What then? Do you not say that it is a plant of paradise, and that before it was cut it had been granted to flourish in gardens?
I do.

Come, then, and turn your thoughts to that ancient Adam. Count all humanity as contained in him, as in the firstfruits and root of the race. Consider this as well: he had been made in the image of his Creator and appointed to rule over the things on earth. Through his life of holiness he was, as it were, in the hand of God, all but a plant of paradise, flowering and most noble. But he was deceived by the bitter malice of the serpent and carried away from his original state, and was then caught having disregarded the divine command. Then, at that very moment, he was torn from his first place and root. He slipped from the hand that held him fast in holiness and fell to the ground, that is, from the heights of virtue. He sank feebly down to choosing to mind the things of the flesh, now sick with undiluted wickedness and differing, I think, in nothing from a serpent. So he was stripped of the kingship and glory he had at the beginning, and sent out of paradise and its delight. Or did the divine Moses not tell us these things?
He did indeed.

When the lawgiver saw him brought down to this degree of baseness, he fled in a sense, and loathed the wickedness that was in him. For Moses fled and left the serpent. It is written: "The holy Spirit of wisdom will flee deceit, and will rise up and depart from foolish thoughts." For holiness and impurity cannot be reconciled with each other, nor can light and darkness, or righteousness and unrighteousness.
True.

So the rod's falling from Moses' hand would signify this. At the beginning the one made after the divine image was a plant of paradise, in the glory of kingship and in the hand of the Creator. But he slipped to the ground by choosing to mind the things of the flesh, and because his bitterness had reached its extreme, he was like a serpent in the eyes of the Godhead. Moses, however, was commanded to stretch out his hand and take hold of the tail, and at once it was reshaped into what it had been at first. It was no longer a serpent but a rod again, a plant of paradise. In the same way, when God the Father was pleased to sum up all things in Christ and to re-create what had been made into its original state, he sent us his Only-begotten from heaven. The Son is the right hand, truly the worker and saviour of all things, as in the verse: "The right hand of the Lord has wrought power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me." Then, at that very moment, he took hold of humanity lying on the ground. He freed us from the beastlike bitterness of baseness and sin, and through sanctification brought us back to royal honour and to a gentleness that leads to virtue. He gives the ancient dwelling place to those who believe, and first of all, as firstfruits, to the thief crucified with him: "Truly, truly I say to you," he says, "today you will be with me in paradise."
You have made your argument excellently and correctly. But tell me this: why does he command him to take hold of the tail, and not the head or the middle?
It had to be done this way, my friend, because taking hold of the tail, and not the middle or the head, serves the mystery.
How so?

The head is the beginning of every animal, so to speak, and the tail is its end. For the present, then, let us count the whole human race as a single animal. Christ took hold of the tail, that is, of those at the end, the last, for he came down in the last times of the age. Moses took hold only of the tail, yet the transformation ran up to the very head, for the serpent was changed into a rod completely. In just the same way, Christ laid hold of those at the end, yet the reshaping that comes through grace extends to the whole race and reaches the very head, that is, Adam. For it is written that "Christ died and rose for this purpose, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." So, together with those at the end, the redemption of those at the beginning is also accomplished.
Your argument is persuasive, and the explanation is not off the mark.

To make him most firmly settled in his faith on this point, God also had him perform two other divine signs. For it is written immediately afterward: "The Lord said to him again, 'Put your hand into your bosom.' And he put his hand into his bosom, and his hand became leprous, like snow. And he said again, 'Put your hand into your bosom.' And he put his hand into his bosom and brought his hand out of his bosom, and it was restored again to the colour of his flesh." Observe how worthy of God this is. What is done here fits among the things that are most wondrous, and like the first sign, it carries within it a disclosure of the mystery of Christ.
Explain it, then; I do not yet understand at all.

Leprosy is a disease of the flesh that is beyond the power of physicians and cannot be overcome by their skill. Under the ancient commandment given through Moses, the leper is unholy and unclean, and he is also greatly detested among those who honour the customs of the Greeks. Anyone who suffers it is already half-dead in a way, and a corpse is abhorrent and unclean. So the ability to heal a leper is counted as something supernatural, beyond our human limits, belonging only to the divine and ineffable nature and its power. That is why Christ was marvelled at when he called out with authority to the leper, "I will; be clean." The all-working voice, which raises even the dead from their tombs, performed the miracle on him, a miracle that overcame death and corruption. So God commanded Moses to hide his hand in his bosom, then to take it out from the bosom's covering and show it leprous through and through. When Moses had hidden it in his bosom a second time, God at once showed it freed from what had befallen it. In this way the Israelites would understand that Moses, armed as it were with an unspeakable and ineffable power, would stand up for the wronged, who were wickedly yoked under the greed of the Egyptians. This explanation is not deep, but it is useful for the history. But I think those who examine the meaning of the passage closely must ask what it means to hide the hand in the bosom, what it means that once outside the bosom it became terribly leprous, and also how it was cleansed. For he freed it from the disease by putting it into his bosom.
Well said. Examining each point would benefit us more than a little.

It seems to me, then, that the marvel points to something like this, as in a shadow. The human being made after the divine image was, as it were, nursed in the bosom of God. As long as he had not yet trampled on the commandment given to him, he was clothed in God's care and love, and he remained pure and sanctified and knew nothing of the deadness that comes through death. But when he went out from God's shelter and friendship by leaning toward evil, he was plainly shown to be unholy and abominable, sick with the uncleanness of death. But God the Father has received us again in Christ, clothed us with divine grace, and holds us, as it were, in his bosom through adoption. So we cast off our impurities, and with them the deadness that came from the ancient curse, and we spring back to what we were at the beginning. For it is written of Moses' hand: "It was restored to the colour of his flesh."
That was very elegantly said.

The third sign after these proclaims the mystery of Christ most clearly and openly. For God spoke to Moses again as follows: "If they do not believe you or listen to the voice of the first sign, they will believe you because of the voice of the second sign." Then he made clear what this was, saying: "And if they do not believe these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some of the water of the river and pour it on the dry ground, and the water you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground."
