For the last sign given to the world was the death of Christ and the cleansing through water and blood, with the holy body added as well, which the dry ground signifies. That water and blood flowed out for us from his holy side when it was pierced by the spear I will not discuss, since everyone knows it very well. But one can also learn clearly from the sacred Scriptures that the Saviour's death has been called a sign. Many miracles had already been performed, yet the Pharisees, who would dare anything, came to Christ as though none had happened. "Teacher," they said, "we wish to see a sign from you." He answered them: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." So the first help we received in Christ came through the law of Moses, for "he gave the law as a help," as the prophet says. And Moses took hold of the tail. The second cleansing, again in Christ, came through the holy prophets and through the voice and mission of John. The prophets said, "Wash yourselves; become clean," and John called people to the baptism of repentance. The third sign, which is said to be the last, is the death of Christ, and faith follows upon it. "If they do not believe you," he says, "or listen to the voice of the first sign, they will believe the voice of the second sign." You see that he states quite plainly that faith will follow neither the first sign, that is, the help given by the law, nor the cleansing in between, that is, the cleansing through the holy prophets and perhaps through John, but only the voice of the last sign. For the mystery of Christ is not voiceless. With a lofty, ringing proclamation it calls everyone throughout the whole earth to the cleansing through water and blood, and also to the new life that comes from partaking of the holy flesh. The law, then, served the announcements made beforehand about Christ, but by itself it is not really capable of saving anyone. I think one could show clearly that Moses admits this too, in the present passage. God had said, "I will be with you," and had first persuaded him with miracles, yet Moses pleaded: "Lord, I have not been capable before yesterday or the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant. I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." And the Lord said to Moses: "Who gave man a mouth, and who made the deaf and the mute, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you are to say." And Moses said: "I beg you, Lord, appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send." For the law is not strong, nor is it sufficient to save the whole earth and to rescue humanity from the tyranny of the devil. Moses knew well that he was slow of tongue and weak of voice, especially once God had begun to converse with him and commanded him to speak about God. "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel," he says: "I am He Who Is. This is my name." For the law is slow of tongue when it comes to articulating properly the account of Him Who Is, nor can it initiate anyone into the august and ineffable nature worshipped in the Holy Trinity. It is weak of voice too, for it could speak only to the Israelites, and barely even to them. It was heard only in Judea, while all the other nations, so to speak, never received its proclamation into their ears at all. Therefore the divine Moses foresaw the one who was fully able to give his hearers a precise and polished account of God and to proclaim it easily to the whole earth, that is, Christ, and he said: "I beg you, Lord, appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send." For Christ is the one who is truly able, and the law also announced beforehand that in due time, by the good pleasure of God the Father, he would be appointed for this. Moses' refusal, even after the divine promise and after he had been shown many signs, would be a type of Israel. Israel shrank from and refused the divine ministry of the gospel under Christ and the obedience it called for. After countless words about faith and many displays of wonders, they kept their hardness of hearing and remained disobedient. And Moses refused twice. For there were two periods in which Israel was unruly and hard to lead. The first was the time of Moses, Joshua and the Judges. The second came right after it, the time in which the prophets arose, and John, who stood, as it were, on the borderland between the apostles and the prophets. For he was the end of the prophetic ministry and, so to speak, the firstfruits of apostolic splendour. But Moses' refusal provoked God to anger, and from then on it shifted the matter to another dispensation, as it were, through which those brought low by the greed of the Egyptians were to be saved. "The Lord was angry with Moses and said: 'Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he will speak for you. And behold, he will come out to meet you, and when he sees you he will rejoice within himself. You shall speak to him and put my words into his mouth, and I will open your mouth and his mouth and teach you what you are to do. He will speak for you to the people. He will be your mouth, and you will be to him in the things that concern God.'" For the law had stumbled, being feeble, and the Israelites had been very disobedient, so Christ was added: the true Levite, the great high priest. He was ranked with those under the law as a brother because of his humanity. He spoke to Moses as God, but as a prophet he was taught by the Father, even though he is Lord: "For I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, and I will put my words into his mouth, and he will speak to them all that I command them." Christ himself also said: "I do not speak on my own; the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak." So Christ addressed the people and became a mouth for Moses, interpreting the law to us spiritually, while Moses in turn is to him in the things that concern God. For Moses seems in some way to be closer to God, since Emmanuel came under the law and promised to keep what was given through the all-wise Moses, saying: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfil them." Christ, then, is a clear guide into the mysteries. He turns the things of the slow-tongued law into clear speech, and reshapes, as it were, the weak voice of the letter into a most resonant interpretation. For in Christ the law is spiritual, and his proclamations are brothers to those of old, just as Aaron was Moses' brother.
So the law, as far as it depended on itself, was feeble, for it brought nothing to perfection.

Just so, I say. And from what follows one could also see how petty, so to speak, the way of life under the law was. For it is written: "Moses went and returned to Jethro his father-in-law, and said to him: 'I will go and return to my brothers in Egypt, and see whether they are still alive.' And Jethro said to Moses: 'Go in good health.' After those many days the king of Egypt died. And the Lord said to Moses in Midian: 'Go, depart for Egypt, for all those who sought your life are dead.' Then Moses took his wife and children, set them on the beasts of burden, and returned to Egypt."
And what is there in this? I cannot see or say on what grounds anyone could reasonably find fault with life under the law.

And yet, Palladius, if you look more sharply into the meaning of the passage, you will see that the matter is full of a great deal of blame. The divine Moses had been appointed for his mission, yet he did not run straight to it and leave the things of the world behind. Instead he let himself be divided by fleshly concerns as well, and first told his relatives about his departure. He did not set out from the land of the Midianites until he learned that the tyrant of the Egyptians was dead, for he was very much afraid of dying. Only when God had told him beforehand and freed him from these fears did he at last take his wife and children and go down into the land of the Egyptians to carry out what he had been commanded. These things would be a type of life under the law, which is divided in a way and looks in both directions, toward divine things, I mean, and human things. For it is not free of earthly and worldly concern, nor is it wholly sacred. The way of life of the gospel, by contrast, is not divided at all toward the things of the flesh, that is, toward the affairs of the world, but dedicates to God entirely, as it were, those who have come under Christ. For "those who belong to Jesus Christ," he says, "have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." Indeed, when one of the disciples came and said to Christ, "Teacher, let me first go and bury my father," he was taught the wholly sacred way of life, for he heard at once: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead." And the divine Paul writes to some: "When God was pleased to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood." But Moses does consult. For life under the law is divided, as I said, and still lies under the fear of death. Moses was afraid to go down to Egypt because he shrank from death. But this too has been abolished in Christ. The holy Paul will confirm it when he speaks about Christ and about us: "Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free all those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives." So now the minds of the saints treat even death itself with defiance. For Paul said again: "For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain." And again: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?" Life under the law is gripped by the terrors of death, while the way of life in Christ has escaped them and makes this its boast. This becomes clear when sacred Scripture cries out that death reigned from Adam until Moses. But who else could have abolished death, shaken down the power of corruption, and saved, along with those who believe, those who were once tutored under the law, except our Lord Jesus Christ alone? "Not an elder, not an angel, but the Lord himself saved them," says a prophetic oracle. Again, you can see the mystery of this very clearly, as in a type, in what happened to the blessed Moses. When he had already left the land of the Midianites and was hurrying on to Egypt, God said: "As you go and return to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your hands." And after some other things it says: "And it happened on the way, at the lodging place, that an angel of the Lord met him and sought to kill him. And Zipporah took a stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: 'The blood of my child's circumcision has stood.'" Will you need a long explanation to make this clear, or is the meaning plain to you?
No, it is not plain. I do not understand at all what this event is showing us, as in a shadow.

My friend, do you not agree that it is true that human nature became subject to death because of that ancient curse? For it was said to us, in the person of Adam, the firstfruits and topmost root of the race: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return."
Certainly.

So, since the beginning of the race fell sick with the death that comes from sin, the condition necessarily passed on to us as well, and the plants springing from the root were ravaged along with it. For the fruit of a corruptible body is corruptible. So death reigned over everyone, all the way to Moses himself, that is, to the times of the law. The angel's attempt on Moses at that time, then, is a clear and vivid type of death's power lasting until Moses and of human beings being subject to corruption. But Zipporah, his wife and partner, prevailed upon the destroyer and drew him away from Moses by circumcising her own child with a stone, pleading and saying: "The blood of my child's circumcision has stood." She says that the blood "has stood," but she does not mean that the flow of blood had stopped. That, I think, would never have turned the destroyer away from his intention to kill. Rather, she means something like this: "What God willed has been done and fulfilled, that is, the circumcision of the child." It is as if someone were to say, "The type of this matter has stood," or perhaps, "The account of it has stood," meaning, "It has come to its end and has been shown."

Then who might Zipporah be understood to be, for us? What are the stone and the circumcision done with it? And how was the divine angel prevailed upon, so that Moses escaped the death that hung over him and was owed by him, once the child was circumcised?

The passage is obscure, and the meaning of what we are asking about is truly hard to reach. But trusting in God, I will speak once more, as far as I am able. Zipporah was the daughter of the priest of Midian, a man of another race and not of the blood of Israel. She fulfils for us the type and figure of the Church from the Gentiles, which was called to God out of worldly worship, as it were. For somewhere it is said to her through the voice of David: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, for the King has desired your beauty, for he is your Lord.” She was called, then, as one following the law and all but joined in marriage to Moses, the tutor who leads us well to the mystery of Christ. For the law teaches the elements: it brings us back to the first principles of the oracles of God, and it sows in us, as it were, the knowledge of the mystery of Christ through riddles and shadow. So it was that Christ said to the Jews, who had set aside even the most holy Moses himself: “Or do you think that I will accuse you to the Father? The one who accuses you is Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” Since we have taken Zipporah as the figure of the Church from the Gentiles, the child born of her will surely be a type of the new people. These are the believers who have received a spiritual infancy in Christ and a rebirth to God, whom David somewhere called “a people being created.” So the newborn child in Christ, that is, the new people who come through faith, turns death aside by circumcision. For the pebble is a symbol of the unbreakable nature, whose strength and toughness are signified as in a hard stone. Indeed, when Joshua son of Nun had brought the Israelites across the Jordan, he circumcised them with knives of stone, prefiguring the circumcision in Christ through the Spirit. For the rock is Christ, and, as I said just now, the pebble that circumcised Zipporah’s child also points to him in type. Then death fled as well, and the one seeking to kill honoured the mystery of circumcision in Christ and departed from Moses. Through this event we are told in a riddle that death departed not only from those counted worthy of circumcision in Christ, but that the thing itself, I mean the mystery of Christ, also came to the help of the fathers. For as we all died in Adam, so too the grace that comes through Christ extends to all. For this is why he died, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. So at the time of the new people’s circumcision, the life of the fathers was also accomplished with it. For they live to God, since they are destined to live; this too the sacred word has told us. And the time of the circumcision understood in the Spirit is the coming of Christ. As God he is older than Moses, but he is second and after him insofar as he appeared as a man for the ministry on our behalf. For notice that God appointed Moses first and then joined Aaron to him. In this way he prefigured that Christ would be revealed second in time to the mission and ministry of Moses. Christ was equal to Moses because of his humanity, but he held a divine and incomparable pre-eminence because he was begotten of God the Father. You can see this too, if you wish, from the sacred Scriptures themselves. For it says: “Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; so they did. Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron his brother was eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.” Do you hear how the two were equal in having reached their eightieth year, even though Aaron came after Moses in ministry? So it is with Christ. In one respect he is equal to Moses because of his humanity, and he is second in the order of the divine plan. But he surpasses him and is exalted far above him, as he is in Godhead and in the glory that belongs to the holy Trinity.
How clear and vivid the explanation is!
What then? Is there not something else besides this that is worth looking at?
What is it?

The Israelites did not escape from the land of the Egyptians in any other way. They would not otherwise have been freed from a slavery so grievous and so hateful to them. Or rather, they would not have escaped at all from the death that fell on the firstborn in Egypt and from the destroyer’s hand, which was so hard to flee, unless they had sacrificed the lamb as a type of Christ, who takes away the sins of the world. They smeared the doorposts with the blood, according to the law laid down for them through Moses. But they were making the mystery of Christ a weapon, as it were, and a rampart for their own souls. For the death of Christ is a remedy that undoes death, and those who share in the mystical blessing are stronger than corruption, according to the words: “Truly, truly I say to you, whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” When they had eaten the lamb, they ate unleavened bread with it. In this way the type points to the excellence of the gospel teachings as unleavened and most pure food, which would nevertheless not come without sweat, nor without the bitterness of afflictions. That is why eating bitter herbs together with the unleavened loaves shows that the guileless and most pure life in Christ will not be without bitterness. So the bitter herb must necessarily be taken in together with the unleavened food. For “all who wish to live in Christ will be persecuted,” it says. Yet those who suffer this are blessed. For if they suffer with him, they will also reign with him, as it is written. My discourse has not wandered off into anything unseemly, has it?
Not at all.

That it is impossible to escape the death that comes from sin, and the greed of the devil, except through the sanctification that is in Christ; and that justification is not in the law, but in Christ.

So then: the rite of the sacrifice had been carried out very well by the Israelites. The firstborn of the Egyptians had now perished, and Christ, as in a type, had driven the destroyer away from those who were sanctified. Then at last the Israelites rushed out of the land of their masters and hurried to reach the land promised to them. Yet they did not run straight to it; instead they were led along roundabout routes, off to one side, as it were, of the straight road. For again Scripture writes as follows: "When Pharaoh sent the people out, God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was near. For God said, 'The people may change their minds when they see war, and turn back to Egypt.' So God led his people around by the road through the wilderness toward the Red Sea."
What, then, is hidden in this passage too?

We must examine it closely, if you agree. Notice that a straight road lay before them, and they could have arrived quickly after a short journey ("for it was near," it says, meaning the land of promise). Yet he plainly led them by another road, a long way around. The Creator of all did so because he knew beforehand how ready the people of old were to fall away, and how uncontrollably they were still inclined toward cowardice.
The passage is still no clearer to me.

Then we must go on to the spiritual interpretation. People who set out from a worldly life and from demonic greed, as if from a land of Egypt, are led to sanctification and to the hope that is with God by a road that is straight and very short: faith in Christ and the justification that comes through him. As Paul wisely said: "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim). For if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved." God did not allow the people of old to travel this road, so close at hand and so short. Instead he devised a kind of circuit that does not run straight: the law, with its roundabout words and riddles, which made for a longer and far from effortless schooling. In this way they would have the things in shadows as a kind of practice for the more perfect things, and would be instructed in the mystery beforehand. Then they would not be terrified by every chance fear into running away and falling away from Christ. Instead, having been trained beforehand and, so to speak, having learned what is truly beneficial, they would be readier to long for the truth and pursue it eagerly, and would keep their love for God firmly grounded and unshakable. So the law was a tutor that led by a long road, as it were, and not a straight one: the worship according to the letter. Christ, however, did not lead in this way. He showed us the road that is straight and near, the road of faith. He reforged us for courage, so that from then on we must stand like men against our adversaries, gladly endure suffering for the sake of the good, and nobly resist the schemes of the devil, saying perhaps the words of the prophet: "See, the Lord helps me; who will harm me?" And what instills such admirable courage in us could surely be nothing else than the power from on high, that is, sharing and communion in the Holy Spirit.
I understand what you are saying, and I admire your sharpness of mind.

The words that follow would at once point to the time of salvation through Christ. "In the fifth generation," it says, "the sons of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt." For we have been redeemed from slavery, and also from toil spent on vain distractions and from the misery that concerns earth and dust (you understand what I mean). This happened as if in a fifth generation, in the fifth time, according to the gospel parable: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard." It says he did the same around the sixth and the ninth hours. "And about the eleventh hour he found others standing idle, and he said to them, 'Why are you standing here idle all day? Go, you too, and work in my vineyard.'" Notice, then, that the last are sent into the vineyard as if in a fifth generation, in the last times, when the Only-begotten became man and endured being slaughtered for the life of all. Accordingly, the law of Moses prescribed in figure that the lamb should be taken from the tenth day of the first month and slaughtered toward evening on the fourteenth of the same month. In this way the fifth time is signified for us, as on the fifth day, and the words "toward evening" signify that the Savior was slaughtered at the end of the age.
So, it seems, the whole aim of divinely inspired Scripture looks toward the mystery of Christ?

Entirely so. For Christ is the goal of the law and the prophets, since "there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." This is what the Savior's disciple said. The proof is close at hand if we turn to what follows: "The sons of Israel set out from Succoth," it says, "and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness. And God went before them, by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire. The pillar of fire did not fail at night before all the people." Do you see how, when the Israelites had left the land of the Egyptians, God led them in a pillar of cloud and of fire? Christ was depicted by both.
In what way?

First, because he is the pillar and foundation of the truth, wholly unshakable and unbreakable, lifting us high above the earth. In Christ we have been set free from thinking the thoughts of the flesh and wallowing in earthly evils. Through him we are lifted up on high, as it were, setting our minds on things above and living as citizens of heaven. For it is written, "The mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they have been greatly exalted." And somewhere Christ also said, through the voice of David, concerning the earth and the holy apostles: "I have made its pillars firm." For the holy disciples who hold up the earth were made firm when they were clothed with the power from on high, that is, with the grace given through the Holy Spirit. And they themselves were pillars because they were conformed to Christ and made like him in grace through the Spirit. You will understand, then, that Christ has been called a pillar for us for no other reason than the ones we have just given. Now he led them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night, it says, in a pillar of fire, to show them the way. Divine Scripture's custom is to call "night" the time before the Advent, when Satan still ruled as a tyrant and the darkness of ignorance held sway over the people on earth. It calls "day" the time of our Savior's Advent, in which we have been enlightened: we have received into our minds the rays of the true knowledge of God, and we see the Sun of righteousness with the eyes of the heart. Paul will bear witness to this when he speaks of the time before the Advent and the time of it: "The night is far gone, the day is near. So let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk decently, as in the day." Since, then, the former time is understood as night, and the time in which the Only-begotten became man as day, we say that he went before the Israelites in the form of fire, as in the law that condemns and punishes (for fire is a sign of punishment). But he goes before us in the form of a cloud, as in a type of holy baptism and of salvation through water. Or is a cloud not water?
Of course it is.

When the Israelites had left the land of the Egyptians, the one who had long oppressed them, that is, Pharaoh, flared up in anger and set out to pursue them. "He harnessed his chariots," it says, "and took all his people with him. He took six hundred chosen chariots and all the cavalry of the Egyptians, with officers over them all." And again, a little later: "The sons of Israel looked up and saw the Egyptians camped behind them, and they were terrified. The sons of Israel cried out to the Lord." And they openly attacked Moses, saying: "Was it because there were no graves in the land of Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? What is this you have done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? Is this not what we told you in Egypt, when we said, 'Leave us alone, so that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness." To this Moses says: "Take courage. Stand still and see the salvation that the Lord will work for us today. For the Egyptians you have seen today you will never see again. The Lord will fight for us, and you will keep silent." Then the Lord said to Moses: "Why do you cry out to me? Tell the sons of Israel to set out. And you, raise your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea, and dry it up, and let the sons of Israel go into the middle of the sea on dry ground." And God made plain the way he would help them: "The angel of God who went before the camp of the sons of Israel moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them and stood behind them. It came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel and stood there, and there was darkness and gloom. The night passed, and they did not come near one another all night." This is what the historical narrative weaves together for us. But I think we must again look at the precise meaning, applying a keen mind to what is written.
Certainly.

So the Israelites set out, hurrying toward the holy land, while God led them forward and guided them in a pillar of fire and of cloud. For it is impossible, utterly impossible, to reach the holy city above unless Christ leads the way and makes the road of salvation clear. The enemies of this world gnash their teeth at those who have chosen to do this. Yet the law spurs them to courage and encourages those who are afraid. It also shows very clearly that the band of adversaries will fall, since the removal of the Egyptians from their path surely hints at this for us. And God saved those who were afraid of suffering, again as in a type of holy baptism. "Tell the sons of Israel," he says, "to set out. And you, raise your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea, and dry it up, and let the sons of Israel go into the middle of the sea." Or does the inspired Paul not write about the sons of Israel that "all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea"?
I agree.

So those who want to follow Christ and are hurrying toward the city above must not settle down in the law. They must not camp immovably among the commandments given through Moses or love to linger among shadows and types. They must rather break camp and move elsewhere, that is, to holy baptism. This is what the people of old did when, at God's command, they went through the midst of the waves and, as Paul says, were baptized in the sea. Then, and only then, will they have as their helper the mediator between God and men himself, Christ Jesus. For the Word, being God, became flesh. In another sense, too, he is mediator in the divine plan: he regularly goes between those who worship him and those who persecute them, not letting them come together and holding back the attacks of the adversaries. "For the angel of God moved," it says, "and the pillar of cloud, and came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel, and they did not come near one another all night." Here again Christ is signified as an angel and as a pillar of cloud. For his name is called "Angel of Great Counsel."
So when Christ stands between us, we will not come to blows with those who want to make war on us?

That is how it is; you understand rightly. But I will add this too, and I think what seems right to me will not miss the mark. When we have only just chosen to leave the pleasure-loving and worldly life, and have become most eager to follow the laws of God, but have not yet been enriched with the grace that comes through holy baptism, we are not very strong. That is, we are not yet fit to endure hardship, to bear the labors that virtue demands, or to withstand the trial of war. Newly sprouted plants shrink from the harm of the sun's fiercest rays, and they would be badly damaged if they were shaken by violent gusts of wind; they need the aid of the gardener's skill and a fence around them. In just the same way, I think, the human soul that has only just escaped from slavery to the passions, and is changing its course toward better things, and wants to follow the divine law, is tender-minded and easily hurt. It would easily be frightened off at the sight of the sweat ahead [?] and the law of war, and it will think it welcome to return to the state it was once in. Indeed, when the Israelites saw the Egyptians' preparations and lost heart at the mere sight of war, they turned on the inspired Moses, saying: "Is this not what we told you in Egypt, when we said, 'Leave us alone, so that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness." So before holy baptism the human soul is feeble in battle, all too ready for slavery, and very easily terrified. But if it obtains grace and is clothed with the power from on high, it will resist its pursuers most vigorously and fight nobly. With Christ as its general and shield, it will easily drive back the assaults of its enemies. For we will prevail in no other way than this.
Consider, then, what examples you will use to show us this too. Surely you will not be at a loss.

It is easy to show it by a great many. But let us start with the nearest one, from what Moses himself wrote. Those who had lost heart at the mere sight of the Egyptians crossed the Red Sea and fulfilled the type of holy baptism (for they were baptized into Moses, as the wise Paul also writes, in the cloud and in the sea). After that they proved warlike and formidable in resisting their enemies, but only through Christ. This is what is written: "Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim. Moses said to Joshua, 'Choose strong men for yourself, and go out tomorrow and draw up your forces against Amalek. I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand.' Joshua did as Moses had told him, and went out and drew up his forces against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; and whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands grew heavy. So they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side and one on the other. So Moses' hands stayed steady until the sun went down. And Joshua routed Amalek and all his people with the sword. Then the Lord said to Moses, 'Write this in a book as a memorial, and recite it in the hearing of Joshua: I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.' And Moses built an altar to the Lord and named it 'The Lord is my refuge,' because with a hidden hand the Lord wages war on Amalek from generation to generation."
And what would be the meaning of what is written? I do not understand it very well.

But I think it is not hard to see for those who want to. When we consider that Joshua, whose name is also Jesus, receives orders from Moses, what else could one suppose but this: the Word, though he was God, came under the law in his human form. In a certain way he was subject to the commandments given through Moses, and in various ways. At one point he underwent circumcision in the flesh; at another he paid the two-drachma tax. He placed himself among those under the law as one under the law, and he said plainly, "I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it." But although he came under the law because of his humanity, even so he was God, the Savior and Redeemer of the whole people. For he chose strong men from the whole people of Israel and from every nation. I mean, once again, the holy apostles and those called through faith, to whom it may rightly be said: "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." With them he drew up his forces against the ruler of this age. Of this ruler the Master of all, he who conquers all, says: "Now is the judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast out." And the inspired John crowns with a splendid verdict those who conquered with him and through him: "I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have overcome the evil one." Or is what I say not true?
Very true.

Moses said that the battle had to be fought tomorrow. For the achievements of Christ did not appear in Moses' own time. They were accomplished, rather, in the time that came next and close after it, that is, after Moses and the law. Then Moses goes up a hill, to the top of a mound, so that he could watch the battle and the exploits in it of Jesus, the Lord of all. For the sacred instruction of the law also raises us up to a fitting height, so that we can see the strategy of Christ, as it were, from afar. When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Israel weakened and Amalek prevailed. For not all Israel, surely, but those who have honored conformity with Christ by bearing his reproach, that is, the precious cross, have become invincible to the devil himself and to every enemy who wants to ravage them cruelly. For hands stretched out in the air clearly depict the shape of the cross. But those who did not accept the cross became easy prey for their enemies, since they had no one to help them. So when Moses stretches out his hands for us, showing the shape of the cross, and Amalek grows weak and falls, the figure surely signifies to us those who conquer Satan through the precious cross and prevail over their enemies. But when we see him lowering his hands and Amalek then prevailing, we will think of those who have come under the devil's power and been conquered because they were unwilling to accept the cross. To them Christ also said, "Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." Scripture says that Moses' hands were heavy, that they were raised only with difficulty and stretched out very sluggishly to display the precious shape of the cross. By this, I think, it indicates in a riddle that Israel was not very ready to accept the faith, but came most reluctantly and only with difficulty to be willing to take up the reproach of Christ. That is why the inspired Paul rightly calls the cross a stumbling block to Jews. "And they took a stone," it says, "and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side and one on the other." The precious stone, chosen, a cornerstone, held in honor, is Christ. Resting on him (for sitting signifies rest), the more reasonable and teachable among the Israelites, the remnant chosen by grace, spread out their hands, that is, they accept the cross. In this too Christ supports and sustains them, as it were. He is signified by Hur and Aaron, and is understood as judge and high priest at once. For Hur was an impartial judge, and Aaron was high priest, the one who holds together the remnant of Israel chosen by grace, for salvation through faith. I think this is what was said prophetically through the voice of Isaiah: "If the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." So when the adversary had fallen, I mean Amalek, he says: "Write this in a book as a memorial, and recite it in the hearing of Joshua." For through the writings of the holy evangelists the achievements of Christ were to reach far into unending memory. And he said that the writing was to be given into the ears of Jesus, because the writings of the saints are like an offering of praises and tributes to Christ. When Amalek had fallen and been defeated, Moses sets up an altar to God and gives it a name: "My Lord, my refuge." This too would be a type of Christ. For he has become Lord and refuge for us. He conquered the ruler of this age, trampled on the power of death, and offered himself for us as a spotless sacrifice, a fragrant aroma to God the Father. The altar, then, is a type of Christ, and the name "My Lord, my refuge" is both fitting and true for him.
I agree; you understand rightly.

Christ fought the spiritual Amalek with a hidden hand and conquered him. So he prevailed over the nations and, as he himself says, plundered his goods once he had bound the strong man. The flock that had once been under that one, I mean those from the nations, he joined to the older flocks. This is why he said: "And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one flock, one shepherd." According to the Scriptures, Christ is our peace, who made both into one and broke down the dividing wall of partition. In his flesh he abolished the enmity, the law of commandments expressed in decrees, and brought together into one new man both those of the circumcision and those outside the law. Now look again at this great mystery, which is linked with what we have just said, as in shadow and riddles. For Scripture says: "Jethro, the priest of Midian, the father-in-law of Moses, heard of all that the Lord had done for Israel his people, for the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt. And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses' wife, after she had been sent back, and her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom, for he said, 'I was a sojourner in a foreign land'; and the name of the second was Eliezer, for he said, 'For the God of my father is my helper, and he delivered me from the hand of Pharaoh.' And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he received them at the mountain of God. And it was told to Moses: 'Look, your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you, and your wife and your two sons with him.' So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law Jethro, and bowed down to him and kissed him, and they greeted one another, and he brought them into the tent. And Moses told his father-in-law all that the Lord had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, and all the hardship that had befallen them on the way, and how the Lord had delivered them from the hand of Pharaoh and from the hand of the Egyptians. And Jethro was amazed at all the good things the Lord had done for them, in that the Lord had delivered them from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh. And Jethro said, 'Blessed be the Lord, who has delivered his people from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh. Now I know that the Lord is great above all the gods, for this reason: because they set upon them.' And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took burnt offerings and sacrifices for God; and Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God. And on the next day Moses sat to judge the people, and all the people stood around Moses from morning until evening. When Jethro saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, 'What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?' And Moses said to his father-in-law, 'Because the people come to me to seek judgment from God. For when they have a dispute and come to me, I decide each case and make them understand the ordinances of God and his law.' Then Moses' father-in-law said to him, 'What you are doing is not right; you will not be able to do it alone. Now listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you. You be for the people their representative before God, and bring their words to God, and solemnly teach them the ordinances of God and his law, and show them the ways in which they are to walk and the works they are to do. And look out for yourself,'" it says, "'capable men from all the people, and they will judge the people.'" And again, a little later: "And Moses," it says, "listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he told him."
Come now, take each point in turn and explain it to me.

Would you not say that the Midianite was a foreigner and from the nations? He did not spring from the root of Abraham, and besides he was a priest and servant of the self-devised worship current on earth at that time. For, as the common account has it, they worshipped the Most High God, and supposed in their own way that they did so, just as Melchizedek certainly did. But they probably admitted other gods as well, counting alongside him the most eminent of created things: earth and heaven, sun and moon, and the more conspicuous of the stars. This corruption and error is an ancient fault, but it reaches down even to our own day and persists. For some in Phoenicia and Palestine still hold these views in their folly. They call themselves God-fearers, but they tread a middle path of worship, attached purely neither to the customs of the Jews nor to those of the Greeks, but tossed about between both, as it were, and divided. When the Israelites once chose to think this way, the prophet Elijah rebuked them, saying: "How long will you limp on both your legs? If Baal, then Baal; if God, then God." So Jethro too, in all likelihood, followed some such form of worship. When he learned what God had done for the salvation of the Israelites, he was captivated by those holy and admirable accounts and came with his whole household and family to the holy Moses. When Moses saw him, he gladly welcomed him and brought him into his own tent. And he recounts to him in more detail the achievements so well accomplished by divine power, and the wonders beyond all words. For the multitude of those in error, I mean the nations, is called to repentance toward God, first from the reports one might hear about God. Then, after that, they come of their own accord, like deserters, to the divine law, that is, to instruction through sacred writing. So they even hurry into the first tent, for the law is introductory. Then, persuaded by the more ancient narratives, they go on to choose at last to believe that God is one and only, and indeed that they must bear fruit to him. For when the Midianite had heard Moses' account, he said: "Now I know that the Lord is great above all the gods, for this reason: because they set upon them." "And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took burnt offerings and sacrifices for the Lord." Moses, then, is an elementary teacher. He brings us to the first approaches of the true knowledge of God; that is, instruction through the more ancient Scriptures is introductory.
That fits.

But Christ brings to perfection those who have been instructed through the law. And if I say "law" again, understand the Old Testament. Thus with Jethro, Moses used only the accounts about God, and at last brought him to such a change of mind that he openly confessed there is no other God except the one alone, who is God by nature and in truth. And this is the first faith of catechumens: I mean being set free from belief in many gods and accepting the one who is truly and by nature God. Aaron, however, honored Jethro with a place at table and invited him to eat bread. For it says: "Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God." For Christ, the truer Aaron, brings us to perfection with the living bread. And he perfects not only those from the nations but rather, all together with them, those chosen from the blood of Israel, of whom the elders may be a type. And the fact that the bread had to be eaten as before God carries no small suggestion of sanctification. For what is so much in God's sight as the mystical table and sacrifice and those who partake of it?
You put it well.

That when we are perfected through Christ we also rise up from the tutelage of the law to a better understanding, we shall see without effort if we take Moses and Jethro as a clear image of the matter. For the divine Moses sat judging, it says, and all the people stood around him from morning until evening. But Jethro offers a proposal, which Moses respected; he recognized that it was excellent and accepted it. For it says: "Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he told him." Is not the one able to offer the better counsel and proposal to be considered, in every way and without question, superior in understanding as well?
I agree.

That perfection through Christ is better than instruction in the law, and far beyond it, carrying us to a knowledge incomparably higher, the most holy Paul could easily show. Because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ, as he himself says, he most willingly counted the gains of the law as loss and regarded them as refuse, so that he might gain Christ. And to those who still honored only what came through Moses and would not accept perfection through Christ, the prophet Jeremiah said: "How will you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us'? The scribes' measuring line has proved false and come to nothing. The wise are put to shame; they are dismayed and caught. What wisdom is in them, since they have rejected the word of the Lord?" But for us, who do not reject the saving word (for we gladly accept the preaching of Christ), he himself has become wisdom from God. So we have surpassed those under the law in understanding too, and we who were instructed through the narratives of the law, having eaten the bread before God, have been taught both to speak and to think better things. For Jethro gives counsel, and Moses heeds it. Jethro may fittingly represent those from the nations, and Moses those under the law.
You are right.

So perfection through Christ, and the power of his mysteries, both makes us wise and causes us to be seen as stronger than death, since it overthrows the hidden and spiritual Amalek, that is, Satan. And very rightly did the Psalmist say: "In God we shall do mighty deeds, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us." And concerning us who have been made radiant in faith, he cried out again, as if addressing him: "For you are the boast of their strength, and in your name they will rejoice all the day." For we boast in Christ, being saved and having him as a shield of favor, according to the Scriptures. Again, a type and clear image of this for us would be what is written at the end of the Second Book of Samuel. It goes like this: "And David rose in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, the seer, concerning David, saying: 'Go and speak to David, saying, Thus says the Lord: I set three things before you; choose one of them for yourself, and I will do it to you.' So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him: 'Choose for yourself what shall happen: either that three years of famine come upon you in your land, or that you flee three months before your enemies while they pursue you, or that there be three days of pestilence in your land. Now therefore consider and see what answer I shall return to the one who sent me.' And David said to Gad: 'I am in great distress on every side, all three are hard; let me fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are very great; but let me not fall into the hands of men.' So David chose for himself the pestilence. It was the time of the wheat harvest. And the Lord sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning until the hour of the midday meal, and the plague began among the people, and there died of the people of the Lord, from Dan to Beersheba, seventy thousand men. And the angel of God stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it; and the Lord relented of the evil, and said to the angel who was destroying the people: 'Enough; withdraw your hand.' And the angel of God was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. And David spoke to the Lord when he saw the angel striking the people, and said: 'Look, I am the shepherd; I have sinned, and I the shepherd have done wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand be against me and against my father's house.' And Gad came to David that day and said to him: 'Go up, and set up an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.' And David went up according to the word of Gad the prophet, as the Lord had commanded him. And Ornan looked out and saw the king and his servants coming over toward him; and Ornan went out and bowed down to the king with his face to the ground. And Ornan said: 'Why has my lord the king come to his servant?' And David said: 'To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the Lord, so that the plague may be held back from the people.' And Ornan said to David: 'Let my lord the king take it and offer up to the Lord what seems good in his eyes. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering, and the wheels and the oxen's gear for wood.' Ornan gave it all to the king. And Ornan said to the king: 'May the Lord your God bless you.' And the king said to Ornan: 'No, but I will surely buy it from you for a price; I will not offer to the Lord my God a burnt offering that costs me nothing.' So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, and David built an altar there to the Lord and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. And Solomon enlarged the altar at the last, because it was small at first. And the Lord heeded the prayers for the land, and the plague was held back from Israel."
And what, again, would be the meaning in this? How very hard to grasp the interpretation is!

Hard to grasp, admittedly, and truly hard to capture. But I will state the gist of the passage, having gathered it well into a few words and turned it over in my mind. Observe then, Palladius, as in a mirror and in faint outlines, the mystery of Christ and the manner of the dispensation on our behalf.
Then please do so, since God grants the power to understand.

Listen, then, for I will now go on to say what must be said. Because of God's wrath, death consumed the people of the Lord, and until the hour of the midday meal the destroyer prevailed, with no one to stop him. But when he was about to lay his hand on Jerusalem, God held him back. Having seen the angel, David implored the Lord, saying that he himself had sinned, and that it was better and more just for the shepherd and leader to die rather than the sheep, since they knew nothing. Then, at God's direction, he raised an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan, which he bought together with the threshing oxen for fifty shekels. And when he had built the divine altar so well, he offered sacrifices on it, burnt offerings and peace offerings. And so at last the plague stopped, and the death that had been so terrible was cut short. And the sacred text noted that the altar was small at the beginning, but that Solomon enlarged it at the last. Would you not say that this, in brief, is the gist of the passage?
I would. Now explain how the meaning may become clear.

Do you not know that human nature admittedly slid down into death and corruption, having provoked the Creator to wrath in the first fruits of our race, that is, Adam? He set aside the divine commandment in the beginning, and so he heard: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return."
True.

So from the morning, that is, from the first times of the present age, death consumed those on the earth until the hour of the midday meal, that is, until the time of the table. For when the time of the holy table arrived for us, clearly the mystical table in Christ, at which we eat the bread that comes from heaven and gives life, then the death that had long been so terrible and fearsome was abolished, because God relented. And the destroyer was barely turned aside: he wished to lay his destroying hand even on those who dwell in the holy city, the spiritual Jerusalem, and only then, when God relented, was he barely held back. For God says: "Withdraw now; it is enough." The holy city is the Church, whose inhabitants would be those who are brought to perfection for sanctification through the living bread. The divine David also mentions this city, so holy and admirable, when he says: "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." For Christ, who is life and the giver of life, has made his dwelling in us. That is why God drives the destroyer away from those who have been sanctified, since he can no longer prevail after the time of the holy table has been revealed, the time hinted at by the hour of the midday meal. So Christ delivered us, understood in the person of David. For when he saw death devouring those on the earth, he became our advocate before the Father. He offered himself for us and willingly submitted to death, and he turned the destroyer aside by saying that the sin was his own. Not that he had committed the sin, but, according to the Scriptures, he takes away our sins and suffers for us, and he was numbered among the lawless, though he knew no sin; and he became a curse for us. And he says that the shepherd should suffer rather than the sheep, for as the good shepherd he laid down his life for the sheep. Then, prompted by God, the divine David set up an altar at the place where he saw the destroying angel standing, now idle (for it says he saw him by the threshing floor), and there he offered to God burnt offerings and peace offerings, these being the kinds and forms of sacrifice under the law. By the threshing floor you will understand the Church. When death came to it, it stopped at last and was abolished, and the destroyer drew back his hand, which had long been so terrible and destructive. For the Church is the house of him who is life by nature, that is, of Christ. We say the Church is a threshing floor by way of likeness and image. On it, like sheaves or ears of grain, are gathered those who are cut off from worldly life by the word of the holy reapers, that is, the apostles and evangelists. Thus they may be brought together into the courts above, and carried as clean wheat into the Master's granary, the heavenly Jerusalem, once they have laid aside the more useless and superfluous things and thoughts, which are understood as being like the chaff. Christ said somewhere to the holy apostles: "Do you not say, 'There are four months more, and then the harvest comes'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest. The one who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life." And again: "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest." By the spiritual harvest, I think, he means the multitude of those who were going to believe, and by the holy reapers he means those who have in mind and on tongue the divine word, which is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow. The blessed Baptist also indicated the Church by the name of threshing floor, when he said somewhere about Christ: "I baptize you with water, but one mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire." This spiritual threshing floor, then, I mean the Church, Christ bought for fifty shekels, that is, at no light price, for he gave himself for her. And he set up the altar in her. And since he himself is the priest (for he became high priest), he also offered himself as the sacrifice, in the form and type of the threshing ox, and became a burnt offering and a peace offering. For in Christ the dividing barrier has been removed, and we who were long separated and cut off because of sin enter together, through him and in him, into the presence of God the Father, having abolished that ancient enmity. For he is our peace, according to the Scriptures.
Shall we then understand Christ as the threshing ox? How do you mean?

My friend, did not the law given through Moses call the holy disciples threshing oxen for us? For it said in a riddle: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing." The blessed Paul understood this very clearly: "Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he not speak entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman ought to plow in hope, and the thresher to thresh in hope of sharing in the crop." So the blessed disciples too are oxen, after the image of the first, that is, of Christ. But Christ is a threshing ox in another sense as well. For through him come the cleansing and the laying aside of superfluous things, I mean distractions and the fleshly thoughts of the world, which are food for the flame, just like chaff. And once the altar was raised, on which were the peace offering and the burnt offering, the affliction was removed; for the Lord heeded the prayers for the land, and the plague was held back. For when Christ offered himself as priest for us, death was abolished and corruption overthrown, and the almighty God now in a sense holds his ear ready for the prayers of all. For he says: "While you are still speaking, I will say, 'What is it?'" And the statement that the altar was small at the beginning and was later enlarged signifies the growth that the Gospel would make over time, and that the holy Churches were narrow in the beginning but broad, as it were, in the times that followed. For the altars are continually being widened, as other Churches are always being added to the first ones, and the peoples are spreading out into a countless multitude. They have been redeemed through the sacrifice in Christ, and they have him as priest, as the holy, fragrant, cleansing victim, as the admirable altar, and as master of the Church, which is figured by the threshing floor.
How clear and vivid the explanation is! It has been skillfully done.
For would you not say yourself, without any hesitation, that Christ is the life and redemption of all?
I would, be assured. That is what I believe.

For one died for all, he who was worth as much as all. He made his own life a ransom in exchange for ours, putting the devil's malice to shame and, so to speak, halting the accusation of the sin that tyrannized over us, and its unbridled tongue in charging all people.
In what way, do you mean?

Sin had reigned over those on the earth, who, as it is written, had leaned strongly toward evil from their youth, with the heart of all people set firmly on holding it necessary to accomplish evil deeds and wanting to do so. So we necessarily fell under the penalty of death as well. For the transgression of the divine law and the setting aside of the Master's will carry death as their penalty. The Creator took pity on human nature, corrupted as it was, and the Only-begotten became man. He bore a body that was by nature subject to death and was called flesh. He did this so that by enduring on our behalf the death that sin had hung over us, he might abolish sin and put an end to Satan's accusing, since in Christ himself we have paid the penalties for the charges of sin. For he takes away our sins and suffers pain for us, according to the prophet's words. Or were we not healed by his bruise?
True. For he was wounded for our sins, and was in affliction and under the blow.

So sin has been undone because Christ suffered for us, and I do not think it could still cry out against those who have been sanctified through Christ. The prophet Zechariah will show us this clearly, speaking as in a vision: "And the angel who spoke in me went out and said to me, 'Lift up your eyes and see this thing that is going out.' And I said, 'What is it?' And he said, 'This is the measure that is going out.' And he said, 'This is their iniquity in all the land.' And behold, a talent of lead was being lifted up, and behold, a woman was sitting in the middle of the measure. And he threw the stone of lead into her mouth. And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, two women were coming out, and there was wind in their wings; they had wings like the wings of a hoopoe. And they lifted up the measure between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who spoke in me, 'Where are they carrying the measure?' And he said to me, 'To build it a house in the land of Babylon and to prepare it, and they will set it there on its prepared place.'" Shall we take each detail in turn and consider how it stands?
By all means.

The prophet saw a measure going out from Jerusalem, and when he asked what it might be, the angel said: "This is their iniquity in all the land." It is perhaps as if he were saying: "In this measure the offenses committed from time to time by people throughout the whole earth are measured." When our sin has reached a clear quantity, then the Lawgiver, grieved, brings on the penalties. But often, out of his innate love for humanity, he holds out and bears with offenders, and he does not become wholly indignant before the measure is full. Indeed he said to holy Abraham: "For the sins of the Amorites are not yet full, even now." And to the Pharisees, who had raged beyond all restraint, Christ said: "Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers." So as the measure goes out, the talent of lead is lifted up, and the woman who fills the measure is cast into its middle, or rather she received the stone of lead into her own mouth. Then the divine angel says: "This is lawlessness."
Your meaning is not yet very clear.

Then it will be, and before long. The talent of lead would be Christ himself. He is lifted up, that is, exalted through the cross, and is seen resplendent with the dignities of the Godhead. For God highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name. He shuts the mouth of sin, as is sung in the Psalms: "And all lawlessness shall stop its mouth." This is the sin that cried out against those who had sinned through weakness and been justified in faith. For it is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns? And since Christ suffered for us, how could it follow that we ourselves should still be required to pay the penalties for our own offenses?

Very rightly said. For we have been justified in Christ and have thoroughly repelled the outcry of sin. But I would most gladly learn from you why Christ is signified by lead, while lawlessness appears in the figure of a woman.
This too is easy to see from the sacred Scriptures. Christ is likened to many other things as well, through qualities in the images that signify what is understood about him.
Such as what?

He has become for us a base and a security, an unshakable footing and an unbreakable foundation, and for this reason he has been called a stone. For it says: "Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a chosen stone, a precious cornerstone, and whoever believes in him will never be put to shame." Again, he is the splendid and admirable treasure of the Church, our spiritual wealth, and he has been called a pearl. For it says: "The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. When he found one pearl of great value, he went away and sold all that he had and bought it." Through himself he joined us to God the Father, having abolished the enmity in his body, as it is written. Indeed, speaking to his Father and God in heaven about those who have been justified by faith in him, he said: "Father, I desire that just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us." For this reason he has been called a tin stone, since things that are joined together are soldered with tin. And somewhere God said through the voice of Zechariah, pointing out to us his own Son as one who would come and go forth at the appointed times: "And they will rejoice and will see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel." In the same way, then, he calls him a talent of lead here too. I will explain the reason for this as well. When base silver is melted together with lead, it is thoroughly purified, because the lead naturally draws into itself the dross of what is burned with it. Christ has done something like this in us too. He was mingled with us, who were base, both bodily and spiritually, and so he melted away the dross in us. For he takes away our sins, so that because of him and through him we may be pure and made bright. Indeed, the prophet Jeremiah lamented over the people of the Jews, who did not accept the purification that comes through Christ, saying: "The bellows has failed from the fire, the lead has failed; in vain the silversmith works the silver, for their wickednesses have not melted away. Call them rejected silver, for the Lord has rejected them." You see, then, how the divine Scripture knew that silver cannot be purified without lead. So since Christ purged us who were base, he is likened to lead, and he stops up the mouth of sin, which appears in the form of a woman. A woman is a symbol of both weakness and pleasure, and all lawlessness is done through these. When the mind has first been corrupted by pleasure in some chance thing or another, and so has had its sinews cut, it gives up the labors that lead to virtue, and the human soul falls into sin. That is why some are called lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. And the prophet calls out to those who have grown sick with sin through weakness of soul and have gone slack toward wickedness: "Be strong, you slack hands and paralyzed knees."
So much for that. But tell me: what might the pair of women be meant to show, who carry the measure and the lawlessness away to the land of the Babylonians?

The mouth of lawlessness, my good friend, has been stopped through Christ. For we have been justified in him and set free from every charge, and the accusation of lawlessness against us has ceased. This was the purpose of his saving dispensation toward us: that for our sake, in our likeness and on our behalf, he should go to death, though he came back to life again, for it was not possible for life to be overcome by death. But some have disobeyed the gospel of Christ. They have not accepted redemption from sin, and so they carry it again as a burden, hanging it on their own heads through weakness of mind, softness of understanding and unmanliness of soul. These people are carried about by every evil spirit, and as they are driven with great violence into every kind of uncleanness, they pursue base things with the greatest possible eagerness. The wing is a sign of eagerness, and he says it is a hoopoe's. This is a kind of bird that is always running about the foulest-smelling swamps and gathering its food from mud and filth. So all who spend their eagerness on defilement may fittingly be said to have the wings of a hoopoe. They too are like women and effeminate, and so they are conformed to the sin that tyrannizes over them. Just as those who are under Christ and with him have been conformed to Christ through sanctification, so too those who have taken lawlessness on as their burden and have chosen to live with unclean wickedness are conformed to it and share its form. They carry the measure to Babylon and seek a house for it there. I think this too signifies, in a riddle, that if someone does not choose what comes through Christ, or love the stopping of sin's mouth, because his eagerness is for uncleanness alone, he will depart from the holy Jerusalem, that is, from the holy mother of the firstborn, the beautiful city above. Carrying sin as an all but unbearable load, he will dwell with the Babylonians, that is, he will have his portion and lot with the godless idolaters. For those who have scorned the redemption that comes through Christ are on a level with the godless. Indeed the Savior says: "If your brother sins, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take one or two others along with you, so that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector." So it is not unclear, but rather is testified to us throughout the divine Scripture, that all justification and all redemption are in Christ.
Well said.

That whoever has been called by God to justification and has been redeemed must follow him, and must reject the slackness that leads to wickedness, and must strive instead to live lawfully and with vigour.

It is a perilous thing, then, it seems, Palladius — I would even call it utterly loathsome and steeped in every absurdity — not to love to play the man against baseness and sin. Instead some go soft, as if melting into outlandish pleasures, let an effeminate weakness settle into the mind, and desert their boldness for virtue. Yet through Christ it is entirely possible to rise to anything at all that is praiseworthy. Besides, the most holy Paul spurs us on, saying: "Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might."
Well said.
"For we shall do valiantly in Christ." Yet no one, I think, could succeed without sweat in overpowering the passions with youthful vigour, or in strengthening his own mind to stand upright for this.
I agree.

So it is a splendid thing and worth gaining. Those who fall back cannot capture it, but those who have learned to value toil obtain it easily. It is written: "A man in toils toils for himself and drives off his own destruction." To suppose that the most excellent things can be achieved with little sweat is, I think, ignorant even to imagine. Would not the most precious of all things for us be to save the soul and to fight to the utmost for one's own life?
Most certainly.

Now to which athletes would you think renown, once it is plainly won, chiefly belongs? To those who compete correctly and with training, and for whom winning is a matter of real concern? Or to those who most gladly dissolve into luxuries and have preferred the life of ease to the best one?
And how, or on what ground, could anyone dispute that victory would least befit those who are sick with sloth, while the power to prevail belongs to the worthier?
Shall we say, then, that the power of glory properly belongs to those who bid farewell to the duty of toil and have chosen to relax and live in luxury?
Certainly not.
Good repute, then, will follow those who love toil the most, and without contests no one could succeed in becoming illustrious.
Agreed.

We must go straight, then, Palladius, toward what is praised, and attend to courage in the pursuit of virtue, and to a great stoutness of heart. This is admired in the divinely inspired Scripture, and it is familiar and dear to the souls of the saints. So the divine David too called out to those who had firmly set themselves toward this, saying: "Be courageous, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord." And as one who had achieved this very thing before all others, he prides himself on it and says: "The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" For the stumbling blocks around us are countless. A multitude of demons greater, I think, than any number provokes us to sin. Besides this, there is the ferocity of our innate pleasures, which is no small thing. Love of money and arrogance assail us, and envies, which are neighbours to murder, and hatred and slanders — and what similar evil does not? Those who are easily led away barely touch with the tip of a finger, so to speak, the duty of bearing such things nobly. They carelessly hand the victory to the enemy and are like "a half-boiled beet," in the prophet's words, as though thrown to the ground and, in a way, brought under the feet of wickedness without a fight. But those who love virtue and are good, who aim at the glory from above and long to share in eternal life, meet the assaults of their own passions most nobly and boldly. They put the flesh to death and rise up against the impulses that are in it and come from it. In this way they skilfully thrust aside every form of baseness and sin and achieve the holy and blameless life. To them the divine Paul also calls out, saying: "Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one." For the spiritual full armour is most fitting for the saints. The Savior himself also commands that we must aim at it, though in another way: "Let your loins be girded," he says, "and your shoes on your feet, and your lamps burning." Being girded signifies being belted up and, as it were, tucked in, ready to endure hardship for the sake of the good and for love of God. Having the feet shod signifies preparedness and eagerness for departure from the world, as people about to set out at once wherever the divine law may wish us to go. The burning lamps signify that we should not put up with living as in darkness and ignorance, but should rather make our way toward every admirable thing in the light that comes through Christ. To the Jews, who in their madness would not do this, Christ called out: "While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you." Readiness for virtue, then, and courage yoked with prudence, would make the lover of piety brilliant and conspicuous.
Well said.

For we shall not find renown in loving ease. Only if someone chooses to sweat will he, with difficulty, become brilliant and highly esteemed. So while the sons of Israel were still living in Egypt, the profane Pharaoh set over them harsh and bitter taskmasters. But they made that unwanted and forcibly imposed hard treatment an exercise in endurance, and so in truth they were benefited rather than wronged. For Pharaoh feared the Hebrews when he saw them growing into a countless multitude. Attempting most villainously to check their surge and growth in this, "he set over them," it says, "taskmasters, to afflict them in their works." But for them the scheme turned out the opposite way. The affliction inflicted on them became the occasion of their growth in number, as God managed the matter and set his own grace, as it were, against that man's villainies. "For the more they humbled them," it says, "the more they multiplied and grew strong." For Satan brings afflictions, gnashing his teeth at the saints. He always deliberately leaps upon those whom God claims as his own: "For his foods are choice," it says. But those who toil in these things will become better than they were when they are tested, and steadfastness in contests certainly makes them more glorious. So by the very things through which he means to grieve and harm, he most of all benefits them, against his will. And through the means by which he supposed he would overcome them, he makes them stronger. Pharaoh's crafty contrivance came to an unexpected end, and he perceived, late and with difficulty, that what he did to harm them was actually benefiting them. So he immediately changed the manner of his plot. He summoned the midwives of the Hebrews and said: "When you act as midwives to the Hebrew women and they are about to give birth, if it is a male, kill it; but if it is a female, keep it alive." But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they kept the males alive. His unholy and murderous plan against the race proved fruitless, since God did not allow the midwives to act impiously. So he then turned to open injustice. No longer content to do harm secretly, he now openly chose war and decreed a cruel death for the newborn. "For Pharaoh commanded all his people," it says, "saying: Every male that is born to the Hebrews, throw into the river, and every female, keep alive." He had no concern at all about the female, for a woman is unwarlike and not sharp in understanding. But the male troubled him on both counts, as wise and most warlike. So a womanish frame of soul, effeminate and feeble, is most pleasant and wholly agreeable to the murderous dragon — I mean Satan — and so is one that suffers from unfitness for wisdom.
