But eagerness for courage is hateful and abhorrent to him, as is whatever is better than softness and superior to cowardice, and whatever is exceedingly prudent. For this reason he keeps the female alive and in a way sets aside his murderous plan and design against it. For it is foolish, I think, to seek to fight those already laid low, who are sick of their own accord with a love of being under the yoke. But he chokes the male, as it were, by plunging it into the trials of temptation. It seems to me that the divine David sings of this too, saying: "If the Lord had not been among us when men rose up against us, they would have swallowed us alive; when their wrath was kindled against us, the water would have drowned us; our soul has passed through a torrent."
So it is.

Observe now the manner of the plot. First he tormented them with savage toils, devising most villainously to keep them from growing into a great multitude by the very means through which he thought to harm them. The wrong was still secret, and the tyrant's aim was not yet very evident. But, as I said just now, the grace of the one who pities was set against it, and being humbled, they grew all the more in strength and number. Next, he wanted to arm the midwives against the Hebrew women, but God did not allow this to succeed either. Then, as a third and final way of plotting, he ordered all his own people to choke the male, no longer bothering to gain his advantage by stealth. In the same way Satan wars invisibly against those who play the man, and arranges his plot in a threefold manner. He begins the battle with villainous schemes, hindering the mind's progress toward virtue, for he arranges for it to be worn down by unexpected toils and to grapple with hard contests. When he can do no harm by these, because God comes to our defence, he often stirs up those who are our own in faith and of the same people, and tries to whet them to hostility and battle. Paul will bear witness to this when he says: "In dangers among false brothers, in dangers from my own people." And if he should fail in this too, because the one who presides over the saints instils the fear of God into them, as he did long ago in the midwives, he then openly rouses his own shield-bearers to savagery and murder. But even so we shall hold fast to our love of boldness and our zeal for courage, knowing that what is hateful to him is precious to God. For God holds in account, and deems worthy of his care, whatever rises above softness.
I am persuaded. But I think we can see this again from the holy Scripture itself, for there is surely no lack of thoughts on it.

Then, God granting, let us speak. In the book called Numbers, which is a book of Moses, it says: "The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tent of witness, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying: Take the sum of every kindred of the sons of Israel, by their kindreds and by their fathers' houses, according to the number of their names, head by head. Every male from twenty years old and upward, everyone who goes out in the army of Israel — number them by their companies; you and Aaron, number them." This makes it quite clear that the male, the most warlike, the one who has come to maturity, is entered in the divine register and in God's book. By maturity I mean spiritual fitness and "the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." For the male who has reached the twentieth year and beyond is counted, I think, for no other reason than this: so that we too may understand what is rejected and unapproved, namely what is feeble and imperfect in understanding. We say these qualities belong to those who are still quite young and have not yet come to the measure of maturity that the divine law recognizes and defines, that is, the twentieth year. But what is male and in its prime is precious, counted, and known to God by multitude, by families, by heads, and by name. To those who play the man in this way and have advanced to this measure of understanding — the holy apostles — Christ said at one time: "Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven." At another time he said: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground without my Father who is in heaven. But even the hairs of your head are numbered." By saying that even their hairs are counted, he shows very well, I think, how exact is his care for them. So the male in its prime is in God's book. The census was carried out through Moses and Aaron, so that through both of them we may understand the one Christ: lawgiver, as in Moses, and high priest, as in Aaron. For he became for us at once lawgiver and a holy and innocent high priest. Through his mediation, those who play the man and are more eminent in virtue are registered in the divine books. The wise John also addressed them, saying: "I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have overcome the evil one." These, then, would be the ones we spoke of just now: "Every male from twenty years old and upward, everyone who goes out in the army of Israel." And you may see from what is written next, Palladius, that the Creator, as a lover of virtue, treats them with care and deems them worthy of his concern. For God — obviously it is he — said again to Moses and Aaron: "And with you there shall be men, one from each tribe, each a ruler; they shall be by their fathers' houses; and these are the names of the men who shall stand with you." Each tribe sets over itself the most renowned and most warlike man as its leader and champion, the head of its counsel and the one who proposes what must be done. These would be a type of the angels set over the chosen, over those inscribed in the book of life. For it is written concerning every righteous person: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them." That we are kept safe by the help of angels according to God's will would be clear from every quarter, and I think it superfluous to gather the proofs at present, though those who wish can very easily do so if they choose.
So the registration of those who play the man would take place through Christ, as in the type of Moses and Aaron.
So I say. And the passage in the blessed Daniel carries us on to the next argument on this point, since it offers a not implausible suggestion.
Which passage do you mean?

He saw the Father as one of venerable age, crowned with white hair and conspicuous in garments like snow. And he said: "And books were opened, and the court sat; and I looked, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was brought before him; and to him were given the rule and the honour and the kingdom." For when the Only-begotten came to be in our form, then the Father also opened books. He released from judgment those who were liable for sins, and granted to those who play the man that from then on they should be inscribed and counted among the choirs above and be kept in God's memory. And I hear the blessed David singing about those who behaved outrageously toward Christ: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous." For they had been honoured by the kind and loving assent of God the Father, but they fell through weak reasoning, having sinned out of unmanliness against the life in Christ. They were invited to the wedding, but they answered the holy servants who invited them to the supper softly and slackly. One said, "I have bought a field"; another, "I have married a wife, and I cannot come." You hear them saying everywhere, "I cannot." For the human mind that has turned aside toward worldly love of pleasure is powerless and feeble for doing the things of God, and such a person will have no share in the heavenly and divine feast.
So only what is mature and courageous, and already in some way sensible, is in God's register and in the book of the living, and everything that is not such is unapproved? Or how is it?

If you bring an exact and alert mind to the Scriptures, you will know the truth. For it is not only those in their prime, who have reached the twentieth year, who are registered. It is also commanded: "every male." Or do you not grasp what I mean?
I understand.

Then consider this. Suppose we carefully work out what courage in Christ means, and the right means for accomplishing virtue well. Those who have advanced to that height of glory, as already courageous and most warlike, having left boyish thinking behind, will have their own registration. Then would not each of us, my friend, have his own proper and fitting place of registration and glory, proportioned to the brilliance of his deeds?
I say so.
For the one who is not on their level will by no means be among the holy apostles — far from it.
True.

Nor again do we say that one who is not such will be ranked with those made exceedingly brilliant by manifold virtue, who have practised the most lawful achievement of life. Yet it is not unclear that he will inherit according to his own measure.
You are right.

So inasmuch as we have believed in the Savior and Redeemer of all, and through baptism have been enriched with the strength that comes from heaven and from above — for we have put on the power from on high, sealed with the Holy Spirit — we too have been placed, as it were, in the rank and reckoning of males, and have been counted in God's book. Yet here too there is a difference. Those who are more sacred and holy are, as it were, first in the registration and nearer to God. Faith in Christ is one; yet not all who have believed are alike and equal in conduct and life, but "one in this way, another in that," in the words of the blessed Paul. So those who excel in dignity of life, and are therefore holier, have the first rank in the divine registration and in God's memory. But those who have less in sanctification, because they have less in virtue, are surely second somewhere in the registrations as well.
And how could this too be made clear?

From the Scriptures, for our argument is not rash. After the count he made of the males who were in their full prime, the God of all again laid out for us another manner of registration. It goes like this: "The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, saying: Number the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, by their kindreds, by their clans. Every male from a month old and upward you shall number. And Moses and Aaron numbered them by the word of the Lord, as the Lord had commanded them." When the registration had been made in this way by clans and by fathers' houses, he immediately gives the whole total, saying: "The whole number of the sons of Levi, whom Moses and Aaron numbered by the word of the Lord according to their clans, every male from a month old and upward, was twenty-two thousand." And he adds at once: "And the Lord said to Moses: Number every firstborn male of the sons of Israel from a month old and upward, and take their number by name. And you shall take the Levites for me — I am the Lord — instead of all the firstborn of the sons of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the cattle of the sons of Israel. And Moses numbered them, as the Lord had commanded him. And all the firstborn males, counted by name from a month old and upward, according to their numbering, were twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites instead of all the firstborn of the sons of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites instead of their cattle, and the Levites shall be mine; I am the Lord. And as the ransom of the two hundred and seventy-three of the firstborn of the sons of Israel who exceed the number of the Levites, you shall take five shekels a head, by the holy didrachm; you shall take twenty obols to the shekel. And you shall give the silver to Aaron and his sons, as the ransom of those among them who are in excess." How deep a matter this is, Palladius, and how hard it is to grasp precisely and exactly what is laid down here!
Well said; but even so, put your mind to the test, trusting in Christ, the giver of every good thing.

Understand, then, that in the first registration what was sought was every male of twenty years — that is, the sensible and courageous, in their prime and able to accomplish whatever God may wish. But let what we have said on this suffice, for I think it has been dealt with quite adequately. In these two registrations, every male of the tribe of Levi is entered in the divine and sacred count. From the rest of the multitude it is no longer simply every male, but the firstborn, and all of those counted are from a month old and upward. The count of the Levite infants is twenty-two thousand, and that of the firstborn is twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three. Then God decrees that the Levites must be dedicated in place of the firstborn. But since the common people are found to exceed them in number by two hundred and seventy-three heads, the lawgiver ruled that a ransom must be brought for them to the tribe of Levi. In this way the Levites would perform the ministries and offer the worship on their behalf as well, receiving this from them as a kind of wage for their undistracted attendance. Or would you not say that this is the sense of the passage?
I would.

Then I will say this, and once again my argument will not stray from the mark, but will keep to what is likely and not unpersuasive. Where the point was a reminder, and as it were a search in type, of the courage and prudence understood in Christ, the males were enrolled, and their bodily age was not left unclear. But since it was also necessary, besides these, to mark out very clearly the enrollment made in faith and love toward Christ, a distinction is woven in, one that can be seen among believers. For some, together with receiving the faith, also practice holiness in works and service under God; while others do not make their consecration complete, being divided toward the things of the world. For this reason the lawgiver rightly commands that the holy be preferred to the other, understood in type in the Levitical race, and he ordered that it hold the first place in the enrollment. That is why he mentions the Levitical first, and after it, somehow yoked to it, comes the male and firstborn. For what is understood as spiritual courage and as conformity to Christ, who is the firstborn, is held in very high honor with God. Thus the divine Paul writes to some who were faltering in the faith and had grown effeminate in cold thoughts: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." So everyone is acceptable, even in the book of God, who is firstborn, as it were, by being formed after Christ, male and most prudent. Note that, as I said just now, from the other tribes not every male without distinction is counted, but only the firstborn; for not every man is distinguished in faith and in conformity to Christ, since many have not believed. Only the firstborn is registered and counted, because of the Firstborn who is among us and among many brothers. Among the Levites, however, every male, simply and without distinction, is enrolled and reckoned; for what is holy belongs wholly to God. Those enrolled are a month old and upward. And what is the reason? That the infancy in Christ of those who have believed is not rejected by God, and the very tender age is like a symbol of simplicity in Christ and of spiritual infancy. For just as we said that, in the case of the most warlike, the enrollment was rightly and blamelessly made from twenty years upward, so we say that the age of one month would be a clear sign of infancy in Christ. Paul too says something of the kind: "Brothers, do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature."
Shall we suppose, then, that we will share with the saints in whatever they may achieve by their own efforts, as they act bravely and strive as hard as they can to win approval?

Certainly, if they truly are such. They themselves are filled with divine gifts, having won the gift by toil and sweat and having pressed on through countless contests; and they fill us too with what has been given to them out of God's love. Thus the divine Paul said to some of the believers: "For I long to see you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you." Or do you not say that the blameless and unerring knowledge of God, and an exact understanding of all the best things, is a heavenly gift and a spiritual grace?
Yes, since the thing is life-giving: to know clearly who is by nature and truly the Creator of all things and God, and what kind of life, the best path, leads to long-lasting and endless life.

You are right. Teaching us this very thing, Christ himself charged the holy apostles, saying: "You received freely; give freely." And the splendor of the saints would be of profit to others in another way too: in their good deeds our failures are somehow obscured, and our God, who loves virtue, looking to the courage of the more illustrious, remits the charges against the weaker. Thus the people of Israel, having turned uncontrollably to disobedience and leaving no wickedness unpracticed, inevitably provoked the lawgiver against themselves; and when he was about to exact punishment for their outrages from those who had grieved him so savagely, the prophet Jeremiah brought him supplications. And what did God say to this? "Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem," he says, "and look and take note, and search in her squares, to see whether you can find a man, whether there is one who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to them, says the Lord." And he said that he would remit even to Sodom the punishment by fire, if there were five holy and good men in it. So the splendor of the saints sometimes secures for even great sinners that they not be punished at once, as though it shamed the divine anger and reined in the wrath. And to those who have genuinely received the faith but cannot rise to such courage as to be able to win by their own labors the filling with divine gifts, the saints all but share out their good deeds, training them as far as possible and leading them on to whatever pleases God, and making them partners in their own brave deeds; and what they themselves find with difficulty through very many toils, they instill into the souls of others. That we will share with the saints in the splendor that is in them, and be partners in their brave deeds, since God out of gentleness and love for humanity as it were mingles and blends our failures with their achievements, and joins what is lacking to what is more perfect so that it may be acceptable, would become clear once again from this as well.
What do you mean?

The Moabites and Midianites were unholy and barbarous nations, and they occupied the land of promise which the sons of Israel were to inherit. When war was now close at hand and on their doorstep, since they were about to perish at any moment and were unable to march out against the forces of Israel, they tried by the art of magicians and by their own unholy practices to shake off their enemies. But when, for all they did, they did no harm, because God was shielding Israel and turning the false prophet Balaam to blessing, although he had been hired to curse, they found themselves at last in the utmost perplexity. They reasoned among themselves that they could not harm Israel in any other way unless Israel offended the God who protected them; then, if they chose, they could join battle with them while they were stripped of help from above. Knowing that the male is hot and prone toward the female, and that youth is not secure against the most abominable pleasures of that kind, they sent out women who had made themselves beautiful, for unseemly intercourse with the Israelites. By their charms everyone who was easily prone to the sicknesses of the flesh was very readily carried away and, following the women's wishes, was drawn little by little away from the worship of God. And together with fornication they fell sick with apostasy as well. For it is written: "And the people were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor." God said this very thing through the voice of the prophets too: "And the people that had understanding was entangled with a harlot." The lawgiver was indignant at this, and with every reason, and the matter did not go unpunished for Israel. For because of it they were at once in unbearable disasters, as those who had committed fornication were destroyed by the hand of brother and neighbor. And God at once directed them to undertake war against the Midianites, saying to Moses, the initiator into holy things: "Avenge the sons of Israel on the Midianites, and afterward you will be gathered to your people." And Moses spoke to the people, saying: "Arm men from among you, and draw up in battle array before the Lord against Midian, to execute the Lord's vengeance on Midian. A thousand from a tribe, a thousand from a tribe, from all the tribes of the sons of Israel, send out to battle." So they counted out from the thousands of Israel a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for battle. And Moses sent them, a thousand from each tribe and a thousand from each tribe, with their force, and Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest, and the holy vessels and the trumpets for signals in their hands. And they drew up for battle against Midian, as the Lord had commanded Moses, and killed every male. And they killed the kings of Midian together with their slain: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, the five kings of Midian; and Balaam son of Beor they killed with the sword together with their slain. And they took captive the women of Midian, and their households, and their livestock, and all their possessions, and they plundered their wealth; and all their cities in their territories, and their encampments, they burned with fire. And they took all their plunder and all their spoils, both of man and of beast, and brought the captives and the spoils and the plunder to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to all the sons of Israel, to the camp at Araboth of Moab, which is by the Jordan opposite Jericho. And Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the leaders of the congregation went out to meet them outside the camp. And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds who were coming from the battle; and Moses said to them: "Why have you kept every female alive? For these were the ones who, at the word of Balaam, caused the sons of Israel to fall away and disregard the word of the Lord in the matter of Peor, and the plague came upon the congregation of the Lord. Now kill every male among all the little ones, and kill every woman who has known lying with a male; but all the young girls who have not known lying with a male, keep alive." When God had uttered these commands, chosen young men were gathered for the needs of the war, and from every tribe there came together the hardiest and most proven, so that what excelled in each might become the boast of the whole, and the splendor of the part might pass to the entire fullness, according to what Paul wisely said: "If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice together."
You understand rightly.

So the most valiant host of chosen men marched against the Midianites, with Phinehas the priest among them, together with the holy vessels and the trumpets called "of signals." For Christ, our great high priest, is always a fellow-soldier and ally to those who act bravely; and angels also contend alongside them, indicated as it were by the holy vessels. For the rational spirits in heaven are holy and ministering vessels, appointed by God to help us. No less present are the trumpets for signals, that is, the words of those who speak of God, which show very clearly how we must prevail over our enemies, that is, over the passions within us. So the priest, that is, Phinehas, is a figure of Christ; the holy vessels, of angels; and the trumpets for signals, of those who have proclaimed the divine word aloud to us. For in this way we shall overcome without toil those who oppose us, in Christ, saying what is sung in the Psalms: "Through you we will gore our enemies, and in your name we will bring to nothing those who rise up against us." This is just what the Israelites did: having laid waste every city and district of the Midianites, they brought the captives to Eleazar the priest and to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel. For the achievements of the saints are like holy offerings to Christ, the high priest of all, and are not hidden from the peoples, according to the saying: "For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor secret that will not be known and come to light." So the spoils of the captivity are brought before the priest and all the people, in type and by divine dispensation. Moses, however, rebuked the victors for not having carried out the matter according to an exact and wholly irreproachable rule; for, he says, they ought not to have kept the males alive, nor the females who had experience of marriage. The literal account is plausible enough: for it was necessary, truly necessary, to cut off the males of the land that was very soon to be under them, since they would shortly come to manhood and strength and become enemies of the people; and to destroy the females along with them, since they had been the cause of stumbling and, if spared, would perhaps be so again. But as far as spiritual contemplation is concerned, I think one might see the following elegantly indicated to us in these things.
What sort of thing do you mean?

The chosen men of the tribes did not remain free of blame, although they had won the victory. By this it is signified very clearly that complete blamelessness will never belong even to those who act bravely. For even what seems rightly done by us would by no means escape reproach and charge, when God examines it closely and tests it. That is why it is written: "If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall stand?" And again: "Cleanse me from my secret faults, and spare your servant from those of others; if they do not gain dominion over me, then I shall be blameless." So it is possible sometimes to see, even in the brave deeds of the chosen, a holy reproach, which the knowledge of the lawgiver discerns but which escapes us; for we by no means understand, according to the saying: "Who will understand his transgressions?" And Isaiah says somewhere that all our righteousness is like the rag of a menstruous woman, because it can never be in a wholly fine and blameless state. And Paul, most wise, having written, "For I am conscious of nothing against myself," says, "but I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who judges me." Yet Moses' reproof was not addressed to all indiscriminately, but only to the officers of the army, and to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds. For "the mighty will be mightily examined," and the strictness of the law bears above all on them: "For to whom they entrusted much," it says, "of him they will ask much." That is why the Savior's disciple also wrote: "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, knowing that we shall receive a greater judgment." So the charge against all is brought upon the officers and those set over the ranks; for those under command always do well through the vigilance of their leaders. That is why it is written to the peoples under their hand: "Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they keep watch over your souls, as those who will give account." After the killing of the women and children, the divine Moses does not allow the warriors to lodge in the camp unwashed, but orders that they must first be purified, saying: "And you shall encamp outside the camp seven days; everyone who has killed and who has touched the slain shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day, you and your captives; and every garment, and every vessel of leather, and all work of goats' hair, and every vessel of wood you shall purify." You see that even the best and most esteemed among us, the race of the chosen, is not entirely blameless; "For no one is clean from filth," even if he is very much one of those who are accustomed to excel; for perfect holiness is reserved for the age to come. So he settles the victors outside the camp and says they must be purified on the third day and on the seventh. The third day signifies for us either the third period, in which the cleansing through Christ took place, after the time of Moses and the time in which the choir of the holy prophets appeared; or the time of the resurrection, in which Christ came back to life, having nailed to the precious cross the bond that stood against us and having endured on our behalf the suffering that sets us free from sin. The seventh, on the other hand, leads us to understand the time at the consummation of the present age, in which, having entirely shaken off the burden of sin and entering into our allotted portion of holiness, we shall be with Christ, spending a pure and purified life in the blessedness that is in Christ.
That is well said, in my view.

Besides this, you would also marvel at the mystery that follows. For Eleazar the priest immediately takes up after Moses' speech and says to the men of the army who came from the battle: "This is the ordinance of the law which the Lord commanded Moses: as for the gold and the silver, the bronze, the iron, the lead and the tin, everything that will go through fire shall be cleansed, only it shall also be purified with the water of purification; and everything that will not pass through fire shall go through water. And you shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and you shall be clean, and after this you shall come into the camp." Note that Moses was first to show the victors the time for their scouring clean, but not the manner. For the law proclaims in advance the time of the cleansing through Christ. Second, and after Moses, the priest, that is, Eleazar, spoke. For Christ gives his ordinances after Moses, and he no longer shows those who act bravely the time of the cleansing, since he himself was the time; rather, he introduces the manner, and now at last sets the mystery itself before our eyes, interpreting the precise aim of the law. For he commanded that whatever among the vessels could withstand the intensity of fire should be passed through fire; but those things that have no natural strength, but are frail and somehow more liable to suffer complete destruction (he means clothing, and things made of leather and wood), should be carried through water. Thus, in the vessels of gold and silver and in the others, he hints to us in a figure of those for whom the cleansing through Christ came about as though in fire and water. For we have been baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire. So the carrying through fire and water of what was gathered from the captivity indicates precisely our own cleansing: we who were once something like a devil's wealth, which Christ acquired for himself when he entered the house of the strong man, plundered his vessels and bound the strong man. And Eleazar says that the victors will enter the camp only when they have washed their garments on the seventh day, and so will be clean. For the perfect cleansing, the putting off of all filth, will be in the last times of the consummation, as I said just now, when sin is utterly destroyed and human nature is brought back to its original and most ancient beauty. "For then," it says, "there will be a pure way, and it will be called a holy way; and no unclean person shall pass along it, but those redeemed by the Lord shall walk in it." I think, then, that my account has not missed the mark of clarity. But if anyone should choose to understand it in another way as well, we say this: he commanded that each victor's vessel, whether it happened to be of gold or silver or bronze or made of some other material, should go through fire; for, as blessed Paul writes, "The fire will test what sort of work each one's is." And he commanded that some things go through water; for the words of the Psalms hint to us that the souls of the saints are tested in no other way, except that it is in such modes as these. Thus David sang: "You have tested us, O God; you have tried us with fire, as silver is tried; we went through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment."

But, my good friend, the more studious might perhaps say to us: "Your account has shown us adequately how the chosen men once drew up for battle against the Midianites and won, and in what way they scoured off the pollution of the war. But it is now time to give full assurance whether we too shall truly share in the daring of those who act bravely and partake with them in their achievements, even though we are not wholly their equals in virtue but somehow fall short of their courage. For this is what your account promises us."

Indeed, the law on this point is right at hand and close by, offering a very clear demonstration and an approach that is not steep. "And the Lord spoke to Moses," it says, "saying: Take the sum of the spoils of the captivity, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation, and divide the spoils between the warriors who went out to battle and the whole congregation. And levy a tribute for the Lord from the men of war who went out to battle, one soul out of five hundred, of the men and of the cattle, of the oxen and of the sheep and of the donkeys; you shall take it from their half, and you shall give the first-fruits of the Lord to Eleazar the priest. And from the half belonging to the sons of Israel you shall take one out of fifty, of the men, of the oxen, of the sheep, of the donkeys and of all the cattle, and you shall give them to the Levites who keep the charge of the tabernacle of the Lord." And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the Lord had commanded Moses. For the divine command was carried out at once: the spoils were counted with fine precision, they were divided in halves, and the portions set apart, that is, the first-fruits, were rendered to the Lord, that is, to Eleazar the priest and to those of the tribe of Levi. Now, is your mind proof against forgetfulness, and strong enough to run back to what we said at the beginning?
What was that?
Did not the sacred account say that a thousand from each tribe were brought together for the needs of the war?
It did indeed.

We stated clearly and plainly that the splendour and good repute of the part will extend to the whole. God's gentleness and love for humanity arranges this very well for us too. As from a single, most fragrant incense made of many different ingredients, one fragrance from all may then rise up to God, and what is less highly esteemed may somehow share the splendour of what is most highly esteemed.
True. That is exactly what our discussion set out to examine closely.

Look, then, at God laying this down plainly for the Israelites. The chosen thousand from each tribe went to war against the Midianites. Having won the victory, I suppose, with toil and sweat, they at once divided what they had taken in the war with the whole congregation, and the rest of the people were honoured by the achievements of those who had fought bravely. For he says: "Divide the spoils, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation; divide the spoils between the warriors who went out to battle and the whole congregation." The inspired Paul also hinted in some way that what is somewhat lesser, and falls behind the greatness of the others, will share in the good repute of those who are especially chosen and more distinguished. He listed the saints of old who won good repute through faith and whose glory shone out because of their exact piety toward God, and then said: "These all died in faith without receiving the promises, since God had foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us." And he writes to others as well: "You are already made perfect; you have become kings without us. I wish you really had become kings, so that we too might reign with you!" Do you see how those of lower rank will be made perfect together with those of high standing, and how those who are not as strong as the chosen are blessed together with them? The inspired David also sings somewhere: "May you be blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth. The Lord has blessed the house of Aaron; the Lord has blessed the house of Israel; the Lord has blessed those who fear him, the small together with the great." Those called small are blessed together with the great. They cannot boast of equal strength, and they fall short in eagerness to endure hardship. Yet they may be equal in zeal and faith, and they gladden Christ with whatever strength they have. Moses and Eleazar could be a type of the one Christ, who is both high priest and lawgiver, distributing the spoils to the people with the holy angels standing beside him. The heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation would be a type of those angels. Or do you deny that there are many holy angels on earth, appointed by God to help believers and, so to speak, to lead peoples?
I affirm it. How could I not?

Christ is expected to come from heaven with the holy angels. He will sit on the throne of his glory and give each person the rewards they deserve, with honours in proportion to their achievements. That is why the wise Isaiah says to us about Christ: "Therefore he will be lord over many and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was handed over to death and he was counted among the lawless." In Christ, then, lies the distribution of good things, as was prefigured in Moses and Eleazar. For Christ is lawgiver and high priest at the same time.
You put that excellently.
And is the way the distribution was made not itself worth marvelling at?
Very much so. Those who stayed at home were honoured with a share equal to that of the fighters.

No, not equal, far from it, even though the fighters received half of the whole and the entire congregation the other half. The total number of Israelites came to six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty, with the priestly tribe set apart and left out of the count. The fighting force was a thousand from each tribe. So when the spoils were divided equally and each group received half of the whole, the honours went in far greater measure to the fewer, not to the more numerous. Whatever glory is to be given to the whole people in due time, then, and whatever the measure of the heavenly gift, as it were exactly half of it will be allotted to the chosen, who show themselves worthy of God's visitation. The other half will be given to the whole multitude, even though it is so much greater in number. For many are called, but few are chosen ... [?] for the matter is deep.
I understand. Even if we share in the glory of the saints, it will be in a lesser measure than theirs. That is what your argument hints at, and not obscurely.
You are right. But consider another point besides this. It shows especially clearly how boldly those who fight bravely can approach God.
What do you mean?

God commanded the twelve thousand warriors to bring to the high priest, out of the half of the whole allotted to them, one head in every five hundred, both of people and of cattle. This was their tribute to the Lord. But the Lord required the other multitude to hand over one soul in every fifty to the sacred tribe. Eleazar once again represents in himself the one and only true high priest, that is, Christ. So the offering of the chosen will be dedicated to Christ specially and truly, and, so to speak, personally, face to face, since they bring it to him with no one in between. This is what the blessed disciples did, and those who lead peoples still do it now, making their labours in preaching God's word a personal offering to Christ. The rest of those who are well approved also make their offerings to Christ's glory, but through intermediaries. The saints stand in between, understood as the sacred tribe, for it is said: "A chosen race, a royal priesthood." So these people's reverence and worship toward God passes through the saints. They bear fruit, but their offering does not reach Christ's presence directly. This is the sort of thing done by those who gathered the so-called collections and sent help to the saints in Jerusalem, or who refreshed those dedicated to God by some other service. The gifts of the more eminent, then, are a personal offering to God. The offering of the lesser comes through the saints in between, in second rank, as it were. The first group brings one soul in five hundred, the second one in fifty. Those who are well approved owe fewer debts, so their offering is smaller. The lesser owe far more, so what they bring is greater in number, since what is offered on each person's behalf matches that person's failings. For it says: "The one who is forgiven more will love more, and the one who is forgiven less will love less." So those who are not like the chosen offer ten times as much as they do. This is not because they are more devout or live more decently. It is because they are caught in far more failings and need a much greater cleansing. As the Saviour said: "Whoever has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean." The saints need only a very small cleansing, for nature is sick in this: it cannot be entirely free of sin.
Well said.

The chosen men of the tribes, then, obeyed the divine laws. They divided the spoils of war with the whole congregation and brought their gifts to the Lord as the law prescribed. But the leaders of the chosen men honour God with finer offerings, because their glory is more conspicuous than that of the others. For again it is written: "Then all who had been appointed over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came to Moses and said to him: 'Your servants have counted the soldiers under our command, and not one of them is missing. So we have brought the Lord an offering, what each man found: gold articles, anklets, bracelets, rings, armlets and hair ornaments, to make atonement for ourselves before the Lord.' Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from them, all of it worked into articles. All the gold of the offering that they set apart for the Lord from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds came to sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels. The soldiers had each taken plunder for themselves. Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds and brought it into the tent of witness as a memorial for the Israelites before the Lord." Do you hear how it says that the count of those who had fought was exact, so that no one was left from whom the gift had not been brought, as the divine commands required? And the leaders themselves say they wanted to bring the Lord even what he had not required: anklets, bracelets, armlets and every kind of gold jewellery. The lawgiver had commanded that the gifts be taken from the people and the cattle, and these had been brought as the divine and heavenly ordinance required. But they made a voluntary offering of the choicest of their treasures, and so the leaders of the chosen men outdid the limit of the law in their generosity. Moses and Aaron took these and brought them into the holy tent, laying them up as a memorial before the Lord. So too those who lead peoples and are appointed as rulers honour God with splendid and finer offerings. As though bringing God an ornament and dedicating it to him, they offer the many forms of virtue. In this way they outrun, as it were, even the measure of the law, and win a more brilliant reputation.
What do you mean? Give an example.

Christ ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live by the gospel. Paul was eager to confirm this from a commandment of the law too. At one point he writes that "those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar." At another he uses necessary examples to show that it is entirely blameless, saying: "Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not drink the milk of the flock? Am I saying this on human authority? Does the law not say the same? For it is written in the law of Moses: 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.' Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or is he not speaking entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the ploughman should plough in hope, and the thresher thresh in hope of a share." Then he immediately adds: "If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this right over you, do we not have a stronger claim? But we have not used this right. Instead we put up with everything, so as not to put any obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ." Then again he reinforces the point: "What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer the gospel free of charge." Do you see how he went beyond what Christ and the old law had decided? He had the right to live by the gospel, yet he offered the gospel free of charge, dedicating this to Christ as a voluntary gift. Again, neither the old law nor the new preaching has decreed that people must not marry. Indeed Paul says: "Concerning virgins I have no command from the Lord." But those who are especially vigorous in piety put the flesh to death and bring God a splendid offering: self-control beyond what the law requires. Like an ornament skilfully crafted, they offer the best kind of life, made up of both deed and word. Moses and Aaron brought what had been offered into the holy tent. For the noble deeds of the saints are acceptable to Christ, a treasure and a splendid boast. Through them the saints gain a long, or rather an endless, remembrance and show themselves worthy of God's visitation. That is what is meant by saying the offerings were placed before the Lord. And it is a great and exceptional thing to lie, as it were, in God's sight, for he gives extraordinary honour to those he deigns to look upon.
Your words seem to show us in many ways that we should be convinced of this: bearing fruit is fitting above all for those who are very brave and used to winning good repute.

Well done, Palladius, you understand rightly. This is how the matter stands by its nature, and the sacred scripture will bear witness to it. The Israelites were still camping in the wilderness when God wished to have the holy tent set up for them, as an image and type of the Church from the nations. So again he prescribed that whatever was needed for it should be gathered. He spoke to Moses, the revealer of holy things, as follows: "When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man shall give the Lord a ransom for his soul, so that no plague falls on them when they are numbered. This is what each one who passes over to be counted shall give: half a didrachm, reckoned by the holy didrachm, the didrachm being twenty obols. The half didrachm is an offering to the Lord. Everyone who passes over to be counted, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the offering to the Lord. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than half a didrachm when they give the offering to the Lord to make atonement for your souls. You shall take the silver of the offering from the Israelites and give it for the work of the tent of witness. It shall be a memorial for the Israelites before the Lord, to make atonement for your souls." See, once again the lawgiver says the count must be carried out exactly, and he commanded them to contribute gifts to the Lord, half a didrachm each. He also defines clearly who was obliged to bring it. God did not allow women to do this, nor those who were still children. In this, I suppose, he was rejecting what is feeble, soft and immature in understanding. Instead he enrolled among those who ought to bear fruit the young man who has grown up and is in his full vigour, who passes over to be counted, and for these he set the age of twenty. For according to the law, the only ones worthy to bring gifts to the Lord are those who have risen above a boyish mind and an effeminate way of thinking. They already measure up to a grown man and have reached the full stature that is understood as spiritual and in Christ. These pass over to be counted. That is, they show themselves worthy to come into God's very sight, as is sung in the Psalms: "The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous." The ransoms serve for the salvation of those who bring them, for the work of the holy tent, and as a memorial before the Lord. For the noble deeds of the saints build up churches and serve to adorn the holy tent. At the same time they help bring about the soul's salvation and crown with endless glory those who fight bravely. Or does what I say not seem true to you?
It certainly does.

God, then, decreed that the ransom, that is, the didrachm, was to be collected, and that was the tribute of the brave. But the leaders of the tribes added to what the law prescribed and brought some even greater and more notable things, the choicest of what they owned. For it is written: "And the rulers brought the emerald stones and the stones for setting, for the ephod and the breastpiece, and the blended spices, and the anointing oil, and the blend of incense." Are these things not closely related to what we discussed a little earlier? The whole fighting force brought God the captives, from human beings to cattle, as they had been commanded. But the commanders of thousands and of hundreds added anklets, bracelets, hair ornaments, rings and every kind of worked gold, and Eleazar the priest placed these in the holy tent itself. Here, likewise, the whole body of grown men paid the didrachm, but the rulers in turn brought choice stones for the ephod and the breastpiece, which went to adorn the one who was foremost in the priesthood. For those who lead peoples bring themselves to Christ as an ornament, like precious stones. That is why the prophet, referring to the holy apostles, says: "Holy stones are rolling over the earth." Such was the inspired Paul, who travelled all around from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum to preach. The company of the saints, then, are the precious stones, set there for Christ's glory. They would also be the anointing oil and the blend of incense. They spread the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, and, as though with oil, they enrich the souls of those being initiated with their all-wise teachings and with words given through the Spirit. The incense is a blend, because the knowledge of Christ is made up of two things, since he is God and man at once. Yet he is one from both, Son and Christ, to whom it is said somewhere, by us as well: "Your name is perfume poured out."

So it is the warlike and strong who are counted in God's visitation, and their fruit is the building up of churches and whatever serves God's glory. That is what these spiritual interpretations show us.

You are right. And who could doubt, or on what grounds, that God will grant a splendid and exceptional lot, indeed a share in every good thing, to those who habitually win such good repute? Or have you not heard David singing, "You shall eat the labours of your fruits," and the wise and holy Paul writing, "Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap"?
I have heard it.

No one fights bravely without a reward, and the one who said this is surely right: "God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown for his name." He will by no means forget. He will hand out the rewards for their labours to those who rise above the weakness that forces people into sin, and what is written in Numbers will again give us full assurance of this: "The Lord spoke to Moses and Eleazar the priest, saying: Take a census of the whole congregation of the Israelites, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers' houses, everyone in Israel who goes out to battle." Then, after the count by clans and tribes, it goes on: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: The land shall be divided among these as an inheritance according to the number of names. To the larger groups you shall give a larger inheritance, and to the smaller a smaller one. Each shall be given its inheritance according to those counted, whether many or few." This law concerns the inheritance of those already in their twentieth year. But after the count of the general population, the Levitical race is numbered: "These are the sons of Levi," it says, "by their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites. These are the clans of the sons of Levi." After giving the genealogy of Moses and Aaron in between, it continues about the sons of Levi: "Those counted among them came to twenty-three thousand, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not counted among the Israelites. This was the census taken by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who counted the Israelites in the plains of Moab by the Jordan, opposite Jericho. Among these there was not one man of those counted by Moses and Aaron when they counted the Israelites in the wilderness of Sinai. For the Lord had said of them: They shall surely die in the wilderness. Not one of them was left except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun." Come, then, let us go over each point again briefly, one at a time, and explain it more clearly and distinctly.
Explain, then, and don't hold back, since in matters like these it is a pleasure to go into fine detail.

So then, gathering the sense of the passage before us into a few words, this is what we say. God commands, once again, that those who have come of age, those of an age experienced in war, are to be counted. As we have already said, in the knowledge and the register kept by God, in the book of the living, it is not the feeble and the inactive that is found, nor what is still childish in understanding. It is everything that is already strong and ready for battle against the passions and sin, that has advanced to understanding, and that is already fit to do, and able to accomplish, whatever God may wish. And these divided the land very well, by tribes, by name and one by one. For those of whom the text speaks will be heirs of the holy land and will share in the good things that are hoped for, by tribes and by kindred, as in the words, "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth; blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy," and as in the other beatitudes. For this lot belongs, as it were, to those who have received mercy, to the meek, to the poor in spirit, and to those persecuted for righteousness' sake. Yet the crown of glory is also given one by one and by name, since God honours each person in proportion to his own achievements and measures out to those who act bravely the grace that is their due. Or perhaps this might be understood as a larger measure and a richer distribution: "For a good measure," it says, "pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap." And I think this is exactly what God means when he says, "To the larger you shall give a larger inheritance, and to the smaller you shall give a smaller inheritance; to each, as they were numbered, their inheritance shall be given." For the greater number of names would be a clear type of one who excels and abounds in virtue, since one person wins approval in this way and another in that, as the blessed Paul says. The land is distributed by lot, perhaps in keeping with the words addressed to God, "My lots are in your hands." For the unerring distribution of the good things to come will take place by divine decree, when he who knows everything about us will then determine for each what is fitting as his allotted share. The counting of the Levites, on the other hand, is separate, from a month old and upward. No lot is given to them among the children of Israel, nor were they numbered together with them. For the more priestly race is always somehow the holier. That is why its enrollment is set apart from the others, and why their lot is not with the others but they have a census of their own. Their portion and lot is the God of all himself, according to the saying, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." For while those called poor in spirit are to inherit the kingdom of heaven, and those who have chosen to mourn will be comforted, and the merciful will receive mercy, "Blessed," it says, "are the pure in heart, for they will see God." These would be the ones who are more priestly and holier than all the others, and their lot and portion is the exact vision of God, that is, the knowledge of the Godhead. This is what Christ promised to grant the holy apostles when he said, "I have spoken these things to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly about the Father." The enrollment of the more priestly, as I said just now, begins from a month old. For among the holier, what is recorded in the book of God is not only what is more distinguished in spiritual strength and wisdom, but also everything that lives in the simplicity that is in Christ and is childlike in malice. So the whole more priestly race is recorded, both the wise and the simple. And you may see, Palladius, some such difference in the souls, minds and ways of life of the saints. He has added that there was not a man among those numbered by Moses and Aaron when they numbered the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai, because the Lord had said to them, "They shall surely die in the wilderness"; and not one of them was left except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun. In this he shows clearly that the inheritance, and being written in the book of God, do not belong to the disobedient. They would rather befit those who have received the faith, clearly the faith in Christ. For of the disobedient the inspired David said, "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous." The divine oracle also hints to us in these words that grace is for those who believe. This is why the text says, in a mystery, that the enrollment took place by the Jordan: the one who is baptized is enrolled. Yet Israel has not fallen from hope entirely. For the remnant has been saved, as the prophet says, and its type would be Caleb and Joshua, the only ones left out of all of them, who share the inheritance and are enrolled with those not liable to the charge of unbelief. Notice, wherever it occurs, the enrollment of the saints and the allotting of their inheritance. It is carried out through Moses and through the one foremost in the priesthood, so that, as I said before, through both of them you may understand the one Christ, as high priest and lawgiver. Through him comes all grace, including being entered in the books above, which the blessed Daniel too says he saw. "Books were opened," he says, because the enrollment of all is great and varied, and for this reason the books are many and not one.
Rightly and wisely, then, did the word of Proverbs tell us: "Those who are slothful about wealth become needy, but the courageous are supported by wealth."

For they are indeed supported. They have God gracious to them and standing over them, enriching them with blessings from above, crowning them with exceedingly brilliant honour, and richly adorning them with renowned glories. Or does he not speak the truth when he says, "As I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify"?
Certainly he does.

So, I think, everyone who is vigorous in spirit accomplishes what is for the glory of God: he has trained himself in spiritual courage, has practised standing against enemies visible and invisible, knows how to save both himself and others, and can do all things in God.
I agree.
Would you like us, then, to observe this very thing closely, sketched out as on a panel, in the narratives about the inspired Abraham, which are so profitable to us?
Very much so. Why not?

It is written, then, that Lot lived and made his dwelling in Sodom. But when a terrible and heavy war overran the land, and both the nearby peoples and those from the neighbouring country, together with the rulers they had appointed, took the city by force, Lot was carried off along with those who were driven out, and was taken captive with the others. Then one of those who had escaped came, and "it was reported," it says, "to Abram the migrant. He was living by the oak of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aner, who were Abram's confederates. When Abram heard that his nephew Lot had been taken captive, he counted his own home-born servants, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them as far as Dan. He fell upon them by night, he and his servants, struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is to the left of Damascus. He brought back all the horses of Sodom, and he brought back his nephew Lot and all his possessions, and the women and the people. After he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom came out to meet him at the valley of Shaveh; this was the plain of the kings. And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High. He blessed Abram and said, 'Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your power.' And Abram gave him a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom said to Abram, 'Give me the men, and take the horses for yourself.' But Abram said to the king of Sodom, 'I stretch out my hand to the Lord God Most High, who created heaven and earth: I will not take anything of yours, not a thread or a sandal strap, so that you may not say, I made Abram rich. I will take nothing except what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me, Eshcol, Aner and Mamre; they shall take a share.' After these things the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision by night, saying, 'Do not be afraid, Abram; I am your shield; your reward will be very great.' Abram said, 'Lord and Master, what will you give me? I am departing childless, and the son of Masek, my home-born servant, is Eliezer of Damascus.' And Abram said, 'Since you have given me no offspring, my home-born servant will be my heir.' At once the voice of the Lord came to him, saying, 'This man will not be your heir; another, who will come forth from you, will be your heir.' He brought him outside and said to him, 'Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able to number them.' And he said, 'So shall your offspring be.'" Do you see how ready the saints are to act boldly, and how willingly they endure hardship? As soon as Abraham learned that Lot was in danger, he at once pitied his kinsman's misfortune. Quickly gathering his home-born servants and some of his confederates, who were not Hebrews, he marched readily against those who had done the wrong, overcame them with ease, and freed from captivity both his nephew Lot himself and those who had fallen into the hands of the victors. Then, paying him the honour fitting for a victor, the king of Sodom and Melchizedek, the priest of God Most High, rightly came out to meet him, as it is written. Melchizedek did not meet him empty-handed. He brought the symbols of the priesthood as it was established at that time, bread and wine, and he blessed Abraham and gave him holy words as his prize. So Abraham acted bravely and won the victory. Such, in some way, are always those who are courageous in Christ and whose minds hold a boldness most pleasing to God. As an example and a confirmation of what I am saying, I will add the holy apostles. Satan was easily plundering everything, and those opposed to the doctrines of truth were taking the souls of the simpler people captive; but the apostles resisted vigorously. They armed their home-born servants alongside themselves, that is, those brought up in the sacred Scriptures, together with some of their confederates who were not Hebrews, by which I mean again those who still think the things of the world but contend alongside the saints and emulate them. Acting bravely in this way, they won the victory and snatched the captives from his greed. Some they rescue by dragging them out of idolatry and out of worshipping the creation instead of the Creator; others they rescue from knowledge falsely so called. For so brilliant and noble a courage they gain as their reward the honours that come from those in the world, for "the king of Sodom," it says, "went out to meet Abraham"; and from Melchizedek, the priest of God Most High, they gain the blessing that comes through Christ, who gladdens them with life-giving grace in bread and wine. So, speaking truly of themselves, they say very well, "Blessed are you by the Lord who made heaven and earth." Melchizedek would be a type of the priesthood according to Christ, and the matter will not, I think, need many words to prove it, since Sacred Scripture is enough for that. When the king of Sodom said to the inspired Abraham, the victor, "Give me the men, and take the horses for yourself," he at once swore that he would take nothing at all, except the food of those who had toiled with him and a share for his confederates Eshcol, Aner and Mamre. For the saints fight and contend nobly for the freedom of those who were lost, and enter into every kind of toil, yet they take nothing from the world. Nor do they gather earthly wealth, for they firmly refuse the reproach that would come from it: "So that you may not say," it says, "I made Abraham rich." They accept only food from those whom they benefit. For the worker deserves his wages, and Christ commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should live by the gospel. The confederates, however, do receive shares, since God, I think, blesses those who share the zeal of the saints even in the affairs of this life. Their possessions increase in due measure by just means. For to those who have not yet entirely departed from earthly things, but are divided, as it were, between God and the world, God also distributes earthly blessings. In this way he blessed Jacob, multiplying his flocks.
Well said.

To those who are approved in this way and made illustrious, as now his genuine children, he who knows how to save says that they must not grow faint, and he usefully promises that they will receive an abundant reward. In doing so he puts that feeble and most cowardly passion, fear, as far as possible from the flock of those who fear him; he sharpens them to eagerness by the hope of what has been promised and makes them stronger. So the inspired Paul too, being of this disposition, said at one time, "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me," and at another, "I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness." But the inspired Abraham is deeply distressed, and although he has a home-born son, he is not free of despondency. "For what will you give me," he says, "if I depart childless?" He counts having illegitimate fruit as no better than childlessness. Then God promises the son born of the free woman, that is, Isaac, and says that in him Abraham will be the father of many nations and will have offspring like the stars of heaven. For it greatly grieved the holy apostles to have illegitimate fruit, born as if from a slave woman, that is, from the worship according to the law. They sought rather the one born of freedom, that is, of the New Covenant. This was Christ, of whom Isaac too is understood as a type, being born according to promise and through faith. Indeed the blessed Paul says of the things in the law that he once boasted of: "Whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ. More than that, I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I regard them as refuse, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the one that comes through faith in Jesus Christ." For in Christ they have become fathers of many nations and of countless offspring, just as Abraham did in Isaac. And we will apply what has been said on this point not only to the holy apostles of old, but also to those after them who have received the priesthood and lead the Churches, and indeed to everyone else who is holy and good.
On Courage in Christ.

The aim of the saints, then, Palladius, even if they surpass others in their way of life, should be to claim nothing in the world as their own. That is how they would be wise and strong, full of good hope, and well fortified by favours from above. Be sure of it, my friend: the matter stands no other way. If they keep their minds above the distractions of the world and its passing desires, they will find their enemies very easy to defeat and will overcome their opponents quite readily, because God shakes their power before the battle. But if they too are caught by worldly passions and entangled in more earthly desires, they will lie open to those who have set out to pursue them, easily overrun and very easily captured. Shown to be stripped of the protection from above, they will lie before their enemies like prey ready for the taking.
And what proof is there of what you have said? I would like to know clearly.
The sacred Scripture, which usefully tells of what happened to the people of old. Did not the divine Paul himself say that those things were written for our instruction?
He did. And what they show will bring us no small benefit, for the shadows were types of the truth.

Then let us speak now. Having crossed the Jordan, the Israelites attacked Jericho. Following the divine commands, they set out to take it by siege, expecting to overcome and capture it at once, and their best fighters were there, equipped according to the custom of war. For it is written: “And Joshua son of Nun went in to the priests and said to them: Command the people to go around and encircle the city, and let the fighting men pass by, armed, before the Lord.” In the same way, when Christ gives the command through the voice of those who lead us, we take the field against our enemies. We choose to fight not against blood and flesh but against principalities and powers, and against the law that has seized tyrannical control in the members of the flesh. Then we shall be in the sight of God, fitted out, as it were, with the divine and spiritual full armour (for “our weapons are not fleshly,” as Paul says), and made splendid by the glories of righteousness. So the God and Master of all looks upon his best fighters, clad in the bright armour of righteousness. This is what is meant by the armed fighting men passing by as though before Christ. To come under God's watchful care is truly a precious thing and much to be prayed for, since it is not unreasonable to think that God punishes those who have grieved him by turning away from them. He says: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you.” When the siege had dragged on to the seventh day, Joshua son of Nun again said to the sons of Israel: “Shout to the Lord, for the Lord has given us the city. The city shall be devoted to destruction, it and everything in it, to the Lord of hosts, Sabaoth. Only Rahab the harlot you shall spare, with everything in her house. But keep yourselves from what is devoted, so that you do not covet it and take something of what is devoted, and so make the camp of the sons of Israel a thing devoted to destruction and destroy us. And all silver and gold, bronze and iron, shall be holy to the Lord; it shall be brought into the treasury of the Lord.” He allowed the men who had fought bravely to enjoy the rest of the spoils, but all silver and gold, bronze and iron, he says, must be brought into the treasury of the Lord. For this was what was called “devoted,” that is, what is set apart from everything else and reserved for God. But Achan set the commandment at nothing: “Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah,” it says, “took some of what was devoted. And the Lord was angry with the sons of Israel.” I think this teaches that those who steer their minds, made strong in Christ, clear of worldly pleasures and the distractions of this life, who have chosen to win distinction with the weapons of righteousness, and who have already come under Christ's watchful care, should desire nothing that the world admires: not wealth, not glory, not power or rank, and not the unholy doctrines of Greek wisdom. Silver may serve as a type of the splendour that comes with honours and high rank, for it is a bright metal; gold is a type of wealth. Bronze may signify the resonant tongue of the world's wise men; and iron, which is very hard and resists every other material, strength and power. Suppose someone chooses to take a share of these. Even if he holds the highest rank with God, is counted among the warriors, and has become distinguished for spiritual courage, he will offend God. Having chosen to grieve his comrade-in-arms and helper by turning aside into what is false, he will fall under the wrath that follows.

Well said; I would agree. But tell me this, turning the discussion briefly away from the matter at hand and the story. Why were the silver and gold, the bronze and iron, given to the Lord? Why were they not rather sent out of the camp, either as perhaps useless or as able to defile? After all, the force of the spiritual interpretation has shown them to be abominable.

Because, Palladius, all splendour, all wisdom and wealth, and strength as well, are fittingly and devoutly dedicated to God. His are the glory and all splendour, wealth and wisdom and power. If someone receives these from him and is enriched from the treasury of the Lord, with spiritual wealth, I mean, so that he has spiritual glory, understanding and strength, he will be admired and envied. But if he wants to take these things from the world, he will be loathsome and hateful to God, who loves virtue, and will be subject to judgement and punishment. For love of pleasure always follows wealth; arrogance lives right next door to splendour and high rank; greed is fastened to power; and the wisdom of the world brings ugly doctrines, even if those who wrote them had a resonant tongue. Paul says something of this kind: “If anyone among you is wise, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” So Achan offended God by taking not from the treasury of Christ but, as it were, from the world of Jericho. The harm that followed from this, the consequences of divine wrath, did not fall only on the man condemned for these things but afflicted the whole congregation. Cut off from the help that comes from above, Israel, once so hard to defeat, became powerless and weak.
And how, or from what source, can we learn that this account is true?

From what is written next. After the events at Jericho and the brilliant and vigorous deeds done there by all Israel, “Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, saying: Go up and spy out Ai. And the men went up and spied out Ai, and returned to Joshua and said to him: Do not let all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and take the city. Do not lead all the people there, for they are few. So about three thousand men went up there, and they fled before the men of Ai. The men of Ai killed about thirty-six of them, pursued them from the gate and crushed them on the slope; and the heart of the people was terrified and became like water.” The men who had taken cities, laid waste whole countries and conquered the most savage nations without effort now met men from Ai they could not defeat. They barely escaped and withdrew with losses. Yet at the start they had not even wanted the whole body of fighting men under arms, and had openly declared that the city could be defeated very easily, even by a few. “Do not let all the people go up,” they said, “but about two thousand men.” At this unexpected blow, a disaster beyond all expectation, Joshua was deeply dismayed. He tore his clothes and fell down before God, astonished at what the cause could be. And God said: “Get up; why have you fallen on your face like this? The people have sinned and broken my covenant which I made with them; they have stolen some of what was devoted and put it among their own goods. The sons of Israel will not be able to stand before their enemies; they will turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become a thing devoted to destruction. I will not be with you any longer unless you remove what is devoted from among you.” When Achan had been pointed out, Joshua questioned him, saying: “Give glory today to the Lord God of Israel; make your confession and tell me what you have done, and do not hide it from me.” Achan answered Joshua and said: “It is true that I have sinned before the Lord God of Israel. This is what I did. Among the spoil I saw a fine embroidered mantle, two hundred didrachms of silver and a tongue of gold weighing fifty didrachms. I coveted them and took them, and see, they are hidden in the ground inside my tent, with the silver hidden beneath them.” You see that the thief himself says he saw among the spoil an embroidered mantle, two hundred didrachms of silver and a tongue of gold weighing fifty didrachms, and that he coveted them, that is, that he came to an unlawful desire for them. The mantle is thought to be a soldier's garment; they say it was a cloak woven in many colours. A soldier's garment is a symbol of greed, since the military class has always had a natural fondness for grabbing more than its share. Silver, again, is a type of worldly splendour, and the tongue is a type of the sweet-spoken wisdom of the Greeks. Such indeed are the tongue and learning of the Greek sages: golden, as it were, and highly prized for the brilliance of their style. Once the sin had been uncovered, Joshua had Achan punished, for he had not wronged himself alone. He had spread the harm caused by his own unrestrained desire to the whole congregation. Perhaps this is what was said to us so well and so plainly through the voice of Paul: “Drive out the wicked person from among you; a little leaven leavens the whole lump.” Have I shown you clearly, then, from the first case, that of Abraham, that the saints' glorious strength remains undamaged and their power to defeat their enemies follows easily, if they choose to seek nothing from the world? And from the case of Achan, that things turned out the opposite way for a man who swerved from the straight path and leaned toward the things of the world?
Certainly; the argument is clear.
