That the saints must be seen to be of one character in every way and not double-minded becomes clear from the plain words of the law: “A man's gear shall not be on a woman, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment, for whoever does these things is an abomination before the Lord.” To God it is equally an abomination and a most unsightly spectacle to have a reputation for nobility while being soft, which is what it means for a man's gear to be on a woman, and to suffer from softness while being courageous, which likewise is what it means for a man to put on a woman's garment.
What exactly do you mean?
Is not hypocrisy a wicked and disreputable thing in the eyes of both God and men?
True.

Suppose, then, that someone loves pleasure and lacks self-control, and his very deeds show him to be so, and yet he fabricates a reputation for decency for himself. Would you praise such a man, Palladius?
Certainly not.
And what of the man who truly is orderly and decent? Will you not think that he ought to stay firmly fixed in the same mind, and not be known as anything other than what he is?
I do.

Then let the brittle, soft mind of certain people never sneak in under a reputation for courage; that is what “A man's gear shall not be on a woman” means. Nor let the truly strong seek softness; that again is what “A man shall not put on a woman's garment” means. The baseness is equal in both cases, and both offences are an outrage against virtue.
Softness, it seems, is a dangerous thing, and it does real harm.

Have no doubt about it at all. This passion is utterly to be rejected and hateful to God. That is why anyone who happens to be guilty of such offences is even struck from the sacred rolls. For I say that a man who is truly strong and noble must never carelessly let his own mind be shattered. He must keep it above all fear and hesitation and, firmly grounded in faith in God, say: “I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me.” And he must refuse, as something that brings destruction and makes us rejected by God, any choice to set his mind on earthly things. Indeed, it is written again in Deuteronomy: “If you go out to war against your enemies and see horse and rider and an army larger than yours, you shall not be afraid of them, for the Lord your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. When you draw near to battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people and say to them: Hear, O Israel: today you are going into battle against your enemies. Do not let your hearts faint; do not be afraid or shattered, and do not turn aside before them; for the Lord your God, who goes out with you, will fight beside you against your enemies to save you. Then the scribes shall speak to the people, saying: Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, so that he does not die in battle and another man dedicate it. Has any man planted a vineyard and not enjoyed it? Let him go back to his house, so that he does not die in battle and another man enjoy it. Has any man become engaged to a wife and not married her? Let him go back to his house, so that he does not die in battle and another man marry her. And the scribes shall speak further to the people and say: Is any man afraid and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, so that he does not make his brother's heart as fainthearted as his own.”
I too would say that those who trust in God must excel in virtue and show courage in every good thing whatever. But I cannot see how, or in what sense, some are sent away from the war as unfit.

Do you not know that no one could win God's approval, and no one would even choose to endure toil for the sake of devotion to him, unless he regarded life in this world as a temporary stay in a foreign land? This was depicted for us beautifully and clearly, as in an image and in types, in the lives of the saints. The divine Abraham lived as a foreigner in tents and moved from place to place, and all Israel in the wilderness broke camp often and lived in tents. The prophet David too takes great pride in this when he says to God: “Spare me, for I am a foreigner on the earth and a sojourner, like all my fathers.” And he eagerly welcomed the dwellings above, saying: “How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.” Such people set their minds on things above and thirst for the dwellings in heaven, which the Saviour himself promises to those who love him, saying: “I am going, and I will prepare a place for you, and I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be there with me.” So the man who builds a house and devotes himself eagerly to working on it is a type of the man who cannot bear to regard the present life as a temporary stay. The man who plants a vineyard is a type of the man who loves possessions and gain. And the man who is about to be engaged to a woman stands for the man who is mad for women, softened by luxury, and has given his mind over to the desires of the flesh. That is why they leave the sacred army of fighting men when the herald calls. The herald anticipated what men in the grip of such passions would likely think and say, and he called it out ahead of them. Is it not true that people who suffer from such things somehow love to keep themselves out of hardship in times of persecution? They do not follow the zeal that springs from love of God, because they reflect that if they should suffer anything in the struggle, they would lose their houses and possessions and the things they desire and hold dear. That is why they are seen to be so timid and ignoble. So the scribe cried out what those men would likely think and say, striking the ignoble man with veiled reproofs and witty taunts, the man who makes excuses for his weaknesses and gathers worldly pleasures as a kind of food for his cowardice. For this reason God commanded the herald to make the last proclamation naked and undisguised. “And the scribes shall speak further to the people,” it says, “and say: If any man is afraid and fainthearted, let him go to his house, so that he does not make his brother's heart as fainthearted as his own.” He all but says plainly: “The man devoted to earthly things, who builds houses, plants vineyards and gives in to the pleasures of the flesh, will certainly be cowardly and weak. Such a man is entirely unfit and will do harm to others, for bad company corrupts good morals.” And sometimes the man who is most easily overcome by cowardice drags the strong and courageous down into unmanliness. So the divine Paul also rebuked some who wanted to stop him from going up to Jerusalem. He said: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Note too that the excuse of those invited to the wedding feast was: “I have bought a field,” and “I have married a wife, and I cannot come.” This is how it is written in the Gospel, in the parables. And if you like, it is not hard to find proof of this from ancient examples as well.
Tell me, then, without delay; you will do me a great service.

Very well. As we have read in Numbers: “After this the people set out from Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men for yourself to spy out the land of the Canaanites, which I am giving to the sons of Israel as a possession. You shall send one man from each tribe, according to their ancestral clans, every one of them a leader. So Moses sent them out from the wilderness of Paran at the command of the Lord, all of them men who were leaders of the sons of Israel.” After listing those who were sent, by tribe and family, it goes on: “And they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, near Lebo-hamath.” And a little further on: “And they came as far as the Valley of the Cluster and spied it out. From there they cut a branch with a single cluster of grapes on it and carried it on poles, along with some of the pomegranates and figs. They named that place the Valley of the Cluster because of the cluster that the sons of Israel cut there. After spying out the land, they returned from there after forty days. They went and came to Moses and Aaron and to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back a report to them and to the whole congregation, showed them the fruit of the land, and told him: We came into the land to which you sent us. It is a land flowing with milk and honey, and this is its fruit. But the nation that lives in it is bold, its cities are strong, walled and very large, and we saw the descendants of Anak there.” Do you see how the most easily frightened and timid of those who spied out the promised land plainly admitted that the land was rich in vines, fertile and heavy with ripe fruit? Yet they wove into their report things meant to make people afraid. They called the nation living there bold, they kept on about strong and walled cities, and so they drove Israel from the hope of conquest and frightened them into cowardice.
That is so.

But those wise and spirited men, Caleb and Joshua, stood against their quibbling. They said to the people and to the holy Moses: “No! Let us go straight up and take possession of it, for we are well able to overcome them.” Yet the men sent with them would not stop, insisting that the land of promise would be hard for the Israelites to take. Then it says: “And the whole congregation raised its voice, and the people wept all that night, and all the sons of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them: ‘If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or in this wilderness! If only we had died! Why is the Lord bringing us into this land to fall in war? Our wives and our children will become plunder. Now, then, it is better for us to go back to Egypt.’ And they said to one another: ‘Let us appoint a leader and go back to Egypt.’” The whole congregation sank to this depth of wretchedness and cowardice. Joshua son of Nun tried, as it were, to bring them round to courage. He tore his clothes and poured out countless praises of the land, but they would not take heart. Instead their senseless faintheartedness grieved God, who was defending them, and they made the fulfillment of their hope depend on their own strength. So in the end God swore an oath, saying: “None of these men shall see the land that I swore to their fathers, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.” Can anyone doubt it, then? The coward who shirks toil and is small in faith destroys others along with himself and corrupts them with bad company, and he will fall away from his inheritance and from his hope in God. But the strong and most valiant man will be set within that hope and will be known to God.
There is no doubt. The demonstration is enough.
So, as we said at the beginning, a person caught up in worldly pleasures is unfit for the spiritual battle.
Very much so.

I would add this, since I think one ought to hunt very eagerly for whatever is profitable. Someone who has only recently begun to practice any virtue at all is not yet fit for battle, and he is very easily carried off toward wrongdoing.
What do you mean?

It is written in Deuteronomy: “If anyone has newly taken a wife, he shall not go out to war, and no duty shall be laid upon him. He shall be free at home, and for one year he shall make glad the wife whom he has taken.” Well then, Palladius, should we attend only to the bare letter? Does the lawgiver, who loves virtue, really keep the fighting man at home and refuse him the chance to win distinction because trivial dalliance with a wife has got the better of him and he puts love of the flesh ahead of what is necessary?
I would by no means concede that this is what the lawgiver intends. But there seems to be some persuasive reasoning behind it.
Then I will go back to what I said and repeat it: a man who has taken hold of virtue but has not yet fully achieved it is easily carried off toward its opposite.
Explain how, because I am not quite following.

Solomon says somewhere: “Say that wisdom is your sister, and make understanding your close friend.” We make the virtues our own, as it were, when we have worked as hard as we can to bear fruit in them. One person, perhaps, has wisdom in knowledge; another has trained himself in gentleness and freedom from anger; or someone has whatever other such virtue he chooses to achieve. Is a mind that has only just begun to show goodness in these things fit to be tested and tried straight away? Suppose someone who has only recently come to live with wisdom meets people who twist what is right. Since he is not yet standing firmly or steadily grounded in understanding, won't he be twisted himself, rather than prevail and fend off the harm they do?
So it seems.
And if someone provokes a man who is practicing gentleness but has not yet been trained in it, won't he easily slip into anger?
I think so.
But a seasoned wise man will fight it out with the clever, and he will vigorously set the fruits of right reasoning against their tricks?
True.
And what about someone who has achieved gentleness? Isn't he hard to move to anger, even if people sometimes try to goad him into it?
I agree.

The law is right, then. It elegantly depicts the virtue that lives with the saints in the form of a wife, and it says: “If anyone has newly taken a wife, he shall not go out to war, and no duty shall be laid upon him; he shall be free at home. For one year he shall make glad the wife whom he has taken.” The law does not let someone who is, so to speak, newly set in place, and whose zeal for the good is still fresh, be weighed down with toils and persecutions. Instead it lets him stay at leisure and by himself, as it were, so that, kept warm, he may be bound fast by love for virtue. We shall find that the holy apostles did something similar. When they wrote to converts from the Gentiles who had just been called to the knowledge of God, they said plainly: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than this: that you abstain from fornication, from what is strangled, and from blood.” With wise accommodation they left aside the heavier commandments and told them to keep a few necessary ones, because they knew how little hardship people just brought into the worship of God could bear. And so the God of all spares such people his wrath and his charges against them, even if they lose heart as they travel the unfamiliar road of toil. Afterward, however, he does exact penalties and subjects people to the stirrings of his wrath. By then they are no longer weak because toil is new to them. Rather, they are falling back into what is pleasant and smooth and very readily pouring themselves out into what does not befit them. For isn't virtue uphill? Isn't the road to it rough? And mustn't anyone who has chosen to achieve it sweat?
I agree.

Surely, then, it was not unreasonable, or rather it was holy and fitting, for those just brought to this to be trained with indulgence. Their zeal is not yet firmly established; they walk on tender feet, as it were, and still suffer from weakness. The seasoned man, by contrast, should be hardened with toils and fears, since by now he is carried along, as if by necessity, toward endurance and obedience.
You think excellently.

And the matter is quite clear if we are willing to look closely at what happened to the ancients as a type. For it is written: “Moses led the sons of Israel away from the Red Sea and brought them into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water to drink. Then they came to Marah, and they could not drink the water of Marah, for it was bitter. That is why he named that place Bitterness. And the people grumbled against Moses, saying: ‘What shall we drink?’ Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a tree. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet.” The Israelites had just left the land of the Egyptians and thrown off the heavy, unbearable yoke of slavery to them, and at God’s call they were hurrying to move to the land promised long ago to their fathers. The first hardship to meet them was a lack of water. They found water only barely, after long toil, and even then they could not enjoy it without hardship, for it was bitter, as Scripture says. But when wood was mixed into it, it was changed into something pleasant and sweet, because God had shown the divine Moses how to do it. So it is with us. We are being trained by divine law to choose to follow God, who draws us out of slavery to the passions and sets us free from the tyranny of demons. While we are tested, we must sweat and so be crowned with the wreath of approval. We must waste away the things of the flesh by the toils of ascetic discipline and, as one charms a fearsome beast, subdue with thirst and fasting the untamed impulse that always looks toward pleasure. When we want to achieve self-control, our first battle is against the flesh and its concerns, and I do not think anyone could practice virtue any other way. So the thirst that came upon the ancients in the wilderness is a type of the toils of ascetic discipline, and bodily exercises are the first fruits of training. Notice that they were not sent into war at the very start. Those who have only just begun to master the passions and achieve virtue are not immediately set to wrestle against principalities and powers, because they are still feeble and not yet very secure. Instead they are tested by the toils of the flesh, and God measures the heaviness of the toil to the condition of those being tried. This, I think, is what is meant by the words: “No temptation has seized you except what is human. But God is faithful,” it says, “and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear; with the temptation he will also provide the way out, so that you can endure it.” The sweat poured out for virtue is very bitter, but Christ refashions it into something pleasant and sweet, for he is called the tree of life and is the tree of life. He himself said somewhere in the Gospels: “If they do these things when the wood is green, what will they do when it is dry?” There he calls himself green and flourishing wood. And it is a tree that God shows to the divine Moses, because only the Father reveals the Son, since only he knows him: “No one knows who the Son is except the Father.” So in Christ, the tree of life, bitter things are sweet and unbearable things bearable, and things that by their own nature usually destroy become necessary for life.
What do you mean?

Toils are very bitter and waste away the body, but they make the soul a sharer in eternal life. Paul said as much: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” And again: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” If that is true, who would ever choose to endure such harsh toils without the sweet hope that is in Christ?
No one at all, I think.

Consider, then (for we must go back, Palladius, and recall what came at the beginning), how Israel was thirsty in the wilderness and grumbled against the all-wise Moses, yet fell into this faintheartedness without punishment. They paid no penalty and suffered nothing from God’s wrath, even though God usually punishes those found guilty of this. At the beginning, someone still in training for virtue is shown mercy even if he sometimes stumbles. Afterward, though, excessive faintheartedness cannot be pardoned, nor can unbridled running off after strange desires. In fact, the holy Scripture says this about the sons of Israel in Numbers: “They set out from the mountain of the Lord on a three days’ journey, and the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before them on a three days’ journey to seek out a resting place for them. Whenever the ark set out, Moses said: ‘Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered; let all who hate you flee.’ And when it came to rest he said: ‘Turn, O Lord, the thousands of ten thousands in Israel.’ And the cloud overshadowed them by day when they set out from the camp. The people were grumbling wickedly before the Lord. The Lord heard and was angered, and fire from the Lord blazed up among them and devoured part of the camp. The people cried out to Moses; Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire died down. And the name of that place was called Burning, because fire from the Lord had blazed up among them.” And after this, again: “Setting out from Mount Hor by the road to the Red Sea, they went around the land of Edom, and the people lost heart on the way. The people spoke against God and against Moses, saying: ‘Why have you brought us out of the land of Egypt to kill us in the wilderness? For there is no bread and no water, and we loathe this worthless bread.’ Then the Lord sent deadly serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and many of the sons of Israel died.” So you see that the whispering, grumbling people was consumed by fire and by serpents. They set out from the mountain of the Lord with the ark leading them forward and searching out rest ahead of them; Moses was praying and interceding, and the cloud was overshadowing them. Yet they called the bread from heaven worthless and raised a great outcry against God and Moses. For this reason some of them inevitably became the work of fire, and the others died at once from the bites of bitter serpents.
And what should we notice further in both accounts? And what is the mountain of the Lord?

By the mountain of the Lord I think it means Sinai. The Creator of all came down upon it in the form of fire and was seen by all the people, as it is written, and there he gave as oracles the laws about what must be done: “For there he set ordinances and judgments for the sons of Israel.” But it was Christ who was giving those laws even then. That is why he calls the laws given through Moses his own words. He said: “Truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until everything is accomplished.” And: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” Come, then, let us leave aside the coarse surface of the history and look at the finer spiritual meanings. Some have already been counted worthy to see God and know him, and with the eyes of the mind they have beheld the brightness of the divine nature as if on a mountain, that is, at a supreme and lofty height, for God’s glory and nature are beyond all things. They have presented themselves to Christ, as it were, through faith; they have heard his words, and they have promised obedience, as Israel also did then when it said: “All that the Lord your God has said we will do and hear.” These people will enjoy the care that truly befits them and will receive a solicitude sufficient for their salvation. For they will have Christ himself as their leader and defender, going before them to seek out rest for them. Christ was the first, for our sake and on our behalf, to set himself against Satan, who had conquered of old. He fasted and was tempted in the wilderness so that we might have rest, seeing Satan conquered, fallen and laid beneath our own feet. That is why he said: “In the world you have tribulation, but take courage: I have conquered the world.” And again: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the Enemy.” He was the first, for our sake and on our behalf, to engage death. He destroyed its power and sought out rest for us, renewing us to incorruption. He was the first to enter paradise; he prevailed, as it were, upon the turning sword and removed the sin that shut us out. For he himself paid our debts on our behalf, and by his wound we were healed, as it is written. He was the first to ascend to his Father and God, opening the way above for us and preparing the dwellings above in advance. That is why he said: “I will go and prepare a place for you.” So Christ was prefigured in the ark, as it were. The ark was built of wood that does not rot, and it enclosed the divine law, which is the Word of God. You can see that the mystery of Christ resembles this, for the Word was God in an incorruptible temple. The ark, then, went ahead to seek out rest for the Israelites, and Christ too goes ahead of us in the ways just described. Besides this, he fulfills the office of mediator and becomes our advocate with the Father and the propitiation for us, just as Moses did of old. When the ark set out, Moses said: “Arise, O Lord, let your enemies be scattered; let all who hate you flee.” And when it came to rest: “Turn, O Lord, the thousands of ten thousands in Israel.” Long ago the Only-begotten said through the voice of the Psalmist: “Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord.” When he arose to help us, his enemies fell, and those who resisted him and fought against the divine glory fled. For on the cross he triumphed over principalities and powers, and by dying he abolished the ruler of this age, as it is written. Then, having come to rest, as it were, and completed his whole saving plan through his resurrection from the dead and his journey up to the Father, he turned the whole earth and made thousands of ten thousands his own worshipers. “For when I am lifted up from the earth,” he said, “I will draw all people to myself.” So Moses’ prayer is a type of Christ’s mediation in his human form, as he prays and asks the God and Father for the best things for us. As the divine John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world.” Furthermore, we also have him as our protector, understood in the overshadowing cloud. Let anyone justified by faith in him hear this: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.” In the Gospel parable about paying the wages, some also say: “We have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.” By “the scorching heat” and “the burden of the day” I think they mean the fierce, fiery heat of untamed pleasures, or perhaps of temptations. So Christ has become our helper and protector for salvation. Some, however, have been counted worthy to see God and have heard the divine proclamations for themselves, and by confessing their faith they have in a sense already promised obedience. When these people change for the worse and reject the one who goes ahead of them and leads them, I mean Christ, who seeks out rest for them, who intercedes as mediator, and who is understood as their protector in the type of the cloud, then they are called to account for their own folly, quite rightly, and undergo the savage penalty of fire. This, I think, is what the wise Paul himself meant when he said: “For if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.”

So those who through sin have rejected the whole saving plan that is understood in Christ will be fuel for the fire. The grumbling, it seems, signifies apostasy and an unwillingness to accept the salvation he offers. And this is so even though they have tasted grace and have, in what they have already experienced, a secure pledge of what is to come.

So I say. Others too lost heart and raised the same outcry. They whispered feebly against God and Moses and called the manna from heaven worthless bread, but they were destroyed by the serpents. Likewise, those who dishonor the Savior and Redeemer of all by their ingratitude, count the gift of freedom as nothing, and even disparage his life-giving Word and the gift given through the Spirit as useless, will fall prey to the bites of the murderous dragon. But those who are not caught in such monstrous faults will escape both wickedness and the punishment and penalty that hang over it, and they will prove stronger than their enemies: “For they shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the dragon.” It is settled, then, and the facts themselves bear witness to it: it is dangerous for those already trained to grow slack and fall back into cowardice. They are no strangers to winning approval through toil; sweating for virtue has already become familiar to them, a well-worn road.
It is settled indeed, and it is true.

Our discussion has made it clear to us that grumbling against God is hateful to God and deserves punishment. Faintheartedness, even when the hardships in between seem small, amounts to a kind of accusation or outcry against the gentleness of the Savior. But it is no less accursed to love slackness, and, when one could delight blamelessly in the divine gifts themselves and be fed by the words that come from above and through the Spirit, to break loose without restraint toward perishable pleasures and the impure love of the flesh. To choose evil things instead is plainly an insult to what is better and saving. To rank earthly things above heavenly ones, though they are full of the deepest foulness, is a most unholy verdict of the mind. The prophet Isaiah rightly all but weeps over this when he says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, who put darkness for light and light for darkness.” We shall find that the Israelites fell into just such evil failings. Right after they were punished for grumbling, they fell sick with a desire that was its neighbor and partner, a desire for all the most shameful things. By spitting, as it were, on what came from God, and scowling in their impiety at the good things from heaven, they inevitably provoked the Judge against themselves. For it is written: “And the mixed multitude among them felt a craving, and the sons of Israel sat down and wept and said, ‘Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish we used to eat in Egypt for nothing, and the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic. But now our soul is dried up. There is nothing at all before our eyes but the manna.’” And Moses heard them, it says, weeping clan by clan, each man at the door of his tent; and the Lord’s anger burned very hot, and in Moses’ sight it was evil. Or would you say it does not deserve the wrath of God, and the condemnation of holy men, that people already trained should sink to such softness and such cowardly reasoning? They were so overcome by the wish to go back to such outlandish impurities, and so paralyzed by lack of self-control, that they wailed like boys, as though they could not bear the sharp assault of desire.
You are right.

The all-wise Moses was distressed and terribly downcast over this. He cried out openly that he could never carry by himself a people so easily swept into frenzy and rebellion. So God appointed men to help him and share this burden, seventy in number, and he made them more distinguished by the gift of the Spirit, for they prophesied in the camp. And to Moses he says: “And you shall say to the people: Purify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, because you wept before the Lord, saying, ‘Who will give us meat to eat? It was good for us in Egypt.’ The Lord will give you meat to eat, and you shall eat meat. You shall eat meat not for one day, nor two, nor five days, nor ten days, nor twenty days, but for a whole month, until it comes out of your nostrils and makes you sick, because you disobeyed the Lord who is among you and wept before him, saying, ‘Why did we come out of Egypt?’” This grieved the Redeemer deeply: that Israel thought nothing even of slavery, and counted the hardships in Egypt as nothing, for the sake of meat and the most foul-smelling vegetables. Hot and sharp pleasures often persuade us too to think slavery under the devil bearable, and to bind ourselves under the yokes of sin for the sake of perishable and earthly desires. Yet even then he let them eat meat, not for one day, nor perhaps for ten, but for thirty days, which signifies how long his anger against them lasted. And now too he allows those who have inclined without restraint to worldly pleasures to share in fleshly things if they choose, sometimes for long periods. This is how he is said to have handed some over to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting. But for the Israelites the food turned to sickness. And for those who love fleshly things, and prefer perishable earthly things to the spiritual manna, which is the word of God, the venture will end in death. This, I think, is what is meant by “Whoever sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh.” The cure for such a sickness is perhaps this: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh. For the flesh wars against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other.” So if the Israelites had been willing to count the supply of manna as delight enough, the manna that is the spiritual bread of angels and a type of the sweetness given through the Spirit, they would not have carried out the desire of the flesh, nor reaped corruption from it. The people’s graves are very conspicuous. There, it says, they buried the people who craved, as in the saying, “They shall be a spectacle to all flesh.” The people who suffered this were called “the craving people,” in line, I suppose, with what is said about certain others: “whose glory is in their shame.” Their name came from their sin. The reproach for their cowardice was written forever over those who died so pitiably, and what made them notable was the very thing for which they were condemned.
True.

Those who have truly chosen to love learning, then, must above all reject impatience in hardships, feeble grumbling and ungrateful idle talk. Above all they must reject what is somehow more unholy than the rest: longing for the defilements of wickedness and love of the flesh. Such a person wavers between two ways, and the hamstring of his mind is lame. For it is written: “Woe to cowardly hearts and slack hands, and to the sinner who walks on two paths.” I think that those who value endurance and steadfast patience above everything must remember Christ’s words: “If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me.” That is: if anyone wants to be my disciple, let him come eagerly through sufferings like mine, and walk and love the same path, as it were. Such a person will rest with me and live with me. This is what he himself asked of God the Father for us, saying: “I want them to be with me where I am.” We are also with Christ in another way: while we walk on earth, we no longer live in a fleshly way but a spiritual one, and we are eager to make what pleases him our lodging and our rest. You have the type of this written in Numbers: “On the day the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony. And in the evening there was over the tabernacle something like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was continually: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night. Whenever the cloud went up from the tabernacle, the sons of Israel set out after it, and in the place where the cloud stopped, there the sons of Israel encamped. At the command of the Lord the sons of Israel will encamp, and at the command of the Lord they will set out. All the days that the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the sons of Israel will remain encamped. When the cloud lingers over the tabernacle many days, the sons of Israel will keep the charge of God and will not set out. And when the cloud covers the tabernacle a certain number of days, they will encamp at the word of the Lord and set out at the command of the Lord. And when the cloud stays from evening until morning, and the cloud goes up in the morning, they will set out, by day or by night; and when the cloud goes up, they will set out. Whether for days or a month, as long as the cloud continues to overshadow it, the sons of Israel will remain encamped and will not set out, for at the command of the Lord they will set out. They kept the charge of the Lord at the command of the Lord through Moses.” When the holy tabernacle had been raised in the wilderness, he says, the cloud filled it. Then he commanded the Israelites to set out with it and halt with it, and urged them to watch with great care for the departures, whether up or down. By this he showed how perilous disobedience is for those inclined to be careless. That is the historical sense. Now let us look at it spiritually. As soon as the truest tabernacle, that is, the Church, was raised up and dawned upon the earth, it was filled with the glory of Christ. The covering of the ancient tabernacle with the cloud signifies, I think, nothing other than this. Christ has filled the Church with his glory. To those who live in ignorance and error, as if in night and darkness, he shines out like fire and pours spiritual illumination into them. To those already enlightened, who have the spiritual day in their hearts, he gives his shade and shelter, and enriches them with spiritual dews, that is, with the consolations that come from above and through the Spirit. This is the meaning of his being seen in the appearance of fire by night and in the appearance of a cloud by day. It was necessary, truly necessary, that those who are still infants should have illumination and radiance to lead them to the knowledge of God, and that those above them, who have been made bright through faith, should have shelter and help, so that they could nobly endure the scorching heat of this present life and the burden of the day. For “all who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted.” When the cloud sets out, the tabernacle sets out with it, and when the cloud halts, the tabernacle settles with it, and the Israelites did the same along with it. For the Church follows Christ everywhere, and the holy multitude of believers is never parted from the one who calls them to salvation.
And how might we understand our setting out and our halting, with Christ leading us forward and guiding us?

In a way it makes little difference to our argument here, since setting out and halting together with the cloud shows us, as it were, a type of the wish to be with God. But if we apply our mind to the finest ideas we can, we shall say this as well. The first setting out is from unbelief to faith, from ignorance to knowledge, and from not knowing who is God by nature and in truth to knowing clearly the Lord and Maker of all things. A second setting out, which follows that one and is beneficial, is from wickedness and licentiousness to a desire to do and think what is better. A third, more excellent than this and more glorious, is from what is lacking to what is complete, in both conduct and doctrine. Do we not advance little by little toward the growth that is understood to be in Christ, progressing to mature manhood and rising up to the measure of the stature of his fullness? This is perhaps what the divine Paul celebrates for us when he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call.” When we set out spiritually from ignorance to knowledge, from lack of learning to understanding, from unbelief to faith, and keep advancing in virtues, do we not move from place to place? And as we pass from one disposition or habit to another, are we not already like people who make a practice of traveling?
I understand what you mean.

But no one could manage either to set out from wickedness or to arrive at better things and in a way pitch his tent among them, unless Christ is with him and leading him. That is why he told the holy disciples: “Apart from me you can do nothing.” So setting out with the cloud when it set out, and resting with it when it rested, would hint in a figure at being with God and doing everything with him. But it says they will set out at the command of the Lord. This shows, I think, that those who believe they must follow in Christ also need a word that spurs them to courage and to the good order that befits the saints. For it says: “Let all things be done decently and in order.” What is written next is again a type of this. For God spoke to Moses, the revealer of sacred things, as follows: “Make yourself two trumpets of hammered work; make them of silver. They shall serve you for summoning the congregation and for breaking camp. When you blow them, the whole congregation shall gather to you at the door of the tent of testimony. If they blow only one, all the rulers, the leaders of Israel, shall come to you. When you sound a signal, the camps that are encamped on the east shall set out. When you sound a second signal, the camps that are encamped on the south shall set out. When you sound a third signal, the camps that are encamped by the sea shall set out. When you sound a fourth signal, the camps that are encamped on the north shall set out. They shall sound a signal for their setting out. When you gather the congregation, you shall blow, but not sound a signal. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets, and this shall be a perpetual statute for you throughout your generations.”
What, then, shall we say the pair of trumpets means, and the different signals? And why did he command that they be of hammered work and made of silver?

There are two trumpets because the preaching of exhortation in the churches is twofold. One kind leads believers to correct doctrine and exposes the teaching of perverse men as counterfeit. Such was the teaching of those who forbid marriage and who taught, quite inconsistently, abstinence from foods that God created to be received by the faithful. Among these I would also count the teachers of the Jews. They set aside as stale what the divine law honored and approved, and held it of almost no account, and they ordered their pupils to rely on their own teachings and on human commandments. Others again foolishly taught that those justified by faith must be circumcised, so that they might boast in another’s flesh, as it is written. But of them it was said: “Away with the dogs, away with the evil workers.” The other kind of preaching guides us toward moral improvement and makes the road of life in Christ shine white. The trumpets are of silver. This signifies the brilliance of both kinds of teaching and their perfect purity, as the nature of the material neatly suggests. With the trumpets, it says, let the people be summoned to the tabernacle. For by preaching we gather into the churches those who are, as it were, in their own tents. Once they have come together, we persuade them to set out from more shameful things to things fitting for the sanctified, and we skillfully re-educate them to move, so to speak, from wickedness to the good. Or does not the word lead the reasonable person, the genuine lover of life in Christ, to correct doctrine and to reform of character?
So I say.

So there are two trumpets that gather the people to the tabernacle. But if they blow only one, it says, all the rulers, the leaders of the sons of Israel, will come to you. For I take it that even those more perfect in their habits need exhortation and encouragement, though not as much as the multitude of the others. That is why two trumpets barely summon all the rest, while one is enough for the chosen. A little suffices for the wise man, and if he is given a starting point he will supply what is missing, as the saying goes: “Give a wise man an opportunity, and he will be wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will gain in learning.” Then he commanded four different signals to be made, so that by them the camps on the east and the southwest, the north and the south, might break camp and set out. I think this signifies the four written Gospels, through which the whole world is taught doctrinal and moral knowledge together. And if we should also propose another interpretation, we shall not hesitate at all, for we count the pursuit of what is useful above sleep and sweat. We shall find four kinds of preaching among us, by which the whole earth will achieve the best and truly approved life. One, the first, is that by which we customarily call to the knowledge of the truth and the reception of divine light those who have worshiped the creation rather than the Creator, and who say in their ignorance to a piece of wood, “You are my father,” and to a stone, “You gave birth to me,” as the prophet puts it. The other three kinds of preaching would properly suit those who already believe, since the Savior too taught that there are three kinds of life and conduct. For he said that the seeds sown on good soil bore fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. So for each of these there is a kind of preaching especially suited to it. We would not be acting rightly if we tried to help with the same undiscriminating words both those who are divided between God and the world because they are lawfully yoked in marriage, and those who have chosen the most excellent and ascetic life, or the life befitting the priesthood. To the first we shall say: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife,” and whatever else it befits married people to think and do. To the ascetics and those who have resolved to endure: “Put to death your earthly members: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire.” And: “The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” To those called to the priesthood: “The lips of a priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth,” and whatever the most wise Paul urges in his letters to Timothy. Am I wandering away from the point in my explanations and drifting off into something wrong?
Not at all.

Notice that he assigns the use of the trumpets only to those whose lot it is to serve as priests. I think he is entrusting to the teachers of the people, those sanctified for the priesthood, the word that initiates into the mysteries and also spurs people on to desire virtue. That, I think, is why he says to Moses, “Make yourself two trumpets.” And as if sealing the matter by law, he says: “The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets, and this shall be a perpetual statute for you throughout your generations.”

So we shall take the different kinds of signal as the kinds of preaching suited to each group of those who seek to win approval. In this way we shall set out and halt together with the cloud. That is, we shall walk spiritually with Christ and rest with him.

Well said. The words of a prophet will also persuade us to think this. They run: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to do justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?”

That walking with the Lord your God is a fine thing, worth everything, and rich in the glory that belongs to courage, how could that not be clear? But what is meant, again, by “to be ready”? Please explain it to me, for I would like to know.
Gladly. When eagerness to think and do the things of God lies right at our feet, and nothing hinders us or drags us back toward a debased mind, that, I think, is being ready to walk with God.
And who, in general, do we say are those who want to follow God, yet do not choose to do it with their whole soul, but sink down into weakness and shrink from endurance?

Those who are slow, who only barely bring themselves to want to think on what would please God, but do not yet hold fast with an undivided mind to a way of life fit for saints. They allot to love for God only a small share, so to speak, of the zeal and eagerness that is in them, and have resolved to spend all the rest most wastefully and rashly on the distractions of this life, on profitless sweat and bitter cares. The men of Reuben and Gad could serve as a type of these. For again it is written in Numbers: “Now the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad had a great number of cattle, a very great number. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and the place was a place for cattle. And the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad came and spoke to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the leaders of the congregation, saying: ‘Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo and Beon, the land which the Lord delivered up before the sons of Israel, is a land for cattle, and your servants have cattle.’ And they said, ‘If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants as a possession, and do not take us across the Jordan.’ And Moses said to the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben: ‘Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here? And why are you turning aside the minds of the sons of Israel from crossing into the land that the Lord God is giving them?’” Then, after reproaching them besides with their fathers’ disobedience and with what befell those fathers because of it (“for they died in the wilderness,” he says, “without so much as seeing the land of the promise”), he goes on: “And see, you have risen up in place of your fathers, a brood of sinful men, to add still more to the fierce anger of the Lord against Israel. For you will turn away from him, to leave him yet again in the wilderness, and you will act lawlessly against this whole congregation.” “And they came to him and said: ‘We will build sheepfolds here for our cattle, and cities for our households; and we ourselves will arm and go as a vanguard ahead of the sons of Israel until we have brought them to their own place. And our households will live in the walled cities because of the inhabitants of the land. We will not return to our houses until the sons of Israel have each been allotted his inheritance. And we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because we have our lots on this side of the Jordan, toward the east.’” You see that for the sake of their cattle and possessions, and of their love for their wives and children, such men would never have crossed the Jordan at all. They would not even have brought themselves to whet themselves for war and battle, nor would they have wanted to share with the others in glory and in the good things that were hoped for. It seemed best to them, and most desirable, to stay where they were without so much as setting foot in the waters of the Jordan. But when Moses reproached them and persuaded them to be afraid and to look out for the wrath of God, they barely promised to cross the Jordan along with the others and to share with them the toils of war and battle. Yet they do not say that they will also share in the allotment, because they have, or have received, their lot on the other side of the Jordan. Such in their ways are those who are bound tight by the cares of the present life. They devote, as it were, their whole heart to choosing to set their minds on the things of the earth, give barely a little thought to what is necessary, and do not make the things of God their concern. For “many,” he says, “are called, but few are chosen.” Those, then, who are counted among the called because of their faith, but are not yet numbered among the chosen because they have given themselves over to pleasure, are sometimes slow and very hesitant, perhaps even about the grace of holy baptism itself. They shudder at enduring, for God’s glory and their own benefit, the labors that befit the saints, and at being persecuted along with the true believers, should the time lead to that. But when the divine law reproaches them, and the wrath of God sometimes strikes them with fear, they come hesitantly to saving baptism and share the labors of the chosen, either fasting with them more moderately, or sometimes even sharing the zeal of the churches under attack. Yet they are not yet persuaded to despise the things of the world, but return, as if to a lot of their own assigned to them, to the pleasures and delights of earthly things. That is why Christ said to those who love uprightness and are most earnestly striving to be devout: “Take heed, lest your hearts ever be weighed down with the worries and cares of this life.” Or would you not say the thing is harmful, my friend?
I would; how could I not?
If you turn the keen eye of your mind on what is written, you will greatly admire the beauty of the image.
In what way?
Those who, for the sake of cattle, children and wives, sheepfolds and buildings, have let hesitation creep in about the best things are Reuben and Gad.
And what does that mean?
Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn, while Gad was born of Zilpah, the slave woman.
True.

So the called are firstborn through their faith, and as far as grace goes they have received from God the choicest lot; but they are not lovers of freedom, because of their leaning toward baser things. For we say that those who have been justified in faith have been called to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. But the firstborn who does not love freedom is rather a partner and fellow lover with those who have not escaped the shame of slavery.
Very well said.

But now that my discourse is nearing the shore and, as it were, casting out its mooring cables, it occurs to me to say, and to remind you again, that we must act like men in facing anything whatever that leads to our benefit, and regard our labors as training in virtue. We must be disposed in no other way than this: that it is God who saves, and who grants us the power to overcome our adversaries, even if they should set against us strength far greater than our own. That we do not shed our sweat in vain when we endure the labors undertaken for virtue, Moses will teach us when he says in Deuteronomy: “And you shall remember the whole way by which the Lord your God led you in the wilderness, to afflict you and to test you, and so that what was in your heart might be made known, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” And he does not allow us to be sick with unmanly cowardice, if we look carefully at the hand that shields us. For again he writes as follows: “But if you say in your heart, ‘This nation is greater than I; how shall I be able to destroy them?’ you shall not be afraid of them. You shall surely remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all the Egyptians: the great trials which your eyes have seen, the signs and those great wonders, the mighty hand and the uplifted arm, how the Lord your God brought you out. So will the Lord our God do to all the nations of whom you are afraid.”
That we must cleave to God alone, who is God by nature, and love him with our whole soul and heart.

Well then, Palladius, it seems we have now given a sufficient account of courage as it is understood in Christ, and of spiritual strength. But I think we must once again look carefully at the means by which these qualities may come to be in us.
You are right.

Come, then. Let us turn the eye of the mind all the way around and direct it to a close examination of our own affairs. Let us consider very carefully which path will make us illustrious and let us bind on, like a crown, the verdict of approval given for everything praiseworthy. Or do you think I am wrong to choose to be so discerning in these matters?

Not at all. I would say myself that we must first be sharpened by the challenge to courage, and must choose the things that would make a person illustrious and lead him straight along the way of a blameless life.

Then let us say at once that every house rests on its foundation, and a ship begins from its keel. In the same way, for anyone who has chosen to live rightly, the foundation and starting point of the groundwork is the knowledge of the truth and the pure teaching of faith in God, who is one and true by nature. "For if you do not believe, neither will you understand," says the sacred Scripture. And those who do not yet understand will inevitably fail to do any of the necessary things, because they do not know how to act rightly. Or would you not agree that, if we are to win good repute, we must weigh everything we are to do, provided we have made it our concern to do rightly the things we ought to love?
I would.

Faith, then, is the nurse of understanding, and understanding tests what we ought to do. So when the God of all set over the people of Israel the law given through Moses, as a kind of tutor and wise guide, he first laid down the knowledge of the one and true Godhead as a sort of groundwork and unshakeable beginning. He did not think they could reach a blameless and pure life, that is, be ordered by the law that teaches the finest things and submit to its commandments, unless they first took faith in God into their minds as an outer rampart and bravely resisted the pleasures that sharpened them toward slackness. It was necessary, truly necessary, for the people of old first to put away the error of many gods, like a sickness of the soul, and to be firmly grounded in faith in God, who is one by nature and in truth. That is why the first law shone out to them before all the others: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my ordinances." It was necessary, truly necessary, for those who were to keep the commandment inviolable to be cowed by stern terrors. So he calls himself a jealous God, who lays the sins of fathers upon their descendants, if, that is, they choose to live as their fathers did and to rival the faults of their ancestors. We certainly do not say that the sins of the fathers fall on those who have done no wrong at all, since God has declared plainly: "Fathers shall not die for their children, nor children for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin." But if the descendants follow the mind of their fathers and become zealous for their ancestors' impiety, the wrath may well reach them too. And even if the God who is above all should somehow, out of his innate love for humankind, spare the first generation from punishment, he still brings at last upon the second or third the wrath that from the beginning befitted and was owed to that profane race. So he frightened them into fear by calling himself a jealous God. But he also strengthened them in faith another way, by promising to show mercy to thousands of those who love him. To these he added a neighbouring commandment, a sister to the first: "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold guiltless anyone who takes his name in vain." Some people did exactly this. They attached the title of God to wood and stones, and in their ignorance they brought him who is above every name down to the handiwork and labour of human hands. Somewhere God spoke about them through the voice of Isaiah: "A carpenter chose a piece of wood, set it up by measure, fitted it together with glue, and made it in the form of a man, like the beauty of a human being, to set it up in a house. He cut wood from the forest that the Lord planted and the rain made grow, so that people might have it to burn. He took some of it and warmed himself, and they burned it and baked bread on it. The rest they made into gods, and they bow down to them." And after other things: "Know that their heart is ashes, and they go astray." These are the people who take the name of the Lord in vain. Those who have now escaped the devil's snare and come to know the true God must not, I think, sink back into cold thoughts. Nor should they foolishly honour what is base in this matter by letting themselves be dragged back into thinking that there are other gods, or supposing that any exist at all besides the one who truly is. For "even if there are so-called gods and lords, in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him"; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things, and we in him. We will by no means narrow the nature of the Godhead in the Jewish manner to the one God and Father alone. Rather, we widen it, so to speak, into a holy and consubstantial Trinity. And while we distinguish by the character of the persons and the distinctiveness of each hypostasis, we gather it again into one God because the substance is the same. Him we will serve and him we will worship, calling on the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For "there shall be no other gods besides me," he says; and again: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." Since the Father is one God, the Son one Lord, and the Holy Spirit one, proceeding, we will neither shut the one God out of true lordship nor banish the one who is truly and by nature Lord from being God. For lordship certainly follows on deity by nature, and the glory of deity in turn follows on lordship in truth.
You have spoken very rightly and very wisely indeed.

We will acknowledge one God, then, Palladius, and count no other at all besides him. We will drive as far as possible from our souls that unholy and profane double-mindedness, which is truly boastful and insolent, so that the sacred word may not cry out against us as well: "How long will you limp on both your legs? Either Baal is Baal, or God is God." We must be seen to be single-minded, not divided in mind and unsteady, ready at any moment to fall away to what is improper. For I would call limping on both legs and liking to be tossed about one of the most godless things of all. The ancient law, indeed, punishes the unsteady person with death, for it says: "Whoever sacrifices to gods, except to the Lord alone, shall be utterly destroyed." So to rise up against the divine glory, to try to hand out to whomever one pleases what belongs to it alone, and to bestow it on those who are not gods by nature, is the most shameful of diseases. Better, it would be an indictment and charge of the utmost impiety. Anyone who is truly genuine and dear to God must therefore be free of such things. He must not only cleanse his heart but never so much as let the name of an idol pass over his tongue. For it is written: "You shall not make mention of the name of other gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth." What is shameful to know is not harmless to speak. Those who have chosen to honour sincerity in faith in every way should remember the blessed Paul, who writes: "For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance." Through holy baptism these people were once brought to share in the heavenly and divine grace, and they received the true and life-giving word about the resurrection and the kingdom of Christ. If they choose to run back to where they began and fall into the old sickness, they will not be renewed and cleansed by a second baptism. "For their unbelief will not nullify the faithfulness of God," as the inspired Paul says. Nor will we write off divine grace as unreliable because some have turned back and despised it. Rather, the Judge of all will punish those who do not shrink from sliding into such impiety that they trample the Son of God underfoot, treat the blood of the covenant as common, and insult the Spirit of grace, by whom they were sanctified and became sharers in the divine nature. Think of a soldier who throws away his shield and runs from battle. He must not be honoured with a second set of insignia but punished at once, and made to pay the penalty for his cowardice. In the same way, I think, those who so outrage a grace this venerable and admirable should not be honoured with a second gift of the Spirit after setting aside the first, but should be subject at once to punishment. Those who have once been enlightened ought to reach such a disposition and steadiness of thought that they know the one God who is God by nature, loathe anyone who brings in anything else besides him, and make it the finest of their desires to fall upon idols, overturn temples and count the objects of Greek worship as nothing. An ancient word will teach us this too. For it is written in Numbers: "The Lord spoke to Moses at the west of Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: You are crossing the Jordan into the land of Canaan, and you shall destroy all the inhabitants of the land before you. You shall remove their lookout places, destroy all their molten idols, and remove all their pillars." Do you see that those who had crossed the Jordan were to do away with altars and sacred precincts and to pry up the very idols and pillars without hesitation? To spare such evils at all would be a clear sign that one is not firmly grounded and does not dedicate a blameless heart to God. Yet he says plainly concerning the godless and wicked: "You shall not bow down to their gods or serve them as they do, but you shall utterly tear them down and smash their pillars to pieces. And you shall serve the Lord your God, and I will bless your bread and your wine and your water, and I will turn sickness away from you. There shall be no one barren or sterile in your land; I will fill up the number of your days." So it is quite plain what happens for those who are firmly grounded, who hold fast with a sound mind to the God of all, and who have made it their concern to give clear proof of it. Overthrowing the altars and pillars, those playthings of people corrupted in mind, will win them divine gifts.
True.

"For if you pull down what is made by hands," he says, "and serve God, having come to hate their customs, I will bless your bread and your wine and your water." The saying is mystical and deep. For those who truly belong to God, sharing in the mysteries of Christ and the grace given through holy baptism will bring spiritual blessing. But for those who are still double-minded and stirred toward apostasy, they bring wrath and condemnation. For such people, what is there of the dreadful that partaking of the spiritual blessing is not? And this, I think, is what the wise Paul said: "Whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of Christ unworthily eats and drinks condemnation on himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." "But let a person examine himself," he says, "and then eat of the bread and drink of the cup." So sharing in the holy mysteries, he says, will bring blessing to those who truly love God above all. They will also be freed from sickness, that is, from the weakness that easily gives way to wrongdoing and carries a person off into cowardice. And there will be no one barren or sterile among them, he says. For every God-loving and holy soul is most fruitful and richly laden with holy fruits, by which I mean, once again, the glories that come from virtue.
That is so.

He does not let us have a heart that is easily shaken. Instead he skilfully turns us toward choosing what is steady in faith and secure in piety. Sometimes he reschools us toward the better with fitting reasoning. He bids us shun sacrificing to idols or worshipping them, or rather turn from it entirely as something that brings destruction, and he shows that this sickness is full of the worst slander, or rather of the highest impiety. At other times he sets fear over us, I mean the fear of punishment, as a kind of tutor and noble guard, and so turns us from every side toward what pleases him. So in Deuteronomy the blessed Moses says: "These are the ordinances and judgments that you shall take care to do in the land that the Lord, the God of your fathers, gives you as an inheritance, all the days that you live on the earth. You shall utterly destroy all the places where the nations you are dispossessing served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every leafy tree. You shall tear down their altars, smash their pillars, cut down their groves and burn the carved images of their gods with fire, and you shall destroy their name from that place." The sages and learned men of the Greeks, and the poets above all, give the names Oreads and Hamadryads to certain nymphs, or rather demons. And there were some who chose to honour their gods on the local heights. They set up altars on the mountains and were eager to sacrifice oxen there, and around the finest trees they planted groves and set up images of demons, and slaughtered sheep. But those who had come under the God who is God in truth and by nature had to fear nothing, to overthrow the playthings of those in error, and to keep as far as possible from their customs. So he says again: "When the Lord your God destroys before you the nations whose land you are going in to inherit, and you dispossess them and live in their land, take care that you do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed before you. Do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How do these nations serve their gods? I will do the same.' You shall not do so to the Lord your God. For they have done to their gods the abominations that the Lord hates; they even burn their sons and their daughters in fire to their gods." The lawgiver does well to forbid all imitation of those in error and to bid them keep far away from the pitiless slaughter of children. He exposes those bloodthirsty, falsely named gods as corrupters and destroyers of humankind, and shows that their worshippers savagely dishonour the laws of natural affection for the sake of what pleases those gods. For "God created all things that they might exist, and the generative forces of the world are wholesome, and there is no kingdom of Hades on earth. But through the envy of the devil death entered the world." The divine will overturns death and destroys corruption, and it hates that what exists should cease to exist; for he created all things that they might exist, as it is written. But those whom the greed of the demons has caught in the net of error offer to Satan the destruction of those who were born for life and the death of those created to exist, as if these were delicacies and the finest, most fragrant incense. Very fittingly, then, he chose to show that their practices are full of the worst slander, of nature wronged and of the cherished laws of love for children trampled underfoot. In this way he stirred the noble, evil-hating mind of his hearers to honour and eagerly choose whatever he himself wills and commands. These things, then, were legislated long ago to overthrow their unholiness. He also decrees death for anyone who tries to win over someone who is firmly grounded and has received the knowledge of the truth out of love for God. For again he spoke thus: "If a prophet or one who dreams a dream arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder he told you of comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us go and serve other gods whom you have not known,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or of the one who dreams that dream. For the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love your God with all your heart and with all your soul. You shall walk after the Lord your God, fear him, keep his commandments, listen to his voice, serve him and cleave to him. And that prophet or that one who dreams the dream shall die, for he has spoken to lead you astray from the Lord your God." How holy this law is, and how worthy of God! If the laws require that those who murder bodies must by all means be put to death, how could the man who brings deadly error upon a soul not justly face the same danger? For he throws into the pits of destruction what is better than the body, as the Saviour himself said. God judged that the deceiver and charlatan must pay the penalty for bloodshed. And he decrees the same penalty also for those who have yielded an easily swayed and fickle mind to such people. For when a person could easily have escaped by coming to his senses and returning to the truth, he asks, why did he willingly run off toward wrongdoing? "If there is found among you, in one of your cities that the Lord your God gives you, a man or a woman who does what is evil in the sight of the Lord your God by transgressing his covenant, and they go and serve other gods and worship them, the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which he did not command you and which was not declared to you; and you inquire thoroughly, and indeed the report is true and this abomination has been done in Israel, then you shall bring out that man or that woman who did this evil thing, and you shall stone them with stones, and they shall die. On the evidence of two or three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; he shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness. The hand of the witnesses shall be the first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people; and you shall remove the evil one from among you." When God is wronged in the worship that is his own, it is not safe to show pity. And it does great harm to go soft at the wrong moment out of an unmanly fondness for one another. This, I think, is what the Lord meant: "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." At such a time let the law of affection go hang, let the power of natural love depart, and everything else that belongs to human kindness. Let God, so to speak, be served by a pious harshness. Or do you not think it right that those who fall away without any excuse should be punished without pity? For they grieve the glory that is beyond all things, and they do not shrink from insulting without restraint the one whom they ought rather to have gladdened by earnest steadfastness.
Right indeed. How could it not be?

I will also recall what he said to the people of older times: "What wrong did your fathers find in me, that they went far away from me, went after empty things and became empty themselves?" And somewhere, as if astounded at the sheer folly of the people of Israel, he says: "The heaven was appalled at this, and the earth shuddered greatly, says the Lord. For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water." I would think, and with good reason, that those people have missed all good counsel who turn away from the worship of God and serve the creation instead of the Creator and Maker, or who plunge into an even more shameful error and worship the works of their own hands. Yet if they had chosen to think rightly, they could easily have seen, from the creation of the world, the beauty of the nature that is above all things and beyond words, and from the good order of created things they could have perceived the commander, ruler and craftsman of this universe. But some of the ancients spurned this venerable and admirable way of thinking and "exchanged gold for bronze," as the Greek poets say. For they gave up the duty of worshipping the God who is God by nature and turned like children to a useless worship of empty things. They poured shame and ridicule on their own heads and chose of their own accord to fall away from the help that comes from above. So God said: "As a thief is ashamed when he is caught, so shall the children of Israel be ashamed, they and their kings, their rulers, their priests and their prophets. They said to the wood, 'You are my father,' and to the stone, 'You gave birth to me.' They have turned their backs to me and not their faces, and in the time of their troubles they will say, 'Arise and save us.' Where are your gods that you made for yourself? Will they arise and save you in the time of your affliction? For your gods were as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem were the altars where they sacrificed to Baal. Why do you speak to me? You have all acted lawlessly against me, says the Lord."
A terrible thing indeed, my friend.

But sometimes someone counted among us, who is not yet firmly grounded, puts on a feigned and counterfeit love for Christ, and wraps himself in the appearance of being dear to God as if in a fleece. He will prove a bitter and unholy beast, a trickster and a turncoat, so that at home and by night (I mean in secret) he gives himself to the worship of demons. No doubt he thinks that he too can escape God and outwit the mind of the ineffable nature. Anyone could show with very little effort that a man who chooses to think this has taken up the more shameful parts of the folly of the Greeks. The wise men among the Greeks thought it right to say that the sun, the great luminary, sees all and hears all, though it is created and generated and was made by God for this very purpose. They thought that whatever had been received into the rank of God must be enriched with the prerogatives of the divine nature, and a prerogative of the highest nature is to know and observe all things. So much for them. But to us God called out long ago: "I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Will anything be hidden from me?" For nothing escapes the one who is truly God by nature. And let blessed David instruct us when he says: "Understand, you senseless among the people; you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, will he not hear? He who formed the eyes, does he not perceive?" Some said, I think, out of lack of understanding: "The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand." Is it not utterly foolish to say that the giver of knowledge does not know, or to think that he who gives hearing to the creatures he made does not hear?
That is altogether implausible.

Then, according to the Scriptures, we must worship the Lord God alone and wholeheartedly, and no other besides him. For it is written: "You shall be perfect before the Lord your God." Spiritual perfection means being founded in faith, being blameless in worship, and having the irreproachable beauty of love toward God.
That is what I say.

Then, Palladius, take those who would never choose to worship other gods, that is, the creation instead of the Creator, but who are somehow persuaded by the false divinations of idolaters. Shall we acquit them of blame and accusation? Or is it safe for those who are truly genuine believers to declare them free of the charge of apostasy?
By no means.

Astrological sorcery, omens, false divinations and demonic deceptions would befit, I suppose, only those who are most outlandishly eager to bring that inglorious and accursed idolatry into their minds.

You are right. The divine word also commands us to loathe the shamefulness of such things. It runs as follows: "When you enter the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or his daughter in fire, anyone who practises divination, who reads omens, who interprets birds, a sorcerer, one who chants spells, a medium, a watcher of portents, or one who consults the dead.
