For everyone who does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God." And a little later it says again: "You shall be perfect before the Lord your God. These nations, whom you are about to dispossess, will listen to omens and divinations; but the Lord your God has not granted this to you. The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; [you shall listen to him in everything, as you asked of the Lord your God] at Horeb on the day of the assembly."

Well said, my friend. We will not follow watchers of portents or necromancers. Nor will we accept the flights of birds as something true, whether they move to the right or to the left, toward the west or toward the east; such things are the height of folly. Instead we will make Christ the leader of all, who for our sake became a prophet like us. From him we will receive the knowledge of what we need, and on him we will wait, telling the lying words of demons to go and wail and bidding them farewell. For just as giving life and ruling over all things belongs by nature and properly to God alone, in the same way, I think, so does the knowledge of all things. It is a property of his nature to know clearly what is to come, and to hold the knowledge of all things gathered, as it were, within himself. Or is this not a wise and accurate account?
Certainly it is.

Then we shall sin against him, and the charge [?] will touch the supreme glory itself, if we believe that profane and unclean spirits possess the very things by which he is adorned and made exceedingly glorious. If we are so disposed, it will be time to imagine foolishly that Satan too can give life, and even that he is a creator, if we grant him, and say he naturally possesses, the things that are pre-eminent above all and belong properly to the nature of God. And knowledge of what is to come is a proper and pre-eminent good of the highest nature. Or is what I say not true?

Very true. For through the voice of Isaiah he says to some who were ascribing to the creation what belongs to God: "Remember these things and groan; repent, you who have gone astray; return in your heart, and remember the former things of old: that I am God, and there is no other besides me, who declares the last things beforehand, before they happen, and at once they were accomplished; and I said: All my counsel shall stand, and all that I have planned I will do." For he set before his hearers the power to declare the last things before they happen as a sign, so to speak, that there is no other besides him who is God by nature and in truth.

Well said, Palladius. But as we go on examining the truth very carefully, I would like us to consider this as well. If we are at all counted among those who wish to live rightly and according to the gospel, how can we still follow the flatteries of false divinations? And if we heed them, as though some word of theirs were true, shall we not be ruling that the Savior's voice must be false? For he said to the boastful and insolent Jews: "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and the father of it." How then can a liar be unerring? And how can he who does not stand in the truth be anything but false in his speech, wholly and in every way? Is it not now plain to everyone, Palladius, that if we credit the voices of demons with truth, we shall be convicting Christ of falsehood and saying that the Truth tells lies?
It seems we would.

Besides, let me add this to what has been said: Christ has taught us not to accept the words of unclean spirits, even if they should ever wish to offer us the truth, a path untrodden and utterly unfamiliar to them.
What do you mean?

Do you not hear what the holy evangelists have recorded? The demons came to Christ crying out loudly and piercingly: "Ah! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? You have come to destroy us. We know who you are, the Holy One of God." But he, it says, rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. Yet why, one might reasonably wonder, did Christ rebuke those who were crying out the truth? What he did was surely for our benefit. Through it we are taught that we must not attend to their words, even if they choose to proclaim the truth itself and say what is plainly genuine. For sometimes they weave falsehood together with truth and so ruin their hearers. They do it in just the way one sees people take away the taste of bitter things by mixing in honey, and try by the admixture of sweetness to steal away whatever would otherwise be unpleasant.
So it is altogether dangerous to pay attention to the deceptions of oracle-mongers.

God sets the penalty for this at death and counts it among the worst evils. He spoke thus in Leviticus: "And the soul that follows mediums or enchanters, so as to go whoring after them, I will set my face against that soul and destroy it from among its people. And you shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy." And a little later again: "And any man or woman among them who becomes a medium or an enchanter shall surely be put to death; you shall stone them with stones; they are guilty." First he forbids anyone to be fond of following knavish astrological divinations or necromancies, saying that this is as far as can be from a holy way of life and wholly unfitting for those devoted to God. Then for the second group he decrees death and says that they too are guilty. He does not allow us to show mercy to those who have already gone so far in wickedness as to become a snare of death, a trap for innocent souls, a door of destruction, a pitfall of Hades, and every such evil. But I think it is wise and sound to reflect that God would not have fixed so bitter a penalty, one that goes beyond every evil, on people who could know what is to come and tell it to others, if they were truly able to speak of the future. For a word of truth is not punished; it is lying that is accursed. But if someone is caught doing this, and doing it as though it came from God, he has slandered the ineffable nature itself. By ascribing falsehood to the Truth as though it belonged to it, he will go to his end bearing a penalty equal to his crimes. For the word does not rebuke those who are from God (perish the thought!) but those who practise these things as though they came from God, because they did not keep their prediction free from falsehood. Since they do not speak from the truth [?] but say whatever they please, and what comes from themselves, they have therefore gone astray.
Then is this how we shall discern whether it is God who gives the oracle, or whether they are speaking their own words?

Certainly. The divine law will at once persuade us of this as well. For God spoke thus in Deuteronomy: "If you say in your heart, 'How shall we know the word that the Lord has not spoken?'—whatever that prophet speaks in the name of the Lord, and the word does not come to pass, that is the word the Lord has not spoken; the prophet spoke it in impiety; you shall not spare him." Do you hear that he says the failure of what was foretold will be clear proof that an oracle was not given by God? For truth loves truth. He says something similar through the voice of Jeremiah: "I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord. I have heard what the prophets say, what the prophets prophesy in my name: lies." Then, after severely censuring in between those who despised the divine laws, he gives truth as the clear proof of what is from God and what is not. For he said again: "The prophet who has a dream, and the prophet to whom my word comes, let him relate my word in truth." So if anything turns out to have missed the truth, it would at once expose the one who begot it as a liar, speaking from his own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written.
Would you like us to examine one question that bears on this, or shall we pass it over and go wherever your discourse leads us?
Indeed, Palladius, discussing what is necessary brings us no small benefit, so I would have good reason to blame you if you did not say freely what you think. Speak, then, without any hesitation.

If some do not speak from the mouth of the Lord, but belch out, as you say, what comes from their own heart, how then did that medium bring up holy Samuel for Saul, dead as he was, to make clear to him how things would end for him? For some think that this is exactly how it happened and that it was not otherwise.
And do you yourself not think so, and will you reason better about it? Or do you foolishly say that the soul of that righteous man was really forced to come, and came when a wretched woman called?
I could not say for certain. But examination would show the truth, I suppose.

Well said. Then let us first inquire into this, before anything else: do they pry into these things, work their marvels and accomplish them through God, or through evil spirits whose business this practice is?

Who would sink to such absurd reasoning as to think that necromancers, mediums and enchanters work these marvels through God? For I remember the law, which fixes the ultimate penalty for anyone who chooses to do this. Then is it not madness to think that someone condemned to death is not at odds with God? He will surely not fight against his own laws.

Your thinking is excellent. But shall we suppose that the souls of the saints, once released from their bodies, have been cast aside and held of no account, and have now come to such misery that they are subject to evil and unclean spirits, and must follow against their will wherever those spirits may choose to steer them? Yet the wise John, who composed for us the book of Revelation (a book honored by the verdict of the Fathers), clearly affirmed that he had seen the souls of the saints beneath the divine altar itself. But if the demons drag them even from the mansions above and carry them down unsparingly from the most holy places, with no one to stop them, then heaven is open to every demon. Presumably the gate of paradise is opened to them as well, and the flaming sword, it seems, gives way, not only to let them come and go, but also to let them carry out openly any of those who have come inside, if they wish. Is this not to make a mockery of our hope in Christ, and to show that the life of those we admire is thrice wretched?
So it seems.

And indeed it is plain enough. How was it better for the marvelous Paul to depart and be with Christ? If, after we have left earthly things behind and come to be with Christ, we are going to be subject to the hostile spirits, then faith is emptied, as it is written. Everyone, I think, would then vote that being at home in the body is incomparably better than being with Christ, and that the latter is harder to bear. For while we still spend our days in this life, we are not yoked to the devil's will; rather, we tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, as the Savior said. How then, once we are with Christ, shall we be worse off? And how does he speak truly when he says: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hands. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand"? Perhaps the most wise Peter, too, deceived the athletes of piety toward Christ when he wrote: "So let those who suffer at the hands of others according to his will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator." But if Satan overpowers a soul entrusted to God, leading and carrying it off wherever he pleases from time to time, how could he who presides over the saints, and has received each one's spirit as a deposit, be thought faithful? It is nonsense, then, and dreadful madness, to think that the prophet's voice [?] was really dragged down by the frigid incantations of a most loathsome woman from the places allotted to it.
Then how should we explain what was seen? For I think such shameful things should not even be spoken of, nor even entertained in bare thought.

We will set out the sacred text itself, and then make clear what comes to mind, holding fast in every respect to what is fitting. It runs as follows: "And Samuel died, and all Israel mourned him, and they buried him in Ramah, in his own city. And Saul had removed the mediums and the wizards from the land. And the Philistines gathered and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered every man of Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa. And Saul saw the camp of the Philistines, and he was afraid, and his heart was greatly dismayed. And Saul inquired through the Lord, and the Lord did not answer him, neither in dreams, nor through the Urim, nor through the prophets. And Saul said to his servants: 'Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, and I will go to her and inquire through her.' And his servants said to him: 'There is a woman who is a medium at Endor.' And Saul disguised himself and put on other clothes, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night. And he said to her: 'Divine for me by your spirit, and bring up for me whomever I name to you.' And the woman said to him: 'Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has destroyed the mediums and the wizards from the land. Why then are you laying a snare for my life, to have me put to death?' And Saul swore to her, saying: 'As the Lord lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this matter.' And the woman said to Saul: 'Whom shall I bring up for you?' And he said: 'Bring up Samuel for me.' And the woman saw Samuel, and she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul: 'Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!' And the king said to her: 'Do not be afraid; tell me whom you have seen.' And the woman said to him: 'I have seen gods coming up out of the earth.' And he said to her: 'What did you perceive?' And she said to him: 'A man coming up erect out of the earth, and he is wrapped in a double cloak.' And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and did obeisance to him. And Samuel said: 'Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?' And Saul said: 'I am in great distress. The Philistines are making war on me, and God has turned away from me and no longer answers me, either by the hand of the prophets or in dreams. And now I have called you to tell me what I should do.' And Samuel said: 'Why do you ask me, when the Lord has turned away from you and is with your neighbor? The Lord has done to you as the Lord spoke by my hand: the Lord will tear the kingdom out of your hand and give it to your neighbor David. Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord, and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek, therefore the Lord has done this thing to you this day. And the Lord will deliver Israel along with you into the hands of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons with you will fall, and the Lord will give the camp of Israel into the hands of the Philistines.'" Can you still have any right to doubt that Saul wasted away, condemned by his own verdicts? Because he feared the weakness of the forces gathered on his side for the battle, he wanted to learn from God what was to come. But when God kept silent and revealed nothing, he turned to grieving the One who had chosen to be silent. He resorted to necromancy, and yet [?] the wizards—by whom I mean those who suppose they know what is to come. Then he says, "Bring up Samuel for me," not because incantation or the art of magicians could bring the soul of the saint, but because those who practise divination always use a formula of this kind. I have learned that they bewitch demons with certain secret words and chant spells over water, and then see phantoms and shadows and, as in a mirror, the forms of certain people; perhaps the demons cleverly disguise themselves and take on the shapes of those who are named. And so at first the woman said, "I see gods coming up out of the earth." Then comes this: "And the woman saw Samuel," it says. There is nothing hard about a shadow and phantom of blessed Samuel, in the same and similar form and shaped by demonic power, being seen. So if anyone thinks that the prophet's soul was truly called back, and credits the woman's words with truth, then since she says she saw gods coming up from the earth, let him also indulge the lie that belongs to the customs of divination, and indeed suppose that there really are gods of that sort, ones that rose up from the earth, even though God by nature is one and only.

You are right. But someone will say, I think: "Yet it foretold the truth about the future when Saul was eager to inquire." And we have spent no small amount of discussion proving that truth is not found in unclean spirits.

No indeed. Light and darkness, Christ and Belial, are incompatible and do not belong together. Yet to those who provoke him and habitually grieve him, God sometimes reveals what is to come, even through those through whom it least ought to come, presumably by holy angels sounding it into the human mind. When those who have chosen to be curious inquirers learn it, they will waste away utterly, and they endure that foreknowledge as a kind of first installment of the wrath and punishment hanging over them. For God rests upon the holy prophets and often shares with them not only gloomy things, over which one might sit down in sorrow and weep, but also things that will bring good cheer and prosperity to some. But to unholy and most accursed lovers of divination he reveals the evils that will befall them.
And what would be our grounds for believing this, and where would they come from?

From the sacred Scriptures, of course. For what happened to those of old was written down for us as a type and as a way of initiating us into the mysteries. Or do you not know that Balak son of Zippor, the ruler of the Moabites and Midianites, dreaded the invincible and unbreakable multitude of Israel, and, convinced that he would very soon perish along with the other nations, hired Balaam? "Come," he said, "curse Israel for me." When the envoys arrived, Balaam said, "Lodge here tonight, and I will give you the answer that the Lord speaks to me." He was seeking cold, demonic little dreams, and probably expected them to come to him through incantation and sorcery, yet he said that the Lord would speak to him, for he pretended to receive divine utterances. But even if Holy Scripture uses the customary language of sorcerers, we would not, if we think rightly, suppose that the God who is God by nature and in truth puts the truth into the souls of the profane as though out of love, or speaks with a polluted man, a sorcerer and an idolater. Yet Scripture says, "God came to Balaam and said to him, 'Why are these men with you?'" And when he had reported the reason for their coming, it says, "God said to Balaam, 'You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people, for they are blessed.'" See how plainly the blessed angel, speaking in the person of God, turns the deceiving, idly babbling sorcerer away from seeking to curse the people whom God had blessed, and from setting the inventions of human ill counsel against the decrees from above. This was not because the curse had any power to harm. It was so that the man who had unreasonably entertained such a hope might be clearly and plainly assured, and others through him, that Israel would never fall to the Moabites or Midianites, since God was shielding it and fighting on its behalf, and walling about with his favor the people who were devoted to him and blessed. These things the divine angel said, and he commanded Balaam to act accordingly. But since the seer was being lured by promises of gifts to make the journey, perhaps supposing that he really would have power, the blessed angel let him go, yet appeared in the middle of the road with a flashing sword. In this way he taught him plainly that if he wished to curse those who were blessed, his war would be against God and the angels. When Balaam arrived at the Midianite's court, he set up altars and ordered oxen to be sacrificed. But at once he became a prophet, not his usual lying self; by a divine and ineffable power he was turned, against all expectation, to the very opposite. He did not curse at all, but instead blessed Israel and plunged Balak into bitter grief. For it is written: "Balak was angry and struck his hands together, and Balak said to Balaam, 'I called you to curse my enemy, and look, you have blessed him now for the third time.' And Balaam said to Balak, 'Did I not tell the messengers you sent to me, "If Balak gives me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot transgress the word of the Lord to do good or evil of my own accord; whatever God says to me, that I will speak"?'" It is customary for false seers to use deceitful language of this kind, calculating that those eager to inquire will think they will certainly hear the truth from them. But understand that speaking the truth is foreign to the art of the enchanter and the magician. It may sometimes come from God, when he sorely afflicts [?] the souls of the profane by foretelling what is to come.
I am convinced.

That God hates such sorceries and idle tales and brings them to nothing becomes clear when he says, "I am the Lord God," and further, "Who else will scatter the signs of ventriloquists and divinations from the heart, turning the wise back and making their counsel foolish, establishing the words of his servant and making the counsel of his messengers come true?" Divinations that come from the heart he shows to be stale and false. But every word of his own Servant, that is, Christ, he establishes; and the counsel of his messengers, that is, whatever the heralds of faith in Christ wish to speak, he shows to be full of truth, bearing witness to it with signs and wonders and the other workings of the Spirit. And elsewhere again he said, reproaching some for the things they had corrupted against the law of God: "Stand, then, with your enchantments and your many sorceries, which you have learned from your youth, and see whether you can be helped. You have wearied yourself with your counsels. Let the astrologers of the heavens, who gaze at the stars, stand up and save you; let them tell you what is about to come upon you." You see, then, how God exposes accursed astrological sorcery as laughable and entirely useless. And to learn that unerring truth belongs to him alone, as does the power to speak without error about things expected to come, hear him saying through the voice of Isaiah: "Remember these things and groan. Repent, you who have gone astray; turn back in your heart, and remember the former things of old. For I am God, and there is no other besides me, declaring the last things before they happen, and at once they are accomplished. And I said, 'All my counsel shall stand, and I will do all that I please.'" To God alone, then, who is beyond all things, we will ascribe the power to know clearly and foretell unerringly what is to come. Everything else is mere drivel and old wives' tales, buffoonery and imposture, coming from those who, with corrupted minds, speak from their own hearts, as it is written, and make falsehood a means of making money.
True. That is how it is, and not otherwise.
Let us therefore keep away from this too. Let us leave the crooked path and walk the straight one, devoted single-mindedly to God and confirming the truth by the words of the saints.
Yes, indeed.
And why should we not also count this as hateful, and say that it belongs to Greek godlessness: the fondness for purifying oneself, say, with fire and water, and by other such means?
Most certainly. That is why a divine oracle said clearly: "There shall not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or his daughter in fire."

How well the law addressed us on this, and forbade us to do it! The whole business, I think, is full of folly and devoid of the best and wisest reasoning. In what way will the nature of fire benefit us? How could torches carried round in a circle deliver the sinner? The blast of fire does melt the dross out of bronze or some other such material. But how will it remove the defilement of mind and soul? Are these things not laughable, the inventions of silly notions?
Absolutely.

I would very gladly say to the learned men of the Greeks, who invented such shameful practices and passed them on to others: What are you doing, noble and wise men? You punish in Hades that Tityos whom you say sprang from the earth, setting vultures around him to feast on his liver, because he admired a woman's beauty and fell sick with desire. You say that a stone hangs over Tantalus, and you tell the young the myth that he pays the penalty for an unbridled tongue. You bind Ixion to the long, ever-turning revolutions of a wheel and say that he endured this punishment, one quite in keeping with the gods of your delusion. Yet yourselves and others, though caught in dreadful and utterly outlandish evils, you release with fire and branches, as you suppose, and grant the washing away of charges even to those who stand utterly condemned. Tell me, then: did you impose a harsh and inescapable penalty on Tityos and those just named because they happened to lack fire? And yet the one who among you is the greatest of thieves and the bringer of fire to mankind, Prometheus I mean, if he ever existed at all, had fire in abundance to use, and had it before the rest. Yet your myths sing that he too was bound in unbreakable chains, and they say that crook-taloned vultures flew down upon him, just as upon Tityos, as dreadful and savage punishers. Grant it, then, grant purification by fire, not only to those, but also to any of you who rage with lust after other men's daughters or wives and do what is unlawful. Let these too be released from the charge by fire, and let the indictments vanish along with the offenses! But in the case of others there are at once courts and indictments, and the laws' hatred of wickedness is roused. Yourselves, though, who indiscriminately practice an utterly shameful and foul-smelling life, you think you can free from every defilement, deceived by cold and childish toys, and taking as your ministers for this the most polluted of all men, who along with their dress abandon manly reason and lower themselves to the manners and ways, the bodies and minds, of women. How then will such a man purify anyone? In this state you are doing something like this: as if someone, say, thought he was anointing himself with perfume while he was smeared with the most hideous filth, and then supposed he was carrying out very well what had come into his head.
You speak well, and I would agree with you, since what you say is true.

I will pass over the folly in this, and say nothing for now about the ministers of purification, and return to the matter itself. And I will say that one could catch the worshipers of demons choosing to live most senselessly and ignorantly, neither understanding how to cleanse themselves nor having learned accurately what defilement and profanation truly are. Adulteries, and passions still more savage than these, sodomy and murders, slanders and envy, false divinations and deceits, fraud and perjury: these would be the stains and defilements that pollute soul and body and are hard to wash out. Yet neither fire nor springs of water could scour these away. But they neglect, I suppose, even to know that these things stain the soul and fill the mind with stench, while they keep away from dead bodies and loathe what has decayed, dishonoring the laws of nature. Moreover, they sagely condemn, on their own authority, whatever foods they choose, and if they happen to touch them even unwillingly, they jump up at once and rush to purification by fire or water, as though merely by abstaining from these things they would be holy and pure. So completely are they defeated by opinion and out of their minds that one might very fittingly say to them: Woe to you, unbridled and ignorant, who strain out the gnat and swallow the camel! For they count as nothing what truly has the power to defile, and they shudder excessively at things from which no one suffers any harm. So if one of them goes to a tomb and comes upon the monuments of the dead, he throws off his cloak and shaves his head, cutting off his hair as defiled. Yet the divine law has taught us that we ought to shun these practices and refuse to imitate them. For again it said: "You shall not purify yourselves; you shall not make yourselves bald between your eyes for the dead." The learned men of the Greeks tell of a god Apollo, whom they also call Phoebus, that is, pure and undefiled. They say he is the same as the sun. So in Greek usage they used to say phoibazein and phoibasthai for purifying and being purified, according to their own opinion and their own laws. The divine oracle therefore keeps us away from such shameful and unseemly practices. It is not right to regard the death of bodies as a defilement of the soul, nor to think that the sight of a corpse imprints a stain on the hearts of those who see it, nor again to shave off one's hair on that account. The whole business is utterly stale and full of groveling opinion. The law, then, does well to say, "You shall not purify yourselves," for such purification will not benefit the soul. Rather, it harms it, robbing it of the knowledge of the most profitable path and carrying it away from the pursuit of what is beneficial. Let us consider it this way. Among us there are the laws of those who rule on earth, prescribing to people everywhere what must be done and forbidding what must not. Yet no one could escape the penalties for transgressing them unless the king's clemency granted him remission. In the same way, whoever disregards the divine laws would not become clean unless he had been granted this by divine assent. If we have transgressed laws of fire or water, and the reckoning of sin looks to them, then let the water wash away the indictment, let the fire melt away the filth, and let them remit the charges, on their own authority, to whomever they choose. But if the one who says to God, "Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight," speaks the truth, since there is one Lawgiver and Judge, why do they abandon the Lord who has power to punish and to release, and slide into old-womanish notions, assigning to fire and water the power to free them from the charges against them? Away with such ill counsel, man! Approach the one who alone is God by nature, and at once you will hear him say: "I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember them." This is true purification; this is spiritual brilliance. For we have been scoured clean, having gained forgiveness of sins through faith in Christ, sanctified by the washing of regeneration, and having enriched ourselves with the divine grace of the divine Spirit, who, like fire, consumes as so much rubbish the defilement that has settled in our minds. That is why the divinely inspired Scripture rightly says that we have been baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire.
Shall we, then, reckon the error in this matter as also a part of idolatry?

Certainly. The thing is full of godlessness. And it would be fitting to rank and count alongside these the belief that human affairs are governed by the will of others, and that authority over our lives belongs not to ourselves but to whatever powers the inventors of such implausible doctrines choose to make up. For they set Fate, Fortune and Birth over our life, I know not how, as helmsmen of a sort, and they say that none of us wills or is master of what he does, but that each is led, as if by a binding necessity, to whatever seems good to those in control. What could be more irrational than this? How could Satan have done the human race a greater wrong than when he disposed it to think and reason this way? For how could anyone still plan what is good, and ever go willingly to do it? And if he has fallen into more shameful things and thought what he should not, how could he blame himself, and, melted with grief, change his mind to think and do what is better? Just as those who speed across the sea and choose to sail must be driven by the winds from the stern and forced in every direction toward wherever the driving wind wishes, so too, according to them, we must surely yield to wherever Fortune chooses to carry us, and to the winds of Fate, which are so hard to escape. Or will you too not think that this has been rightly said?
How could I not?
Then it is utterly foolish to crown the good and fair-minded man with praise and count him worthy of honor, and to regard the wicked and licentious man as loathsome and despicable.
What do you mean?

I mean, Palladius, that according to them Birth and Fortune have prevailed, and they sweep the thrice-wretched race of those on earth in either direction against its will. Nothing in us is voluntary. For is not whatever is by nature able to move something the cause of motion in the things moved by it?
I agree.

Come, then, apply the same reasoning to human affairs. Measure our condition, and look closely at the depth of evil we come to, if it is not by our own voluntary inclinations that we go and hasten this way or that, but we are mastered and, as it were, brought under the yoke of others who can lead and drive our affairs wherever they choose. For if we reason consistently, we will no longer attribute any of our actions to ourselves; rather, we will lay the causes of everything on those who are accustomed to steer every one of them as they please. So the just man will be cut off from all praise, just as the unjust man will be cut off from punishment and from any need to be punished.
You reason most correctly.

In vain, then, do the inventors of such doctrines admire Solon of Athens, and Draco and Lycurgus, as introducers of the finest teachings and discoverers of the best laws for the Greeks. What benefit is there in them anymore, if nothing is in our power and our affairs depend instead on others? The man who is ignorant of the laws would then stand on an equal and like footing with those who know them, if those who are willing have no share in freely doing whatever they might choose. And I say that the teachers of the laws turned out to be most unjust, even though they won for themselves the greatest possible reputation for justice. For they laid down, I know not how, that the negligent must be punished and pay bitter penalties for transgression, and they handed down rules, as it were, for the young, and highly praiseworthy methods of education, either as though it were in our own power to choose to live honorably, or else thinking I know not what. Someone, I think, might say: "Well done, Solon, you legislated for the people of your time. But surely you also needed to persuade Fate to allow those under your laws to think and do what they wished. Yet you legislated without having persuaded her. Perhaps you yourself laughed at the myth, and knew that we are masters of our actions, and drove unjust and blind Fortune out of human affairs. Otherwise you would not have thought it right to regard the pious and law-abiding man as the best citizen, raised to the reputation of the highest virtue, and on the other hand to count as useless and among the most shameful the man who says goodbye to the laws that counsel us to pass through life in uprightness."
You have put that most wittily and very well.

What then, my friend? Shall we not say that the instructions and precepts, and indeed the exhortations to virtue, that fathers give their sons and teachers their pupils are futile, if one must sometimes tread a path one has not chosen and follow a course of life one does not will?
Certainly.

And if someone is provoked against his own children, or against others who have done wrong, and administers a just rebuke, would you praise such a person? Or would you count it unjust that those responsible for all our evils are, I know not how, left uncensured, while those who are led to these things against their will and by necessity are made to suffer the penalties?
So it seems. The argument is very persuasive.

You will also see from this that their view is full of the most extreme impiety. They shake God, the helmsman and overseer of this universe, from the glory that belongs to him. Then they go so far in their audacity as to strip him entirely of what is his to boast of, and by their own vote they hand control of our affairs to whatever happens to come into their heads. And they do this even though they see that all creation is not carried toward its proper ends by unsupervised motions. For what is there in the world, of all that concerns creation, that is not done in due order? What existing thing has not kept its own rank, and all but cries out the name of the one who ranked it? It shouts that it is yoked under laws and governed by the will of the one who has the power to rule, I mean God. That is why the divine Paul says: "For his invisible attributes, his eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things he has made, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became futile, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools." And how could they not have become fools, when they advised themselves, and others too, to think things contrary to what is right? Yet why, one might ask, do they drift about on such wretched reasonings, when the fable does not please even your own poets? For those poets thought it right that the management of what we do should depend not on anyone else but on ourselves. Homer, for instance, says in his poems that your noblest and highest Zeus spoke with the other divinities about the adultery of Aegisthus and its punishment: "Oh, how mortals blame the gods! For they say that evils come from us, but they themselves, through their own recklessness, suffer woes beyond what is allotted." Why, he means, do some people accuse the gods, as though they had their evils from them, instead of crying out against their own sin, which plunges them into misfortunes, even those "beyond what is allotted," that is, beyond Fate, or beyond what Fate decrees? So if anyone chooses to live rightly and to spend his time in this life with the greatest prudence and fairness, he will walk upright and swim safely through dangers. The fruit of a right and undistorted judgment is that he will not be caught in evils, and the saying is true. For it lies with us to look both ways, I mean toward the good and toward its opposite. Those who have held in regard what is by nature admirable, and the path to uprightness, will come to the good estate of virtue. But those who turn aside to the opposite and prefer wrongdoing to better things ruin their own life. They will be caught as their own murderers, convicted as terrible destroyers of their own heads. That it lies with us to look both ways, as I said just now, and that when we sink back into pleasures we fail in the pursuit of what is beneficial, will be clear from another of their poets, who proclaims it aloud. This was Euripides. He put on the stage a woman sick with unbridled pleasure, and then somehow showed her philosophizing and saying: "Women of Troezen, who dwell in this farthest forecourt of the land of Pelops, before now, in the long night hours, I have pondered how the life of mortals is ruined. And it seems to me that they do not do worse because of the nature of their judgment, for many have good sense. Rather, this is how it must be viewed: we know and recognize what is good, but we do not carry it out, some from idleness, others because they prefer some other pleasure to the good. And life has many pleasures: long gossip, and leisure, a delightful evil."

Do you see how the ancients thought it right not to blame Chance, or the horoscope, or Fate, as though it drove us by force away from the uprightness we know and from whatever we learn to be good? For the life of those on earth is ruined, she says, "not because of the nature of their judgment"; that is, not because they have a judgment evil by nature, but because they are unwilling to carry out the good they know. And what is the reason for this? Either sloth, she says, has bound them to idleness, or one of life's pleasures has run in instead and risen up against what is beneficial. It has carried them off from the pursuit of what is necessary and beguiled the mind by making the road to laziness look smoother. We could heap up countless such passages from their writers on top of these, and very easily. But who would doubt that a sufficiency is pleasant to the hearers? So we will drive the crowd of them out of our discussion.

You are right. But if you like, as they say, let these things go. Consider how you would give a wise answer if some people were to ask what reason might be found for the inequality among us, and for the ups and downs that sometimes go against what people deserve. For one may see the wicked man prospering and rich, while the decent man is often in the opposite condition, though he is full of the highest praises.

It is truly a matter hard to see and very hard to reach, Palladius. I would say that wanting to pry into it goes beyond the measures of humanity and lies far above them. We must yield to the divine judgments. If we choose to think rightly, we will ascribe knowledge of God's ordering of things to the supreme and pure Mind alone, and turn to what lies in our hands, which, as the Scriptures say, we find only with effort. But since I think we must help with argument as far as we can, come, let us also go on to that. Just now we refuted the stale opinion of the godless. We used no reasonings foreign to the matter, but showed from necessary conceptions that the horoscope does not hold the helm of the human mind. Nor has a hard and inescapable yoke of Fate been thrown upon us. Rather, each person's will is master of the actions that lie in his choice, and it is up to us to choose to do what seems best, whether good or bad. For my part, I would reckon the forms of prosperity by what the holy Scriptures have judged to be good. They do not lie in the things in which this loathsome and earthly flesh luxuriates, but in those by which the soul, which is above the body, can come to share in eternal life. These, I think, would be the pursuits of virtue and the splendor that comes from faith and works. If these are not open to all who wish to live soberly, whether they are bad or good in character, let those who would refute it come forward. But consider that doing right freely, in whatever one wishes, lies in our choice, and that all are empowered to choose spiritual prosperity and to share equally in the glory from above. If, then, some have more, holding the advantage in wealth or in the paltry glories of this world, let this not carry us off to godless opinions, prised loose from true knowledge, so that we think the yoke of Fate and Chance has been laid on our affairs. Rather, let anyone who wishes indict the greed of the wealthy, who have made their own private good, as it were, what would be common to all if there were no such thing as greed. And let him inquire instead into the will of the Maker. Wishing our affairs to be ordered and seen to be on an equal footing, he commands the rich to sell the wealth they have gathered and distribute it to the needs of the poor, and he does not allow them to love glory and preeminence. That God awards equality to those on earth is not hard for us to see even from the very structure of the body. For nature does not distinguish between the poor man and the rich, the lowborn and the illustrious, the noble and the despised, or the man held in glory in this life. She passes through all alike, without partiality, completing each with the same parts into a well-fitted shape and beauty. There is one road for all into birth and one laying aside of life. She does not free one from the snare and catch another in it, but brings on every created being an end that is harsh and inescapable. Tell me, then: is it still hard to see, or rather is it not now plain to everyone, that the aim of the divine will is for those on earth to live in equality? Listen to him, if you will, speaking also through one of the prophets: "Did not one God create us? Is there not one Father of us all? Why has each of you forsaken his brother?" So if some set aside what the Maker wills, having a free inclination toward whatever action they choose (for the Creator honored our nature with freedom), that has no bearing on the argument, since some people also disregard our own laws. But no one in his right mind, I think, would find fault with the lawgivers. He would rather blame, and very reasonably, those who chose to despise what is necessary. So when some people, as they sin, say, "Perhaps it pleased Chance," or, "This was Fate's purpose for me," what drivel, you people, shall we call this? Why do you indict what does not exist, without condemning your own frivolity? But the divine Scripture will proclaim the truth to those who have chosen not to walk uprightly: "A man's folly ruins his ways, and in his heart he blames God." So those who set the horoscope and Fate and fickle Chance over our affairs, rather than assigning the management of affairs to God, have missed the true opinion. Yet Christ says: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father in heaven. Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows." For the Creator provides for those on earth, yet he allows each one to do what seems best and to walk whatever road he wishes. And since the human race on earth fell sick with straying, he at once gave the law as a help, as it is written. It is therefore dangerous for anyone who has received faith in Christ, and has passed beyond that ancient error, to be carried off by old wives' tales to things he should not believe. He would be swept away from sound opinion into thinking that Chance and Fate, which do not exist at all, steer this universe, or man.
Most dangerous. Such a person would surely and in every way sharpen the Judge against himself.
What then? Do you not agree that it is utterly shameful, and truly next door to these evils, to observe days and hours and seasons and years, and the waxing and waning of the moon's cycle?

Very much so. The divine Paul makes this a charge, quite clearly, against those who have been saved from among the gentiles, when he says: "Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to beings that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements? Do you want to be enslaved to them all over again? You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear for you, that perhaps I have labored over you in vain."

So the observance of hours and days, and I would add of seasons, is wholly unfitting for those who are not ignorant of the one God who is God by nature. It is still more unfitting for those who have been known by him through faith and called into the close fellowship that comes through grace. Whoever chooses to do this goes backward and lets go of his boast in Christ. He has no longer kept his own mind free, but foolishly slips back under the yoke of the ancient error. He gives the elements of the world the honor that belongs to God, and crowns with the highest glories things that were called into being at the Maker's bidding. By "elements of the world" Paul means what are, so to speak, the parts of the universe: seasons and months, and their measurement, which is carried out by hours and days. Time is continuous and flows ever onward, but God subjected it to measures and numbers by breaking it up, as it were, into seasons, hours and days, which come round again and again. For it was fitting, fitting indeed, that beings whose coming into existence had a beginning, and who before long will reach the end of their own life, should have time of a like kind: time, I mean, that begins and ends, and that matches, as it were, the nature of things that do not always exist. Seasons, hours and days, then, have brought nothing else to those on earth except their circuit and its exact measurement. Why, then, do some people invent fables that are laughable even to think of? They say that some hours bring good and others do not, and they observe them with great exactness. They credit the hours with the power to bring prosperity or its opposite on whomever they may choose, or on whomever it is necessary for them to fall. Is this not drivel already, and a dreadful derangement of mind, a devilish snare maliciously laid?
I agree, and it is evident.

As we were saying, they tried to persuade us to hang our affairs on the Fates and Chance and the will of others. They made our diligence look pointless and drew us away from caring for ourselves. In the same way they fit us out here too with the same error. They say that what comes from days and hours hangs over those on earth as though by a yoke of necessity, running a course that cannot be escaped. And the strange thing is this (for such a tale is fit only for old women): they see countless failures following their nonsense about these things, yet they do not allow experience to expose the fraud. Instead, they write off certain hours and days as bad and pass the same verdict on the moon's waning phases. What, I wonder, would they say then? Suppose someone chose to list and name, within a single hour and perhaps a single day, those who are prospering and those caught in the worst misfortunes. Yet what is bad by nature would be to everyone exactly what it naturally is. So if a given hour or dawn is harmful to those on earth, why does the harm it brings not pass to all alike? Why are some in the most enviable circumstances, while others are sometimes ruined and, filled with evil to the utmost, become a byword in life and the plot of a tragic stage? Those who are willing to look closely can see what it is most profitable to know and to practise. On the very same day, perhaps even at the same hour, one man is caught in adultery or murder and pays bitter penalties to his judges. Another, meanwhile, revels in praises for his self-control, his decorum and his exceeding goodness. But no day or hour would prevent the licentious man from being self-controlled, nor would it spur the decent and orderly man on to disorder and licentious pleasures. Rather, it was the will, free toward anything whatever, and its unfettered inclination, that placed the one in the former state and the other in the latter. So it lies with us, and not with the natural qualities of the seasons, to fare well or otherwise.
So it seems. The argument is straightforward.

They especially dread the fifth and the eighth day. They "make excuses for their sins," but they have not escaped the notice of anyone of sound mind, adrift as they are on chilly old wives' reasonings. Foolishly they attach to these days the birth of certain Furies and the appearing of demons more savage than the rest, together with penalties and punishments and other such things, and the wretches do not blush. And when the moon's disk, which was full before, shrinks back toward less (for in this way, waning and waxing, it rounds out the cycle of the monthly intervals, as its Designer saw fit), they stop all work and put off journeys. They think that our affairs wholly and entirely wane along with that heavenly body, and that human life melts away with its turnings toward less. But if I may say something with a smile at their folly, they take on a fear fit for oysters and the most wretched of vegetables. Bodies of that sort, perhaps, or even greater and more important ones, may be naturally affected in sympathy, for a reason the Creator knows. To probe into such things is hazardous, and to leave them alone is no loss. But the matter will stand far off from the human mind and lie a long way from it. For even if that heavenly body wanes, the self-controlled and well-ordered man will be no less so. The mind will not sink toward less along with its light, nor will the nature of things be changed for the worse or the better, compelled by the powers of the moon. For it always somehow follows that those who do the best things must share in every good, while those who do base things receive what is most fitting for them. And I marvel at this: when the moon is waning and creeping toward the end of the month, for those of them who are moneylenders, and very fond of money, the interest grows and the lenders' purses get fatter. Yet somehow they have supposed that everything else must shrink and sicken along with the moon. Or would you not say that this is full of absurdity and stupidity?
Certainly.
To bring long arguments against such foolish notions is pointless, I think. Their ugliness is sick of itself, even if no one says a word. Let us go on instead to that other point now.
Which one?

It seems to me that Satan loathes the fifth and the eighth day, and the moon's backward path from the full, that is, the time of the conjunction, the fourteenth day. Being utterly cunning and keen in mischief, he weaves other pretexts around them, but his real reason is this. The seasons, or days, in which he came to slip from his tyranny over us, when the Only-begotten shone upon us in human form and in our likeness, he perhaps cannot bear to grasp even in bare thought.
What do you mean?
Is not the time of our Savior's coming, Palladius, counted for us as the fifth time?

I understand what you mean, from the gospel parable. Christ said that the man who hired workers for the vineyard went out at about the first hour, the third and the sixth, the ninth and the eleventh, that is, in the last time, in which he appeared and shone upon us.

Very sensibly and quite rightly said. And what then? Do we not say that he was handed over on the fifth day of the week? And that the whole economy of salvation, through which we have all been saved, came then, as it were, to its beginning, when he who became man for our sake endured the saving cross on our behalf?
Indeed.
And did he not abolish death and come back to life, despoiling Hades, on the eighth day, that is, on the first day of the week?
No doubt of it.

Indeed, the ancient law prescribed that circumcision in the flesh, a figure of circumcision in spirit and truth, be performed on the eighth day. The circumcision that surpasses that ancient one, namely the spiritual one, is participation in the Holy Spirit. It is the grace given in the beginning, which Christ renewed for us after he came back to life from the dead, when he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." The blessed Paul also says somewhere, "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed." Now the day of this saving and longed-for sacrifice was the fourteenth of the moon. So the law clearly proclaimed in advance the time of our Savior's sacrifice, which we say he endured for the life of the world. "On the tenth day of the first month," it says, "let them take for themselves a lamb for each household; they shall gather according to the number of persons. It shall be kept until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening." Do you hear how the victim was taken by the people of old on the tenth and kept until the fourteenth? This is so that you may understand the fifth time, in which he became man and underwent death for us, when the moon, which is appointed to rule the night, was already waning. The thing is a figure of a mystery. It seems to hint faintly at the backward course of the devil's greed, and at his sinking, as it were, little by little into feebleness and utter weakness. For in a way he bears the figure of the moon. He too rules the night, that is, those who are still in darkness and drowsing, who do not have the light of the knowledge of God. Inspired Scripture is accustomed to liken the herd of those who wander astray to night. Listen to what the Lord of all says to the Jews when Jerusalem was slipping back into idolatry: "I have likened your mother to night; my people has become like one who has no knowledge." Do you see that he calls "night" those who have no knowledge of the true Godhead, the one that is God, of course, by nature? So the enemy of all hates the seasons and days in which he was destroyed and we were saved. And whoever hates them along with him will belong to his portion and share his lot with him: the necessity of being punished without end.
Then we shall class these things too as part of truly profane and God-hated idolatry, just as we do, of course, the idle tale about the so-called horoscope.

You may be quite sure that it is no different, as the very test of events has shown. Besides all this, we must also utterly detest the habit of devoting ourselves to useless augury, to whisperings and incantations. For through lightness of mind some among the Greeks have slipped so far as to think that knowledge of our affairs resides even in the birds that dart through the air. So they busy themselves with their flights toward the east and toward the west, to the right and to the left; and if a crow happens to be seen cawing somewhere, they prick up their ears and receive it as though it were the truest of truths, and go home rejoicing. And the wretches do not blush in the least at ascribing the power of so venerable a thing as prophecy to birds. They have made up an imposing argument for themselves, or so they think among themselves: “For the gods,” they say, “show signs through them.” But we say that the apostate angels are not gods, those by whom good and admirable prophets have been appointed for us, knowers of the future: the cawing crow, and indeed the swift-winged hawk, and the tawny doves, to use the Greeks’ own phrases, and the other birds besides. Prophets well worthy, to be sure, of those who sound their twitterings about us into them! And blessed are you too, and enviable, to have obtained such divine spokesmen! But it seems you have forgotten, admirers though you are of the opinions of your own poets, that even they saw fit to laugh at the thing, and to regard it as nonsense and in no way necessary. For Homer says: “Ah, my friend, let the birds be, whether they go to the right, toward the dawn and the sun, or to the left, toward the misty gloom.” And Euripides clearly and openly declares how futile it is to watch the flights of birds. He says that Theseus raged against Hippolytus, his own son, and set about driving him from his native land. And when Hippolytus said, “Without testing oath or pledge or the utterances of seers, you cast me out of the land untried,” Theseus replied: “This tablet, which has received no lot, accuses you convincingly; as for the birds that roam above my head, I bid them a long farewell.” And surely the voice of God would be trustworthy, and its credibility better than that of writing on a tablet, since it is not unlikely that we humans speak falsely; but never to err belongs to God, and the truth is what is dearest to him. Yet Theseus certainly knew that the birds roaming above one’s head are nothing at all. So we must by no means ascribe knowledge of the future to demons; rather we shall assign it to God as his special prerogative. Bird-omens, then, will be nothing but trickery, and faith in them a plain proof of an unsound mind. And the law itself says somewhere, “You shall not practice augury,” knowing the thing to be loathsome and utterly detested by God, who rules over all.
That is how it seems to me as well.

Again, this furtive whispering, fit for old women, would be a species and form of sorcery. That is why the divine Moses, in setting out for us the laws from above, always joins these offenses together and, as it were, makes incantation the sister and kin of witchcraft. “There shall not be found among you,” he said, “one who practices divination, one who reads bird-omens or utterances, a sorcerer, an enchanter, a watcher of portents, a ventriloquist, or one who inquires of the dead.” Now incantation is diseased with utter shamefulness and lies deep in evil, yet somehow some are carried away by it, saying that those who practice such things invoke the name “Lord Sabaoth” as they chant over the sick. In this way they strive to establish that the practice is no longer shameful. But they seem to be carried off into deception and folly by a cold and feeble reasoning; for this very point is what is most grievous about the matter. We utter “Lord Sabaoth” to the God of all, wishing to glorify him, and we allow no other being whatever to bear such a title. For there is one and only one Lord of hosts. But these people casually toss so transcendent and most glorious a title, or rather doxology, to whichever of the demons that play along with them they choose; to the actors of their wonder-working they grant the glory most fitting to God alone, flattering and being flattered, and paying the extremity of so dreadful an impiety as recompense for their help in whatever they choose. For the throng of demons is always fighting against God and greedy for glory. We must therefore not be carried away along with them by their evil counsels, but rather keep as far away as possible, and pay no heed to wicked healers or wonder-workers, the demons, who demand blasphemies as a kind of wage for the games they play with us. As for you, if you are in pain in some part of your body, and you truly believe that “Lord Sabaoth” and other such titles, which the divine Scripture ascribes to the One who is God by nature, will release you from the ailment, pray for yourself and utter the words yourself. You will do better than those people, for you will be giving the glory to God and not to unclean spirits. And I shall also recall the inspired Scripture, which says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.”
So let augury, and incantation too, be ranked, if you agree, among the things condemned by the law, and among those held in the most shameful and loathsome repute before God.

Certainly; and I would add that we also insult God in other ways, and that a man would be liable to indictment and to account for impiety toward him if he chose to swear falsely, or to say anything blasphemous and offensive against the supreme and most high glory. The first is punished with utter wrath and unchecked penalty, the sickle, as it is written, destroying the perjurer’s home and shaking it down completely: “For it will enter,” he says, “into the house of the thief, and into the house of the one who swears falsely by my name, and it will lodge in the midst of his house and consume it, both its timbers and its stones.” The other incurs death and a penalty beyond all evils. We must therefore not swear falsely; or rather, we must not swear at all. For this is what the Savior taught us, saying: “Let your Yes be yes, and your No be no; anything more than these comes from the devil.” Those who are reputed to be people of dignity, who have made virtue as it were their housemate, will have no need of an oath at all; for the life of such people is held in high esteem among lovers of piety, and people are loath to distrust them; and if they happen to say anything, it is at once crowned with the belief of those who hear it. Let our life, then, be of good repute, and the need to swear will, I think, fall entirely idle. But if it should happen that some at times make light of the respect due to the saints, let God be the one sworn by; let no one drag in the name of anything else. For some, heedlessly sliding into lax degeneracy, pretend that it makes no difference, saying “By heaven,” or “By Justice,” “By Adrasteia,” “By the light,” “By the lamp.” And gathering other such things as they please, they perhaps even think they are being pious, pushing aside the divine name while gilding with the glory fitting to God the things that were called into being at his nod. We shall find that Israel at times suffered from some such error. For admittedly they built the temple in Jerusalem for God, and prided themselves greatly on this very thing, believing that they had attained the boasts of piety and won very notable glory; yet they were caught out, having heedlessly paid little attention to what had been declared to them through the all-wise Moses. But God taught that the thing would bring them no glory, and that he does not delight in buildings of stone, saying: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me? Or what is the place of my rest? says the Lord.” For God fills all things; he rests in heaven, but he pervades the earth as well. The divine is not subject to quantity; rather, just as it is farthest removed from any bodily imagining, so too is it removed from place and from any appearance of being quantified. But once the Jews heard him say, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet,” they fell into unsound notions and began swearing by heaven, calling it the divine throne, and likewise by the earth, as lying beneath God’s feet, and even by Jerusalem, for, they said, it is the city of God who rules over all. And this although the more ancient saints had used “As the Lord lives” whenever an oath was needed. But the Savior exposed the counterfeit in this most foolish notion of the Jews, saying that one must not swear, either by heaven, because it is God’s throne, or by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, or by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. For what they said in their nonsense, the Savior uttered to good purpose, showing that their supposed reverence in these matters was fabricated through and through and invented from who knows where. Let this error too, then, be gone. For we have been taught, whenever an oath is needed, never to invoke anything else, but rather to make Yes, yes and No, no our sure and trustworthy pledge. The law too said: “If a deposit should be lost while in someone’s keeping, and the one who gave it demands an assurance about it, an oath of God shall be between them both.” And men swear by what is greater, for so the wise Paul has told us. And we say that something is greater than man, if we understand it rightly, not in the sense that it perhaps excels in size, or in understanding and wisdom and glory, but in the sense that it is such, in comparison with us, in its very being.
I don’t understand what you mean.
And yet, Palladius, the argument seems to me clear and plain. Do we not say that many created things, and heaven besides, differ incomparably from human bodies in size?
Certainly.
And do not the angels surpass us in understanding and wisdom and subtlety of body?
They do, and in honor too.
And in brightness and bodily glory, I mean, is not the nature of the sun incomparably better?
It is better.

It is settled, then, that each of these might reasonably be superior to us in the respect in which it naturally prevails. Shall we, then, make these things what we swear by, setting aside the mention of God as superfluous?
By no means.
It seems, then, that what is greater than man is that which is supreme by nature and differs from created things in its whole being, that is, God.
Well said.

Let Yes and No, then, among those who have chosen to live the best life, serve as the use and force of an oath, and let this be firmly fixed; for being believed will follow from it. But if someone dishonors Yes and No, then let the use of oaths turn to what is greater than we are, or rather greater than the whole creation. And as for blasphemy, what more should I say about where it stands and into what evil it carries those who practice it? The ancient law requites it with bitter death, and Christ himself has condemned it to inescapable and endless evils: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” By Spirit he means the nature that is above body, which is God; and whoever dares to let loose an unbridled tongue against it will reap the fruits of his unrestrained mouth. For “a fool’s lips lead him into evils,” as it is written, “and his bold mouth calls down death.” That is why the divine Psalmist also said: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips; do not incline my heart to words of wickedness.” And these would be the most unholy outcry against God and against the ineffable and pure nature.
So those who are eager to walk the straight path blamelessly, and cannot bear to offend God, must be firmly established.

So I say. For to those who approach God not from a sound heart but from a suspicious and corrupted one, which has chosen to suffer from feebleness and instability, the prophet says: “How long will you limp on both your hams? If it is Baal, then Baal; if God, then God.” For to be neither wholly sound in faith nor yet settled in error is to limp on both, and it destroys sincerity on either side. The occasion of so rotten and brittle a disposition would be, I think, that some make their love for God fabricated and not genuine: they pretend to want to be Christians, yet do not do so with their whole heart, nor out of reverence for the truth, persuaded by it and honoring what is right. Rather, they are either hunting for what pleases them, or else, as though trying to charm away the fear of danger and the savage onset of misfortune, they make a show of having come to the faith, so that they may have many who choose to share their struggles and take on their cares. But such people will be given the lowest regard, and their lot will be among the most abject; utterly dishonored and cast off, barely managing to be counted worthy of life, they will be caught out when God examines what is hidden within us. Such were the men from Gibeon. They once approached Joshua and earnestly begged to be joined to the people of God; but their approach was not free of malice, nor simple and honest, as though from love of God, but made in hypocrisy and deceit. At first they escaped notice. But when they were caught acting treacherously, and were exposed as malicious and double-minded, they were assigned to the lowest rank: they became woodcutters and water-carriers for the whole congregation. You see, then, where insincerity will bring a man, and failing to honor with a sound mind the spiritual fellowship with the saints. For some at times deceive, not, I mean, Christ, who knows all things, but rather those who are in his type, that is, the leaders of peoples. Just as those men then deceived Joshua, who was put forward as an image and type of Christ, so these too slip in under the cover of deceit, holding out hypocrisy to mask the wickedness hidden in the depths of their thoughts and minds. But when they are found out, for it is impossible to escape notice, they will be saved only barely, receiving the servile and lowest lot; for deceit is the fruit of an ignoble mind. But we, whose aim is to think soundly about the things of God, and who care nothing for the rest, will cleave to our own Master and the God of all, with a simple heart, with an upright mind, with an undivided love that cannot bear to suffer from double-mindedness, but departs completely from Greek customs and ways of thinking, and goes as far as possible, and with all speed, from the things condemned by the law. For in this way we shall be perfect before the Lord God, as it is written, and glorious and approved together with the other saints in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
On Love for the Brethren.

The law crowns with the highest and fullest praise the first and supreme commandment, Palladius, namely: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength." It adds, "And your neighbour as yourself." Christ himself says plainly that on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets, and the divine Paul too calls love the fulfilment of the law, because it does no harm to the neighbour. Our discussion has, it seems to me at least, dealt sufficiently with the first of these, as far as we could. It went up and down and, as it were, all the way round, and gave a worthy account of how we might love God completely and wholly without blame. Come, then, let us look into the neighbouring and sister commandment, and make a careful study of love for our neighbour. Let us trace closely the means by which a person may come into the fair circle of virtue, win the highest reputation for skill in it, and walk in goodness with God and with men, as the divine Samuel says. For I hold that love for our brothers must be practised gracefully together with love for God, since to fall short in one is to fail in both, according to the words of John. He wrote this: "If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for whoever does not love his brother, whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he has not seen? And this commandment we have from him, that whoever loves God should love his brother also." So the two perish together and rise together in splendour. These virtues are like next-door neighbours to each other. Like an inseparable pair of horses, they carry the one who has trained himself to drive them well to one outstanding and most perfect beauty, that of piety toward God.

Well said. And since our aim is to labour over these things, come now, gather proofs from the holy Scriptures for each point, and try to tell me how love for our neighbour might be fulfilled in all its purity.

Very many paths lead us there, for it is written, "Your commandment is exceedingly broad." But I think one can gather skill in each of our actions from no other source than the law, for a prophetic word said that it was given to us as a help. And so the lawgiver, rousing us to remember his decrees continually, says: "And you shall lay these words on your heart and on your soul, and bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be unshaken before your eyes. And teach them to your children, to speak of them as you sit, as you walk on the road, as you lie down and as you rise. And write them on the doorposts of your houses and of your gates, so that you may live long, and your sons' days may be many on the land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, as the days of heaven are above the earth." And he showed clearly in Numbers what "Bind them on your hands" means. For it is written this way: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: Let them make tassels for themselves on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and you shall put a blue thread on the tassels of the corners. It shall be on the tassels, and you shall see them and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them. You shall not turn aside after your own thoughts and after your own eyes, after which you go whoring, so that you may remember. And you shall do all my commandments and be holy to your God. I am the Lord your God." First, then, he commanded us to inscribe the law carefully in our hearts. Then, knowing that forgetfulness is a grievous sickness of the mind, he commands that the commandments be marked on the doorposts as on a tablet. Moreover, he says it is of real benefit to bind to the right hand little tablets, perhaps, that carry the law and have the oracle written on them, and also to hang the tassels and the blue thread from the garments themselves.
And how could tassels and a blue thread remind us of the divine laws?
Do you not say that the law was spoken to the people of old in riddles, and as it were in shadows?
I do.

Is not the binding of the blue thread to the tassels, and to the hand itself, a riddle meaning that we must choose to think and do the things of heaven and keep the laws from above in mind? For I think the ethereal body of the sky is likened to the Indian stone, I mean the hyacinth. Like the sky, it is a mixture of brightness and darkness, holds something watery in its depths, and gives off a trembling, diffuse appearance. So the law deliberately commanded that the blue thread should hang from the garments themselves and also from the hand, as if quietly saying: "Let the oracle from heaven be a garment, a clothing for your mind and thought, and let the law be the judge of right deeds." For the hand is a symbol of action, and what we do in keeping with the law is surely beyond reproach and has nothing sinister or base about it. The Pharisees, then, made their tassels large and their phylacteries broad, that is, the tablets hung on the right hand. Yet Christ ridiculed them, because they made the practice an occasion for vainglory and not for remembering the law. So it is possible to break the law lawfully, if one does not use the law rightly. And this, I think, is what Solomon said: "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness." The divine commandment, then, must be inscribed on mind and heart. The divine David made the benefit of this plain when he said of every righteous man: "The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not slip." For it is, I think, quite clear that whoever has the divine law in his mind will surely be well grounded and stand firm in virtue.
So it is.

So long and continual study of the law drives out forgetfulness, which is like a murk and mist over human thought, and carries us toward what is straight, that is, what pleases God. And the lawgiver does not stop there. He devises something better still, and sets the hope of everything most to be desired as a kind of bait to make us eager to do what is required. For again he said: "If you walk in my ordinances and keep my commandments and do them, I will give you rain in its season, and the earth shall yield its produce, and the trees of the plains shall give their fruit. Your threshing shall reach to the vintage, and the vintage shall reach to the sowing, and you shall eat your bread to the full and dwell securely in your land. War shall not pass through your land, and I will give peace in your land, and you shall lie down and no one shall make you afraid, and I will destroy the evil beasts from your land." Do you see how much care and gentleness he grants to the person who is fair-minded and hard-working, and who gives way to reverence for the law? He promises to bestow early and late rain, one rich harvest after another, bread to the full and food without stint, and peace besides. It is fitting that the genuine keeper of the law, the insatiable lover of what God wills, should be made drunk with the abundance of heavenly goods.
