The righteous soul is like rich and fertile land, and spiritual consolation from above waters it like rain and gladdens it greatly, so that it puts forth unfailing and, as it were, richly varied fruit of piety toward God. Peace then crowns it, bringing it lasting well-being. So Paul too writes: "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts." Whoever has received such generosity from God will spend a life untouched by war and at peace. The enemy gives way, every adversary falls and comes to nothing, the devil's assault achieves nothing, and all fear easily departs. We shall find this same law written in Deuteronomy as well, for there he spoke this way, with slight changes: "If you will indeed listen to all his commandments which I command you today, to love the Lord your God and serve him with all your heart and all your soul, he will give you the rain for your land in its season, early and late, and you shall gather in your grain and your wine and your oil, and you shall provide fodder in your fields for your cattle." So the study of the law will make skill and good order at home in our souls, so that we can fulfil whatever God wills, while longing for what has been promised makes the sweat of virtue bearable.
True. I would agree, and with very good reason. But now, my friend, it is time to say how one may carry out the law of love for one's neighbour.

Let us turn to that very thing, then. Following the holy Scriptures, we say that God, the Lord of all, commanded Moses to assemble the people and bring them together beneath the mountain called Sinai, clean and thoroughly purified. He directed that they must wash their clothes and keep themselves above pleasure with women for three days. Through things perceptible to the senses and visible, he was signifying things perceived by the mind. For it is fitting that we come, so to speak, into the sight of God as if in bright garments, adorned with the glories of virtue, shining with radiance of mind, and set free from all love of the flesh and from earthly defilements. The law tutors us toward this, just as Moses indeed tutored the people of old, for those things were types of truer ones. And the tutelage given through the all-wise Moses, who leads the instruction of the law on to Christ, foreshadowed this for the ancients. I think one more point deserves attention here. The role and character proper to a tutor are well preserved in the person of Moses. He presented the people not to himself but to God, as lawgiver, teacher and guide to what must be done. So too the law, our tutor through the letter, brought us not to itself but to God the Word, who came down from heaven for our sake. Does our discussion seem to you to be following the track of the truth?
Very much so.

It is written, then: "And Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood beneath Mount Sinai. And Mount Sinai was wholly wrapped in smoke because the Lord had come down upon it in fire, and the smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and all the people were greatly amazed. And the blasts of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice." That God came down upon a mountain is a very clear sign that he does not visit the lowliest minds. Nor does he care to dwell with those whose thinking is earthy and grovelling. He comes rather to anyone whose mind springs upward and, as if it had a towering summit, looks down on human affairs and pictures only the things of God. It might also signify, in another way, that the knowledge of God is lofty and beyond our level, and perhaps attainable, even if only in part, by those alone who have trained themselves to fly to the heights; for "the young of the vulture fly to the heights," as it is written. Notice also that when God came down to lay down the ancient law for the people of old, he did not come where the people were, but high up and far away. For he still stood far off, in the words of the Psalmist, since the Only-begotten had not yet come to be with us in the flesh, nor lowered himself into self-emptying. That mystery was kept not for the people of old but for us. He came to be with us, so to speak, in a glory visible to the eye, leaving behind the heights of the Godhead, and he lived among us as one of us. God came down in the form of fire. Those who were to be tutored by compulsion and law needed to know clearly that, if they chose to be careless, they would have fire to answer to. For the people of old did what pleases God not out of willing love and the free inclination of the mind, but as if out of compulsion and fear. The spirit in them was not one of freedom or of adoption, but of slavery leading to fear. The mountain smokes because the Lord came down upon it in fire, and this, I think, is what is sung in the Psalms: "And he made darkness his hiding place." In another way the smoke might also signify for us the tears that will surely and wholly follow upon contempt, for moisture creeps from the eyes when smoke strikes them. If someone wished to approach these points of contemplation differently, he will take the fire as the illumination given through the law, though not without murk. For the law is dim and unclear, and the shadow cast by the letter is thick and quite able to cloud the eye of the mind. The blasts of the trumpet grow louder as they go on. At the beginning the law's voice was faint and barely audible. But when our teaching advanced to the instruction of the Gospel, when Emmanuel shone forth, the blasts grew louder. For Christ cried out with a piercing voice heard far and wide, which already reaches through the whole world. One can hear him saying through the voice of David: "Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world." Yet at that time the voice of the law went nowhere else, nor did it initiate all the nations. It sounded only through the land of the Jews and tutored one race, the race of Israel. "But Moses spoke," it says, "and God answered him with a voice." Moses asked for the law as a minister, a mediator and servant of the divine decrees. But God answered with his own voice, that is, through the Son, for the Son is the voice and word of the Father. The law is from him, even if it was spoken through angels. Indeed, anyone who wishes can hear him saying plainly: "I who speak am here." And: "I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfil them. For I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things have taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." So he calls the law his own words, for the voice of God spoke it, as I said just now, that is, the Son. Then it says: "The Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, on the top of the mountain, and the Lord called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up. And God said to Moses: Go down and solemnly warn the people, lest they draw near to God to gaze, and many of them fall. And let the priests who draw near to the Lord God be sanctified, lest the Lord destroy some of them." The God who is over all comes down to the mountain, and then Moses, being called, goes up. For no one can possibly spring up to the heights of the true vision of God unless God lowers himself and makes himself accessible to our minds. When he calls, we go up, and even then with difficulty, to a summit that is beyond nature and, as it were, set apart: the true knowledge of him. Christ will bring us this when he reveals to us the Father and God. The mountain is untrodden by the common herd, since the grace of a knowledge so exceedingly lofty is beyond the reach of the many. It can be climbed only by those who know how to make the ascent, or rather by those whom God has called to it, as indeed he called Moses. If anyone, then, is faithful and genuine in the house of God, he too, like Moses, will be chosen and made fit to come near to God, by way of sanctification and knowledge. For in this way we shall be with him as he says: "But you, stand here with me." He also charges that those crowned with the priesthood must be purified, when he says, "lest the Lord destroy some of them." For the priesthood is a very perilous calling. It is not far from danger, but very near it, unless a blameless life is plainly present, for those who minister to the all-pure God must be holy. Then it says: "And the Lord said to Moses: Go, go down, and come up, you and Aaron with you; but let the priests and the people not force their way up to God, lest the Lord destroy some of them." Moses goes up, and not without Aaron, who was a type of Christ. For the law is precious in Christ, and as holy through him it stands near God and with God. The law itself proclaims the high priest and apostle of our confession, according to the Scriptures. So let the law be yoked to Christ through spiritual contemplation, for Moses heard, "Come up, you and Aaron." What God has joined together, then, let no one separate by taking the law away from contemplation in Christ, clinging to the shadow alone and refusing to accept the truth as the image of the types. Yet the priestly race, together with the common people, is told [not] to go up the mountain. For God has not granted to those tutored under the law, nor to those still performing the worship of shadows, to enter into lofty and supreme doctrines about him. This is kept rather for those who have been justified by faith and called in Christ to obedience, and to a knowledge far surpassing the older one. The divine Paul too marvelled at the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ. And the Saviour himself will bear witness, concerning us and those who are of Israel by blood, when he says openly: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given." And concerning the Jews: "Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind." And again he said to those who had come to know him: "But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear." When the God of all had finished speaking about these things, he begins to legislate and to lay down laws about all the highest matters. And he says: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me." He made a fitting beginning for the laws by declaring that he himself was the worker of wonders in Egypt. He was the one who roused, so to speak, the whole creation against the madness of the oppressors. He armed the rains and the hail and displayed transformations of the elements. He sent pitiable death upon the firstborn and poured three days of darkness over them. He grants to whomever he wishes to pass through the midst of the waves, and he crushes those who oppose him without effort. For those who were coming under the yoke of the divine commandment had to know, they absolutely had to know, how great the lawgiver's power is, and that it is not safe for them to offend him who can easily accomplish all things.
How well, and how worthily of God, the lawgiver planned for us! Fear always somehow presses people into obedience, and makes the harsh and unruly as easy to guide as a colt that answers the rein.

Quite right. He forbade the worship of other gods and the making of any idol, likeness or painting. He forbade them to dare to give the name of godhead to the handiwork of image-makers, and he made such things liable to the severest penalties ("For you shall not take," he says, "the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold guiltless the one who takes his name in vain"). After this he sets human affairs in order and lays down the law as a kind of rule to keep everyone's way of life straight. He removes us from all sin, and before all else he points to the time of righteousness in Christ. That is the time of the most perfect redemption, the destruction of wickedness, the restoration to what was in the beginning, and the renewal of life in holiness and love for God. Accordingly he says: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work, but the seventh day is the sabbath, a rest to the Lord your God. On it you shall do no work, you, your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, your ox and your beast of burden, all your livestock, and the stranger who sojourns with you. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy."
And what does this mean? I do not understand it clearly. How could we keep the sabbath day holy?
Would you like us to say a few things about the sabbath and the rest from work honoured on it? That way, what God has declared to us by oracle would become very clear.
By all means.

The Sabbath, Palladius, is the last day of the week, and so, I think, it would signify the time when our Saviour came to dwell among us. That time appeared at the consummation, almost at the very sunset of the present age, but it has become for us the beginning, the door and the way to the washing away of sin, to freedom and forgiveness, to incorruption and life, and to the hope that is to come. The trustworthy word of the holy Scriptures hints in many ways at the sabbath-rest understood in Christ. Sometimes it sketches the ceasing that belongs to it, namely the ceasing from sins, and lays down a most bitter and harsh penalty for the transgressor. At other times it shows in figures the redemption and release into freedom that come with it, and also the preparation for the age to come.
Tell me how, then. I would be very glad to know.

It is through faith in Christ, Palladius, that we keep the Sabbath spiritually. We cease from the distractions of this world, we stop our aimless wandering, we separate ourselves from wickedness, and we slip out from under the yoke of sin; and so we are at last set free for a holiness that is free. Indeed the inspired Paul says of those who had not yet believed: "With whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who disobeyed, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed? So we see that they could not enter because of disobedience. Let us therefore fear that, while the promise of entering his rest remains, any of you should seem to have fallen short." And further on: "So then, a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God." And surely, if the sabbath-rest consisted only in being idle on the Sabbath, how could Israel have failed to enter the rest when it kept the Sabbath idleness? No: the whole matter was a type of the rest in Christ, and of the ceasing from sin of the one who is justified by faith. That is why God commanded that the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath must be stoned to death. The penalty laid on him was a figure of a spiritual and necessary truth. For is not wood that has withered from its own root, stripped and already dried out, a symbol of deadness? And is it not, besides, food for fire?
True.

Such is utterly wicked sin: a kind of deadness, and an unholy feeder of the savage flame for those who love it. So when, in the season of ceasing (from sins, I mean), some cling to dead and fruitless works, and let go of virtue and choose to love the things that will kindle punishments and flames for them forever, they will rightly undergo the sentence of death. For although they need not live dissolutely, they march of their own will toward the punishment that must follow. We who have believed, then, do enter into the rest, as the blessed Paul says. And so through the mouth of Jeremiah God accuses those who, by sinning against the type, defaced the beauty of the truth. He says: "Go and stand in the gates of the sons of your people, through which the kings of Judah come in and through which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah, and all Judea, and all Jerusalem, and those who come in through these gates. Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day; you shall do no work, and do not go out through the gates of Jerusalem, and do not carry burdens out of your houses on the Sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. But they did not listen and did not incline their ear, and they stiffened their neck more than their fathers, so as not to hear me and not to receive instruction." So he commanded not only that they must cease from all work on the Sabbath, but also that they must not go beyond the gates of Jerusalem.
Then what would be the meaning of these things too?

A spiritual one, perceived by the mind, going beyond the types and better than the ancient shadow. He commands those who keep the Sabbath in Christ to come to a halt in every work that is bent on wickedness and looks toward it, and to take up no burden on the shoulder at all. For those who have once truly cast off through faith the heavy load of sin, would it not be sheer madness to load themselves with it again, and to choose to put themselves once more under the yokes that lead to wickedness? And by having them stay inside the gates of Jerusalem, the type signifies that we must not separate ourselves from the holy city; nor does it allow us to be carried outside and slip away by turning aside to something else. By the holy city you are to understand the Church. For already some people, made bright through faith in Christ, who had unloaded profane sin and come within the holy gates of God's house, have been carried off into apostasy. Perhaps it was not an open apostasy, but they leapt out of the holy gate all the same by honouring customs fit for idol-worshippers. So when God declared that those who keep the Sabbath spiritually must remain inside the gates, the type signified steadfastness that cannot be erased, and that we must never slip away from our true devotion to him. That the Church is the city of God, David above all will proclaim aloud: "Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God." And the Saviour himself will assure us of it when he says of her: "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her."
It is settled, then, that we are to cease from all work on the Sabbath, as the lawgiver decreed.

Not from all work without qualification, Palladius. We must think and do the things in which God delights and which bring no small benefit, and to cease from these would win no praise. Not without reason, it seems to me, did the holy Scripture add that the Sabbath day must be sanctified by us: "Remember," it says, "the Sabbath day, to keep it holy." We shall fulfil this very fittingly if we are seen to be diligent in holy works while keeping the Sabbath spiritually. A clear figure of this would be that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and yet blamelessly carry out the sacred rites, complete the sacrifices, slaughter sheep, and do without hindrance everything that serves the glory of God. Did not Christ set this very point against the reproaches of the Jews, when they accused him of breaking the law because he had healed the paralytic on the Sabbath?
I remember.

And a man is circumcised on the Sabbath, as the Saviour says, without the law finding fault. The type urges us, and all but testifies plainly, that for those who keep the Sabbath in Christ, that is, those who cease from sin and are sanctified through faith, it is entirely fitting that circumcision in the Spirit be performed on the eighth day, that is, the day of resurrection; for it was then that Christ was raised. When he had come back to life and broken the power of death, he at once sealed his disciples with the Holy Spirit, and this is circumcision in the Spirit. For he breathed on them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit." Does not Paul too say that spiritual circumcision is performed in this way? He insisted that believers must be circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, that is, by the Spirit. I would add that while we keep the Sabbath spiritually, we would rightly not cease from the works of spiritual courage: crushing our enemies and conquering our adversaries in Christ. As an image of this I will again offer you that ancient Joshua, who together with the Israelites captured Jericho on the seventh day, that is, on the Sabbath.
So it seems that the Sabbath, once it has come to its truth, would bring us rest only from wickedness and sins, and this truth was still only sketched in shadow in the older types.
That is what I say. But in another way it would also show the mystery of Christ very clearly.
What do you mean?

Elsewhere the law said: "If you acquire a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year he shall go out free, without payment." That is in Exodus. In Deuteronomy it says this: "If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh you shall send him away from you free. And when you send him away from you free, you shall not send him away empty-handed. You shall provide for his journey from your sheep, from your grain, and from your [?]; as the Lord your God has blessed you, you shall give to him." For all the time before our Saviour came to dwell among us, Israel was held fast by a spirit of slavery, yoked to a law that punished. But when Emmanuel shone forth in the last times of the age (and the Sabbath has been set before us as a type of this too), the spirit of slavery was taken away. Without bringing anything at all to the Master for their redemption, people were called by his loving grace to freedom and to the glory of adoption as sons. For, as the Scriptures say, those who believed have been justified not by works of the law but by faith. And this, I say, is the meaning of "He shall go out free, without payment." But it says: "When you send him away from you free, you shall not send him away empty-handed. You shall provide for his journey from your sheep, from your grain, and from your winepress." Do you see clearly the power of the mystery of Christ shining through in these words? For we have been redeemed, and the Saviour of us all has set us free without payment. As it is written, we have shared in such extraordinary kindness not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his great mercy. And in setting us free, that is, in releasing us from sins and adorning us with the grace of adoption, he gave us himself as a fine provision for the journey: a blameless victim, led like a sheep to the slaughter for our sake. He also granted us a share in the life-giving blessing, that is, his holy flesh and blood. This, I think, is what it means that those who are called to freedom in the seventh season, that is, in the spiritual Sabbath, by the Master's kindness must be provided for from the sheep, and from grain and wine. That is what the law says. But the Jews sank into negligence and did not care much about keeping the commandments, and God accused them for choosing to act this way. For it is written: "The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I made a covenant with your fathers on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying: When six years are completed, you shall send away your brother the Hebrew who is sold to you; he shall work for you six years, and then you shall send him away free. But they did not listen to me and did not incline their ear. And today they turned and did what is right in my eyes, proclaiming release each to his neighbour, and they made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name. But you turned back and profaned my covenant, each of you bringing back his male servant and his female servant, whom you had sent away free to go where they wished, to be your male and female servants again." Do you see how he does not tolerate the types being set aside, or rather the truth itself being outraged, even while it was still in shadows? For, as it is written, the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. But the Jews dragged back those who had once been released and put them under the yokes of slavery again. They did not keep what was irrevocable, and so they offended against the power of the mystery, setting it aside and dishonouring it, even though it was still in types.
You have spoken quite rightly.

We are justified freely through the grace that is in Christ. We offer nothing in exchange for our own life, nor do we buy the glory of freedom; we gain it through the Master's kindness and love for humankind. He foreshadowed this when he said in Deuteronomy: "Every seven years you shall make a release. And this is the ordinance of the release: you shall release every private debt that your neighbour owes you, and you shall not demand from your brother whatever of yours he holds. You shall grant your brother release from what he owes you, so that there will be no one in need among you; for the Lord your God will surely bless you in the land that the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance to possess." Do you see the truth flashing out in the shadows? For this too would show very clearly our Saviour's saving plan for us. Those who have drawn near to him through faith, and have now been shown to be his own household and his brothers by sharing in the Holy Spirit and becoming partakers of the divine nature, he released from their debts though they had paid nothing. He did not demand from them the penalty for their transgression, although they owed him an account of how they had lived. But those who are still strangers, all but of another race because of their ruinous unbelief, and as far removed as possible from kinship with him, he held liable for their debts. Since their sin is still unwashed, he rightly made them subject to judgment and punishment. And so he said to those who had believed: "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." But to those who despised the true teaching of the gospel he said: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." Do you understand, then, that he promises to set free those who are his own by faith, but said that those who are still strangers and foreigners, dead in their offences, will give account to the judge for their own transgressions?
True.
The Sabbath rest also gracefully portrays the holy delight of the age to come and the sharing in heavenly goods.
Explain how, since I want to understand.

Gladly. The inspired David sings somewhere about the sons of Israel and the almighty God: "He gave them bread from heaven; man ate the bread of angels." By the food of heaven and of angels he means the manna, so that we may lift our minds beyond things that are perceived by the senses and seen, and contemplate the spiritual and divine provision that God pours into the souls of the saints, when he makes God the Word, who feeds the angels and gives life to human beings, dwell in those who have received the faith. For Christ has made his dwelling in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, and we are fed with living bread from heaven, for spiritual health and strength. The manna, then, is a clear and unmistakable type of this. The law commanded the sons of Israel to gather it, without going beyond what was sufficient for each. For it is written: "In the morning, when the dew had lifted all around the camp, there on the face of the wilderness was something fine like coriander seed, white like frost on the ground. When the sons of Israel saw it, they said to one another, 'What is this?' For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them: 'This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat. This is what the Lord has commanded: Gather of it, each of you for those who belong to him, an omer a head, according to the number of your souls; each of you gather it with those of your tent.'" Then, further on, it says again: "On the sixth day they gathered what they needed, twice as much, two omers for each one; and all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses. And Moses said to them: 'This is what the Lord has said: Tomorrow is a holy Sabbath, a rest for the Lord. Whatever you would bake, bake; whatever you would boil, boil; and all that is left over, lay up for yourselves in store until morning.'" And besides this the sacred teacher Moses explained the divine law to them, adding at once: "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord. You will not find any today in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath; there will be none on it." Is it still unclear to you after this, Palladius, that doing nothing on the Sabbath would hold a very clear foretaste, as it were, and outline of the life that will be in the age to come? And gathering, as into a storehouse, what has already been provided? And that the manna is no longer sent down from heaven, but one must make use of what has already been gathered, for enjoyment and nourishment? For when we keep the Sabbath in Christ and come to a complete end of sin, we shall delight in the good things from above. All toil will be taken away, and without sweat we shall find in abundance everything that benefits us.

What you say is true. For the life of the saints at that time will be spent amid good things that are all ready and, as it were, laid out before them. And let us too say to every saint: "You shall eat the fruit of your labours."

Let us then run back to the beginning and, as it were, rein our discussion back, and say this: when the law turned people to the one who is God by nature and in truth, it very fittingly and consistently did not allow them to be ignorant of the coeternal Word, who sprang from him and in him and exists together with him. For after first commanding, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength," and also, "You shall have no other gods besides me," it immediately joined to these the mystery of Christ, adding: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy." This is a good and necessary path, a road of most God-befitting skill, and it brings the most complete benefit to those who learn what they ought to know. Indeed the Saviour said to the Father and God in heaven: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." For teaching about the Son necessarily accompanies teaching about the Father, and the knowledge of the two lies very close together. And so, when the Jews missed the truth by not accepting the Son, yet thought they knew God, he rebuked them, saying: "You know neither me nor my Father; if you knew me, you would know my Father also." For the knowledge of each is included together with that of the other. So, having first laid down as a foundation, as was necessary, precision in the knowledge of God, and having first rooted in them the knowledge of the lawgiver, the law comes down to human matters. Right beside reverence for God, and joined directly to it, it places reverence for father and mother. Through them, with God's consent, we have been brought into being and existence at all, so that they hold, as it were, the second rank after the Creator. For by divine command and an art no one taught her, nature forms within herself the living child that is born, and so takes on, as it were, the glory of a creator. And just as God is the beginning and origin of all things, as Maker and Creator, so each person who has become a parent is, as it were, a root of origin for the child born from them, and the source of its coming into being. The service that father and mother render in bringing about existence is therefore, for everyone on earth, a type of the Creator of all. That is why the law commanded that they be given more honour than others. It neither withholds rewards from those who choose to honour them nor spares from punishment those who will not do so. It crowns a noble and holy disposition with honours, and loads the opposite disposition with evils in the end. "Honour your father," it says, "that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the earth." So the law holds out life, and a span of years as long as possible, as a kind of prize and special reward for those willing to honour their parents, and it hangs death over the arrogant and insolent; and it sets fear over them like a tutor who drives them toward what is right. For it said again: "Whoever strikes his father or mother shall surely be put to death; and whoever curses his father or mother shall die the death." Notice, then, that it punishes every kind of sin against them with the same measure, and it is clearly seen once more setting the rights of parents next to what concerns God. For just as with God an offence of the tongue is punished with death and the utmost wrath, so it is with parents too. Whoever sets aside the divine commandment and chooses to grieve the tutor by his transgressions dies without mercy. And whoever happens to disregard the counsels of father or mother dies by stoning, for the divine law commanded this too. It says in Deuteronomy: "If anyone has a son who is disobedient and provoking, who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and they discipline him and he does not listen to them, then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city and to the gate of his place, and they shall say to the men of his city: 'This son of ours is disobedient and provoking; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.' And the men of his city shall stone him with stones, and he shall die. And you shall remove the evil one from among you, and the rest, when they hear of it, will be afraid." After this, is it still right for you to doubt that honour toward father and mother follows in the footsteps of the honour of God?

Not at all. We are shamed into honouring them by what someone has wisely said: "Remember that through them you were born." And the patriarch Jacob also spoke most fittingly when he said: "Had not the Fear of my father Isaac been with me."

Tell me, then: does not saying that we were born through them clearly show that they are an image of the Creator, who calls into being things that once did not exist? And as for the fact that it is fitting for them to be honoured by us with fear, has he not placed them almost in the very rank of the Master?

Certainly. That is why the writer of Proverbs calls down a curse on certain people, saying: “The eye that mocks a father and dishonors the old age of a mother — may the ravens of the valleys peck it out.” But explain this: how should one understand what was plainly said by Christ, the Savior of all: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me”? I will also recall this: to the disciple who begged leave to bury his father and care for him in his old age, he says, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
Then what is strange in these words? Nothing in them is hard going, it seems to me. The meaning of these passages is quite plain, and very easy to grasp for those willing to think rightly.
And yet the saying is not entirely free of suspicion, for it seems somehow to lead us away from reverence for our parents.

Away with that suspicion, man, and with such counterfeit notions! The Savior’s word does not draw us away from reverence for parents at all. It teaches us to regard reverence for God as older and better. Our own discussion, too, has kept calling reverence for parents close to and second only to the reverence due to God, saying so over and over. Christ himself preserved this order: he brought no charge against those who choose to love their parents, nor did he lay any reproach or indictment on those who have chosen to honor them. But he lays down, most fittingly, that human things should come after God. That is why he does not say simply, “Whoever loves his father or mother,” but has added, “more than me.” Or would you not think it right that love for God should be ranked ahead of love for human beings?
Absolutely.

So he did not let the disciple go, so that he would not think he ought to make reverence for a human being more important than reverence for God, even if that human being is a father, whose claim to be honored is backed by the laws of nature as well. He ranks what concerns himself above what concerns us, for God is beyond all things and highest of all. Yet he by no means allows anyone to count reverence for parents as nothing on the ground that one must think and say that the things of God hold the older and better rank. Indeed, Christ made this very thing a charge against the teachers of the Jews, saying: “God said, Honor your father and your mother; but you say” — so God speaks — “‘Whoever says to his father, Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift,’ need not honor his father or his mother; and so you have nullified the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition.”
And yet the meaning of these words is not very easy to grasp. So explain what exactly the Pharisees’ offense was in this matter.

Somewhere in Leviticus it is written: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: Whoever makes a vow to the Lord of the value of his own life, the value of a male from twenty years old to sixty years old shall be fifty didrachms of silver, by the holy weight.” After saying a few things in between about women and young people, he adds again: “But if he is too poor to pay the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall set his value.” The passage is mystical and deep, and at the proper time we will examine it thoroughly; but for now let us speak of the matter in hand. Some of the Israelites came forward eager to consecrate their own lives to God — still in type and shadow, yet according to the law — pledging the prices set on themselves to those whose lot it was to serve as priests and attend the divine altar. But there were some who longed for such glory (for they wished to be called already sanctified and holy, a divine offering, and every other title of that kind), yet their desire was checked by lack of money, and poverty stood as a hindrance they could hardly get around. The scribes and Pharisees urged them very eagerly to go ahead with it anyway, for such people are great lovers of money and slaves to shameful gain. These would-be votaries pleaded their duty to their parents, and said — truthfully — that they could barely provide the necessities of life for themselves and for their parents, or perhaps scrape together clothing. The Pharisees dared to persuade them to count this as nothing for God’s sake; and if their parents came seeking the usual help from them, they taught them to say to father and mother: “Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift.” That is: “Whatever you receive from me, know that you are damaging a divine offering and laying hands on sacred property; for I have dedicated myself and pledged myself to God as a gift.” And the parents, fearing the penalties for sacrilege and greatly dreading the laws about it, endured it with groaning, and protested that piety toward God had become the cause of their hunger, perhaps even crying out against the divine commandment itself as wronging them in what mattered most. Why, then, does he say, “You have nullified the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition”? Because they ought — yes, they ought — to have honored those who begot them, and not to undo the law that concerns parents on the pretext of piety toward God. So we must neither neglect what befits God for the sake of human concerns, nor need we be altogether careless of human concerns for God’s sake. Rather, giving the preeminence of our love to the source of all things, that is, to God, we should then at once pass on, as in a second and neighboring rank, to those who served our coming into being the honors most fitting to them — bearing in mind, besides what I have said, this as well.
What do you mean?

Our Lord Jesus Christ, showing that reverence for those who gave us birth is among the most necessary of our duties, judged his own mother worthy of care and consideration. When he was already hanging on the precious cross, nailed to the wood, he gave the holy Virgin to his true disciple, and appointing the beloved disciple to look after her in her old age, he said: “Woman, behold your son”; and to the disciple he said, “Behold your mother”; and from that hour, it says, the disciple took her into his own home.
The discussion of this seems to me to have been carried out excellently.

So, having yoked offspring very firmly to their parents and laid on them the yoke of law and necessity, he immediately lays down what sort of people parents in turn should be toward their own offspring, if they are not to drive away what pleases God. Now the most wise Paul, briefly and plainly, instructs children that they must be subject to their fathers; and he said too: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline of the Lord”; that is, “Become their instructors in the best lessons, and direct them toward a God-loving and thoroughly lawful way of life.” The law, as is always its habit, goes about it in a roundabout way, but quite rightly charges fathers to take the greatest care for the decency of their children: “You shall not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, so that the land does not fall into prostitution and the land become full of lawlessness.” For the Creator requires bodily chastity of us before everything else, as a kind of firstfruits of a holy way of life; for bodily things, when they escape the reproach of shame and dishonor, are like the first approaches to spiritual splendor. So it would befit fathers to lead us into what is best of all. But if those who bring up children grow slack and negligent, or rather are caught, against all reason, becoming their leaders and teachers in shameful things, they will suffer the ultimate penalty, as men who destroy their own fruit and cast into the pits of perdition those for whom they would surely have done better even to die — for nature lays this law on fathers too. And a man who puts his own girl on display for the most open shame to anyone who wants her would justly be held to account and made to pay the penalty by the Judge of all, not for her alone, but also for everyone who has slipped into shame. For he has set out a kind of trap and a net of death, and holds them all caught, even if not all were actually caught; for what is judged is not simply the outcome, but the force of the attempt. Concerning such a woman the most wise Solomon also writes: “The woman who is a snare, and her heart a net, a fetter in her hands.” Necessarily, then, the lawgiver says, “You shall not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, so that the land does not fall into prostitution.” For if there is no woman at all around whom the charge of fornication could arise, it is not hard to escape that fall and to keep decency in the body, even if someone is easily drawn to pleasure and his mind is utterly weak and feeble. Having thus far given commands to fathers about their children, he also punishes with death the one who sets his mind on casting his own offspring away into apostasy from God. It is written thus in Leviticus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: You shall also speak to the sons of Israel, saying: If anyone of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes who have joined Israel, gives any of his seed to a ruler, let him surely be put to death; the people of the land shall stone him with stones. And I will set my face against that man and destroy him from among his people, because he gave of his seed to a ruler, to defile my holy things and profane the name of those consecrated to me.”
The law is obscure; it is not yet very clear what it means to show. So explain it — you will do well.

The Moabites and Midianites, the Gergesites and Hagarenes, and certain other barbarian peoples living near the land of the Jews lived by pagan customs: each one’s religion was whatever he fancied, and simply whatever came into his head was worship and service. The Israelites, whose minds were not yet secure and firmly fixed in love for God, were very easily led into apostasy and so ready to fall away that they thought nothing of worshiping, if it so happened, the gods of their neighbors too, and of choosing to share with them the sickness of error that had been theirs from of old and in Egypt. Indeed, they once went mad over the young women of Midian, and, carried away by the charms of the women, joined them in calling on Baal of Peor. So the lawgiver, having clearly foreseen how unsound and brittle their minds were, entirely forbade intermarriage with foreigners, saying very plainly: “You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son; for she will turn your son away from me, and he will go and serve other gods.” Since it was entirely to be expected, and quite naturally, that some of the Israelites would choose to betroth their daughters to the more prominent men among the nations, caught as in a net by wealth so as to think nothing of apostasy, he decrees wrath and death for that act of daring and brings the written law under the words that concern the ultimate penalties. For it was inevitable that the girl given to a foreigner would come to think differently and serve demons; so he subjected the father, as the destroyer of his own fruit, to a punishment of equal weight. So the holy and New Scripture instructs parents to be diligent in bringing up their children in the discipline of the Lord, while the slow-tongued law travels the same road by a circuitous and roundabout way. Having first very properly commanded that fathers must not permit their daughters to do things that lead to shame and licentiousness, it then says that they must also keep their daughters’ knowledge of God unshaken and not allow them to be spent on profane idolatries, even if great wealth were laid before them. For when a daughter is joined by the law of marriage to a foreign husband, even a rich one, is this not a case of “What will a man gain if he wins the whole world but forfeits his soul?”
You have spoken rightly.

One could see quite easily that the gap is no small one between those justified in Christ and those schooled by the law. For the people of old, to become entangled with outsiders and to associate with foreigners was not without harm; but Paul advises us to live in a better and more confident way, saying: “If any man has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away; and if a woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband.” What, then, is the reason for God’s arrangement in these matters? Why did the law of old fear close ties with those of other beliefs, but now no longer? Because the Spirit dwelling in those called in Christ makes them steadfast and gives them an unshakable love for God — the Spirit through whom and in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” — whereas those of old were not yet rich in that gift. For as the divine John says, “The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified.” So all perfection is in Christ, while the law, as it is written, made nothing perfect.
Then would you tell me, since I long to know, how the imperfection of the law might be made clear?

Certainly. Our discussion will proceed to the matter in hand and will examine closely the ways of love toward one’s neighbor, which were brought to the people of old through the writings of Moses in a somewhat cruder form than is fitting.
Go on, then, to this very point, and gladly.

Well then, the law says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” But our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us the law of mutual love in only a few words, making, as it were, our innate knowledge and each person’s own will an advocate for the law: “Whatever you wish people to do to you,” he says, “do the same to them.” For if someone chooses to do to others the very things he would pray to receive, he will not miss the mark; rather, he will go straight along the path of love and win the crown of mutual love.
Well said.

Love, then, is the fulfillment of the law, and greater than faith and hope; for so the divine Paul writes to us. Accordingly, weaving for it, as it were, a many-colored crown of spring flowers, he says again: “Even if I give away all I have to feed others, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing. Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave unbecomingly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, keeps no account of evil, does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth; love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; it never fails.” But these things are evident to everyone, I think, and the discussion of them would grow very long if one chose to gather up minutely everything in the New Scripture. Let us turn now to the shadows of the law and to what was decreed for the people of old while things were still in types.
An excellent plan.

The law was a training in righteousness and a kind of prelude to the noble deeds of the gospel. For it is written: “The beginning of a good way is to do what is just.” The law is a tutor leading us to Christ, and if it is understood spiritually, its view of the life perceived in him will not prove false. It establishes us in righteousness, while the teaching of the gospel carries us further still, beyond it. Now the ways of righteousness are these: first, honor and love toward the one God, who is God by nature; and next, as its neighbor, immediately after it, love toward our brothers and kin, with reverence for parents placed first among these. So the Word advances for us in fitting order: after piety toward God and respect for parents, it urges us to show our kindness to others too. Everywhere the law takes thought for equality, and it is seen laying down that justice be tested with precision. For it is written in Deuteronomy: “There shall not be in your bag a large weight and a small one; you shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, so that you may live long in the land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance; for everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination to the Lord your God.” And again in Leviticus: “In measures and weights and scales, you shall have just scales and just weights and a just chous.” He was eager, and quite rightly, to liken the ways of justice closely to measures, weights and scales. For a straight and justice-loving mind in a way weighs and measures the nature of things, and tests the principle of equality more finely and precisely than one would expect even of those who assay coins on the pan of a balance. It measures out, as it were, to each thing under consideration what is most fitting to it, neither spoiling the beauty of exact equality by excess, nor letting what is adequate in equality be debased by a shortfall. “Let there be just scales and weights, and a just chous,” it says. These, I think, would be types, as it were, and visible examples, showing us the ways by which the principle of exact equality may be searched out and the knowledge of justice will come to light. But understand that the things in the law are kept within measure and have justice as their limit, whereas the things that come through Christ are rich in something greater and run far beyond. For the good lies beyond the just — that is, the glory of the life in Christ.

Well said. For I remember Christ declaring to those justified by faith: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.”

But let these things stand as they are. Let us inquire, if you like, into the measure of the kindness taught by Moses and the glory of righteousness according to the law. One who has most rightly made it his aim to hunt out the knowledge of justice, and who has made it his concern to excel in love toward his brothers, ought to be seen as secure and steady and as what he truly is. His goodness should not be easily shaken, nor light, nor feigned, like one who wants to hide a wolf’s form under a sheep’s fleece; rather, he should be eager to keep the freedom of his own character bare and blameless. That is why the law says: “You shall not walk with deceit among your people, and you shall not hate your brother in your heart.” It also puts the same thing another way: “You shall not put on yourself a garment woven of two kinds”; and again: “You shall not wear an adulterated cloth of wool and linen together.” For deceit and guile are truly dreadful in those reputed to be good, and beyond all reproach. This is among the things God most abhors, and it always has double-mindedness as its sister, together with a kind of twofold and fickle disposition, at which the divine and pure Mind is most sharply roused to anger. For he said somewhere about certain people: “Their tongue is a wounding arrow; the words of their mouth are deceitful; one speaks peaceably to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself. Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a people?” And David says that the one who will ascend the mountain of the Lord is the one who is innocent of hand and pure in heart, who has not deceived with his tongue nor done evil to his neighbor. So the law forbids as most shameful and offensive walking in deceit — that is, choosing to live craftily, putting on the outward form of righteousness while harming one’s brothers, with no regard for the laws of love. And it does not allow us to have a garment woven of two kinds, setting the matter as a riddle: that we should not tolerate having a kind of doubleness in the mind. By doubleness I mean the inward, mental kind — the accursed desire to please people, which is woven, as it were, of two pursuits, each badly corrupted by the other. For what is the life of hypocrites, and what sort of life is it? Is it not to be seen as good in people’s eyes, and to seem good, without actually being good in truth?
Certainly.

So such a way of life is double, woven for us out of unlike wills. But the divine David approves the single-minded and says they are deemed worthy of care from above: “For the Lord settles the single-minded in a house,” he says. God is also said to scatter the bones of people-pleasers; and Paul too loathes the thing, saying: “Am I now trying to win over people, or God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ.”
And to whom on earth is it not evident that being double-minded and playing the hypocrite is truly out of place and as far as can be from strict uprightness?

So freedom from guile is the fruit of a love that is blamelessly formed and fitting for a just and good man. The law also says this is required: someone who truly cares for righteousness and loves his brothers should not think he has earned that name rightly just because he alone refuses to do wrong. He must also become the teacher of his own relatives, and of those who have become close to him in some other way and enjoy the title of kinship with him. Paul too instructs that whoever is to take charge of a church must keep his children in submission, and he makes this the proof of whether he has the right goodness of character or not. He says: “If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he take care of God’s Church?” For this reason the law speaks by way of an example and a vivid image: “If a bull gores a man or a woman and they die, the bull shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull shall be guiltless. But if the bull was in the habit of goring before yesterday and the day before that, and its owner has been warned and has not done away with it, and it kills a man or a woman, the bull shall be stoned, and its owner shall be put to death as well. If a ransom is laid on him, he shall give as the ransom for his life whatever is laid on him. If the bull gores a son or a daughter, they shall deal with him according to this same rule. If the bull gores a male or female slave, he shall give thirty didrachms of silver to their master, and the bull shall be stoned.” Is the oracle clear to you?
Not very.

Then consider what I say, and above all keep in mind the most holy Paul, who wrote: “Is it about oxen that God is concerned? Or is he not speaking entirely for our sake?” So the law compares to a bull the man who is insolent and boastful and strong enough to take advantage of others. For the animal is always somehow proud and haughty, terrible in strength, and its charge is hard to withstand. If such a man, the law says, belongs to the household of someone who has chosen to live a holy life and is, as it were, yoked to him, and if he injures someone, or worse, even destroys him, perhaps crushing him by his acts of greed, the law has ordered that he pay the penalty of death for it. It said he must die by stoning. But it exempts the owner from punishment if he did not know about the man's grasping ways and is not found to be a partner in his wickedness. For the faults of others are not charged to us if they happen to be hidden. The law does not allow the bull's flesh to be eaten. By this it means that we must not share in the impurity of others, and it sketches this in the figure of eating, which is a kind of sharing. Is this not plainly the saying: “Keep yourself pure, and do not take part in the sins of others”?
Certainly.

The law has ruled that the master is condemned along with the bull if he knew of the offense and is shown to have known of the wrongdoing. To be able to restrain wrongdoing and fully prevent the offense, and then not bring oneself to do so with real effort, shows that the man was all but a fellow-worker in it. As far as will and agreement go, he has chosen to join in the work of those who want to commit sacrilege. So let such a man die, the law says, unless the judges impose a ransom and the penalties that apply in such cases. The law looks toward kindness. It takes into account that his part in the sin was consent, a joining in by mere assent. For it punishes more mildly, it says, if the judges so choose. Now take the figure as a guide to the truth. The Judge of all condemns the gravest offenses to death, yet he accepts sinners who offer ransoms that release them from sin: the tears of repentance, the hard labor of contrition, the various works of mercy. For “mercy triumphs over judgment,” as the Scriptures say. The law also makes a precise distinction among the victims. If the bull kills a son or a daughter, it says, let the owner die without pity. But if it kills a male or female slave, let silver be what is demanded for them. What is the reason for this? Surely it is worth looking into. After all, freedom and slavery among us come from greed and are not an infirmity of nature, as sickness, of course, is. For “one God created us, and one is the Father of all,” in the words of the prophet. Does the Creator, then, record slavery as a charge against some people? Does the slave count for less with him too, and does the free man have the advantage in honor? Not at all. “For in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free.” Since the law is a shadow, the son and daughter stand for the free race of the saints. The male and female slave stand for those who are still enslaved and under the yoke of sin. Offending against saints is not the same as offending against sinners, and offenses against the two are not punished in equal measure. Everyone can see that both groups are brothers by nature. But the saint stands out spiritually and on the heights of virtue. He is precious to God, so that he comes into the rank of son and daughter and rises above the human and servile measure. The law also teaches us in other ways to act in holiness and hold fast to love for our brothers. We will set these out one after another and say what comes to mind about each. For it said again: “If someone opens a pit, or digs out a pit, and does not cover it, and a calf or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution. He shall give silver to their owner, and the dead animal shall be his.” In a riddle, this means that we must not put a stumbling block or a cause of offense in our brother’s way. We must not let what is by nature beneficial become useless to anyone. Nor must the things that are necessary for life, for ourselves and for others, be made to look like a road to death. For does not someone who opens or digs out a pit produce something useful and necessary for himself and for others? But do not let what is yours, the law says, become an occasion of danger to someone else. For love, as the inspired Paul says, “does not seek its own,” but takes thought for what belongs to others as well.
I should like to know clearly who the one opening or digging out a pit is, and what the pit is.

What the literal account indicates is not obscure. The law says that a pit must be covered so that no one comes to harm. In other words, it says that whoever has not done this should know that if anything slips into it, he will pay silver to its owner, and the dead animal will be his. But let us rise above the plain sense of the narrative and lift the matter up to spiritual contemplation. Then we will say this. In these words the law seems to give the name “pit” to the knowledge of the divinely inspired Scripture, to the teaching about the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and to understanding of the mystery of Christ. These lie, as it were, in the depths, and they have life-giving power. The Savior himself will bear witness, saying: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” So whoever reads the older writings, searches laboriously into the words of the divinely inspired Scripture, and seeks precise and genuine knowledge closely resembles a man digging a pit. For he is looking for life-giving water, a gladdening spring, and a torrent of delight. But whoever has come so far in understanding that he can hand on the teaching of the mystery in a work of his own is digging out a pit. He makes something new, as it were, not building on the sweat of others but benefiting himself and others through his own. The lovers of “knowledge falsely so called” also dig broken pits, in the words of the prophet. So if anyone digs a pit, the law says, let him take precautions, so that what seems to have been done well does not become a means of ruin for anyone. For we must speak about God correctly and with complete precision, so that we give no one an occasion of stumbling. And this, I think, is what it means for a cover to be placed on the pit: our teaching must not lack the safeguards it ought to have. For if an ox or a donkey falls in, the law says, the one who did the work will make restitution. Again, it does not name the ox and the donkey without purpose but with a deep meaning. It says “ox” so that you may think of the sacred and clean race, and “donkey” so that you may understand the unholy and unclean. For under the law what is unclean is not brought to God as a sacrifice. By the sacred and clean race we mean those already sanctified through faith. By the unholy and unclean we mean those not yet cleansed through holy baptism, who still have the stain of sin ingrained in them. So it is as if the law were saying: If harm comes to someone who has already been baptized and sealed by grace into fellowship with God, or perhaps to someone who is not yet such, the one who caused the stumbling will pay the penalty, and the dead will remain his. That is, the death of the one who suffered will be laid to his account. The Savior himself puts us on guard when he says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.”
You are right.

You can easily see that the law shows us through other riddles as well how perilous it is to sin against our brothers in this way too. For wounding their weak conscience makes our offense an offense against Christ. So it said: “If fire breaks out and catches in thorns and also burns threshing floors, or ears of grain, or a field, the one who kindled the fire shall make restitution.” For it is not right that good things should perish along with what is harmful by nature, or that what is cultivated should be consumed together with what is wild.
What do you mean?

Could not the writings of the unholy heretics, and the empty quibbling of the doctrines held among the Greeks, rightly be compared to the thorns on mountains and in fields? What benefit could come from them to human souls? Or rather, what harm will they not do to those who want to take them to heart? The thorn feeds only fire and nourishes flame. So too the worthless doctrines of those who have gone astray, and the old wives’ tales of the idolaters, kindle for us flames that last forever. But ears of grain and wheat are the most cultivated food. They are fit for people to eat and necessary for their benefit, for they keep us alive. They may stand as a figure of the doctrines of truth, by which we believers are fed on Christ as on living and true bread. The divinely inspired Scripture, in turn, is like a smooth field without rough ground for those who know how to walk through it rightly. For as it is written, “All things are plain to those who understand, and straight to those who find knowledge.” So the thorn is the utterly loathsome and profane loose talk of the perverse. The wheat and ears of grain are the teaching of truth, which is most nourishing and good for the soul. The open field is the divinely inspired Scripture. So when the words of the holy teachers of the mysteries fall like flames or fire on the deceptions of heretics and Greeks, in defense of the doctrines of truth, the law speaks of them as going against the thorn alone. They burn up the writings of those people as useless and wild material, but they must not harm the wheat or the ears of grain. That is, let the teachers of the mysteries stay watchful, so that they do not damage any of the doctrines of truth. Otherwise, the law says, whoever cannot bring himself to do this with care should know this: if anything needed for our benefit is burned up along with the worthless things, he will have to give an account for his carelessness. Do you see, then, how much watchfulness the lawgiver has ordered us to exercise, keeping the sincerity of our love for our brothers unclouded in every way?
I understand.
More on love for the brethren, and against one who steals a calf or a sheep.

So from every side, Palladius, you can see that the ancient law too commands that the words of sacred instruction be kept correct and very precise. And, making sure the matter would not go unpunished for those who make a habit of deceiving the simpler sort, it said again: “If anyone steals a calf or a sheep, and slaughters it or sells it, he shall repay five calves for the calf and four sheep for the sheep. If the thief is found breaking in, and is struck and dies, there is no bloodguilt for him; but if the sun has risen upon him, he is liable, and he shall die in return. If he has nothing, let him be sold for the theft; and if he is caught and the stolen thing is found alive in his hand, whether ass or sheep, he shall repay double.”
The passage is not very clear. But please try to tell me what it is that is being declared here as in a riddle.

The law usefully fixes a penalty for anyone who wants to grasp more than his share, and in a way reins in the man who cannot restrain his desire for whatever his neighbor or his brother may happen to have. So, it says, even if the one convicted of this should die in the very act of stealing, no blame attaches to those who killed him. It also brings disgrace on him by saying that he must be sold if he cannot afford to pay the ransom, driving him by these fears to choose to live rightly. But the hidden sense of the narrative would be quite different from this, and we must state it as well as we can. The calf and the sheep are both clean and sacred, and both are offered to God as a fragrant aroma. But the calf excels in size of body, while the other does not, for the sheep is smaller than the calf. Calves and sheep, then, as clean and most sacred animals, are the holy multitude of those justified through faith: they divide the hoof and chew the cud, according to the law, and they produce cultivated fruits, for the calf tills the ground, and the sheep too is fruitful. The flock of the called is penned in the divine courts, that is, in the churches; but very many are the thieves around it, breaking in and slipping in, drawing away the souls of the simpler sort by manifold deceptions, and all but selling them off to Satan the destroyer. But whoever has done such a thing, it says, shall repay five calves for one, and four sheep for the sheep. For it says that the penalty for the thief should be fivefold for the calf but fourfold for one sheep, imposing the punishment, I think, according to the measure of spiritual stature in virtue of those who are lost. Bodily size would be a type and shadow of stature in virtue; for it is easy to see greater or lesser goodness among believers, since perhaps not all are equal: “But each of us has his own gift from God, one of one kind and another of another.” But if, it says, he is caught still stealing and breaking in and carrying out the works of robbery, as in night and darkness, then let him die; and the deed is not murder, nor is there any charge against the one who did it. For the one who fell was greedy and violent, and was wounded under the law of war. But when the sun has risen, and the time for robbery has already passed, it restrains the hand of the one who strikes and defines the daring act as a charge of murder. For as long as the spiritual thief maims the soul of one who has believed in Christ and drags it away from love toward God, if he is caught in these very offenses, he would not unjustly suffer death as well; for he has killed a soul, which is better than a body. But when the sun has risen for him too in his mind, and true knowledge shines out, as in the order of light and day, it does not allow him to be in danger; for the works of night and darkness are punished, but those done henceforth as in the light are no longer punished. God has judged it right that he be released from the old charges, those committed in ignorance and darkness. And indeed let it be said to those who have come out of sin into the spiritual light: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” So too the Lord justified the divine Paul, who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of violence; for he persecuted the Church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it.
Excellently said.

“But if he cannot,” it says, pay five calves for one and four sheep for one, “let him be sold for the theft.” Do you see how the law plainly records the disgrace of slavery against those whose sin is continual and indelible, and who are unable, so to speak, to ward off the charges with a ransom, because through weakness of will they cannot bear to toil toward repentance and to appease God through the labors it requires? So it rightly says they are to be sold. For it does not allow those so defiled to be counted among those set free by divine grace. Thrust out of the honor fitting for the free, they too will hear: “Behold, you were sold for your iniquities.” But if, it says, he is caught having stolen but not yet having killed—that is, if one of those accustomed to heterodoxy is caught having begun his trickery and deceit against others, but has not yet prevailed and carried his hearers off to destruction—he shall repay double. For the master of the flock will take back what is his, and the charlatan will in addition be called to account; this would be the “double.” And he will undergo a penalty unto death. For what he wished to do to others he would himself suffer, and quite fittingly.

How truly ruinous and dreadful is the business of the deceivers! I think Christ himself also warned of them in advance: “Beware of those who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”

So the law rightly condemns every such person to death, as one would a wild beast. For it is written in Exodus: “If anyone steals one of the sons of Israel, and overpowers him and sells him, and he is found with him, let him be put to death.” And in Deuteronomy: “If a man is caught stealing a soul from among his brothers, the sons of Israel, and overpowers him and sells him, that thief shall die.” For it is not right that the holy race in Christ should be ravaged and carried off into unaccustomed slavery by those who make a practice of this. Just as those who beguile young boys carry them off from their city and homes, strip them of the pride of the free, and put them under the yoke of compulsory slavery, in the same way, I think, those who by intricate deceptions of thought carry off people who have chosen to think rightly and who pursue the life befitting the free, bringing them over to what seems best to themselves, utterly foolish as it is, will rightly face the charge of robbery against human souls; and their penalty is death. “Do not even say ‘Greetings’ to such people,” says the Savior's disciple. He is not training us to be savage in our manners; it is that the sheep is not suited to friendly relations with the wolf, and those accustomed to think differently are, as it were, incompatible with one another: “For what share has a believer with an unbeliever?” And besides this, the divine Paul writes that we must not associate with the sexually immoral of this age. So then, lest some be snatched away from the Church of God as from their father's hearth and carried off into the assemblies of evildoers, selling off, as it were, their own minds by turning aside to wickedness—“for bad company corrupts good morals”—the law fixes death as the penalty for those who have most impiously set their hearts on doing this. And you may see the law again indicating this to us obliquely, through another oracle as well. For it sets the affairs of the world in right order through the more evident interpretation, which anyone who wishes can readily grasp. We will not discard the literal narrative as stale, at least where it is especially useful. For sometimes the letter itself will benefit the hearers, while in its depths it is, as it were, in labor with spiritual things, and holds the force of subtler meanings as in faint shadows. It said again in Exodus: “If anyone deceives a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall pay the bride-price and take her as his wife. But if her father utterly refuses and does not wish to give her to him as wife, he shall pay her father money equal to the bride-price for virgins.” And, as if broadening the divine command for us, the divine Moses says in Deuteronomy: “If a man is found lying with a woman who is married to a husband, you shall kill both of them, the man who lay with the woman, and the woman; and you shall remove the evil from the sons of Israel. If there is a virgin betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of their city, and they shall be stoned with stones and shall die: the girl because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he humbled his neighbor's wife; and you shall remove the evil from among yourselves. But if a man finds the betrothed girl in the open country, and forces her and lies with her, you shall kill only the man who lay with her; but you shall do nothing to the girl. The girl has committed no sin worthy of death; for as when a man rises up against his neighbor and murders him, so is this case: because he found her in the field, the betrothed girl cried out, and there was no one to help her.” Now as for the literal narrative, I think no one will need any explanation in order to understand it, for it is very clear and evident. But it seems we must leave these things aside for the present and take the inner and hidden path.
Certainly.

I say, then, that just as among offenses involving a woman the most grievous of all would be adultery, which dissolves another man's marriage and separates those already joined, so in the same way, I think, among offenses against human souls the most impious and intolerable of all is to set about corrupting not just any soul, but one already in some way married to and united with Christ, the Bridegroom from above and from heaven. For we are united with him through faith and also through partaking of the Holy Spirit: “For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit,” according to the Scriptures. So the law justly assigns death both to the adulterer and to the woman who has prostituted herself: to him because he sowed the seeds of the impiety within him, and to her because, dishonoring the law of faithfulness, she became another's, and, opening her mind to his corruptions, received the defilement that comes from human inventions.
The argument is persuasive.

Then we may very well liken a woman lawfully married to a husband to the soul that is wedded and united to Christ through faith and the Spirit. And we shall take the betrothed virgin to be the soul that has been called to the beginnings of true knowledge but is not yet fully united with Christ. Such a soul is still awaiting, as it were, the marriage and the truer mode of union—the grace of holy baptism and participation in the Holy Spirit—having received the word of catechesis as a pledge and, as it were, the beginning of intimacy. In this way our divine initiator, Paul, brought the Church from the Gentiles to Christ, for he writes: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.” And the Bridegroom himself says somewhere through the voice of the prophets: “And I will betroth you to myself forever, in righteousness and in justice and in mercy and in compassion; and I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord.” If then, it says, the charge of corruption should arise in the case of such a soul as well, let the deed be recorded as adultery; for the betrothed woman is bound, and is henceforth under the hand of the one who will shortly be her bridegroom. But if the wrong takes place in the city, it says—that is, in the Church of Christ and in the city of the living God, inhabited by angels and holy men, guides and teachers who are able to help those in danger and being deceived—let the virgin who suffered it die together with the deceiver.
