For though she could readily have escaped the corruption by reporting it to the teachers who know how to save, she succumbed to the suffering willingly, and she was not led away into evil by necessity. But if, it says, it does not take place in the Church, nor in the city of the living God, but as it were in the open country and in a field, where there was no initiator to help and a great lack of those accustomed to persuade people toward the better, and the deception happened amid a scarcity of teachers, then let only the one who used force be in danger. For in that case what is done is an act of aggression, a suffering without help, and a necessity hard to escape will deflect the charge. Or shall we say that it is not superfluous to censure what was inflicted against one's will, involuntary as it is?
Entirely so; for the law is holy.

Well said. The law examines what is done with great precision, and in a way measures out its anger to fit the offenses: it neither releases lesser wrongdoing entirely from punishment nor puts it on a par with what goes beyond it, but shapes its response, as it were, to match the size of the charges. For it said again: “If anyone finds a girl who is a virgin and not betrothed, and forces her and lies with her, and is found out, the man who lay with her shall give the girl's father fifty didrachmas of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; he shall not be able to send her away all his days.” So the law made the one who lay with a betrothed woman liable for adultery—in the senses already stated, of course. But if, it says, a soul appears in the form of a virgin, still unjoined and not yet pledged to Christ through faith, and then someone is caught defiling it with words that lead to impiety and carrying it off from one error into another—as heretics do, sometimes snatching away people from among the Gentiles and the Jews and persuading them to follow them—he will not find the attempt unpunished. For he will render to the Father of spirits, that is, to God, an account of his offense, which is very aptly figured by a fine of money. But the words “she shall be his wife” are of use for the literal narrative.
I understand what you mean: the law is twofold, both fleshly and spiritual.

And observe how the word of the ancient commandment was not ignorant of what Christ said about husband and wife: “What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.” For “let her be his wife,” it says, “because he humbled her; he shall not be able to send her away all his days.” Besides this, consider how lofty a glory all-pure virginity is; for the word of divinely inspired Scripture knows the loss of virginity as a “humbling” and sees fit to call it so, as though it were the casting off of dignity.
Rightly said.

Having declared the deception of the heterodox to be truly hateful to God and unholy, along with the perversion into wickedness by those who make a practice of corrupting people who have chosen to walk uprightly, and their leading them away to what is improper, the law devised something further, which the divine Paul himself also made one of his best lessons for us, saying: “Do not wrangle over words, which is of no use and only ruins the hearers.” For excessive disputations and a stubborn love of contention over questions beget needless fights and wound the minds of the hearers. Some, out of frivolity, sometimes rashly and ignorantly accept what is neither right nor rightly said, and are eager to praise it; others, passing the harsher verdict on the best things, would be found to suffer from the same lack of education as the first; and very few indeed know how to discern and to put what is beneficial ahead of what tends to do harm. Even these scarcely keep their minds unwounded amid the verbal battles of others. So the law again hints to us that the matter will not go unpunished for those who choose to do it, saying: “If two men are fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out not fully formed, he shall be fined whatever penalty the woman's husband imposes, and he shall pay as assessed. But if it is fully formed, he shall give life for life.” Now it is said that the embryo in the womb scarcely appears in human form, and attains the shape of our body only when the count of the fortieth day has been completed. For this reason, they say, the most excellent Moses, as if giving birth to Israel anew out of the error of Egypt and re-forming it for life under the law, abstained from food and drink: “For I did not eat bread,” he says, “and I did not drink water for forty days.” And we must suppose that Christ too did and endured this for our sake. For in him our nature was being re-formed toward holiness through self-control, since in the beginning, in the first-formed man, it had contracted the defilement of sin and transgression from unrestrained appetite. These thoughts are not implausible; but however the literal account may stand, let it be set aside for now. Come, then, let us examine how one should understand the striking of a pregnant woman by those who make a habit of wrangling over words; for in such matters a very subtle discussion is not unpleasant. The fruit and offspring of the mind, then, would be faith in Christ, which re-forms us toward him through complete knowledge and shapes us into the divine image. And indeed those who have believed, signifying this, I think, cried aloud very aptly through the voice of Isaiah: “Because of fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor and gave birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.” So the spiritual and saving fruit and offspring of the mind would be faith in Christ, which also imprints the divine features upon us. To those who had foolishly slipped from more perfect knowledge into a lesser and more imperfect kind—these were the Galatians—the divine Paul called out: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” For having begun in the Spirit, they were pursuing perfection according to the flesh, having gone over to the worship of the law; for this reason they left the forming of Christ in themselves incomplete, as though miscarrying the good that lay within them as in a womb. Thus perfection in knowledge and purity in faith will establish the form of the Savior in the souls of all of us, and this will be in us like a divine seed. When, then, some are scandalized by certain people's wrangling over words, and the soul that has suffered this miscarries the faith and knowledge it was carrying as in labor and had stored up within its mind, then if, it says, it is not fully formed—that is, if it is still imperfect and less beautiful—the one responsible for the scandal will by all means and in every way undergo a penalty, whatever, it says, her bridegroom, that is, Christ, imposes; “and he shall pay as assessed,” that is, let him also acknowledge the favor shown him, since he has not undergone the full punishment unto destruction. But if, it says, the spiritual offspring of the soul is fully formed—that is, if it is knowledge and faith bearing the form of Christ—he will be liable to the extreme penalty, as being already a murderer. For the death of the soul is the casting off of blameless faith and the loss of sound knowledge. Therefore the law says that it is a defilement to partake of the unholy teachings, and of whatever words may be spoken by a man who has become the devil's prey and, as it were, food for the herd of demons; and it forbids this again, speaking as in a riddle: “And you shall not eat flesh torn by wild beasts; throw it to the dog.” For divine Scripture is accustomed to call a shameless and unclean man a dog. And perhaps to such a one, I think, every loathsome and foul-smelling word would be fitting, composed by Beelzebul himself, as by a wild beast that has devoured the soul that fell under its power and serves it for this purpose; for “no one says ‘Jesus is accursed’ except by Beelzebul.” But for the saints it is altogether unfitting to share in such shameful or counterfeit thoughts and words. For light has no fellowship with darkness.
True.

Again, he has declared by oracle that those whose lot it is to lead, and who are in charge of flocks, ought to keep watch. And he hints at the kind of care this calls for on our part, saying in Leviticus: “You shall not let your cattle breed with another kind, and you shall not sow your vineyard with a different seed.” The multitude under one’s hand may very well be compared to flocks of goats and sheep, or to a vineyard. For the divine Peter heard: “Simon son of Jonah, do you love me? Feed my lambs; tend my sheep.” And concerning those of Israel the prophet Isaiah said: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is a beloved new planting.” It is the mark of a good shepherd, then, not to let an animal of a different kind loose among the sheep, so that they might happen to be mated by a foreign animal, lest a sheep bear offspring of a different nature and fall away from the natural nobility that is in it. And the keeper of vineyards, if he is sensible and has studied to farm as well as possible, would never allow dry grain crops to grow under the vines themselves, lest the vines’ moisture be spent on what is foreign to them and they fall short in their own fruit. Come, then, from the image, as it were, to the spiritual meaning: let us not impiously allow our rational flock to be subjected to what we might call the seedings of heterodox teachers (spiritual seedings, of course) and to the doctrines they introduce by speech. For the fruit of an unlike mind is very ugly, and the words of those who do not share our faith would produce base offspring in those who received them. And since we are vineyards, set in the ranks of orchards, we ought in a way to be crowned with a single kind of fruit and to refuse the double-natured way. For there is no natural likeness at all between wheat and grapes. Let there be no place among us, then, for foreign seeds.
Well said.

In another way too he shows that things of differing ways are incompatible and irreconcilable, and severed from fellowship with one another. As a type he sets forth the most outlandish and utterly monstrous union of the rational animal with what is not rational, but of a different form and alien kind. And so he says in Exodus: “Whoever lies with a beast, you shall surely put him to death.” And more clearly again in Leviticus: “And whoever has intercourse with a four-footed beast, let him surely be put to death, and you shall kill the beast. And a woman who approaches any beast to be mated by it, you shall kill the woman and the beast; let them surely be put to death; they are guilty.” For conversations, and what we might call spiritual minglings and unions, with those whom it least befits, those whose mind has sickened into the utmost irrationality, bring death both to those who corrupt and to those who willingly submit to the corruption.
The law speaks most rightly and very piously.

You would marvel at this too. For it could happen, I suppose, that some people, through the intolerable high-handedness of others, even if perhaps they did not wish to undergo corruption from right thinking to what is crooked, were led astray as if under compulsion, and perhaps not without tears. The law, then, did not think fit to overlook even this class of people and leave them without help.
What sort do you mean?
Those bound tight by the yoke of slavery and held fast under the power of those who bought them.
And in what way did the law come to the help of these too?

It releases them from bond and constraint if the harm concerns the soul, and it has clearly ruled that the one who is wronged may run away if he wishes, with nothing to hinder him. For it said this indirectly in Exodus: “If someone strikes the eye of his male servant or the eye of his maidservant and blinds it, he shall send them away free in exchange for their eye; and if he knocks out the tooth of his maidservant or the tooth of his male servant, he shall send them away free in exchange for their tooth.” As far as an obvious, surface reading goes, it restrains insolence and makes the anger of owners moderate, and it does not want them to go so far as to do the kind of thing that would lead to those under their yoke going free, to the loss of the owners’ own prosperity. It by no means permits outbursts of temper to run unbridled and to be inflicted on nature itself, of which the Creator alone is to be understood as Master. For slavery and the suffering bound up with it are not a natural infirmity, but something introduced by greed. In Christ, then, God the Father at once refashions the whole of nature to what it was in the beginning. For “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” And the shame of slavery is entirely abolished, for Paul writes that “in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free.” Meanwhile the law, training people step by step toward perfection, removes the unrestrained use of power and whatever goes beyond the measure of what is fitting, imposing on those who neglect the law the penalty of releasing those they have wronged. But this concerns the letter and the shadow, if one chooses to understand it this way as well. If, however, the aim of the law is interpreted spiritually, you might approach its insights in another way too, Palladius. For this light of the world we receive and admire with the eyes of the body, but the divine and spiritual light rises in our hearts. And the body’s food is ground fine by the teeth, and so it becomes a path to life; but the divine insights, which are hard and difficult to reach, are all but crushed by the strength of the understanding, as if by a tooth, and they nourish the soul. Indeed Wisdom, spreading for us the divine and spiritual table, says: “Come, eat my bread.” So if a servant should happen to suffer harm in any such matter, because his master goes astray and forces him to slip from correct doctrines into outlandish error, “let the bond be loosed,” it says, “and let no account be taken of the compulsory yoke.” Let the dread of authority be cast away somewhere, and let the one under the yoke go wherever he may find that he can remain unharmed; for nothing was ever better than the soul. And it says, “So that he may be saved, let him be released from slavery.” You can see that this saying is true, and that it is still being fulfilled in our own times. For servants do not tolerate masters who lead them off into error; in this matter at least they generally withdraw their obedience from the authority set over them. Though they have bowed the neck of the body under the burden of slavery, they keep the mind unclouded within them. They are convinced that to know the doctrine of the true faith clearly and without error is worth a very great deal, or rather everything, and they make it their spiritual food, grinding what comes to their ears with the mind as with a tooth, and chewing over the force of the divine thoughts.
How clear the argument is to us, and how right!
The law also accustoms us in another way to love for one another, persuading us to value standing by our neighbors, while abhorring and punishing ways of acting unequally.
What do you mean?

Listen, then. For again it writes: “If someone’s bull gores his neighbor’s bull, and it dies, they shall sell the living bull and divide its price, and they shall divide the dead bull. But if the bull is known to have been a gorer yesterday and the day before, and its owner has been warned, and he has not done away with it, he shall repay bull for bull, and the dead one shall be his.” Do you see the riddle, and how its meaning comes straight through to us, as it were, by means of a very clear example? “If,” it says, “so-and-so’s bull should die, felled by another bull, they shall divide the living bull, and the dead one in turn shall belong to both.” That is, if someone should unwillingly take advantage of and wrong another, let the one who was wronged, it says, enjoy the goods of the one who caused him grief, and let them share their joys in common. This, I think, is what dividing the living bull means. And let the one who gave offense unwillingly, it says, share in the misfortunes of the one who suffered; this, I think, is what dividing the dead one indicates. Do you see, then, how the law, still in riddles and in shadowy fashion, introduces the way of mutual love? Or is this not: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep”?
So it seems.

But if, it says, the one who takes advantage clearly knows that his neighbor will suffer something terrible, because the means of his overreaching have not been removed, he himself shall undergo an equal penalty and pour out the misfortune of the one who suffered on his own soul alone. For this is what is meant in a riddle by “He shall repay bull for bull, and the dead one shall be his.” For the matter does not stop at wrongdoers losing their own goods: they will have a misfortune of their own, and what befell their neighbor will be their own suffering.
How well the argument holds for us!

The divine Paul too set before us a wise law of love for one another, saying somewhere: “Not seeking your own interests, but those of others as well.” For love does not seek its own; rather it looks around also to the interests of others, and to how things may go well for the brothers. This again the ancient letter hints at for us. It runs as follows: “If someone grazes a field or a vineyard, and lets his beast loose to graze another’s field, he shall make repayment from his own field according to its produce; and if it grazes the whole field, he shall repay the best of his own field and the best of his vineyard.” For one who lets his own beast loose on other people’s fields benefits his own affairs and in a way seeks his own interest, but not from things in which his neighbor delights, nor from things any of his neighbors would be pleased with, but from things by which they would be grieved and wronged. We must seek, then, what benefits us, that is, our own interest, not by overreaching against others, but by such means as allow us to pursue it without doing any wrong, while our neighbor’s contentment remains intact. This would clearly be to seek the interests of others as well. Or let a person know, it says, that if he chooses heedlessly to cause his brothers grief and takes no thought for his neighbor, looking perhaps only to his own interest, he will undergo an equal penalty, and his way of seeking apparent advantage will bring about the loss of what is dearest to him. This, I think, is the meaning of “He shall repay the best of his field and of his vineyard.” The sense of these words would also fit, it seems to me, the inventors of heresies, whose loathsome and utterly senseless disciples, like irrational beasts, graze down the Lord’s crops and vineyards, to the condemnation and punishment of the heresy’s inventors. For the loss of their finest possession will befall them, that is, ruin of the soul itself. For in a vineyard, or perhaps a crop, understood as each one of us individually, the best thing in it is the soul.
So we say that it is a fruit of love that one must seek the interests of others, and not only one’s own.

Certainly, Palladius. And while the law requires that love toward the brothers be fulfilled, as most pleasing to God, it wisely does not allow love to be overburdened by excessive and too great exploitation on our part. For even a mind that stands firm, even if it happens to be well established in some virtue or other, is easily damaged by what assails it not moderately but with an onslaught that is hard to withstand.
What exactly do you mean? I do not understand clearly.
Do you not say that gentleness and forbearance are a virtue?
Of course.

But suppose someone heaps griefs and insults on one who practices gentleness and forbearance, and the sort of things that provoke anger. If this is done in moderation, he might sometimes endure it and bear it nobly, and he will make it an exercise in gentleness and freedom from anger. But if someone goes beyond moderation and runs past the bounds of forbearance, it would be no surprise if the virtue, as though overpowered, weakened a little.
Well said. For the good in human beings is somehow tipsy: even when no one shakes it, it can barely stand.

Come, then, if you please, to love itself. It is the preeminent virtue, more excellent than the others. Yet it does not tolerate excessive exploitation. This again the law teaches us in the form, as it were, of a parable and a clear example, saying: “If you enter your neighbor’s harvest, you may gather ears in your hands, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor’s harvest; if you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, you may eat grapes as many as you wish to fill yourself, but you shall not put any into a vessel.” For to gather a few ears by hand, or to pluck a cluster of grapes out of desire or for food, would do no harm; the owner will bear it gladly, I think. This is the law of love, and such a thing does not appear to go beyond measure. But to bring the reaping iron to a neighbor’s goods somehow overflows and oversteps love for one another, and passes into the territory of greed. So this is a clear example that we must not abuse the love of our brothers, but must honor love for one another by being content with enough. It is not inelegant, I think, to apply this saying to certain others among us as well. In the churches they pluck, as a kind of spiritual food, the words of the teachers, which may be spoken on the spur of the moment and extempore; but they do not consent to stop there. Going, as it were, beyond the measure, and putting them as if into a vessel, they store them away in notebooks. They are very eager to learn, but in a way they wrong their brothers’ reputation, because they consign to writing what was improvised on the spot as though it were something carefully composed. But the law, my good friends, I would say to them, has clearly commanded that nothing be put into a vessel.
It is dangerous, then, to pry up a virtue of the soul as if with a lever, and to dare all but to shake a firmly set mind by excessive exploitation.

The saying is accurate. For the God of all has clearly ruled that we must not plot against virtue, but rather share, if we can, in the good things that come from virtue. He sets this out in a faint riddle, depicting in very small things things incomparably higher. For it is written in Deuteronomy: “If you come upon a bird’s nest before you on the road, in any tree or on the ground, with young or eggs, and the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the children. You shall surely let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, so that it may go well with you and you may live long.”
And what does this mean? The riddle is not clear to me.
Do you not understand plainly? That if someone catches a bird that is still nesting or brooding, he may make use and gain of what comes from her; but he must send her away, doing her no harm.
Yes, for that would be the intent of the letter.

Then look at what is hidden, and, unfolding the shadow as it were, contemplate the truth spiritually. Each virtue is like a mother, the source of the good things that come from it: take, for instance, kindness, love of the poor, gentleness, long-suffering. For a person is kind not so much to himself as to others; and those in need would share in love of the poor, and likewise in gentleness and long-suffering. So each virtue is to be understood as a mother, a kind of origin of the good things in it and from it. And the nests, as it were, of the virtues are the souls that travail with them and have taken them into themselves. The law therefore says that those who come upon men in whom virtues are gathered as into a nest should profit from what comes from them, but should not go on to harm virtue, the mother of the finest achievements. And virtue is wronged when someone shakes it in the ways already described.
How deep the riddle is!

Yes, you are right. But, to say something in keeping with the words of blessed Paul: Is it for sparrows that God cares? Or does he not speak entirely for our sake? For the word of the commandment given through Moses sets out for us types of realities, not the realities themselves plainly. And you can see how, little by little, it lifts us up to the ways of the highest love for one another. It tries to persuade us to love even those who have offended us, and to show ourselves above resentment toward enemies, not overcome by evil but rather overcoming evil with good. For it said again, in Exodus: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his beast of burden straying on the road, you shall turn it back and return it to him. And if you see your enemy’s beast of burden fallen under its load, you shall not pass it by, but shall help him raise it.” And in Deuteronomy: “When you see your brother’s calf or his sheep straying on the road, do not ignore them; you shall surely bring them back to your brother. And if your brother is not near you, or you do not know him, you shall gather them into your house, and they shall stay with you until your brother looks for them, and you shall give them back to him. So you shall do with his donkey, and so you shall do with his garment, and so you shall do with anything your brother loses: whatever he loses and you find, you may not ignore. You shall not ignore your brother’s donkey or his calf fallen on the road; do not ignore them; you shall surely help him raise them up.” Do you understand, then, how very elegantly it trains us toward what is already in some measure the supreme and perfect good? It commands us to make our sparing of the beasts of the one who has hurt us an exercise, as it were, in not bearing grudges, and throughout it crowns him with the name of brother. In doing so it restrains, I think, vehemence in anger and excess in pettiness, and brings in the law of nature as a kind of umpire of love. For if you find, it says, a straying beast or a lost garment, you shall keep them safe for your brother; and if one of the animals used to carrying loads slips to the ground, to be crushed under the load itself, you shall work with him and help raise it. This is nothing other than to benefit the owner: an exercise in mercy, a training in kindliness, an effort to thrust resentment far away and to avoid quarrels, so as not to be seen offending against love and the law of brotherly love. It is likely, too, that the oracle hints at something else. For if the lawgiver was so concerned that we should offer help even when one of the irrational creatures is in distress, how much more would sparing human beings please him, and the love owed to those of our own race? So even if an enemy should happen to go astray, let him learn the straight way and through us turn toward what is good for him. So too Christ was pelted with stones by those of Israel, yet he called out nonetheless: “While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you.” And if one of those who have offended us is oppressed by toil and trials and, as if thrown to the ground, is crushed by inescapable constraints, let him, it says, be helped by us, and let the one at odds with us be beyond our resentment. Or is this not: “Do good to your enemies, and pray for those who mistreat you”?
Excellently said.

It befits the saints, then, to share the pain of those who suffer, and not rather to make the very things for which they ought to be pitied a pretext for taking advantage of them, leaping upon those who have been wronged and raging against them still more. And even if someone could carry out his scheme in secret, the law says very well that one must abstain from such crimes. For it said again: “You shall not speak ill of a deaf man, and you shall not put a stumbling block before a blind man.” And yet how is it not better, and most especially fitting for the truly gentle, to keep a bridle, as it were, on the tongue, and to refuse to speak ill of anyone at all, or rather of any human being? For “Do not speak ill of one another, my brothers,” says the Savior’s disciple. But here the law says, “You shall not speak ill of a deaf man,” wishing, I suppose, to signify through a riddle that those who are truly gentle in character must keep away from injustice, even when some people happen to be easy victims. For the deaf and the blind are not free from infirmity: they are sick in body and maimed in their senses, I mean sight and hearing. The deaf man would not hear someone who wants to speak ill of him, nor would the blind man see the one who puts a stumbling block before him. So it is not at all hard to escape notice if someone wishes to plot against them. But those whom they ought rather to pity, as already afflicted by their own misfortune, they will be caught wronging further: crushing the blind man with a stumbling block he does not know about, and sometimes leading the deaf man to smile at insults as if they were compliments, while often striking him in the most vital places. So the wickedness done to both might be hidden, if one chose; but it would not escape the charge of harshness and extreme hatred of others.
True.

That the ancient decree also makes us loving toward one another and compassionate you will learn more easily by listening to it speak. At one time it says, "You shall surely open your heart to your brother who is in need among you"; and at another, "And you shall not wrong a stranger, nor oppress him; for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. You shall not wrong any widow or orphan. If you wrong them in any way, and they cry out and call to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows and your children orphans. If you lend money to your poor brother who is with you, you shall not press him, nor shall you lay interest on him. If you take your neighbour's cloak in pledge, you shall give it back to him before the sun goes down. For it is his only covering, the cloak for his nakedness; in what will he sleep? If then he cries out to me, I will hear him, for I am merciful." Do you hear how, after setting out the sweet lesson of love for one another, he added the threat of his anger? And how he all but kindly explains himself to those who would have to endure it if they did not take care to show compassion to their brothers? "For I am merciful," he says; that is, being good by nature and compassionate as God, I will certainly receive the outcry of the one who has suffered, and will readily pity the tears of those weighed down by poverty. So we must avoid giving the poor man cause to cry out against us. That we ought to share with others, and count love of the poor worthy of the most urgent care, he again earnestly urged in Deuteronomy, saying, "You shall not withhold the wages of a poor or needy man, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the strangers in your cities; you shall pay him his wages the same day. The sun shall not set on them, for he is poor and has set his hope on them; and he shall not cry out against you to the Lord, and there shall be no sin in you." Do you see, then, that he persuades us to dread the outcry of the poor, and so drives us toward love for one another? And the new Scripture, the one given through Christ, which brings in perfect goodness, says, "Sell your possessions and give alms, and behold, all things will prosper for you"; and some of the believers did just that. For they brought the prices of lands and houses and laid them at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as anyone had need. But since the law is an elementary teacher and leads us to the first principles of the oracles of God, it commands generosity in small matters, as a kind of preliminary exercise for the road that leads to this. That is why it says: "When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in your field, you shall not turn back to take it; it shall be for the poor, the stranger, the orphan and the widow, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands. When you gather your olives, you shall not go back to glean what is behind you; it shall be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow; and you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this thing. When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not glean it again behind you; it shall be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow; and you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt. Therefore I command you to do this thing." For in times of good cheer it is good to remember one's toils and former affliction. Such remembrance calls us to love of the poor, and does not let the fullness of prosperity forget the evils of want.
True.

See how very skilfully and elegantly he weans us from what is worse and persuades us to shun hardness of heart, while leading us toward what is better and setting us on the ways of love for one another. He urges us to lend to our brothers if they happen to be in need, but he forbids interest and commands us to refuse any increase. And having further commanded that we must not be burdensome or press hard on debtors, he orders the remission of debts. He writes as follows: "You shall not charge your brother interest on money, interest on food, or interest on anything at all that you lend to the foreigner [?]; you shall not charge interest, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all your works on the land which you are entering to inherit." As far as the lawgiver's own will went, the open-handed and generous use of ample wealth would have been set before us without stint, toward the foreigner and toward brothers alike: "Give to everyone who asks of you," says Christ, "and from one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back." But since the mind of those who are only beginning in righteousness is not strong enough to accomplish the good without fault, the law, acting as a tutor, advances toward it little by little and measures out the manner of righteousness. It requires strict compassion toward brothers and neighbours, but reserves generosity toward foreigners and sharing with all for a more perfect instruction. For the shadows lasted until the time of reformation, and that time was the time of Christ's coming.
Very elegantly said.

So, having further commanded that we must lend, having cut off increase, and having promised a blessing to those who choose to do this, he orders that when seven years have rolled round on the debts, they are to be released. In this they honour the time of the remission of all, that is, the coming of Christ, at which we have all been justified by faith and have gained an amnesty for our old offences, since he nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us and took out of the way the accounts we owed the Judge. He speaks thus again in Deuteronomy: "Every seven years you shall make a release." And this is the ordinance of the release: "You shall release every private debt that your neighbour owes you, and you shall not demand it of your brother, because a release has been proclaimed to the Lord your God. Of the foreigner you may demand whatever of yours he has. But to your brother you shall grant release of your debt, so that there shall be no one in need among you; for the Lord your God will surely bless you in the land which the Lord your God gives you as an allotment to inherit." And again, after other things: "If there is among you one of your brothers in need, in one of your cities in the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not turn away your heart, nor shut your hand against your brother who is in need. You shall surely open your hand to him; you shall lend him as much as he needs, according to what he lacks. Take heed to yourself, lest a hidden word, a lawless thing, arise in your heart, saying, 'The seventh year, the year of release, is drawing near,' and your eye be evil toward your brother who is in need, and you give him nothing, and he cry out against you to the Lord, and it be a great sin in you. You shall surely give to him, and lend him as much as he needs from you, and you shall not be grieved in your heart when you give to him; for because of this the Lord your God will bless you in all your works and in all that you put your hand to." "You shall not be grieved in your heart," he says, "when you give to him"; for "God loves a cheerful giver," in the words of the blessed Paul.
How, then, does this seventh year signify the coming of our Saviour, at which the time of the remission of all was revealed, or rather the manner of it was brought to completion?

Do you not remember that we explained in what has already gone before that divine Scripture customarily likens the whole span of the present age to a week, because the days cycle back to their beginning? The end of the week is the Sabbath, and right next to it comes the eighth day, which brings us, as it were, the new beginning of an age through the resurrection of Christ.
I remember.

Christ, then, came to dwell among us according to the Scriptures at the consummation of the present age, as though, in a sense, on the Sabbath; and it was then that he released all who were bound tight by the cords of their own sins and owed him an account for their transgression. Accordingly, in the Gospels too he likens us to debtors, saying: "A certain man had two debtors; one owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they had nothing to repay, he forgave them both." And besides this, when shaping for us the pattern of prayer, he says, "Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven; give us today our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." So the law was hinting at the divine mystery to us obliquely and in riddles when it commanded the release every seven years. It also sets us on the paths of kindness, teaching us to value love for our brothers above money and persuading us to be ready to give and to share. And for the time being it establishes gentleness toward brother and neighbour as a kind of exercise for a more generous regard toward all.
So it is. I gladly agree with you, since you mean to speak so well.
And you would marvel still more, Palladius, if you learned something greater.
What is that?

The law wants us to advance so far in kindness and love for one another that we consider nothing equal in weight to love for our brothers. It wants us to bear their ill temper so nobly that we are seen to rise above anger, even if they do not behave toward us as they ought to be and to be seen, and choose to grieve us by their lack of affection. You have a type of this too in Numbers: "And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying, 'Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that has befallen us: our fathers went down into Egypt, and we lived in Egypt many days, and the Egyptians ill-treated us and our fathers; and we cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard our voice, and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And now we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. Let us pass through your land. We will not go through fields or vineyards, nor drink water from your cistern; we will go by the King's Highway, and we will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory.' And Edom said to him, 'You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out against you in war.' And the sons of Israel said to him, 'We will go along by the mountain; and if I and my cattle drink any of your water, I will pay you for it. It is nothing; we will go along by the mountain.' But he said, 'You shall not pass through me.' And Edom came out against him with a great multitude and a strong hand. So Edom refused to let Israel pass through his territory, and Israel turned away from him." Do you hear how those of Israel's blood, usefully recounting their miseries in Egypt and setting out the ways in which they had been oppressed from first to last, courteously ask a favour that wrongs no one, all but eager to make their kinsman a helper? For the descendants of Esau were brothers of Jacob. But the others, though they ought to have pitied them and let them do whatever they knew to be useful and beneficial for them, were exposed by the facts themselves as hard, unbending and incapable of sympathy. They barred them from the road, even though the people had said plainly that they would do no damage anywhere to the vineyards or to the produce of the fields, and would not even draw water without paying. And if they would not abandon their request, he not only threatened an attack but was already in arms and drawn up with his whole army. And what happened then? Israel rose above pettiness. "He turned away from him," it says, rejecting any quarrel with his brothers and honouring the law of kinship by great forbearance. Or do you not think this is so?
Certainly I do.

Then we shall reckon that checking our passions and reining in our anger, measuring out penalties in proportion to each person's faults, and, moreover, making our judgments in every case upright and wholly beyond reproach, are the fruit and outcome of love for our brothers.
Quite rightly.

If you wish, you may be persuaded of this again when he says at one time, "And you shall not bear a grudge against the sons of your people"; and at another, "If there is a dispute between men, and they come to judgment, and they judge and acquit the righteous and condemn the ungodly, and if the ungodly man deserves stripes, you shall lay him down before the judges, and they shall scourge him before them according to his ungodliness. They shall scourge him with forty stripes in number, and shall not add to them; but if they go on to scourge him with more stripes beyond these, your brother will be disgraced before you."
And what reason shall we find, in turn, for why the condemned must be beaten with only forty stripes in number? Tell me about this, since it somehow embarrasses some people.

In many ways the mystery of Christ is finely sketched in shadow for us through the ancient commandment, and the saving passion is, as it were, modelled for us—the passion in which and through which we have been freed from everything that has power to harm us and plunge us into incurable calamities. As I said a moment ago, the release of debtors every seven years hints at the time of the remission of all; for we have been justified in Christ, and have been taught to say in our prayers to our Father and God in heaven, "Forgive us our debts." In the same way here, the rule that those who strike, or those who are struck, should go no further than forty stripes in the torment of scourging points to the thrice-longed-for time of the Only-begotten's dispensation in the flesh. At that time we were healed by his bruise, and he was afflicted for our sins, when the people of Israel treated him with drunken outrage and Pilate laid the blows on his back, while we were delivered from penalty and punishment. For of old "many were the scourges of the sinner," as it is written, but Christ was scourged for us. Just as he died for all, so again he was scourged for all, since he, being one, is equal in worth to all. And if you divide the number forty into five times eight, you will find the five and the eight useful for signifying the time. For the Only-begotten came in the fifth time, according to the parable in the Gospel: a certain man was hiring labourers for his vineyard, and he went out about the first hour, the third and the sixth, the ninth and the eleventh. And he rose on the eighth day, destroying the power of death and abolishing along with it the mother of the corruption that came in upon us, that is, sin. Once sin has been taken away, scourges too must cease, and the penalties and punishments it brings. That is why the law does not allow the scourge to go beyond the number forty until the coming of Christ, as it were halting the punishments and signifying the time of remission. For the types are in labour with the beauty of the truth. It should also be known that when Israel had offended, they wandered in the desert until the fortieth year, for God had sworn an oath not to bring them into the land of promise. This was the limit set for the wrath against them. When the time had passed, the wrath was dissolved, and their descendants crossed the Jordan and entered the land, since the indignation did not run beyond the fortieth year. So this too is a clear type, that some are beaten with up to forty stripes. For the time after this is the time of remission, bringing us the mystical crossing of the Jordan, and moreover the knives of stone, that is, circumcision in the spirit, and the generalship of Jesus. For Christ has become our leader after Moses and the law.
I am persuaded.

So, in order that the cases that come up might be judged rightly and impartially, and that the ways of greed might be done away with, he says, "You shall appoint for yourself judges and scribes in all your cities which the Lord your God gives you, tribe by tribe, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. They shall not pervert judgment, nor show partiality, nor take gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the righteous." The law thought, and very reasonably, that those appointed to judge must be seen to rise above the love of gain, and must not, out of regard for certain persons, grant them leave to transgress what is good and blameless. Moreover, it thought they must reject partiality as unholy and weigh each matter according to the law, imitating the Judge of all, that is, Christ, whom the law itself clearly proclaimed in advance, knowing that he is Judge as God. And it spoke thus again: "When you come into the land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance, and inherit it and dwell in it, and say, 'I will set a ruler over me, like all the nations around me,' you shall surely set over yourself a ruler whom the Lord your God chooses; you shall set him as ruler over yourself from among your brothers. You may not set over yourself a foreign man, because he is not your brother." For we must not worship the creature rather than God the Creator. Rather, yielding ourselves as inwardly as we can to the words of truth, and being called as into the holy land—that is, the promise of God that comes through faith in Christ—we must in this way set over ourselves as ruler and judge the Son who is by nature from God, even though he is conceived of as being in the flesh. And he says concerning us, "But I was established as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord." Besides him we shall accept no other at all, nor shall we put our necks under the yoke of strangers; for we have one leader, Christ. The wretched Jews have remained outside through unbelief. Not only did they refuse outright to accept Christ as ruler and judge over them, though he was brought down from heaven by the will and good pleasure of God the Father; on top of this, they have chosen for themselves a foreign man, the son of perdition, that is, the Antichrist, an alien of another race and not even of Israel's blood—even though the law said clearly, "You may not set over yourself a foreign man, because he is not your brother." And they heard Christ himself say, "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive." For Christ came for the glory of God the Father. But in due time the son of lawlessness will come, not for the glory of God the Father—which I think is what "in the name of the Father" means—but the wretch will place the name of divinity on his own head. For he will seat himself in the house of God, proclaiming that he is God. Yet if the Jews kept the law, they would not worship him or ever accept him as Christ; for the law clearly foretold that Christ would spring from the blood of Israel. But they will cast even this aside as stale, and accept a foreign man of another race.
Then they will eat the fruit of their own way, and receive a penalty to match their shameful folly.

Well said; for God, who judges justly, will surely repay each one according to his work. But let us leave these matters there, and let what has been said suffice. Now, to those appointed to judge others and to sit on the seat that befits judges, the law again proclaimed: "You shall not accept a vain report"—that is, a false word full of slander. "You shall not join with a multitude, to turn aside with the majority so as to pervert judgment." And again, after other things: "You shall not pervert the judgment of the poor man in his cause; you shall keep away from every unjust word." Blamelessness in speech is most fitting for those who have authority to judge, and the one who must cast his vote on each of the accused according to the lawgiver's decision must speak rightly. And this too is usefully added: "You shall not pity the poor man in judgment." For judges find it an easy and tempting thing to waver between the two sides when the person on trial is not rich. A man weighed down by poverty is very easily trampled on by greed; yet at times he is quite capable of overpowering the claims of justice, by moving the softer-hearted among the judges to pity. So the law forbids both taking advantage of those in need and misery and pitying them, keeping the beauty of just judgment uncorrupted and making the judge in every case the guardian of equality. "You shall pursue justice justly," it says. Whatever grieves the law, then, even if it seems to be something good, may reasonably be regarded as not free from fault; for "there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness," as it is written. The good therefore requires skill, and pity shown at the wrong time would not escape the charge of wronging the law. Those caught in moderate offences he corrects by the torment of scourging. See how servile and utterly unworthy of free men this is—and do not be surprised, for there was a spirit of slavery in them. That is why stripes no longer follow the decrees given through Christ, as they did under the ancient law. Instead, what befits free men is set before us: splendid and desirable gifts, the firstfruits and promises of spiritual blessings, beatitudes befitting good deeds, and no longer threats but rather invitations to virtue. For Moses spoke to the people of old as a servant to servants and a fellow slave, but Christ, who is truly and genuinely from God the Father, speaks as Son to sons, and to those who are his brothers by adoption.
That is right.

The murderer, however, the law punishes with death. By inflicting like for like it reins in unbridled audacity, and it punishes an anger that can no longer be borne with a penalty that cannot be borne, even for those who have gone to the very limit of evil, though it first examines with great care the intention of the one who did the deed. If the offence was deliberate, it removes mercy. It does not allow love of neighbour to disgrace itself by going soft at the wrong moment and being dragged, as it were, toward leniency in the very cases where that is least fitting. For it said this: "But if anyone attacks his neighbour to kill him by treachery and flees for refuge, you shall take him even from my altar to put him to death." But if the harm the striker did to his victim goes only as far as illness, the law scales the penalty to match and orders the loss to go no further than money. For again it said: "If two men quarrel, and one strikes his neighbour with a stone or with his fist, and he does not die but is confined to bed, then if the man gets up and walks about outside on a staff, the one who struck him shall be free of guilt; only he shall pay for his lost time and the costs of his healing." So much for the law. But the Saviour, bringing in what is perfectly good, says: "Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also." About servants the law lays down the following: "If anyone strikes his male or female servant with a rod, and the servant dies under his hand, he shall surely be punished; but if the servant survives a day or two, he shall not be punished, for the servant is his money." So the law sets death as the penalty for anger carried all the way. Just because we have become masters through greed, God has not allowed us to cut off from life itself those who are under our hand and our yoke. The law urges us to weave mercy in with our anger, and it fixes the ultimate penalty for the one who kills. "But if the servant survives a day or two," it says, "he shall not be punished, for the servant is his money." It all but says: What happened to the victim after he had recovered somewhat is not the work of the striker's anger. For no one would want to lose his own servant, whom he bought with silver and acquired by paying money. If someone becomes a killer unintentionally, the law in turn thinks it right to punish him with perpetual exile. It tempers the punishment with a fitting measure of humaneness, and quite rightly it does not put an unintentional offence on the same footing as deliberate ones. It has ordered three cities to be set apart, which it called cities "of Refuge," and in this way it gathers there those who flee because of unintentional offences. For those who have acted so unhappily it also fixes a time of release: the death of the priest who is set over them and holds the first place. It writes as follows in Numbers: "But if he pushes him suddenly and not out of enmity, or throws any object at him not from ambush, or any stone that could kill, without seeing him, and it falls on him and he dies, though he was not his enemy and was not seeking to harm him, then the congregation shall judge between the one who struck him and the avenger of blood according to these judgments. The congregation shall rescue the slayer from the avenger of blood and return him to the city of refuge to which he fled, and he shall live there until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil." Then, a little later: "And after the death of the high priest the slayer shall return to the land of his possession."
So what releases them from their perpetual exile is the death of the priest we have just mentioned.
That is the outline in the types; and the shadows are in labour with the mystery of Christ.
In what way?

It is not unreasonable, Palladius, to suppose that those caught in sins are, as it were, murderers of their own souls. They did not slide into this misery willingly but were forced, as it were, into transgression and into offending God, because the mind of man is bent on evil from his youth, and because of the law of untamed love of pleasure that has seized tyrannical power in the members of the flesh. So the wretched soul of man is punished with exile from the world and from the body. It settled in the recesses of death as in a city of refuge and remained there for long ages. Only with difficulty was it released, when Christ the great high priest died. He endured death on behalf of all and went down into Hades. He opened the gates to those below and freed them from their bonds, saying to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves."
How clear that explanation is!

The law urged the people of old to win approval not in one respect only, but to be well ordered in everything and in the best condition, so that the man of God might be complete, equipped for every good work. So it also regulates marriage so that it is dignified, and it makes plain how marriage may be conducted blamelessly before both God and men. Fornication and impurity it banishes completely, and sex between males and adultery it puts as far off as possible, saying in Leviticus: "You shall not lie carnally with your neighbour's wife and so defile yourself with her; and you shall not lie with a male as with a woman, for it is an abomination." Such things, it means, show their own condemnation on their face, and the heavy stench ingrained in them is found without effort. No long argument will be needed to convict those who have sunk to such loathsomeness, since they carry from the start so shameful and ugly a reputation and stand indicted by nature itself. So it sets such things aside and examines things done lawfully and not without reason, saying in Deuteronomy: "If anyone takes a wife and lives with her, and she does not find favour in his sight because he has found something shameful in her, he shall write her a certificate of divorce, put it in her hands, and send her out of his house. If she goes away and becomes another man's wife, and the second husband hates her, writes her a certificate of divorce, puts it in her hands and sends her out of his house, or if the second husband who took her as his wife dies, then the first husband who sent her away may not take her back to be his wife after she has been defiled, for it is an abomination before the Lord your God; and you shall not defile the land that the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance." For a man to take as his lawful wife again a woman who has been separated from her husband for good reasons and has endured the outrage of belonging to another is not safe; indeed, it is utterly foolish. For "he who keeps an adulteress," it says, "is foolish and ungodly." Yet just as the law forbids delighting in things that are plainly shameful and condemned beyond doubt, so too it does not allow what is honourable to be slandered as dishonourable. It is an equal offence to judge worthy of affection what is better shunned, and to deprive of affection what one should be afraid to reject. For "Woe," it says, "to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, good evil and evil good, who make light darkness and darkness light." So the law does not allow a woman once sent away to be taken back. Nor does it let women not yet condemned suffer harm from mere talk. Again it said: "If anyone takes a wife and lives with her, and then hates her, and invents charges against her as a pretext and gives her a bad name, saying, 'I took this woman, and when I came to her I did not find the evidence of her virginity,' then the girl's father and mother shall take the evidence of the girl's virginity and bring it out to the elders at the gate. The girl's father shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man as his wife, and now he hates her and invents charges against her as a pretext, saying, I did not find the evidence of virginity in your daughter. But here is the evidence of my daughter's virginity.' Then they shall spread out the garment before the elders of the city. The elders of that city shall take that man and discipline him, fine him a hundred shekels, and give them to the girl's father, because he gave a bad name to a virgin of Israel. She shall remain his wife, and he may not send her away as long as he lives." You see, then, how the law has ordered that a man who unjustly scorned a woman not yet condemned must not leave the court entirely unpunished. I think we must cherish the good with great care, and not rush fickly after our own fancy, choosing to slander what is honourable as dishonourable. Rather we should try to hold in respect a devotion to everything good, and be glad to dwell with what is best so that we may speak well of it. For the one who allows no slackness in the middle of his undertakings brings to completion the aim of whatever he does well. That we ought to be people of this kind the law again hinted when it said: "If you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring bloodshed on your house if anyone falls from it." A house without a coping, with its finishing work never added, is an unsightly thing. In the same way, I think, every good work of ours is quite unconvincing unless it is brought to its proper completion. Nor is that all: danger will also follow those who are negligent. That, I think, is what is meant by someone falling from the house. For "Woe," it says, "to those who do the work of the Lord carelessly." So by countless means the law brings us toward what is profitable. It does not yet set before the people of old food that is solid and fit for grown men. Instead it nurses them with milk like infants, leading them little by little toward the mystery of Christ. The law is spiritual. Insofar as it went no further than shadow and types, it was, so to speak, not edible, nor indeed of any use as spiritual food. But it becomes so when it is reshaped into gospel contemplation and toward the mystery of Christ. You will understand this very well from what the all-wise Moses wrote about it here. For he said in Leviticus: "When you enter the land that the Lord your God is giving you, and you plant any tree for food, you shall purge away its impurity. For three years its fruit shall be unpurified to you; it shall not be eaten. In the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, worthy of praise to the Lord. And in the fifth year you shall eat its fruit. Its produce shall be an increase for you. I am the Lord your God." The writing of Moses is like a richly flourishing garden. It is in labour with a varied growth of ordinances and is thickly planted, as it were, with trees, namely the laws on each matter. But on each tree, it says, you shall purge away its impurity. That is, you shall cut away what is superfluous in the history and strip off what is, so to speak, the woody part of the letter, and you will come to the very heart of the plant. In other words, you will carefully work out the inner fruit of what is commanded and make it your food. "But its fruit," it says, "shall be unpurified for three years; it shall not be eaten." It uses the year to stand for a period of time. There were first three periods in which the law was still unpurified, weighed down by the coarseness of the history and wrapped in shadow as in useless refuse. I say the three periods are those of Moses, of Joshua, and of the Judges. After them came a fourth period, in which the brilliant choir of the holy prophets sprang up. Then the fruit of the law became holy and worthy of praise. For with the holy prophets the things of the law began to be set aside, and things in shadows were no longer even mentioned. Instead the truth was openly proclaimed, and the mystery of Christ's coming was praised. Soon the forerunner was close at hand, crying out and saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near." So in the fourth period the things in the law reached the beginning of their purification, and the fruit was already in some sense holy. But it became edible in the fifth, the period in which Christ came, as the law and the prophets bear witness. That is why it says, "Its fruit shall be an increase for you." For in addition to the gospel proclamations, the instruction of the law too, once it is led up to spiritual contemplation, is most useful to those who love learning. Indeed the Saviour said, "Every scribe who has been made a disciple of the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old." By the new things he means the Gospels, and by the old the things in the law, which make no mean contribution to our knowledge in Christ. To him be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.
On the holy tabernacle, that it was a type of the Church in Christ.

Love for God and for the brethren has glorious grounds for boasting, and through both the law is fulfilled. Whoever has reached this height of good repute will be illustrious and admirable, and will be ranked among the most genuine of all, as Christ cries out and says, "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord." For he will indeed enter, and very readily, into the heavenly Jerusalem, and will dwell in the mansions above, delighting in good things beyond mind and speech. The prophet Isaiah says something of this kind too: "Your eyes will see Jerusalem, rich cities, tents that will not be shaken; the pegs of its tent will not be moved, nor will its cords be broken." For the form of this world is passing away, according to the Scriptures, but the hope of what is to come is very firm and wholly unshaken. But since all these things are being dissolved, as the Savior's disciple insisted, we must be found to be people of a certain kind, holy and blameless before him, honoring him with spiritual sacrifices as Savior and Redeemer, and practicing a holy and choice way of life that accords with the laws of the Gospel. In just this way, of course, the law sketched out for the people of old this so august and worthy life, commanding them to slaughter sheep, to make offerings by blood, to dedicate tithes and firstfruits to God, and thank-offerings besides. Yet it laid down that these things must not be done outside the holy tabernacle. And it set apart the tribe of Levi as chosen for God, making the matter a type for us and pointing to ourselves. For in the divine Scriptures we too are called "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." And we enter into the truer tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man, that is, the Church, not appeasing the Creator of all with calves and goats, but distinguishing ourselves by an upright and blameless faith, and giving off a spiritual fragrance through spiritual fruit-bearing. For it is with such sacrifices that God is well pleased, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, according to the Savior's word.

You have spoken rightly. And I for my part would say that we ought to win approval by sacrifices that surpass the law; I agree with that. But tell me this: was not the old tabernacle pitched in the wilderness as a type for us of the Church from the Gentiles, displaying, still somewhat dimly, the beauty of the truer one?

Certainly. And I said just now that the requirement that those of Levi's blood be chosen out as the best for the sacred ministries would also be a type, in its turn, of those called in faith to a holy and blameless life, I mean the life in Christ.
Would you like us, then, to say a few things about the holy tabernacle and about the priesthood under the law, letting our discussion examine what was solemnly ordained concerning both?

The matter is not without its difficulties; it will call, I think, for long labor and sweat on our part, Palladius, both to be able to understand these things and indeed to explain them. Still, if you agree, let us go through it trusting in God; for you have heard him say plainly, "Who gave man a mouth? And who made the deaf and the dumb, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth."
Go on, then, and take the Giver of wisdom as your helper in this too.

Then I will go on, and indeed I will speak, having gathered the material from the sacred writings with great care. God, the Creator of all, came down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai and laid down laws by which each thing to be done was to be directed toward what is right and genuine. Then, drawing them away from their former error and setting them as far as possible from the false worship of Egypt, he spoke to Moses, who was acting as mediator at that time: "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the sons of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves." For he did not permit them to serve falsely named gods, but commands that they must devote themselves only to the One who comes from above and from heaven, who by his very essence holds power over all things, and whose glory lies not in the fine colors of materials but in showing that heaven is his own. It was in some way necessary that those commanded to depart from their ancient impiety and profane worship should pass over at once to another custom, and come under the worship of the God who is God by nature as under a kind of yoke. For a mind left slack is unrestrained and all too ready to drift away into anything whatever, even the most outlandish; but when fears and care hang over it, it darts quite effortlessly toward what is right and inclines toward what is beneficial. And since we approach the Father through the Son ("For no one comes to the Father," he says, "except through me"), it followed necessarily that he should ordain the types of access through the Son and of fruit-bearing in him, saying: "You shall make me an altar of earth, and on it you shall sacrifice your whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where I cause my name to be named; and I will come to you and bless you. And if you make me an altar of stones, you shall not build it of hewn stones; for if you have laid your tool upon it, it is defiled." He calls Emmanuel an altar of earth, for the Word became flesh, and the nature of flesh is earth from earth. In Christ, then, is all fruit-bearing and every offering; for he himself says, "Apart from me you can do nothing." For just as we have gained access through him, so too every sacrifice of those who have received the faith is acceptable through him. And to those who set up the altar of earth he promises his coming and his blessing: "For I will come to you," he says, "and bless you." For when we had received the types of the truth through the all-wise Moses, the truth itself also shone forth in due time, that is, Christ, through whom and in whom we have been enriched with the blessing from above and from the Father, sealed for adoption in the Holy Spirit; and this too, again, is accomplished in Christ. "And if you make me an altar of stones," he says, "you shall not build it of hewn stones." He does not allow the stones dedicated to God to be wounded by iron. For Christ was the chosen stone, the cornerstone, precious: unwounded by sins, knowing nothing of suffering the devil's blows, not divided between God and the world even though he became flesh, but wholly holy; not divided after the ineffable union, that is, his coming together with the flesh, into God on one side and man on the other, but being one, God and man, the same. For he is in no way divided, as the wise Paul also writes.
So the altar of earth, and the unhewn stones as well, signify Christ, in the ways already described?

So I say, for the law is spiritual, according to the Scriptures. And since it was foreshadowing in riddles the mystery of Christ and the access through him, it was then, yes then, that God planned to display beforehand the form of the Church as well. So he called Moses, and Joshua with him, up onto Mount Sinai. And understand from this that even to the holy prophets themselves the Father is accessible through the Son; for Moses and Joshua go up together. For it is written: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and take firstfruits for me from all whose heart so moves them; you shall take my firstfruits. And this is the firstfruits that you shall take from them: gold and silver, bronze and blue, purple and double scarlet, and spun fine linen, and goats' hair, and rams' skins dyed red, and blue skins, and incorruptible wood, and sardius stones, and stones for engraving, for the ephod and for the full-length robe. And you shall make me a sanctuary, and I will be seen among you. And you shall make it for me according to all that I show you on the mountain, the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings; so you shall make it." Do you see how he urges the people toward the duty of offering what is profitable and most useful for the establishing of the Church, bringing cheerfully what accords with their strength and inclination? For he did not ask only for gold, or for things that many perhaps find hard to come by, but also for goats' hair and rams' skins, showing that even what is small and cheap is not rejected by God, if the one who has chosen to make an offering has nothing more splendid; perhaps it is even on a par with the most precious things, or deserves greater praise. So indeed Christ did not leave unadmired the widow in Jerusalem who brought to the treasury something small and very easily obtained, yet perhaps great for those in the direst poverty, whom even parting with the very cheapest things is likely to wear down. Once the firstfruits had been received, "You shall make me a sanctuary," he says, "and I will be seen among you." For Christ appears in the Church and shines upon those within it, according to the word in the Psalms: "God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us." Observe how, although he had come down upon the mountain in the form of fire and had been seen by all the people (for so it is written), he says, as though he had not yet appeared, "I will be seen among you," once the sanctuary has been raised. The text all but cries aloud, and it is plainly seen, that those visions were shadows of the true sight of God, while the true manifestation is Christ, in whom we have seen the Father himself. Indeed, when the Jews supposed that they had truly seen the God of all on Mount Sinai, he exposed them as utterly senseless in their thinking, saying, "You have never heard his voice or seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe the one whom he has sent." So, "I will be seen among you," he says, once the sanctuary has been raised. This was a type of the Church, which was made in the likeness of the Church above. For indeed he says, "You shall make it for me according to all that I show you on the mountain; so you shall make it." For there was shown to the blessed Moses a type, as I said, of the holy churches, and in many forms, as though in shadow, the One who became man for us was being depicted. Yet on each of the patterns the discussion would be long and drawn out, and full of trivialities. But since some things are proper and suited to the construction of the objects, while others are directed toward the purpose of contemplation, come, let us speak of what is useful for that purpose, and let the rest go.
I do not understand what you mean.

Consider, then, what I mean; you will understand, I think, with very little effort. He commanded that an ark be made of incorruptible wood, overlaid inside and out with pure gold, bearing within it, as it were, the so-called testimonies, that is, the law on tablets. And his instructions about it did not stop there: he further commands that carrying poles be made of incorruptible wood, gilded in the same way, and gold rings, and twisted moldings all around. He fixed the length, breadth and height of the work. Now if someone wished to investigate such things thoroughly in a mystical sense, he might perhaps discover what the ark is, and the testimonies within it, and what the need for incorruptible wood was. But what the gold on the ark might be meant to signify, together with the things put together for use and ornament—I mean the wave-moldings, the twisted borders, the rings and the poles—if someone should busy himself with these, he will find the matter hard. And having no mystical sense to fit to them, he will perhaps talk to excess and heap a crowd of idle words upon the ears of the more studious. And what we are saying holds true not only, perhaps, of the ark; I would add that it holds of the other things too that he commanded to be made.

What you think and say seems to me not implausible. So, setting aside what concerns, as you say, proportion and use, that is, the ornament of the finished works, hurry on to what is necessary for contemplation: explain without delay in what way Christ himself is signified to us through the things that were shown, or rather made.

Then I will try, as far as it is possible to speak and understand. But if I miss the truth, and reach the loftiness of these ideas less fully than I ought, be forgiving. For seeing in a mirror and in a riddle may at times trip up even a precise and sensible mind.
Well said.

The ark, Palladius, would be for us a type and image of Christ. For when we consider the manner in which the Only-begotten became man, we shall see the Word from God the Father dwelling, as in an ark, in the temple taken from the Virgin. For in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, according to the Scriptures. And the testimonies in the ark were the Word of God. Its wood was incorruptible, and it was adorned inside and out with pure and most refined gold. For the body of Christ is incorruptible, held fast in incorruption, as if by gold, by the power and splendor of the indwelling Word and by the nature and life-giving activity of the Holy Spirit. It is for this reason that Christ is said to give life. For since the Word from God the Father is Life by nature, he himself, by the power of his own Spirit, brought his own temple back to life, placing it beyond corruption. For his flesh does not know corruption, according to the words of the holy Paul. And somewhere he also addressed the Jews about his own body: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Peter too says that he was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. The gold, then, is a symbol of the surpassingly brilliant Godhead, overlaid, as it were, upon the holy body and imparting to it, ineffably, its own splendor and incorruption, in a manner known only to the divine nature itself, which is beyond the mind. For if "the righteous will shine forth like the sun in the kingdom of their Father" in due time, what then will be the glory of Christ himself? How can his radiance not be beyond all mind and speech? The poles that carry the ark are of gold, the rings are of gold too, and so is everything on it; for those around him share in his glory, being joined to him in love and sanctification, and being of use. Such were the blessed disciples, receiving divine power from him, enriched by participation with the splendor of the excellence from above, and for that reason performing divine signs.
You have spoken rightly.

And besides the ark, "You shall make," he says, "a mercy seat, a cover of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. And you shall make two cherubim of turned gold, and you shall set them at both ends of the mercy seat. One cherub shall be made at this end, and one cherub at the other end of the mercy seat; and you shall make the two cherubim at the two ends. The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces shall be toward one another; the faces of the cherubim shall be turned toward the mercy seat. And you shall place the mercy seat on the top, above, and into the ark you shall put the testimonies that I will give you. And I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are upon the ark of the testimony, concerning all that I command you for the sons of Israel."
Then what do you say the mercy seat is?

As far as the letter and the shadow go, it was made of pure gold and lay fitted upon the ark; that is why it is called a cover.
