And those adorned with the glories of the priesthood, when they turned toward it and looked at it, were considered to be turned toward God and looking at him. But we say that the mercy seat, if understood spiritually, is the One who became man for us, "whom God set forth as a mercy seat through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness." So Paul says. And John, the wisest of disciples, also writes to us: "Little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world." For through him comes propitiation, and every prayer, and every request for good things. "Until now," he says, "you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and it will be given to you." He himself, then, is the mercy seat. For through him the Father is propitious to us, every prayer finds its goal in him, and through him we draw near, since we are not acceptable in any other way. That is why he says, "I am the way," and "I am the door," and "No one comes to the Father except through me." Yet even though the only-begotten Word of God became like us, lowering himself into humanity and self-emptying, it is still his own by nature to be conceived of in a glory befitting God, and to exist in excellences beyond creation, just as he did, of course, before the flesh. That is why the cherubim stand around the mercy seat, covering it with their wings, turned toward it and always fixing their faces upon it; and their standing on the right and the left is a clear sign that they are its bodyguard. And the fact that the cherubim are always looking toward the mercy seat seems to hint at the intense and, as it were, insatiable longing of the highest powers for the sight of God. The prophet Isaiah also describes the Son in his own proper form, saying: "I saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and seraphim stood around him"; and each had six wings, he says, and with two they covered their feet, with two their faces, and with the others they flew. Now if someone should think that the seraphim covered the face and the feet of God, there is nothing unreasonable in conceiving something of the kind. For if we translate the meaning of "seraphim" into Greek, we shall find that it signifies abundance of knowledge, or an outpouring of wisdom. By their posture, then, these all-wise and highest powers indicate quite clearly that it is not lawful for God's face to be seen by anyone. For the nature that is beyond every mind is wholly invisible, and dwells in unapproachable light, according to the words of the blessed Paul; and "No one shall see the face of God and live," as he rightly said to the most holy Moses. Nor could anyone know his footprints and his ways. For it is written: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" And the blessed David sings, striking up a wise melody: "Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known." For just as one could not see a track in the waters, whether of a man or a ship or the creatures that swim in them, so no one could discern the divine and ineffable ways. The feet would be a type of these. But if someone should suppose that the holy seraphim cover their own faces and feet with their wings, let us understand that it is not lawful to see the beginning or the end of the wisdom or knowledge concerning God. For it too is incomprehensible and beyond the human mind. The beginning of every body is the head, and its end is the feet. The mercy seat, then, is Christ, who even having appeared in the flesh is no less God and Lord, by nature and in truth, having even the highest powers themselves standing around him like servants. And somewhere the sacred word has told us that after Satan departed, giving up his testing of Christ, when Christ had fasted for our sake, angels came and ministered to him; "for they are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation." "From above the mercy seat," he says, "I will make myself known to you and will speak to you," indicating two things by this as well, I think. Either that Christ, though he is man, will speak things beyond human nature, and will not remain only within the limits of the self-emptying, because he is God and from God by nature; for he said, "I and the Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." Or perhaps this: he is known above the mercy seat and the cherubim, that is, in an excellence and glory beyond man and beyond everything that has come into being, of which the very highest and most exalted are the seraphim, even though he became flesh. The mercy seat is of gold, and so are the seraphim themselves. For the glorious and most beautiful nature is God, while created things are in his likeness by participation. And to those who have come to be around him and near him he imparts a share in his own natural brightness, as light reflected onto something near by lights up whatever it meets with its own splendor.
That is right, and our discussion has been polished down to the truth.

After the making of the mercy seat, he sketches the mystery of Christ for us in yet another way, saying, "And you shall make a table of pure gold." He commanded that rings be fixed to it and golden poles be put through them, and he set out very clearly its measurements and the methods of craftsmanship by which it would attain outstanding beauty of the highest form. Then he says, "And you shall set on the table loaves of the presence, before me continually." And he commanded that its vessels be made of gold: bowls and censers, and also ladles and libation cups. Was not the bread from heaven plainly shown to us here, which in due time would be set forth on the holy tables of the churches and give life to the world?
Very much so.

And the bowls and censers, the ladles and libation cups, and the things by which the mystical and most sacred service of the holy table is carried out—would they not be a type of the divine treasures, my friend?
Certainly.

But these things are in Exodus. Concerning the table, and indeed the setting out of the loaves, the lawgiver has spoken his oracle in Leviticus. There he broadens the commandment, as it were, and teaches clearly how the setting out is to be done, saying: "And you shall take fine flour and make of it twelve loaves; each loaf shall be of two tenths. And you shall set them in two rows, six loaves to a row, on the pure table before the Lord. And you shall put pure frankincense and salt on each row, and they shall be for the loaves as a memorial, set before the Lord. On the sabbath day it shall be set out before the Lord continually, in the presence of the sons of Israel, an everlasting covenant; and it shall belong to Aaron and his sons. And they shall eat them in a holy place; for this is most holy to them, from the things sacrificed to the Lord, an everlasting ordinance." In Numbers, again, he pointed to one bread for us, the bread from heaven and from us, for the Word, though God by nature, became one of us and dwelt among us. He said to Moses, the revealer of holy things: "Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land into which I am bringing you, then, when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall set apart an offering, a portion separated for the Lord, the firstfruits of your dough. You shall set apart a loaf as an offering; as an offering from the threshing floor, so shall you set apart the firstfruits of your dough, and you shall give an offering to the Lord throughout your generations." Through these passages one could behold the mystery of the truth without any effort. We will speak of it in its own time, finely and precisely, when our discourse has moved on to another labour of writing. For the present, though, there is one thing, I think, that might fill a person with wonder, Palladius.
What do you mean?

He sets Emmanuel before us in many ways, and here he portrays him again through another figure. For he says to Moses: "And you shall make a lampstand of pure gold; you shall make the lampstand of turned work. Its shaft and its branches and its cups and its knobs and its lilies shall be of one piece with it. Six branches from the second side." Then, after adding the things that serve the adornment and use of the work (I mean the lilies, the knobs and the almond-shaped cups), he declared again: "All of it turned work, from a single piece of pure gold. And you shall make its seven lamps, and you shall set its lamps on it, and they shall shine from the one face. And its oil-funnel and its trays you shall make of pure gold; all these vessels you shall make of a talent of pure gold. See that you make them according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." The lampstand, then, is golden because it bears the type of Christ. For the Son is God by nature and in truth, and to gold, as we determined above, we must liken the divine splendour and preeminence. It is of turned work because Emmanuel is surpassingly beautiful, beyond all words, in his spiritual comeliness. For it is written: "You are fairer in beauty than the sons of men." So the turned work of the lampstand would very well show the distinguished form of Emmanuel, plainly a form befitting God. He also says that branches spring out to the right and left, as from a tree, yet rise together with the central shaft and are raised to an equal height. For the Only-begotten, being one by nature and simple in essence, as God, seems to be manifold through his various operations; yet there is nothing compounded or foreign in him, even if in some way he may be thought not simple in his divine attributes. For he is conceived as light and life, power and incorruption. Wishing to teach that there is nothing adventitious in him, he added, I think: "Let the knobs and the branches be of one piece with it; all of it turned work of pure gold." That is, he is wholly and throughout God. He is not sanctified in the way created things are, nor like the angels, perhaps, who are conceived in their own nature but are made glorious by his grace and glory and anointed with the gift of the Spirit as if with pure gold. Rather, he is by nature the very thing itself, God, the purest and highest nature. The lamps are seven, for the illumination that comes from Christ comes in many ways: "To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge," and "the discernment of spirits," and the rest. And again, seven is the number that signifies perfection. Emmanuel is all-perfect, both in his own nature, as God, and in the distribution of his gifts, which he bestows perfectly on those worthy to receive them. For "he does not give the Spirit by measure," in the words of John, but "from his fullness we have all received." Then he says: "And you shall set the lamps, and they shall shine from the one face." What this placing might be he made clear in Numbers, where he says: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and say to him: When you set up the lamps on the side facing the front of the lampstand, the seven lamps shall give light. And Aaron did so: on the one side facing the front of the lampstand he lit its lamps, as the Lord had commanded Moses." Understand, then, that the seven lamps were turned toward the front of the lampstand and cast their light on those who were looking at it. For the divine and spiritual light does not shine on those who are behind, lying as it were with their backs turned to God. It shines on those who have been brought into his sight through sanctification, and who have already come face to face with him through boldness in faith and the most beautiful dignity of right living. For everything that consists in wickedness and disobedience is abominable and hateful, but obedience and docility are precious and are looked upon by God. So to the Jews, who chose to rage against him without restraint, he says through the voice of Isaiah: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you." But "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous," as is sung in the Psalms.
True.

The inspired Zechariah also clearly mentions this holy lampstand. For he said: "And the angel who spoke in me returned and woke me, as a man is woken from his sleep, and said to me: What do you see? And I said: I have looked, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and its bowl on top of it, and seven lamps on it, and two olive trees above it, one on the right of its bowl and one on the left. And I asked, and said to the angel who spoke in me: Lord, what are these? And he said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, Lord." So the blessed prophet inquired, saying, "What are these, Lord?" The inspired angel inserted a brief account, then interpreted the vision and referred the construction of the lampstand to Christ, saying of its seven lamps: "These are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon all the earth." To speak somewhat crudely, the Godhead sees us with countless eyes and surveys human affairs, "knowing what is in the darkness," as it is written, "and the light is with him." For if God sheds light on us who are in the world, he surely possesses it abundantly, having it before all others in his own nature. Or if some suspect that this is not so, perhaps it is time to cry out to those who choose to think that way: "Understand, you senseless among the people; you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?" For "the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes." Christ, then, illumines and oversees all things. That is why he said through one of the prophets: "I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?" For nothing could escape the mind that knows all things. Or do I not seem to you to have considered these things excellently?
Entirely so.

But the prophet saw something unusual about the lampstand, for there were branches of olive trees, and he inquired further, saying: "What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on the left?" "And I asked a second time," he says, "and said to him: What are the two branches of the olive trees that are beside the two golden spouts, which pour out and draw up the golden oil-vessels?" "And he said to me," he says, "Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, Lord. And he said to me: These are the two sons of fatness, who stand by the Lord of all the earth."
Why, then, did the blessed prophet need to ask again? For he says, "I asked a second time."
Would you not say, Palladius, that it is wise and fitting for those who have chosen to think rightly at all to make their inquiries about any necessary matter precise and carefully refined?
I would.

The prophet, then, saw shoots of olive teeming with tender new growth and called them olive trees, not branches from olive trees. The inspired angel kept silent, waiting for the wiser and truer question. But when the prophet had been roused, and now called them two branches of olive trees and begged to learn what they might symbolize, he was taught at once, for the angel said: "These are the two sons of fatness, who stand by the Lord of all the earth." By the two sons of fatness he meant the people from Israel and the people from the nations, and he says that they stand by the Lord of all the earth. He thus clearly and plainly makes the craftsmanship of the lampstand a type of Christ. Its olive branches, placed to the right and the left and stationed round about it, as it were, are enriched with the oil, which is a type of the Holy Spirit watering the minds of believers, as in the verse "You have anointed my head with oil."
Then why did he not call them olive trees, but rather branches of olives?

Because, my friend, just as slender shoots and freshly grown branches are taken from olive trees and all but transplanted, so believers are transplanted through faith into godliness. Some of them come from the synagogue of the Jews, and others are taken from the multitude of the nations, for not all those from Israel believed, nor did the whole multitude of the nations come in. Branches of olives, then, are those broken off, as from trees, from the Jewish multitude and indeed from the Greek, who have come into the divine light and already, in a sense, luxuriate in the more abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit. This, I think, is what is shown by the olive branches being set as it were beside the spouts of the lamps. The blessed Psalmist also mentions them somewhere, when he sings to Christ, the Saviour of all, about the bride joined to him, that is, the Church, and about her children in faith: "Your wife shall be like a flourishing vine on the sides of your house; your sons like young olive shoots around your table." For having received faith in him, we are given life by sharing in the Spirit and at the holy table of Christ.
Yes, you speak rightly. For he says, "I am the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world."

But concerning the lampstand and what belongs to it, let this be enough from us for the present. Let our discourse now proceed to the bronze altar, the most essential element of the worship under the law. "You shall make," he says, "an altar of incorruptible wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits. And you shall make the horns on its four corners; the horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay them with bronze. And you shall make a crown for the altar, and its cover, and its bowls, and its flesh-hooks, and its firepan; all its vessels you shall make of bronze." The altar, then, was five cubits in breadth and length. It needed measurements, and very ample ones too. For on it were to be offered the pieces of oxen cut apart, and whole burnt offerings, sheep and goats consecrated to God. That is why its grate and firepan, its flesh-hooks and bowls and all its vessels were of bronze: so that they could render their service to the sacrifices of the law without being destroyed by the assaults of the all-devouring fire. The crown and the horns at the corners we will ascribe to the beauty of its form, for nothing is without grace in the eyes of the all-wise God. But come, let us speak of this point again, fixing our minds precisely on what was ordained in each case. He commanded an altar suited and fitting for the sacrifices of the law, yet nothing in it was golden, as one could of course observe in the case of the ark, the lampstand, the table and its furnishings.
What, then, does this mean?
Did we not say, Palladius, that gold very well signifies the preeminence over all things and the incomparable splendour of the divine and pure nature, in a spiritual sense, I mean?
That is so.

Observe, then, that the altar of the worship under the law was entirely without gold. God set this before us as a riddle, and quite a clear one: the law was by no means a source of the Holy Spirit, and the power of the worship in types was not honoured with such a grace. For it was a spirit of slavery that lay upon Israel, whereas the gift was allotted to us through Christ after his return to life from the dead. For he breathed on them, saying, "Receive the Holy Spirit." Therefore Paul too said to the believers: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, by which we cry, Abba, Father." The wise John assures us that the power of the worship under the law was not rich in participation in the Holy Spirit, but that the Spirit was given rather to those justified by faith, when he says: "For the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified." For Christ had not yet come back to life; it was then that human nature was, so to speak, gilded with the Spirit and with communion with him. That, I think, is why he commanded the altar to be made without gold. But it seems that lovers of learning would lose something if they passed over the significance of the bronze from which it was made. For close examination may bring forth something needful, as someone wisely said: "In everyone who takes care there is profit."
What would you have to say about this, then?

Listen. The sacred writing says that the inspired Aaron was appointed priest and leader by a decree from above. But Korah and Dathan and those with them, a savage crowd, most rashly disparaged the decree from above and rose up against the divine laws. They brought censers, coming to this uncalled and of their own accord, and seized an honour that had not been allotted to them. Out of madness and audacity they set themselves up very hotly as rivals to the preeminent priest, who had been chosen out of all the others. Through these events was sketched the madness the Jews would one day show against Christ. For he is our high priest, brought to this office by the decree of the Father. Those men paid the penalty for such shameful attempts, and after them the Jews too will pay it, having made themselves liable to the same charges. Then God said to the holy Moses, and also to Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron: "Take up the bronze censers from among those who were burned, and scatter this strange fire there, for these sinners have sanctified the censers at the cost of their lives. And they made them into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, because they had been brought before the Lord and were sanctified; and they became a sign to the sons of Israel." This is what God said at that time. And in Exodus it is written of Bezalel, who was the son of Uri, of the tribe of Dan, and the master of every craft: "He made the bronze altar from the bronze censers that belonged to the men who rebelled with the congregation of Korah."
What, then, of this?

It would be of great benefit to consider that the ark was made as a type of Christ, and so too were the other things (I mean the lampstand, the mercy seat and the golden table), the people bringing and dedicating whatever each had at hand. For those who bear fruit to Christ and bring him spiritual offerings, of which those gifts were types and shadows, are highly acceptable, to the glory of God the Father. The altar of the worship under the law, however, by its very construction mystically and providentially signifies the provocation and contradiction, and, so to speak, the revolt that took place against the great priest; it is a kind of memorial and forewarning of it. Is the riddle clear to you? Aaron is a type of Christ. The Jews contended against the glory of Christ, and for this reason the altar of the law is spoken against. For the worship in shadows has ceased, and it is rather in Christ that we offer the Father our spiritual fragrance. This too he foreshadowed for us, again as in shadows, when he said: "And you shall make for me an altar of incense of incorruptible wood. You shall make it a cubit long and a cubit broad; it shall be square, and two cubits high. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. And you shall overlay it with pure gold, its grate and its walls round about and its horns." Then, after adding staves for it, and rings and carrying-poles, and other such things, he says: "And you shall set it before the veil that is over the ark of the testimony, where I will make myself known to you as God. And Aaron shall burn on it fine compounded incense, morning by morning; when he trims [?] the lamps, he shall burn incense on it. And when Aaron lights the lamps in the evening, he shall burn incense on it, a perpetual incense continually before the Lord throughout their generations. And you shall not offer any other incense on it; you shall not offer a burnt offering of sacrifice on it, nor pour out a drink offering on it. And Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year, with the blood of the purification of sins, of atonement. Once a year he shall cleanse it throughout their generations; it is most holy to the Lord."
Shall we accept this too, then, as a type of Christ?

Certainly, Palladius. For the truth is that this object would quite easily show its precious and deep mystery to those who have chosen to investigate such things finely and with careful precision. It was made of incorruptible wood and wholly overlaid with gold. For the body of Christ is incorruptible and holds within itself the riches of the divine nature, for "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." And Christ is our firstfruits and the root of the race that is being re-created for incorruption through union with God, even if this is understood of him in a unique sense. The horns of the altar are like outstretched hands, prefiguring the shape of the precious cross. If someone should say that there are four horns, it does no harm to the right understanding of the student. For since the altar is square and has equal sides all round, the horns appear the same from every direction. And what does this mean? In every place Christ is known, and known as crucified, and this is a splendid boast for those who believe in him. So the inspired Paul says: "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." Added to the work are things for its adornment, a twisted crown; for truly Emmanuel is "fairer in beauty than the sons of men." Things for its use were also added, the carrying-poles and the rest. For at the times of breaking camp the divine altar had to be carried in good order. The inspired disciples did this too, carrying Christ about through their preaching, decently and in order, as ministers of God and stewards of the mysteries of Christ. "And you shall set the altar," he says, "before the veil that is over the ark of the testimonies, where I will make myself known to you from there."
Then why, I wonder, was it necessary for the places themselves to be specified?

How deep the subject is, and how very obscure! Yet I will speak as best I can, relying on God, who makes even the blind wise. He says the ark was made of incorruptible wood and pure gold, and that the law was in it, that is, the divine word, or the testimonies. For the thing was a type of the Word who sprang from God, who dwelt among us and came to be in the likeness of flesh, according to the Scriptures. Then he said that a veil, stretched over four pillars, had to hang near the ark. The name given to the veil is "the mercy seat." This too is Christ. For he is the propitiation for our sins, and a mercy seat through faith; Paul called him by this name. The cherubim were also portrayed, as it were, around the mercy seat. They signify very well the service of the highest powers under God, for the Word is God, and also their nearness to him, and indeed their standing by him in ministry. Then God said to Moses: "And I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are upon the ark of the testimony." Now the ark, as I said, was Christ, God the Word in an incorruptible body. But the ark stood on the ground, and the Only-begotten also came down into lowliness, into our low estate. For he took on the form of a slave and emptied himself. Yet he himself is also the mercy seat, set on high and escorted by the powers above. For the Son is known to us not only from the ways in which he emptied himself, but also from the things by which he is God and Lord of all. Even if he humbled himself because of his humanity, having come down by the divine plan into our condition, still "God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name." A type of this too would be the placing of the mercy seat on high, with the cherubim depicted on the right and the left. For where the service fitting to God alone is seen, there surely would be the glory of the Godhead too, and the preeminence of dignities beyond words. "Above the cherubim I will make myself known to you," says the Lord of all. He commands that the ineffable nature is not to be sought among created things, but altogether beyond whatever has been called into existence. For the most fitting account and place for the nature of God is what lies beyond and above everything that has come into being. So the place above the cherubim, even in its visible form in the holy tabernacle, all but reveals the divine nature to us. For this reason he commanded that the golden altar, made as a type of Christ, be placed opposite the one who gives oracles and is understood to be above the cherubim. This signifies, I think, that in Christ our affairs have come, as it were, into the sight of God and before the eyes of the Father. For man had turned away and offended God through transgression and much sin, and Christ set him again before the face of the Father, in himself and first of all. For as a forerunner he has entered heaven on our behalf, "now to appear in the presence of God for us," as wise Paul writes to us. He who always exists with his own Father is said "now to appear," because in himself and first of all he presents human nature in the sight of the Father and removes that ancient estrangement. For he is our peace, according to the Scriptures.
It is settled, then, that the golden altar is again an image of Christ.

Besides this, Christ himself might fittingly be understood as the compound, fine incense. For he himself is the high priest: "Aaron shall burn on it," he says, "compound, fine incense." The incense is compound, for the Word, being God, became flesh. Emmanuel is in a sense compounded for us, since divine nature and humanity are brought together ineffably into a unity beyond understanding. And it is fine, because it does not have the coarseness of worship under the law. "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; in whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin you took no pleasure. But a body you prepared for me," he says. "Then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God." What this will of the Father is, he himself has taught us in the Gospels, initiating us into the mystery: "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day." For he offered himself for us as a fragrant aroma, and for this reason he was also called high priest. So he himself is the high priest, and he himself is the compound, fine incense. Paul will bear witness to this, saying: "Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us reveals the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place. For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life." And he also called out to us: "Be imitators of God, then, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma." The law also set out plainly the time for burning incense, decreeing that everything must be done in order and good arrangement, and by means through which the force of the inner meanings might be well conveyed to us. "In the morning and in the evening," he says, "when the lamps are lit and dimmed." "Evening and morning" indicates what is unceasing and continuous. The requirement to burn incense under the lamps perhaps hints very well at this: when we are illumined by the divine light, then, and only then, are we richly filled with the fragrance of Christ, and so we come to perceive the good things inside the tabernacle, that is, the distribution of the divine gifts that Christ holds out to the worthy. So if anyone has not yet come into the light through faith, he surely has no share in the spiritual fragrance either, since he does not yet know the mystery of Christ. "If you do not believe," it says, "neither will you understand." For faith is the first approach, which leads on to understanding and, as it were, opens the mind to receive the divine light. He calls the incense "perpetual." For there is no time at which Christ does not give off his fragrance in the holy tabernacle, that is, in the Church. And he altogether forbids that a drink offering be poured on it (clearly meaning the altar, which is Christ) or a burnt offering be offered up. For the things of the law have been abolished in Christ, and the shadows are creeping to their end. This, I think, is what the drink offering and the burnt offering are. The prophet bears witness, saying: "Sacrifice and drink offering have been removed from the house of the Lord." For now that worship and service in spirit and in truth have been revealed, the shadows are in a sense superfluous, and what consists in types is altogether vain and useless; for in Christ there is a new creation. Those who seek to be justified by the law after the truth has been revealed have fallen from grace. "You shall not offer other incense on the altar," he says. For in Christ we will accept no other at all. We will call no one in existence "Rabbi." For we have one teacher and guide, and to him alone we will cleave, saying: "Your name is perfume poured out; therefore the maidens loved you. They drew me; we will run after you toward the fragrance of your perfumes." Or is this not the meaning of "You shall not offer other incense on it"? For the fragrance of Christ alone in the Church would be enough for those who are truly sensible, who desire no other scent, as the wretched Jews certainly do. For in their folly they insult the compound, fine incense, that is, Christ, and they have remained without any share in this holy, indeed truly divine, fragrance. Instead they will accept another in his place, the son of lawlessness, the adversary who exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat, as it is written, in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God. He also defiles the divine tabernacle, being alien smoke and, if I may put it so, a diabolical stench. For "his coming," it says, "will be according to the working of Satan."
I understand what you mean, for the point is clear.

He commands Aaron to make atonement on the altar of incense once a year, smearing the tips of the horns with the blood of the purification of sins. For it is, he says, "most holy." The divine Paul will make this clear to you when he says: "But when Christ came as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, he entered once for all into the holy places, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption." For, as he says again somewhere, "Having died once, he dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God." So the divine Aaron entered the Holy of Holies once a year, through the blood of the purification of sins. See Christ again in these things, all but sprinkling his own cross with his own blood, the blood of the salvation and life of all. For the horns are a type of the cross, stretching out this way and that like outstretched hands. So understand that Christ died once, but that he is Holy of Holies by nature, as God. For John speaks the truth when he says: "From his fullness we have all received." The whole creation, visible and invisible, shares in Christ. Angels and archangels, and those still higher than they, and even the cherubim themselves, are holy in no other way than through Christ alone, in the Holy Spirit. He himself, then, is the altar; he himself is the incense and the high priest; and likewise he himself is the blood of the purification of sins.
Yes, you speak rightly. But what exactly the blood of the purification of sins is, I cannot clearly understand.

The law prefigures the cleansing by blood and the sacred victim, I mean Christ, through whom we have been saved and escape the defilement that sin had fused into us. It speaks of this in Leviticus somewhat as follows: "If the whole congregation of Israel errs unknowingly, and a matter escapes the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of all the commandments of the Lord that ought not to be done, and so transgress, and the sin which they committed becomes known to them, then the congregation shall bring an unblemished calf from the herd for the sin, and shall bring it to the doors of the tent of witness. The elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the calf before the Lord, and they shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. The anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the calf into the tent of witness. The priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the calf and sprinkle it seven times before the Lord, in front of the holy veil. And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of compound incense, which is before the Lord, which is in the tent of witness." We shall speak about these things more fully in due course. But observe Emmanuel once again, slaughtered for us as in the calf, freeing us from sin, releasing us from judgment, and delivering us from punishment, passing through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not through calves and goats but through his own blood, having tasted death once for all. For on the cross his side was pierced by a lance, and blood and water poured out. And the projecting horns would be a type of the cross, as we said before.
Well said.
Yet the law, in riddles, ordered that cleansing must come not by blood alone but also by holy water. For this is the most perfect way to cleansing, according to the mystery in Christ.
And how did it show this, or in what way?

It is written: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make a bronze laver with a bronze base, for washing. You shall place it between the tent of witness and the altar, and pour water into it, and Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet with water from it. When they go into the tent of witness they shall wash with water, and they shall not die; or when they approach the altar to minister and to offer up whole burnt offerings to the Lord, they shall wash their hands and their feet with water. When they go into the tent of witness, they shall wash with water so that they may not die; and it shall be a perpetual ordinance for him and for his generations after him." That the grace of holy baptism was prefigured in this is plain enough. For when we are baptized we do not gain the removal of dirt from the flesh; we are freed from the defilements of mind and heart, and we wash away the stains of our offenses, by the grace and loving-kindness of him who calls us to salvation. For we have been justified, according to the Scriptures, not by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ. Observe how Aaron, though holy according to the law, and also those appointed to minister with him, first wash their hands and feet with water, and only then undertake the sacred labors and hurry into the Holy of Holies, free from fear. The law, I think, shows this clearly and plainly, and the fact itself all but cries aloud: even one who seems to be holy according to the law is unholy before God unless he washes in the water, and the power of worship under the law is not enough for cleansing. At any rate they washed beforehand, even though they had been sanctified according to the law; and what is cleansed is surely not what is clean, but what is filthy and unclean. Christ himself said something of the kind: "One who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, for he is clean." And the most wise Paul writes that it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. So the law falls short of sanctification, unless saving baptism is added for those who thirst for intimacy with God. That is why the divine John too, though richly crowned with the highest glories, and knowing how to advance in virtue so far that he had already reached the highest rank, begged the Savior to baptize him, saying: "I need to be baptized by you."
True.

The washing of hands and feet signifies purity and sincerity in action, and in the course we take, as it were, toward each thing that must be done. Once we have practiced this, we are permitted to enter the inner tabernacle, to offer spiritual sacrifices to God, and to consecrate, as it were, the sweet fragrance of the gospel way of life as our incense. He usefully instructs that those who wish to go into the Holy of Holies, and those in charge of the sacred works, must wash, so that they may not die. For to draw near to God without being cleansed is truly a perilous and harmful thing. That is why wise Paul charges us, if we wish to share in the mystical blessing, to examine ourselves and only then to approach. And he reveals that carelessness in these matters is full of danger, saying: "That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world."
It is settled, then, that the sacred laver prefigured for us the grace given through holy baptism.

So it is; do not doubt it at all. And when you have looked at the way it was made, you will be, I think, still more amazed. For it is written thus about Bezalel, who crafted the things in the tabernacle: "He made the bronze laver and its bronze base from the mirrors of the women who fasted, who fasted at the doors of the tent of witness on the day he set it up. And he made the laver so that Moses and Aaron and his sons might wash their hands and their feet from it when they went into the tent of witness; when they approached the altar to minister, they washed from it, just as the Lord had commanded Moses."
And what is this business of the mirrors? And who were the women who fasted?

Many events are not clearly narrated in the divine Scripture but are indicated somehow in passing, as is indeed the case with the matter at hand. Moses did not say where, or who, fasted when the holy tabernacle was set up. But that it happened, no one could doubt, for it is stated, even if not clearly. But let us leave this and go on to that other point, if you agree.
Which?
Of what might the women who fasted be a type? And what does it mean that the bronze laver was fashioned from the mirrors?
Surely it is now for you to explain this too.

Listen, then. The Israelites worshiped idols, for they endured servitude under the Egyptians and spent long years living by their laws. Now it was a custom of the Egyptians, especially of the women, to frequent the temples dressed in linen garments, with a mirror in the left hand and a sistrum in the right, solemnly arrayed as for a sacred rite. Women chosen above all others and initiated into the sacred mysteries were scarcely deemed worthy of such an honor — or rather, such an outrage, for that is the better and truer word. So women of Israelite blood, finding these relics of the worship in Egypt among their own belongings, brought these mirrors as an offering, and they were reworked into the laver. And when the holy tabernacle was set up, they fasted, sitting somewhere by its doors and living in complete purity. The event indicates, I think, that once the truer tabernacle had been revealed, that is, the Church, which the Lord pitched and not man, as the divine Paul writes, the time had come for those once devoted to the glory of the herd of demons to be remade into sacred vessels, fit to receive holy baptism, so that they could shine with glories beyond the law. For this, I think, is the meaning of the bronze laver being fashioned from pagan mirrors, that is, from diabolical heirlooms. In it was the water that cleansed even Moses himself, and served the priesthood under the law for washing — clearly, the spiritual washing. Or would you not say yourself, Palladius, that those who have gone astray and served demons are diabolical vessels?
How could I not?

The women fasted at the doors of the holy tabernacle. This too would be a fine and wise riddle: those justified in Christ do not hurry into the churches with blood, but rather are distinguished by spiritual sacrifices, and bring to God as a kind of gift their self-control, which is a sort of mortification of the flesh. "Present your bodies," it says, "as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your reasonable worship." And again: "Glorify God in your body." So the women who fasted when the holy tabernacle was set up stand as an image of souls that are no longer schooled by the commandments of Moses, but have now displayed a spiritual and gospel way of life. Such souls trample on earthly pleasures, not without sweat, and are well transformed toward unblemished beauty, because they refuse to incur the foul and profane charges that come from love of the flesh. Or is this not our way of life, we who have been called in Christ to sanctification and spiritual leanness?
Certainly.

But let this be enough for now about the sacred vessels. Come, if you please, let us examine the tabernacle itself, how it is placed and how it is built. The subject is deep and beyond our measure, yet I think there is no harm at all in our being glad to gather what is profitable from every quarter, and in attempting, as far as we can, things that lie far above us.
Well said.

If one chose to go into minute detail, the discussion of each item would become long and branch out in many directions. But it should be understood that some of the furnishings lie close to spiritual contemplation and mystical meanings, while others were devised for the adornment and use of the tabernacle. So I will cut the discussion as short as I can, speak briefly and keep the account concise. He said, then: "And you shall make the tabernacle of ten curtains of twisted fine linen, and blue and purple, and twisted scarlet. You shall make them with cherubim, the work of a weaver. The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of one curtain shall be four cubits; all the curtains shall have the same measure. Five curtains shall be joined to one another, one to the other, and five curtains shall be joined, one to the other." So there are ten curtains, and they are tightly joined to one another. For there are many dwelling places with the Father, and those who dwell in them all share, I think, one holy aim and one knowledge of God. For God has called us in peace, as it is written. If you like, you may take the ten curtains to be the full number of the churches throughout the world. They are not scattered into discord or conflicting opinion but united in the Spirit, bound tightly into one, as it were, in the unity that is in Christ through faith. For everywhere and in all of them there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Each of the curtains is four cubits broad and twenty-eight long. The riddle is intricate and subtle, but I think it indicates, darkly and dimly, that the instruction given through the law is also in some way accepted in the churches. That instruction is very narrow because the letter is obscure, but as time stretches out in length, it will have as its end the mystery of Christ, that is, the eighth, or the resurrection that took place on the eighth day. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and it was to him that the divine David cried out: "Your commandment is exceedingly broad." The inspired Paul also writes to those who had preferred the worship of the law to faith in Christ: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children) be enlarged as well. Do not be mismatched with unbelievers." Do you see that wanting to cling to the disobedient Jews, who still speak the things of the law after faith has come, makes one restricted?
I understand.

The fabrics of the curtains are of twisted fine linen, and blue and purple, and twisted scarlet. For the adornment of the Church is of every variety. This is what the inspired David sings, speaking of her somewhere like this: "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe woven with gold, richly adorned." Her adornment and beauty is manifold, namely Christ. He is one by nature, but he is understood through many different figures, such as, for example, twisted fine linen. For the Word who is from God the Father is fine and incorporeal by nature, yet he has in some way been twisted, as it were, through his interweaving with the flesh. So he is twisted fine linen, and he is also like blue, because he is not from the earth but from above and from heaven; for blue is in some way likened to the lofty, upper, ethereal body that reaches all the way to the firmament itself. So he is like blue because he is from heaven, and purple because he is not a slave, as a created being would be, but a king from God and Lord of all. He is twisted scarlet, because, being understood, as I said, in his interweaving with the flesh, and truly being the Word of God, he gave his own blood for us. For scarlet is a sign of blood. The cherubim pictured on the hangings very well indicate, perhaps, that things below have been joined to things above, and that the Church on earth has now been united to the powers in heaven. It should be noted that the most wise Solomon too carved cherubim on the walls of the temple, and the design of the house described by the voice of Ezekiel was made in the same way. The coverings for the curtains are hangings fastened together with loops and rings. Then there are also the outer coverings, skins dyed blue and rams' skins dyed red, which suggest Christ, the protector of the Church: through the blue, again, as from heaven and from above, and through the red color, as having come in the flesh. For the color of flesh is something like this.
I say these things have been interpreted quite reasonably.

The curtains have pillars, a cubit and a half in breadth and ten in length, their capitals and shafts overlaid with gold, and resting on double bases of silver. Here again Christ is understood in each pillar, the support of the Church, the foundation of the truth, as Paul puts it. It is he who establishes and holds all things together. The cubit and a half indirectly suggests that he is perfect in the nature of the Godhead, but lesser, in turn, within the measures of humanity. It is not foolish to say that Christ is entirely perfect, as in a whole cubit, since he is God by nature, but that he is lowered, as in half a cubit, because of his humanity. For nothing among created things is perfect. The Only-begotten, though he was rich, became poor among us and lowered himself into self-emptying.
True.

So the human nature will not be equal to the supreme heights of the Godhead; far from it. That is why, having become one of us and being understood as such, he said, "My Father is greater than I," although in the nature of the Godhead he is of equal measure and in no way falls short of the supremacy of the one who begot him. The length of the wooden pillar is ten cubits. For Christ is entirely perfect, as in the heights of the Godhead, and in divine Scripture the number ten is taken as a sign of perfection. The pillar has a golden capital and a golden shaft as well. For the temple born of the Virgin is enriched with the indwelling of the highest nature. Gold is a symbol of the Godhead, since it surpasses all others, so far as material things go. The base is of silver and is double. For Christ is bright and radiant on earth, in keeping with the words "God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us," and the knowledge of him is, as it were, twofold, since both God and man are understood in him. This, I think, is what it means for the base to be double, as it were, and of silver.
Your interpretation is correct.
But look at this, my friend.
What is it?

Having ordered that the whole tabernacle be extended in ten curtains, he adds in between: "And you shall make hangings of hair as a covering over the tabernacle; you shall make eleven hangings. The length of one hanging shall be thirty cubits, and the breadth of one hanging four cubits; the eleven hangings shall be of the same length. And you shall join five hangings together and six hangings together, and you shall double over the sixth hanging at the front of the tabernacle. And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the one hanging, the one in the middle at the join, and you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the second hanging that joins it." What is the meaning of this, Palladius? He sets up ten curtains. Why, then, are the hangings not equal to them in number, but there is one extra, that is, the eleventh? For he says, "You shall join five hangings together and six hangings together."
I cannot say.
But the arrangement will clarify what we are looking for.
What do you mean?

He says that five curtains were to be fastened to one another, and five others, of the same form and in the same manner, set opposite them. So, since the two sets were raised up facing each other, perhaps from north and south, or from east and west, an eleventh side was then put up in between, separating the ten and dividing them into two. Over it, perhaps, the eleventh hanging is stretched, holding both sides together with rings and loops. Its pillars were like the others, but fewer in number. For the ten curtains, as I said before, extended to a length of twenty-eight cubits, but the eleventh, in the very middle of the others, having the breadth of the five (and each of these is four cubits), is stretched to a measure of about twenty cubits. That is why he says, "And you shall double over the sixth hanging at the front of the tabernacle," so that what was stretched out in excess would not spoil the beauty of the court. In this part, then, the one between the others and, as it were, the eleventh, the holy and divine furnishings were set out, which among themselves depict Emmanuel in various ways. Perhaps the number also indicates that Christ appears in the last times of the age, at the eleventh hour, as it were, and so does the tabernacle that holds Christ, that is, the Church.
There seems to be nothing implausible in thinking that this account is also sound.

After the instructions and types concerning the tabernacle, he says: "And you shall make a court for the tabernacle. On the southwest side the hangings of the court shall be of twisted fine linen, a hundred cubits long for one side, and their pillars twenty, and their bases twenty, of bronze, and their rings and their fillets of silver. Likewise on the east side there shall be hangings a hundred cubits long, and their pillars twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze, and the rings and the fillets of the pillars and their bases overlaid with silver. And the breadth of the court on the side toward the sea shall be hangings of fifty cubits, their pillars ten and their bases ten." Notice, then, that the first curtains were narrow and reached only into the third ten of cubits, for they were four cubits wide and twenty-eight long. But those after them were both broad and long: a hundred by a hundred and fifty by fifty, one side running toward the east, the other toward the west and southwest.
Then what is the riddle?

Is it not clearly what was promised long ago through the voice of Isaiah to the Church revealed in the last times? "Enlarge the place of your tent, and the hangings of your curtains. Fix them; spare nothing; spread out to the right and to the left." For the Church of Christ, though narrow at the beginning, then broadens toward the east and west, and the north and south, and reaches into every place.
True.

Observe that he said all the other pillars, those of the ten curtains and of the one in the middle, were to be overlaid with gold and to rest on double bases made of silver. The reason for this has been explained, I think. But he adorns the pillars of the long, broad curtains on a different principle. He says they must be splendidly adorned with silver from head to foot and must rest on bronze bases overlaid with silver. This too would be a type of Christ: the silver signifies that he shone out like light, flashing with spiritual rays as God, while the silver-plated bronze indirectly suggests to us that the word he spread over the earth, that is, the gospel proclamation, is bright and resounding. For bronze is resonant, and silver is very bright and clear. This is true of the gospel proclamations: one can see that the Savior's word has the clarity and purity of perfect godliness, yet it resounds, as it were, through the whole world. If anyone chooses to see the holy apostles and evangelists represented in such pillars, he will reason rightly. For they are truly silver-plated, as it were, because they have come to share in Christ who gives light. That is why it says, "And may the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us." They are also called "the light of the world," and they stand, so to speak, on silver-plated bronze, for their support is their use of a bright and most resounding word. For it says, "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power." And it is written: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!"
The explanation is deep, but close to the truth.

When the ordinances about the courts have been completed, he turns to the preparation of the oil, the ointment and the incense, saying: "And you shall command the sons of Israel, and let them bring you pure oil from olives, without dregs, beaten, for the light, so that a lamp may burn continually in the tent of witness, outside the veil that is over the covenant. And Aaron and his sons shall burn it from evening until morning before the Lord, a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, from the sons of Israel."
And what does this mean?

Its meaning is most necessary, and I say the riddle is a wise one. The seven lamps, always burning and shining in the holy tabernacle, should very fittingly be compared to the enlightenment that comes through Christ, which is always able to shine on the minds of believers and kindle them, that is, to fill them. For the number seven everywhere suggests the idea of completeness, as for instance in the saying, "The barren woman has borne seven," that is, very many, as many as were needed to be sufficient. Aaron and the other priests after him kindle the lamps. For the enlightenment from Christ is kept unquenched, as it were, in the churches by the diligence of those allotted the priesthood, who make the minds of believers bright by initiating them into right teaching. This, I think, is what the kindling of the lamps from evening until morning means. By darkness I take to mean the deception that comes from the devil, a kind of spiritual night that falls on human minds: the lightless, murky little fables of the unholy heretics. So the Savior's light would be seen continually and unceasingly in the churches, as their teachers rightly interpret the divine and gospel proclamations. The oil is pure, for the right and true teaching about divine doctrines, unmixed with anything worse, is entirely free from all dregs and impurity, as it were. It always rouses the Savior's enlightenment, not by adding anything of its own to Christ's brightness (it would be utterly foolish to think that he needs anything from a human being), but because Christ, who is the true light and the radiance of the Father, appears to the minds of believers as what he truly is through the orthodox words of the teachers.
And why does he say that the oil is to be from olives? This detail is very precise, and perhaps it is in labor with some necessary insight.

You think very well, and I will say what has come to my mind. Those skilled in these matters are accustomed to produce oil for our use not only from olives, Palladius, but also from various other inferior and earthier seeds. The genuine oil will truly come from the choicest olives, while the oil from the earthier seeds is, I say, somehow counterfeit, produced by force and artifice, and not genuine, as it were. So the oil from olives may very fittingly be compared to the genuine and true word, which is supplied to the worthy through the wisdom from above. But the word devised from human notions and demonic inspiration is the oil produced by some people's artifice and huckstering, and its use is counterfeit. Such a word is useless and worthless, contributing nothing at all to the enlightenment of the knowledge of Christ. That is why it is not accepted in the churches, since it has neither the fragrance of the Holy Spirit (for no one says "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit) nor the genuine, unclouded quality of the truth that is necessary for real benefit. Notice that the law says the oil from olives is to be brought by the sons of Israel. For, as I said earlier, the fruit we bring and our spiritual offering to God will be the true word, which does not allow the enlightenment from Christ to grow weak among those being initiated. The lamps are placed and burned outside the veil. For Christ, being light by nature, has no need of light, but he sends his own light into us, who are outside the Godhead because we are created. Inside the veil, by contrast, was the ark, set there as a type and image of Christ.
Well said.

Then he says: "And the Lord spoke to Moses: 'Take for yourself spices: flower of choice myrrh, five hundred shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, two hundred and fifty, and of sweet-smelling cane two hundred and fifty, and of iris five hundred shekels by the holy shekel, and oil from olives, and you shall make it into an oil of holy anointing, a perfumed ointment, the work of a perfumer. It shall be an oil of holy anointing. And with it you shall anoint the tent of witness, and the ark of the tent of witness and all its furnishings, and the lampstand and all its furnishings, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offerings and all its furnishings, and the table and all its furnishings, and the basin and its base; and you shall consecrate them, and they shall be most holy. Whoever touches them shall be made holy. And you shall anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve me as priests. And you shall speak to the sons of Israel, saying: This shall be a holy anointing oil for you throughout your generations. It shall not be poured on human flesh, and you shall not make any like it for yourselves according to this composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever makes any like it, or whoever gives any of it to a foreigner, shall be utterly destroyed from his people.'" About the quality and the composition, and again about the unequal weights of the kinds named, I could say nothing, for truth is dear to those accustomed to think rightly. But oil mixed with perfumes would signify, I think, the sanctification in Christ through the Spirit that is bestowed on those who have received mercy, as in the words "You anointed my head with oil." The tabernacle and everything in it are anointed, for even a place would share in sanctification through the one who dwells in it. The furnishings too are sanctified, in the way that suits them, because they serve in the worship of God, and whoever touches them will be made holy. So the holy and sacred things are not to be touched by those who are still profane; for "what fellowship has light with darkness?" as it is written. He absolutely forbids them to prepare similar oil for themselves. For sanctifying belongs to God alone, and this will truly be reserved to him as his special prerogative. How could a created and made nature ever be able to sanctify others? It possesses sanctification only with difficulty, by participation in what comes from above. One might fittingly cry out to it in the words of the saints: "What do you have that you did not receive?" And John says of the Only-begotten, "From his fullness we have all received." And, "He does not give the Spirit by measure"; rather, being himself the source of sanctification, he measures out the Spirit to the worthy and sanctifies the rational creation. "It shall not be poured on human flesh," he says, although he had ordered Aaron and his fellow priests to be anointed with it. So the sacred race is now above the merely human, since it shares in Christ, who is above creation. That is why, raising us to a dignity above nature, and cutting us off, as it were, from earthly things, he assigns us to the things above; for he says, "Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven, and you are all brothers." The penalty for those who give any of it to a foreigner is destruction; for he says, "Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine." For to offer carelessly to those who are still unbelievers the hidden things, which befit only the holy, is full of danger. What is sanctified is not what is still profane and grievously sick with impurity, but what has already been cleansed through holy baptism.
True.

In the same way and on the same principle, he laid down how the incense was to be prepared, saying: "And take for yourself spices: stacte and onycha, and sweet galbanum, and clear frankincense, equal part for equal part; and they shall make it into incense, perfumed, the work of a perfumer, blended, pure, a holy work. And you shall beat some of it fine, and put it before the testimony in the tent of witness, where I will make myself known to you. The incense shall be most holy to you. You shall not make it for yourselves according to this composition. It shall be holy to you for the Lord. Whoever makes any like it, to smell it, shall perish from his people." Here again the passage suggests to us that what is specially reserved to the nature that is beyond all things is shared in essence by no created being; creation has nothing whatever in common with its Maker and Master, as far as dignity and preeminence of honors are concerned. We will remember that we said the golden altar, and the compounded, fine incense itself, were Christ, and that Emmanuel himself is signified to us through both. So, since the incense refers to Christ (for it is incomparably fragrant), we will not make for ourselves anything after the pattern of that incense. For we will accept no one else at all besides him, as the wretched Jews will indeed accept the son of lawlessness. Such people will be caught compounding for themselves something after the pattern of that fragrant and truly special incense of God the Father, who has made manifest to us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in the Son. Through the Son we too are fragrant, not because we compound the fine incense for ourselves, but because we share in the incense, have been anointed with the grace of the Spirit, and strive to win approval through our way of life in Christ.
So it seems that the mystery of the Savior is depicted for us in everything that was made in the holy tabernacle.
And beyond this you would be quite amazed to learn that even the craftsmen of the holy tabernacle portray Christ, in their own persons, as it were.
How do you mean? I cannot work it out.

Again it is written: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge, to devise in every work: the gold, the silver, the bronze, the blue, the purple, the spun scarlet, the twisted fine linen, the stonework, and to work at the carpentry of wood in all the works. And I have given him, and Oholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan; and to everyone wise of heart I have given understanding, and they shall make all that I have commanded.” Notice, then, how Bezalel directs the crafting, while Oholiab carries out the work.
And what of that?

Listen, then. Judah and Dan were both sons of Jacob, but the one was born of Leah, the free woman, and the other of Bilhah, the maidservant. Bezalel, then, is a clear type of Christ, who appeared to us, according to the flesh, from the tribe of Judah, and who is truly of the free nature—plainly, the divine and supreme nature. And Oholiab would very well signify the apostles and evangelists who worked together with Christ, as being from Jerusalem, the slave woman. For they became God's fellow workers, while he, as it were, labored and crafted all that was needed to establish the holy churches. And all who were wise of heart contributed, out of their own zeal and goodwill, to the works of the tabernacle, and so they fill out the image of the teachers in every age, who make it their eager care to do the works of God and whatever would serve the benefit of the Church of Christ.
More on the same subjects, and on the things in the holy tabernacle
Do you find the account we have given of the holy tabernacle and the things in it clear and sufficient, Palladius?
Very clear indeed, but far from sufficient.

Shall we, then, go back very eagerly to what seems to have been left out of our accounts of it? For I suppose you think, as is reasonable, that we ought to add a discourse explaining how it was erected for us, and when and how the ordinances and laws connected with it were established, along with its dedication, its sanctification and its judgment.
Then go through each of these again; you are thinking rightly.

Well then, I will speak. But you in turn must be forgiving, bearing in mind the utter difficulty of these speculations; and if perhaps I say something somewhere that falls short of accuracy and strays from the proper account, reshape it and set it right. For I shall make you my helper and ally in what I say.
Go ahead, trusting in God.

When the work on the holy tabernacle had been fully completed, and each of the things in it had been made wisely and skillfully after the beauty shown on the mountain, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "On the first day of the first month, at the new moon, you shall set up the tent of testimony." And again, a little later: "And it came to pass," it says, "in the first month, in the second year after they came out of Egypt, at the new moon, that the tabernacle was set up, and Moses set up the tabernacle." So the ancient tabernacle of the Church as understood in Christ was erected, as God willed, plainly displaying the types in itself. But let us inquire, if you agree, into the reasons why it was erected by Moses rather than another, while Joshua is passed over in silence for the present, even though he always stood by the most excellent Moses, went up with him onto Mount Sinai, and fought and took the field against Amalek at Moses' word. For Moses said to him somewhere, "Choose for yourself mighty men, and go out and draw up for battle against Amalek tomorrow." And he drew up for battle, and he won. What, then, is the meaning of this? Is it not worth examining?
Certainly.

If anyone chooses to examine as precisely as possible the meaning of the mystery in each of the things that were done, he will cry out in amazement, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!" For see how subtle and how necessary the sense is in each case. When the divine Moses goes up the mountain, Joshua goes up with him, for the Father cannot be approached in any other way than through the Son. And indeed it is true when it is said, "No one comes to the Father except through me." So even for the saints themselves the approach is in Christ. No one could leap up, as onto a mountain, to some lofty and transcendent contemplation; nor, I think, could anyone come near to God (in the manner of union, of course, that is, through a way of life in the Spirit and in holiness) unless Emmanuel were with him, making what is inaccessible to human beings passable, even a road for horses. And this, I think, is what was said through the voice of Isaiah: "Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and all the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places smooth roads." For in Christ even the uphill ways are smooth for us, the rough ground is passable, and the hard going becomes bare and level. Indeed, as the same prophet says again somewhere, "The way of the godly has become straight, and the way of the godly is prepared." So it is necessary that Joshua goes up with the divine Moses. For, as I said, the Father is approached through the Son, and he is the mediator, joining us to the Father through himself and carrying us up to heights beyond nature. And Joshua drew up for battle with chosen men and defeated Amalek. For Christ chose the saints, of whom the divine disciples became the firstfruits, and conquered the ruler of this age. Yet it was Moses who gave the command, for the Son came under the law, although as God he is the lawgiver. And the battle did not take place on the very day on which Moses spoke, but on the morrow, that is, it was deferred to another time. For the law foretold what was to come, and, if it is understood spiritually, it contains a splendid narrative of the Savior's achievements. For this reason, I think, it was Moses who set up the holy tabernacle as well. For the training given through the law contributes something to the establishing of the Church: it is a tutor leading to Christ, who is the head of the Church and its whole foundation, the pillar and bulwark of the truth, as it is written. And so Christ said to the Jews, "If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me." So Moses too, that is, the training given through the law, builds the Church of Christ, showing the mystery concerning it beforehand, though still in shadows. For the person of Moses sometimes stands for the law given through him, as is rightly said in the Gospel parables: "They have Moses and the prophets."
You are right.

Now, what might it signify that the holy tabernacle had to be set up on one day, and indeed at the new moon of the first month, and in the second year? Come, let us say, tracking down the truth and what seems best to those who will read this. The one day points to the much-prayed-for and saving time in which the Only-begotten, having become man, won those on earth for God the Father by the death of his own flesh. And the time of this is one, once for all; for having died once, he dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him, according to the Scriptures. We shall not expect the Son to die again for ourselves and for the spirits in Hades, nor that there will be a second firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For if there is to be no death, how could there be a resurrection? So we do not speak falsely when we say that the time of this is one, as I said just now, and one day, which the prophet too recalled, speaking as in the person of God: "At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you." And the divine Paul writes, "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation": the day on which Christ came back to life from the dead, having destroyed the grim power of death, when he also appointed the holy apostles as builders, so to speak, and spiritual craftsmen of the Church from the Gentiles, saying, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age." Or would you not say that this is the establishing of the Church?
What exactly do you mean?

I mean the faith handed down through the holy teachers of the mysteries, and the way of life they proclaimed, that is, the life in Christ, and union with God through holy baptism by participation in the Holy Spirit. For this is how Paul addressed us: "You too, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit." Of old, Christ was prefigured in the holy tabernacle as in various vessels: as the golden censer, as the ark, as the lampstand, and indeed as the table and the things on it. But in the present time, I think, each believer is called a house and temple of God, having Christ dwelling within. For he dwells in our hearts through faith, as it is written. He is one and the same by nature, even when he is understood together with the flesh, for "there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things"; yet through the various properties of the divinity he has in himself a kind of manifoldness and is understood in various ways. For he is in us as the Word of God, and wisdom, and light, and life, and the living bread from heaven.
I understand what you mean.

So the time of the incarnation for our sake, and the thrice-longed-for day of the resurrection from the dead, were prefigured long ago when God said, "On one day you shall set up the tabernacle." And one can see, Palladius, that the words "and at the new moon of the first month" were added usefully and necessarily. For just as the beginning of a month is the first of its days, that is, the new moon, so the time of his coming among us is, as it were, the beginning of a new age and the first onset of a renewal of the times. For in Christ there is a new creation; the old things have passed away. And the age that follows this one dawns on us, as it were: for now it is still seen as in hope, but then it will be truly present, when Christ shines upon us again with the holy angels in the glory of the Father, to take with him those who have chosen to walk in newness of life and have patiently gained the riches of the surpassing beauty of the gospel way of life, and to bring them into the glory and kingdom long awaited. That those in Christ are a new creation and, as it were, a new sprouting of times and things would be well shown by the riddle of the first month, in which tender, newly appeared grasses cover the earth, plants bloom again, and the varied beauty of the flowers in the meadows appears, while the fragrance of spring smiles. For it is as though in such a season that Christ called the Church from the Gentiles, saying: "Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come." For human nature, which had withered in death like a plant because of the transgression in Adam and the sin that tyrannized over all of us, blossomed once more. And I hear Christ saying also through one of the holy prophets, "I who speak am here, like spring upon the mountains." For what spring does on the mountains and in the woods, crowning the plants with new growth, our Savior's coming has accomplished in us too.
