It came in due season, as in the second year, and not in the first period, when there were the law and the choir of the prophets, and when death held sway; for death reigned from Adam until Moses. So as in the second year, that is, in the time after the first, in which there was the law, the Church from the Gentiles shone forth, having dwelling within it Christ, the end of the prophets and of the law. Does our account seem to you to be heading straight for the truth?
Absolutely.

For my part, I think the truer tabernacle was announced to us beforehand through the voice of Isaiah, who says, as though to each of those called in faith to righteousness, "Your eyes will see Jerusalem, rich cities, tents that will not be shaken; the stakes of its tent will not be moved, nor will its cords be broken, for all time." For the Church is the city of God, which the divine David also recalled when he said, "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." For it is rich, adorned with gifts from above and from heaven, and it has an unbreakable foundation and permanence, standing secure. For the gates of Hades will not prevail against it, according to the Savior's word.
Your thinking is entirely right and reasonable.

Once the tabernacle had been set up, God, the Lord of all, teaches that the things in it had to be placed in order, and not at random and carelessly, saying: "And you shall place the ark of the testimony, and cover the ark with the veil. And you shall bring in the table and set out what is to be set on it. And you shall bring in the lampstand and put its lamps on it. And you shall place the golden altar for burning incense before the ark. And you shall put the covering of the veil over the door of the tent of testimony, and you shall place the altar of burnt offerings by the doors of the tent of testimony. And you shall set up the tabernacle round about, and set all its things round about." In these words one can see the sacred vessels being brought into the holy tabernacle, but not yet clearly the place that was fitting for each and assigned to it. Would you like us, then, to gather a fine and exact knowledge of these matters from the commands concerning the tabernacle?
Most gladly.

God, then, said to the holy Moses: "And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and spun fine linen; you shall make it with cherubim, woven work. And you shall hang it on four pillars of incorruptible wood overlaid with gold; their capitals shall be gold, and their four bases silver. And you shall put the veil on the pillars, and bring in there, inside the veil, the ark of the testimony. And the veil shall divide for you between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. You shall cover the ark of the testimony with the veil in the Holy of Holies. And you shall place the table outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table on the side of the tabernacle toward the south; and you shall place the table on the side of the tabernacle toward the north. And you shall make a drawn curtain for the door of the tabernacle of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer. And you shall make five pillars for the curtain and overlay them with gold; their capitals shall be gold, and you shall cast five bronze bases for them." So much for these things. Concerning the laver he says something like this: "Make a bronze laver, and a bronze base for it, for washing, and you shall place it between the tent of testimony and the altar." Is the meaning of each of these clear to you?
Not at all; I am at a loss, believe me, and cannot say what it is about.

Then for each of the passages set before us I will seize on what bears on their spiritual contemplation and give an account as clear and distinct as I am able. The holy tabernacle, Palladius, was erected in the wilderness with a twofold arrangement and form, as it were. One part was the innermost, and its name was the Holy of Holies. The first part, surrounding it, was a kind of vestibule, called the Holy Place. In the innermost tabernacle the ark was laid up, with a veil around it on four golden pillars, skillfully made of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and spun fine linen. Since we have already spoken, and I think sufficiently, about the fine linen and the purple and the twisted scarlet, and the blue as well, we shall avoid repeating ourselves. But this much we shall say for the present: the veil on the four golden pillars with silver bases signified at that time the mystery of Christ. Why so? Did not the wise Paul too call the body of Christ a veil, when he said, "the new and living way which he opened for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh"?
You are right.

See, then, as in shadows and riddles, that the Word, who is God and from God the Father by nature, came to be as in a golden and incorruptible ark, the temple taken from the Virgin; for the body of Christ is incorruptible and precious. And having taken the flesh, he was all but hidden, as though behind a veil. We say that the Word from God was hidden, not as though he were confined within a small body, for the Son is everywhere and in all things, but in that he remained concealed for the sake of the divine plan and awaited the time of his manifestation. And the time of his manifestation to all was his return to life from the dead. For before the precious cross he commanded the holy disciples not to make him known; for so it is written. But after he had suffered death and come back to life, he says, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." So the veil hung from the pillars, covering the ark within, and it would be a type of Christ, who is lifted on high by the preaching of the holy evangelists and is seen in the glory of the divinity by those in the holy tabernacle, that is, the Church. The pillars are four, of gold and overlaid with silver, and the evangelists are equal to them in number, brilliant and precious. So the ark lay there, and the veil, made of fine linen and purple and the rest and reaching from top to bottom, kept it out of sight. And from above the veil and the cherubim on the right and left God gave his oracles, showing that he is above all creation. Even the highest of all rational beings, that is, the seraphim, sit beneath the divine and ineffable glory and attend the Son himself as his guard, even though he became flesh and was, as it were, perhaps beneath equality with the Father insofar as he became man. That is why he himself said, "My Father is greater than I." Being equal by nature to the one who begot him, he says he is in a lesser state solely on account of his humanity. Therefore in the holy tabernacle too the cherubim are around the veil, they also attending the Son as God. And indeed God is understood to be above the veil itself, which was a type of Christ. "For I will make myself known to you from there," he says, "and I will speak to you." For the Father is beyond all creation, and beyond Emmanuel himself, not insofar as Emmanuel is understood to be and is God, for he is equal to God in all things, but insofar as he came into the form of a servant and the measure of humanity.
How subtle and deep this argument is!
And yet it does not miss the mark.
I agree.

With the ark placed in this way, he says, "And you shall place the golden altar for burning incense before the ark." That Christ is the golden altar I think we have said sufficiently. It is placed opposite the ark, over which is the veil, with the seraphim around it and God above, as though receiving the incomparable fragrance of Emmanuel. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, as it is written; that is why he himself said, "The Father loves the Son." And we ourselves too are acceptable to God, breathing out the fragrance of Christ's perfume. Paul will confirm this when he writes: "But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes manifest the fragrance of the knowledge of him; for we are the aroma of Christ to God."
You are right.

Let us consider carefully, then, fixing our eyes on what is written, that the ark was set on the side of the holy tabernacle facing southwest and west, and opposite it the golden altar, in the place facing the sunrise. For east and west, north and south, are filled with Christ. And so the place of the lampstand is the south of the tabernacle, and that of the table the north. That Christ is signified by both has already been shown at length: the lampstand shows that Christ is light, and the table and the things on it that he is life and the living bread. But consider this, and observe the mystery: the land of the Jews lies furthest south, while that of the Gentiles lies further north. So from the position of the two, I mean of the lampstand and the table, those who wish will surely be well able to understand that Christ shone as light upon the Jews and proclaimed among them, "I am the light." For he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; and "theirs are the promises," according to the Scriptures. But since they did not accept the light of the truth, he became life and bread from heaven for the Gentiles. Yet the Gentiles are not without light; you may learn this too from the fact that the light of the lampstand reaches even the northern parts of the tabernacle. And since the holy tabernacle was very narrow, there is nothing improbable in the lampstand seeming to stand almost beside the table, even though it occupies the southern place. The type also shows us in another way that when the divine light shines forth, the worthy may be able to partake of Christ as the living and true bread. And the Gentiles have become fellow members of the body of Christ and partakers in him. And again the divine Paul writes: "The Gentiles have become fellow members of the body and partakers" of light, clearly the spiritual light, being filled with the dawning day and with the Morning Star rising in the mind, as one of the Savior's disciples said. With the things in the Holy of Holies thus positioned and arranged, he commanded that a drawn curtain, that is, a veil, be made of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and spun fine linen, and he said that this must be stretched across the entrance of the tabernacle, hanging from five golden pillars with bronze bases. He calls the hanging over the door a "drawn curtain," I think, because it was drawn back on small rings when the entrance was opened, and was drawn across again and spread out over the doors to hide the Holy Place. The five pillars, golden and clad in bronze, prefigure the teachers and leaders of the Churches in what is, as it were, the fifth period, in which the coming of Christ took place. Rightly handling the word of truth, they are precious as gold and resounding as bronze; for their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Through their skillful and divinely inspired teaching of the mysteries they open wide, as it were, the entrances for those who wish to hasten into the Holy of Holies. The Holy of Holies, then, that is, the inner tabernacle, was covered by the veil. Directly adjoining the second tabernacle and joined to it was the first, which contained the altar of burnt offerings, on which every offering by blood was performed, together with cakes and frankincense and every sacrifice and libation; and besides the altar there was also the bronze laver. The altar's place was by the doors of the tabernacle, clearly the outer one, and the laver's place was the very middle of the tabernacle.
And what, in turn, might be understood as the point of this arrangement?

Sacred Scripture is precise, Palladius, and there is absolutely nothing random in it. See how the riddle has shown us the law acting as a tutor leading to Christ. The altar of the worship under the law was placed right at the entrance to the Holy of Holies. For the law barely brings us to the beginnings of the mysteries of Christ, as if to the first approaches to an exact knowledge of him. It in no way brings us into the Holy of Holies, that is, into the inner tent, where Christ appears in many forms: as the Word of God, as light, as living bread, as a fragrant aroma to God the Father. Or would you not say that the preliminary training of the worship under the law was the elements and first principles of the oracles of God?
True.

That the law perfected nothing (for it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins) you would learn at once and with no effort at all by considering also the use of the laver. It stood in the middle of the first tent, bright and conspicuous, washing beforehand with water those who hurried into the Holy of Holies, for the law about this had been laid down for the priests. So the apparent fulfillment under the law is also incomplete. It hints at the cleansing through holy baptism, which washes the holy race, I mean the race of those justified in faith. The divine disciple also addressed them, saying, "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light." We should also know that a curtain was stretched across the door of the outer tent, so that the Holy Place, that is, the first tent, where the altar of the law stood, would not be bare and visible to those outside. Here again, I think, the type shows that the law itself is not plain to just anyone. For the letter has a veil, and it is somehow covered and wrapped in its obscurity, as if in shadows.
That is so.

So in the first tent stood the laver and the altar. In the second, innermost one were the ark and the lampstand, and also the golden censer on which the fine incense was burned, and the table and the loaves. The divine Paul also mentions a golden jar holding the manna. He names Aaron's rod as well, and says that it too was laid up in the Holy of Holies. He was well versed in the sacred Scriptures and knew very well what had been ordained at various times and commanded to blessed Moses by God. But he knows that there was a table and a lampstand in the first tent. He writes this about the two covenants: "In speaking of a new covenant, he has made the first one old. And what is becoming old and growing aged is close to vanishing. Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary. For a tent was prepared, the first one, in which were the lampstand, the table and the presentation of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a tent called the Holy of Holies. It had a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on all sides with gold, in which were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail."
So if someone chose to be inquisitive and said that we ought to give the reasons for the whole arrangement, what account would we give?

That, Palladius, he commanded some things to be done before the holy tent was constructed, and others after it. In Exodus, before the patterns of the holy tent had been shown at all and the commands about it given, he uttered the oracle about the golden jar, knowing what would happen. After the whole tent had been pitched, we will find in Numbers that Aaron's rod was brought into the Holy of Holies. And in Leviticus God gave further laws about the lampstand and also about the table in the first tent. The most wise Paul, who was learned in the law, leaves out none of what took place, but mentions the first, the middle and the last.
Excellently said. Explain each of them, then, clearly and distinctly, for the meaning behind them is surely deep.

Yes, you are right, for that is truly how the matter stands. I will begin my account with the jar. God sent the manna down like rain on the Israelites in the desert, for it was food and bread for them from above and from heaven. But what was done did not stop at the things of the senses. As through type and shadow, it leads us up to understand that in due time the Word from above and from the Father would come to us as bread from heaven. The divine David also indicates this to us when he says, "He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels." We certainly do not say that the manna perceived by the senses is the bread from heaven and of angels. For the spirit is nourished spiritually, while the body is nourished according to its own nature, that is, bodily. The food of angels, the bread fitting for the heavens and the spirits above, is the Word from God the Father. The manna, then, signified Christ. But the type does no good unless the truth has been received. It is a shadow of the truth, which did not come about strictly for its own sake, but to paint in itself a picture of something better. For this reason Christ wisely rebuked the crowds of the Jews because they admired not him as the truth, but Moses, the minister of the types. He said this: "Truly, truly, I tell you, Moses gave you the manna; but the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. I am the living bread." So when God gave the oracle about the jar, he was making the manna an image of the Word who came down from above and from heaven. It is written thus: "And Moses said, This is the word which the Lord commanded: Fill an omer with manna, to be kept for your generations, so that they may see the bread which you ate in the desert, when the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt. And Moses said to Aaron, Take one golden jar and put in it a full omer of manna, and lay it up before God, to be preserved for your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses. And Aaron laid it up before the testimony, to be preserved." We said that the ark, which contained the divine word, signified Emmanuel, for the Word of God was in a holy temple, I mean the one from the Virgin. In the same way the golden jar, which held the manna perceived by the senses, shows us the life-giving Word from above, clearly the one from the Father, dwelling as in a sacred and undefiled body. The jar was also full of manna. For "in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily," in the words of blessed Paul. And "he does not give the Spirit by measure," for Christ is wholly perfect. The jar was laid up to be preserved for the generations of the sons of Israel. For Christ is incorruptible and abides forever, and he is best known in every season and time. And it is before the Lord, that is, in the Father's sight. For when the Only-begotten became one of us, he also entered the Holy of Holies through the greater and more perfect tent, that is, into heaven, "now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf," as it is written. He does not set himself in the Father's sight, but us, as in himself. Yet we had fallen from his presence and, as it were, out of his sight because of the transgression in Adam and the sin that tyrannized over all. In Christ, therefore, we have received access and boldness to enter the sanctuary, as wise Paul told us. For just as we have been raised with him and seated with him in the heavenly places in Christ, so in him again we have come into the presence of the Father. That is enough about the sacred jar. Now, if you agree, let us say how Aaron's rod also signifies Christ.
By all means.

Korah, then, and Abiram, and Dathan with them, came from the tribe and blood of Levi. Scripture says they had been entrusted with a ministry in the holy tent, appointed by decree from above. Yet they thirsted for the glory of Moses and Aaron and seized the honor for themselves, though God had not called them to it. They swelled up into harsh insolence, became exceedingly haughty, and made a denunciation against the two of them that was no longer bearable but utterly intolerable. Like bulls straying from the herd they broke away, and shaking off their service under God, they persuaded others to break away with them in impiety. But they paid the penalty for what they had dared. The earth opened its mouth and sent the arrogant people down to Hades, together with their families, tents and possessions. The Lawgiver wished to make it plain that Aaron had been allotted the highest rank in the priesthood by decree from above, and not by Moses' wishes. So he said to the most excellent Moses: "Speak to the sons of Israel, and take from them a rod for each father's house, from all their leaders by their fathers' houses, twelve rods, and write each man's name on his rod. And write Aaron's name on the rod of Levi, for there is one rod. They shall give them according to the tribe of their fathers' house. And you shall place them in the tent of testimony, before the testimony, where I will make myself known to you. And the rod of the man whom I choose shall sprout, and I will remove from me the murmuring of the sons of Israel, which they murmur against you. And Moses spoke to the sons of Israel, and all their leaders gave him a rod, one rod for each leader, by their fathers' houses, twelve rods. And Aaron's rod was among their rods. And Moses laid up the rods before the Lord in the tent of testimony. And on the next day Moses and Aaron went into the tent of testimony, and behold, Aaron's rod for the house of Levi had sprouted. It had put forth a shoot, blossomed with flowers, and produced nuts. And Moses brought out all the rods from the presence of the Lord to all the sons of Israel, and they looked, and each took his rod. And the Lord said to Moses, Put Aaron's rod back before the testimonies to be kept, as a sign for the sons of the disobedient. Let their murmuring against me cease, and they shall not die." The blossoming of the rod, then, was a clear sign that the divine Aaron, as being of the blood of Levi, had been splendidly and specially chosen for sacred service. But when the account is turned again to spiritual contemplation, the mystery of Christ will shine out once more, though in types that are still very dense.
In what way?

Emmanuel has been appointed by God the Father as both lawgiver and high priest over us, offering himself as the sacrifice for us. As blessed Paul said, "The law through Moses appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever." So the Word came down from heaven and became one of us, "a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tent, which the Lord pitched, not man." But those of Israel's blood did not think he was right. As if setting their own will against his, they assailed him in many ways with the arrows of envy, sparing no slander, no insolence, no outrageous scheme. The wretches were destroying themselves, and in the end they crucified him. Yet the rod from the root of Jesse blossomed again. For Christ sprang up and came back to life, "having loosed the pangs of death," as it is written. Since he is life by nature, being God, how could he be held by death, and not rather overpower corruption? The rod's sprouting, the already flowerless wood's unexpected budding, was a sufficient sign to the ancients that Aaron had been appointed high priest by decree from above. In the same way, we say, Emmanuel's trampling on death and coming back to life in a manner fitting for God is a splendid, clear and fully sufficient proof that he is also God by nature. Indeed, Christ himself could accomplish with ease and without effort anything at all, however far beyond likelihood and reason. Yet to those who asked for a sign he said: "This generation is evil; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." His abolishing death and corruption and blossoming again into life is therefore a truly famous and conspicuous sign. For those who are genuinely well disposed, it is enough to bring them to believe that the Son is God by nature and was begotten of God the Father. For he became "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" and "the firstborn from the dead." The sign has been given to the sons of the disobedient, so that they may know that by decree of God the Father Christ has become our high priest, "holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens," as it is written.
But Aaron's rod blossomed for us, as the sacred text has just shown us, and it blossomed with nuts. What the riddle means I cannot understand.

First of all, Palladius, it is not at all unlikely that the rod was cut from a nut tree, and the ancients were accustomed to use scepters of that kind. But if we must apply an interpretation suited to spiritual contemplation, I would mention something that is widely repeated and that some accept as true. A rod of nut wood, it is said, can cause sleeplessness if it is laid by someone's head, perhaps doing this by natural powers according to the will of God. He who knows all things, the Creator of the universe, will in a way confirm this for us when he says to Jeremiah: "What do you see, Jeremiah?" Jeremiah answers, "A staff of nut wood." And what does God say to this? "You have seen rightly," he says, "for I am watchful over my words, to perform them." The rod of nut wood, then, can reasonably be understood as a symbol of wakefulness. And Christ's return to life from the dead was like an awakening from sleep. That is why he also says through the lyre of the Psalmist: "I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord sustained me."
The account is true.

About the lamp and the table in the first tent, again, it is written thus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, Command the sons of Israel, and let them take pure oil, beaten, for the light, to keep a lamp burning continually outside the curtain in the tent of testimony. Aaron and his sons shall keep it burning before the Lord continually from evening until morning, a perpetual statute for your generations. On the pure lampstand you shall burn the lamps before the Lord until morning. And you shall take fine flour and make twelve loaves of it, each loaf of two tenths. And you shall set them in two rows, six loaves to a row, on the pure table before the Lord. And on the row you shall put pure frankincense and salt, and they shall be for the loaves as a memorial set before the Lord. On the sabbath day you shall set them out before the Lord continually in the sight of the sons of Israel, an everlasting covenant. They shall belong to Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place, for it is most holy. This is his portion from the offerings made to the Lord, a perpetual statute." The oil, then, is pure, and indeed olive oil, that is, made from olives. It is not pressed from other, more earthy kinds of seed, which yield an oil that is spurious and, as it were, adulterated. For the light in the churches is always pure and truly genuine, clearly the light given through Christ in the Spirit, even if it is ministered through the voice of the saints, to whom Christ said, "You are the light of the world." And this is no wonder. He called them brothers and made them his partners, so he would naturally share with them the glory of his own dignities as well. The lamp, then, burns in the first tent too, and the matter may have a twofold meaning. In the inner tent seven lamps shine. They are lit in the morning and pour abundant light on those who hurry in. And the lampstand was Christ, again as in a type, illuminating with plentiful, abundant light those who wish to hurry into the Holy of Holies. For it says, "Come to him and be enlightened." The lighting of the lamps in the morning would also signify the time of the incarnation. For it dawned like a day, and a spiritual light shone out, driving away the darkness of our ancient ignorance and scattering the gloom that had fallen like night on the hearts of all. That is how the prophet called on God about the time of the Savior's coming, saying, "In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will watch." For when would the prayers of all have become acceptable, and when would we who once wandered have stood, as it were, before God, through a spiritual kinship and through obedience and faith, unless the light from heaven, that is, Christ, had shone on us? So in the inner tent the light of the seven lamps was rich and fine, while in the first tent a single lamp gave light. The arrangement shows, I think, that even those being trained under the law were not without the divine light. For the law given through Moses also called people from polytheism to the knowledge of him who is God by nature and in truth. It drew the ancients away from still worshipping the creation rather than the Creator, and persuaded them that they must hold fast to the Maker of all. These things were not achieved in the souls of those being trained without the spiritual light. So, to say it again, the illumination from Christ is rich and abundant for those in the Holy of Holies, but less for those under the law. And this is true, for the shadow in the law in no way equals the gospel oracles in spiritual brightness. The gospel oracles flash their light around the whole world, while the law was a distinguishing mark only for those of Israel.
You have spoken rightly.
It seems, Palladius, that the table and the lamp in the first tent also point to something else.
What do you mean?
The lamp perhaps prefigures for us the divine John the Baptist, and the twelve loaves the choir of the holy apostles.
In what way?

Do you not know that for those under the law in Judea the divine Baptist was a kind of lamp that went before Christ? God the Father announced beforehand about him: "I have prepared a lamp for my Christ." The Savior himself also bore witness to this when he said to the teachers of the Jews about him, "He was the lamp that burned and shone, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light." See how blessed Paul, being learned in the law, all but calls to mind the lamp in the first tent. The lawgiver commanded that it be kept from going out, saying, "Aaron and his sons shall keep it burning before the Lord continually from evening until morning." But the Jews delighted in John for only a very short time, when they ran to be baptized by him and were filled with admiration for him. Then they put him to sleep in death, all but extinguishing the lamp that was meant to shine always. Even if the outrage might perhaps be called Herod's, Herod was still of the blood of Israel. That is why Christ, charging the Jewish people with their insolence toward every holy man, says, "It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem."
So the divine Baptist too was a light and a lamp for those under the law in Judea, by his likeness to Christ and his participation in him.

That is what I say. In the same way, we say that the holy apostles are to be understood as loaves. For there is one bread that is by nature and truly from heaven and life-giving. But in imitation of the one who is so by nature, and by participation in him, the divine teachers of the mysteries are loaves that nourish us for godliness: they instill in us words of life and drive the famine of ignorance out of the souls of believers. The loaves are equal in number to the disciples, for there are twelve. They are laid in two rows, "six on one side," it says, "and six on the other," as though standing round in a circle, with the one who is also from heaven, that is, Christ, lying in the middle. Each is of two tenths, that is, of two perfect measures, for the divine disciples were perfect in both respects, fully equipped for every good thing whatever, outstanding in deed and in word. Frankincense and salt are sprinkled on them. The frankincense signifies fragrance in holiness, the fragrance of Christ; the salt hints at wisdom. For the speech of the saints is not senseless or foolish but seasoned with grace and salt, as it is written, and it gives grace to those who hear. Christ himself said to them, "You are the salt of the earth." The loaves are also set out on the Sabbath day. For the day on which the holy apostles were made known is the time of the spiritual Sabbath, that is, the coming of Christ. Because the people of Israel did not recognize it, Paul says of them, "So then a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God." For they did not enter into his rest, since they did not accept the faith. The spiritual and true Sabbath rest, then, is the time of our Savior's sojourn among us. The loaves are set out in the sight of God, and also in the sight of Israel. For "you shall set them out," it says, "on the Sabbath day before the Lord continually, on behalf of the sons of Israel." God looks on, and continually counts the saints worthy of his care, for "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous," it says. Israel, for its part, is bound to pay heed to them and in a sense to fix on them the eye of the mind, of which the bodily eye would be a type. "But they shall belong," it says, "to Aaron and to his sons, and they shall eat them." For the writings of the holy apostles are set before us as food: before us who have been justified in faith, a holy and priestly race, peoples for God's own possession, chosen, and anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Well said; I would certainly agree. But why are the types of the holy Baptist and of the holy apostles placed not in the Holy of Holies but in the first tent?

First, because the distance between them is great: the things of the saints will not lie where Christ is, but, as it were, outside and among lesser things. For the things of God are set apart and stand by themselves, and a great principle walls off what is human, showing the incomparable distinctness of the natures and the difference in glory. Second, because they came from the Jews and from worship according to the law. That is why the first tent is, so to speak, the fitting place for them, since in it stood, in types, the altar of burnt offerings. Or did not the calling of the holy disciples come from the blood of Israel, and from what was, as it were, the first tent?
It certainly did.

Since our account of these matters is now quite sufficient, let us bring forward, if you agree, the words of the divine Paul, which set out elegantly the testimony concerning the first and the second tent. He writes as follows: "These things having been so arranged, the priests go continually into the first tent to perform their acts of worship. But into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people. By this the Holy Spirit shows that the way into the holy places has not yet been disclosed while the first tent still stands. This is a parable for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper in conscience, since they deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the flesh imposed until the time of reformation. But when Christ came as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, he entered once for all into the Holy of Holies, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption." You see, then, that the priests performed the acts of worship in the first tent but had no access into the Holy of Holies. For such, in a manner, is the worship according to the law: it has its standing in shadows. And these things were of no avail for cleansing and washing away sin. For you heard Paul cry out just now that they are incapable of perfecting the worshiper in conscience. Rather, they were maintained until the time of reformation, clearly meaning the incarnation of the Only-begotten, when the unloveliness of the types gave way to the truth. Once a year, and alone, the high priest used to enter the Holy of Holies, and not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people. The most wise Paul will make this clear to us as well, speaking of Christ as follows: "When he said above, 'Sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and offerings for sin you did not desire, nor did you take pleasure in them' (these are offered according to the law), then he said, 'See, I have come to do your will.' He abolishes the first in order to establish the second. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ. And every high priest stands day after day ministering and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But he, having offered [?] a sacrifice for sins, sat down forever at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified." For having died once, he dies no more, as it is written; and having borne the sins of many, he entered into the Holy of Holies, that is, into heaven, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.

The explanation is clear, so you may spare yourself further toil on that point. But tell me, since I ask: what blood, again, would it be that the chief of the priests was accustomed to bring for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people?

Paul was learned in the law and had studied the commandment given through Moses with the utmost precision. Since the Hebrew people were well versed in such things and had read the law, he speaks to them about these very solemn and deeply secret matters not in lengthy narratives but rather in passing, as a reminder of things already known. But if you agree, I will bring forward the law on this subject too, since you have chosen to be eager for learning and are very thirsty for a precise and finely worked explanation of these contemplations. It is written, then, in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel: If a soul sins unintentionally before the Lord against any of the commandments of the Lord concerning things that ought not to be done, and does any one of them: if it is the anointed high priest who sins, so as to make the people sin, he shall bring for his sin which he has sinned a calf from the herd without blemish to the Lord for sin. He shall bring the calf to the door of the tent of witness before the Lord, and he shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. And the anointed priest whose hands have been consecrated shall take some of the blood of the calf and bring it into the tent of witness, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the Lord, toward the holy veil. And the priest shall put some of the blood of the calf on the horns of the altar of compounded incense which is before the Lord, which is in the tent of witness; and all the blood of the calf he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings, which is by the doors of the tent of witness. And all the fat of the calf of the sin offering he shall remove from it: the fat covering the entrails, and all the fat on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat on them, which is on the thighs, and the lobe on the liver together with the kidneys he shall remove, in the same way as it is removed from the calf of the sacrifice of deliverance; and the priest shall offer it up on the altar of burnt offering. And the hide of the calf and all its flesh, with the head and the extremities and the belly and the dung, they shall carry, the whole calf, outside the camp to a clean place, where they pour out the ashes, and they shall burn it on wood with fire; it shall be burned on the place where the ashes are poured out." These are the things the law commanded to be done if any sin of ignorance should be charged against the one who held first place in the priesthood. It also says that a sacrifice must be performed for the sins of ignorance of the people: a calf is brought and slaughtered in the same way at the doors of the tent of witness before the Lord, the elders of the congregation lay their hands on it, its blood is carried into the holy place, and, in short, everything is done for it just as in the sacrifice for Aaron. Now that Christ is the cleansing of both priests and people (for we have been justified in him, shaking off the defilement of sin) would be clear to anyone even from these things. But let us speak of each of the things written in turn, for in this way our discussion will proceed distinctly and will unfold, as far as possible, what is hidden.
Well said.

The calf, then, which is taken without blemish and without bruise, is a type of Christ, who is truly without blemish and did not submit to suffer the wound of sin. For "the ruler of this world is coming," he says, "and he will find nothing in me"; for he committed no sin, according to the Scriptures. It is brought to the very doors of the holy tent before the Lord, since he did not, as it were, refuse to suffer for the holy tent, that is, the Church, and offered himself for it as a fragrant aroma to God the Father. That is why he said, "For their sake I sanctify myself," saying "sanctify" in place of "bring" and "dedicate as an unblemished offering to God the Father." For what is dedicated to God is said to be sanctified, as somewhere it is written: "It is a snare for a man to sanctify hastily any of his own possessions; for after the vow comes repentance." That the offering is acceptable and well-pleasing is shown by the words "before the Lord." For we already understand what is written about the pair of brothers, I mean Cain and Abel: "God looked on Abel and on his gifts," it says, "but to Cain and his sacrifices he paid no heed." It is plain that he looks upon what pleases him, and turns away in hatred from what is not so. The slaughter is performed after the hands of the one who has sinned have been laid on the calf, and it is done before the Lord. For he takes away our sins and is pained for our sake when he is slain; the hand is a type of work and deeds. Yet he is slain before the Lord, as though the Father consented to the necessity that the Son die for us. For he does not turn away when he sees him slain. He certainly does not approve of the suffering as such, but he knows that it brings salvation to the world for Emmanuel to suffer for us. So it is he who takes away our sins and is pained for our sake, enduring for us his slaughter on the precious cross. Then the priest takes some of the blood with his finger and sprinkles it seven times on the holy veil, which was over the ark; its name is the mercy seat. He also smears the horns of the altar of incense. For Christ has become for us both propitiation and mercy seat. Moreover, in the blood of an eternal covenant he grants us the most perfect cleansing. This, I think, is what the sevenfold sprinkling of the mercy seat with blood means, for the number seven is a symbol of perfection. And his death too gives forth the fragrance of the world's salvation and life and of access to God in faith; for "one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and was raised for them," according to the Scriptures. So the smearing of the golden altar of incense with blood shows the fragrance of his death. The rest of the blood is poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings in the first tent; and blood is a type of the soul. Emmanuel laid down his life not only for the Church from the Gentiles but also for those under the law, that is, for Israel. For we have all been redeemed together by the blood of Christ, Greeks and Jews alike, and Paul will bear witness, saying, "Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of the Gentiles also? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." When the inner parts of the calf have been removed and carried up to the altar, the rest of the body is burned outside the camp. For he himself is the holy victim, fragrant in virtues, of which the inner parts would be types, since the virtues are, as it were, hidden within us and lie inward in the mind. He is also the one who suffers outside the gate, and by the death of his own flesh cleanses those who are defiled; for "the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are defiled sanctify," it says, "for the purification of the flesh." So Emmanuel, being one and the same, both gives forth his fragrance in the holy tents, I mean the Churches, and suffered outside the gate, where, as the divine Paul said, we too must go out, bearing his reproach. The calf is also brought for the sins of ignorance of the people, equally and without any difference, and the meaning of the sacrifice was the same in every case. For Emmanuel offered himself in the same way for small and great, for people and priests alike. Or is what I say not true?
How could it not be?
Would you like us, then, to draw the reins of our discussion back, as it were, and turn again to the accounts concerning the tent?
Certainly.

When all the works had been completed, and the sacred vessels had been well arranged, each in the place best suited to it, God prescribed that they and the tent must be sanctified, saying to the divine Moses: "And you shall take the oil of anointing and anoint the tent and everything in it, and you shall sanctify it and all its vessels, and they shall be holy. And you shall anoint the altar of burnt offerings and all its vessels, and you shall sanctify the altar, and the altar shall be holy of holies." You see, then, the ark being anointed with the holy oil, and the table too, and the lampstand upon it, and also the golden altar of incense; and our long discussion has already shown us clearly that Emmanuel is prefigured in all of them.
True.

Understand, then, what is sung to him through the voice of David: "You loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." And Paul writes, "For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one." It must be understood that, according to sound reasoning, he who as God, together with God the Father, is the giver and bestower of sanctification on all others is sanctified with us according to his humanity; and this is what is called the self-emptying. For he who is holy by nature, as God, is said to have needed God who sanctifies. The blessed Peter says this too: "Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit." So the anointing concerns his humanity, and the sanctification belongs to the flesh, which is not holy by nature but by participation in God. For sanctification comes to created things from outside, and they are enriched with grace by God as something added to them. Along with the others, the altar of worship according to the law is also anointed. For the law too is holy: it calls people to the knowledge of him who is God by nature, it instills in its hearers an understanding of righteousness, and it brings those it trains to the beginnings of goodness. For "the beginning of a good way," it says, "is to do what is just." And the divine Paul writes somewhere, "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good." The law is holy of holies, not in its shadow, but because, if it is turned toward spiritual contemplation, its types proclaim aloud to us Christ himself, who is truly the Holy of Holies. For as God he sanctifies, anointing with his own Spirit those who have come to share in him through faith. Now that the holy tent has been set up and anointed with the holy oil, let us speak of what comes next, if you agree.
By all means.

It is written as follows: "And Moses finished all the works, and the cloud covered the tent of witness, and the tent was filled with the glory of the Lord. And Moses could not enter the tent of witness, because the cloud overshadowed it and the tent was filled with the glory of the Lord. When the cloud went up from the tent, the sons of Israel set out with their baggage; but if the cloud did not go up, they did not set out until the day when the cloud went up. For the cloud was over the tent by day, and fire was over it by night, before all Israel in all their journeys." For when the holy and truer tent, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, was revealed in the world, the light of Christ shone around it, and the cloud, like a kind of spiritual dew richly fattening us with gifts from above, fills the divine temple. But Moses, it says, could not enter. For Israel did not go in, being unable to bear the onrush of the divine light, since it did not understand the mystery of Christ, nor did it accept illumination in the Spirit, nor did it behold the glory of the Lord with the eyes of the mind. With him, as with the cloud in the type, we set out when he departs from the world and goes on high, following in the Master's footsteps; for he opened for us the new and living way, I mean the way to the things above and in heaven. And when he rests and, as it were, encamps, we rest and encamp with him. When the cloud set out, the people set out with it; and when it halted, they encamped with it. For "the cloud was over the tent by day," it says, "and fire by night." For Christ enriches with spiritual gifts those who are, as it were, in day and light, because they have grasped the knowledge of him with subtlety and care and have had their minds made bright; and he enlightens those who are still more ignorant. But there is no darkness at all of worldly deceit in the Churches, since Christ shines around them and floods everything with spiritual light. For we are not of the night or of darkness, but sons of light and of the day, as it is written.
You are right.

To this let us add, without lengthy discussion, an account of the laws concerning the tent, the people's offerings of gifts, and also the departures and encampments; for in this way our discussion would proceed along the right path.
I agree.

The lawgiver and judge decreed that sacrifices must be performed only in the holy tent. In this way, I think, he drew those who might choose to offer them away from the stale false worship of Egypt, where there was much mockery with idols, and a most ugly crowd of falsely named gods that perhaps could not even be told apart by those who chose to worship them. There, too, people were free to sacrifice however they pleased, as one of the Greek sages carelessly put it: "One sacrificed to one god, another to another." So, to draw them away from such a cold and profane practice and most irrational custom, he said again in Leviticus: "Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: This is the word which the Lord has commanded, saying: Any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes among you, who slaughters a calf or a sheep or a goat in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness, so as to make it a whole burnt offering or a peace offering to the Lord, acceptable as a fragrant aroma; and whoever slaughters it outside [?] at the door of the tent of witness and does not bring it so as to offer it as a gift to the Lord before the tent of the Lord, blood shall be imputed to that man; he has shed blood; that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people." So the one who sacrifices outside the tent sheds blood and will be liable to the charge of murder. For he who removes his own soul from the God who is God by nature, and assigns and dedicates it to stones and wood and the deceits of demons, has, as it were, done away with himself and destroyed his own soul. That he did not command every slaughtered animal without exception to be brought to the doors of the tent, but only what someone chose to dedicate to God as a sacrifice, he showed clearly by adding at once: "And they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the vain things after which they themselves go whoring." So he forbids altogether sacrificing indiscriminately to whomever one pleases, and he says, very rightly, that worship must be offered to the God who is God by nature alone.
Our discussion stands in excellent order.

But I think it would benefit us not a little to understand in another way too how profitable and indeed necessary it is that the sacrifices be performed, and the sacred victims offered, only in the holy tent.
What do you mean?
Did we not say that the calf slaughtered at the holy tent for the priest and for the sins of ignorance of the people was an image and type of Emmanuel?
We did.

We say, then, that in this way the mystery of Christ must be celebrated in the churches of God, as in holy tabernacles. He prefigured this for us again somewhere else as well. At the beginning, when he laid down for those of Israel departing from the land of the Egyptians how the lamb was to be slaughtered as a type of Christ, he says: “It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside.” So the heretics, who think otherwise, set aside what pleases God. Beside the tabernacle that is truly holy they pitch another for themselves; they sacrifice the lamb outside, carry it off far from the one house, and divide the indivisible, for Christ is one and complete in all. But our wise Moses, the revealer of sacred things, gives this charge in Deuteronomy: “Take heed to yourself that you do not offer your burnt offering in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God chooses, in one of your cities. There you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I command you today. But you may slaughter as much as you desire and eat meat as your soul desires, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which he has given you in every city. The unclean among you and the clean shall eat it alike, as they would a gazelle or a deer. Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.” To dare to sacrifice in every place, and not to fulfil the mystery of Christ in the house of God, is therefore the offence and indictable crime of a most abominable mind.
Well said. But explain this. The law has forbidden the eating of blood as something corrupt, and quite rightly. What, again, is the meaning of this passage of Scripture?

Then, if you like, let us cite what was decreed on this matter in Leviticus as well. It runs thus: “And any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes who dwell among you, who eats any blood, I will set my face against the soul that eats the blood and will destroy it from among its people. For the life of all flesh is its blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for its blood shall make atonement in place of a soul. Therefore I have said to the sons of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood, nor shall the proselyte who dwells among you eat blood. And any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes who dwell among you, who catches in hunting a beast or a bird that may be eaten, shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. For the life of all flesh is its blood. And I said to the sons of Israel: You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, for the life of all flesh is its blood; whoever eats it shall be utterly destroyed.” See, then, clearly and openly, how blood is taken as a type of the soul.
I understand.

So the law sets apart the blood and withdraws it from the bodies of slaughtered animals. In this it teaches a true doctrine, one that we too accept in faith and that is held in honour in the churches: that the rational soul of man is, I say, immortal, and continues to exist and to think. Death does not destroy it along with our earthly bodies; rather, the Creator releases it and sets it free, and removes it from suffering, having made it a partaker of life. For in the beginning man was made a living soul, when God breathed into him the breath of life; so it is written. We would be accusing the life that gives life to all things of weakness, I think, if we said that what came into being for life from it perishes together with our temporary bodies. Instead we will crown it with the noblest understanding, believing it to be immortal, since this is how the Creator of all, in whom we live and move and have our being, has willed it to be. And this, I think, is the reason for the legislation on this point. But let us go on to other ordinances of the tabernacle. God, then, said in Exodus: “You shall not slaughter the blood of my sacrifice with leaven.” Let the blood that is poured out be unleavened, he says, and for what is brought as a sacrifice to God, no leaven, that is, no leavened fine flour, is to be added to it. For we must be, as it were, cleansed and unleavened (that is, we must not have in our minds anything entangled, so to speak, with wickedness and evil) when we consecrate to God our own souls, of which the blood is a type. The divine Paul too called “a new lump” and “unleavened” those who keep their own soul pure, unclouded and unmixed with wickedness, through faith in Christ, of course, and perfect love. Again he says: “Nor shall the fat of my feast remain until morning”; that is, you shall not offer yesterday's fat as a fragrant aroma. In Leviticus he makes the law clearer still and sets the matter out plainly, saying of the one who brings a sacrifice: “If it is a vow, or a freewill offering that he sacrifices as his gift, it shall be eaten on the day he offers the sacrifice, and on the next day. But whatever is left of the flesh of the sacrifice until the third day shall be burned with fire. If he eats any of the flesh on the third day, it shall not be accepted for the one who offers it, nor shall it be credited to him; it is a defilement, and the soul that eats of it shall be defiled and shall bear its sin.” So the sacrifice of the third day is rejected; and that the one of the day before is refused as well, he made clear when he said: “If you sacrifice a sacrifice as a vow of rejoicing to the Lord, you shall sacrifice it so as to be acceptable for you. It shall be eaten on that same day; none of the flesh shall be left until morning. I am the Lord. He shall bear the sin.”
Then what would be the meaning of these things too?

The law has already shown us many times in what came before that it is the custom of Holy Scripture to divide the whole of time sometimes into two periods, the one in which the law was in force and the one in which Christ shone forth; and sometimes into three, with another period inserted and placed between them, the one in which the choir of the holy prophets shone forth. Yet both in the time of Moses and in that of the holy prophets the manner of worship was the same, still, as it were, among the shadows of the law. But when morning came, that is, when the third period was revealed in its turn, and the spiritual light, which is Christ, flashed round all that is under the sun, and the ancient mist was at last dispersed, then the manner of worship of that former time was no longer acceptable. Whether it be yesterday's fat or sacrifice or that of the third day, it is no longer acceptable, but abominable and rejected before God, and counted as defilement for those who choose to offer it out of season. Or do you not say that it is true that, now that Christ illumines the souls of the saints with the teachings of the gospel and initiates them so well into spiritual worship, the things in the law have become in some way superfluous and useless?

I do. For I will call to mind the divine Paul, who called the boasts of the law refuse and loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ. And I hear him writing to certain people: “I tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to us.”

You are right. Therefore, now that Christ has been revealed and the time of the law and the prophets has passed, it is sin and defilement to cling to a worship carried on as in shadows, and to try to bring God a sheep, or fat, or frankincense; all the more since the Son plainly says to God the Father: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come—in the scroll of the book it is written of me—to do your will, O God.’” For the Son, by offering himself up for us as a spotless victim, put a stop to the things of the law, which could not take away sins; for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets.
Well said.

So after the perfection accomplished in Christ, the Father cannot be approached through the worship of the law, but can be approached through the Son alone. That is why he said: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” That everything not in Christ is unfit for sacrifice and imperfect, while what is through him and in him is acceptable and most holy, may also be made clear from what the law says. In Exodus it says: “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother's milk”; and in Leviticus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When a calf or a sheep or a goat is born, it shall be seven days under its mother. On the eighth day and after, it shall be accepted as a gift, a burnt offering to the Lord. And whether calf or sheep, you shall not slaughter it and its young on the same day.” So he does not allow a newborn lamb, still at the breast, to be slaughtered, showing that what is still imperfect, and as it were small and weak in understanding, is not yet holy, and for that reason still unacceptable to God. Such were certain unwise and small-minded people to whom the divine Paul writes: “For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the first elements of the oracles of God; you have come to need milk, not solid food. But solid food is for the mature.” What is still at the milk and under the breast is therefore imperfect—I mean in understanding and spiritual strength. But let our discussion of these things proceed, as from a type, from things that are perceptible and plain to the senses to things that are beyond sense and grasped by the mind; and you will understand very well that all things have come to be in Christ, both in perfection and in acceptance. For he says that the animals brought and dedicated to God must be seven days under the mother, but on the eighth day and after they will be a gift and a burnt offering to God.
What you say is not very clear.
Do you not say that the eighth day is the day of the Saviour's resurrection, and as it were the beginning of a new age, once the age of the law, which is like the first seven days, has passed by?
I do.

Then what belongs, as it were, to the time of the law, that is, what consists in fleshly worship, is still unholy and unfit to be offered; but everything that is now in Christ, on the eighth day and after, is a gift and well-pleasing to God. For the calling in Christ is unending, and has the resurrection as its beginning. Knowing this, the Son himself said at one time, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself,” and at another, “Truly I tell you, unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
You are right. But what, again, would be the meaning of the rule that a mother must not perish together with her young on the same day?

When he had legislated so well concerning Christ, and had gracefully foretold the perfection that would come through him, he, being God, was not unaware of the disobedience of the Jews and the stubbornness of Jerusalem. He knew that for this reason the people of Israel would be destroyed as murderers of the Lord who had raged savagely against the Son; and yet Jerusalem would not perish utterly, root and all, but would remain, as it were, bereft of her children, awaiting the last time, at the end, when she too will be saved, running behind the nations. For she has been set at the back, that is, behind, as the Psalmist says: “For he will put them at the back.” For all Israel will be saved, once the flock from the nations has first been folded in the divine pens. So the law does not allow destruction to take place as a final and total annihilation, foreshowing that the wrath against the disobedient is tempered with gentleness, and at the same time, I think, laying the matter down as a kind of type of a necessary truth. For the things that exist will by no means pass into nothing, overpowered by unmitigated corruption, but will endure, as it were, by succession, this one preserved in that one and perhaps that one in this, according to kinship or likeness of kind, since God wards off the total destruction of his own creatures. For he created all things that they might exist, and the generations of the world are wholesome, as it is written. It was fitting, moreover, that such things should be foretold and indeed declared among the teachings about Christ, through whom and in whom what was corrupted is saved, and what was in the grip of death has blossomed again into life. For the root of the human race died like a mother, as in Adam; but those who came from it, that is, we ourselves, have blossomed again in Christ, and we exist and are saved, having him as our life and as a second root, as it were, of our race.
How well and how carefully refined this account is!

It is worth adding to what has been said, Palladius, this passage: “You shall not plant a grove for yourself; you shall not make for yourself any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God; you shall not set up a pillar for yourself, things which the Lord your God hates.” See how he removes the worshipper of the truth completely from the deceit that belongs to idols. He by no means permits him to make use of the customs of the Greeks, but urges that he must shake off their practices, even if they contain nothing harmful, and even if they should come about by chance.
What do you mean?

The Greeks would seize on the most flourishing trees and woods thick with foliage all around, and set up altars and sacrifices to the demons there. For it was necessary, yes, necessary, that the altars of demons should have set beside them something to draw the mind away, as it were, as well as worldly delights. Falsehood suffers from an inherent feebleness, but is often beautified with borrowed adornments, just as the indecencies of loose women are. But what need had the divine altar, flashing with the beauty of truth, of outside aids or idle adornments? The divine is not approached through worldly delight, nor by a mind that is somehow slack and attached to fleshly things, but by a sober understanding that looks intently upward and into the heavens. If a divine altar did happen to stand somewhere under trees, as though it had come about by chance, the fact would do no harm at all to the steadfast and genuine worshipper of the Saviour. But since the practice is entirely Greek, we must refuse to imitate it or to resemble their custom. In the same way, for the faithful mind that stands firm in true knowledge, an idol is nothing in the world, and neither is food offered to idols anything; yet it is not permitted to eat it, since another enjoins abstaining for the sake of the conscience of the weaker: “For why am I judged by another's conscience? If I partake with thanks, why am I denounced over that for which I give thanks?” So it is well-pleasing to God, I mean, to refuse to act as the Greeks do, both in the placing of altars and in the customs and manners of worship.
I agree.

That we must bear fruit for the glory of God, and not go into the holy tabernacle with empty hands, the sacred Scripture again made clear to us in Numbers, where it runs thus: “And it came to pass on the day when Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, he anointed it and consecrated it and all its utensils, and the altar and all its utensils; he anointed them and consecrated them. And the leaders of Israel brought offerings, twelve leaders of their fathers' houses. These were the leaders of the tribes, those who presided over the census. And they brought their gift before the Lord: six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon from every two leaders and a calf from each one. And they brought them before the tabernacle. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take these from them, and they shall be used for the service of the tabernacle of witness; and you shall give them to the Levites, to each according to his service. And Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites.” Nor did the gifts of the tribal leaders stop there; others were brought as well. For it is written: “And the leaders brought offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day he anointed it, and the leaders brought their gifts before the altar. And the Lord said to Moses: One leader each day, a leader each day, shall bring their gifts for the dedication of the altar. And the one who brought his gift on the first day was Nahshon son of Amminadab, leader of the tribe of Judah. And he brought his gift: one silver dish, its weight a hundred and thirty; one silver bowl of seventy shekels by the holy shekel, both full of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; one golden censer of ten shekels, full of incense; one bull calf from the herd, one ram, one yearling lamb for a whole burnt offering; and one male goat for a sin offering; and for a sacrifice of deliverance, two heifers, five rams, five he-goats, five yearling ewe lambs. This was the gift of Nahshon son of Amminadab.” The others too brought their offerings in turn, up to the twelfth, in the same way and with equal generosity, each being assigned the particular day appointed for him; for so God had prescribed.
And what, then, is the meaning of so varied an offering?

The matter is, of course, a bringing of fruit, Palladius; but woven into it, I think, is a mystical meaning as well, which carries the riddle up to Emmanuel and to ourselves. I will explain it again as best I can. Since the holy and true tabernacle, that is, the Church, has been revealed in this world, Christ, shining forth in it in many ways, is offered, one might almost say, by us and on our behalf as a holy sacrifice to God the Father, a ransom and an exchange for the life of all, the one who is worth all. For since the Only-begotten became man as one of us, he offered himself to God the Father as a kind of first fruits and firstling of human nature, fragrant with holiness—a holiness that belongs to him naturally and essentially, insofar as he is understood to be and is God, but that he holds as something brought in from outside because of his humanity. Though he himself is one, he was depicted in many ways, as in the offering of the leaders; and Christ is still sacrificed now, as it were, through those who preside in each age, understood in many ways and honoured with various names. And there was an offering each day, the matter hinting at the unfailing and, so to speak, unceasing character of Christ's sacrifice on every day, and at the fruit borne in it by those justified in faith. For worshippers will not fail, nor will there be any lack of gifts brought; Christ will be offered by us and for us, sacrificed mystically in the holy tabernacles. He himself is our first and choicest fruit-offering. For he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, not for himself, according to the blameless account of the matter, but rather for us who are under the yoke and the indictment of sin. And in likeness to him we too are holy sacrifices, dying to the world, since sin has been put to death in us, but living to God the life of holiness and piety. This is what the offering of the leaders seems to suggest to us. Would you like us to examine it piece by piece with fitting reasoning and discuss it as far as we are able, so that it may be clear to us?
Very much so.

From each leader, then, a calf was brought, and the wagons, six in number, were allotted to the sacred work of the holy tabernacle. Then from each came one silver dish and one bowl, both, it says, full of fine flour mixed with oil; one censer full of incense; one ram; one yearling lamb for a whole burnt offering; and a male goat for a sin offering. These were the whole burnt offerings. And for a sacrifice of deliverance, it says, they also brought two heifers, five rams, five he-goats and five yearling ewe lambs.
Explain, then, before anything else, what distinguishes them, and what one would say is the difference between the sacrifice of deliverance and the whole burnt offering.

Listen, then. In the whole burnt offerings the animals were consumed whole and entire by holy and unquenchable fire. No part at all was removed; every part and limb, as it were, went up to God as a fragrant aroma. But the animals slaughtered for the sacrifice of deliverance received only a partial consecration, in the right shoulder, the head and the feet, the kidneys and the liver, and certain other inner parts and entrails. It befits Christ, then, to be wholly burnt, for he is truly holy throughout, entirely fragrant and sacred. But what is proper to us is to be not entirely holy and not wholly sacred, since there is some defilement in us because of the sin that is in us. For no one is clean from filth, and “Who can discern his transgressions?” as it is written. For this reason the law very rightly commanded that the sacrifice of deliverance should not be burnt whole, but consecrated only in part. Is this account clear to you, then, Palladius, and sufficient for you to understand easily?
Very much so.
Come, then, let us go on to the next point: to say something, I mean, about each of the things offered, and also to understand what we need to know for our benefit.
Go on, then.

Each of the tribal leaders, then, offered one silver dish and one bowl, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The dish serves for food and is used for eating dainties, as the Saviour himself showed when John, his true disciple, was eager to learn who would betray him: "He who has dipped his hand with me in the dish," he said. As for the bowl, why should I describe its use, when the thing proclaims it so plainly? Fine flour is a sign of bread, since bread is made from it, and the bread of life is Christ. So, as in the dish and in the bowl, and as in the bread contained in both (for both were full of fine flour), and so as in food and drink, Christ is signified as life and as the giver of life. "Truly I tell you," he says, "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." Scripture says that the flour was soaked with oil, as though the type were singing out the words of the Psalms: "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." The censer, in turn, had the shape and form of an incense-burner and was made like one, and it too was full of incense. For Christ is fragrance and a censer. He does not have his fragrance from outside, as we do, who gain our share in such things by participation in virtue and in the sanctification that comes through godliness. Rather, as God, he possesses in his own nature, from within himself, the riches for which he is admired, and he fills the whole world with a fragrance that is above the world and above creation. For he is God by nature and in truth, and he is very well known to have by his own nature the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father. So the censer is full of incense. Along with these a calf and a ram were brought, and also a lamb and a kid from the goats, offered in addition to the rest; and through all of them the one signified is Christ himself. In the calf he is signified because of its great strength, and because among the tame and clean animals the calf is the foremost and the largest in bodily size; and in spiritual pre-eminence everything belonging to Christ excels, and he himself is foremost and stands above all, with a superiority beyond comparison in every respect. In the ram he is signified because of its perfection; and in the lamb, because of its innocence: "I was like an innocent lamb led to the slaughter," he says, "and I did not know it." In the kid he is signified because of his slaughter on behalf of sinners. For under the Law the sacrifice for sin is a kid; and Emmanuel entered into death for our sake, and we have been redeemed from our ancient offences through the slaughter he endured for us. Or do you say that this too is not true?
How could it not be?

Notice that the calves were brought, but were then given over to the work of the tabernacle, so that during the journeys they might carry it on wagons and spare the priests toil and hardship. For the Church rests upon Christ, and he carries us, not allowing the holy and honoured race, the people skilled in holy works, to fall into labours beyond their strength. This, then, is how the things named are to be referred to Christ. But the animals for the peace offering the leaders brought as though in place of themselves, in a sense consecrating themselves to the holy tabernacle and offering themselves up to God as a fragrant aroma. There were two heifers, five rams, five goats and five ewe lambs. The calf is Christ, and the heifers are we; and the reasoning that applies to both is not out of keeping, but rather true and clear. For the male is always in some way the leading element, held in honour and the highest glory before God, and nature bears witness, confirming the fact. The female is lesser and subordinate, and comes, as it were, behind the strength and glory of the males. So in the male calf Christ is our leader, while we are yoked under him, as it were, far inferior to him in strength and glory, and the gap between us is beyond comparison. For although he became like us (the heifer is of the same kind as the calf), what is his is far, far superior. "Who among the sons of God will be likened to God?" For Christ is at once like us and above us in the pre-eminence of his Godhead, even though he became flesh. There are two heifers, as a type, I think, of the two peoples who have come together into one through him who comes from both and who, through faith, joins them in spiritual unity, the one who is both for us and with us. The rams and the lambs, again, are equal in number, and the kids are no fewer; they indicate the multitude of believers gathered, I mean, in the fifth period, the time of the coming of him who says, "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself." Through the rams is signified the perfection of believers in understanding and their full maturity of spiritual stature, plainly the stature that is in Christ; through the lambs, their simplicity and innocence: "Brothers," he says, "do not be children in your thinking; rather be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature." And through the kids offered for sin is signified our constant need of cleansing and of forgiveness for our offences. That is why we have been taught to say in our prayers, "Forgive us our trespasses."
