For there is no time when those who are truly sound of mind, and who know the weakness of human nature, need not cry out, "Who can discern his trespasses?" and "Cleanse me from my hidden faults." This is a spiritual sacrifice, sending up a fragrant aroma to God for the salvation of our souls.
True.

I said, then, that Christ is signified in the calf, the rams, the lambs, the goats and the rest, and I would not think this account of the matter falls short of what is fitting. But if anyone should choose to transfer the force of these ideas to ourselves as well, there is nothing wrong with applying some such interpretation as this to the passage before us.
What sort of interpretation do you mean?

Under the Law the holy sacrifices were brought by all Israel. The blood of the slaughtered animals was poured out at the divine altar, the action all but depicting, as in a shadow, and indirectly indicating to us, that we ought to consecrate our own souls to the holy God.
Well said.
So the sacrifices were in place of us and on our behalf, and it is we who, in type, are offered in them.
True.

Come then, let us examine properly the offerings brought on behalf of all by the hands of the leaders, and contemplate the beauty of their spiritual meaning. What was offered, then, in silver vessels, that is, the dish and the bowl, was fine flour moistened with oil. Silver is a symbol of brightness, fine flour of life, since it is the source of bread, which sustains life, and oil of gladness. Let us too, then, offer to the God of all a life that is glad in its brightness, through hope in Christ. "Rejoicing in hope," says Scripture. How could those who keep the commandments of our Saviour, and who have cultivated an illustrious life and conduct, not be filled with the highest joy? For them a share in his glory is laid up with God, entirely and without fail. "For you have died," he says, "and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory." So the fine flour is soaked in oil. For the life of the saints holds the gladness that comes from the hope of glory, together, of course, with the brightness that consists in holiness and righteousness. The golden censer full of incense depicts the beauty of the saints, and the fragrance of holiness, as it were in chosen vessels, and then the truly most fragrant gift, as it were, offered to God. Or should we not think, Palladius, that the saints are bright and choice vessels?
Certainly we should.

A calf was offered by each leader, twelve in all. They carry the holy tabernacle, brought two to a wagon and under one yoke, and they are assigned to the service of the Levites. The thing may be a type of the two peoples, no longer divided by differences of doctrine and of life, but brought together and united under the one yoke of the Saviour, enduring and courageous. "Be strong," Scripture says, "and let your heart take courage, and wait for the Lord." The calf is an enduring and very strong animal. Such, surely, are those who have chosen godliness, bearing Christ upon themselves like a yoke, Christ who was prefigured in the holy tabernacle. The divine Paul called the Church his body. And it was said to Ananias about him, I mean about Paul: "Go, for this man is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before the Gentiles." Besides these, a ram and a lamb were offered, indicating the coming to God and, in a sense, the dedication (spiritual, of course) of both the older people and the new. For just as endurance and courage were signified in the calves, in the same way, I think, the sheep clearly show the meek fruitfulness of those justified through faith in Christ. For the animal is meek and also fruitful. Such are all who carefully practise the way of life of the Gospel, to whom Christ himself said, "Give to everyone who asks of you, and do not demand back your goods from one who takes them, and to him who strikes you on the cheek, turn the other also." And Paul too writes, "The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, correcting opponents with meekness." That the offering of a goat must follow the ones already mentioned would show nothing else, I think, than what I said a little while ago: that all, even those who are good in disposition, need the cleansing that comes through repentance and the forgiveness of their offences. Knowing this, the divine David said, "If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand?" So under the old Law the kid is the sacrifice for forgiveness. But now repentance and the plea for pardon are the sacrifice of those of us who approach God in spirit and in truth. "Declare your sins first," Scripture says, "so that you may be justified." And David sings somewhere, "I said, 'I will confess my sin against myself to the Lord,' and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart." Is the account of the leaders' gifts now clear to you?
Entirely so.

I think this too must be said: once the sacrifice had been brought by each and, as it were, on behalf of all, the divine words began to be spoken in the holy tabernacle to Moses, the revealer of sacred things. It is written thus again in Numbers: "This was the dedication of the altar, after he had filled his hands and after he had anointed it. When Moses went into the tent of witness to speak with him, he heard the voice of the Lord God speaking to him from above the mercy seat that is on the ark of the witness, between the two cherubim, and he spoke to him." For when the holy tabernacle had, so to speak, been completed, and the true sanctuary, which is the Church, had been revealed to the world, then indeed the voice of God the Father came to us. For he has spoken to us in the Son, whom we also call the propitiation for our sins, according to the Scriptures. The voice comes from above the cherubim, for God is above and beyond creation, possessing an essential and inherent superiority over all that has come into being. And the Son, the true mercy seat, conveying to us the voices from above and from the Father, said, "The words that I speak are not mine, but his who sent me." So the voice came from above the mercy seat. And you would be greatly amazed if you considered how the tribal leaders came forward. Each was assigned his own particular day on which he was to fulfil what had been ordered and bring his gift, and they came in an orderly way, as the lawgiver determined; yet not in the order of their birth, that is, by age, nor simply at random and in confusion, but rather arranged, as it were, according to a mystical design.
I really cannot grasp what you mean. Explain it to me clearly.
Shall we list Jacob's sons in order, one after another? That way the departure from it in the order of their approach will become very clear.
By all means.

Reuben, then, is the firstborn, and after him Simeon, Levi and Judah, from their mother Leah. Bilhah the maidservant bore Dan and Naphtali, and Zilpah, Leah's maid, bore Gad and Asher; and Leah, in addition to her other four, bore Issachar and Zebulun. Joseph and Benjamin were born of Rachel. So first come the four sons of Leah, the free woman: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah. From the two maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah, come four: Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. After these come four more: two from Leah, Issachar and Zebulun, and from Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin. We must remember that Joseph's portion was divided into two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, who were his sons.
I understand the order of the names perfectly well; now it is for you to explain what remains to be examined in them.

When they came forward with their gifts, Palladius, they did so not by age. First came Judah, though he was fourth in time; after him the ninth, Issachar, and with them the tenth, Zebulun. After these came a second group, as it were: Reuben the firstborn and the next, the second, Simeon. With them was joined Dan, the son of a slave woman. After these came the third rank, made up of three sons of free women: Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin. Last of all came a fourth group, those born of the maidservants. These again were three, Dan, Asher and Naphtali, although by time of birth they came before those placed ahead of them in rank, I mean Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin. Do you not agree that this needs examining?
Certainly; so try to tell me what the explanation is.

The thing is a kind of riddle, as I think once again. It means that what comes through Christ holds first place with God over what is under the Law, and that the first have been made last and the last first. For those older in time and therefore firstborn, that is, Israel, come behind the Gentiles. And those who have the spirit of slavery, the sons of the Jerusalem that is in slavery, will yield precedence in glory to the children of the free woman, who is the mother of us who have been justified in Christ and called to the dignity of freedom through the Spirit of freedom. Notice, if you will, the precision of these insights. The tribe of Judah brings its gift first, the tribe from which Christ sprang according to the flesh. Immediately after it come Issachar and Zebulun, both free and born of free parents. Then come Reuben the firstborn, Simeon, and Gad, who is the son of a slave woman. Through these Israel is signified. Come, let us state what applies to each, gathering it from the prophecy Jacob made about them. The inspired Jacob said, "Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the first of my children, hard to bear and hard and headstrong." And again: "Simeon and Levi are brothers; they carried out wrongdoing by their own choice. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let not my heart lean upon their assembly, for in their anger they killed men, and in their passion they hamstrung a bull. Cursed be their anger, for it was headstrong, and their wrath, for it was hardened." And about Gad he said this: "A band of raiders shall raid him, and he shall raid them at their heels." So in Reuben Israel might fittingly be signified, the firstborn in time, but hard, headstrong and insolent. In Simeon, with whom Levi is joined, Israel is signified as ready for murder, as having killed the saints ("Which of the prophets did your fathers not kill?" he says), and as having, so to speak, hamstrung the bull, who is Christ. For it is not the Jewish people alone that is caught in the act of daring these outrages against the saints and against Christ; Levi too joined with them, that is, the priestly race, those who attend upon the altar, the scribes and Pharisees. That is why, in the prophecies of the patriarch Jacob, Levi is yoked together with Simeon. In Gad, the son of a slave woman and a band of raiders, Israel is signified as base-born in disposition, tempting Jesus and laying snares to do him harm; for they came to him saying, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?" So (to bring the discussion back to where it began) Israel, the firstborn in time, hard, headstrong and insolent, quick to murder, with an accursed wrath, who killed men and hamstrung the bull, base-born and bitter in deceit, laying snares and acting as a band of raiders, has been placed behind those who are in Christ and free; and even if he is free, he comes after us, scarcely coming into the sight of God.
Well said.

You may learn the meaning of what I say by paying attention to what follows as well. Three came next, one after another, bringing their gifts, the sons of the free woman Rachel: Ephraim and Manasseh [?]. Then, after them, came three more, one after another, those born of the maidservants, I mean again Dan, Asher and Naphtali. You see, then, that those born of the free woman enter first and are greatly honoured, while those born of the maidservants follow. Is this not plainly what the inspired Paul himself writes to us? "When the full number of the Gentiles has come in," he says, "then all Israel will be saved."
You are right; the observation is very subtle.

And you will very easily recognise that the matter is not false. For the text immediately confirms it for us from other ideas as well. God laid down that the journeys of the children of Israel, and also their encampments, that is, their camping together, should be carried out in proper order, and he expressly commanded them to go around the tabernacle, in keeping, I think, with what the blessed David elegantly sings: "And I will go around your altar, Lord, to hear the voice of your praise," or again, "I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of jubilation." Something else, too, is hinted at by what they were commanded to do as a type. For we must not separate ourselves from God, but be seen standing near him, as it were, and around him, with no sin coming between, no worldly pleasure keeping us apart, but with an upright disposition of mind and a readiness for everything admirable gathering us into spiritual unity. And it is especially fitting for those who have chosen to win approval in this way to bear fruit. For it is written, "All who are around him will bring gifts." So he commanded them to set out together with the tabernacle and to march around it, and again in an order that was not suited to their ages, nor running without confusion from the first to the last, but grouped and arranged in divisions just as in the bringing of the gifts. It is written thus in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, 'Let the children of Israel encamp before the Lord, each man keeping to his own rank and under the standards of their fathers' houses; the children of Israel shall encamp around the tent of witness.'" Then he shows the place assigned to each: where and how they encamped, and who they were. For he continues thus: "And those who encamp first, toward the east, shall be the division of the camp of Judah with their host, and next to them shall encamp the tribe of Issachar, and next to them shall encamp the tribe of Zebulun." Then he mentions the second group and says: "The division of the camp of Reuben toward the south with their host, and the leader of the sons of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur; his host, those numbered, forty-six thousand five hundred. And next to him shall encamp the tribe of Simeon, and next to him shall encamp the tribe of Gad." And he at once adds a third, saying: "The division of the camp of Ephraim toward the sea with their host, and next to them shall encamp the tribe of Benjamin." And he at once mentions a fourth group as well, saying: "The division of the camp of Dan toward the north with their host; and next to him shall encamp the tribe of Asher, and next to him shall encamp the tribe of Naphtali. All those numbered of the camp of Dan," he says, "are one hundred and fifty-seven thousand six hundred; they shall set out last, according to their divisions." Do you see that Judah and those with him are placed first and have the choice position toward the dawn and the south? For those who are in Christ are in the light and fervent in spirit. Reuben and those with him are second. Third, again, come the sons of the free woman. Then after these come three others, the sons of the maidservants, of whom it is said, "They shall set out last." Is it not plain and in no way doubtful that the second has been honoured above the firstborn and called in before him, that is, those who are in Christ; and that those who are free through faith have been honoured above those born of slavery? For the one group leads because of Christ, who came from Judah; the other scarcely comes behind and has been placed, as it were, in the second rank.
Very rightly said; and I would praise you for such subtle insight.
On the priesthood, and that the priesthood under the law was a type of the priesthood in Christ.

We have now given a quite sufficient account of the tabernacle and of the oracles delivered about it, elegantly refined into spiritual subtlety. It would be fitting, as it seems to me (and I know you will agree), to turn now to the prerogatives of the priesthood, and to show how the priesthood in type and under the law signifies the true priesthood: the one that, in Christ and through him, sanctifies the holy race. By this I mean, once more, those who have been made radiant in faith and enriched with closeness to God through sharing in the Holy Spirit.
It would indeed be fitting, and very reasonably so.

When the holy tabernacle had been completed in fitting order and given the form shown to the divine Moses on the mountain, God proceeded to appoint the priests, and said: "And you, bring near to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons from among the sons of Israel to serve me as priests: Aaron, and Nadab and Abihu, and Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron." So the chosen were called by name to the sacred ministry. For "no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God," as it is written. Let no one, then, take up God's priesthood on his own initiative. Let him wait for a call. If he tries to seize what he has not been granted by the decrees from above, he will suffer the punishment of Dathan and Abiram. And do not be surprised that taking it on oneself is out of place and unseemly for us, since Paul writes even about Christ himself: "He did not glorify himself in becoming high priest, but was appointed by the one who said to him, 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.'" So the words wisely spoken to Moses, "And you, bring near to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons," would again be an image of the call that is spoken of in Christ's case. For what else does "bring near" mean but "make your own" and "summon"? Christ was called, as it were, to be high priest by the counsel of the Father. And in a certain sense the divine disciples were called along with him and appointed his fellow workers in the sacred ministry. That is why they said plainly, "For we are God's fellow workers." And they travelled the whole earth under the sun, ministering the gospel of Christ as priests among the nations. They were called to apostleship through Christ, and that statement is true. But the matter was surely also willed by the Father, since there is one decree governing everything that is done, because the Son is the counsel and wisdom and will of the Father. So Aaron would be a type of Christ, and a kind of advance showing of the priesthood understood in spirit and in truth, though still in rather dim shadows. Notice that Moses is commanded to bring Aaron near to himself. For the law is somehow weak and imperfect if it is cut off from Christ. "For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins." But Christ, by offering one sacrifice for sinners, "has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified." Let those who still love the shadow and the letter, and who set great store by the commandments of Moses, know this: unless they bring near to themselves the high priest and apostle of our confession, Jesus Christ, their zeal for worship in types will come to nothing. For what could the boasts of a life under the law be worth before God, who loves virtue? This is why the most wise Paul says that, because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ, he counts the things of the world as refuse and has chosen spiritual things instead. And this, spiritually understood, is what it means to bring Aaron himself near to oneself.
I understand what you are saying; the argument is clear.

"Bring near to yourself, then," he says, "Aaron your brother." I think he says this in another sense as well, knowing that it contributes a good deal to our profit in spiritual understanding. Mark what I mean. Moses was sent to bring Israel out of their misery in Egypt. Then, seeing that the undertaking far surpassed human power and lay beyond the strength and eloquence he had, he pleaded: "Look, I have not been eloquent, not yesterday, not the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant. I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." God answered: "Who gave man a mouth? Who made the deaf and the mute, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth." Still overwhelmed by the greatness of the deeds required of him, he grew afraid again and said, "I beg you, Lord, appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send." Then God at once appointed Aaron, as a type of Christ, who knows how to accomplish all things with ease. Israel was redeemed in no other way than by Christ being given, in the image of Aaron, as a fellow worker to Moses' halting speech and weakness. You should understand the present passage the same way. Perfecting the weakness of the law in Christ, he brought Aaron into the priesthood and joined him profitably to blessed Moses. For the law would not have been enough for redemption, nor could it perfect the redeemed in sanctification. Christ, however, is redemption and sanctification, with the saints working alongside him, just as Moses worked with Aaron in Egypt at that time, and Aaron's sons with Aaron himself. In a spiritual sense the divine disciples also worked with Christ, the high priest and leader of all. He was able to accomplish everything, and they did not join in as though helping someone weak. They did so as men called to service and chosen for their excellence, and they received from him strength for every task. The divine Paul will bear witness to this when he says, "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me."
So Aaron and the others were chosen and called by name to the sacred ministry.

In addition to this, he laid down that splendid garments befitting the priesthood be made for them, saying: "And you shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honor and glory. And speak to all who are wise in understanding, whom I have filled with a spirit of perception, and they shall make the holy robe for Aaron for the sanctuary, in which he will serve me as priest." Now the most wise Paul advises those justified by faith that they must put on the robe that is truly holy and comes from heaven. He writes: "Put on our Lord Jesus Christ." The prophet Isaiah proclaimed this in advance, speaking as though in the person of the Church: "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness." So the garment that truly brings honor and glory to the sacred and holy race is Christ, a splendid and more than earthly adornment for the souls of the saints. "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ," he says, and the saying is true. But the law adorns Aaron as if in shadows, pointing the glory of his varied vesture toward Christ. A mystical and precise meaning is found practically woven into the making of the handiwork, hinting in riddles at the Savior's glory. See how he says that the craftsmen of the garments were filled with understanding from God, who guided them to richly flowered embroidery and inscribed the glory of Christ on the vestments. The items crafted are the breastpiece and the ephod, the full-length robe, the fringed tunic, the turban and the sash, and others besides, which we will discuss one by one as far as we can. Of the materials taken for the work he said: "And they shall take the gold, and the blue, and the purple, and the scarlet, and the fine linen." Now apply your mind closely once again to the matter before us, and first of all consider this.
What do you mean?
Were not all the things in the tabernacle made of gold and fine linen, of purple and spun scarlet, and of blue as well? And was this not as a type of Christ?
That is so.

Notice, then, that the robe of the one who held first place in the priesthood was made from the same materials, and that it too carried the glory of Christ within it as in an image and in types. The same meanings, and no different knowledge, signify the beauty of Christ. He is known as God, as in the gold. He is known as possessing royal dignity, as in the purple. He is known as the subtle and incorporeal Word, as in the fine linen. He is known as in the scarlet because of the flesh. And he is known in the air-colored blue, for that is the color of hyacinth, because he is from above and from heaven. For is not the Word who is from God the Father both God and king at once?
Of course.
And though he is the subtle and incorporeal Word of the Father, did he not come to be in the flesh? And is he not from above?
True.

So, viewed with subtle contemplation, the materials of the vestments are exactly the same as those of the things made in the holy tabernacle. So much for that. Now it is time to speak of the things woven in various ways for Aaron, for honor and glory. "And they shall make," he says, "the ephod of spun fine linen, the woven work of an embroiderer. It shall have two shoulder pieces joining it, fastened to each other at its two sides. And the woven band of the shoulder pieces, which is upon it, shall be of the same workmanship, of gold and blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen." Having assigned the material already mentioned to the woven pieces, he immediately adds: "And you shall take the two stones, emerald stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel: six names on the one stone, and the remaining six names on the second stone, in the order of their birth, the work of the stone-carver's craft. You shall engrave the stones with the names of the sons of Israel, as one engraves a seal. And you shall set the two stones on the shoulders of the ephod. The stones are a memorial for the sons of Israel."
The meaning of these contemplations seems to be deep. But first try to explain what the so-called ephod is, and how it might have been made.

He commanded that a woven piece be made, shaped like a tunic and reaching down to the chest. It was to be worn over the inner garments that lay next to the skin and reached to the feet, so that, flashing with the radiance of gold and purple, it would awaken in the eyes of those who saw it a sense of awe and holy wonder. He called this the ephod, that is, the "shoulder-piece," because, I think, the garment was short and barely stretched across both shoulders. He clearly prescribed that two stones, emeralds, were to be fixed onto this ephod, bound very tightly with fine threads, and that the names of the tribes were to be skillfully engraved on them, six on each stone. He himself made the reason for this clear to us, saying: "And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel before the Lord on his two shoulders, as a memorial concerning them."
And what shall we think is signified, in turn, by the stones and by what is on them?

Listen, then. The emerald is a pale stone. A brightness swims in its depths, and light seems mingled with darkness, each pulling against the other for the victory. Now, Palladius, when the bodily eye looks up on high and gazes deep into the ether and the heaven, does it not meet with just such a sight? For the uppermost ether is pale, and somehow dark in its depths, and mingled with a moderate light.
That is so.

Holy Scripture, then, makes the stone an image of heaven. And do not be surprised that it also compares heaven to sapphire. For the sapphire is pale and not far from the appearance of the emerald. It is written thus in Exodus: "And Moses went up, and Aaron, and Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And they saw the place where the God of Israel stood, and what was under his feet was like a work of sapphire stone, and like the appearance of the firmament of heaven in its purity." When the Israelites were in Egypt they had worshiped the creation and called the heaven a god. So the Lord of all, to their benefit, appeared to them standing on the firmament itself, so that they might know that he has all things under his feet and, as their creator, is master even of the heavens. Do you see, then, that Holy Scripture makes the stone, which is pale in moderate light, a kind of type and image of heaven? For by nature it gleams dark blue.
Excellently said.

The emerald, then, is a sign of heaven. Israel is written on it tribe by tribe, and it has its place on the ephod. From this we may understand that those who have been enrolled in heaven will wholly and in every way rest upon Christ, who holds them as if on his shoulders and treats the good as his children. The divine Moses said something similar, adorning Israel with the care that comes from God: "As an eagle shelters its nest and yearns over its young, it spread its wings and received them, and took them up on its shoulders." And David too sings to every saint who dwells in the help of the Most High: "He will overshadow you with his shoulders," he says. By "shoulders" here I take him to mean the parts below the neck, at the shoulders, and not at all the back. So those who have been enrolled above will be lifted up on shoulders, as the prophet says, and taken up in his arms, like Ephraim of old. The Savior himself declared this enrollment glorious and admirable, surpassing the beauty of the divine gifts, when he said to the holy disciples: "Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven." He also says that what is inscribed on the stones will be a memorial for the sons of Israel before the Lord, who gazes on them, as it were, in Aaron. For God the Father receives us into remembrance in Christ, and in him we have become known to him and worthy of his regard, as if written in God's book.
Rightly said.

He commands that another adornment be added to this, saying: "And you shall make little shields of pure gold, mixed; and you shall make two fringes of pure gold mixed with flowers, plaited work; and you shall put the plaited fringes on the little shields, on their shoulder pieces at the front. And you shall make the oracle of judgments, the work of a weaver, in the style of the ephod. You shall make it of gold and blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen. You shall make it square; it shall be doubled, a span in length and a span in width. And you shall weave into it a setting of stones in four rows." Then, after listing the names of the stones, he adds: "And let the stones be twelve, according to the names of the sons of Israel, according to their names. Let them be engraved like seals, each with its name, for the twelve tribes." And a little further on: "And Aaron shall bear," he says, "the names of the sons of Israel on the oracle of judgment, on his breast, when he enters the sanctuary, as a memorial before the Lord God."
How deep the matter of the oracle is! Even the way it was made seems to me very hard to grasp.

Then we must set about it and come as close as we can to the truth, even if the steepness of the climb perhaps does not allow us to reach it fully. I would say that seeing very obscure things even in a mirror is better than the alternative, which is not understanding them at all. So I will explain as best I can and as I understand it. He commanded that two little shields be made of pure gold, wider than the circle of a coin but of the same shape, for a coin is round. Then he commanded two fringes of pure gold, mixed with flowers. By "fringes" we mean cords with a varied appearance, as of many colors, for by "flowers" he meant colors. They were of fine linen and purple, gold thread, blue as well, and scarlet yarn. In addition, he says that a square woven piece must be made, in the form of a cube, a span in size and equal on every side. Into it, he says, the twelve stones were to be firmly woven, set three by three so as to form four full rows, with the names of the tribes engraved on them. So the little shields hung from the ephod by golden, many-colored cords. They sat a little lower, though they seemed to be high up, on the shoulders themselves. They touched the chest and hung right over the breasts. And from the little shields, by other cords, the oracle of judgments hung firmly attached and seemed to float on the chest, with fringes hanging from it. To those who saw it the thing was a marvel, gleaming with stones and gold and gloriously worked in the rich colors of the other materials. This too was to be a remembrance for the sons of Israel before the Lord when Aaron entered the sanctuary. Is the shape of the work now as clear to you as it can be?
Very much so. But why is the piece called the "oracle of judgments"?
When we explained the origin of the name, did we not say that the upper piece was called the ephod, the "shoulder-piece," because it stretched over both shoulders?
Yes. What of it?

We say that, by a similar origin and on the same principle, the piece placed at the heart and inner parts was named the oracle (logion) of judgments. For the heart and inner parts are, as it were, the dwelling place of the reason (logikon) within us. And fixed and implanted by nature in our reason is the right and blameless judgment about each thing to be done: just judgment, in other words, and a sense of what fits each case. For is there not a faculty of reason in us that weighs the nature of the things to be done, and separates what is graceless and unprofitable from what is better?
Certainly.

Divinely inspired Scripture usually calls uprightness and just judgment "judgment." So the divine David sings: "Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times." And again he said somewhere: "And the honor of a king is to love judgment." For the honor and glory of a king who loves justice is splendid. So the oracle of judgment is the piece laid on the heart and breast, because it lies, as it were, in the seat of reason, where uprightness in justice resides. On it are twelve stones set in gold, inscribed with the names of the tribes. They would be a type of holy men, who are splendid and precious like choice stones, lying as it were in the mind and heart of Christ. For they are truly worthy of remembrance, because they shine in virtue and are precious in holiness. Golden fringes also hang from the oracle of judgments. This shows, I think, that the vast and countless swarm of noble deeds done by the multitude of the saints is seen, as it were, hanging from it. Indeed, blessed David says that the adornment of the Church too consists in fringes.
The argument is persuasive.

From the oracle of judgments, held fast by golden rings, a many-colored and richly hued cord runs upward, as we said. It passes through both little shields and reaches the very top of the ephod, where the stones of the enrollment are. Surely it is worth seeing what this means too. The riddle seems to me to point once more to something like this: the precious stones, which are in the knowledge and memory of Christ, run toward the enrollment above and win the prize through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. The divine Paul writes this plainly. And elsewhere he says: "Put on the whole armor of God." The king's weapons are golden, and the little shields are golden too, hinting in a riddle at the whole armor of God. So we shall be in God's memory and enrollment in no other way than by taking up the weapons of righteousness and advancing through them in practice. The oracle's being fastened to the ephod would signify, I think, that the things below are joined to the things above, with Christ as mediator. "For he is our peace, who has made the two one," as the Scriptures say, and he has bound humankind to the multitude of the holy angels with the bond of love. We should also note that blessed Ezekiel says the prince of Tyre was clothed with every precious stone, and he lists the very stones that the divine Moses says were set in the oracle of judgments. These were: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx. They were arranged three by three in four full rows. This arrangement sketches for us the steadfastness in faith of those who are in Christ's heart and memory. The grouping by threes is a symbol of faith, as in the Trinity, and the square, equal-sided shape is a symbol of steadfastness. For the oracle that held the twelve stones was made in this way.
I am persuaded.

Besides this, he also orders something else to be joined to the twelve stones, saying: “And you shall put on the oracle of judgment the Manifestation and the Truth, and it shall be on Aaron’s breast when he goes into the Holy Place before the Lord; and Aaron shall carry the judgments of the sons of Israel on his breast before the Lord continually.” He names a Manifestation and a Truth, but he does not go on to say clearly whether he ordered them to be stones, or writing as on a small tablet. I recall the prophet saying: “For the sons of Israel shall remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations.” But whether these too were stones, or the names were written as on a golden tablet, our discussion will not inquire too closely. We shall understand that they were put there as a type of Christ, who is present with the saints. For he says, “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the end of the age.” And Christ is Truth and Manifestation. For in him we have come to know the Father, and he has made manifest to us his good will, perfect and well-pleasing, as the Scriptures say. For Christ said somewhere: “I no longer call you servants; you are my friends, because everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you.” Emmanuel is Truth in another sense as well: he alone is Son by nature and, as God from God, alone holy and alone Lord, while the creation is what he is understood to be only by participation and imitation. So Christ, understood as Manifestation and Truth, is present with the saints. He also brings our affairs before the face of the Father, since he always lives to intercede for us. This, I think, is the meaning of “And Aaron shall carry the judgments of the sons of Israel before the Lord on his breast continually.”
True.

He also orders that a sacred and admirable garment be made, saying: “And you shall make an undertunic reaching to the feet, all of blue. Its opening shall be in the middle, with a border around the opening, the work of a weaver, its joining woven of one piece with it, so that it may not be torn. And on the hem of the undertunic below you shall make pomegranates like those of a pomegranate tree in bloom, of blue, purple, spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, around the hem of the undertunic. The pomegranates shall all be of the same form, and there shall be golden bells between them all around: beside each pomegranate a golden bell and a flower, around the hem of the undertunic. And when Aaron ministers his sound shall be heard as he goes into the Holy Place before the Lord and as he comes out, so that he may not die.” By “an undertunic reaching to the feet” he plainly means a long tunic, well suited to covering the body, running from the neck down to the very feet. It is of blue because it is a symbol of the incorruption from above, that is, of Christ. The inspired David proclaimed something of this kind long beforehand when he said, as if in the person of God, concerning those who perform the sacred rites in the churches: “Her priests I will clothe with salvation.” And the wise Paul writes to us: “Put on our Lord Jesus Christ.” This, I think, is our dwelling from heaven, which we long to put on, the tunic of gladness, the garment of salvation, as the prophet puts it. And the blue color has clearly been said to be a type of heaven. This interpretation is true with regard to ourselves, for we have been clothed with the incorruption from above. But if Christ himself is understood to wear the undertunic reaching to the feet, as in the person of Aaron, the interpretation is no less true for us. For since the Only-begotten is God by nature, he makes his own body incorruptible, and by clothing it with the life from above he set it entirely beyond the greed of death. That incorruption and life are in Christ by nature and not by participation, you will understand from this as well. Since he is God by nature, he said, “I am the resurrection and the life.” Yet as one who receives life in his humanity he says, “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.” So even if it is Christ himself who is understood to be said to be clothed with the incorruption from above, the interpretation would not fall short of what is fitting. On the lower parts, then, pomegranates and bells alternate with one another: the pomegranates woven in, the bells of gold, so that they might ring out truly well and make Aaron’s entrance most conspicuous whenever he hastened into the Holy of Holies. This too is a symbol of the saving and wise dispensation, I mean of the divine preaching of the Gospel, which resounds, as it were, through every city, now that our great High Priest, the spotless sacrifice, has entered the Holy of Holies for our sake, having obtained eternal redemption. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified. The riddle is not obscure: the golden bells stand for the saving preaching, and the pomegranates for cities.
In what way?

A city is enclosed on the outside by a single wall, yet holds within itself countless households. In the same way, I think, the pomegranate is girded on the outside by a single rind, while inside the seeds are walled off from one another by thin membranes and are all but gathered into households. Is that not so?
I agree.

So there is a bell beside each pomegranate, for there is a teacher in each city who, by the ringing and clear sound of the divine doctrines, makes our Savior’s entry into the Holy of Holies plain to all. And the threat of death hangs over those appointed to minister, that is, over Aaron, in the holy tabernacle, if the ringing of the bells does not resound loudly all around. For silence is a dangerous thing for teachers. This is clearly what Paul said: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel!”
So it seems; your judgment is quite right.

Besides this, he says: “And you shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a seal, ‘Consecration to the Lord,’ and you shall fasten it on a cord of twisted blue. It shall be on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things which the sons of Israel consecrate, of every gift of their holy things. And it shall be on Aaron’s forehead continually, so that they may be acceptable before the Lord.” The turban, then, is of blue and the plate of gold. The engraving and the writing on it are the mystery of Christ and a clear prophecy of his mission into this world. For it says, “Consecration to the Lord.” Did not Emmanuel plainly say that he had been consecrated by God the Father?

Yes. I remember him saying to the Jews: “If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

When the Son says that he has been consecrated by God the Father, he means, as it were, that he has been appointed and sent. So “Consecration of the Lord” means his manifestation and mission into this world, but for kingship and glory. For that is how he perfects Aaron, by placing the golden band on his forehead. Christ is Lord and King of all, both by nature and by participation. For being God by nature he emptied himself, coming down into the form of a servant; and he receives kingship in a manner befitting his human state, although from above and from the beginning he sits beside God the Father, ruling all things with him and sharing his lordship. Notice how his turban was made of blue and bears the splendid emblem of kingship, I mean the golden plate. Blue is a sign of heaven; and remember that Christ says, “My kingdom is not of this world.” For Christ is not an earthly king but a heavenly one, who has the whole creation under his feet. And by adding, “And Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things which they consecrate, of every gift of their holy things,” he has clearly shown that all access to God and all perfection are in Christ, and indeed that all justification is in him and through him, together with the putting away of former offenses. For he takes away our sins, and through him we have become acceptable as we bring our spiritual offerings to God the Father.
Well said.

Showing very well that our Savior’s kingship can never be laid aside but is everlasting and extends to endless ages, he says concerning the plate on the turban: “And it shall be on Aaron’s forehead continually.” Where, then, will the brazen and senseless argument of the unholy heretics go, who have babbled that the power of Christ will one day come to an end, and that Emmanuel will hand over the kingdom to God the Father and withdraw from the seats of the Godhead? They pride themselves on such dreadful and worthless doctrines, and to them it is fitting to say: “You are in error, because you do not know the Scriptures.” For look: while God the Father clearly and plainly crowns Aaron with everlasting glory and honor and with the emblems of kingship, they strip him of his crown and all but snatch the sacred turban from the forehead it adorns.
True.

“You shall make a headdress and a sash of fine linen,” he says. Aaron’s attire is that of a soldier, a belt and a helmet, for the headdress has something of a helmet’s form. For Christ has fought for us “with a hidden hand,” as it is written, and “He has bent his bow and made it ready; he has made his arrows for those who burn,” and he has pulled down principalities, triumphed over powers, shaken dominions, and rescued those on earth who were held captive. That the war he waged was not visible or material, nor, so to speak, against flesh and blood, seems to be hinted at in a riddle by the fact that his military equipment, the headdress and the sash, was made only of fine linen, which is very slender. So by this sacred adornment he shows Aaron splendid and admirable. And he adds the command: “And for the sons of Aaron you shall make tunics and sashes, and you shall make headdresses for them, for honor and glory. And you shall put them on Aaron your brother and on his sons with him, and you shall anoint them and fill their hands and consecrate them, so that they may serve me as priests. And you shall make them linen breeches to cover the shame of their flesh; they shall reach from the loins to the thighs. And Aaron and his sons shall wear them whenever they go into the tent of witness or come near to minister at the altar of the Holy Place, so that they may not bring sin upon themselves and die. It is a perpetual ordinance for him and for his descendants after him.” You see that it befits the sons of Aaron too to be seen in military attire. For the whole priestly race is a fighting race; it knows how to campaign and do battle, not against flesh and blood, but to hold back profane sin, contending most openly and with reason for the doctrines of the truth, and taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ, as it is written. And they have linen breeches, which properly cover what is unsightly and unseemly about the thighs. For everything belonging to the saints is entirely dignified, and nothing unseemly is found in them. The linen placed on the parts of the body around the thighs indicates, in a way, that a cooling of the pleasures of the flesh is most fitting for the saints, for linen is cool. Heat toward the most loathsome desires is foreign to every holy person. There is another reason, too, why those who have been allotted the priesthood wear garments and breeches of linen. They must depart from dead works, and a symbol of deadness is what is taken, as it were, from a carcass, I mean from a sheep. So being clothed in linen, and not in woollen garments, again signifies in a type the putting away of dead works; and this is a holy and perpetual law. It will follow that those who neglect what is fitting, and the decorum most suited to them, must surely and utterly die. He has made this clear by saying, after he has stated what they must wear when they minister: “And they shall not bring sin upon themselves, so that they may not die.”
The law is a sure guide: it shows very well what is profitable for each person and makes clear the means by which he may be in the best state.

That is so. He adorns the sacred and chosen race with this kind of vestment, but he also sanctifies them in another way, still in shadow, it is true, yet in Christ. For it is written thus: “And these are the things you shall do for them: to consecrate them so that they may serve me as priests, you shall take one young bull from the herd and two unblemished rams, and unleavened loaves kneaded with oil and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. You shall make them of fine wheat flour. And you shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, together with the young bull and the two rams. And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the tent of witness and wash them with water. And taking the vestments, you shall clothe Aaron your brother with the tunic reaching to the feet, the ephod and the oracle, and you shall join the oracle to the ephod for him. And you shall set the turban on his head and put the plate, the consecration, on the turban. And you shall take some of the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him. And you shall bring his sons and clothe them with tunics, and gird them with sashes, and put the headdresses on them. And the priesthood shall be theirs, to serve me forever; and you shall consecrate the hands of Aaron and the hands of his sons.” He has commanded that a young bull and two rams, with wafers and loaves in a basket, be brought for sacrifice. But first he purifies them in another way, making the act, I think, a type of true sanctification. For after washing Aaron with water he clothes him in the holy vestment. We too, once we have been washed through holy baptism and have scrubbed away every kind of uncleanness, then and only then are enriched with the grace that comes from above and from heaven, receiving the tunic of gladness, in accordance with the words, “Put on our Lord Jesus Christ.” For our discussion has already shown that Christ was represented in many ways in Aaron’s adornment. He also anoints his head with holy oil. And David somewhere sings: “You have anointed my head with oil,” the oil signifying the joy in hope that the saints voice, that is, the gladdening visitation from above. For we who have believed have received mercy and are blessed by the Lord, our minds enriched by the bountiful supply of the Spirit; and the head is a type of the mind. In the same way the priests were sanctified: they were washed with water and anointed with oil, and, once anointed, they put on the sacred vestments and had their hands consecrated, so that they might now seem fit to perform the sacrifices purely and blamelessly from then on. We too, having first been sanctified, made splendid by the grace from above and anointed for spiritual perfection, now with confidence and, so to speak, with pure and all-holy hands, bring our offerings to God, clearly meaning spiritual ones. I think this is also what the blessed David means in the hymn he sings about everyone who goes up to the mountain of the Lord: “Innocent of hands and pure of heart.”
So it seems.

And he laid down how the sacrifices for the priests are to be performed, saying: “And you shall bring the calf to the doors of the tent of witness, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the calf before the Lord, by the doors of the tent of witness. And you shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, by the doors of the tent of witness. And you shall take some of the calf’s blood and put it on the two horns of the altar with your finger, and all the rest of the blood you shall pour out at the base of the altar. And you shall take all the fat that is on the belly, and the lobe on the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, and you shall place them on the altar. But the flesh of the calf, its hide and its dung you shall burn with fire outside the camp, for it is a sin offering. And you shall take one ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram. And you shall slaughter it, and taking the blood you shall pour it against the altar all around. And you shall cut the ram into pieces, limb by limb, and wash the entrails and the feet in water, and put them on the pieces together with the head. And you shall offer the whole ram on the altar as a whole burnt offering to the Lord, for a fragrant aroma; it is an offering of incense to the Lord. And you shall take the second ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram. And you shall slaughter it and take some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron’s right ear, on the tip of his right hand and on the tip of his right foot, and on the lobes of the right ears of his sons, on the tips of their right hands and on the tips of their right feet. And you shall take some of the blood from the altar and some of the anointing oil and sprinkle it on Aaron and on his vestments, and on his sons and on the vestments of his sons with him; and he and his vestments shall be consecrated, and his sons and the vestments of his sons. The blood of the ram you shall pour against the altar all around. And you shall take from the ram its fat, the fat covering the belly, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, and the right shoulder, for this is a consecration; and one loaf made with oil and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread set before the Lord. And you shall put all of these on the hands of Aaron and on the hands of his sons, and you shall set them apart as a portion set apart before the Lord. And you shall take them from their hands and offer them on the altar of burnt offering for a fragrant aroma before the Lord; it is an offering to the Lord. And you shall take the breast of the ram of consecration, which is Aaron’s, and set it apart as a portion set apart before the Lord, and it shall be your share. And you shall consecrate the breast set apart and the shoulder of the portion taken off, which has been set apart and taken off from the ram of consecration, from Aaron and from his sons. And it shall be a perpetual ordinance for Aaron and his sons from the sons of Israel; for this is a portion set apart, and it shall be a portion taken off from the sons of Israel, from the peace offerings of the sons of Israel, a portion taken off for the Lord.” And a little later: “And you shall take the ram of consecration and boil its flesh in a holy place. And Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram and the loaves in the basket by the doors of the tent of witness. They shall eat the things by which they were consecrated, to consecrate their hands and to sanctify them; and no stranger shall eat of them, for they are holy. And if any of the flesh of the sacrifice of consecration or of the loaves is left over until morning, you shall burn what remains with fire. It shall not be eaten, for it is a holy thing.”
How profound the commandments of the law are!

Very profound indeed; you are right. Yet they are not altogether obscure, since the Holy Spirit makes the divine light flash within us. So come, let us again speak about each point as best we can. Our Lord Jesus Christ sanctifies us in countless ways and makes us priestly and acceptable. For through him and in him we have gained access, and we are not unwelcome to God the Father. For us who were subject to corruption and sin, his death, and indeed his life, are most useful and necessary for salvation, and besides these the perfecting that comes through his body and blood. For perfection is in Christ, and not in the law.
Well said.

Look, then, at the means by which we have been so well saved and sanctified and have become priestly and holy in Christ, still in types. The animal brought for sacrifice was a young calf from the herd. It is slaughtered right at the doors of the holy tabernacle, after hands have been laid on it. Its blood was poured against the altar and the horns of the altar were smeared with it; the inner parts are burned like the most fragrant incense, while the rest of the body is carried outside the camp and burned. Christ is the young calf, as one free of the yoke and yet under the yoke. For though he is God by nature, he came under the law because of his humanity. Is not a young calf unaccustomed to the yoke, while belonging to a kind that bears the yoke?
That is so.

So Christ is once again called a calf as part of the divine plan of salvation, so that we may understand at one and the same time both that the Godhead of the Word was unaccustomed to servitude, and that, as regards his humanity, he came to be in the nature that is under the yoke. He is slain, as it were, for the holy tabernacle and for those who laid their hands on him, and these are Levites and priests; for he died for the Church and for those consecrated to him through faith. That his death was sacred, and acceptable as a sacrifice to the God and Father of Emmanuel, you may understand from the blood being poured out on the holy altar and anointing it, and from the entrails being burned as incense. These might also be a type of the inward virtues, the virtues of the mind, which carry a spiritual fragrance, though not in a single way, since the entrails are many: the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver. The rest of the body is burned outside the camp. For Christ suffered outside the gate; so Paul writes. The consuming of the body by fire would signify in outline that his suffering and death would in no way end in dishonour, but would issue in a brilliant and most manifest glory. For the divine is conceived under the form of fire; it was in this way that it came down on Mount Sinai. To destroy the power of death, Christ in the plan of salvation submitted to death, so that he might be glorified by us as God. So death passes into a glory befitting God, having as its end a brilliant return to life; and the lowliness of his suffering, overcome by the highest honours, vanishes into nothing. And this, I think, is what is meant in a riddle by the dead calf being consumed by fire. And by adding, "For it is for sin," he has made it known that Christ's suffering took place for the cleansing of sin, and the matter is not obscure.
Certainly not.

Then the first ram is taken and slain in the same way as the calf. Its blood was likewise poured out on the altar, and it was cut up limb by limb and offered up, the entrails having been washed with water, together with the head and the feet, because it is an offering of incense. Here again Christ is depicted for us, perfect in the perfect ram, having a holy life. This, I think, is what the pouring of the blood on the altar shows; for the blood is a type of life. And it shows that he was dedicated as a fragrant odour to God the Father, both for all together and for each one. And this again is the type: the ram is offered up on the altar both as a whole and limb by limb. We are members of Christ, each in part, and all of us are understood to be one body. That he is holy and wholly sacred, having no stain of impurity, the washing of the entrails indicates very well. The head and the feet are offered up together, signifying that the Saviour's life was fragrant in holiness from beginning to end. For in every animal the head is the beginning, and the feet, as the extremity of the whole body, are the end. Or perhaps it is better to understand the head as a type of the mind, and the feet as a type of the course of practical action. Everything in Christ is fragrant, and both his thoughts and his deeds reach the height of purity; for he committed no sin. For this reason it calls the consecration of the ram whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice; for he is not holy or sacred only in part. It would never befit him, but rather us, sometimes to be weak and to be caught in stumbles; for no one is pure from sins, and we all stumble in many things, as it is written.
And how might someone perhaps suppose that Christ's very life also came about for our sake?

Well, you will see it quite easily if you consider that we became partakers in the transgression in Adam, and all but paid the penalty for his offences ourselves, since the curse ran through to everyone and the wrath was in a sense distributed over the race descended from him. So the Only-begotten came down into human life and dwelt among us, and subjected himself to God the Father. For he became obedient unto death, wiping out the charges of insubordination that came from Adam, and he brought the fragrance of obedience to God the Father, both for all together and for each one, and through him we have been saved. Paul is witness, having written as follows: "Therefore, just as through one trespass came condemnation for all people, so too through one righteous act came justification of life for all people. For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous." So you understand that we have been saved, as in the calf, by Christ dying for us, and that we are fragrant to God the Father through his submission and his life in holiness; for the ram's blood was poured out on the holy altar.
I understand what you are saying.

Depicting the same one for us in many ways, as in shadows, it says, "And you shall take the second ram," and the slaughter is carried out on it as on the first. Aaron is anointed, and the band of priests under him is sanctified, the blood being put on the tips of the right hand and the right ear, and also of the right foot. The priests' vestments too are sanctified by being sprinkled with the blood. Then, the remainder having been poured out at the base of the altar, as God saw fit, the entrails are taken, together with unleavened bread and one cake, both of them moistened with oil; Aaron and his sons bring them, placing them in their own hands, and Moses receives the sacrifice and offers it up. In addition he said that the arm and the breast must be set apart for the priest and be counted among the portions taken off. The name of the victim is "ram of perfection." When the entrails have been burned as incense, the rest of the body is eaten with the bread, and whatever is left over until morning is burned with fire. For this is how the sacred text runs.
How deep the passage is!

You are right; it is very deep indeed, and it is pregnant with the mystery of Christ. For he became for us a ram of perfection, making us complete for everything that is excellent and most distinguished in virtue through sanctification in the Spirit. First of all he gives us a hearing full of blessing, that is, one that is obedient and tractable, well disposed to receive the doctrines concerning him, but unwilling to tolerate whispered chatter and the loathsome, unbridled talk that some produce when they fight against the truth and oppose the doctrines of orthodoxy. For this is the fruit of the holy ear. Indeed the inspired John says to us somewhere: "Brothers, test the spirits, whether they are from God. Every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ is not from God, and every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ is from God." The testing of words would reasonably be carried out nowhere else than in the ear. So the ear will be holy in those who care for exactness and doctrinal orthodoxy. But this is Christ's gift, a present from heaven, and the achievement of the holy blood; for we possess everything excellent in him and through him. Accordingly the hand too was sanctified, which indicates practical activity, and the foot as well, a clear symbol of uprightness in the paths we take. For we must adorn ourselves with holy works and walk well along the path that leads to everything pleasing to God, as is sung in the Psalms: "And I turned my feet to your testimonies," or as in the book of Proverbs: "Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways." Let the sacred and chosen race, then, have a holy ear, and likewise a holy hand and foot, in the ways we have just described; all of them anointed on the right side, and at the farthest part, that is, at the tips. For it speaks of the tip of the ear, and also of the foot and the hand. For every good deed, I think, is noble and right-handed, with nothing of the left-handed awkwardness of wickedness about it, and it reaches to the tips, that is, to the very end or completion. For those consecrated to God ought to be right-handed in holiness to the very end, with endurance. "For let him who began a good work in you," it says, "bring it to completion." And it is altogether out of place to turn back, as it were, shrinking from carrying the good through to its end. Since Moses stands as a type of God, Aaron and his sons bring the sacrifice, but Moses himself receives it, as though God were signifying by this too that he will receive, virtually from hand to hand, the sacrifices offered in Christ by those who have been sanctified in this way, and will not disdain the offering; for it has the fragrance of Christ. And this, I think, is the meaning of the entrails being offered up and burned as incense to him. The breast and the arm from the ram of perfection are the portion set apart for the priest. The arm would be a symbol of strength, and the breast of the heart and the inmost thoughts. And Christ has been given to the holy and sacred race as power and wisdom from God the Father. Or are we not wise and very strong in him?
Of course we are. For it is written that Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, has become these things for us from God.

The meat is sacred food for those chosen for the ministry. It is given together with the unleavened bread, and no one of foreign birth shares in it; or, if anyone does, he will die. For it befits sacred souls to partake of holy food, that is, of the body of Christ, and the blessing is closed to those of another race. By "another race" might be understood the race that is still unbelieving and unbaptized, and besides them those who have been twisted into a heterodox mind, out of harmony with the views of the saints and cut off by their wicked doctrines. Whatever is left of the sacrifice is consumed by fire, since the law does not permit it to be eaten on the following day as well. For there will be, I think, another mode of sanctification for us in the age to come, worked spiritually and no longer bodily, in the way known to God, who transforms all things and changes them into whatever he wills. A mind that is not unintelligent will follow this argument: once corruption has been destroyed in us after we have perhaps risen from the dead, the means by which it might be escaped are no longer needed. So another mode of sanctification will be devised, suited to the state of that time, when Christ is with us. Having said what came to mind, we shall give way to those who understand better. And perhaps the inspired Paul hints at something of this sort when he says, "But when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away," that is, it will come to an end and cease.
So it seems.

These, then, are the things he said must be carried out for the consecration of the priests. And when the priests of Israel had been gathered together and convened in an assembly, he laid down how they were to be publicly installed, saying: "Take Aaron and his sons, and the oil of anointing, and the calf for sin, and the two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread, and assemble the whole congregation at the door of the tent of witness." And Moses said to the congregation [and he did as the Lord had commanded him, and assembled the congregation at the door of the tent of witness; and Moses said]: "This is the thing that the Lord has commanded to be done." And he clothes Aaron in his adornment, and the priests as well. He sprinkles the altar with the oil of anointing seven times, "and all its vessels, and the laver," it says, "and the tabernacle and everything in it, and he sanctified them." For the tabernacle is holy, and the altar is fully enriched with sanctification through the Spirit, not as sharing in the rank of rational beings (for it is not holy in the way that, say, an angel's nature or a human soul is holy), but, as it were, through contact with the sacrifice laid upon it. For even a place in which Christ may be is holy. So having anointed the altar seven times, that is, abundantly, he sanctifies Aaron; for he poured the oil of anointing over him, and in addition offered the sacrifices for him and for his sons in the ways we have just set out. When these things had been completed, he gives a further command, saying: "And you shall not go out from the door of the tent of witness for seven days, until the day is fulfilled, the day of your consecration. For seven days he will consecrate your hands, just as he did on this day, which the Lord commanded to be done, so as to make atonement for you; and you shall sit at the door of the tent of witness seven days. Day and night keep the charges of the Lord, so that you may not die; for so the Lord God commanded me." What procedure was followed for each of the sacrifices, our account has shown well enough. So let us leave off dwelling on these details and go on to the following point. The law does not allow those who have been enriched with a sacred and chosen lot, and who have already been consecrated for the duty of serving as priests, to wander anywhere outside the holy tabernacle, but requires them to sit within until the seventh day; it all but nails them to the doors so that they do not cross the threshold, making their sitting in the holy places a symbol, I think, of steadfastness and perseverance in holiness. For we who have been appointed to attend upon God must be firmly fixed and unshakable in virtue, not straying outside the proper way or running off from a mind befitting priests, but always, as it were, near God and dwelling with him, according to what was said by the voice of the prophet: "Seek diligently, and dwell with me." Moses ordered this to be done for seven days, meaning that one must strive to attend upon God at all times, since seven signifies this; it is as though he said "entirely and continually." And he commands them, while they are within the tabernacle, to keep the charges of the Lord, indicating that obedience is the fruit of attending upon God, along with willingness to do whatever he chooses to ordain. So we must attend upon the Lord of all, since slackness in what is good always ends in the very worst of evils. That, I think, is why Moses added, "so that you may not die."
You have spoken rightly.

Once consecrated for the priestly service, Aaron begins to fulfil what has been prescribed. In what way? Come, let us explain. For again it is written in Leviticus: "And it came to pass on the eighth day that Moses called Aaron and his sons and the council of elders of Israel, and Moses said to Aaron: Take for yourself a calf from the herd for sin, and a ram for a whole burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the Lord. And speak to the council of elders of Israel, saying: Take one male goat from the goats for sin, and a calf and a year-old lamb for a whole burnt offering, without blemish, and a calf and a ram for a sacrifice of salvation before the Lord, and fine flour mixed with oil; for today the Lord will appear among you. And they took them, as Moses had commanded, before the tent of witness, and the whole congregation came near and stood before the Lord. And Moses said: This is the thing that the Lord has spoken; do it, and the glory of the Lord will appear among you. And Moses said to Aaron: Approach the altar, and make your sin offering and your whole burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and your house; and make the gifts of the people, and make atonement for them, as the Lord commanded." If you apply your mind closely to the sacred Scriptures, Palladius, you will see very well that here too the mystery of Christ is plain.
In what way?

On the eighth day Moses, as it were, ceases from serving as priest, and Aaron begins; yet Moses has not fallen silent, even though Aaron is already hastening to the works of the priesthood. For the time of Christ's priesthood may reasonably be understood as the time after the law, that is, the eighth day, on which the resurrection took place, the beginning, as it were, of a new age. For there is a new creation in Christ, as it is written. Now that Christ has been revealed on the eighth day, the things of Moses come to an end, for we no longer worship in types and shadows. Yet the instruction of the law has not fallen silent; for the law is spiritual to those who are spiritual, and it always speaks the mystery of Christ. Moses, then, promised that on the eighth day the glory of the Lord would appear; for the law announced beforehand the time of our Saviour's coming. He further commands that Aaron should first perform sacrifices for himself, and after that those for the whole people. In this, I think, he makes the matter a type of what concerns us now, and indicates very well and clearly that it would rightly befit those chosen for the priesthood, and those who receive sanctification by faith, to be holy and sacred. What the manner of the offering was, we shall explain as best we can. A calf, then, was slain for sin and for the cleansing of those performing the sacred rites. Its blood was poured out at the holy altar, the entrails were burned as incense, and the rest of the body was consumed by fire. The ram, again, was the whole burnt offering, according to the customary law of the whole burnt offering; a male goat was the victim for cleansing the people's sin; a calf and a lamb were for the whole burnt offering, and a ram and a calf for the sacrifice of salvation, the fine flour also being placed on the altar, though perhaps not all of it, but a handful, a portion. Then it says: "And Aaron lifted up his hands over the people and blessed them, and came down after making the sin offering and the whole burnt offerings and the offerings of salvation. And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of witness, and came out and blessed all the people, and the glory of the Lord appeared to all the people. And fire came out from the Lord and consumed what was on the altar, both the whole burnt offerings and the fat; and all the people saw it, and were amazed, and fell on their faces."
What, then, do you say about these things?

The glory of the Lord truly appeared on the eighth day; that is, the Son, the glory of God the Father, was made manifest. For he called him this when speaking to the most sacred Moses: "As I live, says the Lord, the whole earth shall surely be filled with the glory of the Lord." And it is he who makes us sacred: slain for us as in the calf, he frees us from sin, releases us from every charge, and scours away the filth of condemnation. Likewise he is perfected as a ram for an odour of spiritual fragrance; he himself becomes the sacrifice of salvation, sanctifying us with his own blood; he himself is the fine flour moistened with oil, presenting himself on our behalf to God the Father in the gladness of a holy life.
I understand what you are saying.

For my part, I think that the sacrifice for Aaron and for the people elegantly signifies the consecration of the saints to God. Once Emmanuel had been revealed and had made plain what concerned himself, we were called through him to sanctification, acceptable and holy, and we have been dedicated to the Father as a fragrant aroma. For notice that in what was just said the perfecting of the priests was accomplished according to the law, but the priests were in turn sanctified in many ways through him. He was burned like a calf outside the camp for sin. He rose as incense like a ram, duly burned whole. Cut up limb by limb, as if for each and for all, he sanctified them by anointing them with blood, like the ram of the peace offering. Then, when the eighth day had at last appeared (that is, the day on which the glory of Christ became more fully manifest, once death had been abolished and corruption trampled down), priests and peoples from then on bear fruit for God. They do not honour the Lord of all with things foreign to themselves or try to please him with what is external, as Israel according to the flesh did. Instead, they present themselves as a fragrant sacrifice. For in the victims, as in an image, we offer our own souls in sacrifice and bring them to God. We die to the world and to the mind of the flesh, we endure the putting to death of the passions, and we are all but crucified with Christ, so that we may pass over into a holy and blameless life and conduct ourselves as he pleases. The inspired Paul writes something of this kind: "Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our body." And again: "If we endure, we shall also reign with him." If we are conformed to his death and his sufferings, as it is written, we shall also share in the resurrection and the glory. So Christ suffered for us outside the gate, as blessed Paul says, and we too go out, bearing his reproach, outside the gate. Slaughtered in the same way as a young calf and burned whole like a ram, we make the life in Christ a fragrance to God. These, then, were the victims for Aaron and for those with him and descended from him. For the people, the sin offering was a he-goat. And what is the reason for this, when a young calf had been offered to purify the priests? Everything that concerns priests is of higher rank: the offering of sacrifices, and whatever serves for purification and cleansing. A young calf is larger in body than a goat, and so it gives a clear indication of superiority in spiritual matters. The young calf and the lamb for the whole burnt offering hint at the infancy in Christ of those who are consecrated in faith. The calf and the ram signify very well endurance and courage, and fruitfulness in gentleness: the calf is a type of the first, and the ram of the second. The fine flour soaked in oil shows very well the bright hope of the life in Christ. It is not fitting for those who have taken up the life in Christ to be gloomy and tearful. They should be cheerful and glad. This, I think, is the meaning of "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord." For in this way the glory of Christ will shine out purely and clearly, accepting the offerings of the saints with the greatest pleasure, just as God then came down visibly in the form of fire and consumed the victims. He all but treats the good standing of those sanctified in faith as his food and delight. The passage also hints at something mystical. At that time God sent the full force of fire down on the divided pieces, as if he were touching what lay before him, for the Divine is always pictured under the nature of fire. But now, when the spiritual sacrifice is set before him, he touches what lies before him spiritually, not in the form of fire but in the Holy Spirit, and makes it life-giving for those who desire to partake of it. And we have received this as true in faith.
You have spoken rightly.
