"And Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed the people." See here again what is like a first laying on of hands upon the peoples, through Aaron. For the true Aaron blesses everyone, priests and peoples, "the small with the great," as it is written, all but laying his hands on them. The laying on of the hand would be a clear sign of the all-holy Spirit coming down upon us. Before Aaron's sacred service there was no laying on of hands. For, as John says, "the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified."
The argument is persuasive.

He also lays down the form of the priests' prayer, and he places in it words that very aptly foretell what we would receive through Christ. For he said: "Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, saying to them... And they shall put my name upon the sons of Israel, and I the Lord will bless them: 'The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you, and give you peace, and have mercy on you.'" He commands those crowned with the priesthood to bless the people, but he usefully guards against idle thoughts by showing that the hand that blesses is not a human hand but his own, as Lord. For "every good gift and every perfect gift," and every blessing, "is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," as it is written. Christ is the way of blessing. He is the one who distributes heavenly goods to us, and in him and through him all things come from the Father. So the inspired Paul says: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ." We are blessed, then, in the name of God. He also indicates elegantly how this might come about, for he said that the priest who prays must pronounce: "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you; the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace." The blessing keeps us, for it loosens the curse and refashions what had sinned, so that it may be praised in Christ. Paul is a witness of this when he writes: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him; in love he predestined us to adoption through Christ for himself." You see that rejection came about through sin, and that man is made acceptable for adoption, blessed in Christ through participation in the Spirit. He poured out the Spirit on us richly, for he does not give him to the saints in part but bestows him from his own fullness. The shining of God's face would at once bring us mercy, if it is true that in knowing God we come to share in eternal life. For this is what the Saviour said to his Father and God in heaven: "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." No one, I think, would have the least doubt that the Son, who has also appeared to us, is the face of God the Father. For he is his exact imprint, his likeness and his image, and through him and with him we know the Father. Mercy necessarily comes in along with such knowledge. For we have been justified by faith, "not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy." We have laid down the burden of corruption and been changed into newness of life in Christ, because God had compassion on us. There is also another way to take it. If we turn the force of the passage toward the Jews, they truly received mercy when the Only-begotten shone upon them. The law that condemns and punishes sinners without pity lay on them like an unbearable and intolerable burden. But they received mercy when at last, and with difficulty, they gained justifying grace through Christ. They longed to see his coming and cried out to the God of all: "O God of hosts, turn us, and make your face shine, and we shall be saved." So we have all received mercy in the appearing of Christ. Moreover, the lifting up of God's face brings peace. Christ is its giver and arbiter: he sets it before those who believe in him and bestows it on them as his own good. "Peace," he says, "my peace I give to you; my peace I leave with you." When the Father in a way set the Son on high, granting him the name that is above every name and saying, "Sit at my right hand," then, yes then, the enmity that divided us was dissolved and we were joined in peace. This came about because we chose to set our minds on his things and to walk in the Spirit. In the Spirit and through him we have been made partakers of the divine nature, and Christ binds us together into unity. For he said somewhere to the Father: "I desire that, as you and I are one, so they also may be one in us." We are all one body in Christ, and, as Scripture says, "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." That we gained the riches of peace with God when God the Father in a way lifted up his own face (that is, when he glorified the Son), the Son himself makes clear when he says: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself."
You understand rightly. For he is our peace, and through him we have access in the Spirit to the Father.

This, then, is what the law tells us about the priests and their installation. But it states very plainly that the Levitical order must be sanctified, and that only after being purified beforehand in the proper ways should the Levites take up the service assigned to them. In Numbers it says: "Take the Levites from among the sons of Israel and purify them. This is how you shall purify them: you shall sprinkle them with water of purification, and a razor shall pass over their whole body, and they shall wash their garments, and they shall be clean. And they shall take one calf from the herd, with its offering of fine flour mixed with oil; and you shall take a second yearling calf from the herd for sin. And you shall bring the Levites inside the tent of witness. And you shall assemble the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, and you shall bring the Levites forward, and Aaron shall set the Levites apart as a gift before the Lord from the sons of Israel, and they shall be for doing the works of the Lord. And the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the calves, and you shall offer one for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering, to make atonement for them. And you shall set the Levites before the Lord, and before Aaron, and before his sons, and you shall give them up as a gift before the Lord. And you shall separate the Levites from among the sons of Israel, and they shall be mine. And after this the Levites shall go in to do the works of the tent of witness."
Explain very clearly, then, how we should understand the manner of purification that was applied to the Levites.

It is mystical, Palladius, and once again it concerns Christ. For he is our cleansing, the washing away of all filth, and the giver of sanctification. "You shall sprinkle them with water of purification," it says. The wise Paul made this plain when he wrote: "For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ." And what he says is true. For if the types bring some benefit, and the shadow brings salvation, how much more the truth, that is, the blood of Christ? So the water of purification mixed with the ashes of the heifer was a clear symbol of what is called the dying of Christ, which we ourselves also pray to fulfil through faith in holy baptism. As the inspired Paul himself says somewhere else: "For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life." And again he said: "Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our mortal flesh."
And what, then, is the dying of Christ that is spoken of here?

It is to have died to the world and to sins, and to live a sacred and holy life, the life most pleasing to God. Paul again took great pride in this, saying: "For I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." This, I think, is what it means to have died in the world and to have undergone the dying of Christ, and then to live the life that is in him. So the ashes of the heifer mixed with water would hint at the dying of Jesus as it is accomplished in holy baptism. He said that those serving in the Levitical order must also come to share in it, having first, again as in a shadow, put off every kind of fleshly uncleanness. This, I think, is shown very clearly by the shaving of the body's hair with a razor. For the word of God is living and active and sharper, and it cuts away from the mind, like hair and nails, the uncleanness of the fleshly impulses that are innate in us. Sacred Scripture somewhere calls this the law of sin, which dwells in the members of the flesh, wars against the law of the mind and drags us toward what is unlawful. But it is weakened when it is cut, as if by a razor, by the power and working of the Holy Spirit, and even if it somehow grows again in us, it is shorn off all the more quickly. "Walk by the Spirit," it says, "and you will not fulfil the desire of the flesh." A razor does not dig the hair out of us from its root altogether but cuts it as soon as it grows. In the same way the word of God in us does not tear out by the roots, as it were, the impulse of desire that is innate in us (for perfect holiness has been reserved for the age to come). Rather, it puts that impulse to death as it springs up and rises in us, and it tames the law that rages in the members of the flesh. So the removal of hair hints at the purification of the mind, which the divine and sharper word of God works in us. The washing of garments points to a bright and genuine way of life, one that is visible outwardly. For, as it is written, "we take thought for what is good, not only before the Lord but also before men." And he himself says somewhere: "Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." So those who are truly holy and sacred must carry about the dying of Jesus in their own body, purely, both inwardly and outwardly, and must in some way be united with him through holy baptism.
Well said.

He said that the sacrifice for them must be offered in two calves, one full-grown and one a yearling, that is, tender and young. The full-grown one is for the whole burnt offering, and fine flour mixed with oil is burned along with it. The other is burned outside the camp for sin, for that is how sin offerings are completed. And again Christ is in both. He is in the calf of the whole burnt offering as wholly holy, a fragrant aroma for our sake to God the Father, bringing the saints the grace and gladness of the life in hope. For fine flour mixed with oil was offered along with the calf, and this will surely accompany those who have honoured the life in Christ. And he is also in the young calf consumed by fire for sin. For, according to the Scriptures, "by his bruise we were healed." Notice that the full-grown calf is burned whole, but the yearling is slaughtered for sin. This is so that through the two you may understand the one Christ at the same time: most fragrant in a spiritual sense because of his perfection in the virtues, and slaughtered in simplicity and innocence. For he says: "I was like an innocent lamb led to the slaughter, and I did not know." The laying on of hands by the Israelites would show that the priestly race is brought to God as an offering both for all and from all. For it says: "The sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the heads of the Levites." The Levites laid their hands on the heads of the victims slaughtered for them as a type of Christ. They did not do this to bless them, far from it. Rather, by laying on their hands they were in a way pointing to the God who bears our sins and is offered in sacrifice for us, so that he might nail to his own cross the bond that stood against us. In the same way, you will understand, the peoples performed the ordination of the Levites. For they laid their hands on them as if they were appointing them, as chosen men, to serve God in their own place. That was when the laying on of hands was practised. But now that things have changed for the better beyond comparison, the peoples cast their vote for those called to sacred service through Christ, crying out loudly that they are worthy. And they do this in churches, just as the people of old performed the laying on of hands on the Levites at the sacred and divine tabernacle. It is plain, then, that an ordination performed neither in church nor before the people will be contrary to the divine will and outside the sacred laws. Once perfected, the Levites take part in everything that belongs to sacred service. So whoever is not holy in Christ and has not been purified beforehand in the proper way, let him keep far away. For he will not touch the divine altars with impunity.
On the Priesthood.

We have now spoken clearly about the sacred vestments, and also about the sacrifices which God decreed must be performed at the consecration of the priests. But of the countless further things that were divinely spoken after these, about the ministry and purifications, and about the careful propriety needed to live in the most lawful way, polished to spiritual refinement, I think there is one thing in particular that must be said before the rest.
What sort of thing do you mean?

The tribe descended from the blood of Levi was an offering dedicated to God and chosen out of all the tribes. The law granted that race the duty of serving as priests, and God assigned it this privilege as a special honour. Yet he did not let the priestly multitude go entirely unexamined. Nor did he simply open the office to anyone at all merely because they were of Levi's blood. He commanded that very careful inquiry be made, so that no one who happened to suffer from one of the defects the law censures would be unacceptable to God and make the approach to him blemished. Otherwise such a man would all but rush with unwashed feet into the tent of witness and give offence, even without meaning to. And again it is written in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Say to Aaron: A man of your race throughout your generations who has a blemish shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God. No man who has a blemish shall come near: a man who is blind, or lame, or has a mutilated nose, or cut ears, or a man who has a broken hand or a broken foot, or is hunchbacked, or spotted, or bleary-eyed, or a man who has a malignant scab, or ringworm, or has only one testicle. No one of the seed of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall draw near to offer the sacrifices to the Lord, because there is a blemish in him. He shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God. He may eat of the gifts of his God, of the Holy of Holies and of the holy things, but he shall not come near the veil and shall not draw near the altar, because he has a blemish. And he shall not profane the holy place of his God, for I am the Lord who sanctifies them."
Tell me, then: is bodily infirmity a ground of accusation against anyone? Does the Creator indict nature when it has been impaired involuntarily?

Well said, Palladius; you are thinking rightly. Blame and indictment may at times fall on those who turn their own minds willingly toward base things, and who have come to value leaning toward anything at all that is outrageous. But to rebuke the infirmities of the flesh, which happen naturally and involuntarily, is, I think, harsh and unfeeling, and not free from the charge of boorishness. From this we may see that the Creator of all would not have indicted human nature on involuntary grounds. Nor would he have dismissed a man with a bodily infirmity from the ministry appointed for him as though he were unholy. Rather, once again using bodily things as a type, he refines us toward more spiritual counsels. He points to the manifold variety of the passions in the soul, and gives us to understand that such a thing is hateful to God. Did not the divine Paul also say that those chosen for the priesthood must have a glowing reputation in everything admirable? "So that," he says, "the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." He also insisted, very plainly, that the bishop must be above reproach, and he was very exacting in these matters.
I agree. But I should like to learn, believe me, what the meaning is of each of the infirmities we have just listed.

Come then, let us take them one at a time, treating each as a sample, and say what comes to mind. "A man of your race throughout your generations," it says, "who has a blemish shall not come near to offer the gifts of his God." The word is firm, and the oracle is stern. The law is laid down not only for those descended from Aaron at that time. It extends to the whole race, covers all priestly blood, and runs on through all time. That, I think, is what the words "of your race throughout your generations" show. For what is not blameless is always unacceptable to God. No one could name a time when what has been condemned would become dear to him, meaning, of course, infirmities of the spiritual kind. What is prized instead is the blameless: what suffers no corruption from any quarter but is whole, as it were, in virtue and robust in sanctification, what has trained itself well to win approval through patience, and is quick toward constant understanding. So he makes his law about this extend to the whole race, declaring the holy and chosen race to be genuine and his own. At that time this meant the tribe of Levi and the blood of Aaron. Now it means those sanctified in Christ, the great and true high priest, to whom we have been joined through the Spirit, and who have been made sharers and partakers of his own nature. Therefore, having called into brotherhood those justified by faith, he rejoices over them as his partners, saying: "Here am I and the children whom God has given me." Or did not the divine Paul think fit to attribute this saying to the person of Christ?
Certainly.

So he bars from serving as priest anyone with any of the defects named, as being infirm and an object of mockery. "For a man who is blind or lame," it says, "shall not come near to offer the gifts of God." Even taken in the bodily sense, the thing is plainly unsightly. When a man's eyes have wasted away, or his foot is not planted firmly and cannot walk straight, would it not be better for the priest to keep still? Otherwise he does not know where he ought to go, or he goes amid laughter, using someone else's feet and eyes. But not much needs to be said about this. Let us instead say what is necessary for our knowledge and spiritual contemplation, passing quickly over the coarse literal sense of the history. By "blind," then, he seems to mean the extremely simple and witless. What the eye is to the earthly body, the mind may be called in the soul. It is lit by the divine light and opens its eyes to beauty itself, the pure beauty. With the subtle and nimble movements of its thoughts, so to speak, it springs eagerly upward toward accuracy of belief, and it knows how not to miss doctrinal correctness. This, I think, is what is said in Proverbs: "Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids nod toward what is just." And somewhere it was said to the mother of the Jews, who did not see rightly: "Behold, your eyes are not good, nor is your heart, but they are only for your greed, and for shedding innocent blood, and for your wrongdoings, and for murder, to commit them." So the man who is blind in the spiritual sense is unfit for sacred ministry. This is the wholly senseless man, maimed in mind and understanding. Also unfit is the lame man, that is, a man who does not know how to walk uprightly and is not strong enough to walk properly. Blindness, as I just said, is a symbol of utter lack of understanding. Lameness, in turn, is a symbol of a broken and feeble movement and eagerness, the kind a person might show in each of the things that ought to be done. Perhaps it is fitting to call out to those so maimed: "Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees." Christ himself also accused the Jewish peoples of refusing to make straight paths toward him. Instead they turned aside into lameness and slipped away from right reasoning. "Foreign sons," he says, "lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped away from their paths." Lameness of mind and blindness, then, stand on a par and are very close to each other, since their afflictions are alike. The one makes useless what is precious in understanding, the other what is strong in good works. Next, the law said that the man with a mutilated nose must be rejected, and with him the man with cut ears. One might apply the following account to them. The sense of smell tests foul odours and the sweetest ones, among things whose nature is to have a scent. This sense is very good at telling apart what can delight from what perhaps cannot but is of a different and worse kind. In the same way the human mind [?], if it happens to be sound in its own faculties, presses vigorously toward discerning the quality of things and will test each one exactly. Like an excellent money-changer, it tests everything, holding fast to the good and abstaining from every form of evil, as it is written, and so it will be highly approved. It rejects as counterfeit whatever among our actions is in any way base and false-stamped, and readily accepts what is beneficial and better. A flattened nose, therefore, signifies something not quite healthy and sound in our perception. It is by perception that we discern each thing well, giving the better verdict to the best things and the worse to the more shameful. By it we are, and are called, wise and shrewd and everything of that kind. Smell is, as it were, the actual quality of the things the mind perceives, rising up to the mind. A cut ear would suggest, it seems to me, hardness of hearing. When the hearing has been cut, I would say the affliction is being only partly compliant and not wholly docile in obedience. Or it is being unable to listen blamelessly to sacred things, especially the Scriptures. Some people actually do this, most foolishly turning the soul's readiness to listen toward what they should not. These would be, in the words of the most wise Paul, the people with itching ears, who turn them away from the truth, devote themselves to spirits of error, and swerve aside into profane empty talk. The man with cut ears, then, would suggest a maiming of the inner, spiritual hearing, and a corruption from what is right toward what is worse. And if anyone is seen to have a broken foot or a broken hand, let him withdraw, it says, and be ranked equally with the others. A man whose foot or hand happens to be crushed, though not wholly disabled, leads us to think of someone who cannot fully set about his work. His gait, that is, his activity, is not wholly beyond reproach, I mean in his conduct and in a most lawful life. These, again, would be either those who do the work of the Lord negligently, on whom a woe is pronounced by the voice of the prophet, or those who pursue justice unjustly, as it is written. Note that a moderate maiming of the leg is placed on a par with complete lameness in the spiritual sense and is reckoned the same. For not doing good rightly will be counted equal to being entirely unable to do any good. It is fitting that lameness should stand for "not at all," and the fracture for "not soundly."
So it seems.

Next he lists the hunchback, the spotted man and the bleary-eyed man among the most disqualified. By the hunchback we mean someone who is, as it were, bent over and looks downward in his mind. He has inclined toward the passions of the flesh and fixed his eye on earthly things (his spiritual eye, clearly). He has come to such a state of mind that he hates being straightened up, I mean toward setting his mind on things above. Here belong the charges against the Jews, about whom it is written: "Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their back forever." The spotted man is one who has what is called a freckle on his very forehead. This infirmity is a kind that darkens the surface of the skin. It takes away from those who suffer it even the possibility of escaping notice, since it blossoms on the eyebrows themselves and spreads over the whole face. Such a man is spotted in the bodily sense. In the spiritual sense he signifies someone shameful who is naked and open about it. His face, so to speak, is not clean, and the ugliness of his life is plain for all to see, so that perhaps he does not even know what one of the wise rightly said: "The wise will hide their own shame."
What do you mean?
Are there not, Palladius, countless passions in us?
Yes. What of it?

Just this, my good friend: each person is sick with whatever he is sick with. Yet often, overcome by shame before his brothers, he makes it a serious concern to seem healthy and to keep his faults from being noticed.
Well said.

But suppose someone has reached such shamelessness that he thinks nothing of choosing to sin openly, and completely disregards the honour owed to decency. Would not anyone think that such a person had gone far away from the sacred and holy race?
Very much so.

Such a man, then, the law calls "spotted," since he does not know how, or cannot bear, to hide the infirmity and passion that has befallen him. The bleary-eyed man is one who is not at all deprived of sight but cannot see soundly. Such would be those who have understanding, but in whom the choice to think rightly is not seen. Some, he says, see the good but turn the inclination of their own wills toward what they should not. Others, though capable of sharing in correct doctrine, all but wreck their own minds themselves. They launch into a most unseemly hunt for ideas and admit nothing sound into their belief about God. Such are, above all, the children of heretics, and the Jews as well, who believe that the Father is God but most senselessly thrust away the Son who has come forth from him by nature. Therefore what the prophet sings is true of them: "They have eyes, and do not see." Seeing is of no benefit unless one also takes care to see soundly. In the same way we rightly said that lameness and a broken foot are ranked equally. To walk unsoundly is no different at all from being entirely unable to walk, meaning, of course, the path of our affairs and the road of our deeds.
Well said.

"And no man shall come near to minister who has a malignant scab on him, or ringworm, or has only one testicle, or anyone in whom there is a blemish." The malignant scab must be compared with the most monstrous of the passions. They flood the mind with sharper currents and go beyond all measure. They begin in pleasure but end in bitterness. Would you not say that in every sin one can see both a measured and an unmeasured degree of evil?
What do you mean?

Take someone overcome by bodily pleasure. Could he not suffer this either moderately or beyond measure? Some are merely overcome and are sick in a restrained way. Others reach the very extreme of evil and are sick with a pleasure that runs uncontrollably wild, so that they slip even beyond the natural passions.
I understand what you mean.

In each kind of evil, then, whatever has swerved outrageously beyond reason, and beyond the measures that are customary and found among most people, may be called the malignant scab. Ringworm, besides, is any passion that keeps creeping outward and advances toward the worse without ceasing. The divine law wants us to contract and reduce whatever passions befall us. You will understand something of this kind when you hear: "If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins." Passions that go unrebuked always creep toward what is more shameful. They seize the heart and mind and lead to utter destruction. So we must rebuke what is base, while the sobriety within us restrains it by repeated returns to what is better and removes it little by little. By the man with one testicle, besides, he means, as I think, the half-man, someone who has had complete manliness cut away, so to speak. "For neither fornicators," it says, "nor the effeminate will inherit the kingdom of God." He calls such people effeminate because, though they were given a man's nature, they betray their manliness. They grow soft in mind and body and willingly break down into what is weak and womanish. It is likely, too, that the man with one testicle points to something else as well. We usually call someone "a man" when he is strong and firmly knit and quite capable of accomplishing whatever he may choose. A half-man may reasonably be understood as one who is not wholly strong and not altogether quick to do what befits him. It is not fitting for someone devoted to God to bring him a courage cut short and a mutilated strength, and so to be partly weak. Rather he should "act like a man and be strong," as it is written, with an eagerness beyond reproach and ridicule. So the man charged with a blemish is admittedly unfit for holy service. But he is not barred from partaking of the holy food. "For he shall eat of the holy things," it says, "but he shall not come near the veil and shall not draw near the altar." Those who are still subject to weaknesses hidden within the mind may partake of the blessing of Christ. They do not partake in the rank of the saints, for advancing in sanctification, firmness of mind and steadfast perseverance in all that is best. They partake in the way that befits the sick: to put away evil, to put an end to sin, to deaden pleasures and to recover spiritual health. Since Christ is a new creation, according to the Scriptures, we too receive him into ourselves through his holy flesh and blood. Being refashioned into newness of life through him and in him, we may then put off the old man, which is corrupted by deceitful desires, as it is written.
You have spoken rightly.

He forbids the practice of the sacred works, then, to those who suffer from a spiritual affliction that is ingrained, as it were, and cannot be cast off. For whatever is always sick with passions that have grown into it is by no means holy. But suppose one of those who are blameless in themselves and irreproachable for ministry happens to suffer from these common passions, which do not last. He commands that such a man must not be left unrebuked, saying: "Speak to Aaron and to his sons, and let them keep away from the holy things of the sons of Israel, so that they do not profane my holy name in whatever they themselves sanctify to me. I am the Lord. Say to them: Throughout your generations, any man of all your seed who approaches the holy things which the sons of Israel sanctify to the Lord while his uncleanness is on him, that soul shall be cut off from me. I am the Lord your God. And if a man of the seed of Aaron the priest is leprous or has a discharge, he shall not eat of the holy things until he is cleansed. The same applies to whoever touches anything made unclean by a dead person, or a man who has had an emission of semen, or whoever touches any unclean creeping thing that defiles him, or a man through whom he is defiled by any uncleanness of his. The soul that touches these shall be unclean until evening. He shall not eat of the holy things unless he washes his body with water. When the sun sets he will be clean, and then he shall eat of the holy things, for they are his bread. He shall not eat what has died of itself or been killed by wild beasts, so as to be defiled by them. I am the Lord. And they shall keep my ordinances, so that they do not incur sin because of them and die because of them, if they profane them. I am the Lord who sanctifies them." He is saying this: those who bring the sacred offerings, that is, the things sanctified by the sons of Israel, whatever they dedicate to God as a sacrifice, must not profane his name. They would profane it by bringing the offerings without first being purified, while the uncleanness they happen to have incurred is still unwashed. Otherwise, he says, let them know that they will at once pay the ultimate penalty. For "I am the Lord" means: I am not a falsely named god, against whom a person might sin without committing any offence. What could we do to wood or stone that would make us answerable for it? So he corrects them with very strong terrors, to keep them safe from uncleanness, and he usefully lists the ways in which we may incur it. In this way the ministers may know the path of the propriety that most befits them, and the means by which they may be acceptable and clean, as they pass through the life most pleasing to the lawgiver.
You have spoken rightly.

So he excludes the leper and the one with a discharge from the sacred ministry, and says that such a man must have no share in the holy things until he has thrown off what has befallen him and is entirely free of the disease. To these he adds, as suffering an uncleanness of the same kind, the one who touches any uncleanness of a soul, or the one from whom an emission of seed goes out, and also the one who touches a creeping thing, and a man who has any kind of flux that defiles. In its true and blameless intent, I think, the law is not censuring bodily ailments. It is still speaking in types, through things that are bodily and perceived by the senses, and through them it shows what takes place in souls. Leprosy, then, is a symbol of deadness: it consumes and devours the flesh, changes it into an unnatural state, and alters the appearance of the body. A discharge of seed is the casting away of fruitfulness, as nature flows out into nothing. Such, one might see, is a human mind that has been led astray into corruption and is all but consumed into barrenness, since it can understand nothing of what is necessary for salvation. Such were Hymenaeus and Alexander, who thought and said that the resurrection had already taken place. To these may be added those who turn without restraint to anything at all that is outrageous, and simply throw away the fruit of their own mind on stale and licentious pleasures. So the leper and the one with a discharge, that is, the one held fast by the works of deadness (and the works of deadness are the passions of the flesh), and the one who does not keep uncorrupted his inner fruitfulness, which is plainly the hidden fruitfulness of the mind, must withdraw, he says, from the holy things until he is cleansed. For as the divine Paul said, "Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning his body. But let a person examine himself," he says, "and then eat of the bread and drink of the cup."
Very well said.

Observe, then, Palladius, how precise the law is. It has not proceeded against the leper and the one with a discharge alone. Along with them it also condemns anyone who happens to touch those who suffer these things, I mean the leper and the one with a discharge. "And the one who touches," it says, "any uncleanness of a soul, or from whom an emission of his seed goes out, shall be unclean."
And what harm could come from this to those who touch them?

None at all, at least in the obvious sense, for bodily contact will not defile a person's soul. But the law is spiritual, and here again it teaches us in riddles that those subject to passions of the soul are unclean and charged with defilement. Those who touch them, that is, who cling to them, are defiled along with them. This plainly means a relationship of shared will or shared action. For "bad company corrupts good morals"; and "the believer has no share with the unbeliever"; and light is hostile to darkness and cannot be reconciled with it. It is also true that "with the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the elect you will be elect, and with the crooked you will be perverse." Suffering the most outrageous passions will be grievous not only for those who suffer them. Those who become like-minded with them and share their opinions will be defiled with defilements no less than theirs. He showed this at once by adding: "Whoever touches any unclean creeping thing, it will defile him, or a person by whom he is defiled through any uncleanness of his; the soul that touches them shall be unclean until evening." We say that the bitter and venomous creeping things are, and are rightly called, those to whom this saying would fit: "The venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." These would be, before all others, those who pervert what is right and din into the simpler folk the word that brings destruction, carrying them off to thoughts that are not good and to a perverted opinion about God. Perhaps they would also include those who say, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die," and those who drag the minds of the more ignorant toward the pleasures of the world. Others again are unclean and can defile those who touch them, that is, those who come near them, according, I mean, to the law of disposition. These are the people of whom the most wise Paul says somewhere: "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or a drunkard, or a robber, or greedy, or an idolater, do not even eat with such a one." Or do you not agree that what most befits the holy and chosen race is neither to fall into such evils nor to mingle with those who suffer them?
Certainly.

So whoever touches these, he says, will be in uncleanness until evening. "He shall not eat of the holy things unless he washes his body with water and the sun sets; then he will be clean, and afterward he shall eat of the holy things, because it is his bread." In addition to these things he also forbids eating what has died of itself or been killed by wild beasts, since it is well able to defile. See, then, Palladius, the putting away of all filth and the release from charges. These could come to be in us in no other way than through Christ alone, and at the time of his coming.
What do you mean?

Everything before the coming of the Only-begotten was uncleansed and still in defilement, and had no share in life. He showed this by saying, "He shall be unclean until evening, and shall not eat of the holy things." Or did Emmanuel not come in the last times of the age?
Yes, the statement is clear.

And we have been made alive by eating the bread that is truly holy and from heaven, that is, Christ, when the time had come to its end, as though the sun were setting and closing the measure of time into evening.
Quite so.

This is why the defiled person is unclean until evening and has no share in the holy and life-giving food while he waits for the time of cleansing. But once he has washed in water and the sun has set, he is clean, and the bread from heaven is his own. For it has been granted to those sanctified through water, in holy baptism I mean, to be blessed through Christ. He himself is the living bread, and he again is the one who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. That the setting of the sun signifies the time of our Savior's coming you will clearly see from what God says about the lamb to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: "Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them take for themselves a sheep by households, and it shall be," he says, "kept from the tenth of the month until the fourteenth, and the whole multitude of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening." For the time in which Emmanuel appeared to us is called the tenth hour, close to evening itself, that is, to the end of the present age. What has died of itself or been killed by beasts brings defilement on those who touch it, in a spiritual sense, no less than leprosy does. What has died of itself plainly signifies what is completely dead and without life, as in the works of the flesh. What has been killed by beasts signifies the soul that has fallen under the devil. It is a saving thing to depart from a man who has chosen to think dead thoughts, who is lifeless in mind, and who feeds Satan, as it were, upon himself (for Satan devours whatever souls he seizes). How could this not be clear to those who are truly sound in mind and who strive their hardest to keep as far as possible from everything that usually defiles?
So it is.

Our discussion has now crept on to this point of precision. The aim of the law is that the holy and life-giving foods be shared not by the defiled but by the blameless. So he at once distinguishes the classes very carefully. He has defined who would be worthy of the blessing and able to hasten toward it, and he made clear for whom it is fitting to be driven away from the sacred foods, saying: "No foreigner shall eat holy things; a priest's sojourner or hired servant shall not eat holy things. But if a priest acquires a soul bought with silver, he shall eat of his bread, and those born in his house, these too shall eat of his bread." He excludes the foreigner and the alien as defiled and still unwashed, that is, the one who has not yet believed and does not know the true God. For how could those who cannot be bound to Christ, the great and true priest, through a spiritual and inward kinship, become sharers in his bread? We will not give holy things to dogs, and no one would throw the spiritual pearls before swine, as the Savior himself said. So the foreigner has no share at all. To him he joins the sojourner and the hired servant. These again, in my view, would be those who live for the world and conduct themselves by its ways. By thinking only of the things of the flesh they have made the earth their homeland, as it were, and they are only sojourners in bare faith, that is, in their love for Christ. As far as words go they are good and reasonable, but in their deeds and in the ways of true piety they have strayed very far indeed. Hired servants, again, are those who perhaps chose even to believe, which is all they did, not out of reverence for the truth. As a kind of wage for seeming to be Christians, they hunt for the favor of certain people and fawningly insinuate themselves into the good graces of those who can benefit them. They make piety a means of gain, and they mold fair speech around themselves like a mask, as a cover for their greed. As far, then, as the force of the law goes, if the sojourners and hired servants are ranked with the foreigners and kept as far as possible from the holy things, they will be with them. Since their faults are almost brothers to the others' faults, they will justly undergo a penalty of the same kind. He said that sharing in the holy things must be granted to the members of the household. "For they shall eat," he says, those born in the priests' households and whoever the priests may have purchased. By "acquired," "bought with silver" and "born in the house" he means the one who is genuine in faith, a member of the household in spirit, and "bought with a price," as the blessed Paul says. For Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, as it is written.
True.

He further commands that "if the daughter of a man who is a priest marries a foreign man, she shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things." He has plainly honored the member of the household by allowing him to share in the holy things as one who is genuine. But those who belong to his household must firmly refuse to become fondly attached to people who are not their own in faith or way of life, or who have not been enriched with a kind of kinship that comes from virtue. This would not be unclear to anyone willing to look closely into the sense of the sacred Scriptures. In the passages already read he made the leper unclean, and the one with a discharge as well, and he made anyone who came near them, joined to them as it were by contact, a sharer in their defilement and uncleanness. In the same way here he says that the priest's daughter, even if she happens to have a holy kinship, will gain nothing from it if she is joined to another, that is, to a foreigner, one who is in no way her own and not of the blood of Israel. Let this, then, be the historical sense. But as the law is carried over for us into spiritual contemplation, we say that by the priest's daughter he means the soul reborn of water and spirit by the power of Christ and called through faith to sanctification. Yet even such a soul, he says, may have no share in the holy things if she becomes a foreign man's, that is, if she is joined to people who are not truly holy and have no spiritual relationship with God. For bodies the manner of union would be bodily, and for spirits it would be spiritual.
And who do we say have been led astray into this?

Those against whom the solemn word of wisdom gave warning, saying, "Son, do not let ungodly men lead you astray, and do not consent if they urge you, saying, Come with us, share in blood." We will also add those who have ignorantly turned away from the right faith and run after the flesh. They do not accept the words given through the Holy Spirit but give heed to spirits of error, through the hypocrisy of liars whose minds are seared. Thrusting away their kinship with Christ, these have truly become foreign men's. They have received diabolical seeds, and in their error they bear the fruit of error and destruction. So a soul is cast out, even if it was once sacred and holy, when it is caught in such shameful defilements. For everything that becomes abominable and defiled through attachment to base and unholy men is utterly unholy. Next to this he at once delivered another law by oracle, which runs as follows: "And if a priest's daughter becomes a widow or is divorced, and has no offspring, she shall return to her father's house as in her youth; she shall eat of her father's bread." The historical sense is clear, I think, but we must go on to the inner and hidden meanings. If a soul, he says, is cast out as condemned, and is then seen to be without a husband, that is, without the spiritual bridegroom, and has no fruit from virtue, let her run back to what she was at the beginning. Let her return swiftly to her own father's house, seeking kinship with God, plainly through repentance, and then she will eat of his bread. Nothing prevents us from applying the force of these words also to those we mentioned just now. If, he says, a sacred and holy soul is led on by profane men and slips into error and receives the defilement of alien doctrines, and for this reason becomes like a widow sent away by God, but then somehow comes to her senses and learns how she slipped, let her return to the Father. For he receives those who have strayed, if they are seen to be clean of the unholy seeds sown in them and to carry no remnant of the loathsomeness of those who led them astray. In this way he gathers them in with the holy worshipers, setting himself before them as bread from heaven, as life-giving food. I think that through these laws the lawgiver also hints at something else for us. He foretells, as it were, the apostasy of the synagogue of the Jews, the penalty for it, and the kindness that will come upon it in due time, which will bring it back to return by God's mercy and restore it to its original state. For "if the daughter," he says, "of a man who is a priest marries a foreign man, she shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things." As far as teaching and instruction go, the divine Moses became a kind of father to the synagogue of the Jews. She was, then, a priest's daughter, for Moses too was a priest, being of the blood and tribe of Levi. But his daughter became a foreign man's. She thought very little of what God had ordained and in a way disregarded the seeds from above. She has studied teachings that are the commandments of men and bears fruit to the opinions of others. This is why God accused her, saying to her through the voice of Jeremiah: "Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not been defiled. You sat by the roads for them like a forsaken crow, and you defiled the land with your fornication and your wickedness, and you had many shepherds as a stumbling block for yourself." But these are the ancient charges against the synagogue of the Jews. Akin to them are the new charges concerning Christ himself. For she refused entirely to accept the bridegroom who is from above and from God the Father, and she heeds the words of the scribes and Pharisees. So she has become a foreign man's, and for that reason she has remained without a share in the holy things, for she did not eat the bread from heaven, that is, Christ. You see the charges, and the penalty that Christ at once brought on those who committed such impiety. Observe now also how they have received mercy and been restored to their original state. "If a priest's daughter," he says, "becomes a widow or is divorced, and has no offspring in her, she shall return to her father's house as in her youth, and she shall eat of her father's bread." For the synagogue of the Jews was shown to be a widow and divorced because of her impiety toward Christ. She has remained in sins, possessing none of the spiritual goods, and has continued so for a long time. But she will return to her father's house. She too will be called through faith to God, she will claim with us the Creator of all things as her Father, and she will become a sharer in the blessing of Christ. The word of the prophet will make this mystery clear to you, for he spoke thus: "For the sons of Israel shall remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar or priesthood or manifestations. And after this the sons of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and their king, and they shall be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last days."
The word is true.

So the sacred things, that is, the holy things, are fit to eat and suitable to share in for those who are unblemished, as far as it depends on themselves. But they will no longer be set before those who are not sound, or who have been defiled through their relationship with others. For it is written, "With the crooked you will be perverse." Even for those who are truly sacred, it is not without penalty to treat the holy things as if they were for common use and to think they differ in no way from other things. He declared this at once, saying: "And if a person eats holy things in ignorance, he shall add a fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest. They shall not profane the holy things of the sons of Israel, which they set apart for the Lord, and so bring on themselves the iniquity of trespass by eating their holy things; for I am the Lord who sanctifies them."
I do not quite understand what you mean.

You will learn it quite clearly, for there is nothing difficult in it. The things dedicated as a pleasing aroma, calves perhaps, or sheep, were carried up to the altar in part, with the entrails, the feet, the head and the fat, and sometimes the kidneys, being set apart for it. With the remains they fed the priests. For "those who eat the sacrifices are partners in the altar," as the divine Paul said. It was therefore necessary that the prescribed portion of what was offered be consecrated to God according to the law that applied to each kind, and that the ministers be sustained by the rest of the body of the sacrifice. But if anyone kept the whole gift entirely for himself and allotted it to his own needs, burning nothing, the law charged him with having eaten holy things. This is what the sons of Eli the priest did: they seized and profaned the sacred things before the sacrifices, and they said most impiously to those who came to sacrifice, "Give meat for the priest to roast." But those acts were deliberate and blatant outrages, and they were punished accordingly. But if it should happen, he says, that someone does something of this kind because he is overtaken by forgetfulness or does not know exactly what the laws require, let him pay a penalty. Let him repay the equal amount without delay and add the fifth to it, that is, a fifth part of the value. In this way he will be released from the charges and will ward off the harm that comes from ignorance. If what is done in ignorance is not free from indictment, what would anyone think of what comes from folly and audacity? Those who have charge of sacred things must therefore refrain from seeking to claim anything for themselves before the sacrifice. Otherwise let them know that they have committed grievous offenses, will pay the penalty, and will fall under divine wrath. Or do you not agree that this is true, my friend?
Entirely so.

He made clear that those who serve as priests must be holy and washed clean, and must shake off quite vigorously any mindset that is, so to speak, dead and grown cold and does not breathe toward virtue, when he said: "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: They shall not defile themselves for the dead among their people, except for the relative nearest to them: for father and mother, for sons and daughters, for a brother, and for a virgin sister who is close to him and has not been given to a husband; for these he may defile himself. He shall not defile himself suddenly among his people, so as to profane himself. And you shall not shave your head bald for the dead, and they shall not shave the edges of their beard, and they shall not cut gashes into their flesh. They shall be holy to their God, and they shall not profane the name of their God; for they offer the sacrifices of the Lord, the gifts of their God, and they shall be holy." Another person's death would be no defilement at all to a man, if one looks into the true meaning. But bodily deadness would be a type of the deadness within, in souls, and whoever comes near that is bound to be defiled by it, whether by consenting to it or by doing the same things. It befits the holy to depart from dead works and keep as far from them as they can, and it is good not to keep company with those who are sick with such things. For it is written: "Whoever touches pitch will be defiled." Anyone who does not refuse to cling to another will very easily share in his wickedness. Yet the law allows the consecrated to incur defilement without blame for father and mother, for children and brothers, and indeed for close kin, by going to their lifeless bodies. It does so out of respect for nature, overlooking the offenses that belong to the type, so that those whom God knows may not seem hard-hearted, haughty and unfeeling, especially since the law says plainly: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you." There is also another way and another reason, we say, why the consecrated were barred from mourning. They were ministers of life, and offered sacred things to God for the undoing of death (for the undoing of death is the death of Christ, prefigured by the sheep and calves). How then would it be consistent for them to be weighed down by grief over death? So too the inspired Paul writes plainly to those who have been baptized into Christ in the hope of life and resurrection: "I say this so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so too God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, and will raise them with us." So the law permitted the consecrated to go to their very nearest dead. But it sets limits to the matter, and does not let them abandon what most befits them by going too far and beyond what is needed, so that the august honor of the priesthood may not be wronged. It forbids them to strip their heads bare as others do, or to shave off their beards and disfigure the face; and the impious practices of Greek frenzy, I mean cutting the flesh, it commands them not even to entertain in thought. To share the grief of one's kin is nothing unreasonable; but to lose all decorum would be ugly and utterly senseless. For "let all things be done decently and in order," it says. And the Savior himself has commanded us to put the things of God before even what the old law says is owed to parents, saying: "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me."
Well said.

So he commands that the priests must by no means defile themselves over the dead. And showing us in other ways as well that the holy has no agreement or affinity with the profane, he laid down laws about marriage, going on at once to say: "As for every priest, they shall not take a harlot or a profaned woman, nor shall they take a woman put away by her husband, for he is holy to the Lord his God, and you shall sanctify him. He offers the gifts of the Lord your God; he shall be holy, for I the Lord who sanctify them am holy." The woman who has truly played the harlot and been defiled is sick, clothed in the charge of shameful deeds, and her condemnation is beyond dispute. But the woman who has been put away is by no means free of blame either, for she would not without cause suffer being driven from her husband's hearth. Those brought into so august a ministry must therefore abstain not only from the evils that carry the most manifest and open condemnation, but also, I think, from anything at all that is attended by a reputation for wickedness, an unfavorable opinion, and the indecency of many suspicions. The passage also seems to hint at the calamity of the synagogue of the Jews. Because she played the harlot with many shepherds, as it is written, Christ did not accept her into spiritual communion: he, the all-pure priest, who offered himself to the Father on our behalf as a choice gift, who is holy with us as regards his humanity, although he himself sanctifies all creation, as God from God. He made the meaning of the mystery clearer when he said: "And if the daughter of a man who is a priest is profaned by playing the harlot, she profanes the name of her father; she shall be burned with fire." For the synagogue of the Jews has been given over to the flame as unholy and profane, since she followed the opinions of the scribes and Pharisees and devoted her whole mind to the commandments of men. Therefore she very justly heard the prophet say: "How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, she who was full of justice?" Having played the harlot, then, and paid no heed at all to her heavenly and spiritual bridegroom, she has become food for fire. So the prophet Jeremiah too, shedding bitter tears over her, says: "A fair olive tree, well-shaded in appearance: so the Lord called your name. At the sound of her circumcision a fire was kindled against her; great is the affliction upon you. Her branches have become useless, and the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you." So the form that spiritual harlotry takes is turning away from uprightness and seeking to attach oneself to shameful and unholy teachers.
So I say.

The types in what has been said are rather faint, and not very clear in the case of the other priests, but they shine out, as it were, in Aaron, who bore the image of Christ. For again he said: "And the great priest among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil has been poured and who has been consecrated to put on the garments, shall not uncover his head of the turban" — that is, shall not take off the mitre — "and shall not tear his garments; and he shall not go in to any dead person; he shall not defile himself for his father or for his mother; and he shall not go out of the holy place, and he shall not profane what has been sanctified for his God, because the holy anointing oil of God is upon him. I am the Lord. He shall take as his wife a virgin of his own kin. A widow, a woman put away, a profaned woman and a harlot — these he shall not take; he shall take as his wife only a virgin from his own people. And he shall not profane his offspring among his people. I am the Lord God who sanctifies them." You see clearly Emmanuel, the Anointed, still in types, named as it were in Aaron. For he was anointed with the Spirit, according to the Scriptures, being himself the all-perfect priest. Therefore he holds the glory of the priesthood beyond any loss. "He shall not uncover his head of the turban," it says; that is, he shall not lay aside his priestly dignity. For it was said to the Savior and Redeemer of all: "You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek." And "the others became priests in great number, because they were prevented by death from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, holds a priesthood that does not pass away. Hence he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him." So the inspired Paul has written. Not removing the turban from the head, then, would indicate that his priesthood cannot be lost. And if it is said, "He shall not take off the mitre from his head," you will understand very well that his kingship is perpetual and unshakable; for the mitre, which bears the golden band at the very front of the forehead, would be a symbol of rule and kingship. "Nor shall he tear his garments," it says. This is what some are accustomed to do over the dead; but the thing is entirely foreign to Christ. Life itself could hardly suffer the anguish caused by death. Nothing at all is dead to it; rather, it is the undoing of death and the overthrow of corruption. Indeed the Savior once rebuked those who wanted to wail over the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, saying: "Go away and do not weep; the girl is not dead but asleep." It was truly out of place for them to shed tears as over a dead girl when the Life of all, that is, Christ, was present. And if he wept over Lazarus, we say that this was the fruit of his tender affection and of the divine gentleness that feels for us. For he pitied our nature, tyrannized by death, and his tear was its release from suffering.
So it seems.

That there is nothing profane in Christ in any way is indicated indirectly by the statement that the high priest must keep apart from deadness and go to no dead person at all, even setting aside here the honor due to father, mother and brothers. See how wise the law is, and how it gives no small weight to the propriety befitting its meanings. In the case of the other priests it showed regard for nature, and granted the consecrated leave to perform the customary rites without blame for their very nearest dead, those related by blood. It was not much concerned about sin in the shadow. For the charges were written with us in view, and the type concerned human beings, and it is nothing strange if some defilement clings to them. For we all stumble in many ways, and our nature is sick with wrongdoing. But in the case of the great high priest, that is, Christ, reverence has been kept pure even in the type itself, and unadulterated in the shadows, so that the beauty of the truth might not be misrepresented as though it had been wronged in them. For Christ is free of all profanation; he knows no sin and is beyond all defilement, or rather he belongs to spiritual radiance and purity. He dwells within all holiness, and his radiance in this respect is [?], because it rests on the laws of his nature and he is always the same and unchanging. This, I think, is what is meant by: "He shall not go out of the holy place, and he shall not profane what has been sanctified for his God." And it says very well that he must take a virgin as his partner in marriage, and it rules out the woman who has been driven away. She too may be a type of the synagogue of the Jews; for she has been cast out of union with him, and he says of her through the voice of the prophet: "She is not my wife, and I am not her husband." But Paul betrothed the Church of the Gentiles to Christ as a pure virgin, without spot or wrinkle, or rather holy and blameless. Thus, as applied to the Church of the Gentiles and to the mother of the Jews, the riddle would be true and the type not unlovely. But if anyone wishes to turn the force of these meanings fittingly to the case of each individual, we say that Christ has no union with profane and unholy souls; but with souls that are all-pure and clean, like virgins, he unites spiritually, makes them fruitful and calls them his own kin. For "whoever does the will of my Father in heaven," he says, "is my brother and sister and mother."
You are right.

What sort of men those chosen for sacred service must be, what they should rightly be eager to do, and what they should keep free of, he has clearly declared. But it was also wise, of course, to state openly how they must perform their sacred service, and to regulate by laws the kinds of sacrifices and everything that is offered, so that the matter might be blameless for them and they might perform their ministry in a way most pleasing to God. So first of all he says: "You shall not go up by steps to my altar, so that you may not expose your nakedness upon it." But how could that happen, someone will ask at once, since he gave the priests linen breeches, "to cover the nakedness of their flesh," as it says? If they had to dart up high, then, it would have done them no harm, since their nakedness was covered. What, then, do we say is the aim of the law? To the worshippers of idols it seemed glorious and necessary to set up altars high in their sanctuaries, and they paid little attention to the need to be decently clothed. So the law skillfully takes what was customary among them, sets the divine ministers right toward something better, and leads them from a bodily type, as it were, to spiritual contemplation. "You shall not go up by steps to my altar," it says, "so that you may not expose your nakedness upon it." That is: Let the divine minister who has been sanctified for my service seek what is lowly, and not leap up to the heights. Let him renounce arrogance, so that he may not be seen as indecent and unlovely. For a swollen mind is unlovely and utterly indecent, and a most grievous sickness of the soul. For it says: "The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord." And the disciple of the Savior writes: "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation." For he will pass away like the grass, and will differ in no way from the flowers of the field.
I agree.

He said, then, that the minister must be free of pomp and disdain. And how he may perform his sacred service in the most lawful and irreproachable way, you will learn quite clearly; for it is written in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the whole burnt offering. This whole burnt offering shall be on its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn on it; it shall not be quenched. And the priest shall put on a linen tunic, and he shall put linen breeches on his body, and he shall take up the burnt remains, whatever the fire has consumed of the whole burnt offering, from the altar, and place them beside the altar. And he shall take off his robe and put on another robe, and he shall carry the burnt remains outside the camp to a clean place. And fire shall burn on the altar, and it shall not be quenched; and the priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall pile the whole burnt offering on it, and he shall lay on it the fat of the peace offering; and fire shall burn continually on the altar; it shall not be quenched." The fire of the altar, then, is perpetual and entirely unceasing, and it is not foreign or from outside, but its own, that is, from above and from heaven. And what does this mean? Our holy altar is filled with the glory of God, and the divine and ineffable nature is likened to the form of fire. The passage also seems to point very well to something mystical.
What do you mean?

Did we not say that Emmanuel himself is the divine altar, as in a type, through whom we draw near to the God and Father, worshipping rationally and all but offering up the fragrance of our virtues and the holiness of the gospel way of life? For: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your rational worship."
We did; I remember it.

See, then, that he does not allow the fire that came down from heaven upon the altar to die out, or to wither and depart, as it were, but has it be with the altar always and dwell on it without ceasing. And John the Baptist testified concerning Christ: "I have seen the Spirit descending from heaven in the form of a dove, and it remained on him. And I did not know him," he says, "but he who sent me to baptize said to me: He on whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining on him, this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." So the Holy Spirit was prefigured, still in shadows, descending upon Christ in the form of fire and remaining on him always. For the fire of the altar never sleeps and never ceases. That the Spirit is likened to the nature of fire, the blessed Baptist assures you when he says to the crowds of the Jews: "I baptize with water, but among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." And he said: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire." For we have been baptized not into fire that can be perceived by the senses, but in the Holy Spirit, who like fire melts away the defilement in our souls. Therefore it is also written of Christ: "Behold, he comes in like a smelter's fire and like the fullers' herb; and he will sit smelting and purifying, as silver and as gold." So the fire of the altar is unquenchable. For the Holy Spirit remained in Christ, although the Spirit exists in him by nature, inasmuch as he is understood to be, and is, God. And the law also said that the fire was the altar's own. For even if the Only-begotten became man, and is said to have come to share in the Spirit in a manner befitting his humanity, nevertheless the Spirit is his and in him, and truly his own. And if anyone chooses to apply what is said here to each of those who have been sanctified through faith in Christ, as though each in some way were also understood as a divine altar, the interpretation is profitable. For it is fitting that holy men, who have dedicated their own life to Christ, should be seen to be warm and fervent in the Spirit, and that always — not sinking into coldness through worldly pleasures, but rather rekindling their mind in holiness toward love of God and desire for virtue. For this is the way of rational worship. Such, then, is the meaning of the altar. But he also adds a command that is useful for the historical sense. He says that the ashes must be carried out not by someone else, a stranger, that is, one from another tribe, but rather by the service of the consecrated. Observe how the law allows nothing that belongs to the divine ministry to be thought trivial, or unworthy of the priests' own hands, so that it could be handed over to someone who is not sacred; for holy things are not to be trodden by the unclean. And the divine altar itself is not to be touched. And so that those chosen for sacred service might know the surpassing holiness of the divine altar, he attaches reverence even to the priestly vestments themselves. For, as a wise provision, he does not permit them to appear outside the tabernacle in their sacred garb. Let consecrated things not consort with the unclean, he says, and so, contracting defilement from outsiders, wrong the reverence due to the holy tabernacle. For this reason he lets them gather up the ashes dressed in priestly garb, but has them change their clothes when they carry them outside and leave the holy places. He gave an oracle akin to this through the voice of Ezekiel as well, who writes thus: "And he said to me: The chambers toward the north and the chambers toward the south, which face the open spaces, these are the chambers of the holy place, in which the priests, the sons of Zadok, who draw near to the Lord, shall eat the most holy things; and there they shall lay the most holy things and the sacrifices, those for sin and those for ignorance; for the place is holy. No one shall enter except the priests. They shall not go out of the court of the holy place into the outer court, so that those who bring offerings may always be holy; and they shall not touch their vestments in which they minister, because they are holy; and they shall put on other garments when they come into contact with the people." So the priests' garments themselves are holy and not to be mingled with the multitude. And the whole burnt offering goes on night and day; for the fragrance of Christ never ceases. And the very life of the saints, if understood as a kind of whole burnt offering, has a fragrance that never ceases; for they are the fragrance of Christ, offering to God as sacred service the glories that come from the works of the gospel way of life.
What you say is true.

How the whole burnt offering is to be performed is not unclear from what we have said. And how the sacrifice too may be performed quite rightly, he commands, saying: "This is the law of the sacrifice, which the sons of Aaron shall bring before the Lord, in front of the altar. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the sacrifice, with its oil and with all its frankincense that are on the sacrifice; and he shall bring it up to the altar as an offering, an odor of fragrance, its memorial portion to the Lord. And what is left of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place; they shall eat it in the court of the tent of witness. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it to them as their portion from the offerings of the Lord. It is most holy, like the sin offering and like the trespass offering. Every male among the priests shall eat it. It is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations from the offerings of the Lord. Whoever touches them shall be made holy." The things offered as whole burnt offerings indicate the complete and total dedication, as it were, of those who are exceptionally holy; but the sacrifice indicates a life that is holy in part and lived under God. An exact figure of this is the fine flour carried up in the priest's handful with the oil and the frankincense. For a life consecrated to God, even if perhaps only in part, must certainly be fragrant and enriched with the richest hopes. Or do you not say that every good work of ours is most fragrant?
Certainly.
And what about this: is it not done by us in good hopes?
Yes; for what comes from God will surely follow.
So frankincense, and fine flour moistened with oil, hint to us at a life that is fragrant and very rich.
Well said. But what would be the life that is holy only in part, as far as we are concerned?

It is the life that has not reached the summit of a way of living befitting the saints, and does not travel the path that climbs so very high, as perhaps the Voice, that is John, did, or the holy apostles. Yet it does not lose its claim to reverence merely because it may fall short of the very lofty life we have been describing. Is not the life of those who live in the world and raise children, if they choose to live uprightly, in a sense divided between God and the world, as the blessed Paul says?
It is divided. How could it not be?

So the partial consecration of the fine flour, with its fragrance and cheerfulness, was a type of the life that is not wholly devoted to God but stands in the middle, as it were, looking both ways. The law says that this offering will serve as a memorial of the one who has brought it through the ministry of the priest. And we truly gain a place in God's remembrance through the deeds by which we bear fruit and give off a sweet fragrance. Christ acts as mediator and brings to God both the one who is wholly holy, ranked as it were among the whole burnt offerings, and the one who is not entirely so because he is divided with the world, as a kind of partial sacrifice. The sacrifice is unleavened, for it is fitting that everything we do for the glory of God be done with purity. Indeed, the Saviour commanded us to shun praying while standing in the middle of the marketplaces, putting on a gloomy face when fasting, and making an unseemly blast of trumpets when we show pity to our brothers. For this is a leaven that profanes holy things. What is done for the glory of God should be free of any charge of pleasing men, for then the victim would be truly unleavened and holy. The rest of the sacrifice is a portion and food for the priests. Every male eats it in a holy place. That the holy things are consumed by the priests in a holy place preserves reverence for our more mystical teachings. That every male eats it gracefully suggests that effeminacy is truly an unlovely and unholy thing for those chosen by God. For it makes a man profane, removes him from spiritual blessing, and shows him to have no share in the good things that God has allotted to the saints. Judas too grew soft and turned aside to shameful gain. This came from an unmanly and ignoble mind, and for this reason he remained without a taste of the good things from God and had no share whatever in what has been given to the saints.
So it is.

This, then, is the law for the sacrifice offered by the flock. But in another way it commands that the sacrifice offered by the priestly race be brought, saying: “This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day you anoint him: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual sacrifice, half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening. It shall be made on a griddle with oil; he shall bring it mixed, rolled, a sacrifice of broken pieces, a sacrifice for a fragrant aroma to the Lord. The anointed priest who succeeds him from among his sons shall make it; it is a perpetual law; it shall be wholly carried out. And every sacrifice of a priest shall be wholly burnt and shall not be eaten.” Observe then, Palladius, the precision of the law and its great subtlety in securing what befits the priesthood. Since it commanded that the sacrifices of those of the flock should not be wholly burnt, because their life is not entirely holy but divided, as it were, between God and the world, it rightly sets apart those chosen for sacred service and places them in a higher rank. It says that the sacrifice for them must be wholly burnt, with the fine flour that is brought being burnt as incense to God morning and evening, that is, through the whole day and at every season. For the one who has been chosen is in some way always holy and has an unceasing fragrance (spiritual fragrance, clearly). He is not divided between God and the world, as some are, but attends on his own Master constantly and without distraction, devoted to him wholly and entirely, and crying out, as it were: “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” So the tenth of fine flour would be a sign of a life that gives off a fragrance to God at every season.
