But it says that he shall offer it on a griddle, mixed with oil, and in broken pieces. In a riddle, I think, the griddle signifies to us painfulness; the mixing with oil, abundance in cheerfulness; and the broken pieces, the tender and, as it were, easily broken state of the hearts of the saints. For a life that is completely and wholly holy will certainly be accompanied by labours, by abundance in hope toward God, and by a heart that is thoroughly easily broken, since an unbroken heart would be the least fitting thing. For it is written: “A broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” But the devil's heart is set hard like a stone, like an anvil that cannot be beaten out; for so Holy Scripture says. The law also extends to all time, being fulfilled in the successions of those who serve as priests. For they must follow the good repute of those who went before them and show themselves imitators of their fathers' glory, walking in the footsteps of their worship and bringing to God the fragrance most dear to him, not partially but wholly. This, I think, is the meaning of “Every sacrifice of a priest shall be wholly burnt.”
So we shall offer ourselves and be dedicated to God for a fragrant aroma, following in the tracks of the life of the saints and keeping to their sacred services, the spiritual ones, clearly.

Certainly, Palladius. But wiping away defilement and escaping sin could not come about or be found in anyone except through Christ alone, in whom and through whom is all cleansing, who endured the saving slaughter on our behalf. One can learn this, and without going far, from the neighbouring ordinance that is joined to it, which runs thus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the sin offerings before the Lord; they are holy of holies. The priest who offers it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tent of witness. Everyone who touches its flesh shall be sanctified. And if any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment, whatever it is sprinkled on shall be washed in a holy place. And the earthen vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken; but if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, he shall scour it and rinse it with water. Every male among the priests shall eat them; they are holy of holies to the Lord.” The victim for sin, then, would be none other than Emmanuel, who is the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. He is slain in the place of the whole burnt offering. For Christ is not holy partially, as we are (for he committed no sin), but is wholly fragrant and sacred, and supplies sanctification to all others. For even though he was reckoned among the lawless and, in the divine plan, was numbered among the condemned, the Father knows that the death of the Son is holy and sacred. That is why it says: “In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall also slaughter the sin offering; it is holy of holies.” For just as the Son is God of gods, so he is also Holy of holies, himself sanctifying the whole creation by his own Spirit, inasmuch as he is by nature from the Father and is truly God. It says that the priest who brings the sacrifice shall eat it. For each of those brought into the sacred ministry, I think, will gather the fruits of his own labours and harvest the reward of his own ministry. The remainder of the sacrifice is eaten in holy places and in the court of the holy tent. For the mystical things are offered in the churches, and in them the chosen race is counted worthy of the holy table of Christ. Wherever a lawful priest serves, the place will be holy. The sacrifice and the sprinkling of the blood sanctify the one who touches them. For we approach the holy things for no other reason than to partake of the holy Christ through the ineffable and spiritual sacrifice. The vessels that serve the sacrifices are also purified, so that things that have served holy rites should not belong to anything else or be put to human uses. This law has been kept and is preserved in the churches. And that blessing is fitting for those who act manfully, the law again makes clear, saying: “Every male among the priests shall eat them.”
The meaning is clear.

In addition, he lays down how the manner of the sacrifice, that for sin, I mean, may be carried out rightly: which parts of it are to be food for those who minister, and which are set apart for a fragrant aroma. For it is written thus: “And all the sin offerings, some of whose blood is brought into the tent of witness to make atonement in the holy place, shall not be eaten; they shall be burnt up in fire. And this is the law of the ram for trespass; it is holy of holies. In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the ram for trespass before the Lord. And he shall pour the blood at the base of the altar all around; and he shall offer all its fat from it: the loin, and all the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat on them, that which is on the thighs, and the lobe on the liver together with the kidneys; he shall remove them, and the priest shall offer them on the altar as an offering to the Lord; it is for trespass. Every male among the priests shall eat them; they shall eat them in a holy place; they are holy of holies. As the sin offering, so also the trespass offering; there is one law for them: the priest who makes atonement with it, it shall be his.” He forbids the inner parts of the victims to be made into food. For it must, he says, be dedicated to God alone and offered to him. This, I think, is what “it shall be burnt up in fire” indicates: that it is to be dedicated and [?] plainly assigned to the divine nature alone, which is above all things, and of which fire is a type. When the ram of trespass is sacrificed, the blood is poured at the base of the altar; for the death of Christ is holy and sacred, and fragrant too. For the inner parts are offered up: the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver. These, I think, as I have also said elsewhere, would serve as a type of virtue, not of one virtue but of many kinds. For the ways of virtue are very many. We have therefore been justified in Christ, who endured death for us and dedicated himself for a fragrant aroma to the God and Father. And that we shall not minister to God without reward he makes clear, saying immediately next: “And the priest who offers a man's whole burnt offerings, the skin of the whole burnt offering that he offers shall be his; and every sacrifice that is prepared in the oven, and every one that is prepared on a grill or on a griddle, shall belong to the priest who offers it. And every sacrifice mixed with oil, and every one not mixed, shall be for all the sons of Aaron, to each an equal share.” This law too is preserved in the churches, and it ensures equality among those who officiate, distributing to each without distinction the portions of the bloodless sacrifice. Knowing this, Paul writes: “So also the Lord commanded that those who attend the altar should live from the altar.” And those who offer the sacrifices are sharers in the altar, as he himself again says somewhere.
So it is.

He also regulates the sacrifice of praise and prescribes how it should be done, saying: “This is the law of the sacrifice of salvation which they shall offer to the Lord. If he offers it for praise, he shall offer along with the sacrifice of praise six [?] loaves of fine flour kneaded with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and fine flour mixed with oil. With leavened loaves he shall offer his gifts at the sacrifice of praise of salvation; and he shall bring one of all his gifts as a portion set apart for the Lord. It shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the sacrifice of salvation; and the flesh of the sacrifice of praise of salvation shall be his. And on the day it is given it shall be eaten; they shall not leave any of it until morning.” He commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves, although elsewhere he said clearly and plainly: “All leaven and all honey you shall not offer to the Lord your God. As an offering of firstfruits you shall offer them to the Lord, but they shall not be placed on the altar for a fragrant aroma to the Lord.” Would you not say, then, Palladius, that close inquiry into these things is profitable?
Very much so.

Come, then, let us say what the meaning of this arrangement might be, inquiring into it as far as we can and taking the hidden path. Very much in keeping with the law, the divine David, striking the spiritual lyre, says: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord,” expressly calling the sacrifice of praise the cup of salvation. We too bring our praise, as a multitude in the churches, in unity of spirit, brought together through faith as into one body and one soul; for it is written: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul.” But we also often offer our doxologies one by one, quietly in our homes, both by day and by night; and this is a regular practice among the godly. Or is what I say not true?
How could it not be?

Whether the victim is offered by us as a multitude in the churches, or the rite is performed in other places, by one person perhaps, or by two or three or even more, those who are accustomed to sing hymns and have gathered for this purpose stand together without distinction. For together with those already cleansed through holy baptism, the catechumen too joins in offering up the victim; and after he has joined with the perfect in offering praise, he withdraws from the more mystical rites and is excluded from the sacrifice in Christ. That is why the law rightly foretold this arrangement and commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves and with unleavened wafers, each of the things named, I think, signifying a kind of life. The leavened bread will be a type of a way of life not yet cleansed through holy baptism, nor wholly freed from worldly uncleanness; the unleavened wafer, of the life already washed clean in Christ through faith, that of the perfect, I mean, to whom the divine Paul also called out, saying: “So let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” And again: “Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.”
Excellently said.

Besides these, the fine flour, which has not yet been brought into unity, as it is in a loaf or a wafer, but still remains, as it were, in grains, hints at those who offer praise individually, each on his own. For we are acceptable to God when we offer our doxologies, both each of us separately and all together as one, as a multitude. Oil is poured on the sacrifice of praise, signifying the cheerfulness of the act, and that mercy from God will in every way and by all means follow for those who are accustomed to offer it. For it says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” And the disciple of Christ writes somewhere: “Is anyone among you discouraged? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms.” So he clearly prescribed that the sacrifice of praise be performed with leavened loaves, with unleavened wafers, and with fine flour still in grains. One of each is offered, and of the fine flour as it were a single handful; a sheep is slaughtered and its inner parts are sacrificed according to the law, and the rest is food for those appointed to officiate, the law thus showing that the priesthood is not without gain. And he further commands, saying: “On the day it is given it shall be eaten; they shall not leave any of it until morning.” From this, again, one may perhaps understand something like this: when the time has gone by, and the present age has passed like a day, another manner of glorifying God will be devised for us, beyond those we know. For when they had been set free from Pharaoh's tyranny, they rejoiced and said under the law: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.” But some of the saints, foreseeing in the Spirit the achievements of our Saviour's coming, which are incomparably more splendid and surpassing, cried out: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” And this was: God has gone up with a shout, having despoiled Hades and said to those in bonds, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” In the same way, I think, when death has been abolished and sin wholly undone, there will be a manner of praise befitting that time. For we shall sing of greater things, and, enriched with good things beyond mind and speech, we shall crown Christ, the giver of all good things to us, with more splendid praises, together with the God and Father. For, it says, “as for prophecies, they will be abolished; as for knowledge, it will cease. Now we know in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will be abolished.” And indeed Christ himself said somewhere: “I have spoken these things to you in figures; but the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly about the Father.” Since, then, there will in due time be a more perfect knowledge in us, we shall also sing our hymns more loftily than now.
The argument is persuasive.

Having laid down for each sacrifice the rule that suits it, and having explained very well how it is to be performed, he at once makes the officiating priest a sharer in the altar. For it is written as follows: “And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You and your sons and your father’s house shall receive the firstfruits of the holy things; and you and your sons shall bear the sins of your priesthood.” Then, adding that they must attend to their sacred duties with an alert and sober mind, he says: “And behold, I have given you charge of the firstfruits from all the things consecrated to me by the sons of Israel; I have given them to you as your portion, and to your sons after you, as a perpetual ordinance. And this shall be yours from the consecrated holy things of the burnt offerings: from all their gifts, and from all their sacrifices, and from every trespass of theirs, and from all their sins, whatever they render to me from all the holy things, it shall be yours and your sons’. In the Holy of Holies you shall eat them; every male shall eat them, you and your sons. They shall be holy to you. And this shall be yours from the firstfruits of their gifts, from all the offerings presented by the sons of Israel. I have given them to you and to your sons and to your daughters with you, as a perpetual ordinance; everyone who is clean in your house shall eat them. Every firstfruit of oil, and every firstfruit of wine and of grain, their firstfruits, whatever they give to the Lord, I have given them to you. All the first produce that is in their land, whatever they bring to the Lord, shall be yours. Everyone who is clean in your house shall eat them. Everything devoted among the sons of Israel shall be yours, and everything that opens the womb of all flesh, whatever they offer to the Lord, of man or of beast, shall be yours. But the firstborn of men shall surely be redeemed with a ransom, and the firstborn of unclean beasts you shall redeem; and its redemption shall be from a month old; the valuation is five shekels, by the holy shekel, which is twenty obols. But the firstborn of calves, and the firstborn of sheep, and the firstborn of goats you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall pour out their blood against the altar, and you shall offer up the fat as a burnt offering, for a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And the meat shall be yours, as is the breast of the offering; and like the right shoulder, it shall be yours. Every portion set apart from the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel set apart for the Lord, I have given to you and to your sons and to your daughters with you, as a perpetual ordinance; it is a covenant of everlasting salt before the Lord, for you and for your offspring after you.” From this too, then, you understand, I think, and quite clearly, that he has plainly assigned every kind of sacrifice and offering to the sacred and chosen race, including what comes “from every trespass and from all sins”, that is, the victims offered for every trespass and sin. For the name given to victims offered for sin is “sin”. That is why our wise Paul too applied the term of the law to Christ, saying: “We beseech you on Christ’s behalf, be reconciled to God; for him who knew no sin he made sin for us.” For the Son was sacrificed for our sins, according to the Scriptures, as an innocent lamb. That the law gives the name “sin” to the victims offered for sin, God will make clear when he says through the prophet concerning the priests: “They shall eat the sins of my people”; that is, what is offered for the sins of my people shall be food for the priests. He therefore allots to them the remainder of every sacrifice and orders that it be eaten, but only in a holy place, he says, and by every male. What the reason for this is, we have already said. But in the passage we have just gone through, the firstfruits of oil, grain and wine, the redemption payments for the firstborn, and indeed the devoted things, are no longer to be eaten by males only, nor in the holy court, but rather in the priest’s house, and they are available for the enjoyment even of the daughters, and of every acquaintance and close member of the household. And the distinction is one that must be observed. For the remains of the sacrifices are fitting for the use of the sanctified alone, and are not to be common food; and a holy place is what befits them. But the remaining things, which have been brought in the manner of gifts, he takes as having, so to speak, a secondary standing; and they will be available to the whole household of the priests, provided only that a person is clean, that is, not profane: according to the law, not uncircumcised, not a foreigner, not a leper, not one with a discharge; but according to the intent of the new Letter and the safeguarding of the Church, not unholy and unbelieving, but devout and God-loving. For it is above all fitting that those who have been brought into the divine priestly service should love to associate with those who are good in character and whose minds are full of love for God. And by adding to this, “It is a covenant of everlasting salt before the Lord, for you and for your offspring with you,” he commanded that what he said elsewhere too be kept without fail: “The salt of the Lord’s covenant shall not be lacking from your sacrifices. With every gift of yours you shall offer salt to the Lord your God.” The sacrifice was sprinkled with salt, the figure signifying that it must be consecrated to God with understanding, and so, as it were, make the offering most savoury to him. For bread will not be eaten without salt, as it is written. “You are the salt of the earth,” Christ declared to the holy apostles.
Well said.

These, then, are the laws by which the sanctified ought to perform their priestly service. But those who have been chosen, and have received the best of lots for themselves, must keep away from profane company and from worldly care, under which even a well-steadied mind may grow drunk and all but be shaken loose toward outlandish pleasures. This he will make clear when he says in Leviticus: “You shall not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter the tent of witness or approach the altar, so that you may not die; it is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the unclean and the clean. And you shall teach the sons of Israel all the ordinances which the Lord has spoken to them by the hand of Moses.” Observe, then, that they must be watchful, and that to lay hands on the sacred service with a darkened mind and an anxious heart, drunk with worldly drunkenness, brings death; for some are drunk without wine. For at times the mind, unable to walk straight, wanders off toward what is unseemly; the sacred rites collapse, and what is done is no longer done in good order but is scattered as though off the straight road. Those who suffer this must offend God and endure bitter penalties for their negligence. So it is necessary to be watchful, shaking off the drunkenness that comes from worldly care. The Saviour himself urges us to do this, saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with anxiety and the cares of this life.” And what the way of sobriety is for us, or how we shall remain unprofaned and clean and beyond punishment, he indicated at once. For “distinguish”, he says, “between holy and profane, and between clean and unclean; and you shall teach the sons of Israel all the ordinances which the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses.” This plainly means that priests ought to shake off drunkenness and keep away from men who are not holy but profane and unclean. And one would do this, I think, quite easily if he himself is unprofaned and clean; for “every creature”, he says, “loves its like, and a man will cleave to his like.” And besides this, they ought to be wise and able to teach; for whoever is set over the rational flock must be sober and able to teach. Very well indeed does he say “you shall teach”, that is, you shall make it plain, so that the hearers may be able to perceive that the law is a tutor and speaks the mystery of Christ. For nothing in it is hard to grasp or needs explaining unless it is understood spiritually; the historical account is perfectly simple and free from the shadows of obscurity.
Further on the priesthood.

So much for now, then, about the priests and Aaron. But I think we should add to what I have said the ordinances about the Levites that seem to have been left out. That way the discussion will be complete.
Go on, then, and explain it clearly; you are thinking rightly.

In setting the best order for the sacred services, he places the Levitical rank under the high priest. He says in Numbers: “And you shall speak to the Levites and say to them: When you receive from the sons of Israel the tithe which I have given you from them as your inheritance, you too shall set apart from it an offering to the Lord, a tithe of the tithe. Your offerings shall be counted to you as grain from the threshing floor and as an offering from the winepress. So you too shall set them apart from all the offerings of the Lord, from all your tithes, whatever you receive from the sons of Israel, and from them you shall give an offering to the Lord, to Aaron the priest. From all your gifts you shall set apart an offering to the Lord, or from all the firstfruits the part of it that is consecrated. And you shall say to them: When you set apart the firstfruits from it, it shall be counted to the Levites as produce from the threshing floor and as produce from the winepress. You shall eat it in any place, you and your sons and your households, for this is your wage in return for your services in the tent of witness. You shall incur no sin because of it, since you set apart the firstfruits from it. And you shall not profane the holy things of the sons of Israel, lest you die.” Do you see the mystery of Christ, still as if in shadows, yet shining out beforehand in types? For the one who receives tithes has himself been tithed, as the blessed Paul says. In that earlier time the type was in Melchizedek. In the time of Moses it was preserved again in Aaron, who signified in himself Christ, the priest of priests, the one who leads and presides over the holy tent, that is, the Church. He is the Holy of holies and the God of gods, and all the fruit we bear is owed to him. For it is written: “All who are around him shall bring gifts.” But the things of Moses are still in types, while now the true guardians of the gospel's ordinances gladden their Redeemer with spiritual fruits.
Well said.

He shows in the following way that the Levitical tribe is chosen and set apart from the others. The Creator commanded that the people be counted and that an exact reckoning be made of the common multitude. He did not do this because he did not know their number. For the drops of rain are numbered by him, as it is written, and nothing could escape that pure mind. He did it so that those who read the sacred Scriptures might know very clearly that those who belong to God and bear the name of his people are entered in the registers kept with God, and in the book of life. They are counted among those he knows, and are already in the remembrance of the Lord of all. So the people were enrolled, but God set the chosen and sacred tribe apart, so to speak. He did not let it be ranked equally with the others anywhere, but reserved for it, as it were, the preeminent portion. He said to the most wise Moses: “See that you do not count the tribe of Levi along with the rest, and do not take their number among the sons of Israel.” For the lot of the saints is exceptional, and their privileges are preeminent. Perhaps the registration is also in other books, for the inspired Daniel saw not one book but, as he himself says, “The court sat, and books were opened.” So the registration corresponds to the measure of each person. The tribe that was allotted and dedicated to the divine services is set apart, as it were, from the rest of the multitude. He immediately made clear the manner of the Levites' service, saying: “Take the tribe of Levi and set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall minister to him. They shall keep his charges and the charges of the sons of Israel before the tent of witness, to do the work of the tent. They shall keep all the vessels of the tent of witness and the charges of the sons of Israel in all the work of the tent. And you shall give the Levites to Aaron your brother and to his sons the priests; they are given to me as a gift from among the sons of Israel. And you shall appoint Aaron and his sons over the tent of witness, and they shall guard their priesthood and everything concerning the altar and what is within the veil. And the outsider who touches it shall die.” So the Levites are assigned as fellow workers of a sort and, so to speak, as assistants to the priests. For they will keep his charges, clearly meaning Aaron's, and all the vessels of the tent of witness, and the charges of the sons of Israel. Their share in the work extends this far. But he sets Aaron over the tent, and his sons with him. “For they shall guard,” he says, “their own priesthood and everything concerning the altar and what is within the veil.” That is, they shall guard the secret and more mystical things, and whatever those who attend at the divine altar customarily do. In the strict sense the type points to Christ, whom the Father set over his house, and we are his house. Those who serve as priests with Aaron would signify quite clearly the holy and admirable choir of the holy apostles, who work together, as it were, and minister together with Christ. For they became God's fellow workers, stewards and managers of the mysteries of God, and also ministers through whom we have believed. If anyone chose to look closely at the order of the Church as well, he would rightly marvel at how the law prefigured it. To bishops, as those appointed to lead, and also to those of the lesser rank, I mean the presbyters, the altar and the things within the veil have been entrusted. It would be fitting to say of them: “And they shall guard their priesthood.” But of deacons it would be fitting to say: “They shall keep the charges of the tent, and all its vessels, and the charges of the people.” Do they not themselves give orders, calling out in the churches? Sometimes they tell the people that it is time to sing hymns, and to stand in good order, and often to keep silent. They rouse them to prayer. When the bloodless sacrifice is being performed, they themselves bring the more sacred of the vessels, and they keep careful watch over everything that is needed.
Certainly.

So those who preside serve as priests, while the Levites assist the order of the Church's priesthood, as the letter of the law proclaimed in advance. The common people are excluded from every sacred function, and the threat of the ultimate penalty hangs over those who seize this honor. For he will die, it says, if anyone comes to it of his own accord without God's choice resting on him.
True.

So the Levitical tribe is not included in the registers of the others, but it is recorded separately, and in the book of God. “For the Lord spoke,” it says, “to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, saying: Number the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, by their clans, by their kindred. Number every male from a month old and upward. And Moses and Aaron numbered them at the word of the Lord, as the Lord had commanded them. These were the sons of Levi by their names: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. These are the names of the sons of Gershon by their clans: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath by their clans: Amram and Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. And the sons of Merari by their clans: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their fathers' houses.” Observe this above all, Palladius, for the point calls for close attention. The people were enrolled from twenty years old and upward. The precision of the law did not, I think, consider what is still feeble and powerless worthy to be written in the book of God. What is vigorous and already in its spiritual prime might rightly be admitted to the rolls of the saints. So the law makes bodily age an apt figure of spiritual age. It set apart as chosen those in their prime, and passed over the immature, the weak and the still childish, without entering them in the sacred book. But for the Levites the registration began from a month old. For the Lord of all welcomes very gladly the infancy in Christ of his elect, just as he certainly welcomes their wisdom. To excel in both, I mean in understanding and in the simplicity that is in Christ, is something exceptional. So the inspired Paul says: “Brothers, do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.” And Christ himself says somewhere: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” The simplicity of the saints, then, is acceptable. The numbering is by name, and also by clans and families. For God grants his special attention to those he chooses to honor, one by one, as a body, and by kindred. The Savior himself will make clear how exact God is in these matters when he says to the holy apostles: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father in heaven. Even the hairs of your head are all numbered.”
Well said.

Besides this he further laid down that a second registration of the Levitical people should be made, and that each group should be assigned the service proper to it. He said: “Take a count of the sons of Kohath from among the sons of Levi, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, from twenty-five years old and upward to fifty years, everyone who enters to minister and to do all the work in the tent of witness. This is the work of the sons of Kohath in the tent of witness: the Holy of holies. When the camp sets out, Aaron and his sons shall go in and take down the overshadowing veil and cover the ark of the witness with it. They shall put on it a covering of blue skin and spread over it a cloth entirely of blue, and they shall insert the carrying poles. Over the table of the presence they shall spread a cloth all of purple, and on it the dishes, the censers, the cups, and the bowls for pouring libations; and the bread shall always be on it. They shall spread over it a scarlet cloth, cover it with a covering of blue skin, and insert the poles through it. They shall take a blue cloth and cover the lampstand that gives light, with its lamps, its tongs, its snuffers, and all the vessels for the oil that they use in their service. They shall put it and all its utensils into a covering of blue skin and put it on carrying poles. Over the golden altar they shall spread a blue cloth, cover it with a covering of blue skin, and insert its poles. They shall take all the utensils of service that they use in the sanctuary, put them into a blue cloth, cover them with a covering of blue skin, and put them on carrying poles. They shall put the cover on the altar and spread over it a cloth all of purple. On it they shall put all the utensils they use in their service there: the firepans, the forks, the bowls, the cover, and all the utensils of the altar. They shall spread over it a covering of blue skin and insert its poles. They shall take a purple cloth and cover the basin and its base, put it into a covering of blue skin, and put it on carrying poles. When the camp sets out, Aaron and his sons shall finish covering the holy things and all the holy utensils, and after this the sons of Kohath shall come in to carry them. But they shall not touch the holy things, lest they die.” The registration from a month old teaches that even the innocence of the saints pleases God and is acceptable to him. But only the age set by the law, from twenty-five to fifty years, was assigned to the sacred works. This shows, I think, that whatever is sensible and vigorous, both already and still, performs for God the exceptional and blameless service. A man who has reached twenty-five years is already such, and one who has gone on as far as fifty is still such. A man who has passed his fiftieth year has already begun, somehow, to decline toward the end of his strength. He is no longer in his unblemished prime, but creeps, as it were, toward the ailments of old age. No one who is unwise or feeble could minister to God blamelessly, if indeed it is true that whatever looks toward virtue is the work of strength and of an excellent mind. And it is this that has received the lawgiver's praise.
So I say.

The service of those from the clan of Kohath was the Holy of holies, and the priests went in before them and covered these things. For everywhere what ranks higher is more honored, and all things with God are in order; nothing at all is disordered. The Levitical tribe is in subordinate service, placed beneath the sacred ministry of those above it. The holy ark and the golden altar of incense, and also the lampstand and the utensils of service, are wrapped in blue skins and cloths. The blue signifies to us what is from above and from heaven, for that is the color of the upper sky in its depths. We have already shown at length that the sacred vessels are types of Christ, who is from above and from heaven. The table also has a cloth all of purple in addition to its blue wrappings. The altar of burnt offerings has a scarlet cloth, and the basin, too, has a cloth all of purple over its blue coverings. The table, which holds the loaves set out, signifies the bloodless sacrifice. Through it we are blessed as we eat the bread from heaven, that is, Christ. He became like us, yet even so he was and is God, coming from above and from the Father, and above all things as King and Lord of the universe. The purple cloth spread over the table, that is, the purple covering, would be, as it seems to me, a figure of Christ's kingship. The altar of burnt offerings was clothed with a scarlet cloth, and we shall take the scarlet-dyed cloth as a type of blood. For Christ was sacrificed for us and on our behalf, and went up like a lamb onto the divine altar as a fragrant offering to God the Father. Besides the blue, the basin's covering was a cloth all of purple. The basin depicts in itself the type of holy baptism, which washes us in holy waters to put away sin and carries us into the kingdom of heaven. Holy baptism is from above and from heaven, and the blue color is its figure. Do I not seem to you to have explained these things very well, considering how hard such contemplations are to grasp?
Certainly.

Such, then, was the service of those from Kohath. The Gershonites, and likewise the Merarites, were registered in the same way, from twenty-five years to fifty, by name, by houses and families. The service of the clan of Gershon was the skins of the tent, the coverings, the hangings for the doors, the curtains of the court, and the surplus pieces; for so it is written. That of the clan of Merari, which is also a Levitical clan, was the pillars of the tent, the bases, the capitals, the pegs and bars, the screen of the outer tent, and certain other things besides. Those of Gershon and Merari carried what was entrusted to them from place to place with the help of wagons, but the Kohathites went along carrying the Holy of holies on their shoulders. For it is written thus in Numbers: “And the leaders of Israel brought offerings, twelve leaders of their fathers' houses. These were the leaders of the tribes, who were in charge of the census. They brought their gifts before the Lord: six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon from every two leaders and an ox from each, and they presented them before the tent. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Accept these from them, and they shall be used for the work of service of the tent of witness. You shall give them to the Levites, to each according to his service. So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites. He gave two wagons and four oxen to the sons of Gershon, according to their service, and four wagons and eight oxen to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they have charge of the service of the sanctuary; they are to carry it on their shoulders.” Do you hear how the others were accustomed to transport things on wagons, while the Kohathites alone carried the sacred things on their shoulders?
Why was that?

Because what is higher and more sacred always involves more sweat. In every way and at every point it is accompanied by the need to toil, and beyond that to endure hardship, and not in equal measure with the others. This falls to those who are holier and, in a sense, nearer to God. Or is what I say not true?
Quite so.
In such order, then, the Levitical tribe performed its service. But I for my part think the matter fulfills the type of a mystery.
What do you mean?

The two clans, Gershon and Merari, seem to hint at the peoples under the law, I mean Israel. The Kohathites, on the other hand, seem to hint at those sanctified in Christ through faith. The former had charge of the curtains of the court, the skins of the tent, the coverings and the pillars, the capitals and bases, the pegs and hangings, and, as the sacred text says, “all the surplus.” That word signifies what is not essential to the service. The latter were entrusted with carrying the Holy of holies, the things through which Christ is signified. He is signified not in one way but in many ways and many forms: as ark, as table, as golden lampstand, and as golden altar of incense. For although he is simple in nature, being God, he is made known in many ways through the variety of his works. The Word of the Father is admittedly living and active, and he is also life and light and the scent of a spiritual fragrance. So all who devote themselves to the commandments given through Moses have the surplus of the tent as their service, for the law is of no benefit unless it is understood spiritually. But all who have been entrusted with the Holy of holies are surely holy in Christ. They carry nothing surplus, but bear, as it were, Emmanuel himself.
Well said.
Consider this too, if you like.
What do you mean?

Those entrusted with the surplus of the holy tent carry it on wagons. But the Kohathites carried the Holy of holies neither on wagons nor on anything else at all; they went along with it placed on their own shoulders.
What does that mean, then?

My friend, I would say it means that the law is burdensome, a load hard to bear. A clear sign of this would be that the surplus things were not carried on the shoulders, because those under the yoke were weak. That is why the inspired disciples said to those who, after coming to faith, were turning to the worship of the law: “Now, then, why are you testing God by putting a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither you nor your fathers have been able to bear?” But the Kohathites place on their own shoulders the things through which Christ is signified, and so they make the burden light and easy to carry. Is this not clearly what Christ himself said: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light”?
So it seems.

I would add this as well to what has been said, for it would help considerably toward full conviction. In the first registration of the Levites, those from Gershon were placed first, then Kohath in the middle, and Merari last; these are the Levitical clans. But in the second registration, the one from twenty-five years, Kohath is placed before the others and is named first. After him, and last, come Gershon and Merari, whose service is the surplus of the tent. Each of these two clans has only two families, while the other extends to four. Do you understand the riddle, then?
Not at all.
Israel was called first. But the flock of the Gentiles ran in ahead, and Israel was placed after it. So the last have become first, as the Savior said, and the first last.
True.
And it is clear that the Jewish people are few in number, while the countless multitude from the Gentiles far exceeds them.
Of course.

That is why God says to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: “And now let me alone, and in my anger I will consume this congregation, and I will make you into a great nation, far greater than this one.” The whole Levitical band was honoured with ministries of this kind, and the limit set on their sacred service was that they should be placed under the one who held precedence and act under the hand of Aaron. But experience itself showed that to aim higher than this, and to seek more than what God had allotted and appointed to them, brought punishment and destruction. For again it is written in Numbers: “And Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, spoke, with Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, son of Reuben; and they rose up before Moses, and with them two hundred and fifty men of the sons of Israel, leaders of the congregation, chosen members of the council, men of renown. They gathered against Moses and Aaron and said to them: ‘Enough of you! The whole congregation, all of them, are holy, and the Lord is among them. Why then do you rise up against the congregation of the Lord?’ When Moses heard this, he fell on his face, and he spoke to Korah and to all his congregation, saying: ‘God has visited and known those who are his and those who are holy, and he has brought them near to himself; and those whom he has chosen for himself he has brought near to himself. Do this: take censers for yourselves, Korah and all his congregation, and put fire in them, and put incense on them before the Lord tomorrow; and the man whom the Lord has chosen, he shall be holy. Let this be enough for you, sons of Levi.’ And Moses said to Korah: ‘Listen to me, sons of Levi. Is it a small thing to you that the God of Israel has set you apart from the congregation of Israel and brought you near to himself to perform the services of the tabernacle of the Lord, and to stand before the tabernacle to serve him? He has brought you near, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you; and do you seek the priesthood as well?’” The descendants of Kohath, whose service was to carry the holy of holies on their shoulders, ignorantly leapt at what lay above them and contended for the rank of the priests. They snatched honours for themselves, as it is written, disregarding the divine command, unholily overrunning the laws of the sacred service, and counting the honours of those set over them as worth very little indeed. For they said to Moses and Aaron: “Enough of you! The whole congregation, all of them, are holy, and the Lord is among them.” You hear how they dishonour the measure allotted to them, and all but say that the high priest's honour is common, not only to their own clans but to everyone else too, and that there is nothing exceptional or more distinguished about it at all, even if those who received the office by God's own vote might be said to stand above them. This is plainly to find fault with the decisions made from above and to count the lawgiver's will as nothing. Yet the divine Moses, with his customary gentleness, appealed to them as to men who were sick, and, perceiving how great a wrath was about to fall on them, rebuked them, saying: “Let this be enough for you, sons of Levi.” It is no small thing for you, he says, that the God of all has chosen you out of all to perform so august and admirable a service. But they remained bitter and hard, unbridled in their arrogance, until their madness brought them to such an evil end that the earth opened its mouth, swallowed them up with their families and tents, and overwhelmed them in an unheard-of destruction. For they went down alive into Hades, as it is written. It is unholy, then, and carries a sentence of death before God, to rise up against the head and refuse to yield to those who have been placed in charge and have received the preeminent honour from God. But it is the fruit of the highest understanding to take pride in whatever one has and to give thanks for it, and not to leap recklessly at what lies beyond one's measure, nor to covet what has not been given, imagining that things governed solely by the decrees from above are common and open to the many.
Well said.
So sacred things stand in an order that admits no confusion; for it is fitting that they should be so, and not otherwise.
You are right.

He assigns a sort of common allotment to both: the gifts brought by those under them, and whatever anyone offers to God as a dedication and a sacrifice, these, he says, must belong to priests and Levites alike. For the God of all spoke thus to Aaron: “In their land you shall have no inheritance, and you shall have no portion among them; for I am your portion and your inheritance in the midst of the sons of Israel.” And to the sons of Levi: “Behold, I have given every tithe in Israel as an allotment in return for their services, all the service they perform in the tent of witness. The sons of Israel shall no longer approach the tent of witness and incur a deadly sin; the Levite himself shall perform the service of the tent of witness, and they shall bear their sins. It is a perpetual statute throughout their generations, and among the sons of Israel they shall inherit no inheritance; for the tithes of the sons of Israel, whatever they set apart for the Lord, I have given to the Levites as an offering, as their allotment. That is why I have said to them: Among the sons of Israel they shall inherit no allotment.” And in Deuteronomy, going back over the same word, he says something like this: “The priests, the Levites, the whole tribe of Levi, shall have no portion and no allotment with Israel. The burnt offerings of the Lord are their allotment; they shall eat them. They shall have no allotment among their brothers; the Lord himself is his allotment, as he told him. And this is the priests' due from the people, from those who offer sacrifices, whether a calf or a sheep: you shall give the priest the shoulder, the jaws and the stomach; and the firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first of the shearing of your sheep you shall give him. For the Lord has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand before the Lord God, to minister and to bless in his name, he and his sons, all their days.” Observe, then, how the priestly race is not ranked with the people but is in a sense fenced off from the rest, not only by the practices of their service but already by the difference of their hope. To those who live a groveling life, who cling to earthly things and thirst for temporal things that pass by like shadows, it might fittingly be said: “This is your portion, this is your lot, the portion for your disobedience to me, says the Lord.” But to those who have prized a holy and blameless life and have already been chosen for their virtue, it is very well said: “In their land you shall have no inheritance, and you shall have no portion among them; for I am your portion and your inheritance, says the Lord.” Indeed, when someone once came to the Savior and asked him how he might have eternal life, he said: “You know the commandments: You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal,” and the rest. And when the man declared openly that he had kept such things, and went on to ask, “What do I still lack?”, he answered: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” Those who wish to serve God without distraction, and who think they must follow him, must therefore leave earthly things behind, make him alone their allotment, and be fattened on their hope in him, as is sung in the Psalms: “Delight in the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act.” So he sets apart the tithes for the Levites as a recompense for the labour of their service. For the labour of the saints does not go unrewarded; their honours are exceptional and their privileges splendid. “Do not be anxious,” says the Savior, “about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear; but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” Again, he calls the victims slaughtered for sins “sins.” These too would be types of Christ, who was sacrificed for us and endured slaughter in order to abolish the sin of the world; and the offerings for sin are to be eaten only by those who perform the sacred rites. For it is fitting that not unholy souls but chosen and pure ones should partake of the holy body of Christ, souls to whom one might apply the words: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession.” To those appointed to the service are reserved the shoulder and the jaws, and the stomach as well. For the chosen race must possess what is practical and active, and that is the shoulder; and also speech, clearly the speech of teaching, of which the jaws are a type; and besides this the stomach, which very aptly signifies fruitfulness. For must not the one who is truly known to God be active, highly eloquent, and also most fruitful?
Certainly.

So he made the Levitical race without an allotment, giving himself to it as its special allotment. Yet he wisely did not let it seem to be set entirely apart from the others by receiving nothing at all. Instead he measured the matter out, as it were, granting a little for necessary use. For it is written thus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses on the western plains of Moab by the Jordan, opposite Jericho, saying: Give orders to the sons of Israel, and they shall give the Levites, from the allotments of their possession, cities to dwell in; and they shall give the Levites the pasture lands around the cities. The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and the lands set apart for them shall be for their cattle and all their four-footed beasts. The lands adjoining the cities that you give the Levites shall extend from the wall of the city outward two thousand cubits all around. You shall measure outside the city two thousand cubits on the east side, two thousand cubits on the south side, two thousand cubits on the west side and two thousand cubits on the north side, and the city shall be in the middle of this for you, with the bordering lands of the cities. And you shall give the cities to the Levites, the six cities of refuge, which you shall grant so that whoever has killed someone may flee there.” For the saints are permitted, even in this world, to possess the necessities of life, as much as suffices for the necessary needs of the body. “If we have food and clothing,” he says, “we shall be content with these.” And anything beyond that is not without harm. So small towns and dwellings and surrounding fields, and these measured out, were assigned to the holy ministers. For God judged it right to act in this way: neither indulging them with more than they needed or with what leads to luxury, nor oppressing them beyond measure by excessive restriction, but usefully removing both severe want and whatever causes distress. He measured sufficiency against need. He also commands that the cities of refuge be entrusted to the Levites, placing in the care of those who perform the sacred rites the people who had suffered most and stood in need of the greatest help. Here, I think, is a type for the churches: that they should take care of prisoners. “Remember those in prison,” he says, “as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you too are in the body.”
True.

That the hope of the holy ministers is secure, and that their allotment is perpetual, he again indicated in a riddling way, somewhat like this. For it is written toward the end of Leviticus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land that I am giving you, the land that I am giving you shall rest, Sabbaths to the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, for six years you shall prune your vine and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be Sabbaths, a rest for the land, Sabbaths to the Lord.” Having prescribed the Sabbath rest, and ordered that the land be left unsown and unplowed in the seventh year, he goes on to add: “And you shall count for yourself seven rests of years, seven times seven years, and you shall have seven weeks of years, forty-nine years. You shall make a proclamation with the sound of the trumpet throughout all your land in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month; on the day of atonement you shall make a proclamation with the trumpet throughout all your land. And you shall sanctify the year, the fiftieth year, and proclaim release throughout the land to all who live in it. It is a year of release; this shall be a sign for you, and each one shall return to his possession, and each of you shall return to his family. This is a sign of release: the year, the fiftieth year, shall be for you.” What the reason is for leaving the land itself fallow, and what the year of release signifies, we shall examine at the proper time; what will be stated now is that the Levites' allotment is exceptional. Meanwhile, he writes again as follows: “If anyone sells a dwelling house in a walled city, its redemption shall last until a full year of days has passed; its redemption shall be within that time. If it is not redeemed before a whole year has passed, the house in the city that has a wall shall be confirmed securely to the one who acquired it, throughout his generations, and it shall not go out in the release. But the houses in villages that have no wall around them shall be reckoned as the field of the land; they shall always be redeemable, and they shall go out in the release. As for the cities of the Levites, the houses in the cities of their possession shall always be redeemable for the Levites; and whoever buys from the Levites, the sale of their houses in the city of their possession shall go out in the release. For the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession among the sons of Israel, and the fields set apart for their cities shall not be sold, for this is their perpetual possession.”
And what is it, then, that the law is saying? I do not understand it very well.

Listen, then. As for buildings in a town that people buy from their owners, the sellers, he says, may reclaim what they sold up to the end of one year. But if this does not happen, once the year has passed, the buyer, he says, is to be owner, and from then on beyond any written claim. If, on the other hand, it is a field or a farmstead, it may be recovered at any time, he says, provided the seller pays the buyer back the money he received. If the seller does not have the means to pay and take it back, he commanded that it be released in the fiftieth year, without the former owner paying anything. For the law counted the profits the buyer had drawn from his long possession as repayment of what was owed. These, then, are the laws God laid down for the common people. But he set the Levitical properties apart, as it were, and in a special honour of their own, saying that they are always redeemable and forbidding them to be sold outright: “For this,” he says, “is their portion and their allotment.”
Does the law's purpose, then, my good friend, go no further than this for us, and would examining it yield nothing at all of what really matters?

Then how would the law still be spiritual? And how is it not worth considering what the sacred Scripture means, and why town properties cannot be redeemed once a year has passed, while those outside, in the fields, can be redeemed at any time? But one can see that the all-wise God is not much concerned with the history as such, so long as the spiritual meanings come flowing down and the features of the truth are revealed with full precision.
Explain, then, what it is that the law is saying.

This matter of the sale, Palladius, is obscure and very steep to approach, even if one chose to consider it in purely abstract terms. Still, I will explain it as well as I can and as it comes to my mind. But let me ask you, and you tell me: for those who make a practice of ravaging cities and countries, who would be easy to capture, and without much sweat? Would you say those inside the walls of strongly towered cities, or rather those in the fields?
And who would not see that? Those in unwalled fields are the easiest to capture.

You are right. And who do you think live better and more reasonably: townspeople, who are acquainted with laws, or those brought up more rustically in villages? Surely those in the fields will look after their own safety more feebly, while those within towered cities will take the better counsel and will reckon, in accordance with law, what they need for their benefit, when the time comes for counsel and deliberation.
True, even if they too have perhaps suffered defeat.

Indeed, one might sometimes pardon those in the field for being captured and for failing to take the best counsel, for they are unwalled and less prudent than those in the cities. But one might blame the others, and quite reasonably, I think, if after warding off their enemies and keeping their own property safe from the assaults of their adversaries, they then betrayed it of their own accord and, already defeated by their own cowardice, fell into their adversaries' hands.
Well said.

Consider, then, the Jews, who inhabit the holy city, of which the God of all says: “And I will be to her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I will be her glory in her midst.” Besides this, they have also been made wise by the law. That is why they used to say: “Blessed are we, sons of Israel, because what pleases the Lord is known to us.” Would you not say, then, that such people would be very hard indeed for the assaults of the demons to break into, if they chose to live rightly and submit to the divine laws?
Certainly.

But the herds of the nations, having a more rustic mind and one easily stirred to frenzy, would fittingly be taken without any sweat at all by Satan the plunderer, being stripped of help from above and far from rich in the law that serves as a tutor.
So it seems.

So the Jews inhabit a walled city girded with help from above; they have the minds of townspeople and were not ignorant of God's will; and yet they disregarded what was fitting, carelessly threw away the allotment assigned to them, and fell from their exalted hope. Unless they sober up from their drunkenness, as it is written, and recover what is theirs while the year of redemption is at hand, that is, the coming of our Savior, they will remain forever after under the power of the buyer, that is, Satan. “For behold,” he says, “you were sold for your iniquities, and for your sins I sent your mother away.” But the multitude of the nations, being entirely without help and suffering from a rustic and ignorant mind, and therefore driven out into slavery under others, can always be redeemed, because God has pity on them. For they will regain their own allotment, called to freedom in the year of release, when Christ set all that is under the sun free from the greed of the demons, rescued it from the snares of sin, justified it by faith and sanctified it in the Spirit, cancelling by his own cross the bond that stood against us. But the Levitical properties cannot be alienated; for the allotment is securely kept for the saints, and their hope stands on a firm foundation. Thus Christ said somewhere about Mary, so eager to learn, that she had chosen the good portion, which would not be taken away from her. Yet for small and great, priest and people, and all without exception, redemption and the security of hope are in Christ.

So Israel will sell off its own allotment, because it did not recognize the year of redemption; but the nations will take possession of the hope, and through Christ there will be a recovery of the goods that belong to our nature.

That is what I say. And the God of all will put the seal of truth on our argument, signifying the same thing in another way through the voice of Ezekiel, in the measuring of the house: “Thus says the Lord: If the leader gives a gift to one of his sons out of his inheritance, it shall belong to his sons; but if he gives it to one of his servants, it shall be his until the year of release, and he shall give it back to the leader; only the inheritance of his sons shall be theirs. And the leader shall not take any of the inheritance of his people so as to oppress them and drive them from their possession; out of his own inheritance he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that my people may not be scattered, each from his possession.” Is this oracle clear to you, and can you see even its bare historical sense?
Not at all; but I would be very glad to learn.

By “leader,” Palladius, he means the high priest, the one who has been allotted to lead the peoples under him. Since suitable and exceptional allotments were assigned to the holy ministers, and he commanded that these be preserved for them forever and never be lost, he necessarily makes the following plain. If it should happen, he says, that one of the leaders, that is, of the ministers, distributes some part of his own allotment to his own children, let what was given stand firm, he says, and let the gift be inalienable for the one who received it. For the allotment does not pass to someone of another race, but from priests to holy persons. But if he should grant it to one of his servants, the recipient, he says, will not hold it securely; his allotment will certainly revert to the leader in the year of release. He further commands the minister to refrain from coveting the allotment of others; for this, I think, is what is meant by “the leader shall not take any of the inheritance of his people.” Has this explanation been enough to make the matter clear to you?
Quite enough.
Then let us go on to examine it spiritually. For the things in the law are types, and the form of the truth is engraved in the shadows.
True.
So allotments that pass from fathers to children are secure and lasting, while those that pass from masters to servants are forfeited and go back again; for that is what sacred Scripture said.
I understand.

But we who have been justified by faith have one leader, Christ, who has an inheritance of his own, that of God the Father. That is why, when he addressed him in the form of a prayer, he said, "All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them." And somewhere the inspired Psalmist sings that "having ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men." For some he appointed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; and to one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, and other gifts akin to these. In short, he enriches the souls of those who love him with his own good things. So the possession of what has been given is secure and firmly established for those who are holy ministers and free. But for those who have the spirit of slavery, that is, for those of Israel who do not accept the faith of freedom but still lie under the yoke of profane and abominable sin, even the grace given through Moses (that is, the knowledge contained in the law, which leads like a tutor toward the truth) is to be cast off and taken away. They have no inheritance at all with the saints, and no portion with Christ. "For to the one who has," he says, "more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away." That Israel is disinherited, since it did not accept the faith and was not made illustrious with the dignities that belong to freedom, the Savior made plain, bringing the force of this very law, as I think, into the open. For he spoke thus to those who had chosen to disobey: "Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." Observe, then, that inheriting is fitting for the free, and certainly not for those under the yoke of slavery; for it is sons who remain in the house, he says, and not slaves.
That is most elegantly put.

And when the law adds, "The prince shall not take from the inheritance of his people to give an inheritance to his sons," it hints at something like this: that Christ, who is our leader, would never allot to any of the sanctified an inheritance unfitting for them. For is there not, as it were, one portion and one inheritance for those who have not wholly dedicated their lives to God, and another, a special one, for those who have been chosen and have reached the lot of splendor that is in Christ?
How could it be otherwise?

So it is unseemly for the saints to seek to receive from Christ the things that befit those who are in the world and who follow a way of life that is not wholly sanctified. Rather they should seek nothing of the flesh, but everything divine and spiritual. This is how the Savior himself instructed the holy apostles to frame the words of their supplication, shaping their request very well to what befits saints. "Pray, then, like this," he says: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." So to those who ask improperly for what the leader does not give, we shall say, "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly." And that the one who says to God, "You will repay each according to his works," speaks the truth, the law again hints to us when it says, "For this reason the prince shall not take from the inheritance of his people to give an inheritance to his sons, so that," it says, "my people may not be scattered, each from his inheritance." For a particular inheritance has been prepared, as it were, for each person, and the portion God gives is in proportion to what each has accomplished. Or perhaps, one might say, it is also because it is utterly out of place for the sanctified to turn aside and covet what those who mind the things of the world possess; for these things are temporary and of the flesh, and pass by like shadows.
So it is.

So particular inheritances, and indeed cities set apart from the rest, are the privileges God gave to the holy ministers; yet he designates the one renowned Jerusalem as common, so to speak, to all of them. For he spoke thus in Deuteronomy: "If the Levite comes from one of your cities, from among all the sons of Israel where he is sojourning, as his soul desires, to the place that the Lord your God chooses, he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God like all his brothers the Levites who stand there before the Lord. He shall eat an allotted portion, apart from the sale of his family patrimony." For since God is one, those who have been brought into this office and chosen by the vote from above must everywhere join themselves to the priests. This is kept even now in the churches, and the law is honored among us. Each of those chosen for the priesthood has his own city and his own lot, yet he is received to share in the sacred ministry even if he happens to go from one city or region to another; he eats with the priests and is honored according to the laws of love. But the law seems to me again to hint at something mystical as well. Throughout the whole inhabited world there are countless regions and cities in which holy and God-loving human souls minister to God by living lawfully, conducting themselves according to the Gospel, and offering him, as it were, sacrifices for a fragrant aroma, clearly a spiritual one: faith, hope, love, endurance, gentleness, love for the poor. For with such sacrifices God is well pleased, according to the Scriptures. Yet all of these hasten together, as to one common mother, to the heavenly Jerusalem, the church of the firstborn, the beautiful city above, the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man. There we shall minister more purely, when sin has been wholly removed from us, and lion and dragon, basilisk and asp have been brought to an end. "For there," he says, "shall be a pure way, and it shall be called a holy way; no lion shall be found there, nor shall any of the evil beasts go up there." There we shall eat an allotted portion, for it is written, "You shall eat the fruits of your labors." Or is the repayment of good things not proportionate to each person's labors, even if it comes in greater measure through the Master's generosity? "For a good measure," he says, "pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap."
You have spoken rightly. But tell me this: were the Levites not permitted to perform sacred rites while they were in their own cities and villages?

Not at all. For there was one tabernacle, and one altar on which all the sacred rites were performed, and one temple in Jerusalem, which Solomon built to fulfill the pattern of that ancient tabernacle. The law flatly denies that anyone may sacrifice outside the holy tabernacle. For those who wished to do so the penalty was destruction, and the sentence of ultimate punishment hung over them. For it said clearly: "If anyone sacrifices a sheep or a calf in the camp and does not bring it to the doors of the tabernacle, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people." At that time it was altogether necessary for those who wished to sacrifice to come to the temple and to the holy city itself, and to complete the sacred rites lawfully, with those of the blood of Levi presenting the offerings. You can hear this clearly from God, who says plainly in Deuteronomy: "You may not eat in your cities the tithe of your grain, your wine, and your oil, nor the firstborn of your cattle and your sheep, nor any of the vows you vow, nor your freewill offerings, nor the firstfruits of your hands. You shall eat them before the Lord your God in the place that the Lord your God chooses for himself, you and your sons and your daughter, your male and female servants, and the Levite and the proselyte who is in your cities; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in everything you set your hand to. Take care that you do not forsake the Levite as long as he lives on the earth." For the Divine is unapproachable, and sacrifice without a Levite is unacceptable; for the Levites act as mediators, imitating the Mediator between God and men, that is, Christ. And that the Church is one and the mystery of Christ is one, and that a sacrifice not performed in the church is unlawful, indeed rejected and unable to please God, the law showed plainly by saying that the sacred rites must not be performed outside the holy tabernacle. How much care was given to such matters you will learn from this too. It was not unlikely, indeed it was true, that the many cities scattered throughout Judea were separated from Jerusalem by long distances. And how hard and laborious it was for those who wished to sacrifice the firstfruits of grain, or of oil and wine, to carry them over so long a road! The toil involved might perhaps have made some reluctant. But it would have been unseemly, indeed utterly out of place, for the beauty of the truth to be undone because the thing was difficult and not easily managed for those who lived farther off, with the Israelites failing to bring their sacred offerings to the holy tabernacle. So, in order that all the obstacles in the way might be usefully removed for us, and the law on this matter might from then on be carried out as the lawgiver intended, Moses gave instruction and interpreted the divine will in Deuteronomy, saying: "You shall set aside a tithe of all the produce of your seed, the produce of your field year by year, and you shall eat it before the Lord your God in the place that the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon. There you shall bring the tithes of your grain, your wine, and your oil, and the firstborn of your cattle and your sheep, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God all your days. But if the way is too long for you and you cannot carry them, because the place that the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there is far from you, since the Lord your God will bless you, then you shall exchange them for silver, take the silver in your hands, and go to the place that the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there. And you shall spend the silver on whatever your soul desires, on oxen or sheep, on wine or strong drink, on whatever your soul desires; and you shall eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice, you and your household, and the Levite who is in your cities, because he has no portion or inheritance with you." Do you see the skill of the law, how it levels the steep places, makes the hard roads quite passable, and eases what is very difficult? This, I think, is what is said through the voice of the prophet: "The way of the godly has been made straight, and the way of the godly is prepared." And note that the Levite is included everywhere and of necessity, the law showing us plainly that the God of all would not accept a sacrifice from an unconsecrated hand, offered in discord with the law.
Then the Levitical order is held in the very highest honor.

Entirely so, Palladius. For the priest is a type and an imprint of Christ. Emmanuel has been named the Mediator between God and men, the apostle and high priest of our confession, according to the Scriptures, who entered once for all into the Holy of Holies, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. And by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified, according to the Scriptures. Observe also, if you like, how in another way the priest is crowned with the glory of Christ. For Christ cried out to us expressly, saying, "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." And through the voice of a holy man it is set down in the sacred Writings, "There is one lawgiver and judge," while the inspired David sings that "God is judge." The lawgiver, assigning this splendid dignity to those of priestly blood, says somewhere in Deuteronomy: "If a matter in judgment is too hard for you, between blood and blood, between judgment and judgment, between plague and plague, between dispute and dispute, matters for judgment in your cities, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the Lord your God chooses there, and you shall come to the priests the Levites and to the judge who is in office in those days; and they shall inquire and declare the judgment to you. You shall act according to the matter they declare to you from the place that the Lord your God chooses, and you shall take care to do all that is laid down for you. According to the law and according to the judgment they tell you, you shall act. You shall not turn aside from the word they declare to you, either to the right or to the left. And the man who acts arrogantly and will not obey the priest who stands to minister in the name of the Lord your God, or the judge who is in office in those days, that man shall die, and you shall remove the evil one from Israel. And all the people will hear and be afraid, and will not act impiously again." You see that the law clearly charges those who choose to bring a complaint on any ground to make the priest their judge and arbiter. "But you shall take great care to do according to all that is laid down for you." For "the lips of the priest shall guard judgment, and they shall seek the law from his mouth," in the words of the prophet. The priest does not make law himself in the least; rather he conveys straight on what the lawgiver decided, expounding it impartially, and as an excellent umpire of justice he weighs each judgment with precision. For this reason a charge of savagery and contempt follows those who choose to disobey, and the penalty decreed is the one that surpasses all evils, namely death. "For whoever disregards the priest," it says, "who stands to minister in the name of the Lord God shall die." Great, then, and truly wonderful is standing before God and ministering to him. Whoever dishonors God's minister will be subject to judgment and punishment, and whoever spurns the divine dignity will pay a bitter reckoning for his contempt. We shall find that our Lord Jesus Christ himself was also concerned that this law be respected. For he addressed the crowds of the Jews thus: "The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the seat of Moses; so do whatever they tell you, but do not do as they do." So let no one judge the priest, even if he seems somewhat lax, even if he is sluggish in choosing to live according to the law; rather, let each give him ready obedience when he interprets the law. For his failings come from his own will, but what he expounds belongs to God. The things of God, then, must not be dishonored on account of what is human.
Certainly not.

That the office of the priesthood is splendid and truly conspicuous you will learn from this as well: both its beginning and its end are most notable. No one could escape notice when he is brought into the sacred ministry, or when he is called by God to the dwellings above in heaven and hands the priesthood on to another. That is why Christ also said that those who minister the proclamation of the Gospel to the nations, and also to those of Israel, would be conspicuous in every way and would receive a glory on which all eyes are fixed.
