"For no one who lights a lamp puts it in a hidden place," he says, "or under a bed or under a bushel, but on the lampstand, so that all who come in may see the light." And that this is truly said, I mean that the minister of God will be in glory, conspicuous and admired, let the inspired Isaiah also persuade you when he cries out: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion."
That these things are so is clear to anyone. But tell me how the type of this was also sketched out for us in the sacred words.

Indeed, my friend, you can see quite effortlessly how the matter is described, though still in cruder types. For God spoke thus in Numbers to the most holy Moses: "Take Aaron and Eleazar his son, and bring them up Mount Hor before the whole congregation. Strip Aaron of his robe and put it on Eleazar his son, and let Aaron be gathered to his people and die there." And Moses did as the Lord commanded him. He brought them up Mount Hor before the whole congregation, stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son, and Aaron died on the top of the mountain. Do you understand, then, how Aaron is brought up as he is about to die and come to his end, and with him the one who is to take up the priesthood after him, that is, Eleazar? The mountain would signify being visible and lofty, and conspicuous in glory. So from now on let this be said to everyone who is brought into the sacred ministry: "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden."
That those who wish to attend the churches must be pure and washed clean of the stain of sin, and so present themselves before God.

I think enough has now been said about the tabernacle, and about the priests and the Levitical ministry, and I believe it has been examined in detail. Those who choose to live rightly, and to bind on their own heads, like a crown, the complete beauty of the life in Christ, would do well to urge one another on eagerly, as it were, saying: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will declare to us his way, and we will walk in it." Then some, having heard so glorious and helpful a call, almost leap for joy, saying: "I was glad when they said to me, 'We will go to the house of the Lord.'" So then, Palladius, what is the aim of those who hurry to go into the house of God? Where is their mind looking, and what are they eager to accomplish as they make their way to the holy and divine tabernacle?
Well, my friend, the matter is not obscure. It is written: "Worship the Lord in his holy court"; and: "Take up sacrifices, and come into his courts."
So people enter the house of the Lord and his courts bringing sacrifices on their own behalf (spiritual ones, clearly), and also coming forward to offer a worship of the mind.
That is what I say.

Shall we suppose, then, that those who wish to go in should simply rush in? Should they go in without washing off their sin or freeing themselves of foulness? Should they go in without scraping off, as it were, the filth of fleshly love, with their mind still steeped in it and their heart rusted? Not at all. They should rather be adorned with the brightness that is in Christ, glittering with the many-colored beauty of the virtue most dear to God.
Certainly. I say that we must come before the eyes of the Lord only after every stain has first been rubbed out of our thoughts.

You are right, since the law treats the sick person as hateful, even as something to be cast out, and sends him away from the company of the saints. The divine Paul understood this very well when he wrote: "Drive out the wicked person from among you." I would not call this the fruit of a savage character. It is a wise device for safety. "For a little leaven," he says, "leavens the whole lump." The sacred law also foreshadowed this for us in riddles. It is written in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone with a discharge, and everyone unclean through a corpse. Whether male or female, send them out of the camp, and they shall not defile their camps, where I dwell among them. And the sons of Israel did so." Is it not true to say that the burden of the law is exceedingly heavy and really hard to bear? You see how it prescribes a penalty even for illnesses that no one chose, although people overtaken by such misfortunes ought to be pitied. One might well ask, and with good reason, why it made the leper homeless and banished him. Why did it do the same to the one gripped by the affliction of a discharge, and to the one unclean through a corpse?
I cannot see why; perhaps you will explain it yourself.

I think, then, that God had no great concern for crude, bodily matters, since through them he was prefiguring for us the divine and spiritual worship. What lies outside the law is punished, and whatever has clearly overstepped what is fitting I would call subject to judgment and penalty. But a bodily illness could in no way offend against the laws. It would therefore rightly lie far beyond any charge, and no one could have any grounds to accuse it. Or is it not clear to everyone that no one is sick willingly, and that everyone, I think, prays above all for good health?
True.

So even if the passage has something unlovely in its literal, historical sense, there is no harm, provided the spiritual meaning is worked out well according to the lawgiver's intention. Leprosy, then, is a deadening of the flesh, and a disease that devours more than any other. That is why the divine Moses, when Miriam had become leprous, was terrified and deeply disheartened, and implored, saying: "O God, I beg you, heal her." For he said: "Let her not become like a stillborn child coming out of its mother's womb, with half of her flesh eaten away." As for the discharge, why should I describe what kind of affliction it is? No one is ignorant of it. That some are unclean through a corpse means this. For the people of old, the law counted it a kind of defilement to touch one who had departed or to come near a dead body, and so it showed that deadness is hateful to God, who is able to give life to all things. The law also took the matter another way, as a figure, crude as it were, of the deadening of mind and soul. A mind that loves sin is dead and chilled, used to having no share in the noble deeds that lead to life. Yet if someone happened to die, his relatives by blood and kin had no choice but to gather and perform the customary rites over him. These too were unclean according to the law, though not wholly or forever, since there was a way for them to be purified. There you have a sufficient explanation of the history.
Certainly.

Come, then, let us transpose it into spiritual contemplation and say this. For us, the leper signifies the person spotted with the various passions of youth. These are the works of the flesh, which the most wise Paul himself listed for us, saying: "fornication, impurity, idolatry, enmities, strife, fits of anger, jealousies." The other, the man with a discharge, signifies the one who lives always and without restraint in defilements, and who squanders for nothing the aptitude nature gave him for virtuous and admirable fruitfulness.
What do you mean?

To discuss all the cases would take very long. For now I will use one clear and very vivid example to prove what I said. Take those who have a gifted mind, polished as it were, and who apply it to the teachings about the truth. Will they not bear a remarkable fruit: the beauty of correct and accurate doctrine?
Certainly.

But others do not choose to think and act this way. They turn aside from the road they ought to take and make their mind an advocate of unholy doctrines, or show it to be a servant of the wickedness in the world, and so make it a begetter of deceit and fraud. They waste nature's aptitude for the good and gain nothing useful from it. Such people give us a very good picture of the man with a discharge, and in their own ways they display a sickness of the soul that is akin to the bodily affliction.
You are right.

The one unclean through a corpse surely signifies the person who has shared in the deadness of others and has carelessly filled himself with other people's offenses. To such a person the divine David says somewhere: "If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you cast your lot with the adulterer." Doing what is unlawful ravages and deadens soul and mind, and so does approving of those who do such things. Whoever consents to the sins of those who commit them becomes their partner, and he is by no means blameless. That is why Paul too says: "Keep yourself pure, and do not share in the sins of others." This, I think, is what it means to be defiled by a corpse in the spiritual sense.
So it seems.

Was he not right, then, to command the leper, the man with a discharge, and the one unclean through a corpse to depart from the assembly? He did not allow those whose uncleanness is hard to wash away to mingle with the choirs of the saints. "For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?" as Scripture says.
Then it is dangerous to go into the house of God with unwashed feet, so to speak.

Most dangerous indeed, if it is true that no one offends God without paying for it. In Deuteronomy he also shuts others out of the holy court, saying: "One who is crushed or cut off shall not enter the assembly of the Lord. One born of a prostitute shall not enter the assembly of the Lord. An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord; even to the tenth generation he shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, and even forever. This is because they did not meet you with bread and water on the way when you were coming out of Egypt, and because they hired Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia against you to curse you. But the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam, and the Lord your God turned the curses into a blessing, because the Lord your God loved you. You shall not address them with words of peace, nor with what is to their advantage, all your days, forever."
I would like to learn who should be understood by the crushed and the cut off, and by the Ammonite and the Moabite.

Listen, then. There is not just one way of making eunuchs, Palladius. It is said, and has been found, to be twofold. Some are castrated, with their male parts torn away. Others still have them, but crushed and entirely useless. And sometimes people cruelly and wickedly cut off the part of the body that produces children. Such men are incapable of a man's functions, even though by nature and age they count as men. Now the male parts are a symbol of manliness. So we should take the crushed man to be one who has not had his manliness wholly torn out of soul and mind, so to speak, but somehow keeps it within himself in a shattered state, still directed toward good things. The cut-off man is one who has thrown it away altogether and is deprived of the qualities that best befit men. Not caring to be manly in a sound way is almost as blameworthy as refusing to be manly at all.
What do you mean by that?

Some have sunk back into fleshly desires. They have let go of all the reins, as it were, and given passion its head, flinging their mind, rotten and unmanly, to the pleasures that lead to licentiousness. Others, again, admire self-control and sometimes take up splendid efforts toward it, but they dread the struggle and cannot bear the assault of pleasure, and so they end in feebleness. Will you not rightly call the one who has wholly given up the effort toward manliness "cut off"? And will you not regard as "crushed" the one who intends to be manly but can no longer achieve virtue? In this way you elegantly transpose bodily afflictions into qualities of character, and take the things perceived by the senses as an image of things spiritual and more hidden.
Certainly.

Along with these the Ammonite and the Moabite were also shut out, as unholy and utterly loathsome. They fell on the saints like lions and showered the arrows of envy and malice on those who enjoy good repute. The Ammonites would be a type of the pitiless heretics. The Moabites, for their part, would be a type of those who still lie prostrate in idolatrous errors and under the wickedness of demons. Both are hateful to God, and both are sick with a kindred boldness against the saints.
I do not quite understand what you mean.

You will understand very well, and before long. The Ammonites, being descended from Esau, were close kin and of one blood with the sons of Jacob, that is, with Israel. Yet somehow the descendants of Esau disregarded nature itself and betrayed the bond of kinship. From then on they rushed fiercely and relentlessly against those who were close to them by blood, namely the Israelites. When Israel was leaving Egypt and passing by the land of the Ammonites, he begged the inhabitant, as a brother, to let them go by, or to let them pass through and take pity on them as people who had been wronged. But he would not yield. Why do I say only this? He even took up arms and made war. And he would have done terrible harm, had Israel not turned away at the divine bidding. The text runs as follows: "And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying: Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that has befallen us. Our fathers went down into Egypt, and we lived in Egypt many days, and the Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers. And we cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard our voice, and he sent angels and brought us out of Egypt. And now we are at Kadesh, a city at the edge of your territory. Let us pass through your land. We will not pass through fields or vineyards, nor drink water from your cisterns. We will go along the king's highway; we will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory. And Edom said to him: You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out against you in war." And after some other things: "And Edom came out against him with a great multitude and a strong hand. So Edom refused to let Israel pass through his territory, and Israel turned away from him." Is the account not clear and plain now?
Not entirely.

Do you not see that though they were joined to the Israelites by the bond of kinship, the facts themselves proved them heartless and hard, no different from wild beasts? They ought to have pitied them as brothers, toiling as they were in sweat and labor, yet they came out to ravage them. That is why the law says: "They shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, because they did not meet you with bread and water when you were coming out of Egypt." That is, they are shut out because of their utter lack of compassion and their savage ways, which had passed over into impiety. You can see that the heretical peoples and their leaders behave this way toward us who have chosen to walk straight. They have come to know one and only God the Father and to accept faith in the Son and the Spirit, though not entirely soundly. To that extent they have a false appearance of brotherhood with us, but in their way of thinking their kinship is a bastard one. When we are being persecuted they do not come to our aid. Instead they load us with their own wickedness as well. "For they went out from us, but they were not of us," as it is written. "For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us." Their gentleness is feigned, and they are not in the habit of doing what serves his glory. To them the Savior himself might very fittingly say: "Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters." Do you not think the God-hated workshops of the heretics resemble the Ammonites, sick as they are to an extraordinary degree with a lack of compassion and of love for God?
Certainly.

Consider the Moabites too, if you like. They are openly the bitterest enemies of those who wish to serve God, the one who alone is God by nature and in truth. They worshiped idols and put their confidence above all in divinations and sorceries, and they were excessively fascinated with the flights of birds. Gnashing their teeth at Israel's prosperity, they hired Balaam and arranged for him to curse. But by the ineffable power of God the soothsayer's mouth was turned to blessings they did not want. Such is the war the pagans wage against us. They envy the glory of our Savior and stir up all the strength of the devil against us. But divine grace from above shakes that strength down, pours feebleness over the herd of demons, and turns their scheming into a cause of gladness [?].
Certainly.

The holy places are barred to the Ammonites and to the Moabites as well, and very rightly. Those whose crimes are kindred and whose boldness is of the same kind should fittingly suffer equal penalties. Notice also how carefully the law protects. It removes the saints from them completely and charges them not even to want to enter into conversation with them, so to speak, saying: "You shall not address them with words of peace, and you shall not speak what is to their advantage, all your days, forever." Is this not plainly what a pair of saints, Paul and John, also taught us? The one said: "If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not greet him." And this, I think, is the meaning of "You shall not address them with words of peace, nor with what is to their advantage." The other said: "After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a heretical man, knowing that such a person is perverted." This is the meaning of "You shall not speak what is to their advantage." For the law says that we must give way to the thoroughly perverted as to madmen, saying: "Walk by the light of your fire, and by the flame that you have kindled." But the Ammonite is shut out until the third generation, and the Moabite until the tenth. By the length of time, I think, God shows us how great his indignation is against each. The heretics' penalty is lighter, as is reasonable, for one might say of them what is said of the Jews: "For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." The wretches think they speak correctly and are wise, and so they have deceived themselves without noticing. They fight against the doctrines of the truth, and in the grip of a counterfeit zeal they think they are defending God's glory when they oppose those who walk straight. But the Moabites, that is, the pagan hordes, fight against the divine glory openly and nakedly, without any concealment. That is why the law hung a heavier penalty over them. Still, both are banished from the sacred precincts as profane and hated by God.
So even being fond of talking with outsiders and people of another mind is not without harm, as far as defilement is concerned.

You understand very well. That is why the law walls off those who have been washed and made pure, and who already belong to God, from those people's foulness, saying: "And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land that you are entering to inherit, and he removes great, numerous and mighty nations before you: the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations, numerous and great and stronger than you; and when the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, then you shall strike them down and utterly destroy them. You shall make no covenant with them, and you shall show them no mercy, nor shall you intermarry with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son. For he will turn your son away from me, and he will serve other gods." So the law is a safeguard. "You shall make no covenant with them," it says. What is still profane cannot be reconciled or joined with what has been sanctified. Neither can what lies in mist and darkness be joined with what has been enlightened, nor the unacceptable with what has been accepted, nor what is thrust out of the holy and divine tabernacle with one who goes into it.
Then what is the law's forethought in this? Why does it separate the pure entirely from the profane in this case too, even when someone stands firm in virtue?

Because the fear is very great, my good man, that even one who seems to stand firm might somehow be shaken in an unfitting direction and carried away from what is proper. Perhaps someone might force him, or pleasure might provoke him, or the inclination toward wrongdoing that lies within our nature might drag him down into it. Our nature always leans somehow toward the bad, and the divine word bears witness to this for us: "For the mind of man," it says, "is intently set on evil from his youth." If you wish, I can give you a clear proof: what the story tells us the daughter of Jacob suffered.
You mean Dinah, I suppose. I think so.

Exactly, Palladius. It is written thus in the book of Genesis: "And Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, when he returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he camped in front of the city. And from Hamor the father of Shechem he bought, for a hundred lambs, the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent. And he set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel. Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to observe the daughters of the inhabitants. And Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the land, saw her. He took her and lay with her and humbled her. And his soul was drawn to Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the maiden and spoke to the maiden according to her mind." Observe, then, that while she still lingered and lived in her father's tent, where he had called upon the God of Israel and where a venerable altar had been raised, she was still undefiled and still in the glory of her virginity. But when she ran out of her father's tent, left the sacred place and mingled with foreign women, she was at once forced into an unaccustomed defilement and was no longer a virgin. At first she was subjected to another's pleasures against her will, but afterward she came to the point of wanting to be with the man who had taken advantage of her. For "he spoke," it says, "according to the maiden's mind."
So it is.

Then let us set what the senses perceive alongside as an image of spiritual things, and say this. A soul that lives in an exceptional way of life as in a tent will be all-holy and pure and free of all foulness. But if it should go out somewhere and hurry after the daughters of foreigners, that is, if it should search into and pry into the life of those who are in the world, it will corrupt its gifted and noble mind. For those whose aim is to live splendidly, living alongside the base cannot be without harm. The divine David, however, was never found wanting to go outside the holy tabernacle. On the contrary, among the things he prayed for most was to linger in it and dwell close by, saying: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple. For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of my troubles; he sheltered me in the hidden place of his tabernacle." By the divine and holy tabernacle, I think, he means here the steadfast and unshakable firmness of the holy way of life. Having entered into it, as it were, he could not be captured by the passions that wanted to ravage him.
So it seems.

What then? Would one not learn more clearly and more truly that dealings with foreigners can sometimes bring about the very worst defilement, even in those believed to stand firm, if one cited as proof the end of Solomon's life and what happened to him on the very threshold of old age?
What do you mean?

He was so illustrious and celebrated that he won a glory beyond all comparison. Yet he passed over into what is ugly; or rather, he leapt down ignobly to the very last extreme of impiety toward God. Here is his story. It is written in the First Book of Kings: "And Solomon was magnified above all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom. And all the kings of the earth sought the face of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which the Lord had put in his heart." But this man, so renowned and celebrated, who had advanced so far in wisdom that he was a source of boundless wonder even to the most discerning, was prised loose by pleasure in wicked women. It drew him, as it were, out of the divine tabernacle itself and cast him into the pits of idolatry. For this is what is written about him: "And King Solomon loved women, and he took foreign wives, and the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabites, Ammonites, Idumeans, Syrians, Hittites and Amorites, from the nations of which the Lord had said to the sons of Israel, 'You shall not go in to them, and they shall not come in to you, lest they turn your hearts away after their idols.' To these Solomon clung in love. And he had seven hundred wives who were princesses, and three hundred concubines. And when Solomon was old, his foreign wives turned his heart away after other gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father. And Solomon went after Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians, and after their king, the idol of the sons of Ammon; and Solomon did evil before the Lord, and did not follow the Lord as David his father had." Does not the man said to have suffered such things deserve to be lamented? He who raised up that famous temple in Jerusalem, who asked for the wisdom that sits beside the divine throne, who was admired for his incomparable understanding to the very ends of the earth beneath heaven, who shone like the morning star upon cities and lands, was overcome by shameful women. He went after a most loathsome pleasure, and he is caught having fallen into such folly that he utterly disregarded piety toward God itself. Beyond dispute, then, it is perilous to keep company with foreigners. It is also a most terrible thing to be overcome by fleshly pleasure. Such a person is unclean and hateful to the all-pure God, and without virtue he cannot enter the holy and divine tabernacle. Nor could he offer an acceptable sacrifice. For it is written in Deuteronomy: "There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no fornicator among the sons of Israel; there shall be no tribute-payer among the daughters of Israel, and none made to pay tribute among the sons of Israel. You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God for any vow, for both are an abomination to the Lord your God."
How severe the law is, and yet how very profitable!

Well said, Palladius; you understand rightly. I think you would be still more astonished if you considered that, by firmly blocking the smooth road to pleasures, the law drives away the licentious and the unbridled. See how it lays its charge both on those who wish to practise shameful defilement willingly and by their own choice, and on those who usually bring others into it by compulsion. By what it forbids them to do, it makes them safer, and it leaves them hard put to find any argument strong enough to defend themselves. For the charges are no longer charges of ignorance. From now on the indictment is for negligence and an insubordinate mind.
What do you mean?
Do not some people turn to fornication of their own accord? And do not women and youths who want to earn wages sell the bloom of their youth to other people's incontinence?
Yes.

And what of this? Are not some overcome by shameful gain? They hand over their maidservants to anyone who wants them, or the males they may have happened to buy, and so these wretches make money. Of them the prophet says: "And they sold the girls for wine, and drank." For it is true that some sink to such a pitch of baseness and impurity that at times they impiously dare to levy tribute even from shameful things like these.
I understand.

So some commit fornication willingly: they are carried away into the evil themselves and go to it by their own decision. But the "tribute-payers" would be those who, as of necessity, pay tribute to others and gather the wages of licentiousness for those who bought them.
You are right.

The law, then, forbids the practice entirely. It declares unholy anyone convicted under this charge, shuts him out of the holy tabernacle, and at once makes the divine altar inaccessible to him, saying that his sacrifice will not be received and his vow will not be accepted. For it is true that vows paid from a prostitute's hire are not pure. In the same way the law makes the price of a dog hateful and utterly abominable. By "dog" I think it means someone ready for impurity who simply throws himself at anyone who approaches. The "price of a dog" is what is perhaps paid to him in exchange for himself. So let the law cry aloud: "There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no fornicator among the sons of Israel." And let the most wise Paul join in, shouting: "Flee fornication. Every sin a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body." And let him also call those who nobly spring toward the glories of self-control to strive after better things. For he said again: "I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is, what is good and pleasing and perfect." Or would you deny that putting away shameful things is a truly holy and all-pure sacrifice?
I would certainly call it that; how could I not?

When we depart from fleshly pleasure, God rejoices. But he is greatly displeased with those who turn aside to weakness, and he brings punishment on those who choose to fall back after the flesh. For hot and unbridled pleasure sometimes drives a person by force even to apostasy from God. That this is true, the account of Solomon would at once show. But before him Israel is found to have been led astray into this very thing in the wilderness. For it is written: "Israel stayed at Shittim, and the people were profaned by committing fornication with the daughters of Moab. And they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices and worshipped their idols. And Israel was initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor, and the Lord was angry with wrath against Israel. And the Lord said to Moses: Take all the leaders of the people and make an example of them to the Lord before the sun, and the wrath of the Lord's anger will turn away from Israel." Do you see how the divine and most gentle nature is in a way provoked by us, and is all but driven to anger against its will? For the thing is fit for beasts: I mean going mad over the beauty of women. It is utterly unholy, too, to dare to take unbridled pleasure in exchange for piety toward God. That is why they are made an example to the Lord before the sun; that is, they were hung on upright stakes turned toward the east. This was the form of their punishment, and the figure all but cries out plainly and declares that no one caught in such offences could escape the all-seeing and undeceivable eye of the judge, or get away unpunished. Instead, as the prophet says, he will lie as a spectacle to all flesh, suffering bitter penalties for his wrongdoing.
So by "before the sun" it means being punished openly and, as it were, being made an example in the sight of God.

Exactly. And our discussion has not strayed from its aim. Those who commit fornication, or who have been prostituted, must give account to God for so cold and profane a life; hidden things are manifest, and what is in each person will be plainly known. The lawgiver sketched this for us once more through another law. For it is written in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If any man's wife goes astray and, scorning him, disregards him, and someone lies with her and has intercourse with her, and it is hidden from her husband's eyes and she conceals it, and she is defiled, and there was no witness against her and she has not been caught; and a spirit of jealousy comes upon him and he is jealous of his wife, and she is defiled; or a spirit of jealousy comes upon him and he is jealous of his wife, and she is not defiled; then the man shall bring his wife to the priest, and shall bring the offering for her, a tenth of an ephah of barley meal. He shall not pour oil on it nor put frankincense on it, for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, a sacrifice of remembrance, which brings sin to remembrance. And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the Lord. And the priest shall take pure living water in an earthenware vessel, and some of the earth that is on the floor of the tabernacle of witness, and the priest shall take it and put it into the water. And the priest shall set the woman before the Lord and uncover the woman's head, and he shall put into her hands the sacrifice of remembrance, the sacrifice of jealousy; and in the priest's hand shall be the water of proof that brings this curse. And the priest shall put her under oath and say to the woman: If no one has lain with you, if you have not gone astray to be defiled while under your husband's authority, be free from this water of proof that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray while married, if you have been defiled and someone other than your husband has lain with you — and the priest shall put the woman under the oaths of this curse, and the priest shall say to the woman — may the Lord make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the Lord makes your thigh waste away and your belly swell. And this water that brings the curse shall enter your belly, to make your belly swell and your thigh waste away. And the woman shall say: So be it, so be it. And the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of proof that brings the curse, and he shall make the woman drink the water of proof that brings the curse. And the cursing water of proof shall enter her. And the priest shall take the sacrifice of jealousy from the woman's hand, and shall set the sacrifice before the Lord and bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take a handful of the sacrifice as its memorial portion and offer it up on the altar, and after this he shall make the woman drink the water. And if she has been defiled and has utterly escaped her husband's notice, the cursing water of proof shall enter her, and her belly shall swell and her thigh waste away, and the woman shall be a curse among her people. But if the woman has not been defiled and is pure, she shall be innocent and shall conceive seed." So far the law. I would say that the divine Paul neatly gathers up what is written here in a few thoughts when he writes to us: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad."
I think this is rightly said. But explain to me in detail each of the things ordained.

The woman suspected of adultery, when she faces a charge without proof, he commanded to be brought to the priest and to stand before the eyes of God. This, I think, signifies that all are to stand before Christ. Next, the offering brought for her is barley meal, not sprinkled with frankincense, not moistened with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy that brings sin to remembrance. It is clear, then, that from each person's life a kind of odour rises, as it were, to God. For those who have let themselves slide into negligence, it brings an indictment for every outrageous deed; for those who have striven eagerly to live rightly and well, it bears witness to their genuineness. That is why we say, and with good reason, that the offerings of those not under suspicion consist of fine wheat flour, with frankincense added and oil poured over it. For a life that is properly human, of which fine wheat flour would be a figure, is sure to be reckoned as fragrant and cheerful by God, who loves virtue. But barley meal would be a very clear sign of a bastard life, fit for beasts. For it is somehow more like a beast, and not at all fitting for a human being, to be incontinent in appetite and to want to rush unbridled into outrageous pleasures. That is why the woman accused of a bastard life brought barley meal to God, without frankincense and oil, that is, without fragrance and cheerfulness; for it is a sacrifice that brings sin to remembrance. And where sin is remembered, how or from where could cheerfulness come? For the one on trial is not hoping for crowns but fearing punishment and fire. Besides this, the woman is brought before the judge with her head uncovered, that is, not in her usual and fitting adornment. And what could the reason for this be? The charges are of indecency, and the indictment is for abomination. Remember that Paul, being learned in the law, does not allow a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered, citing the law of nature as proof that she must be covered: "For her hair," he says, "is given her as a covering." So the woman, accused of indecency, was no longer adorned. She is uncovered in another sense too. For all things are naked before the eyes of the judge, and no one at all could escape the notice of him who searches hearts and minds, as he says through the prophet's voice: "I am a God near at hand, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?" But again, the law hints in a riddle that Christ is the judge. For it said that living and pure water must be put into an earthenware vessel, together with some of the earth that is in the tabernacle. Then, when the words of the curse had been washed off into the water, it ordered the woman suspected of fornication to drink. And if she is guilty of the charge, it says, her belly will swell and her thigh will waste away; but if she is free of the accusation, and what was suspected of her is not true, she will conceive seed.
What, then, is the meaning? Or how could Christ be signified to us by the things just named?

By the living and pure water you will understand the life-giving Word of God, who is truly pure and has no share in sin at all, and who came to be in flesh as in an earthenware vessel. For how or on what grounds could anyone doubt that flesh is dust and from the earth? By the earth from the tabernacle you will understand him who entered death for our sake; for it was said to human nature: "You are earth, and to earth you will return." And by the words of the curse you will rightly understand him who became a curse for us by being hung on a tree. For it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." So when Emmanuel, who is God by nature, penetrates to the depths of the human mind, he will convict and punish those guilty of offences; but those not caught in them he will make fruitful. For this, I think, is the meaning of "she will conceive seed": the bodily condition signifies the fruitfulness of the soul.
Excellently said.

Fornication and the passions of the flesh debase a person and estrange him from intimacy with God; for "those who are in the flesh cannot please God." By "flesh," I think, he means the fleshly mind; that is how the text would be rightly understood. But in addition, a bent toward baseness, a savage cast of character, and a decline into every kind of outrage make us abominable and unholy. For it is not enough for us merely to conquer fleshly passions. We must also excel in gentleness of character, show ourselves most attentive in love toward the brothers, and be seen crowned with the glories of righteousness. Besides this, we must keep a subtle and well-trained mind within ourselves, one that approaches teachings about God without distortion and in every inquiry into doctrine preserves what is blameless. Such people are perfect, truly lacking none of the highest goods. For the divine Paul also told us that the man of God must be complete; and by "complete" he means one equipped for every good work and well fitted to achieve virtue successfully. Or is that not so?
Of course it is.

See, then, how the law, sketching human characters in riddles, brings in many irrational animals, as well as kinds of birds and water creatures, and so benefits us in countless ways. And do not be surprised at this, since at times it compares us even to plants, according to the natural quality of each, neatly indicating what belongs to each of us. For God said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, hinting at the fragrance (clearly, spiritual fragrance) and the lofty virtue of those who through faith in Christ have blossomed into life: "And I will make living water in the desert, and rivers in a dry land, and I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box tree, the myrtle, the cypress and the white poplar." And again: "And instead of the thornbush the cypress shall come up, and instead of the fleabane the myrtle shall come up." By "thornbush" and "fleabane" I think he aptly names souls that are still untamed and appear like wild thorns in the eyes of the Godhead. Sometimes, too, the venerable company of the saints is compared to stones: "For holy stones are rolled upon the earth." And the Saviour said that the kingdom of heaven is like leaven and like a mustard seed. So it is the custom of divinely inspired Scripture to make human things plain through many very vivid examples.
I agree.

Observe, then, that Scripture usefully brings forward countless kinds of animals, as well as birds and swimming creatures. Some it condemns altogether as unclean, while others it accepts and clears of reproach. It does this so that those who serve God may rightly know what conduct would make them unacceptable, and what they must wisely avoid in order to be far from blame, to shine, to be worthy of acceptance, and to be honoured by the verdict from above. The law on this reads as follows: "And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say: These are the animals that you may eat from all the animals on the earth. Every animal that divides the hoof and has its hoof cloven in two, and chews the cud among the animals, these you may eat. But of those that chew the cud, and of those that divide the hoof and are cloven-footed, you shall not eat these: the camel, because it chews the cud but does not divide the hoof; it is unclean for you. And the hare, because it chews the cud and does not divide the hoof; it is unclean for you. And the rock badger, because it chews the cud and does not divide the hoof; it is unclean for you. And the pig, because it divides the hoof and is cloven-footed, but does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not eat their carcasses; they are unclean for you." Now Christ says very plainly: "It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person." And it was said somewhere to the inspired Peter, when the sheet was let down from above by its four corners, with all the four-footed creatures and birds pictured on it: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." When the disciple cried out, still fearing the observance of the law, and said, "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean, nor has any profane meat entered my mouth," God spoke again: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." And the inspired Paul writes: "Food will not commend us to God." So it is not at all unclear that the law is far from declaring anything that exists profane; rather, it knows that to the pure all things are pure. Instead, it takes the natural character of each animal and applies it skilfully to the qualities of human character, and so benefits us greatly. You may learn from this, too, that what I say is true and beyond doubt. For the law is seen to command that creatures condemned by everyone be loathed: I mean the camel and the rock badger, the night raven and the cormorant, the gecko and the shrew, and things even more disgusting than these. Is not the lawgiver's aim plain in these, my good friend?
Certainly.

Then the traits naturally present in certain irrational animals must be carefully transferred to the qualities of human character. Each animal, so to speak, portrays in itself the manner of some type of person and indicates what that person's traits are. Or are we ourselves not somehow in the habit of calling those who are very hot-tempered, very strong and bolder than others boars or lions or something of the sort, and of calling the gentle and quiet, who have a humble mind, sheep and doves, and sometimes of crowning them with the name "Calm"? In this way we apply to each person's manners a fitting designation drawn from more obvious things.
True.
Let us go on, then, to the aim of the law, and inquire very carefully into what exactly it enjoins.
Let us go on.

The glories of righteousness, and in a word of all goodness, spring, it may be, from each person's own will. But they are accomplished, I think, in two ways, and so they have in themselves a twofold expression.
What do you mean?

Either we do some good toward ourselves: cutting away pleasures that are unnatural and blameworthy, putting to death our members that are on earth, settling the mind into gentleness in the Spirit, practising poverty, and keeping our mind pure and unclouded as far as we can. Or else we carry out good efforts toward our brothers: showing guilelessness to those who have chosen to hurt us and have offended against us without love, helping the sick, comforting the grieving, turning back to the straight path those who have strayed through ignorance, leading them by the hand toward what is better, supplying the needy, and being very eager to accomplish whatever God would take pleasure in. Is not the way of righteousness, then, in some sense twofold, accomplished both toward ourselves and toward others?
So it seems.

The law, then, always likens such a person to a split hoof, that is, a cloven foot. For the foot would be a symbol and type of our journey of practical action. Indeed we say that those who are very eager to go blamelessly toward what brings benefit pass along with an upright foot. And David sings somewhere, "For my foot has stood in uprightness", that is, "I have walked in righteousness and uprightness, and I have hated what is perverse." And of those who love sin he says, "Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their ways." So the foot is a symbol of our walk in deeds. And the cloven hoof would be a clear type of our being able to walk rightly and irreproachably on both sides: in what concerns ourselves, and also toward others.
The argument is persuasive.

Suppose, then, there is someone who knows how to walk rightly and skilfully on both, able to benefit both himself and others in the quality of his conduct, I mean. Suppose that he is also sensible and very wise, and gives his heart to the words about God as a kind of lodging and dwelling place, always turning over within himself, this way and that, the meanings of the divine doctrines, and for that reason searching them out often and wisely, grinding fine, so to speak, the thoughts he has come to know so exactly. He will surely be like an animal that brings up the cud: it is always bringing back up the food in its belly and putting it under its teeth, so that it may be ground still finer and, made fine for digestion, pass on to its benefit.
You put it well.

The law says that an animal is clean if its foot ends in a cloven hoof and it also brings back up the cud from its belly. For a person who is by nature excellent and good toward himself and others, and who has also acquired a love of learning and practice in knowledge (knowledge of God, clearly), will be complete in virtue and blameless in all that concerns himself, with respect to everything that is admired. And if someone should come to share in such a man (through learning from him, I mean), and as it were feast on his teaching, and become his imitator and choose to emulate one so distinguished and exceptional, he will be unprofaned and pure. For he will be living with one who is pure, and he will at once show his own character to be an impression, as it were, of the other's understanding and love of good learning. This, I think, is what it means that we must eat of every animal that by nature divides its foot into a hoof and brings up the cud. For the law says that such are clean, according to the explanation just given.
I understand what you mean.

So the law has pointed in a riddle to the excellent person who is perfectly fitted for virtue, using an animal that is cloven-hoofed by nature and brings up the cud. Again, it enjoins that it is good and profitable to make a habit of shaking off anyone not of that mind, anyone who limps, as it were, toward the good and lags behind on the way to perfection in virtue. It does so by giving its approval neither to those that bring up the cud without having the cloven hoof, nor to those cloven-hoofed by nature if they lack the cud. Instead it records them as unclean and counts them among the things that defile. Thinking rightly, then, and recasting what was said in riddles into the truth, we affirm that the cloven foot is a type of practical activity and of the quality of one's conduct. And we define the cud as a sign of reasoning in accord with piety, and of doctrinal knowledge that is correct and well practised. Or is it not so?
Certainly it is.

It follows that a person who boasts of good works but falls short of doctrinal correctness, and does not hold the words of truth in his mind, would rightly be considered incomplete in virtue and far from deserving admiration. And it is true that the reverse is just as plain: doctrinal correctness and the sweet care for the divine words would do nothing to give us a reputation for perfect virtue unless the brilliance of good works were joined to them. For the one who is skilled in both will carry off the verdict of perfect approval, while the one who lacks either will have only a feeble claim to be admired for goodness. The Saviour too indicates something of this kind when he says that the one who teaches but does not also do will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, while the one who has both done and taught will be great and distinguished. So according to the law, the one who falls short in either is unclean. And that we ought to keep away from such people and in no way be seen to have any share with them, he made clear by saying, "You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses." For, he says, you shall not associate with them while they live; and if one of them should happen to die, you shall keep your own mind unprofaned, not so much as touching, so to speak, what they have produced, namely their sayings and their foul writings. For such things are the remains of a man's life. This is just what the uneducated heretics are in the habit of doing. Those who became leaders in the ignorance that is in them have admittedly gone astray, and they have handed down to their own disciples the remains, as it were, of their own impiety. The disciples receive these very gladly and lodge them in their minds, and so they carry a defilement that is hard to wash off, as if they were touching the flesh of carcasses, which is full of the foulest stench and uncleanness.
True.

As an example of what does not divide the hoof but does bring up the cud, then, the law takes the camel, a strong and huge animal, and the hare and the rock badger, which are the most insignificant-looking of practically all creatures. By naming the extremes, I think, it takes in everything together and leaves out none of those in between. It is as though it said: from the very lofty and highest down to the small and the very lowest, everyone of this kind is abominable and unclean. For there is no partiality with God, as it is written. If someone is great and imposing, raised on high by wealth and worldly glory, he will receive an inglorious and dishonourable verdict if he is held guilty of the charges of wickedness. If someone is small, living in poverty and obscurity, he will be condemned as unclean unless he can boast of virtuous ways. Nor could anyone make his lowly state an excuse, claiming that the just Judge must have pity on him, when he lacks good works, that is, works of piety and virtue. So the camel, and the hare and the rock badger, would be no obscure type of the small and the great. The law also puts forward the pig as unclean, because it divides the hoof but is not also made by nature to chew its food again, that is, to bring up the cud. In this way it shows that boasting in works, apart from reasoning in accord with piety, is feeble and useless. For just as faith without works is dead, so too, conversely, good order and decency in works are surely dead when knowledge of God is absent and reasoning in accord with piety has not taken up residence in our souls. Such goodness stays below; it bends down toward the earth and seems somehow afraid to lift its eye upward. We will find not a few who have suffered something of this kind. Sometimes they lead a dignified and pure life, yet they have not come to know the God who is God truly and by nature, and they fix the eye of their mind, as it were, only on the things of the earth. Such a person too is unclean, for no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules, as it is written.
So it defiles us, then, under the figure of the pig and indeed of the others as well, if we are liable to the charges the law brings.

You have spoken quite rightly. And the law is not content to set before us images of the unclean through these creatures alone, or ones like them. Having chosen to benefit us through the whole of creation, as it were, and richly setting before us knowledge of what is useful and fitting, it also goes through the kinds of creatures that live in the water and the flocks of birds. Its purpose is that, by inquiring very carefully into what is natural to each, we may be able to perceive what is pleasing to God and what he rejects and hates, and so, pursuing a life wholly in keeping with the law, we may make a most vigorous escape from everything that usually defiles. So the law spoke again, in this way: "These you shall eat of all that are in the waters: everything that has fins and scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, these you shall eat. But everything that has neither fins nor scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, of all that the waters belch forth and of every living creature in the water, is an abomination, and they shall be abominations to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall abhor their carcasses. Everything among those in the waters that has neither fins nor scales is an abomination to you."
But what the difference is between these, according to spiritual contemplation I mean, you yourself will have to explain. For I do not understand it at all well.

Certainly. I will tell you as best I can, recasting into plain terms what the law has taken up by way of examples. All the creatures in the waters that the Creator of all has fashioned so well according to the pattern of fish row along, as it were, with the strokes of their fins, and move strongly and very swiftly wherever they choose. When the sun sends the warm impact of its ray down into the waters from above, they swim up and all but venture to leap out of the waters themselves, refusing to stay always below; and they easily slip through the nets of those who hunt them. But those that have no scales and fins, that is, those that live in hard shells and are clothed in a shell grown onto them, know very little of what is above. They always burrow down into the weed below and love muddy places. They are feeble and easily caught, and anyone who has once spotted them can take them without breaking a sweat. That is a clear and true account of the creatures themselves. Now let us move on from images and types to plainer things.
Please explain it, by all means, and go on gladly.

Signifying for us, elegantly, the distractions of this life and the bitter flood and confusion of affairs in it, the Psalmist sings, "This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number, small creatures together with great." For fish are a very apt likeness of those who dart here and there, sometimes for nothing that is needed or of benefit, and gather up only those things that can make them carnal and prepare them to endure pointless labours.
You put it well.

The disciple of Christ also rebukes people of this sort, saying, "Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a city and spend a year there, and trade, and make a profit.'" And a little later: "Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.' But as it is, you boast in your arrogance." So we swim like fish through this broad and spacious sea, that is, the world; for each person's life is different. Some have not altogether given themselves over to sin. They do know weakness at times, being caught up in the greedy desires of the flesh, and they do not choose to keep clear of other faults either; for we all stumble in many ways, as it is written. Even so, they shake off as unseemly any desire to behave shamefully in the open. No one could persuade them to sin openly and without cover; they take great care to escape notice. For the wise will hide their own shame, as it is written. This, I think, is what it means to have scales serving as a covering. And they often swim up to the heights, for they do not always look downward but also set their minds on things above, and they easily escape those who would like to net them for destruction. This, one might say, is to use fins in a spiritual sense and to make the movement of the mind fervently warm.
What you say is reasonable, for the riddle does somehow lead one to think that this is its meaning.

But some sin without any restraint, practising wickedness naked, as it were, and completely uncovered. Of them it may well be said, "Their glory is in their shame." They always incline toward uncleanness, wallowing in the lowest mire, and they are in truth mere brute creatures, or something of that kind. Such people would be wholly and utterly feeble and easily caught, tyrannized as they are by pleasures in every kind of outrage. Or is not the life of the reprobate something like this? Prostitutes and harlots, the utterly shameful and most counterfeit tribe of effeminate men, those who shine on the stage, those whose love of the flesh cannot be satisfied, and those who love to stray into profane idolatry: all these live a truly accursed life, one that sinks to the most shameful defilements. So the law declares clean those who have been weak in human ways but have not turned away altogether; who swim up, as it were, toward the heights; who have not settled down among earthly things alone but have also set their minds on things above, being divided, as it were, between God and the world. But it declares unclean those who go wholly over to choosing, without ceasing, to do and to think the things of the flesh and the world, who have stripped off all shame in these matters and are used to behaving shamefully naked and uncovered. And it usefully removes us from fellowship with these, while not disparaging fellowship with the others. For it is not safe to walk alongside the wicked, but it is safe to walk with the more upright. For it is written, "He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be known for it." And Paul too writes, "If anyone who is called a brother is greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a one."
Well said; the point certainly contributes to our benefit.

This, then, is what the law says to us in riddles about swimming creatures and those that live in the waters. Then, widening, as it were, the range of examples it sets before us, it goes on to the flocks of birds, saying, "And these you shall abhor among the birds, and they shall not be eaten; they are an abomination: the eagle, and the griffon, and the sea eagle, and the vulture, and the kite and its kind, and the ostrich, and the owl, and the gull and its kind, and every raven and its kind, and the hawk and its kind, and the night raven, and the cormorant, and the ibis, and the purple gallinule, and the pelican, and the swan, and the heron, and the plover and its kind, and the hoopoe, and the bat. And all winged creeping things that go on all fours are an abomination to you. But these you may eat of the winged creeping things that go on all fours: those that have legs above their feet with which to leap upon the earth. These you may eat of them: the locust and its kind, the attakes and its kind, the snake-fighter and its kind, and the grasshopper and its kind. Every winged creeping thing that has four feet is an abomination to you, and by these you will be defiled. Everyone who touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening." Is the meaning of these words clear to you?
Not in the least.
Do you not see, then, that, just as with the others, the natural properties of each of the creatures named would be images of characters and of different kinds of conduct?
What do you mean?
Would you like us to discuss them in turn, distinguishing each one carefully?
By all means.

The law, then, rejects the eagle, the griffon, the sea eagle, and the vulture too. For these birds fly through the heights, love to glory in the very highest places, and despise what is below; for it says, "The young of the vulture fly in the heights." Such, in a way, is the boastful and excessively haughty person, who has a puffed-up mind within himself, is accustomed to look down on a modest and moderate way of thinking, and has not the least liking for keeping company with the lowly. Along with these it also condemns the kite and its kind, and the raven and its kind. By these is clearly signified the race of men who know how to seize what belongs to others and are clever at wrongdoing: the kite is a type of the first, and the raven, the blackest and darkest of birds, of the second. For those who are keen in wickedness are somehow dark and not evident to everyone, keeping the depravity of their character hidden from most people within themselves. And those sick with accursed arrogance always have this growing alongside it: the desire to take advantage of whomever they can, to besiege them with all sorts of wicked devices, and so to plunder them, and that insatiably. That is why the law at once adds, "and the ostrich and the gull". For these, I think, are the most insatiable of birds, always gathering up whatever comes their way. Then it says, "and the hawk and its kind, and the night raven, and the cormorant, and the ibis, and the purple gallinule, and the pelican, and the swan". These in turn would depict those who cruelly and savagely plot against others and fasten upon whomever they can without restraint, so that they do not even shrink from bringing danger and fear for their lives upon some. For the hawk swoops fiercely on every weaker bird, goes after sparrows, and kills them once it has seized them; while the cormorant, the ibis and the gallinule, and I would add the pelican too, rage against fish and make their destruction their food. Such, in their ways and in the savagery of their character, are all those who think nothing of destroying others for the sake of their own pleasure. They have thrust aside the law of mutual love and offended against the ordinances of charity, and they would rightly hear this from us too: "Do not seek your own interests, but those of others; for love," it says, "does no wrong to a neighbour." Again, the law said we must reject the owl, the heron, the plover and their kind, the hoopoe and the bat. These, I think, are lovers of the night: they delight in darkness and have made a practice of flying in it as their greatest pleasure, while they hate the light of the sun and cannot bear to do anything in it. Such would clearly be the workers of evil. For what Christ said is true: "Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds may not be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be revealed as having been done in God." Also unclean, it says, are the winged creeping things that go on all fours, such as, for example, flies and anything close to them. These are countless, small and contemptible, and incapable of flying to any height. What reason the law had for coming down even to these is something we must look into. When it was speaking of the beasts, after naming the camel it added the hare, showing that those charged with wickedness are equally unclean, whether great or small (for there is no partiality with God, as it is written). In the same way here, it mentions the eagle, naming the most kingly of birds, and then comes down again to the smallest of the creatures that bear wings, putting small and great on the same footing if one is a doer of outrageous deeds and cannot escape being condemned. It does, however, exempt from this class the grasshopper and the locust and those like them, because of their strength, which enables them to leap up: they do not in the least love to linger below, but often rise up on high and spring about with ease. Such, in a way, is the person who lives a worldly life but has not wholly lost his share in other kinds of goodness and in love for God. Such a person is not completely bound to earthly things or settled among things below, but has in some measure made a practice of setting his mind on things above, and at times wins approval as he leaps up toward the heights and flies above earthly things. But whoever touches the unclean and is defiled must wash his garment, and toward evening, the law says, he will be clean. In this it very clearly points to the mystery of Christ, through whom we have been cleansed, being enriched with forgiveness through holy baptism at the time, evidently, of his coming among us. That coming took place, as it were, toward evening, that is, when the present age was already moving toward its end. Or do we not say that the Word of God became man in the last times?
Certainly we do.

The law also says that a person becomes profane in another way: whoever touches, say, a wild beast, or any other of the unclean animals. It spoke as follows: “And everything that walks on its paws, among all the beasts that go on all fours, is unclean to you. Everyone who touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening, and whoever carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. These are unclean to you. And these are unclean to you among the creeping things on the earth: the weasel, the mouse, the land crocodile, the shrew, the chameleon, the spotted lizard, the lizard, and the mole. These are unclean to you among all the creeping things on the earth. Everyone who touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until evening. And anything on which one of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether any wooden vessel, or garment, or skin, or sack. Every vessel with which any work is done shall be dipped in water, and it shall be unclean until evening, and then it shall be clean.” To this he added that every vessel on which any of their carcasses falls will be defiled: an earthenware jar, a leather vessel, a garment, food and drink, except, he says, a spring of water, a cistern, a gathering of water, and seed. Now by the wild beasts the law seems to indicate the most savage of robbers, who count as nothing even murder, the evil beyond all evils, and who all but devour whoever crosses their path, destroying without pity, with all mercy stripped away. By the mouse and the weasel, and the creatures near and like them — I mean the land crocodile, the lizard and the gecko — it indicates the timid and unmanly kinds of thieves who prowl about at night. They love to do harm to people secretly while they sleep, but they are terribly afraid of being caught and shun the wakefulness of those they wrong. For are not the weasel and the mouse most thievish things, and easily frightened? Do they not dive into their holes in the ground if anyone makes a noise? And would not the land crocodile and its kin most gladly forage by night rather than by day?
True.

Everything, then, that has to do with robbery is unclean, whether a man is beastlike in his ways and has bloodthirsty hands, or whether he pilfers small things, like the mouse and the weasel, and scales walls and roofs after the manner of the mole and the gecko. And if anyone touches those who are defiled in this way, he will share in their guilt, for fellowship with such people makes a person unclean altogether and in every respect. The defiled vessels would stand as a type of human beings, for a man is a kind of vessel. Yet the law exempts a spring of water, a cistern and a gathering of water from having to be defiled, even if something defiled under the law should happen to fall into them. I think it does this so as not to let those under the law regard the matter as utterly burdensome and hard to bear, and find the keeping of the law impracticable, since in this case they would suffer harm in what is most vital. For then they would sometimes have to abandon cities and houses, because their water had been defiled and its necessary and indispensable use taken from them. So the law relaxed strictness in the literal matter for the sake of what was necessary and useful to those under the law.
That is a convincing explanation.

He says that the carcass even of clean animals is unclean, just as the others are, and adds that it too will defile anyone who touches it. He writes as follows: “If one of the animals that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until evening; and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening, and he shall bathe in water and be clean. And whoever carries its carcass shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.” This, I think, plainly means the saying: “If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber, do not even eat with such a person.” For if anyone at all among those held in repute for holiness, already cleansed and received through faith into spiritual fellowship, undergoes the deadness that comes from sin, let him be loathsome, it says, and hateful; for being defiled by dead works, he surely defiles whoever clings to him. But if anyone does incur the defilement, let him be made clean through water toward evening. And what this means the word has already clearly shown us. Notice that it says that the one who eats of their carcasses will be unclean, and so will anyone who merely touches them. It does not acquit of blame and accusation the one who shares in their deadness, nor indeed does it declare anyone guiltless who even comes close and draws near. For I think we must soberly keep away not only from doing the same things as the wicked, but even from merely keeping company with them. “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled,” it says, and the saying is true. That the law adopted what is useful in these examples for the shaping of character can be learned from what follows. For it said again: “You shall not make your souls abominable with any of the creeping things that creep on the earth, and you shall not be defiled by them, and you shall not be unclean through them, for I am the Lord your God.” For what defilement could the death of an animal, or touching the dead creature, cause to a human soul? What harm could food do, which goes into the belly and is expelled into the drain, as the Savior said?
None, I think; you understand it rightly.

So I say that, like the most skillful sailors who leave no rope untried, we must get clear of defilements and steer into the life most pleasing to God as into a calm, waveless shore. For he could become approachable to us in no other way than this alone, and it is easy to see that this is true. For again it is written in Exodus: “Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the sheep into the wilderness and came to the mountain of Horeb. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, ‘I will turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not consumed.’ When the Lord saw that he drew near to look, the Lord called to him out of the bush, saying, ‘Moses, Moses.’ And he said, ‘What is it?’ And he said, ‘Do not come near here. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.’” Do you see, then, that no one could come near the all-pure God without first washing every stain from his own soul, and freeing his foot from all the deadness found in deeds — that is, his spiritual walk toward what he ought to do? For is not a sandal the remains of a dead animal?
Of course.

So the sandal is a type of deadness. If anyone lays this burden down and breaks the bonds that would bring him to ruin, he will come near to God and become his intimate, and will moreover be fit to save others as well. Thus Moses was appointed to his mission and to the redemption of the children of Israel. And a sacred word has told us: “Son, if you become wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbor.”
Well said.
Well then, shall we not add that other point to these?
Which one?

When the God who rules over all was about to descend in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai, Moses was commanded to make Israel ready to see God. The manner of their preparation the Master of all himself laid down. For the Lord said to Moses: “Go down and solemnly charge the people, and purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their clothes, and let them be ready for the third day; for on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.” So those who long for intimacy with God must first be purified, as must those whose aim is, as it were, to stand beside him and serve him with strength and eagerness for every good thing. Such a person would then not be unfit even to behold God himself in some way, as the Savior said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” You will see the divine Abraham too, if you like, advanced to this same splendor. Come, let us recount in turn what concerns him. It is written thus: “And the Lord said to Abraham, ‘As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. And this is the covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations: every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male child among you shall be circumcised at eight days old, throughout your generations, both the one born in your house and the one bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring. The one born in your house and the one bought with your money shall surely be circumcised. So my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be utterly cut off from its people, for he has broken my covenant.’” Then it says: “And Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all those born in his house, and all those bought with his money, every male among the men of his house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskins on that very day, just as God had told him.” What, then, was the reward of his obedience, and in what way did circumcision benefit him? We shall learn from what follows. For God appeared to him, it says, by the oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent at midday. “And he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men stood over him. And when he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them, and bowed down to the ground, and said, ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let some water be brought, and let them wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. And I will fetch bread, and you shall eat, and after that you shall go on your way, since you have turned aside to your servant.’ And they said, ‘Do as you have said.’” For circumcision in the flesh would be a very clear type of the spiritual circumcision in the Spirit, by which Christ removes all defilement from our minds. For we have been circumcised, in the words of the blessed Paul, “with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the flesh.” For having stripped off, as it were, the old self, which is corrupted by deceitful desires, and having all but cut away the pleasures of the flesh by the keenness and power of the Spirit, we shall show ourselves already in some measure worthy to be granted the sight of God and to become a holy lodging of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this generation — I and the Father will come and make our home with him, and lodge in him,” said the Savior. Nor does the recompense for goodness stop there. Being now received into intimacy with God, we shall come to know the things that are in him, clearly through his own revelation, just as the divine Abraham was taught about the overthrow of Sodom; for God shared his counsel with him as with a friend. Observe, then, how countless are the good things that leaving defilement behind would bring us in return. That is why Paul too says: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship.” And the prophet Jeremiah also cried out plainly: “Wash your heart clean of wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved.”
So we must approach the all-holy God, not with a profaned soul, but with a holy and blameless life. In this way we shall come straight to what is fitting.

Exactly so, Palladius. And it will not take much effort, I think, for you to see that the argument on this point holds true, if you choose to study the lives of the saints eagerly and with a mind attuned to them. For the divine Paul said that what happened to the ancients as types was written down as admonition for us. That we must approach God clean and washed, then, one could learn thoroughly from the following as well. Dinah, Jacob's daughter, being a virgin of marriageable age, went out from her father's tent to look at the daughters of the people of Shechem. But Shechem son of Hamor would not leave her in peace. He at once fell in love with the girl and was swept by unrestrained desires toward what he fancied. Going about it in a brutish way, this foreigner, still uncircumcised, forced the Hebrew virgin. Jacob's sons found the matter unbearable, and they brought the law of war against those who had so impiously outraged a Hebrew woman and their sister.
