The divine Jacob was distressed and became very fearful, suspecting that his whole family would be wiped out. But God took him up and saved him once again, and it is worth seeing how. It is written thus: “Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, ‘You have made me hateful, so that I am odious to all the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number; they will gather against me and cut me down, and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.’ But they said, ‘Should they treat our sister like a harlot?’ And God said to Jacob, ‘Arise, go up to the place Bethel and live there, and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.’ And Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, ‘Put away the foreign gods that are among you, and purify yourselves, and change your garments; and let us arise and go up to Bethel, and let us make there an altar to the God who heard me in the day of my distress, who was with me and kept me safe on the way by which I went.’ And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands and the earrings that were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree at Shechem and destroyed them, to this very day.” You see that the Master of all took up the righteous man in his terror and commanded him to build an altar for a fragrant aroma, a splendid offering for the salvation and help that was to come to him. And Jacob, recognizing clearly that this had to be done, ordered them first to purify themselves, removing the falsely named gods from their midst and changing into other garments. This, I think, at once signifies sincerity in faith and a life free from profanation. To love to cleave to God single-mindedly, with a mind undivided and not inclined to be sick with the remnants of the demons' deceit, would rightly be understood in the removal of the foreign gods; and the changing of garments would mean putting on, as it were, a pure way of life. For the most wise Paul saw fit to write in the same way. Or do you not hear him say plainly: “Put off the old self, which is corrupted by deceitful desires, and put on the new self, which is being renewed after the image of its creator”? And by “the putting off of the flesh” he means laying aside the pleasures of the flesh. Solomon too writes somewhere: “Let your garments be bright at all times.” I would say, and I think I have understood it quite rightly, that our wise Solomon would never descend to such trifling as to urge us childishly to revel in bright clothes; rather, he compares to a bright garment a life that has been, so to speak, washed and set free from all filth. Otherwise, how could anyone put on our Lord Jesus Christ? Would you not say, my friend, that one who is clothed with the glories of the gospel way of life accomplishes this completely?
Certainly.

And if one turns to the celebrated Joseph himself, he will find that he neglected nothing of virtue, but understood that God would work with him in everything whatsoever and come to his aid, if only he utterly refused to be defiled. For although he could have lived at his ease and indulged himself freely in luxuries, letting himself run with the fiery leaps of youth toward whatever was sweet and pleasant and be carried along by unchecked impulses, he did not do this — far from it. Instead he counted the portion that is with God the better one, and preferred the labors of self-control to everything that fattens for the moment. For he knew that the stirring of the flesh is sweet at first, in a way, and bewitches the mind as if with honey, since there is pleasure in such things; yet in the end it is no longer sweet. For punishments and penalties at once, and every evil of that kind, will hang over the head of the one who has sinned. Would you like us to recount a few of the things written about him?
By all means.

“Now Joseph,” it says, “was handsome in form and very fair to look upon. And after these things his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, ‘Lie with me.’ But he refused, and said to his master's wife, ‘Because of me my master pays no attention to anything in his house, and he has put everything he has into my hands. There is nothing in this house greater than I, nor has he kept anything back from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this wicked thing and sin before God?’ And though she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie with her or to be with her. But one day Joseph went into the house to do his work, and none of the household was inside, and she caught him by his garments, saying, ‘Lie with me.’ And leaving his garments in her hands, he fled and went outside. And when she saw that he had left his garments in her hands and fled and gone outside, she called the people of the house and said to them, ‘See, he has brought in a Hebrew servant to mock us. He came in to me, saying, “Lie with me,” and I cried out with a loud voice. And when he heard that I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garments with me and fled and went outside.’” Do you see how the woman tried to force him into bed against his will, while his mind stood firmly fixed on self-control, overcome by nothing at all? He was still a big boy, barely seventeen or so, with the first growth of beard, at the height of the pleasures, amid the most fiery stirrings and, so to speak, harsh and undisciplined desires. For youth as a class is always somehow given to unbroken impulses of craving, and does not readily bear the bridle of self-control. But the divine Joseph was unshaken. He did not have the undisciplined slackness of youth, nor was he afraid because he was a foreigner and a servant — he had been forced into both by his brothers when they sold him to the Ishmaelites. Since he proved stronger than that most abominable pleasure and the impulses toward licentiousness, the woman slandered him and turned the charge back against the young man; the one who would not yield to her demands she called an assailant. From then on the young man was a prisoner; but he was preserved by divine grace, and soon won, as the reward of his self-control, rule over the whole land of Egypt. So even if the matter involves labors, even if heavy toil lies ahead on the way to the glories of self-control, it is of little account to one who has chosen to love God wholeheartedly. For he will have — yes, he will have — praise to match and rewards of equal weight. That is why the divine David also marvels at the most praiseworthy young man for his endurance in this, saying: “Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; his soul passed through iron.” By “iron,” I think, he means the hard and unbreakable onset of toils, through which one can subdue sin, depart from all filth, and attain the holy and most pure life — I mean the life of the gospel and in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
That we must stand before God pure and washed clean, and that our cleansing, again, is in Christ.

From every line of argument, Palladius, we have gathered a clear and evident proof that we must go into the house of God in the most fitting way, bright and washed clean, and gaining closeness to him through sanctification. For then we shall find God gracious, watching over our affairs, so to speak, with his whole eye and granting the care most fitting for the saints. "To whom shall I look," he says, "but to the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?" For truly the one who is so disposed will lift up holy hands, and his cry will reach the very ear of the Godhead, so that, having obtained whatever he may pray for, he will say in great joy: "He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears." Or have you not plainly learned this from the divine David, who sings to us that "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer"?
I have.

It is not right to doubt that the saying is true. But how are we to go about wiping off our defilements? For no one understands his own transgressions, and we all stumble in many ways. Our nature is sick with a readiness to sin, and is very easily carried away into wrongdoing, since our inclination toward what is base in some way smooths for us the road of outlandish and loathsome pleasure.
You speak well. I would agree without hesitation with one who has chosen to speak rightly.

For the flesh that is from the earth has already fallen sick with the law of sin within it, and the human mind is very easily swayed to turn aside toward evil from youth, as it is written. That is why the sacred word rightly frowns upon us: "All have turned aside," it says, "together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one." But since there was no turning away from evil, God the Father sent us his own Son from heaven as Savior and Redeemer, to justify by faith and release from punishment, to make the feeble exceedingly strong, to enlighten what was darkened, to turn back what was straying, and to drag what had been made subject to the devil's greed out of his grasp.
In Christ, then, we shall wipe off the shame that comes from sin, and, thus scrubbed clean and keeping as far as possible from every blemish, we shall approach the God and Father through him.

You understand very well. One can hear the holy prophets themselves proclaiming aloud this grace, so admirable and so longed for. The most wise Micah says something like this: "Who is a God like you, taking away iniquities and passing over injustices for the remnant of his inheritance? He has not kept his anger as a testimony, because he delights in mercy." And another says: "Remember these things, Jacob and Israel; do not forget me. For behold, I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like darkness." One could gather a great many passages from the divine Scripture that show very well the truth of these matters, but to pile up more on things that clear and evident faith already accepts is, I think, superfluous.
That the matter is evident is clear to everyone. But for my part I would like to examine the cleansing in Christ also from the figures of the law.

Look, then, if you please, and let us proceed in this way. The law commanded those who were defiled and those liable to charges of transgression to offer sacrifice, and it distinguished two kinds of sacrifice. Some depict Emmanuel slain on our behalf; others depict us ourselves dying to the world and offering up to God our own life and salvation as a fragrant aroma. For do we not live the divine life of the gospel by putting to death our members that are on earth and freeing the mind from worldly distraction and from more earthly pleasures?
Certainly.

So the sacrifice is the spiritual cleansing effected, as it were, in the death of Christ, while the vow and the gift, on our part, consist in dedicating to God an orderly and holy life. The law specifies beforehand and clearly testifies that the offerings in these matters must be without blemish, and that for good and necessary reasons. Since some of the victims offered signified Christ as slain for us, while others prefigure us as all but burning our own life as incense to God, it says for this reason that they must be unblemished and in no way afflicted with any defect. For Christ is unblemished, since he committed no sin; and God would not accept us either while we are still in our defilements and sick with the foulness of sin. So it is written in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons and to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, and say to them: Any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes who have joined them in Israel, who offers his gifts in fulfilment of any of their vows or as any of their freewill offerings, whatever they offer to God as a whole burnt offering, what is acceptable for you is an unblemished male from the herds, from the sheep, or from the goats. Anything that has a blemish in it they shall not bring to the Lord, because it will not be acceptable for you. And a man who offers a sacrifice of deliverance to the Lord, whether to fulfil a vow or as a freewill offering or at your feasts, from the herds or from the sheep, it shall be unblemished to be acceptable; there shall be no blemish in it. One that is blind or broken, or has its tongue cut, or has warts, or a malignant itch, or ringworm, they shall not bring these to God, and you shall not give any of them as an offering on the altar to the Lord. A calf or a sheep with its ears cut or its tail docked you may make into slaughter-offerings for yourself, but it will not be accepted for your vow. One with crushed testicles, or squeezed, or castrated, or torn, you shall not bring to the Lord, and you shall not do this in your land. And you shall not offer any of these as gifts to your God from the hand of a foreigner, because there is corruption in them and a blemish in them. They will not be accepted for you." See, then, that the law clearly and openly instructs both those of Israel's blood and those who came from outside and were admitted among the people (I mean the proselytes) that the sacred offerings must be very carefully inspected for blemishes. For it said that what we bring must be male and unblemished, that is, strong and superior to the passions. For softness and an effeminate mind, and also being sick with an inward, intellectual defect within the mind, are wholly unacceptable to God and rejected by him. Or would you not say that anyone in whom these things are seen is unholy?
How could I not?

So what is feeble and, as it were, slack is rejected, while what is strong, as pictured in the nature of males, is acceptable, provided it is also unblemished. Such things would serve us as a clear type of Christ. For Emmanuel is both male and unblemished, since he is truly the power of God and did not know sin. He is male in another sense too: the male always has precedence and ranks above the other, and besides this it is the one most fitted to lead. And he is set over all, is incomparably superior, and rules the universe, even though the Son became like us and the shepherd was, to good purpose, counted among the sheep. Unholy and to be sent away among the victims are the blind, the broken, and the one with its tongue cut, the one with warts, with a malignant itch, and with ringworm, and the one with its ears cut or its tail docked. Further, it says, if any animal should have its male parts crushed and so suffer the condition that necessarily turns it into a eunuch, it too is excluded. For this, I think, is what "crushed and squeezed, castrated and torn" means.
Should we then apply these things to our own characters and ways of life?

Certainly. For in no other way than this would the law be spiritual for us. God would take no account of worship in shadows, nor would he ever have laid down its laws, unless he were prefiguring in it the surpassing beauty of the truth.
Well said. Go on, then, with your account of each item, and explain again what each would mean.

I shall, and very gladly. By "blind" it seems to mean the one without wisdom and understanding, who has no divine light within himself, that is, the enlightenment that comes through Christ in the Spirit; and the one who is still senseless and unbelieving is wholly unholy: "For if you do not believe," it says, "you will not understand." By "broken," in turn, it means the one who is infirm in every way and has nothing sound in him at all, who cannot walk straight, that is, has no strength to do anything good, and is wholly lacking in the vigor that is in Christ and in the Spirit. Something like this happened to those of whom it is written through one of the holy prophets: "Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing weakness upon this people, and fathers and sons together shall be weak in it; neighbor and companion shall perish." But the divine Psalmist brings before us those who have been justified by faith in Christ, joyful, singing and saying: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption." By "tongue-cut," I think, it means the one who does not know how to speak rightly and is unable to utter the word of faith that we proclaim, as it is written, the appeal to God from a good conscience. But that they too will throw off such a disease at the coming of Christ the prophet makes clear when he says: "And stammering tongues shall quickly learn to speak peace." So the tongue-cut is the one who still stammers and has not yet been taught to speak the peace that comes to us from above and from the Father, that is, Christ, or the things concerning him. Those with warts, a malignant itch, and ringworm, we say, are those who have within themselves a mind subject to passion and are sick with much corruption in their sins, who do not even consider that they ought to diminish them, but rather let them creep on toward greater shame and spread toward what is worse. For warts, malignant itch, and ringworm are always seen to advance; they somehow tend toward a worse condition and little by little spread over the whole flesh. Such too are those passions in our souls that are not checked but, as if with an unrestrained impulse, always run on toward the worse. The one with ears cut, and in addition the one with a docked tail, would signify the disobedient one who will not listen, and the one who is not seemly in every respect. Is not the damage to hearing in those whose ear has been cut off?
Very much so.

And animals without a tail: would you yourself grant that they are of the finest form? Not at all; they suffer from great unsightliness. So the unseemly and unlovely person is the one indirectly signified by the animal that, as it may happen, has no tail. It also rejects what is male as far as nature goes but cannot perform the functions of males, I mean the crushed and the castrated. Such again would be those who have a reputation for manly courage in virtue, but are no longer active toward the glories of virtue; they are, as it were, dry and fruitless, deprived in many ways of the ability to bear fruit. For a vast throng of unholy passions forces us into feebleness and impotence, and besides this into being unable to bear fruit. For this reason, I think, the law calls the eunuch by many names: "crushed," it says, "and squeezed, and castrated and torn." For the passions in us are very varied, leading us, as it were, by many a path to feebleness and impotence.
The argument is persuasive.

He also declared that it is abominable, besides these things, to offer sacrifices to God through a foreign hand, saying: "And you shall not offer gifts to the Lord your God from the hand of a foreigner." By this it is signified figuratively that the Father can be approached through Christ alone. For he is our truly unblemished and great high priest, the mediator in the divine plan; as the divine Paul writes: "Through him we have access in the Spirit to the Father." So those who choose to consecrate their own souls to God the Father, with Christ as mediator, must be free from blemish: "For you shall be holy," it says, "as I am holy."
Excellently said.

Having laid down the manner of sacrifice as regards cattle and sheep, he goes on through other figures as well, urging very well that those accustomed to approach God must do so without blemish. For he said again in Leviticus: "Every sacrifice that you offer to the Lord you shall not offer leavened; for you shall not offer any leaven or any honey from it as an offering to the Lord. You shall offer them to the Lord as a gift of firstfruits, but it shall not be brought up onto the altar as a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And every gift of your sacrifice shall be salted with salt. You shall not leave out the salt of the covenant of the Lord from your sacrifices; with every gift of yours you shall offer salt to the Lord your God." Leaven, then, would be a type of shrewdness, and by no means only of the blameworthy kind, but also of the other, I mean the good and praiseworthy kind, which the word of Wisdom promises to give even to the innocent; for the term "shrewdness" is in a way neutral. Honey, in turn, sometimes hints indirectly at bodily pleasure, as when it says: "Do not pay attention to a worthless woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot." But sometimes it presents a figure of good sweetness. For it is written: "Eat honey, my son, for the honeycomb is good, that your throat may be sweetened." The law, then, forbids leaven and honey to be brought as a burnt offering and sacrifice. It accepts them from the one who brings them as a gift and as firstfruits, but in no way carries them up to God as a fragrant aroma.
Then explain again what the riddle means.

The matter is hard to grasp, Palladius. What could it mean that these things are not rejected, and yet are not carried up as a burnt offering and sacrifice? Is it not an uphill task to see? I think, then, that sometimes even shrewdness on the part of a holy and good soul, if it is exercised at the right moment and has piety toward God as its motive, is not rejected by him; yet it will not be ranked on a level with fragrant virtue, nor would it be counted as a spiritual sacrifice. For simplicity is more precious to God. Indeed the sacred Scripture admires the divine Jacob, saying: "And Jacob was a guileless man, dwelling in a house." Shrewdness is far removed from all who are innocent. Yet the Savior himself said to the holy apostles: "Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves." Innocence is precious to God and in another respect superior to everything; but shrewdness and craft befit the work of the apostolic mission, and the blessed Paul made use of them at times, constantly escaping an untimely death at the hands of his enemies. So shrewdness in pursuits that are according to God would be acceptable, but would in no way be counted as the fragrance of virtue if it were judged by its own nature. In the same way honey, taken as a type of fleshly pleasure, would indicate, I think, this worldly life that is not freed from fleshly pleasures. For marriage is honorable, serving the bearing of children, and blameless according to the law when it is entered into in Christ. Yet it will not count for anyone as a power of virtue, nor will it be ranked equal with the glories of self-control. The blessed Paul also writes to those who are married: "Do not separate from one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and supplication." And again: "Come together," he says, "so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control." And to this he added: "I say this by way of concession, not of command." Do you see, then, that he grants a concession to those who are married? How then can something that is dealt with by concession be a virtue? But concerning the virgin he says that she is more blessed if she remains as she is, that is, unmarried. So honey is not rejected, for marriage is acceptable; yet it is not a fragrant aroma, as the ways of virtue are. Salt, moreover, is sprinkled on the sacrifices, for I think we must offer sacrifice wisely and sensibly, well equipped for every good thing whatever. For what is graceless and insipid would be least fitting for those who have chosen a life of piety. That is why the Savior too said to the holy disciples: "You are the salt of the earth." And Paul also writes: "Let your speech be seasoned with grace and salt, so that it may give grace to those who hear."
It is settled, then, that good sense and graciousness are signified by the salt.

So it is. And now that we have carefully distinguished the ways of offering sacrifice, I think we must next consider, from the sacred Scriptures themselves, how those who are sick with sin may escape the disease and ward off the harm that comes from wrongdoing. It is written, then, in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: If a soul sins unintentionally before the Lord against any of the commandments of the Lord, concerning things that ought not to be done, and does any one of them; if the anointed high priest sins so as to make the people sin, then for the sin he has committed he shall bring to the Lord an unblemished young bull from the cattle for sin. And he shall bring the bull to the door of the tent of witness before the Lord, and lay his hand on the head of the bull before the Lord, and slaughter the bull in the presence of the Lord. And the anointed priest, whose hands have been consecrated, shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of witness; and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the Lord, in front of the holy veil. And the priest shall put some of the blood of the bull on the horns of the altar of compounded incense that is before the Lord, which is in the tent of witness; and all the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of whole burnt offerings, which is by the doors of the tent of witness. And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the loins, and the lobe on the liver he shall remove together with the kidneys, just as it is removed from the bull of the sacrifice of deliverance; and the priest shall carry them up onto the altar of burnt offering. And the hide of the bull and all its flesh, with the head and the extremities and the belly and the dung, they shall carry out, the whole bull, outside the camp to a clean place where they pour out the ashes, and they shall burn it on wood with fire; it shall be burned on the ash heap." This is what it says concerning a ruler who leads the people under his authority into sinning along with him against what is fitting. And immediately it added to this: "But if the whole congregation of the sons of Israel errs in ignorance and a matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one thing, out of all the commandments of the Lord, that ought not to be done, and they offend, and the sin they have committed in it becomes known to them, then the congregation shall bring an unblemished young bull from the cattle for sin." And it states very clearly that this bull must be offered according to the same pattern as the first.
What, then, would be the meaning of these things?

It is clear, Palladius, and not hard to grasp, at least for anyone of sound mind. In Christ is the cleansing of priests and of people, small and great, and in short of all. This holds even if we are caught offending one by one, whether because we did not know the divine law or because we were perhaps forced against our will into what is least pleasing to God, the Lord of all. That is why the inspired David cried out to us: "Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance." And since God is good by nature, kind and compassionate, and not unaware of the weakness of our nature, blessed Job all but openly accuses him of delaying and holding back from forgiving some people their sins. He says this: "Why did you not make my lawlessness forgotten, and cleanse my sin?" The law, then, cried out besides that in Christ, and in him alone, those held fast by their sins will be justified through faith. For he is the one slaughtered for us like a calf at the doors of the holy and divine tabernacle, so that he might open wide for us the way inside. He is the one who takes away our sins, as the prophet says, and this, I think, is what the laying of hands on the calf signifies. He is the one who entered the Holy of Holies through his blood and obtained a holy redemption for us, and by one offering perfected forever those who are being sanctified, in the words of blessed Paul. He is the one who sanctifies the Church by the sprinkling of his own blood, and does so abundantly. For it says, "The priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger before the Lord." And again: "For we have come to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel's." Abel's blood cried out to God, condemning the murderer, but the precious blood of Christ, the Savior of us all, speaks better things to God on our behalf. For it was poured out as the ransom for the life of all. The calf's blood was poured out at the base of the altar, for the death of Christ is truly holy and sacred. The inward parts are offered up: the fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver. For everything in Christ is fragrant, both what is visible and what is hidden; the Word was holy, and there was nothing in him that was not pure. The skin and the rest, however, are burned outside the gate, for the law does not leave even the place of his suffering unwelcome to us. That is why the inspired Paul said to us: "Let us then go out outside the gate, bearing his reproach," that is, the cross borne for us and because of us. And the Savior himself says somewhere: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me." The most sacred Paul seems to understand "outside the gate" to mean "outside the world." For the will to follow Christ removes us from worldly life. Paul will bear witness again, for he spoke thus of Christ: "Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." Though the saints walk on earth, they strive no longer to live in an earthly way, but rather to have their citizenship in heaven. For the defiled, the cleansing is ash with water. For the Savior's passion is the ransom from sin. He sanctifies us through water, by which we gain not the removal of dirt from the flesh, as it is written, but the washing away of the defilements in our souls. For "Wash yourselves and become clean," as the prophetic word commanded us long ago.
So in the calf, as in an image and in types, the death of Christ, suffered because of us and for us, is sketched in outline.
You understand very well. And besides this, I think you would be amazed if you looked at another point too.
Which one?

The law says that if the leader sins together with those subject to him, or if the multitude under his hand sins by itself, the victim will be a calf. But if the leader is caught in faults of his own, "let him bring," it says, "a male goat from the goats." And if it is one of the people, the victim is no longer to be male but female. If you like, I will also read the laws that follow these. They say this: "If the ruler sins and unwittingly does one of all the commandments of the Lord his God that ought not to be done, and so offends, and the sin he committed in it becomes known to him, he shall bring as his gift a male goat from the goats, without blemish, for sin. He shall lay his hand on the goat's head, and they shall slaughter it in the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offerings before the Lord; it is a sin offering. The priest shall put some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger on the horns of the altar of whole burnt offerings, and pour out all its blood at the base of the altar of whole burnt offerings. He shall offer up all its fat on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offering. So the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin, and he will be forgiven." And besides this: "If a single soul among the people of the land sins unwittingly by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord that ought not to be done, and so offends, and the sin he committed in it becomes known to him, he shall bring a female goat from the goats; he shall bring her without blemish for his sin." And after explaining how the sacrifice is to be performed, it says: "If he brings a sheep as his gift for sin, he shall offer a female without blemish." Do you see, then, Palladius, the depth of the mystery, as it was prefigured for the ancients in a mirror and in shadows? The offering of victims is matched, as it were, to the size of the offenses. The calf was for the ruler and for the people, perhaps because both had fallen sick with one common sin. But one kid was for one person, that is, for a single soul. For Christ offered himself both for all at once, as in the image of the calf, a heavy and great victim ("For where sin increased," it says, "grace abounded all the more"), and for each person individually, like a kid and a sheep. This is because, I say, he was made like those under sin and was reckoned among the lawless, according to the Scriptures; and the kid is a type of the lawless person, being fruitless and dry. Indeed Christ sets the saints on his right like sheep, and the workers of lawlessness on his left like goats. So one might see his glory and his surpassing greatness as in the calf, while his being made like us, and even being reckoned among the lawless, you will understand through the goat. He was also slaughtered as a sheep, because of his innate gentleness and the surpassing meekness of the sacrifice. For it says: "He was led like a sheep, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth." But if the one guilty of offenses happened to be a leader, the goat was male. If it was someone among the people, an individual, the victim was female, whether it was a sheep or from the goats. And in the difference between the victims the law points to the wisdom of our Savior's dispensation. For the male is somehow always the one who leads and holds first honor, while the female follows and holds second place. So the cleansing through Christ is in proportion to each one's faults, both for those who preside and lead and for those under their hand, the individuals and the subjects. For leader and people would not fall into sin with equal guilt; the leaders, surely, would fall with greater. Therefore they are scoured clean by a richer grace.
I understand what you mean: the male is better than the other.

And you can see in Christ the difference as regards glory. He is ruler and, by common confession, guide of all things, as God and Lord. But he also became, as it were, second in rank because of his humanity, and was placed under the law, so as to lead the way.
The interpretation is persuasive.

The law also adds other kinds of defilement, and for each of them again it foretold a purification, to be fulfilled in Christ. It said this: "If a soul sins, and hears the voice of an oath, and he is a witness, having either seen or known, and he does not report it, he shall bear the sin. That soul which touches anything unclean, whether a carcass, or an unclean animal killed by beasts, or the unclean carcasses of abominable things, or the unclean carcasses of cattle, or touches human uncleanness, any uncleanness of a person by touching which he would be defiled, and it escaped his notice, but afterward he knows it and so offends; or the lawless soul that rashly declares with its lips that it will do evil or do good, in anything whatever a man declares with an oath, and it escaped his notice, and then he comes to know it, and he sins in one of these: he shall confess the sin in which he has sinned, and he shall bring to the Lord for what he offended, for the sin he committed, a female from the flock, a ewe lamb or a female goat from the goats, for sin. And the priest shall make atonement for him concerning the sin he committed, and the sin will be forgiven him." Observe, then, that the law puts the one who hears the voice of an oath and makes nothing at all of it, the one guilty of other defilements, and also the one convicted of perjury, into one equal and identical class of offense. For contempt for God is truly an extraordinary defilement and leaps up to the very extremity of evils, and this offense is close and akin to fleshly uncleanness. Or should accursed perjury and contempt for an oath not be put on an equal footing?
Certainly. In both cases the charges are always about evenly matched.

So for these too release will follow through confession and the slaughter of a ewe lamb, that is, of a sheep. For it says: "Declare your transgressions first, that you may be justified." And the divine David also exclaims: "I said, I will confess my lawlessness against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart." Yet confession alone is not enough for a complete washing. What frees us entirely is the death of Christ, who suffered for us and took the sins of us all upon himself, as in every kind of tame animal: I mean the calf, the sheep and the goat. And as if leaving those who are in defilement and uncleanness no excuse for neglecting the sacrifice, the law urges that anyone who has no calf or sheep should honor God with what he has at hand and can afford. It says: "If his hand cannot afford enough for the sheep, he shall bring to the Lord for the sin he committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and one for a whole burnt offering. He shall bring them to the priest, and the priest shall offer first the one for sin. The priest shall pinch its head at the neck but not sever it, and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the wall of the altar. The rest of the blood he shall drain out at the base of the altar, for it is a sin offering. The second he shall make a whole burnt offering as is fitting. So the priest shall make atonement for him concerning the sin he committed, and he will be forgiven." The turtledove and the pigeon may very properly be compared to our Lord Jesus Christ, because the one is the most melodious and talkative of birds, and the other comes as near as anything to the height of meekness. Both qualities were in Christ. For the turtledove from above, from heaven, charmed the whole world with the proclamations of the Gospel, as if pouring out a clear and sweet song and making plain the will of God the Father. As the inspired John says: "He whom God has sent speaks the words of God." And he called us to imitate the meekness and gentleness that were in him, saying: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." So, the law says, the priest shall take the turtledove and pinch it with his fingernail, for that is how small, light birds are slaughtered. Yet he shall not cut it off altogether; plainly, the head is meant. For this is how the death of Christ was accomplished: not for division, but for union. Accordingly, when at the beginning the law was laid down about the Passover, God commanded that the lamb be sacrificed, but "It shall be eaten," it says, "in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside." For Christ is in no way divided, but is one and whole, both in each and in all. He himself is our peace, gathering us into unity, both with one another in oneness of soul and, through himself, with God in the Spirit. So the fact that the bird is sacrificed, and yet its head is not entirely severed from the neck, indirectly showed that the death of Christ has brought us not division but union. And the sprinkling of the tabernacle and everything in it with the bird's blood would signify that he sanctifies the Church with his own blood. One turtledove is for sin, and the other for a whole burnt offering, and Christ is understood through both: dying for us, offered whole as a burnt offering to the Father for a fragrant aroma, and indeed giving himself up as the ransom for the life of all.
Well said.

The law even lowers the manner of sacrifice to something very easily obtained, and orders it to be made in proportion to each person's means. In this way it cuts off on every side any hesitation over the best things, and leaves those who choose negligence without excuse. Again it writes this: "If his hand cannot find a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall bring as his gift for what he sinned a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for sin. He shall not pour oil on it or put frankincense on it, because it is for sin. He shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a full handful of it and put this memorial portion on the altar of the Lord's whole burnt offerings; it is a sin offering. So the priest shall make atonement for him concerning the sin he committed in any one of these, and he will be forgiven. What remains shall belong to the priest, like the sacrifice of fine flour." But here the manner of sacrifice no longer points to Christ. Instead it hints to us at the life of the one who makes the offering, his approach in Christ and his consecration to God. For fine flour is offered, and fine flour is the source of bread, and bread is a type of life. But the law says that the flour must not be sprinkled with frankincense or moistened with oil, and it states beforehand the wise and necessary reason for this: it is for sin. From sin cheerfulness, which is understood in the oil, must be wholly and entirely far removed, and so must fragrance, which is perhaps understood in the frankincense. No one would dispute that the sin in us is truly a gloomy and odorless thing. Virtue, on the other hand, will always somehow be rich in cheerfulness, through hope in God, which is full of fragrance, as in a spiritual richness. So the fine flour without frankincense and oil is a type of a life that has no cheerfulness and is bare of fragrance. But in Christ even this life will be changed to cheerfulness. It also receives fragrance in faith, and is offered to God through him who scours clean the defiled and spiritually washes those caught in uncleanness. For it says that the priest shall take a handful of the fine flour and offer it up on the altar of whole burnt offerings to the Lord. For our access is in Christ, and through him we who are defiled draw near. We are justified through faith and are dedicated to the Father as a fragrant aroma. We are no longer offering ourselves, but Christ who is in us, and so we have the spiritual fragrance.
What you say is true.

Besides this, it may happen that some offend God by stealing something consecrated, or by going back on what they promised and not offering it at once, and so through their negligence incur the charge of forgetfulness. The law cleanses these too. For it is written: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If forgetfulness comes over a soul, and it sins unwittingly in the holy things of the Lord, he shall bring to the Lord for his offense a ram without blemish from the flock, valued in shekels of silver by the shekel of the sanctuary, for what he offended. And what he sinned against the holy things he shall repay, and he shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the offense, and he will be forgiven." It is truly a terrible thing to steal anything consecrated and dedicated to the glory of God. In the same way, failing to pay what was promised will be condemned, and on no small charges. For it says: "My child, if you vow a vow to the Lord, do not delay to pay it; it is better for you not to vow than to vow and not pay." And the inspired David sings somewhere: "Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God." The sons of Eli were also punished for filching some of the holy things and appropriating what belonged to God. What, then, would be the forgiveness for this sin? How might someone free his foot from guilt and be released? First, by making restitution richer than what was taken, for it says, "He shall add a fifth"; then, by bringing a purchased ram for sacrifice. This would be a type of Christ, whom the leaders of the Jews in a sense bought for thirty denarii, which they paid to the disciple who betrayed him. So in Christ there is forgiveness also for offenses against God. And it is easy to see that he would also release us from wrongs done to other people, for anyone who has read the law that comes next. It runs as follows: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a soul sins and wholly disregards the commandments of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor about a deposit, or about a partnership, or about robbery, or has wronged his neighbor in some way, or has found something lost and lies about it, and swears falsely about any one of all the things a person may do and so sin in them, then, when he has sinned and offended, he shall give back what he seized by robbery, or what he gained by wronging another, or the deposit entrusted to him, or the lost thing he found, whatever it was about which he swore falsely. He shall repay the principal itself and add a fifth to it; he shall give it to the one to whom it belongs on the day he is convicted. And for his offense he shall bring to the Lord a ram without blemish from the flock, at the value of what he offended. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord, and he will be forgiven for any one of all the things he did and offended in it." Do you see how the manner of cleansing runs evenly and is fulfilled in both cases? He is to repay with interest and to offer a ram. The law very rightly commanded that both the charges against God and those against brothers and kinsmen must be driven off. Justification in Christ is by no means partial; it is rather a complete washing away of whatever tends to stain. That is why he also said: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life." And if the one who has gained justification by faith through Christ has escaped judgment, it is entirely necessary to say that he has escaped the charges, and that no kind of accusation could prevail against such a person, I say. For "it is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns?" So if by our deeds we make amends to the brothers we have grieved, we will find the justification in Christ ready at hand. Thus Zacchaeus the tax collector, too, when he was called to apostleship, promised not only to follow the one who called him, but also to repay fourfold whatever he had taken wrongfully. For I think that those who are going to make Christ dwell within them through the Spirit must first wash off their stains and scour away their offenses, and so present their own soul to him bright and spotless. Just so the inspired Psalmist, being in a good state of such virtue, cried out: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music." For dyes sink into wool that is clean, but if any trace of dirt remains, the color put into it is at once easily removed, since it has no secure hold there. In the same way, participation in Christ enters into holy and pure souls, but would not settle at all in souls that are not so disposed. For "the holy spirit of wisdom will flee deceit," as it is written, "and will not dwell in a body in debt to sin." So by making amends to those we have wronged, and by cutting away our brothers' grief through acts of friendship, we will free ourselves from all guilt and gain the forgiveness that is in Christ.
Very rightly said.
Would you like us, then, to gather other lines of thought besides these, and to explain both the charges that arise from defilements and what has been prescribed for the cleansing of each?
By all means. In this way the discussion of these things would bring us a more abundant benefit.

It is written, then, in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone who has a discharge, and everyone made unclean by a corpse. Male and female alike, send them outside the camp, so that they do not defile their camps, where I dwell among them." Now it is clear to anyone, I think, that in these matters the law could not reasonably be thought to censure us for things that happen by necessity and against our will. For on what grounds would a bodily ailment be punished, and how could someone who has fallen into illnesses of the flesh justly incur the law's condemnation? So it is wise, and indeed necessary, to take bodily things as an image and type of the diseases in our souls. In this way the law would be spiritual, and what God has declared on each matter at various times would be a holy verdict. It would not bring penalties on those caught by diseases they never chose. Its rebuke would be holy because it falls on those who can be charged with wrongdoing.
Very well said.

The law commands, then, that the leper be sent out of the camp, but it makes the testing in his case very exact, and it orders that the disease must be examined. It says: "And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: If a man has on the skin of his body a scar with a bright mark, and an infection of leprosy appears on the skin of his body, he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons the priests. The priest shall look at the infection on the skin of his body. If the hair in the infection has turned white, and the infection appears to lie deeper than the skin of the body, it is an infection of leprosy. The priest shall look and pronounce him unclean. But if there is a bright white spot on the skin of his body, and it does not appear to lie deeper than the skin, and its hair has not turned white, but it is faint, then the priest shall isolate the infection for seven days. On the seventh day the priest shall look at the infection, and if the infection remains as it was before him and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall isolate him for a second seven days, and on the seventh day the priest shall look at him a second time. If the infection is faint and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is only a mark. He shall wash his clothes and be clean. But if, after the priest has seen him and pronounced him clean, the mark changes and spreads in the skin, he shall show himself to the priest a second time. The priest shall look at him, and if the mark has spread in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is leprosy." The matter calls for subtle discussion, Palladius, and its explanation is not easy to grasp. But I think we must concentrate our minds and say briefly what the law means. First I shall explain how the two ailments differ. Leprosy is a very grievous affliction of human bodies, hard to escape and consuming, and it works by deadening the flesh. The sore at once becomes hollow, because the skin is eaten away and keeps sinking deeper, since the corruption always creeps downward. That, I think, is why the hair growing on those places withers and turns white, and perishes with the ground beneath it like a plant. Such, then, is leprosy. The white patch, on the other hand, is a disorder of the flesh that resembles leprosy. But it does not drive the damage deep, and it does not carry the feeling of the disease to the inner parts. It floats, as it were, on the very surface, barely showing on the body. It does not turn the hair white or spread unchecked. With very few remedies it is easily reined in, and the affected flesh returns to health. So leprosy is plainly a deadening, while the white patch falls under some suspicion of leprosy but is not in truth the same thing, leprosy and deadening. The law therefore condemns the leper as unclean, because he has already suffered deadening. But it frees from the charge the one who suffers from the white patch, because he has come under suspicion of leprosy but has not yet become leprous. So, the law says, if there is a scar with a mark and an infection of leprosy, and it appears deeper than the skin, and the hair also turns white, probably because it is dying along with the flesh beneath it, then it will certainly be leprosy, for the deadening is creeping deeper. But if there is a white patch with a mark, without hollowness in the skin and without the hair turning white, the law says it must be examined by the priest and isolated a second time. For it is quite possible that the mere passing of days, by testing the ailment, will sometimes show the exact truth to those who investigate. If the hair changes colour and the skin becomes hollow, the white patch has turned into leprosy. But if neither of these happens, "Let him be released from the charge," it says. For the ailment is not leprosy, but something that resembles leprosy and comes very close to it, namely the white patch. The plain sense and the explanation of the matter have been set out well enough. But come, let us speak of spiritual things and take up the hidden meanings that the mind perceives.
What a fine and profitable thing!

We who are being made alive in Christ, and I mean being made alive spiritually, must depart from dead works and go as far from them as we can. These, I think, are the works through which the soul is deadened and the mind grows cold, because it has turned without restraint toward the things of the flesh and of the world. For if it is true that "whoever sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh," and that "those who live according to the flesh cannot please God," how, or on what grounds, could anyone still doubt that they will also die? So whoever has defiled his soul and mind, and is full of the world's wickedness, is dead and held fast by the works of death. If anyone chose to call such a condition a truly spiritual leprosy, he would not be wrong. Such a person, then, is unclean in the eyes of Christ. For "the priest," it says, "shall pronounce him unclean." At the divine judgment seat he will be counted among those who are deeply in love with sin, and he will hear: "Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you." But to the white patch and the scar with a mark we must compare those who still have only bare desires and have not yet turned the thought into action. Or would you not say it is true that pleasures and thoughts spring up in us before the deeds, and rise ahead of them, as it were, calling us toward something the law condemns?
I would. I remember blessed David saying: "Before I was humbled, I went astray."

You are quite right. Before the deeds are done, the mind is certainly already at fault, for it has been in labour with the pleasure beforehand. Yet while the sin still lies only in the desires, the mind stands in the middle ground, looking both ways and free to lean toward whichever side it chooses. It has not yet suffered deadening, but it has come very close to evil and carries the passion as if in birth pangs. The Saviour's disciple has clearly told us something of this kind: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God.' For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death."
True.

Therefore dying, as in leprosy (I mean the spiritual kind), and as in the deadening that sin brings, would occur not in the desires alone but when deeds are actually carried out. As long as the evil is still in the mind's birth pangs, there is not yet deadening, not yet death. For not all sin leads to death, as the Saviour's disciple said. Such a person is still only under suspicion of suffering what brings death. And we said that the white patch is something like leprosy, or close to it. "The priest," it says, "shall look at the one held by the affliction," by which I mean the white patch. If it is seen not to be changing into leprosy, he shall not pronounce him unclean but shall rather isolate him. For even being in desires and close to evil does not escape rebuke before God. But if the affliction does not change and has not turned toward the worse, "let him be clean," it says. So it is excellent and truly saving to refuse deadening, I mean the deadening that lies in deeds and somehow already chills the mind in their very accomplishment. Besides this, it is wise to try very hard to turn away from the passions, even when they are seen to occur still only as bare desires. For this, I think, is what it means to depart both from leprosy itself and from the white patch. You have learned that Emmanuel, who is God by nature, our great High Priest, watches over our affairs with the greatest care. He admits those who have washed away what is base, but sends out of the camp of the saints those he sees to be defiled.
What you say is true.

For "you shall be holy," it says, "because I am holy." And note that it says the one freed from the charge will be clean once he has washed his clothes. Here the law foretells the cleansing through water, and in types perceptible to the bodily senses it sketches out for us the mystery of holy baptism.
I understand.
See, then, Palladius, how great the earnestness of the law is. It moves our thoughts, as it were, to the opposite side, and by every means it shows us what leads to our benefit.
What do you mean?

For it said again: "If an infection of leprosy occurs in a person, he shall come to the priest, and the priest shall look. If there is a white scar on the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is healthy, living flesh in the scar, it is a chronic leprosy in the skin of his body. The priest shall pronounce him unclean and isolate him, because he is unclean. But if the leprosy breaks out all over the skin of his body, and the leprosy covers all the skin of the infected person from his head to his feet, wherever the priest looks, then the priest shall look, and if the leprosy has covered all the skin of his body, the priest shall pronounce him clean of the infection, because it has all turned white, and he is clean. But on any day that living flesh appears in him, he shall be unclean. The priest shall look at the healthy flesh and pronounce him unclean. The healthy flesh is unclean; it is leprosy. But if the healthy flesh is restored and turns white, he shall come to the priest. The priest shall look, and if the infection has turned white, the priest shall pronounce the infection clean, and he is clean."
And how are we to understand the way things are reversed in this case?
Don't you understand that we affirmed leprosy to be a partial deadening in living flesh, and that the one held by the disease was cast out as defiled?
I understand.

Notice, then, that the matter is turned around for us again into its opposite. For if, it says, someone becomes a leper through and through, held fast by deadening and with nothing healthy in him, then let him be released from the charges of defilement: he is clean. But if there is any trace of living flesh left in him, "let the priest," it says, "record his uncleanness," for the living flesh will make him unclean, and he is a leper. This too will incur the same charges as leprosy.
I cannot understand what you mean. If partial leprosy defiles people, how could complete and total leprosy show them to be clean?

The matter calls for subtle discussion, Palladius. But we shall not suppose that the precision of the law brings us an interpretation that conflicts with itself and, as it were, works against us. A wise and necessary meaning, beyond reproach, fits each case. Come, let us state it, if you agree.
By all means. I am thirsty, and you will be speaking to me to my great delight.

There are two ways, I think, in which we shall achieve the most law-abiding life before God, who loves virtue. In the first, we live to him and refuse the deadening that comes from passions and sin, and this means not suffering leprosy, for leprosy is produced when partial deadness occurs in a living body. In the second, through a good deadening and by no longer consenting to live in the world's way, we shall bind on, like a crown, the verdict given to all the best. For the divine Paul writes thus to certain people: "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus." Living in Christ, then, and eager to accomplish what pleases him, we shall hate being deadened, that is, deadened by passions and sins. And having died to sin, as it is written, we shall thrust away any life in it, if we think rightly.
Explain this to me still more clearly, for I do not quite understand.
Do we not say, Palladius, that Christ endured death for us so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them, that is, for Christ?
We say so, beyond dispute.

We live to Christ, then, when we conduct ourselves according to the Gospel and loathe the deadening that comes from sin, that is, the death that comes from the passions. Indeed, the divine Peter writes of Christ: "He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness." For I think that those who care about living splendidly must keep far away from everything capable of deadening them, and work hard to be rid of defilements.
You speak well.

Therefore whoever has chosen to live to Christ, following the commands of the Gospel and thrusting away the deadening that comes from sin, will be the least likely of all to suffer the affliction that resembles leprosy.
I am convinced.

This, then, is one way in which we can please God. But there is another, which can rightly be accomplished as follows. We must put to death our members that are on earth, namely fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, and in some sense appear already to have died to sin, and that completely, no longer living in it. The divine Paul will assure us of this, saying: "What then shall we say? Shall we go on in sin so that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?" Just as, when we choose to live to Christ, the law subjected partial deadening to penalties, so too, when we are dead to sin, living in it would again be a defilement and would not escape the law's indictment. That is why it says that if leprosy covers the whole body, as a kind of deadening spreading over every limb, it would signify the one who has died to sin, and there is no longer any defilement in the body. For he is clean, it says, who has died to sin wholly and completely, giving it no room and not allowing it, so to speak, to make its home in him. But if, it says, living flesh is seen in him again, the living flesh will make him unclean. For to live to sin at all, even partially, makes the sufferer abominable. "A little leaven," it says, "leavens the whole lump," and the saying is true. But if the living flesh is restored, it says, and turns into leprosy, let the charges be dropped: he is clean. For he has been freed even from living partly to sin, because his mind has moved over to the praiseworthy deadening and has made a truly beautiful change. To sum up what I have said, then: if we live to God, let nothing in us be dead; if we have died to sin, let nothing of sin be alive in us. For this is the shining road of a life fit for saints, a life with nothing in it open to reproach.
Well said.

The law distinguishes such afflictions still more finely. Even if there is suspicion or appearance of leprosy, it says, perhaps in a wound that has scarred over, or in a part of the body that was once burned, let the priest again use the same care and examinations. If what seemed to break out white does not change into leprosy, let him be clean, it says. But if the white patch clearly changes into leprosy, he will be unclean and abominable. Through these things too the law hints to us about the ailments of our souls, which are countless. They may have been healed by gentle treatment and brought in time to scar over, so to speak. But if our negligence somehow stirs them up again, Christ our great High Priest will examine them and will pass a judgment that is entirely right. For if, it says, the disease advances only as far as thoughts, the sufferer is by no means free from rebuke, since he will be isolated; yet he is not utterly rejected, nor wholly deadened. But if the affliction passes beyond thoughts and desire itself, it has already undergone a complete change for the worse, and it will subject the one who has fallen ill again to the penalties for defilement. We must therefore take the greatest care not to awaken passions that have already been lulled to sleep, nor to reopen the wounds of the mind and run back to where we began. Otherwise we too shall hear a saint crying out: "What the true proverb says has happened to them: The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow that was washed returns to wallowing in the mud."
You seem to me to speak rightly and very reasonably.

This, then, is what the law tells us about leprosy, both in scars and in wounds. It goes on to add: "And if a man or a woman has an infection of leprosy on the head or in the beard, the priest shall look at the head." If there is any hollowness in it, it says, with the skin wasting and sinking, and the hair also turning white, such a person will without question be a leper and unclean. But if none of these things occurs, let the one who has the white patch shave his head or beard, it says. Once his hair has been stripped off in this way, let him come to the priest and be examined. If the mark or white patch does not spread, but stays in place, as it were, or shrinks, let him again be clean. For the affliction is not leprosy, but only a suspicion and an appearance of it.
What, then, would these things mean?

Defilement in us is twofold, Palladius: of the flesh and of the spirit. The flesh is stained by its own monstrous and unholy passions. Soul and mind are stained most of all by straying from correct doctrine toward what is worse, and by the corruption of sound faith; and further by deceits and frauds, perjuries, whisperings, conceit, quarrels, jealousies, and everything near and akin to these, which brings down an equal outcry against wickedness. In these passages, then, the law seems to be speaking to us of the passions of the soul, and to mean the ailments that tend to arise in the mind. For the head is a type of the mind, and the beard of sensible understanding, since the beard too is a sign of maturity. So the High Priest of all, that is, Christ, watches over our affairs and examines them closely. He will look into the mind itself and test our inner and hidden thoughts. If there is some corruption or change, either from right belief to what is not right, or toward a base character and ill will, which he abhors above all, he will drive such people away again as defiled and pass a verdict that pronounces them wholly unclean. This, I say, is what it means to suffer leprosy in the head or the beard. But if the mind is only at the beginning of the affliction, as it were, and is not seen to have turned wholly to the sickness I spoke of, he is isolated and given moderate penalties. Yet he will not be wholly unclean, nor estranged from God. Once he has washed his clothes he will be clean, that is, he will receive the justification that is in Christ as his help. The shaving of the hair, which presents the wound bare to the priest, would signify that everything is cleared out of the way, as it were, so that the sight lies naked and unobstructed before the eyes of the Godhead, to look upon as it wishes. For "no creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes," as it is written.
True. For he said somewhere through the voice of a saint: "I am a God who is near, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?"

Look now, Palladius, at how much more finely the law speaks. It leaves out nothing that we need to know, and by placing each matter under its own rules it benefits those who hear it. For, as it is written, no one understands his transgressions, and we all stumble in many ways. Our nature suffers from weakness and slips easily into wrongdoing; and "No one is clean from filth," and, as Holy Scripture says, "not even if his life on earth were but a single day." That is why the divine David sings to us: "If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? For with you there is propitiation." See, then, how the law kindly lets go the charge for such transgressions, and in gentleness cleanses those who through human frailty have fallen into failings that are almost bitter to them and against their will. For it said this: "If a man or a woman has in the skin of his flesh bright spots, shining and whitish, and the priest looks, and behold, in the skin of his flesh there are bright spots, shining and whitish, it is a tetter; it breaks out in the skin of his flesh; he is clean." And yet, if we look into it closely, having a tetter would be an affliction of the flesh and close to leprosy. But it does not involve deadness, nor anything utterly past hope. Our transgressions are somewhat like this: they are admittedly afflictions, but not unto death and the ruin of the soul. The judge is not overly exacting, for "He knows our frame," and he is not unaware of the weakness of our nature. So out of his innate love for humankind he grants forgiveness. And this, I think, is what "A tetter is clean" means. But small faults also sometimes arise in the mind, even in good people: brief fits of irritation, for example, moderate stirrings toward anger, faint-heartedness toward one's brothers, sometimes a longing for petty, empty glory, and other passions of this kind. These tend to occur at times even in those whose life is blameless and who are truly pure. For they are human, and in a way common to everyone who lives the life of flesh and blood. So the law again sketches these too in a riddle, saying: "If a man's head loses its hair, he is bald; he is clean. If his head loses its hair at the front, he is bald on the forehead; he is clean." The involuntary loss of hair would be an affliction of the head, and we were saying just now that the head is named as a figure of the mind; for the head is the dwelling place of the mind, at least in the opinion of some.
I remember.

So the afflictions of the bodily head would fittingly represent the ailments of the mind, but small ones again, of the kind it is right should be followed by remission. The law, then, frees us from every human affliction and from the involuntary defilements that may befall us, since our nature must suffer weakness. To be freed from passions altogether does not belong to the present time but would suit the age to come, in which sin will be shaken from its foundations and we shall pass into a life wholly free of harm. "But if," it says, "there is a reddish scar or mark on the bald head or on the bald forehead, it is leprosy, and he shall be unclean." For sometimes even small passions grow into the force of serious offences, and they defile terribly if we do not check them but leave the way to what is worse open and entirely unrebuked. Let me give an example. Someone sometimes grows a little angry, and the passion has taken hold in the person; let it be checked by gentleness, so that the small transgression does not grow and little by little become a charge unto death against those who suffer it. This is the leprosy that may break out on the bald spot: the slide from nothing toward worse things, shown as in a figure. Rightly, then, I say, did blessed David say: "Be angry, and do not sin."
How deep this discussion is.

Very much so. For you notice, I imagine, that I am speaking with great subtlety, and that I cannot understand or express such insights without sweat. But that those who are impiously sick with open offences cannot escape notice, even though the smallest and hidden faults sometimes go unrecognized, you will also learn from the following. You will recall that it says those who suffer baldness are clean, kindly remitting our small failings, as we were saying just now. But if leprosy appears on someone's bald spot, that is, when the passion moves from small things to worse, then, then indeed it says it becomes manifest and shameful, and has no plea that could speak in defense against the charges. That is why it says: "And the leper in whom the plague is, let his garments be loosened and his head uncovered, and let him cover himself about his mouth; and he shall be called unclean all the days that the plague is upon him; being unclean, he shall be unclean; he shall sit apart; his dwelling shall be outside the camp." The loosened garments and the uncovered head would indicate quite clearly that he behaves shamefully without concealment. The covering about the mouth means that he has, so to speak, no defense and can say nothing when God charges him with uncleanness. And the requirement to leave the camp would again be a figure of his no longer dwelling with the choirs of the saints, but, as though banished from the holy multitude, having no share in any good thing.
How terrible and dreadful a thing!

Entirely so, Palladius; and that is why the divine David said: "Remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance; according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness' sake, O Lord." Throughout, as it were, the law displays the exactness that is in it, even down to articles—wool, I mean, and woof and warp and anything made of leather. "If leprosy appears," it says, "and the affliction befalls one of these, let the priest examine it again and set the plague apart; and if the mark does not change for the better, let it be consumed by fire. For it is a persistent leprosy," it says. However, it orders that the affected thing be washed; and if after this the affliction appears ingrained, it then gives it to the fire as utterly useless. Here again, perhaps, it is comparing our condition to wool and woof, warp and skins. For who could doubt, or on what grounds, that God has no concern about wool or woof or the other things? We shall grant, then, that it is the gravest of offences, after the cleansing and washing that Christ works in us, not to be rid of our defilements but to take a persistent stand in them. For if Christ benefits us not at all by washing us, he hands us over to the fire to be punished, just as the priest under the law, when washing had done the woof or warp no good, then burned it.
So it is.

By leprosy, then, the law fittingly signifies deadness, so to speak, in works. From this one can see how elegantly it brings the notions of more hidden things into clear, perceptible view, and makes intelligible things plain through examples drawn from the flesh. Setting before us, as it were, a rich knowledge of the defilements in souls, and making what happens spiritually vivid as though in bodily ailments, it declared again in Leviticus: "Any man who has a discharge from his body—his discharge is unclean. And this is the law of his uncleanness: one who discharges seed from his body, from the discharge with which his body is affected through the discharge—this is his uncleanness in him; all the days of the discharge of his body, with which his body is affected through the discharge, it is his uncleanness. Every bed on which the one with a discharge lies is unclean, and every article on which the one with a discharge sits shall be unclean. And whoever touches his bed shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and shall be unclean until evening. And whoever sits on the article on which the one with a discharge has sat shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and shall be unclean until evening. And whoever touches the skin of the one with a discharge shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and shall be unclean until evening. And if the one with a discharge comes near one who is clean, that person shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and shall be unclean until evening." And besides these things it says that every article on which the one with a discharge sits shall be loathsome and detestable; and even if he washes his hands in water, this too will be defiled. And if anyone touches his skin, he will certainly share in the charge of uncleanness; and if he comes near any who are not yet defiled, they will certainly incur the charge of uncleanness. Therefore he too was sent out along with the lepers and expelled from the camp, unapproachable and kept apart, defiling by the mere touch of his hand anyone at all who came upon him.
And what affliction in the soul would resemble the bodily discharge of seed? For the law is spiritual—or is it not so?

Certainly; you are right. But consider this: the discharge from the body in a way wrongs nature's fitness for bearing fruit. It lets the supply of seed go to waste and slackens the tension of the members, and so brings about an involuntary ruin, so that those gripped by the affliction remain in long and continual defilement. Know, then, that from a bodily and evident ailment we have an image of what happens in the mind. For the mind too is ruined when it labors most wastefully at things that are not fitting and devotes the effort of its own activity to nothing that is necessary, so that it bears no genuine fruit but is always somehow carried toward what does harm, and suffers an uncontrollable descent into more shameful things.
What do you mean, for example?
Did not the divine Paul tell us, my friend, that man was created for good works?
Indeed he did.

So man was allotted a nature rightly and suitably disposed toward anything whatever that is praiseworthy. Or do you not say that this creature is capable of wisdom and of all knowledge? And that he could easily achieve temperance and courage, and justice too, if he chose to carry out what is fitting and to follow the divine laws?
I agree.

But suppose he abandons these things and becomes no longer wise but foolish and senseless. He does not incline his own will toward the things that usually lead to truth, but prefers to be carried outside what is fitting, and leaps down to destruction along with those who make a practice of perverting what is right. He neither holds the best and blameless belief about God, nor travels blamelessly along the road of conduct. Would it not be true to say that such a person, in a spiritual sense, has a discharge of seed, since he spends to no purpose the very means by which he might have borne fruit for God?
I would say so, be assured.

And what if he gives up working righteousness and glorying in the noble deeds of courage, and is seen instead to be unjust and slack, given over to pleasures? Would you not think he suffers the same as the man with a discharge, spending on more shameful things the fitness for the good that his nature possesses, and choosing the loss of spiritual fruitfulness for nothing of any use?
I would think so.

The law, then, ordered that people keep as far as possible from the man with a discharge, teaching us to withdraw as much as we can from those who have turned toward wickedness, and to shake off resolutely those whom God himself would loathe as suffering continual defilement. For it is truly not without harm to cling to the wicked. It is true, as it is written: "Whoever touches pitch will be defiled." Indeed, the man with a discharge defiles every article he happens to touch—his bed, his skin, vessels, water, and wooden articles. Through these riddles the law indicates that a person would share in the uncleanness that is in him even by merely coming close to him in spiritual disposition. For it is written: "Keep yourself pure, and do not share in other people's sins." Yet even the passions that seem past hope, and the ailments hidden in the depths of our thoughts, and simply all the weakness in us, Christ removes, along with the cleansing that comes through him—something the law could not do.
