For, as it is written, no one is justified by the law. And you will see that this too is not false if you attend to what is written next. For it says again: "If the man with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his garments, and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean. And on the eighth day he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and bring them before the Lord to the doors of the tent of witness, and give them to the priest; and the priest shall offer them, one for sin and one as a whole burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge." It does cleanse the man with a discharge and free him from the affliction, then—but in Christ, through water and blood. For he shall count for himself, it says, seven days for his cleansing, and wash his garments, and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean. The extension of the cleansing to the seventh day surely signifies that those who have chosen to turn from worldly wickedness and to do what is more fitting must be scoured by virtuous conduct throughout their whole life and for all the time they live. For the week, as a measure of time, contains completion and a return to the beginning, as when a period has already reached its end. And it says very well that the cleansing through Christ and the purification by water must come and necessarily be added to our own virtuous efforts—holy baptism being understood here in the washing of the body and the garments—while the purification through blood evidently accompanies it. For on the eighth day, it says, he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons. The eighth day, again, would signify for us the time of the dispensation in the flesh, when Emmanuel underwent slaughter for our sake—he who is truly the eloquent and most melodious turtledove, who by his own blood has perfected for ever those who are being sanctified. That Christ's death possesses every fragrance (for it was accomplished for the life of the world and for the destruction of sin) would be shown by there being two turtledoves, one sacrificed for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering. And that Christ became a propitiation for our sins, according to the Scriptures, it showed by saying: "And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge."
Well said.

In this way, then, the divine law declared to us that the man with a discharge must be thoroughly cleansed. But anyone who has an emission is defiled by it, whether it is involuntary or voluntary and springing from natural impulse—voluntary, I mean, as in intercourse with a wife according to the law of marriage, and involuntary, as perhaps in dreams at night. For it says again: "And a man from whom an emission of seed goes out shall bathe his whole body in water, and shall be unclean until evening. And a woman with whom a man lies with an emission of seed—they shall bathe their bodies in water, and shall be unclean until evening." For the charges against both are equal, and there is no difference. Now in the case of the chronic discharge, what was described for us was an affliction that is, so to speak, long and continual; but in the present case the aim of the law seems to be to show that a person will be defiled even if he does not suffer complete and total ruin, but is seen to have suffered it even partially and rarely. The Savior's disciple indicated something of this kind: "For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law." For one who has offended once—that is, who has transgressed at all, even in one thing and in part—must surely be liable to the charge. So according to the law a person is unclean even if he does not go to the extreme of defilement, but is caught having suffered it even in part. Yet he is not utterly cast away; he too is cleansed through water in Christ. Therefore the statement that the defiled person is unclean until evening would very well indicate the time of the Lord's coming. For Christ came at the consummation, when this age had all but reached its very setting; and through him and in him we have washed off all the filth of sin, and we who were held fast in offences have been freed from charges both small and great. And that before the time of his coming it was not possible to wash away defilement (for, according to the Scriptures, no one was justified by the law), you can learn from its saying plainly: "He shall be unclean until evening."
I understand what you are saying, and your account is true.

To these the law adds the regulations about a woman who has a flow of blood and who suffers on her own account an unchecked flow by which she must be defiled. Just as with the man with a discharge every article, every bed, every garment, and everyone who touched him or came near him was defiled, so it is with her. And the law frees her too in the same way as him: by washing with water, by the sacrifice of turtledoves, and also by the atonement of the priest who mediates. But the law, raising us up, as it were, to spiritual thoughts and not allowing us to dwell on the ailments of the flesh (for these were taken as a figure of the inward and spiritual things of the mind), clearly adds: "And you shall make the sons of Israel cautious about their uncleannesses, so that they do not die in their uncleanness by defiling my tent that is among them." For when we have been cleansed and sanctified through Christ, then, then indeed we truly draw near in radiance and shall no longer defile the holy tent; rather, being pure, we shall worship the all-holy God purely, as we go to the churches.
Excellently said.

That human nature had long been sick with defilement, and could be scoured clean in no other way than through Christ, the truly sacred and holy sacrifice, you will know very clearly if you examine another oracle in this law as well. For it is written again in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If a woman conceives and bears a male child, she shall be unclean seven days; as in the days of separation for her menstruation, she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. And for thirty-three days she shall remain in her unclean blood. She shall touch nothing holy and shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification are fulfilled. But if she bears a female child, she shall be unclean twice seven days, as in her menstruation, and for sixty-six days she shall remain in her unclean blood. And when the days of her purification are fulfilled, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a year-old lamb without blemish as a whole burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, to the door of the tent of witness, to the priest; and he shall offer it before the Lord, and the priest shall make atonement for her and cleanse her from the source of her blood."
Who, then, is the woman who gave birth? And what, again, would be the law's aim concerning her?

It seems we must speak with great subtlety. For the substance of this commandment is very sharp and not easy to grasp; but let us investigate as far as we can. This, at least, Palladius, is something I marvel at before all else.
What do you mean?

The law is aimed at every woman who gives birth to a male or a female, and makes its condemnation of us as general as possible. Yet the holy Virgin, from whom we say Christ was born according to the flesh, is exempt from this reproach. Look, if you will, at how precise the law is. “A woman,” it says, and perhaps not every woman without distinction, but “if any woman conceives by seed and bears a male, let her be unclean.” But the divine body came into being from the Holy Spirit. It was formed in the holy Virgin in a way beyond words, and paid little regard to the laws of nature. For the firstborn of the saints, the firstfruits of those who have been granted rebirth from God through the Spirit, had no need at all of the sowing of seed. Of these it is plainly said: “They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.” So the holy Virgin escaped the law's denunciation. She did not conceive by seed at all, but brought forth the divine infant by the working of the Holy Spirit. The woman who gives birth and is therefore unclean would, by any reasonable and blameless understanding, be human nature. For the present we will give nature the role of the woman. The law accuses her and calls her guilty of defilement because she gives birth to corruption. She does not remain in the state in which she first received her existence from God, since she was made for incorruption. Instead she has been carried off course into the necessity of decay. She was condemned for the transgression, and nature has borne a penalty contrary to nature, the punishment of the divine curse. For, as it is written, “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living, and the kingdom of Hades is not upon the earth. For he created all things that they might exist, and the generations of the world are wholesome. But through the envy of the devil death entered into the world.” So nature is defiled by corruption that was brought in from outside, and by death, which gained the mastery through the devil's envy and has sin as its root. It is also defiled in another way, because what is born is conceived in carnal pleasure. The inspired David seems to hint at something like this when he sings: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother craved me.” So nature is unclean, because it undergoes corruption as a result of transgression and curse, contrary to what God willed. For he created all things that they might exist, (sic) and the saying is true.
Then go on to explain how one might be freed from uncleanness.

The law itself, Palladius, showed us the way while it was passing sentence. “Let her be set apart as unclean for seven days,” it says. “And let her count another thirty-three, and she shall remain in the blood of her uncleanness.” This of course refers to a male child. “But if she bears a female,” it says, the separation is doubled, and so is the count of the further days. So if the child born is a male, the mother is unclean and in defilement for seven days and thirty-three, that is, forty. If it is a female, she is unclean for twice seven and sixty-six, that is, eighty.
And what, then, is the reason for this?

Once again the law uses physical examples to lead us up to an understanding of more hidden things, and draws the things of the senses like a picture of spiritual contemplation. Those who are learned in these matters say that if what has been conceived in the womb is male, it barely takes shape after forty days have passed. If it is female, it is slower to reach that point, since it is weak and feeble. They say that it needs twice forty days, that is, eighty, to take a distinct shape. So the woman who bears a male is unclean for forty days, while the mother of a female remained in defilement and uncleanness for a full eighty days, that is, until what is in the womb was precisely formed and had reached human shape. For her purification, as the law prescribes, a lamb and a turtledove were slaughtered at the door of the holy tabernacle, with a priest acting as mediator and performing the sacred rites. And the law said that the male child must be circumcised, as it prescribes, that is, on the eighth day. Such is the meaning of the letter. But let us rise to spiritual contemplation and explain how the nature that gave birth to us for corruption and uncleanness has shaken off its defilements and escaped uncleanness and the denunciation of the law. For it has already spent long ages in separation, that is, away from the face of God. These were the ages before the Lord's coming, during which death reigned from Adam to Moses and sin in its many forms held sway over those on earth. But on the eighth day, that is, after the time of the law and that ancient Sabbath rest, we have been circumcised through the Spirit with a circumcision not made with hands. We have also been formed into Christ and have become partakers of his divine nature. So we have shaken off the charges against us, the filth has been wiped away, and all our defilement is gone. For we are no longer born for corruption because of the transgression in Adam, but for life and incorruption because of the justification in Christ. He endured slaughter for our sake as the true and spotless lamb, as the divine and spiritual turtledove. In no other way have we been saved. Or is that not so?
It is entirely so, for the riddle is very clear.
That we must offer spiritual sacrifices and gifts to God.

What has been said is enough, I think, to show that we must set about nobly to wipe away sin and to be cleansed through Christ. He is able to scour away all the filth in us and to melt it down by the working of the Spirit, and he knows how to make us washed and holy. That is why the sacred word cried out to us in advance about the working of the Spirit that was to come upon us, saying: “Suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he is coming, says the Lord Almighty; and who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears? For he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb, and he will sit refining and purifying, as silver and as gold.” The inspired Isaiah agrees with this, saying: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will purge the blood from their midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.” Well then, Palladius, is the righteousness we understand to be in Christ achieved by us simply by being scoured clean and wiping off our ancient defilements? Tell me, would that be enough to win us a glory fit for saints, and will it crown us with the highest honours? Or will our state be something better, so that we may rightly adorn our heads with the highest praises? Will we bring God a kind of spiritual offering and a truly sacred dedication, a life of sanctification and holiness, and carry through a spiritual worship very well?
I say the latter.

Indeed, this agrees with the sacred laws, is pleasing to God, and is among the things most approved. God commanded that people cease from all work on the Sabbath, and he allowed no one to do anything at all. He says in Exodus: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work; but on the seventh day is the Sabbath, a rest to the Lord your God; you shall not do any work on it.” Clearly the type points to the spiritual keeping of the Sabbath. Christ himself has called us to this, so that we cease and take respite from every fleshly work and every wicked pursuit. We have shaken off the burden of sin, and we love to keep away from wickedness and to stay idle from what lies outside the law. Such a Sabbath rest was beyond the reach of those of Israel, for they never entered into the rest of Christ, as blessed Paul says. But Christ has given us rest and has persuaded us to keep the Sabbath spiritually. We give ourselves freely to virtue and practise a noble idleness from transgressions.
Excellently said.

Yet even in the past God laid it down that everyone must be idle on the Sabbath. Still, those crowned with the divine ministry and appointed to attend the holy tabernacle went on performing the sacred rites. As the Saviour says, they profaned the Sabbath and yet were blameless, and they did not face the charge of having broken the law. So we too will cease from earthly pursuits in Christ, fulfilling the spiritual keeping of the Sabbath. But we will not abstain from the sacred works, by which I mean our duty to bring God spiritual sacrifices and spiritual offerings. Following, as it were, in the footsteps of Christ, as it is written, we will sacrifice ourselves. We will honour the God of all not by slaughtering sheep or with the blood of calves, but rather by dedicating ourselves to him as a fragrant odour. For, in the words of the Psalmist, we will please him more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs.
You think rightly. But come now, go on again, and sketch for me from the sacred Scriptures the passages that describe this splendid and admirable worship.

God, then, said in Leviticus, clearly to all of Israel: “If any man among you brings gifts to the Lord, you shall bring your gifts from the livestock, from the cattle and from the sheep. If his gift is a whole burnt offering from the cattle, he shall bring a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the door of the tent of witness, acceptable before the Lord, and he shall lay his hand on the head of the offering, so that it is acceptable for him and makes atonement for him. And he shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall bring the blood and pour it around on the altar that is at the doors of the tent of witness. When they have flayed the burnt offering, they shall cut it into its pieces. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall put fire on the altar and heap wood on the fire. Then the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall heap the divided pieces, the head and the fat on the wood that is on the fire on the altar. The entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all of it on the altar. It is a burnt offering, a sacrifice, a fragrant odour to the Lord.” Is this not a clear type of the life of the saints, and of their complete closeness to God in spirit and sanctification? We are portrayed in the tame animals, I mean the calf and the sheep. We die to the world by putting the flesh to death, so that we may live to God through the way of life of the Gospel. And we go up, as it were, as a truly spiritual and most fragrant sacrifice to the Father through the Son. Come, let us again discuss each detail, as precisely as we can. Each person dedicates his own life as a kind of gift to God who rules all things, but each does so as it is given to him and according to his measure. As the most wise Paul says, each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and another of another. The sizes of the animals, or rather their differences in kind, show inequality and unlikeness, and this perhaps obliquely signifies differences in spiritual strength and in understanding. A person may be great, like a calf, and very strong, or he may have less, like a sheep, and come behind the perfect. Either way, he brings himself to God as an offering, and as a whole burnt offering, that is, as a complete consecration. His life is not divided toward the things of the world but is wholly and entirely acceptable and sacred to God. Let the manner of the sacrifice be like this: “Let the victim be male and without blemish,” it says. For the saints are always in some way conformed to Christ, who is truly male and without blemish. The male depicts his sovereignty, and the lack of blemish depicts his supernatural and unsurpassable holiness. For we have one Master, incomparably all-pure, Emmanuel. Besides this (for that must be said too, and I think it necessary), those consecrated to God should be male and unblemished. They should have nothing effeminate about them and should not slacken into sluggishness. They should be strongly inclined to act manfully and keep within themselves a mind that is manly and, as it were, wide awake. And I would add that they must be pure and blameless, as far as human nature allows. For the inspired David sings somewhere, and very wisely: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to the innocence that is in me.” God measures human goodness by its own standard, since the goodness of the holy angels clearly rises above it and far exceeds our measure. So let the sacred victim be male and unblemished. It is brought to the very doors of the holy tabernacle. For we are made perfect nowhere else. In every way and without fail, it is in the churches that we will be acceptable to God the Father, with Christ bringing us as our priest. For through him we have gained access, and he himself opened for us the way into [?]. He entered the Holy of Holies as a forerunner on our behalf and showed us the true path. God commanded them to lay their hands on the calf, and by this he obliquely signified that in a type they bring, in place of themselves, an image of the need to live holily by being dead to the world, and so they perform the slaughter of the beast most fittingly. See, then, how the shadow gives shape to the truth for us. The calf was slaughtered before the Lord, and the blood was poured out on the altar. Being dead to the world and putting fleshly impulses to death is most pleasing to God and worthy of his watchful gaze from above. Perhaps the divine David sings of something like this when he says somewhere: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.” The death of the holy ones will be like a sacred dedication to God. I do not at all mean the bodily death that comes to everyone. Rather, the word would signify the death they are accustomed to endure, dying to the world and living to God in holiness and sanctification. For we cannot achieve the holy life unless we have first died to the world. Peter writes about Christ: “He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live to righteousness.” So the slaughter of the calf seems to show dying to sins and enduring the death that is precious to God, which he sees fit to watch over. For it says, “They shall slaughter the calf before the Lord.” And the pouring of the blood on the altar would signify, I think, the consecration of life and the dedication of the soul to the glory of God. The victim is flayed and cut up limb by limb. The flaying suggests the stripping and laying bare, as it were, of what is in us. The dismembering shows very well that the word of God reaches down to the joints and marrow. For it says: “The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.” When the priest kindles the fire, the divided pieces are laid on the altar with the head and the feet, and also the entrails, washed in water. For all that belongs to the saints is fragrant, and nothing that has been entrusted to them is rejected by God. In the type, the flesh would stand for their coarser and bodily life, so to speak, for this too is reverent and all-pure. The head is a sign of the mind, and the entrails of thoughts and desires. The feet, in turn, are a subtle riddle for the practical life and for the course of one’s deeds.
How penetrating your account is!

Yet it holds the truth, even though it darts past us as if in mist and darkness, for the law is deep. “If his gift to the Lord is from the sheep,” it says, “from the lambs or the kids, for a whole burnt offering, he shall bring a male without blemish. He shall lay his hand on its head, and they shall slaughter it at the side of the altar toward the north, before the Lord.” This too is cut into pieces, and its entrails are washed in the same way as the calf’s. Again he decreed that it must be carried up onto the altar, and the same spiritual interpretation would hold here too. But there is one difference: the lamb was slaughtered at the side of the altar toward the north.
What, then, is the meaning of this?

Do you not know that the land of the Jews lies rather to the south? And do you not know that the regions toward the more northerly sea have been divided among the countless flocks of the nations, settled in their lands and cities?
True.

So the slaughter of the lamb on the more northerly side is a riddle. It means that the flocks to the north will also be holy to God. Indeed, the Saviour foretold this about the flock from the nations, saying: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.”
I understand what you mean.

The God of all wants those who choose to fulfil what is prescribed to rise above sluggishness and all reluctance. So he smooths the road of fruitful offering, in a way, and commands that the sacrifice may be carried out even with things smaller than a sheep. He says: “If he brings a burnt offering from the birds as a gift to the Lord, he shall bring his gift from the turtledoves or from the pigeons. The priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head, and the priest shall put it on the altar and drain its blood at the base of the altar. He shall remove the crop together with the feathers and throw them beside the altar, toward the east, into the place of the ashes. He shall break it at the wings but shall not divide it, and the priest shall put it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering of sacrifice, a fragrant odour to the Lord.” See again how excellently and skilfully the saints are kept in a form that conforms to Christ. For he himself is truly the turtledove from above, whose voice sounds most clearly, and likewise the gentlest dove. So in the Song of Songs it is written about him: “The voice of the turtledove was heard in the wilderness.” And he set himself before us as a type and pattern of the greatest and highest gentleness, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart.” But see, the saints too, because they have taken on the form of Christ, have been carefully granted a fitting and admirable share in equal goods, as it were. For they too may fittingly be understood as turtledoves. They send forth the divine and sacred word to their hearers and are eager to make songs and melodies to the glory of God. So they say: “My tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, on your praise all the day long.” They also live the life that is in Christ and go along the gentlest path of the way of life of the Gospel. To those who wish to strike them on the right cheek they turn the left as well, and to those who force them to go one mile they freely offer to go two, if they wish. So they consecrate themselves to God as a fragrant odour and as a whole burnt offering, in the form, as it were, of turtledoves and pigeons. Then the priest wrings off the head and places it on the altar, having poured out the blood. For the mind of the most sacred saints is truly holy and in the highest degree fit to be dedicated to the all-pure God. It is filled with good thoughts and breathes the fragrance of the ointment of the true knowledge of God, for, as it is written, “the thoughts of the righteous are judgments.” That the life of those who live in the fear of God is also holy becomes clear from the rule that the blood must be poured at the holy altar, for blood is a type of life. The crop of the birds, that is, the gullet, is removed with the feathers and thrown out as completely useless. This too would be a clear sign that the life of the saints has been shown to be above bodily luxury, so that it already seems, in a way, not even to need a belly to hold food. For such, in some sense, is the life of the most devoted ascetics. They disregard food and perhaps even the belly itself, wasting away the flesh and putting pleasures to death, and they have become free and released from everything worldly and superfluous. This, I think, is the casting away of the feathers. Birds need their plumage, and we too need the things that serve this earthly body in its needs. I mean clothing and the means of getting food. On top of these there are the things by which these are obtained: earning money to fight off the onset of want, soft beds, and things of that kind. These are useful and necessary to those who live on earth and in bodies. Yet the saints count them as nothing. They dismiss the possession of such things as a pointless nuisance and go through life in the world with bodies almost naked and unclothed. They grant to the needs of the flesh, and only reluctantly, whatever comes to hand and is easily obtained. When the feathers have been plucked and the gullet, or crop, removed, it says, “He shall break it at the wings but shall not divide it,” and then he shall carry it up to the altar. The breaking of the wings would be a type and clear example of not thinking haughty thoughts. The mind of the saints should not fly high but should rather go along with the lowly and, as it were, seek what is below. For the mind of the boastful is always lifted up and carried to the heights. It cannot bear to settle down with those who are humbler, and it despises a modest and lowly spirit. So the breaking of the wings hints at the putting away of boastfulness. The not dividing shows that they have dedicated their own life to God entirely and, so to speak, in every way, without being divided toward the things of the world. The wise Paul also said that those who are married are divided. Holy, then, is the mind of the saints, and holy their life. It is superior to bodily luxury, free from worldly care, and beautiful in its modest spirit, and it is undivided toward the things of the world. That is why it is dedicated to God as a fragrant odour.
So it is.

He brings the forms of sacrifice down to things smaller still, things that are at hand all year round and can be obtained without sweat. In this way, I think, he widens for small and great alike the road to winning God’s approval. For it is written: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” The God who loves virtue does not judge sincerity simply and entirely by the size of the offering. The humble person who gives what he has, and chooses to honour God with whatever he has and can afford, stands equal with those who excel. So he said again: “If a soul brings a gift as a sacrifice to the Lord, his gift shall be fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it; it is a sacrifice. He shall bring it to the sons of Aaron, the priests. The priest shall take from it a full handful of the fine flour with the oil, and all its frankincense, and shall put its memorial portion on the altar. It is a sacrifice, a fragrant odour to the Lord.” Do you see how it hints at the lowliness of the one who brings it? The divine law calls him simply “a soul,” even if he is very obscure in this life. In this too it shows that the supreme nature is equal and impartial toward all, just as when it says again: “All souls are mine.” For the Divine shows no partiality, as I said just now. So if one of those who have no standing in the world, it says, chooses to bring a gift to God, the form of the sacrifice will be fine flour, but soaked in oil and mixed with frankincense. Much of our discussion has already made clear that the fine flour is a type of life, the oil a type of cheerfulness in hope, and the frankincense a type of the fragrance of good deeds and right actions and of a life wholly in keeping with the law. So the law says, and very rightly, that those who choose to gladden the God of all within themselves must dedicate and consecrate their own life to him. They must not be gloomy over the sweat of toiling for virtue (for the inspired Paul says, “Do not grumble”). Their life must be filled with spiritual fragrance, for then the priest will offer up its memorial to God. For in Christ we will approach God the Father through spiritual sacrifice and gain a place in his memory as well. Through the very things by which we usually win approval, we will show that we are worthy of remembrance and have come to be known by God in Christ.
Most elegantly said.

To this he adds: “If you bring a gift, a sacrifice baked in an oven, as a gift to the Lord, it shall be of fine flour: unleavened loaves kneaded with oil and unleavened wafers spread with oil. If his gift is a sacrifice from a griddle, it shall be fine flour kneaded with oil, unleavened. You shall break it into pieces and pour oil on them; it is a sacrifice to the Lord. If your gift is a sacrifice from a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil. If you bring a sacrifice of firstfruits to the Lord, you shall bring new grain, roasted and crushed into grits for the Lord. You shall bring the sacrifice of firstfruits and put frankincense on them; it is a sacrifice. The priest shall offer up its memorial portion from the grits with the oil, and all its frankincense. It is a burnt offering to the Lord.”
How deep a thing the law is! Explain, then, how we may apply our minds even to such fine details without straying from the mark.

This, I think, is worth noticing: the foresight of the law and its great skill. You will see it in every way. It accepts even the very smallest offering, and everywhere grants to this too fragrance and cheerfulness. You have surely learned this from Christ himself, who says: "And whoever gives one of these little brothers a cup of cold water to drink, only in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward." Something of this kind must be considered here as well, and we must applaud the lawgiver's kindness with the praises fitting to him. For, as I said, he accepts the offering even if someone chooses to fulfil the prescribed rites with the very cheapest things. Whether it is bread, he says, or a single cake, whether it comes from an oven or from a pan, or indeed from a griddle, and even if it is not of wheat at all but groats and crushed grain, that is, meal made from pulses, let what is brought be moistened with oil, and let it in turn be enriched with frankincense laid upon it. In these things the passage seems to hint at the way the saints win approval through burning, toil and crushing. For the oven and the griddle, and indeed being ground fine in a mill, would surely be signs of the crushing and toil of those who are tested as through fire. That is why those who travel this glorious path cry out: "For you have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined." And the divine David sings to us: "A broken and humbled heart God will not despise." Anyone who considers the purpose of the frankincense and the oil will see that for those who have toiled in this way it would fittingly follow, in every respect, that they become the fragrance of Christ, and moreover that they must receive mercy and be richly fattened with the grace of the Spirit. For are not the things in the law hints and shadows of subtle riddles for us?
Certainly.

So we shall offer ourselves to God, putting ourselves to death to sin and undergoing this sacred death in a spiritual sense, yet living to righteousness, as it is written. As a kind of thank offering we render to him our own life, glorious and blameless and adorned with the glories of love for God. We shall learn this clearly from other laws too. For it is written in Leviticus: "If his gift to the Lord is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he brings it from the cattle, whether male or female, he shall bring it without blemish before the Lord. He shall lay his hands on the head of the gift and slaughter it before the Lord at the doors of the tent of witness. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall pour the blood around the altar of whole burnt offerings. And from the sacrifice of peace offering they shall bring an offering for burning to the Lord: the fat that covers the belly, and all the fat that is on the belly, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is by the thighs, and the lobe on the liver he shall remove together with the kidneys. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall carry them up to the altar, on top of the whole burnt offerings, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar: an offering for burning, an odor of fragrance to the Lord." The calf, then, is without blemish, for those who go up to God as an odor of fragrance must be pure and as far as possible from every blemish. It was slaughtered at the very doors of the holy tent, with the hands of the one bringing it laid upon it, and the reason for this has been stated clearly. The fat on the belly was carried up for sacrifice, as were the two kidneys, with the fat on them removed together with them, and the lobe of the liver. The fat on the belly would signify, I think, the good condition of the mind, so to speak, and the richness of the inward parts that have been excellently nourished by the spiritual provisions supplied through the Spirit. For in irrational animals, and in human bodies as well, good feeding produces fatness; but the richest participation in divine gifts fills the mind of the saints with every good. Therefore they would be sacred and choice for God, as an odor of fragrance. The kidneys, again, would be a type of the discerning activity within the mind, by which what tends to do harm is rejected, and what is beneficial is chosen and judged worth taking. The divine Paul also writes: "Test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every form of evil." Since the kidney is a discerning organ in the body (for it separates out what is superfluous very well, letting into the system what is useful and beneficial, and skilfully distributing it to whatever parts and in whatever amount is fitting), we may reasonably take the kidneys to mean the discernment of the mind. So the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they have in their minds, are sacred and an offering to God. For those devoted to God are approved and exacting money-changers: they always reject what is base as counterfeit, but are accustomed to honour with an excellent verdict whatever tends to benefit. In this sense, I think, the divine Psalmist too, who was accustomed to win approval, cried out to God: "For you have possessed my kidneys, O Lord." The lobe of the liver signifies to us nothing other than the activity of the soul, that is, the movement of the mind by which it is impelled toward desires. Some who have examined such matters closely say without hesitation that every animal has its desires in the liver. So the lobe of the liver too must be dedicated to God, that is, what is, as it were, the very source of all our desire, as the Psalmist sings: "Lord, all my desire is before you." A person may take pride in himself and sing out this solemn and admirable utterance if he directs his longings only toward what pleases God and is found thirsting to do whatever He himself wills.
I agree; you understand it rightly.

For a sheep, again, and indeed for a goat, he lays down the same law, and the sacrifice was carried out for them in the same way. The difference in the size of the animals elegantly suggests the measure of piety and approval among those who are accustomed to bear fruit. One must be thought of as bearing fruit richly and surpassingly, as in the calf; another moderately, as in the sheep; another more modestly still, for a goat is smaller than a sheep. And this, I think, is the fertile earth's yielding a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, according to the parable in the Gospels.
I am persuaded.

That the repayment of reward is in proportion to each person's good deeds, and that God will allot to those who have chosen to act nobly rewards equal to their sweat, the Saviour himself will assure us. He says that the talents were not distributed in equal fashion, and he sets those who did well, one over ten cities and another over five. For each person's life is weighed, as it were, in a balance, and the repayment will surely balance our virtues. And no less, as I said, the law given through Moses will show us this. For it says again in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land where you are to dwell, which I am giving you, and you make whole burnt offerings to the Lord, a whole offering or a sacrifice, to magnify a vow, or as a freewill offering, or at your feasts, to make an odor of fragrance to the Lord, whether from the cattle or from the sheep, then the one who offers his gift to the Lord shall bring a sacrifice of fine flour, a tenth of an ephah, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil. And you shall prepare wine for a libation, a quarter of a hin, with the whole burnt offering or with the sacrifice. For the one lamb you shall prepare this much, an offering for burning, an odor of fragrance to the Lord. And for the ram, when you prepare it as a whole burnt offering or as a sacrifice, you shall prepare a sacrifice of fine flour, two tenths, mixed with a third of a hin of oil; and you shall offer wine for a libation, a third of a hin, as an odor of fragrance to the Lord. And if you prepare one from the cattle as a whole burnt offering, or as a sacrifice to magnify a vow, or as a peace offering to the Lord, then with the calf he shall offer a sacrifice of fine flour, three tenths, mixed with half a hin of oil, and wine for a libation, half a hin, an offering for burning as an odor of fragrance to the Lord. So you shall do for the one calf, or for the one ram, or for the one lamb from the sheep or from the goats. According to the number of those you prepare, so you shall do for each one, according to their number. Every native-born person shall do so when he brings such offerings for burning as an odor of fragrance to the Lord. And if a proselyte joins you in your land, or whoever may be among you in your generations, and he makes an offering for burning, an odor of fragrance to the Lord, then as you do, so the congregation shall do for the Lord. There shall be one law for you and for the proselytes who live among you, an everlasting law throughout your generations; as you are, so shall the proselyte be before the Lord. There shall be one law and one ordinance for you and for the proselyte who lives among you."
Then where are we to see the equal share and the proportion, as you put it, in whatever someone does?

Do you not hear, my friend, the law saying plainly that if someone chooses to fulfil vows and whole burnt offerings, and he sacrifices a lamb, he is to add to the offering a tenth of an ephah of fine flour and a quarter of a hin of wine and of oil? (These, I think, are measures in the Hebrew language.) But if it is a ram, it says, the accompanying offerings are increased, that is, to a third, for a quarter is a smaller measure than a third. And when a calf is offered, the fine flour and the rest go beyond the third again, and come finally to a half.
I follow. So what does this mean?

You surely know that fine flour from wheat is a type of life, and oil a type of cheerfulness; for it is written, "to make the face cheerful with oil." Wine is a sign of the spiritual gladness that comes from above, through the Spirit; for "wine," it says, "gladdens the heart of man."
I understand.

So in proportion to the fruit each person bears, God also supplies life, with cheerfulness and gladness. We certainly do not say that in living, or in being made alive by God, there is a greater or a lesser; that would be nonsense. When we say "life," we mean the splendour of that life, in which one person may perhaps surpass another, while another stands lower than others. Yet he is not without honour and glory, for "star differs from star in glory." So here too the difference between the victims is an image of the glorious life of the saints, and by the quantity of the accompanying offerings it portrays for us the measure of glory. And by adding that the proselyte is not to use other laws, he showed that those from the nations, together with those of Israel's blood, would bow their necks to the Saviour's yoke and would go by way of the same sacrifices and spiritual achievements. For there is one way for all into intimacy with God the Father, and that way is Christ. As the divine Peter said, "There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
The argument is put excellently and with great skill.

We shall by no means be speaking falsely when we affirm that the ways of winning approval are various, and that God will allot rewards in balance with each person's measure. The most wise Paul too will make this clear when he says: "He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully." And David cried out beforehand: "And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me." Or would you not say that the righteousness of Paul, for example, is different from that of anyone, whoever he may be, who has not yet reached such a level (I mean in spiritual strength) that he can plainly cry out: "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world"?
Certainly.
What then? Shall we not grant that the cleanness of John's hands is different from that of someone else who is only beginning to rise toward the way of life of the Gospel?
We shall; how could we not?

Then tell me: will the judge of all, who is just, demand from us a righteousness that keeps pace with the achievements of the saints and is entirely like them? Or, having tested the measure of the strength that is in us, will he demand nothing more than what each person has and is able to accomplish?

That is what I say too; for Christ said, "From the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will ask much." And clearly the converse is also true: surely little will be asked of one who has received less.

Look, then, at what is written in the law, and at how God asks of each person what is in proportion to that person's measure. Since he is the fount and source of a gentleness and love for humankind beyond words, he sends away none of those who have run to him in faith. He accepts each one with whatever he has and receives spiritual gifts, everywhere excusing what is beyond a person's strength. The law on this matter in Leviticus runs as follows: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If a man vows a vow to the Lord as the value of his soul, the valuation of a male from twenty years old to sixty years old shall be fifty didrachms of silver by the holy weight, and the valuation of a female shall be thirty didrachms. If from five years to twenty years, the valuation of a male shall be twenty didrachms, and of a female ten didrachms. From one month to five years, the valuation of a male shall be five didrachms of silver, and of a female three didrachms of silver. If from sixty years and upward, if it is a male, his valuation shall be fifteen didrachms of silver, and if a female, ten didrachms of silver. But if he is too poor for the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; as the hand of the one who vowed is able, so the priest shall value him." For some came forward, enrolling themselves for sanctification and as an offering to God, and gladly dedicating the number of didrachms fixed by the law. But if someone was not very well off, that is, one of the humbler sort, the payment was no longer according to the law; instead the priest serving at the time assessed him and fixed a debt equal to his means. This, then, is the more evident account and sense of the letter. But I consider it necessary to remind those who devote themselves most studiously to the sacred words that Christ once addressed the Pharisees and recalled this very commandment clearly and plainly. They had shifted their anchorage to some faded way of life not recognized by the law, "teaching as doctrines the commandments of men," as it is written, and they came to him saying, "Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread." At once the Saviour answered them: "Why do you too transgress the commandment of God? For God said, 'Honour your father and your mother, that it may go well with you'; but you say, 'Whoever says to his father and his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is a gift," shall not honour his father and his mother.' And you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition." For the Pharisees, who loved money and were extremely greedy for gain, wanted to see as many people as possible going to the enrolment under the law, so that their purses might grow fat with what they collected with insatiable hand from each person who came. But it was natural that some would shrink from the enrolment, having poverty as no ignoble excuse for their hesitation, and also the need to care in their old age for their fathers and mothers out of what they themselves earned, and that with no little sweat. As soon as the accursed Pharisees learned this, they urged such people to go readily to the dedication. They no longer thought as was fitting, and they set at nothing what the law decreed, I mean, to fulfil very fully the reverence owed to parents and to take care of them; rather, they urged them, as it were, to bid farewell to fulfilling these customary duties. Since under the law it was a crime and an indictable offence to appropriate anything offered for God's glory, and "gift" was the name for dedicated things, they taught people to say to parents who asked for help: "Whatever you would have gained from me is a gift," that is, "whatever I might give you is a dedicated offering, and know that you have offended against the law by pilfering and impiously taking what belongs to God's glory." And the authors of these most shameful inventions affirmed that inhumanity toward parents was blameless in those who had chosen instead to dedicate their property to God according to the law. This, I think, is the meaning of "Whoever says to his father or his mother, 'Whatever you would have gained from me is a gift,' shall not honour his father or his mother." In other words: let it be permitted not to honour one's father, nor indeed to show reverence to one's mother, for those who say, "Whatever you would have gained from me is a gift," that is, "what I might perhaps benefit you by giving you is a divine gift, and you will be a thief of sacred offerings."
I say that this has been put rightly and truly.
Since the historical sense is now clear to us, let us go on to the spiritual meaning and take hold of the contemplation that lies beyond things perceived by the senses.
Let us go on.

Each of us, Palladius, who has been justified in faith and sanctified in the Spirit has become a sacred offering to God. And each of us owes his own life to Christ. For, as the divine Paul said, "We were bought with a price, and we are not our own." And again: "One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and was raised for them." For through himself he acquired us for God the Father, laying down his own blood for us as a kind of price. So we approach Christ, the Saviour of all, through faith and sanctification, and in return for what he has done for us we bring the dedication of a life lived in piety. But the manner of this offering would be understood, quite reasonably, to be various and not one. Some rush toward it without much vigour; others with warmer zeal, as it were, with a vigorous understanding and a wakeful mind, and they press on with the keenest impulses to accomplish whatever must be fulfilled and to be able to carry out what pleases him. These would be, according to what the historical sense suggests, those from twenty years old up to sixty. For up to the sixtieth year the body remains vigorous and its movements are at their most active, and the mind is by then settled and in some way strong, and very well suited to receive whatever it chooses to learn. And he who knows our frame, as it is written, surely recognized some such age in souls as well. For the discourse surely passes from likenesses drawn from bodily things to spiritual ones. Whether, then, it is a male or a female, those who are still in the prime of spiritual age are to bring what is prescribed. The male, as with fifty didrachms, brings the complete and most perfect fruit of spiritual service, which through the seven times seven is clearly seen to reach the highest goal and to be attested as perfection. The female, again, as with thirty didrachms: for though she wins less approval than the male, she nevertheless brings, as befits her own nature, the fruit that is in perfection and toil, as signified by the three decades. The one from five to twenty years, if a male, makes a deposit of twenty didrachms; if a female, ten. For from the age of five, I think, and barely even then, the mind begins, as it were, to open its eyes to understanding. It is still childish and weak, but it is advancing toward what is better, and the body is growing toward ever greater vigour. Or do you not understand what I mean?
Very much so.

So the fruit from each person is measured to match his spiritual strength. And everywhere the female comes behind the male, often by half. That the vessel is weaker, the divine Paul has clearly testified. She falls short of the natural gifts of men, and she keeps silent in the churches; for she has not been entrusted with the word, and she is by no means as strong for the achievement of virtue as the male is seen to be. And from one month old, it says, up to five years, five didrachms for the male and three for the female. And yet what fruit could come from infants? The passage, then, is hinting to us at a child newly born in Christ, those for whom, as the sacred Paul said, milk is the fitting food. For those who have just been called through faith and are still infants, the fruit is small. Knowing this, the divine disciples, when they wrote to those from the nations, said that, although so very much gospel commandment had been given by Christ, they needed only to keep away from fornication, from what is strangled and from blood; and they said that those who did this would do well. For a mind that is still tender and infantile should not be weighed down with very heavy burdens. The law added that from those sixty years and above there should be required fifteen didrachms for a male and ten for a female. For what has already declined into feebleness and weakness could hardly be very fruitful, just as aging plants, as their roots grow old, are evidently sluggish in producing ripe fruit. So God, who is truly just and compassionate, receives fruits in proportion to each person's zeal and fitness of mind. He neither disregards what is weak and past its prime nor dismisses it as feeble, nor does he leave the vigorous without reward; rather, he widens, as it were, the way of winning approval for those who wish it, in whatever way each one is able. And those who are weaker in condition, and perhaps also of little understanding, he himself will keep as his own, measuring the fruitfulness of each according to his strength. This, I think, is the meaning of "He shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him according to what the hand of the one who vowed is able."
How finely drawn the argument is!

So then, Palladius, we must offer up to God, like a fragrant odor and as a debt owed, a holy way of life and the glories of an exceptional life. You have surely learned that one of the saints wrote: "Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and offer him the firstfruits of your fruits of righteousness." The people of old thought to honor him with sacrifices of oxen and with incense, for this was the path of life under the law. But we who are now in Christ through faith walk the better and superior road. We will offer God worship in spirit and in truth. We will, as the saying goes, let out every sail so that we can nobly carry out what we ought, and we will honor God with spiritual and holy offerings. For I say that we must remember the one who speaks plainly through the all-wise Moses: "You shall keep what goes out through your lips." That is, whatever you vow, hasten to fulfill it, and very promptly. In such matters delay is not without cost. "If you vow a vow to the Lord," it says, "do not delay to pay it. It is better that you not vow than that you vow and not pay."
True.

And indeed one could learn the wise aim of the skill needed for fulfilling vows and promises from no other source but the law, and learn it without error. For it is written: "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." Are we not guided by the divine law as by a light? Could one not speed along a straight and unerring road, having its rays as a kind of lamp?
How could it be otherwise? For the divine David also sings somewhere: "The commandment of the Lord shines far, enlightening the eyes."

How, then, shall we win approval as we live the glorious and all-pure life and render to God a splendid offering, the ways of exceeding goodness? You will know it quite clearly, since God also instructs us through other oracles. In Numbers it goes like this: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If a man or a woman makes a great vow to consecrate himself in purity to the Lord, he shall keep himself pure from wine and strong drink. He shall not drink vinegar made from wine or vinegar made from strong drink, and he shall not drink anything prepared from grapes. He shall not eat fresh grapes or raisins all the days of the vow of his purification. Of anything that comes from the vine, from the wine of the pressed skins to the grape-seed, he shall eat nothing all the days of his purification. No razor shall come upon his head until the days that he vowed to the Lord are fulfilled. He shall be holy, letting the hair of his head grow long all the days of his vow to the Lord. He shall not go near any dead person. For father or mother, for brother or sister, he shall not defile himself for them when they die, because the vow of his God is upon him, upon his head. All the days of his vow he shall be holy to the Lord. And if anyone dies suddenly beside him, the head of his vow shall at once be defiled. He shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day he shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the doors of the tent of witness. The priest shall offer one for sin and one as a whole burnt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he committed concerning the dead person. And he shall consecrate his head on that day on which he consecrated to the Lord all the days of the vow, and he shall bring a year-old lamb as a burnt offering for trespass. And the former days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled."

This oracle is not easy to understand, least of all unless the law is subjected to careful examination. For not shaving the hair but letting it grow long and hang down, and keeping away from wine and vinegar and raisins and even grape-seeds: what kind of worship could that be?

None, Palladius, in truth, if one were to consider the thing simply as it is by nature. Yet the aim of the law is remarkable. It skillfully recasts the customs of the Greeks into something more fitting, and it elegantly turns even what seems pointless into an image of the gospel life. So if anyone aims to consecrate himself to God by the great vow, that is, by the highest way of life and the straight and blameless path of perfect righteousness, let him keep far from wine and strong drink. That is, let him free his mind from everything that can intoxicate it and usually clouds it. These things, I think, would be worldly thinking, earthly desires, the cares of the flesh, and pointless distractions. Some of the priests suffered this, and the prophetic word lamented them in words like these: "For priest and prophet were beside themselves because of wine, from the drunkenness of strong drink." And the prophet also says about others: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their tendril from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is bitterness, their wine is the rage of dragons." Still others are said to give their neighbor a muddy, overturning draught to drink. So the law shuts out the mind of the consecrated from everything that knows how to intoxicate. And it says, very rightly, that they must have no share in vinegar either. By vinegar, I think, it means unnatural and perverted pleasures. It also forbids the use of raisins and grape-seeds, and so it does not allow the mind to stoop even, so to speak, to the old remnants of the pleasures within us. Wine, then, and everything made from it have been condemned by the law for this reason, I believe, and for no other. Now that we have spoken of the other things, come, let us say what the command to let the hair grow long for God might mean. The most foolish children of the Greeks followed their unnatural customs and lived like irrational beasts. They let their hair grow, claiming that they were growing it for demons. One would cut it off at set times for the mountain nymphs, another for a river, and for them the practice was a form of worship. But Moses, the wisest of men, or rather the all-wise and supremely skillful God through Moses, made similar laws, because the Israelites found the error they had learned in Egypt hard to wash away. He moved them little by little by means of their ancient habits and ways, so that they would no longer attach their reverence to demons but to the God of all, as through type and shadow. For this reason he also laid down the laws about sacrifices, and he accepted the blood sacrifices unwillingly. Indeed, he said plainly through the voice of Isaiah: "For who required these things from your hands?" So among the Greeks the custom was utterly irrational, but the law teaches better things, and by reason it reshapes into good order even what seems pointless. Do you want us to discuss each detail as well, so far as we can?
Very much so.

Do you not know (for I will remind you) that the sacred text has made the head a figure of the mind, since it is the mind's dwelling place? For that is how the divinely inspired Scripture understands it.
I agree. What of it?

Hairs are the fruit of the head and spring up like growths that are part of our nature. In the same way, thoughts and everything that comes from the mind would be the fruit of the mind. They well up in us in the same manner and form, as it were, a beautiful and flourishing head of hair that adorns the mind. We must therefore not keep the mind within us bare and stripped of good thoughts. Rather, it should be teeming, as it were, and growing long hair for God: that is, an exact knowledge of whatever is best. Through this knowledge it will explore the divine beauty itself, whatever it may be. It will clearly survey things hidden as if in the depths, and it will grow rich in the principles of perfect rectitude. So it will be able to gain an entirely blameless knowledge of God and walk the most unerring path, I mean the path to all that is admirable. Or will you not say that such a person has already, in a sense, sped to the very limit of all praise?
Very much so.

And what of this? When the head is shaved and stripped bare and the hair is cut "in Christ" [another reading: "to the skin"], would this not bring a suspicion of dishonor on anyone to whom it might happen?
I understand.

Indeed, God says to the mother of the Jews, I mean Jerusalem: "Shave and cut your hair for your delicate children. Make your widowhood broad like an eagle, for they have been taken captive from you." For shaving brings insult and dishonor, and it is most fitting for those who mourn.
Well said.

Bare, then, and utterly dishonored, and full of shame is the mind that does not have within itself the things that make it admired. Among such minds one would very reasonably count the dull-witted and those who hold a corrupt opinion of God. They worship stones; that is, they senselessly dare to give reverence to the creation rather than to the Creator and Maker. They think and say what is entirely perverse. They shake off the true and blameless faith, and instead they leap upon whatever anyone may babble out of foolishness. All this happens because their mind is not thickly covered with good thoughts.
Excellently said.

Let the mind, then, be filled with thoughts that lead to rectitude and with insights it has found into every admirable thing, and let these crown it like a head of hair. Such a person is wise in the highest degree and is well prepared at last to receive into himself the illumination that is in Christ through faith. Such a person has trained himself in a noble and choice life and is distinguished by such a mind. The divine oracle commands him to keep far from everything that naturally defiles, to withdraw from the works of the flesh, and to cast as far away as possible everything that tends toward deadness and corruption. This, surely, is what it hints at when it says that one must not go near the dead or be ready to be defiled by a corpse. The law shuts him out from such a thing completely, and it places what pleases God above even reverence toward parents. For it says: "For father and for mother he shall not go in." When virtue is being achieved, away with love of the flesh! Let God hold the foremost and better place, above kinship by blood. This is what Christ himself said: "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me." The Savior himself also taught us that the things of God rank above reverence for parents. One of those already numbered among the disciples came to him and said, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." But he said, "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead." By "the dead" he meant, I think, those who have chosen to set their minds on the things of the world and have not kept away from the works of deadness.
So it is.

This, then, is the manner of the all-pure and exceptional way of life according to the law, or rather as it is in spirit and in truth, for the law is a shadow. But if it should ever happen, it says, that the consecrated person is defiled by a corpse, then let him cut off his hair and shave his head bare, since his hair has now in some way become unholy. "And on the eighth day he shall bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons." Let him also bring, it says, a year-old lamb; "and the first days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled." Suppose the consecrated person grows careless of what is fitting, turns aside to the things of the flesh, and is defiled by ways that lead to deadness. Then it will surely follow that he must forfeit the glories of the all-pure way of life, and he will, as it were, bring utter dishonor on his own head. For shaving hints at something of this kind. And since he has toiled in vain through all the time that has passed, he will lament his lost sweat. This, I think, is the meaning of "The first days shall not count." He says something similar through the voice of Ezekiel: "The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on the day he sins, and the lawlessness of the lawless shall not harm him on the day he turns from his lawlessness." So if the consecrated are somehow defiled along the way, they will suffer the loss of what they have already accomplished. Yet the loss they suffer from this is not beyond escape, for they are washed clean in Christ. He offers himself for us to God the Father, like a turtledove and a dove. He is sacrificed as a lamb, and he justifies us by the death of his own flesh. That is why he commanded that the one who has undergone shaving should offer sacrifices as a type of Christ, who justifies the ungodly, strengthens the weak, raises up the fallen, turns back the straying, and washes the defiled.
Excellently said.

But I think that if we apply our minds a little to what lies before us, we can perceive another depth of subtle and hidden meanings. The law, not without forethought, spurs us on to this when it says of the one who grows his hair for God: "If someone dies suddenly, the head of his vow shall at once be defiled. He shall shave his head on the day he is cleansed; on the seventh day he shall be shaved. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest." "And he shall consecrate," it says, "his head on that day." He was also commanded to bring a year-old lamb.
One who has learned from Christ might well ask what the riddle means. Tell one who is eager to learn what it points to.
Then I will speak as well as I can. But you, for your part, be forgiving if I stray at all from the road, for the subject is difficult and the riddle obscure.
Agreed.

The head of the body, Palladius, represents for us the mind, which dwells within it, for so it seemed good to the divine and sacred Scripture. So we compare to hair and locks the thoughts that naturally spring from the mind and within it, by which we are guided to the knowledge of anything that exists. For these are what well up for us from the head.
I remember.

So in us too the mind is, in a sense, unshorn and grows its hair long for God when it is full of good thoughts. But it is bare and stripped, afflicted with a most shameful baldness, if it holds no correct ideas about God and does not grow rich in the best and irreproachable knowledge of all that must be done.
True. We were discussing this just now.

Before the Savior came, then, Israel was called through Moses to the knowledge of God, and that is why it was also sanctified. In a way it made to God the vow of purity. On Mount Horeb it clearly promised to keep the law, saying: "All that the Lord God has spoken we will do and hear." So it had its mind full of the law's instruction. It was, as it were, growing long hair for God, namely the glories of the commandment given through Moses. But they were defiled by a corpse, for they killed Emmanuel. The death of Christ was truly holy, but for those who killed him the charge of killing the Lord was a defilement. So the law now commands them to shave off the instruction of the law like a head of hair. It practically commands them to cut away the things in types on the seventh day, that is, the things before the eighth day. On the eighth day Christ came back to life, renewing us to incorruption and refashioning us for a new life, the life of the gospel. So the one who has cut away the things before the eighth day grows his hair again and consecrates his head after the eighth day. The mind grows its hair again no longer with types and shadows as before, but with the very teachings of faith and truth. Or do you not think that those who have been justified by faith must be stripped, as it were, of the honor of worship under the law? In its place they must grow the knowledge of the gospel way of life and take it into mind and heart, since it is far better and superior to what was there in the beginning.
What do you mean?

Paul was learned in the law. Did he not cry out clearly and openly about those ancient glories of the law? "Whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ our Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as rubbish, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ."
I have heard it.

He also rebuked others for honoring the circumcision of the law after the mystery of Christ. "You have been cut off from Christ," he says, "you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen from grace. But we through faith await the hope of righteousness." And he said that the old commandment had been made useless because it was not without fault, and that another had been brought in to replace it, that is, the commandment of the gospel.
True.

So the riddle shows that the instruction of the law had become rather idle. It orders Israel, which made the vow, to shave, as one that has been defiled by a corpse, that is, as one guilty of the charge of killing the Lord. And it orders Israel to consecrate to God a different head of hair, as it were, after the eighth day, that is, after the resurrection. This new hair is the precise and finely wrought refinement and instruction of the gospel's commands. And the law commanded the one who grows his hair to offer turtledoves and pigeons after the eighth day. In this too it set down a sign of the one who cleanses the defiled, that is, Christ. Both birds signify him: the turtledove shows him to be most melodious, and the dove shows him to be most gentle. The law, by contrast, was slow of tongue and lacked gentleness, for it imposes penalties on wrongdoers at once. A lamb is also offered together with the birds, so that Christ might be understood through all of them. Through the birds he is understood as coming from above and from heaven, and through the lamb as coming from below and from earth. For the Word, being God by nature, became flesh. But even so he was and is God. He frees us from the shadow of the law, and he plants the knowledge of his own commands in the hearts of all. And he makes us truly holy, cleansing us with his own blood, according to the Scriptures.
So it is.

"But if," he says, "the course of the vow is brought to a good completion, let it then be completed by the one who lets his hair grow after the eighth day." And he lays down how this is to be done, saying: "And this is the law of the one who has vowed: On the day that he completes the days of his vow, he shall bring it himself to the doors of the tent of witness. He shall bring his gift to the Lord: one male lamb a year old without blemish for a whole burnt offering, one ewe lamb a year old without blemish for a sin offering, one ram without blemish for a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened bread of fine flour, loaves kneaded with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, together with their grain offering and their drink offering. The priest shall bring them before the Lord, and shall make his sin offering and his whole burnt offering, and he shall make the ram a sacrifice of peace offering to the Lord with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall make his grain offering and his drink offering. And the one who has vowed shall shave the head of his vow at the doors of the tent of witness, and shall put the hair on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering. The priest shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, one unleavened loaf from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the one who has vowed after he has shaved his head; and the priest shall bring them as an offering placed before the Lord. It shall be holy to the priest, in addition to the breast of the offering placed and the shoulder of the portion set aside. After this the one who has vowed may drink wine. This is the law of the one who vows, whoever vows his gift to the Lord for his vow, apart from whatever else his hand can afford, according to the measure of the vow that he vows under the law of purity." For the one who has paid to God his vow to purify himself as he ought has, as it were, unloaded the grossness of the Mosaic narrative and freed his mind from worship in types and shadows, as from a long and heavy head of hair; and having, like hair growing back, the truly purifying knowledge and instruction of the decrees given through Christ, he will be holy and consecrated, and acceptable besides. He will offer himself up to God as a fragrant aroma, and will dedicate, as an acceptable sacrifice, the glorious and blameless refinement of his own way of life. For he will bring, it says, his gift: a year-old lamb for a whole burnt offering, and again a ewe lamb for sin, and also a ram for a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened loaves moistened with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. By the lamb one may reasonably understand the infancy in Christ of the one who brings the sacrifice, and by the ram what is mature in understanding and, as it were, in bearing fruit. For he says: "Brothers, do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature." Between them comes the ewe lamb, for sin. By this, again, it is easier for us to see that even the life of those who are highly purified, who are understood to live in the simplicity and innocence that is in Christ and have been perfected in soundness of mind, is not entirely blameless, but certainly needs cleansing. For no one will possess complete freedom from reproach; it is reserved for Emmanuel alone, and will remain his own prerogative, to say in truth: "For the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me." So in the lamb, the ewe lamb and the ram one may see what I have described; and in the unleavened loaves is signified the guileless and pure life. For the most wise Paul too writes somewhere to the sanctified: "Clean out, then, the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened." And in the wafer is signified the relish and, as it were, the sweetness of the life of the saints. We shall therefore offer ourselves: as in a lamb, because we are infants in Christ; as in a ewe lamb, in turn, because of the weakness of our nature and how easily it is driven into wrongdoing—for the female is a type of weakness; as in a ram, as mature, having reached the measure of the stature that is in Christ; as in unleavened loaves, as pure; and as in wafers, as sweet—yet as having received mercy through Christ. For we have been justified not by works of righteousness that we ourselves have done, but according to his great mercy. That is why the oil was rightly poured over the loaves. The priest, again, acts as mediator, and brings first the sin offering, then the whole burnt offering, and third, after that, the ram of the peace offering. For when Christ mediates and brings us to God the Father, we shall be acceptable, bringing supplications for our own sins and asking forgiveness for our former offenses. And we are burnt whole in a spiritual sense, that is, entirely and completely, holy and consecrated, and shall be dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma, not divided toward the things of the world; for the whole burnt offering was consumed entirely by the fire. And we shall also dedicate thank offerings for our own salvation and life, not honoring God with perishable and earthly things, but bringing him, as a gift worthy of acceptance, a life that is pure, unleavened, sweet and holy; for such, in some way, is the life of the saints. And when the priest has brought the sacrifice according to the law, "Let the one who has vowed," it says, "have his head shaved at the doors of the tent of witness, and put the hair on the fire."
And what do you say this means?

The paying of the vow, and, as it were, the fulfillment of what was promised. For we shall not understand the shaving here in the same way as when the one defiled by a corpse shaved off hair that had by then become utterly dishonored and profane. Rather, as one already perfected in Christ, who has grown another head of hair after the eighth day, he dedicates to God, as in a type, what he promised.
