And the sign that the offering has been accepted by God is that the hair is consumed by fire; for the sacred Scripture always ascribes the form of fire to the divine nature. Indeed the divinely inspired Moses said: "Our God is a consuming fire," likening, I think, the all-powerful character of the divine and undefiled nature to fire. And notice that the shaving at the completion—that is, the end of all our righteousness and purification—takes place at the doors of the tent. For how could whatever purity and righteousness we produce bring us into the Holy of Holies on their own, when they are by no means free of blame and fault? For no one is entirely clean of filth. But Christ brings us in, setting us free without holding our wrongs against us and releasing us from every sin. For he has entered as a forerunner on our behalf—not, surely, for himself, but smoothing the way in for those outside the doors, who have in some way already come to the very threshold of the holy tent.
True.

For he is said to have opened for us a new and living way. And after the man has been shaved on arriving at the very doors of the holy tent, and has also consumed the hair with fire, "The priest," it says, "shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, and a loaf and a wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the one who has vowed"; and taking them back again, it says, he shall bring them as an offering placed before the Lord, and it shall be holy to the priest, as is also the breast of the portion set aside.
Then what might the law mean to show?

In the divinely inspired Scripture the shoulder, or arm, is always understood as a type of one who is strong, or of achievements accomplished in strength; the unleavened loaf, again, as a type of a holy and pure life; and the wafer kneaded with oil and made into a cake would display in itself what is gracious and sweet. The role of the mediating priest one might very reasonably assign to Emmanuel. So the one who has achieved the highest purity and has brought a splendid offering to the all-pure God—works done in strength (spiritual strength, clearly), as in the shoulder of the ram; a blameless life, understood as in the unleavened loaf; and also the sweetness and charm of the life of sanctification, as in the wafer—placing these, as it were, in his own hands, offers them up to God through Christ the mediator, who receives the offerings, so to speak, from hand to hands, and in this especially honors the truly genuine worshiper with the highest honors. That is why it says that the one who thus completes the holy and all-pure vow, having placed them on his own hands, will give to the priest an offering placed and set apart, assigned to him, just like the breast of the ram, as the lawgiver determined. Just as we say that the shoulder indicates achievements of strength, or strength itself, so the breast of the ram indicates understanding and mind. For we have our understanding in our inward parts and in the breast. The divine Scripture often draws no distinction here, and sometimes makes the head a type of the mind, sometimes uses the breast to signify understanding. Holy, then, and set apart, brought, as it were, from hand to hand, and readily acceptable through him to God the Father, are the spiritual strength of those who are being purified, and their understanding as well—if indeed it is true to say that the saints could never achieve what pleases God in any other way than through spiritual strength and a good understanding.
Well said.

He commanded that the shoulder be taken boiled, driving away from the strength of the saints whatever is, so to speak, raw and beyond the bounds of what is fitting. For those dedicated to God must not be harsh or have an untempered mind, but must strive to accomplish the works of virtue gently, tenderly and with great skill. In this way and no other would the achievements of the saints be good and edible to God, having nothing raw or hateful about them. You have learned, I think, that the life of purity [?] is saving food, since Christ calls it, as it were, his own, saying to the holy disciples: "I have food to eat that you do not know about." And remember that he commanded the lamb to be sacrificed as a type of Christ, and further laid down, saying: "You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted over fire"—calling "raw," I think, what is unacceptable and, so to speak, hard to digest. So he says that the shoulder must be taken boiled, since what is unboiled signifies what is neither pleasant nor edible, and therefore unacceptable.
How very subtle and true the argument is!

We must therefore render our pledges to God, and whatever anyone vows, let him carry it out without delay; for not doing such things promptly is among the most dreadful and dangerous of faults—so I myself would say, and so does the sacred Scripture itself. For if, thinking rightly, we reckon it among the most outrageous things to be convicted on a charge of lying, how would it not be among the most shameful to pledge and promise something to God and then break the promise? So for everyone who has vowed and delayed, and still more for one who shrinks from paying altogether, he records it as sin. But he releases from the charges those who have nothing at all of their own, but are yoked, as it were, by a binding tie and are under another's hand. It is written thus in Numbers: "And Moses spoke to the rulers of the tribes of the sons of Israel, saying: This is the word that the Lord has commanded: A man who vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath, or binds himself with a bond concerning his soul, shall not profane his word; everything that comes out of his mouth he shall do. And if a woman vows a vow to the Lord, or binds herself with a bond while in her father's house in her youth, and her father hears her vows and the bonds with which she has bound her soul, and her father keeps silent, then all her vows shall stand, and all the bonds with which she has bound her soul shall remain upon her. But if her father firmly forbids her on the day he hears all her vows and the bonds with which she has bound her soul, they shall not stand, and the Lord will cleanse her, because her father forbade her." And even if, it says, a woman is lawfully joined to a husband, let the same law hold. But for a widow and a divorced woman he makes the bonds stand, and says very rightly that the promises must be carried out in every way and by all means; everywhere he makes the one who is free and outside the yoke liable to the charges if she chooses not to do what she promised, while he reasonably releases one who is not so placed, who is unable to act and is under others. For on the masters—the father, I mean, and the husband—if they agreed and, as it were, consented to the vows of those under their hand and authority, he brings the charge of impiety if they choose not to fulfill what was promised. But to those who refuse he grants that they must be released from sin; for offerings to God are the fruits of free choice, not of compulsion.
On the Feasts of the Saints.

Let this, then, be what we have to say about purity, about matters of prayer, and also about priests. Next, I think, we must set out very carefully what recompense for their labors might come from God, and toward what people must turn so that they may be enriched with the honors that come at the end and share in the hope that lasts for ages.
You put that very well.

For it would be fitting, Palladius, that those who have practiced the glorious and chosen life, and have reached such a measure in this outstanding way of life as to win the best verdict of all, should live in lasting happiness. They would keep festival and rejoice, with Emmanuel as the leader of their festal gathering, resting on hopes that are firmly grounded.
It would indeed be fitting, and what you say is true.

Shall we, then, look closely at the feasts held in figure and under the law, and describe the manner of the sacrifices offered at them? As far as we can, we will carry the force of their ideas over into the truth.
I would like that. How could I not?

Well then, I think I have weighed very clearly what it would be fitting to examine closely, while I was also pondering these matters. So come, come, before anything else let us look into this: when, and for what reasons, the sacred Scripture said we must keep festival. In this way our discussion would go straight along its proper course. Moreover, it will nobly avoid seeming to have been put together without skill.
Go on, then, wherever you please. You will benefit me, and very richly.

Once, when the Israelites had gathered in the wilderness at the foot of Mount Horeb, the God of all set out the law that defines what we must do. After laying down countless beneficial decrees, he went on to add: "Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me." Then he made clear what these times would be, for he said at once: "Take care to keep the feast of unleavened bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time of the month of new things, for in it you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before me empty-handed. And you shall keep the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits of your labors, of whatever you sow in your field, and the feast of completion at the end of the year, when you gather in the fruit of your labors from your field. Three times in the year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God." Keeping the feasts to God would be most fitting for those who act like men. It would not suit those who are slack, with a feeble mind inside them that is always softened toward the things of the flesh and the world. He showed this when he said: "Three times in the year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God." For what is male deserves to be watched over from above, by God, in the ways we have already described. And he did well to make it law that holy feasts must be kept. People who were just setting out on the right course of instruction, and were already in some way coming under the yoke of God, had to be shown, really had to be shown, very plainly the goal of the life lived under the law: that it would surely and in every way end for them in delights and gladness, spiritual ones, of course. That is why he gave them the law. He wisely set apart what by its nature does harm, praised what leads to benefit, and laid before them the path of the way of life and conduct that pleases him. Then he let them understand that one day their toil would end in delights. So the first feast falls in the month of new things. The second, its immediate neighbor, is the feast of the harvest of firstfruits. The third and last is the one at the end of the year, when our crops have been gathered in, in the seventh month of the year. Or is this not what the sacred Scripture says?
I agree.

Then we must bring forward what belongs to each of these times, and examine as well as we can how each feast ought to be celebrated, and for what reasons. At that time the compassionate God was commanding the Israelites to leave the land of the Egyptians, throw off the yoke of their unbearable bondage, and move to the land of promise. Pharaoh, however, resisted what had been decreed. He even spoke a boorish word against the ineffable glory, saying, "I do not know the Lord." Again and again he insisted that he would not let the Israelites go, and so he was punished with plague after plague. Since he remained unyielding and kept up his unbroken madness against God, the one who holds authority over all sent the destroyer against the firstborn of the Egyptians and decreed death in a single night. But God took care that the flocks of the Jews should not suffer the evil, and that they should be as far as possible from the hand of the destroyer, or rather, of wrath. And there was no other way for anyone to bring this about than through Christ, who is life and the giver of life, since he sprang from the Father, who is life by nature. So the law prefigured the mystery concerning him, and it speaks as follows: "The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year. Speak to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel and say: On the tenth of this month let each of them take a sheep for his father's house, a sheep for each household. And if there are too few in the household to be enough for a sheep, he shall take with him the neighbor who lives near him, according to the number of persons; each shall be counted in for the sheep according to what is enough for him. Your sheep shall be perfect, male, a year old; you shall take it from the lambs and from the kids. You shall keep it until the fourteenth of this month, and the whole assembled congregation of the sons of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening. And they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat them. They shall eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, and they shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted over the fire: the head together with the feet and the entrails. None of it shall be left until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it. Whatever of it remains until morning you shall burn in the fire. And this is how you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover. And I will pass through the land of Egypt on this night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast, and on all the gods of the Egyptians I will execute vengeance: I am the Lord. And the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are, and I will see the blood and shelter you, and no plague shall fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. And this day shall be a memorial for you, and you shall keep it as a feast to the Lord throughout all your generations; you shall keep it as a perpetual ordinance. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and from the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats leaven, that soul shall be cut off from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day. The first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be a holy assembly for you. You shall do no work of service on them, except what must be done for every soul; only this may be done by you." Shall we, then, go through each point carefully yet briefly, and say what is fitting? For "we shall give the wise an opportunity, and make things known to the righteous," as it is written. They, for their part, may add what they have of their own, and become far better.
Certainly.

So it is at the beginning of the year and in the first month that the mystery of Christ shines forth. For a new age has come for us, the time of our Savior's coming among us. It changes everything for the better and remakes, very thoroughly, into the newness of creation what was growing old and aging and close to vanishing. For what is in Christ is a new creation: the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. And we too no longer live in the manner of Moses. Rather, we have been carried over into the life of the gospel, as Christ renews us through the Spirit.
You are right.

Each one takes the sheep, and the diners gather in numbers into one house. For although by nature each of us exists as a separate individual, and we are divided in that sense, we have come together into a spiritual unity in Christ. Now there is in us one soul and one heart. The victim is a sheep, or else one from the goats. It is a sheep because of its incomparable gentleness and innocence, and also its fruitfulness: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer." It is a lamb because he was sacrificed for us and handed over for our sins, according to the Scriptures. And it is a kid because, according to the law, the offering for sins is a kid. The sheep is perfect and male. "Perfect" signifies that it is free from every blemish, sturdy and healthy. For Christ is without blemish and beyond every passion, and so truly perfect. Emmanuel is perfect in every respect, since he has of himself and by nature all that makes him God. "Male" signifies that he is the leader of all. For the male is always the most fit to rule, and the female everywhere holds the second rank. The sheep is taken on the tenth of the month, but sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth. This is because the mystery of Christ is not newly revealed. It was not first recognized only when the Jews saw fit to treat him outrageously. The knowledge of it came long before the passion, for the saints proclaimed it in advance, the law cried it aloud, and the holy Scripture prefigured for us the mystery concerning him. So for a time we had the lamb among us, as a matter of foreknowledge. It had not yet been sacrificed, but we knew that it would be slaughtered toward evening. For Christ's death took place in the last times of the age, when time had in some sense already reached its very sunset. The lamb is slaughtered by the whole multitude, for he died for all. Those who brought a lamb for their own salvation were to know that they had been bought with a price and are not their own. One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised. Since he was handed over for our transgressions, he is said to have died because of us. In this sense it is we who slaughter him. Those on whose account he had to die would plainly be all but the authors of the passion, even if the deed was carried out by others. He showed at once that the sprinkling of the blood saves those marked with it when he said that the entrances of the dwellings must be smeared with the blood. I mean the doorposts and lintels of the doors. For the mystery of Christ blocks the way in against death and, as it were, makes it impassable. It is settled, then, that we too, anointed with the precious blood, will be stronger than death and will think nothing of corruption, paying no heed to the destroyer. For the blood of life, that is, of Christ, rescues us. He says that the meat of the lamb must be consumed in one night. For the time of the saving passion is truly one, and "having died once, he dies no more," as it is written: "death will no longer have dominion over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God." The meat is roasted and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The roasting hints at Emmanuel being made perfect, so to speak, through sufferings. For "it was fitting," it says, it was fitting, "that the author of our salvation be made perfect through sufferings." Eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs is a riddle that sketches something else. We ourselves, before whom Christ is set so that we may share in him, must be rid of the spiritual leaven, that is, of malice and deceit. Above all we must love to endure suffering for love of him and to bear bitter toils, following after him who entered into death for our sake. To spur us on to this he says: "A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a slave above his master. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too. If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they call the members of his household." The law forbids eating it raw, or boiled in water, although I think no one would have eaten it raw even if the law had said nothing. In a riddle, then, it indicates that the mystery of Christ is neither unapproachable through extravagant falsehoods nor watery and feeble. The finest of the Greek poets and writers, and those who were skilled with words, wrote down the rites of their gods. In doing so they tell wild lies and offer stories that are raw, as it were, and unacceptable to the human mind, and there is much in them that is watery and sickly. Adulteries, passions for women, the corruption of boys, castrations, maidens transformed into trees, and other utterly shameful and ugly things besides: such are the little myths current among them. But everything in Christ is truth. It is readily accepted and nourishing to the mind, and there is nothing slack or watery about it. For it draws those who are willing to understand toward good order instead of letting them loose into luxury and love of the flesh, as the frigid old wives' tales of the Greeks, of course, do. Do you clearly understand what I mean?
Entirely.

Whoever has become a partaker of Christ by sharing in his holy flesh and blood must also have his mind. He must love to walk in the way of inward good deeds and understand well what concerns Christ. The law would indicate this at once when it says that the head must be eaten together with the feet and the entrails. Did we not say that the head is a figure of the mind, and that the feet everywhere signify our progress in deeds? And again, did the entrails not point to the inner and hidden parts of the victims?
That seemed the right way to understand it. But tell me this: what would Christ's mind be, what his walk, and what the hidden things?

Christ's mind would be to think only of whatever looks to the glory of God the Father, and to want to carry out what pleases the one who begot him. For he says: "I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." The divine disciples chose to think and act in this way, and so they declared plainly: "But we have the mind of Christ." Indeed, they taught us to say in prayer: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your will [?]; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth." Do you see that, having become of one accord and one mind with Christ, they clearly affirm that they have his mind? This, I think, is what eating the head of the lamb means. Christ's walk, in turn, was to endure as he did, nobly, and not to shrink from death, so that, as Paul says, he might save sinners. We too ought to be fully ready for this, and readily spend even our bodily life for our brothers. So one of the holy disciples said: "Since, then, Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought on his behalf." Paul, for his part, rebukes some people, saying something like this: "Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." And Christ himself commands us to follow in his own footsteps, saying: "Whoever does not take up his cross daily and follow after me is not worthy of me." In every other way too, and through every virtue, Christ's walk and way is holy. By the entrails you are to understand the hidden and secret teaching about him. For the Only-begotten, who is God by nature and came forth from God, became flesh and dwelt among us. Though he is the image and likeness of the one who begot him, he lowered himself into emptying and into the form of a slave. Let us then welcome into our souls not only the human and outwardly visible side of Emmanuel. If we also fill our own minds with his very entrails, that is, with his hidden mysteries, we will enjoy good spiritual nourishment. He said that the lamb must be consumed in that one night, with nothing at all left over to remain until morning. And he does not allow a bone to be broken. The first of these signifies that in the age to come Christ will sanctify and bless those devoted to him through faith and holiness in some other way. He will not, it seems, nourish them again with his own flesh and give them life by his blood, as he does now. Since death will already have been abolished and corruption utterly undone, the way in which he sanctifies will be spiritual. So the morning, I think, would signify nothing other than the age to come. The second, I mean that the bone must not be broken, leads us up to thoughts about Christ and persuades us to follow the words of those who spoke from God. For the divine evangelist took the prophecy in a more bodily sense and applied it to Christ, saying: "The soldiers did not break his legs, so that the scripture might be fulfilled: Not a bone of him shall be broken." They eat the lamb with their loins girded, their feet shod, and staffs in their hands. In short, they are dressed like people used to traveling, and quite rightly. For we too, as though made ready to depart in spirit, eager to journey out, as it were, from the distractions of this world and keen to pass over to whatever is best, will partake of Christ in all purity and cleanness. We are not in the habit of lingering fondly over temporary things. Instead we run nobly toward what is fixed and abiding. Departing from the impurities of the flesh, we leap over to spiritual refinement, remembering Christ's words: "Rise, let us go from here." That is why those who eat the lamb as a figure of Christ wear the dress that suits travelers. But it must be eaten in haste. For it is the Lord's Pascha, that is, a crossing, or a crossing-sacrifice. The time has come when we must cross over from the wickedness of the world and hurry to do what pleases God. Not to do this with all haste, but to delay and hold back, as it were, while still clinging to our old evils: how could that not be most dangerous? And so the divine Paul says: "Run so that you may obtain it." We must therefore go to partake of Christ through faith. We must trample down all sluggishness and let no delay creep in, but go in all haste. In this way we will cross over from sins to justification and from death to life. Rubbing off the shame of slavery, we will be enriched with the glorious grace of adoption.
Excellently said.

When these things had been very carefully observed, and indeed carried through to completion as the lawgiver intended, he says that he will pass through and, as it were, go about the whole land of the Egyptians, destroying the firstborn and executing vengeance on the gods of the Egyptians. That is, he will exact a penalty from everything among them that is lofty and exalted, and ranked almost among the objects of worship because of its glory, for so hard and disorderly a mind and for its excessive arrogance. But he promised to shelter the sons of Israel, because their doorposts had been smeared with the blood, which he called a sign that they belonged to him. "For I will see the sign," he says, "and I will shelter you." For when God brings wrath and fury upon everything lofty and high, as the prophet says, and condemns to death the licentious and wicked man who has ceaselessly neglected piety toward him, only those escape and have no share in the punishment who have been sealed with the good seal and sprinkled with the blood of Christ. For you have heard him say, "Truly, truly I say to you, whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life; but whoever does not believe will not see life, but the wrath of God will remain on him." Those who have been sanctified, then, through partaking of Christ (in the mystical manner, clearly), and anointed with the holy blood, are sharers of eternal life, friends and intimates of God the Father, and stronger than death. He says very well that they must hasten to fulfil the law concerning this without ceasing. For we shall never cease keeping the feast in Christ, removing leaven from our own borders, that is, from the whole land in which we may happen to live. Those who have been called through faith to the justification that comes through Christ, and who keep the feast spiritually, must not do so in the leaven of wickedness and evil. Rather, purging out the old leaven, they must be reshaped for the better and now be seen as a new lump, with all their kin and their whole households, and those throughout the land. This signifies that the holy multitude of those who have received the faith is very great and countless. He said that the first day of the week must be called holy, and the seventh also a holy convocation. By this, I think, the law shows that in human life the time at the beginning was holy, as in Adam, the forefather of the race, before he had broken the commandments and disregarded the divine precepts. But holy too, and far greater, is the time at the end, that is, the time in Christ, who is the second Adam, refashioning the race from what had happened in between into newness of life, in the Spirit. He also enjoins that the sabbath must be kept on the seventh day, refraining from all work. For it would be most fitting for those who have entered through faith into the rest of Christ to abstain from now on from every fleshly work, from earthly pursuits and vain distraction, and rather to hasten to accomplish only what leads to incorruptible life and whatever makes people venerable and holy. For as the wise Paul writes to us, "Whoever has entered into his rest" (clearly Christ's) "has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his own."
True.

This, then, is what the divine oracle said to us. And the divine Moses, conveying the command to the Israelites, said: "Go and take for yourselves a lamb according to your kindreds, and slaughter the Passover. And you shall take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in some of the blood that is by the door, and put it on the lintel and on both doorposts, from the blood that is by the door. And none of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning. And the Lord will pass by to strike the Egyptians, and he will see the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, and the Lord will pass by the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike." Now the taking of the lamb by fathers' houses, or according to kindreds, would indicate, I think, spiritual kinship, that is, sameness in faith and concord. For we will not keep the feast with those who have chosen to hold corrupt opinions, nor will we share the holy and life-giving sacrifice with those accustomed to think otherwise than is right and true, but only with those of like mind, our brothers in unity of spirit and sameness of faith. The hyssop, moreover, is joined to the blood of the lamb by design. What the reason for this might be I will tell you briefly. Hyssop, Palladius, is said to be an herb, and physicians indeed admire it as quite able to dissolve powerfully the impurity in the bowels and to thin out congealed phlegm, because of the strength of its natural heat. So the blood is joined, as I said just now, with the hyssop, the type indicating to us indirectly that the precious blood of Christ frees us not only from corruption but also from all the impurity hidden within, and does not allow us to grow cold and sluggish, but rather makes us fervent in spirit. And the law again hints that it is necessary and profitable for those who have once been deemed worthy to partake of Christ to keep their life in sanctification secure and steadfast, for it seats those who have eaten the lamb within doors, so that they may not leave their houses and be destroyed together with the Egyptians. For it is not right to doubt that anyone at all of those numbered among the sanctified, who has virtue as a kind of house, will, if he should somehow depart from sanctification, perish with the rest and be subject along with them to the punishments that are brought upon those sick with a licentious and incurable life. That is why the divine Psalmist says to us, "Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities." Notice, then, how he says, "You shall not go out of the door of your house until morning." For holy Scripture likens the present age to night, and the age to come, which we await, to day. So blessed Paul, seeing the present age already drawing to its end and the age to come near, almost at the doors, called out, saying: "The night is far gone, the day is at hand. Let us then put off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk decently as in the day." So "until morning" would signify the whole of life, that is, until the coming time is revealed. And how would this happen for us? At the end of each person's life the coming age has, as it were, already arrived. For it is true that whoever has undergone death has been justified from sin (for God has shut him in, as it is written), and he is kept for the judgment seat of Christ, and he will be presented just as he was when his own end overtook him.
I understand what you are saying, and the argument is very sound.

In this way, then, the mystery of Christ was sketched in shadow for the people of old when the lamb was sacrificed at the appointed time, the very time at which Emmanuel himself truly endured slaughter for the life of all. So the divine Paul writes that Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us. The divine oracle also told us that the rites must be performed and the form of the feast carried out in the second month as well, if some unavoidable impediment should happen to exclude us and keep us from fulfilling what was prescribed in the first month. Shall we set out the divine saying itself and say what is fitting about it?
By all means.

It is written, then, in Numbers: "And the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, in the first month, saying: Speak, and let the sons of Israel keep the Passover at its time, on the fourteenth day of the first month toward evening; you shall keep it at its appointed times; according to its law and according to its ordinance you shall keep it. And Moses told the sons of Israel to keep the Passover at the beginning of the fourteenth day of the month in the wilderness of Sinai. As the Lord commanded Moses, so the sons of Israel did. And there came men who were unclean by reason of a human soul, and they could not keep the Passover on that day. And they came before Moses and Aaron on that day, and those men said to him: We are unclean by reason of a human soul; let us not then fail to offer the gift to the Lord at its time among the sons of Israel. And Moses said to them: Stand here, and I will hear what the Lord commands concerning you. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: Any person who becomes unclean by reason of a human soul, or is on a journey far off, among you or in your generations, shall still keep the Passover to the Lord. In the second month, on the fourteenth day, toward evening, they shall keep it; they shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs at night; they shall leave none of it until morning, and they shall not break a bone of it. According to the law of the Passover they shall keep it. And any person who is clean and is not on a journey far off, and fails to keep the Passover, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from its people, because he did not offer the gift to the Lord at its time; that person shall bear his sin. And if a proselyte comes to you in your land and keeps the Passover to the Lord according to the law of the Passover and according to its ordinance, so shall he keep it; there shall be one law for you, both for the proselyte and for the native of the land."
And who might those be who are unclean as by reason of a human soul, and who make this their excuse for being unable to keep the Passover? I would very much like to know clearly, I assure you.

The historical account of this is very long. I recall God crying out to the sacred initiator Moses: "Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone with a discharge, and everyone unclean by reason of a soul." We have already worked through the discussion of these matters sufficiently. But I will say this, as useful for the present. Holy Scripture calls "unclean by reason of a human soul" one who has been defiled by a corpse. For it was forbidden even to touch a lifeless body, and the ancient decree charged with impurity even those mourning one of their near kin by blood. That is why they were sent out of the camp. Through these things, again, the law prefigured that anyone who has shared in another's deadness, in character and conduct, will be unholy and full of spiritual impurity. For those of whom Christ might say, "Let the dead bury their own dead," are dead in their conduct. So whoever has associated with those accustomed to think and do dead things, or has come near them (I mean by choosing to think and do the same), is to be sent away outside the divine court, and the Church of the firstborn, and the flock of the saints. Such is the riddle of the law. But as for the true meaning, the one most fitting for us who are spiritual, we shall consider that those unclean by reason of a human soul, who for that reason keep the feast in the second month and slaughter the victim as a type of Christ according to the law of the Passover, are none other than the Jews, defiled by the murder of Christ and charged with impurity for their drunken outrage against Emmanuel. For such people have necessarily slipped away from our holy feast. They come late and have missed the time at which the author of the life of all was perfected through sufferings. Yet by the mercy of him who wills to save all, in the times after this, as in a second month, they too will partake of Christ and will keep the feast with the saints who were called in due time, that is, clearly, those from the Gentiles. For see how those in Egypt, having at once wiped off the filth of idolatry, slaughter the lamb in the first month and spring up to the beginnings of faith. And those anointed with the blood of the Lord will count the destroyer as nothing and will be superior to corruption. But the others, as in a second year and a second month, approach with difficulty and confess their defilement. They clearly affirmed that they had become unclean by reason of a human soul, they ask to receive the blessing, and later, after the first, they fulfil the feast. "For when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in," it says, "then all Israel will be saved." And the prophet foretold somewhere about them: "And afterward the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they will be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last days." For in the last times Christ, who according to the flesh is of the seed of David, will be sought by those of Israel who are left.
What you say is true, for Israel has been set in hope.

That it is not blameless, but rather among the most perilous things, not to keep the feasts to Christ, he made clear immediately, when he said that one who is neither unclean by reason of a human soul nor on a long journey, and has no unavoidable impediment, will be subjected to the utmost penalties if he does not choose to do what is prescribed. We may understand the one unclean as by reason of a human soul to be, as we said just now, the Lord-slaying Jew. And the one on a long journey, as it were, somewhere outside Jerusalem, that is, the holy Church of our Savior, is he who says to the wood, "You are my God," and to the stone, "You gave birth to me"; he who worships the creation rather than the Creator; or he who is sick with some other error. For it is true that every good man, who holds an unadulterated belief about God, may be thought to be near him, while everyone who is not so has strayed, gone away, and is far off. So we who are neither unclean by reason of a human soul, like the Jews, nor on a long journey, like the Greeks or the heretics, shall offer the sacrifice eagerly and without delay, and honor the feasts of the Lord. And the proselyte will keep the feast with you under the same law, and will rejoice with you as you rejoice. For those who, from time to time, embrace the glories of faith in Christ we make partakers of the bloodless sacrifice and call to share in the holy table. I think it also necessary to add this: a custom has prevailed in the churches, derived, I think, from this law, that if the fourteenth day of the moon falls outside the first month, they examine the second, adjacent month and look for the appointed day in it, so that the true time of the feast may not be missed. And the matter stands just as it was declared beforehand in the ancient law.

You have spoken rightly. But tell me this: did the law not perhaps permit anyone at all, even if he were on a long journey and as far as possible from Jerusalem, to keep the Passover without reproach?

Not at all. He commanded them to sacrifice only in the holy city, where Solomon also built the ancient temple. In Deuteronomy Moses addressed the sons of Israel in these words: “Keep the month of new grain, and you shall keep the Passover to the Lord your God, because in the month of new grain you came out of Egypt by night. And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen, in the place that the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there. You shall not eat leaven with it. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the bread of affliction, because you came out of Egypt in haste, so that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of Egypt all the days of your life. No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, and none of the meat that you sacrifice in the evening on the first day shall remain overnight until morning. You may not sacrifice the Passover in any of your cities that the Lord your God gives you, but only at the place that the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there. You shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening at sunset, at the time when you came out of Egypt, and you shall boil and roast and eat it in the place that the Lord your God chooses.” The land of the Jews was filled with countless cities and villages, yet God laid down that the sacred rites and the law of the Passover must be performed in the holy city alone. In this, I think, the letter of the law sketches out for us very well in shadow that it would not be right, nor is anyone permitted, to perform the mystery of Christ in whatever way he likes, that is, in any place at all. For the only place fitting for it, and truly most proper to it, is the holy city, that is, the Church. In her there is a lawful priest, the sacred rites are performed by hallowed hands, and incense is offered to God who rules all things, and a pure sacrifice, as the prophet's voice says. So the heretics, who pervert what is right, make nothing of the law on this point. They sacrifice the lamb not in the holy city, nor by the hand of those chosen through the Spirit for sacred ministry, but, as the divine Paul writes to us, seizing the honor for themselves and offering it in every place. Like insolent and unruly bulls, they rush without discernment toward whatever alone seems good to them. But they, cultivating great unruliness and a bent toward madness, will pay a bitter penalty to the judge of such schemes. Let us for our part return to the well-trodden and straight road, and examine this point in the law just cited. You heard it say plainly, “Keep the month of new grain, and you shall keep the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen.” And yet, someone might say, why is it that when he laid down the Passover law for those in Egypt he commanded only a single lamb to be sacrificed, and we shall not find him mentioning sheep and calves? Did Moses, then, miss what was fitting? By no means. For in Numbers God added a law that oxen and rams should be brought along with the lamb, saying: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, is the Lord's Passover, and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first day shall be a holy convocation for you; you shall do no servile work. And you shall offer whole burnt offerings, an offering by fire to the Lord: two young bulls from the herd, one ram, seven year-old lambs; they shall be without blemish for you; and their grain offering shall be fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths for the one bull and two tenths for the one ram. You shall make a tenth for each lamb, for the seven lambs, and one male goat for sin, to make atonement for you, besides the perpetual morning burnt offering, which is a continual burnt offering. In this way you shall do each day for seven days, a gift, an offering by fire, for a fragrant aroma to the Lord; besides the perpetual burnt offering you shall make its drink offering. And the seventh day shall be a holy convocation for you; you shall do no servile work on it.” That according to the law the Passover must be kept in the first month, and indeed on the fourteenth day, we have already said. And what the eating of unleavened bread is meant to show, and the Sabbath rest, and besides these the naming of the first and the seventh day as holy convocations, our discussion has already shown clearly. So let us stop lingering over these things and go back to the manner of the sacrifices. There are two calves for burnt offerings and sacrifice, one ram, and lambs seven in number, all unblemished and a year old; and the sacrifice with them is fine flour moistened with oil. But not in equal measure: three tenths for each calf, two for the ram, and one for each of the lambs. Then a male goat is also brought for sin. “And all these,” he says, “besides the continual burnt offerings.” Behold, then, Palladius, the death of Emmanuel bearing fruit in many, just as he himself said clearly and truly: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” For the lamb is slain as a type of Christ, in the first month according to the law, and on the fourteenth day. Calves, a ram and lambs are brought in addition for sacrifice and burnt offerings, signifying in type, as I think, both the multitude of those called through faith to sanctification and the measure of their spiritual vigor. For if Christ had not died for you, we would not have been accepted as a fragrant aroma to God the Father. But since he has been perfected through sufferings, we follow straight after him, offering ourselves to God the Father as a sacred dedication and a truly spiritual sacrifice. There are two calves, because there are two peoples: I mean Israel and those from the Gentiles. There is one ram, for we are made one in Christ, “who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of partition, and abolished the law of commandments in ordinances, so that he might create the two into one new man, making peace,” as it is written. And there were seven lambs: for all of us who have become one in Christ are a broad flock, running under the hand of the one chief shepherd of all. Gathered, as it were, out of two flocks into one, and distinguished by a pure and blameless life, we continue in the world because of him who for our sake endured slaughter among the lawless and for the sin of all, and who is also signified in the goat. By mentioning calf, ram and lamb, the law hinted at the three distinctions in the God-loving way of life of the saints: the highest, I mean, the middle, and the one still lesser and inferior. For the bodily size of the animals represented the degree of spiritual vigor. Did not the word of the gospel way of life also say that the most fertile soil yields fruit in three degrees?
Yes: “One,” it says, “yielded a hundredfold, another sixty, another thirty.”

It is settled, then, that difference in virtue and variety of life are well sketched in the number of the victims and, as it were, in their bodily bulk. There is the supreme and surpassing level, as in the calf; the middle level, falling short of the perfect, as in the smaller ram; and one sinking still lower, in the lamb. For the lamb is smaller than the ram, just as the ram is smaller than the calf. Accordingly, the measure of fine flour, which is a type of life, is added in proportion to the size of each: three tenths for the calf, two for the ram, and one for the lamb. But he said that all of it must be moistened with oil, for what comes from God will surely follow in proportion to each one's measure. In the life of glory and blessedness, too, there will be a great difference. To some the highest will fittingly belong; to others one lesser, yet still in honor and glory; and to some one lower and humbler still. For star differs from star in glory; and even among the holy angels themselves, I say, the measure of glory comes in many degrees. Yet in whatever measure it may be, the life of the saints has gladness; they are bound to rejoice and to be enriched with the good things that come from God. For see how the oil was poured not only on the three tenths but also on the two and on the one. He calls the lamb slaughtered in the holy tabernacle in the morning and again toward evening the continual sacrifice and burnt offering. From this again we may learn that the fragrance of the holy tabernacle is great, and that the sweet odor of the Churches and of the saints in them is truly unceasing. For they spread abroad the fragrance of Emmanuel and perform the mystery of Christ, offering the bloodless worship to God. This, I think, is what it means for the lambs to be burnt whole in the morning and toward evening: for a whole span is grasped through its beginning and end and what lies between. So from beginning to end there is fragrance in the Churches, as in Christ the lamb.
Well said.

The law next joins another feast to the first, and all but links the very seasons together for us, saying in Numbers: “And on the day of new grain, when you offer a new sacrifice to the Lord at the feast of weeks, it shall be a holy convocation for you; you shall do no servile work. And you shall offer burnt offerings for a fragrant aroma to the Lord: two young bulls from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished year-old lambs. Their grain offering shall be fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths for the one bull, two tenths for the one ram, a tenth for each lamb, for the seven lambs, and one male goat for sin, to make atonement for you, besides the perpetual burnt offering. And you shall make their sacrifice for me—they shall be without blemish for you—and their drink offerings.” According to the laws of the Hebrews, the lamb was slain in the first month. In the next, neighboring month it was customary to gather in the produce of the fields—I mean the early pulses—and a sheaf of grain, once the wheat had been reaped. So it is the season of new grain, in which what has been sown in the fields must be gathered in. This feast too, he says, is a convocation, and it is to be kept as the law requires, free from toil and sweat. For at feasts it is customary to rest and to keep as far as possible from heavier labors. From this one might learn once again that for those who keep a holy feast to God it would be utterly unfitting to commit inglorious and thoroughly wicked sin; rather, giving the mind rest and, as it were, filling it, they should delight in pursuits that lead to virtue. Offered as burnt offering and sacrifice are two calves, one ram and seven lambs, fine flour soaked in oil, and a male goat. Where the riddle of the law points we have just explained, and we will not repeat ourselves. But this we must say: the season of new grain represents the mystery of our Savior's resurrection. For human nature blossomed anew first in Christ, having rubbed off corruption and cast away for good the oldness that came from sin. That is why it took great pride in this, saying: “Let my soul exult in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness.” By “a garment of salvation” and “a robe of gladness” it surely meant the incorruption that comes from above, from heaven, and in Christ. The law concerning this festival makes the riddle clearer and plain through a great many details, saying in Leviticus: “Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land that I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest, and he shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord to be accepted for you. On the morrow of the first day the priest shall lift it up. And on the day when you bring the sheaf you shall offer an unblemished year-old sheep as a burnt offering to the Lord, and its grain offering two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, a sacrifice to the Lord, a fragrant aroma to the Lord, and its drink offering a fourth of a hin of wine. And you shall not eat bread or roasted new parched grain until this very day, until you offer the gifts to your God. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings. And you shall count for yourselves from the morrow of the Sabbaths, from the day on which you bring the sheaf of the offering, seven full weeks; until the morrow of the last week you shall count fifty days.” For Emmanuel's death on our behalf is truly a saving feast. He paid our debts for us, and it is true that he himself takes away our sins and suffers pain for us, and by his bruise we were healed. For he nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us, and by it he triumphed over those who once held power on earth—I mean the principalities and powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness, and above all, Satan. Close beside it follows another feast, no less than the first: the return to life from the dead, which shakes off corruption, shears away sin, and transfers us to a new life in sanctification and incorruption, death having been abolished. For we have stripped off the old man and put on the new, that is, Christ, or in other words the way of life and the life that is in Christ. Behold, then, behold the firstfruits of renewed humanity, that is, Christ, in the figure of a sheaf, as the first produce of the field and the firstfruits of the crops, brought as a sacred offering to God the Father. Or have we not sprung up in the world like ears of grain?

Yes. That is why Christ himself said of us to the holy disciples: “Do you not say, ‘There are still four months, and then comes the harvest’? Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest; and the one who reaps receives wages, and so does the one who gathers.” For he likens our condition to ears of grain and wheat.

So Christ is understood as a kind of firstfruits of the ears and as new fruit in the form of a sheaf: the firstborn from the dead, our way to resurrection, who transforms all things into newness and frees them from oldness. For “the old things have passed away,” it says; “behold, all things have become new”; and “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,” according to the Scriptures. The sheaf was lifted up before the Lord; for Emmanuel, raised from the dead, the new fruit of humanity, as it were, in incorruption, ascended into heaven, so as now to appear on our behalf before the face of God the Father. He was certainly not bringing himself into the Father's sight, for he is with him eternally and, as God, could never be parted from the Father. Rather, he was bringing into his sight, in himself, us who were outside his presence and under wrath because of the transgression in Adam and the sin that tyrannized over us. So in Christ we gain the privilege of coming into the presence of God, for he now deems us worthy of his gaze, as people who have been sanctified. And see how the law also prefigured for us the time fitting for the resurrection, that is, the third day. For “on the morrow of the first,” it says, “the priest shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord.” And the day reckoned from the first, not as “tomorrow” but as “the day after the morrow,” is surely the third; and Christ came back to life on the third day.
True.

Along with the sheaf an unblemished sheep is also offered, with two tenths of fine flour brought with it, again mixed with oil. For he who is portrayed, as it were, in the sheaf and the firstfruits of the crops is also taken as firstfruits from a flock—a flock that lives in the richness of grace and the gladness of the Spirit. That is why he says that fine flour, oil and wine must be offered together with the sheep. The fine flour would be a sign of life, as we have said many times, the oil of richness, and the wine of gladness. He is offered again also in the bread and in the roasted parched grain. The parched grain (chidra), he says, consists of pulses—so called, I think, because as they are ground they are poured round the mills that thresh them. Through this too Christ might be understood by us as a new lump, to whom we have been conformed; and we have been commanded to keep the feasts after cleaning out the old leaven, so that we too may be called a new lump, in the likeness of him who opened for us the whole way to newness of life, that is, Christ.
You put it well.

He further commands that they abstain from the new crops and make nothing of them into food while they wait for the offering of the sheaf. “You shall not eat the new produce,” he says, “until this very day, until you offer the gifts to your God.” For the only fitting time to share in the new and undefiled life would, quite reasonably, be the time when Emmanuel shone forth. Before him no one at all was able to refashion us into new life; but he himself is the firstfruits, as it were, and the first of those created for incorruption, inasmuch as he appeared as a man and in the flesh with us, through his likeness to us. And straight after this he presented us with a vivid prefiguration of holy Pentecost, saying that seven weeks must be counted from the bringing of the sheaf. For after the day of the Savior's resurrection we who believe count seven weeks together and keep the feast.
How clear the explanation is!

That the season of our Savior's resurrection brings those sanctified in the Spirit and justified by faith to the point where they can bear the fruit of the new and genuine life, he showed clearly by saying immediately afterward: “And you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord. From your dwelling you shall bring loaves as an offering, two loaves; each loaf shall be of two tenths of fine flour; they shall be baked leavened, as firstfruits to the Lord. And with the loaves you shall offer seven unblemished year-old lambs, one calf from the herd, and two unblemished rams, and they shall be a burnt offering to the Lord, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, a sacrifice, a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And they shall offer one male goat for sin, and two year-old lambs as a sacrifice of peace offering with the loaves of the firstfruits. And the priest shall set them with the loaves of the firstfruits as an offering before the Lord, with the two lambs; they shall be holy to the Lord; they shall belong to the priest who offers them. And you shall proclaim this day a convocation; it shall be holy to you; you shall do no servile work on it. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwelling.” For Emmanuel is the firstfruits and, as it were, the first produce of the creation that is being remolded into newness, and he is understood to be the first among us as bread and a new lump. And we, taking the same path thereafter, in likeness to him, have also been called a kind of new lump. A clear type of this too would be the bread brought from the new crops. Yet he says that not one loaf but two must be offered; for there are two peoples, even if they appear to have been brought into unity through Christ the mediator. “Yet they shall be baked leavened,” it says. What, then, is the riddle? Come, let us say, after looking carefully, as far as we can, into the depth of the law. Is it consistent to understand leaven here as the leaven that stands for wickedness and falsehood? Then how is this not folly? How could we still call free from evil those who have been refashioned for the newness of the gospel way of life? Or how could this be understood as newness? And how could anyone still be called a new lump if some remnant of leaven remains in them and they have not been wholly freed from unholy and loathsome wickedness? We must therefore conceive, in the manner fitting for such contemplations, another kind of leaven—one that has nothing in it deserving blame, but is even admired in the divinely inspired Scripture. The Savior compares the glorious and beneficial power of divine, gospel teaching to leaven, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened.” For the life-giving power of gospel teaching, sinking into mind and heart, transforms soul and body and spirit, as it were, into its own quality. So it would be fitting to suppose that the peoples, offered in the form of the loaves, have been leavened with this kind of leaven, and that each loaf is of two tenths because the type is describing to us in a riddle the twofold character, so to speak, of the teaching.
What do you mean?
Would you not say, Palladius, that it is through a twofold instruction, that of the law and that of the gospel, that we shall be holy and acceptable to God, and so go on into a new and choice life?
I would.

This is just what the Savior himself made plain to us when he said: “Therefore I tell you that every scribe who has been made a disciple in the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old.” For those whose minds are versed in what was decreed through Moses and filled with that ancient commandment given in types, and who have then become rich in the new, gospel knowledge besides, may well boast, I think, of a twofold instruction.
You have spoken rightly.

But the multitude of those prepared for newness of life was not depicted for us in the loaves alone. The law further commands that seven lambs be offered with one calf and two rams, with a drink offering, of course, following the victims, that is, wine poured out, a fourth of a hin, which in our language is called six xestai. So again the seven lambs would be a type of the flock of believers, who are still infants in Christ—for the lamb is a symbol of infancy—yet who are advancing, as in spiritual strength and courage, toward perfection and toward the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.
What do you mean by that?

Having named the lambs, and then put the calf in between, he adds the rams. The lambs would be a type of the flock; the calf, of strength and manliness, for that animal is robust; and the rams, finally, of full maturity. So believers, by making a habit of manfully overcoming earthly things, leap up to perfection, the perfection understood as being in Christ. For the rams, full-grown in age, signify very well in themselves the measure of spiritual perfection. And there are two rams, for perfection in Christ is in a sense twofold in us, understood as being in deed and in knowledge. "For whoever does and teaches them," it says, "shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." Again, wine is poured over the victims, for gladness will surely follow those who have been eager to press on to the perfection understood as being in Christ. "For wine," it says, "gladdens the heart of man." And a kid was slaughtered for sin, and two lambs are also brought with the loaves as a sacrifice of salvation. And what does this mean in turn? Emmanuel died for our sins, being depicted in the kid, and he makes holy and acceptable our new life, our change into a new lump, and the dedication and consecration, reaching to soul and body, which we are accustomed to undergo, all but dying together with him who for our sake was among the dead, so that we may live with him. Something of this kind the wise Paul also writes to us, saying: "Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him, then, through baptism into his death, so that, just as Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life." So he was slaughtered for our sins, and we have been buried with him, undergoing a death that is not bodily, but putting to death our members that are on earth, and living no longer to the world but rather to Christ, and through him to the Father. See, then, the lambs dying together with the slaughtered kid, and the loaves burned along with them; for our consecration is acceptable, and the new, evangelical life is a fragrant aroma, being shaped in some way to the sufferings of Christ and following in imitation of him. "For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him"; and if we are sharers in his sufferings, we too shall have a share in his glory. Such a sacrifice, it says, is rightly called a sacrifice of salvation. For Christ saves those for whom he endured slaughter, since he removes them from sin and makes those who are buried and die with him superior to death and corruption, in the manner already described.
How deep the discourse is, and how obscure the matter of the law!
It is a riddle, Palladius, a kind of indistinct shadow of subtle and finely carved ideas.
Well said.

The law, then, named three seasons at which it would be fitting for us to keep festival. "Three seasons of the year," it says, "you shall keep festival for me." Since we have already discussed two of them sufficiently, would you like us now to say what the third is and for what reason it would be celebrated? For you have heard, I think, the reason for each: the first was profitably celebrated because Christ, having endured death for the salvation of us all, has saved us; the second because, having destroyed corruption, he came to life again and renewed us into new life. The season of the first was the first among the months of the year, at the very beginning; that of the second was its immediate neighbor and joined to it, the time when the reaping iron would naturally be busy among the ears of grain and the other crops had to be gathered in. For the produce of the fields is beyond counting. Come then, let us also say what is fitting about the third festal season, inquiring very carefully how and for what it should be carried out; and let us ask the law for knowledge of this and take it from the sacred Scriptures themselves, for in this way our discussion would advance toward the truth. Do I not seem to you right in saying and considering this?
Entirely so.

It is written, then, in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, saying: In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, there shall be for you a rest, an everlasting memorial of trumpets, a holy convocation to the Lord. You shall do no servile work, and you shall offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord." The seventh month, then, seems to us to hint at the season of the consummation and the last times. For in the seventh month, my friend, all the produce of the fields is no longer to be gathered to the threshing floor; rather, it ought already to be shut up in each man's storehouses. The season of fruitfulness has passed, the beginning of winter is already rising, plants wither and flowers fade. Come then, let us apply the features of the season to ourselves and say that, as this age is already creeping toward its end, and as that time is, so to speak, hanging over us and about to arrive, when those who love sin must be punished, each person, if he is wise, will heap up the fruit of his own labors and carry it into the storehouses above. And he will remember Christ saying: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but rather store up treasures in heaven." Since, then, now that Christ has risen, the words of the holy initiators bring us to remembrance of the consummation (for they have cried out again and again, "It is the last hour"), let what each person has, it says, be gathered from now on into the storehouses above. "But on the new moon," it says, of the month in which you shut up the fruits, "you shall have a rest, a memorial of trumpets." For each person stores up the good things won by his own sweat and will take thought and care for eternal delight and rest, remembering that, as the inspired Paul says, "The Lord himself, with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven." "For the trumpet will sound," it says, "and the dead will be raised incorruptible." "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad." Let us remember, then, this sacred and most fearful trumpet, when the most glorious festival of the saints is also a holy convocation, as those who lived in hope now receive as their portion a rich recompense for their splendid deeds of virtue. It is necessary, therefore, that we, rising through thoughts of these things to great virtue, should cease from every work that knows no profit at all but rather tends to defile. For this, I think, is what Paul also wisely told us: "The time has been shortened from now on, so that even those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who use this world as though not abusing it."
So it seems.

Then he says: "On the tenth of this seventh month is a day of atonement; it shall be a holy convocation for you. You shall humble your souls and offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord. You shall do no work on this very day, for it is a day of atonement for you, to make atonement for you before the Lord your God. Every soul that is not humbled on this very day shall be cut off from its people. And every soul that does any work on this very day, that soul shall perish from its people. You shall do no servile work; it is an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations in all your dwellings. It shall be a Sabbath of Sabbaths for you, and you shall humble your souls; from the ninth of the month, from evening to evening, you shall keep your Sabbaths." He said that humbling, fasting, the offering of whole burnt offerings, and moreover ceasing from all work must be observed. By the fasting he sketches the mortification of fleshly desires; by the whole burnt offerings, dedication as a fragrant aroma, not partial but complete and entire; and by the rest and the requirement to withdraw entirely from works he elegantly signifies that nothing earthly should be accomplished any longer. Or will you not think that those who have now reached the end of the times, who remember the sacred trumpet of the last days and keep the Judge in mind, and who for that reason are carrying off the wealth of their spiritual fruitfulness to the storehouses above, must put pleasures to death, be seen to be superior to bodily passions, already offer to God the fragrance of a virtuous way of life, and go far off and keep themselves apart from pursuits that lead to vanity? These, I think, would be the things of this world and the evil distraction of life.
I will think so; how could I not?

Well then, will not those who are superior to the passions and put to death their members that are on earth (fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire) be dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma, and be counted among the whole burnt offerings, making the thing a kind of ransom and atonement for their own souls?
Very much so.

The lawgiver therefore called the day of fasting a day of atonement, and very rightly and lawfully, since he puts to death the flesh and its works and makes the ways of virtue give off fragrance. But whoever does not cease from every worldly work will be altogether and utterly in the worst of evils, as he clearly showed when he said that whoever neither fasts nor offers the whole burnt offering, and whoever outrages the law concerning rest, will be cut off from his people. And by saying that the season for these things is a Sabbath of Sabbaths, he left us to understand that it is, finally, a rest of rests, that is, a laying aside of works complete and in full measure, clearly of the works that lead to wickedness and sin. With this age coming to an end and time all but growing old, what share at all could zeal for vanity still have in us? Shall we not rather set our minds on better things, keeping the rest most pleasing to God and withdrawing entirely from our own distractions?
You speak well.

Again he lays down a law: "And on the fifteenth day of this seventh month," it says, "when you have completed the produce of the land, you shall keep festival to the Lord seven days. On the first day a rest, and on the eighth day a rest; and you shall take on the first day the beautiful fruit of a tree, and palm branches, and leafy branches of trees, and willows and branches of the chaste tree from the brook; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God seven days of the year, an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations. In the seventh month you shall keep it." Do you perceive, then, that when the produce of the fields has been gathered into the storehouse and each man's fruits have been well collected, the far-famed festival of Tabernacles is very near, which hints at the life in paradise and restores man to a share in what was at the beginning? For we say that Tabernacles is the spiritual and truer putting-together of human bodies, and their coming back to life out of the intervening corruption into incorruption. The first day is a rest, and so too is the eighth. For before the transgression at the beginning, before most wretched sin had invaded us and laid on us the yoke that is truly heavy and hard to bear, we led a life in paradise that was relaxed, free, and without any toil, as in Adam, the beginning and root of the race. But when Christ came among us, even the intervening state of toil ran back to the beginning on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath-keeping under the law, or the fullness of the time of the law; and having driven the heavy and profane yoke of sin from our souls, we have ceased from all wickedness, since Christ calls us to this through faith, saying: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." So the first day of the week is a rest, hinting at man's original state. And likewise the eighth is a rest, on which Christ came back to life, having nailed to his own cross the bond that stood against us; and one died for all, so that, taking us out of death and sins, he might deliver us from penalty and toil, and that through him we might gain the rest that was at the beginning. "On the first day," it says, "they shall take the beautiful fruit of a tree, and palm branches," and the other branches. By this we may understand, as though the thing itself were crying out, that God again grants us in Christ the delights of paradise, though in the meantime we had slipped away from them through the transgression at the beginning. For we were driven out in Adam, but we have been brought back in through Christ. You have heard, I think, him saying to the robber crucified with him: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." For Christ has prevailed upon the turning sword, and entry is now open to those who have believed, since he is reshaping everything to what it was at the beginning and restoring it to what it was of old. The branches come from evergreen plants, signifying in themselves the perpetuity of grace and, as it were, the unfading nature of hope. "For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable," as it is written. And the joy of the saints is truly unending. The wise Isaiah also will cry out, saying: "Everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads; praise and everlasting gladness shall overtake them; sorrow, pain, and sighing have fled away." In the decrees about the festival there is also some mention of the requirement to rejoice from the brook. For it said that on the last day of the week, that is, on the eighth, water should be drawn from the brook and the believers should rejoice in this way. And Christ is a spiritual and heavenly brook, watering the souls of those who worship him with streams from above. Accordingly he said through the voice of the prophets: "Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing brook, the glory of the nations." And the inspired David also cried out to the God and Father of all: "How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The children of men will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the brook of your delight." For it would be fitting, and very reasonably so, for the citizens of paradise to partake richly of Christ and to rejoice in the abundant bounty of the Spirit.
It would indeed be fitting; you put it rightly.

Observe how the festival was celebrated only in Jerusalem, and it was in every way necessary for those from all Judea to gather there. This too would be a sign that all who have lived a glorious and approved life must be gathered into the city above, the heavenly Jerusalem, to be with Christ there and to keep the festival with him; but for those who are still unbelieving, who do not accept the grace of the resurrection but have rather rejected so venerable and deep a mystery, destruction will be the penalty laid up for them, to be then altogether and utterly in every evil. For they will go down to punishment. And the prophet Zechariah would be a faithful witness of this, saying: "And it shall be that whoever of all the tribes of the earth do not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, these too shall be added to those. And if the tribe of Egypt does not go up or come there, upon them too shall be the downfall with which the Lord will strike all the nations, whoever does not go up to keep the festival of Tabernacles." So we shall reckon that the thrice-longed-for festival of Tabernacles is the resurrection of all bodies, which have Christ as their firstfruits; for he has been called the firstborn from the dead, and truly is.
Your understanding is entirely right.
But do understand this.
What do you mean?

In the words of the law that we have just brought forward, the perpetual sacrifice was named, and the new moon too, and the sacred offerings on the Sabbaths, and the fast as well, and besides these the much-desired festival of Tabernacles. And everywhere, for each of the things mentioned, the law added, "You shall offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord." But what kinds of sacrifices we should offer, those fitting for the new moon and for the Sabbaths, and again for the fast, and those to be offered at Tabernacles itself, or what the perpetual sacrifice is, the lawgiver passed over in silence in Leviticus; in Numbers, however, he expands his account of these things and sets it out in great detail. Would you like us to speak of each in turn, taking them one by one as far as we can?
Certainly.

It is written as follows: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel and say to them: My gifts, my offerings, my produce-offerings for a fragrant aroma you shall take care to offer to me at my festivals. And you shall say to them: These are the produce-offerings that you shall bring to the Lord: two unblemished year-old lambs a day as a perpetual whole burnt offering.
