The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the second lamb you shall offer toward evening; and you shall offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sacrifice, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil. It is a perpetual whole burnt offering, the sacrifice that was made on Mount Sinai as a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And its libation shall be a quarter of a hin for the one lamb; in the holy place [another reading: in a vessel] you shall pour a libation of strong drink to the Lord. And the second lamb you shall offer toward evening; according to its sacrifice and according to its libation you shall offer it as a fragrant aroma to the Lord." Do you understand, then, how the divine law insists here that the offering of sacrifices is especially fitting for the festivals? For I think that at them we must in every way and altogether make the ways of life in Christ give off fragrance to God, treating them, as it were, as incense, and bringing ourselves to God as a sweet-smelling whole burnt offering, in keeping, I suppose, with that very rightly spoken saying: "Present your bodies, then, as a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God, your reasonable worship." And he says, very fittingly, that the perpetual sacrifice must be carried out with one lamb slaughtered in the morning and another toward evening, with fine flour burned along with them and oil and wine added; for at every season, unceasingly and from beginning to end, in the holy tabernacle, that is, in the Church, we give off fragrance in Christ through every virtue. For the lambs being burned morning and evening would again be a figure of him who for our sake and on our behalf rose up to the Father as a fragrant aroma, and carried up with himself, as it were, the life of those who have believed in him, a life full of gladness, as in the hope of sure glory and kingdom. And in addition to this, there is the need to rejoice in everlasting delights; and a sign of such a life would be fine flour soaked in oil and moistened with wine. The thing, then, is a sacrifice of salvation, like the one performed through Moses on Mount Sinai. For it is written in Exodus, when he had laid down the laws of God Almighty for all that was to be done: "Rising early in the morning," it says, "Moses built an altar at the mountain, and twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel; and he sent the young men of the children of Israel, and they offered whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice of salvation to God, calves." It will make no difference, I think, to the meaning of the sacrifice whether the victims are lambs or are perhaps called calves; for in both the type of innocence is preserved, which one would attribute above all to the person of Christ, who says through the voice of Jeremiah: "But I was like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed; I did not know." And if anyone should choose to say, in another way, that the morning and evening sacrifice in the holy tabernacle was conceived with reference to the time of humanity, that it was fragrant before the transgression in Adam and became so again in the last times, in Christ and in the life understood as being according to him, he would not miss the mark and would reason wisely; for that is the nature of the matter.
I am persuaded.

He defines the sacrifices on the Sabbath, saying straight away: "And on the day of the Sabbaths you shall offer two unblemished year-old lambs, and two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice and libation. These are whole burnt offerings of the Sabbaths on the Sabbaths, in addition to the continual whole burnt offering and its libation." The manner of the sacrifice is no different from the one we just spoke of; these follow in its footsteps, differing in nothing. But note this, my friend: the perpetual sacrifice has a continual ministry and is performed every day according to the law, whereas the Sabbath sacrifice is not offered every day but on the Sabbaths themselves. So that they might not think the daily perpetual sacrifice sufficient and become somewhat careless about offering the Sabbath sacrifices, he necessarily added: "This is the whole burnt offering of the Sabbaths on the Sabbaths, in addition to the continual whole burnt offering and its libation."
So it is settled that, in addition to the perpetual sacrifice, the Sabbath sacrifice is also performed according to the law?

It is settled; it would not be right to doubt it. For when we too keep Sabbath in Christ and have entered into his rest, we will offer to God the spiritual fragrance twice over, as it were, if indeed it is true that for the ancients the boast of righteousness in the law was fragrant. For "the law is spiritual," and "the commandment is holy and just and good," in the words of the blessed Paul. Yet the way of life in Christ is preeminent, and the Sabbath-keeping in the Spirit surpasses righteousness in the law in fragrance.
Well said.

To these he adds: “And at the new moons you shall offer a whole burnt offering to the Lord: two young bulls from the herd and one ram, and seven yearling lambs without blemish; three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for the one bull, and two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for the one ram; a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for each lamb, a sacrifice, an odour of fragrance, an offering to the Lord. Their drink offering shall be half a hin for the one bull, a third of a hin for the one ram, and a quarter of a hin of wine for the one lamb. This is the burnt offering month by month through the months of the year. And one male goat from the goats for sin to the Lord; it shall be offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, with its drink offering.” This is a perpetual and unceasing sacrifice, so that each month, besides the daily one, which is the continual offering, there is also the one at the new moons. Here again the explanation will not be of a single kind, though the riddle is quite clear. The spiritual and truer new moon may fittingly be understood as the new age in Christ, now that the first age, the one under the law, has passed away. But in another way too the new moon may serve us as a type of the age that is to come after this one. That age is not yet present, yet it has its beginning in the resurrection of Christ, through which we have passed over into newness. We have been enriched with the Spirit as a pledge of grace and with a sure hope of life in incorruption, and in blessedness and sanctification we are being transformed back to what was in the beginning, going back, as it were, and being conformed to the age to come. What, then, is the sacrifice fitting for the new moons, that is, for the spiritual new moon in Christ, and indeed for the life of the age to come? It is to die to God, no longer living entangled in sins, but departing wholly from the more earthly way of life, so that we may live with Christ. So too the inspired Paul writes to those who have been sanctified in the Spirit and justified in Christ, and who have been schooled in the powers of the age to come: “If you died in Christ, why do you submit to regulations as though you were living in the world?” And again: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.” See, then, how those who are accustomed to win approval die to God in a holy manner, in differing measures of spiritual vigour, and at once reap the rewards of their goodness. For two bulls are sacrificed, and one ram with them, and seven lambs without blemish. Through all of these the multitude of the saints is depicted for us: as excelling in the highest virtue, through the bulls; as settling somewhat lower, into the second rank as it were, in the ram; and again in a lesser and humbler virtue, in the lambs. There are two bulls, because there are two peoples; and one ram between them, because of the union of the two into oneness in Christ. And again there are seven lambs, for the people of the saints is in the most perfect fullness. Being two, and one by spiritual union, they may fittingly be understood as the most perfect multitude. For the flock of believers is very broad, in the simplicity that is in Christ and in the childlikeness that accords with him. Observe how three tenths of fine flour are set apart for the one bull, and half a hin, that is, six sextarii, of oil and wine. For the ram, two tenths of fine flour, and a third of a hin for what is poured on. For each of the lambs, the sacrifice is one tenth of fine flour, and the libation a quarter of a hin, that is, of oil and wine. For in proportion to each one's labours, and indeed to their powers in virtue, the measure of life will be allotted by him who judges justly—life, I mean, in glory and blessedness, and indeed in oneness with God, and in spiritual gladness. Or have we not often said that the fine flour serves as the type of life, the oil of richness, and the wine of spiritual gladness?
Yes indeed.

Then again a male goat is added to the sacrifices, slaughtered for sins, as a type of Christ. For our sacrifice is acceptable and pleasing to God because of Christ's saving passion. And this, I think, is what the Saviour himself said to the holy apostles: “Without me you can do nothing.” So of necessity Christ's fragrance is added to our fragrant offerings, in some way mingling itself with ours and rising up with them to the Father. For we are acceptable in no other way than through Christ alone.
Excellently said.

These, then, are the rites performed on the Sabbaths and new moons. “But in the seventh month,” he says, “on the first day of the month, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall do no laborious work. It shall be a day of signal for you. And you shall offer whole burnt offerings for an odour of fragrance to the Lord: one young bull from the herd, one ram, and seven yearling lambs without blemish.” Three tenths of fine flour go with the bull, two with the ram, and one with each of the lambs, and the liquids poured on—oil and wine, I mean—follow in proportion: half of what the Hebrews call a hin, then a third, and a quarter. What the meaning of the feast may be, he has indicated by saying, “It shall be a day of signal for you.” For it signals to us the last trumpet, sounded by the voice of the angel, at which all the dead will rise and those in the tombs will be raised, as we have already said. He has also commanded that on the tenth of the same month, on which the fast falls—a fast that depicts in itself the putting to death of fleshly desires and the departure from earthly passions—the same sacrifice must be performed in the same manner as on the first day. And what the meaning of these rites is, according to the explanation suited to spiritual contemplation, we have stated sufficiently.
I will remember.

He also lays down what sacrifices we should offer as befitting the Feast of Tabernacles, and says: “And the fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be called holy for you. You shall do no laborious work. And you shall celebrate it as a feast to the Lord for seven days, and you shall offer whole burnt offerings, an offering to the Lord for an odour of fragrance: on the first day thirteen young bulls from the herd, two rams, and fourteen yearling lambs; they shall be without blemish. Their grain offerings shall be fine flour mixed with oil: three tenths for each bull, for the thirteen bulls, and two tenths for each ram, for the two rams; a tenth for each lamb, for the fourteen lambs; and one male goat from the goats for sin, besides the continual burnt offering, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings.” Then each day one bull is taken away, while the rest of the sacrifice remains the same in manner and measure. For there are two rams, fourteen lambs, and one male goat. So on the second day twelve bulls were offered, eleven on the third, ten on the fourth, nine on the fifth, eight on the sixth, and seven on the seventh. You see, then, that each day only the number of bulls decreases, while the number of rams and of lambs remains the same, as do the fine flour and the liquids poured out.

And what does this mean, my friend? Why are there thirteen bulls at the beginning, decreasing each day as one is quietly taken away, while again there are two rams and fourteen lambs, with a male goat added to the victims?

The meaning of these ordinances is hard to discern, Palladius, and the matter is obscure by nature. But I will try, as far as I can, to say what has come to my mind. You yourself will adjust it for the better if I do not shoot straight at the mark.
I will do so.

It seems, then, that the divine oracle depicts for us both the tutoring under the law of those from Israel and the calling of those who have been brought into sanctification through faith. The riddle of the sacrifice shows, I think, that there were two periods in which the flocks of the Jews may be understood to have been tutored toward the knowledge of God and in the way of life under the law. And what would these periods be, if not surely the one in which Moses was still living, along with Joshua and the judges, and the one of the prophets up to John the Baptist, who, according to the Saviour's word, had something greater than a prophet's mission and ministry? Now the sacred Scripture indicates that in these two periods there were some who walked the path of life praised in the law, though not in equal measure, nor entirely alike in strength and spiritual vigour. For some, perhaps, belonged to the highest measure, of which the bull is a type. Others, again, to the one understood as the middle measure; and the sign of this would be the ram. And a third group besides these belonged to the measure that falls a little short and sits lower, as one may of course perceive from the bodily size of the lambs. For is not the ram smaller than the bull, and does not the lamb fall below the size of the ram?
I agree; how could it be otherwise?

So the animals named would be a very clear type of each one's measure—plainly, the measure of goodness. And since what is eminent and choice is always somehow fewer in number than the second and the third, being rare, there are for this reason thirteen bulls, but ten [?] rams and fourteen lambs. And since we say that there are two rams, the number of the victims is doubled: instead of seven lambs there are fourteen calves [?], and two rams. Or is it not likely that many became venerable and holy, and could boast of being blameless according to the righteousness of the law? Just as the divine evangelist has written for us about Zechariah and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.”
I agree; for God somewhere reproached the mother of the Jews, saying: “How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, she that was full of justice, in whom righteousness lodged?”

So there was a righteousness according to the law, by which some could well become highly approved in obedience to God, even though the law did not by any means bring them to perfection in sanctification.
Well said.

So bulls, rams, and lambs were sacrificed to God as signs of Israel's calling, with its highest, its middle, and its still lesser members; and the number of bulls kept growing smaller, because the chosen, the eminent, and the most approved kept failing, the times always suffering from a scarcity of them—up to the seventh day, that is, the coming of our Saviour, at which the spiritual Sabbath rest and the cessation from works that lead to sin at last sprang up. For we have been justified in Christ when the present age is already ebbing toward its end. And a sign of this, again, would be that the Sabbath stands last in our whole week. For this reason the law wisely halts the offering of the ancient sacrifices at the Sabbath—that is, the calling under the law and the priestly service according to it—and brings in, as it were, the calling in Christ in its place, saying: “And on the eighth day you shall have a closing festival. You shall do no laborious work on it, and you shall offer a whole burnt offering, an offering for an odour of fragrance to the Lord: one bull, one ram, and seven yearling lambs without blemish. Their grain offerings and their drink offerings for the bull, the ram, and the lambs shall be according to their number, according to their proportion; and one male goat from the goats for sin, besides the continual burnt offering, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings. These you shall offer to the Lord at your feasts, besides your vows and your freewill offerings, your burnt offerings, your grain offerings, your drink offerings, and your peace offerings.” Do you hear the law saying plainly, “It is a closing festival”? For worship in shadows and instruction in types came to an end on the eighth day, on which Christ came back to life, and the time of the circumcision in the Spirit broke in. For the ancient multitude of those who had been called was shut out, suffering under the charge of unbelief, and in its place there sprang up, as it were, the new people: excelling in spiritual strength, for this is the bull; perfectly approved, as in the fullness of maturity, for this is the ram; and having the exceptional beauty of childlikeness and innocence in Christ, for this is the lamb, though it is to be understood as a most perfect multitude. That is surely what is indicated by saying that there are seven lambs. And the male goat follows too. For the new people is approved in Christ through faith, rising up to God as an odour of fragrance, as we have often said.
So it is.

That we shall keep Sabbath in Christ, entering into rest—since we must cease from worldly pursuits and no longer bear earthly care, but rather delight ourselves in the Lord, as it is written, and have with him the choicest inheritance—he will make clear when he says in Leviticus to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: “Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land that I am giving you, you shall let the land that I am giving you rest, Sabbaths to the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be Sabbaths. It shall be a rest for your land, Sabbaths to the Lord. You shall not sow your field, nor prune your vineyard, nor reap what springs up of itself in your field, nor gather the grapes of your consecrated vine. It shall be a year of rest for the land, and the Sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, for your male servant and your female servant, for your hired worker and for the sojourner who stays with you; and for your cattle and for the wild animals in your land all its produce shall be for food. And you shall count for yourself seven Sabbaths of years, seven times seven years, and you shall have seven weeks of years, forty-nine years. And you shall proclaim it with the sound of the trumpet throughout all your land in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month. On the day of atonement you shall proclaim it with the trumpet throughout all your land. And you shall sanctify the year, the fiftieth year, and proclaim release on the land to all who dwell in it. It shall be a year of release, a signal for you, and each one shall go back to his own property, and each shall go back to his own family.” Do you see, then, how the law permits plowing and sowing and tending vineyards before the seventh year, but commands release from care for these things in the seventh? For when we keep Sabbath in Christ we are released, having set aside earthly care and departed wholly from vain distractions. For seven weeks of years—that is, for ages of ages—we shall continue among goods that are ready and set before us, plainly delighting and feasting in the spiritual goods that come from God. For there will be a time of release for all of us throughout the whole world, at the end, when each one will hasten to his own property, that is, to the inheritance fitting for him and allotted to him by God. For just as there are differences in the lives of the saints, so also in their rewards, God measuring out the recompense in proportion to each one's good deeds. He also makes mention of the trumpet that proclaims these things. For the time of our Sabbath rest—in Christ, that is—and indeed of release and the allotting of the inheritance, is the resurrection from the dead that will come in due season through the trumpet and the voice of the angel. In it the radiant multitude of the saints will hear Christ say: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” May we too attain it, by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
